div.head: PRAEFATIO EDITORIS.

p.s: Augusti Boeckhii quae hoc volumine continentur orationes prope omnes eisdem sollemnibus celebrandis sunt habitae, Regis Borussorum augustissimi nataliciis laetissimis.
accedunt duae orationes singulares:
ea, quae in universitatis Berolinensis dedicatione est habita, et Friderici Guilelmi Tertii laudatio funebris.
Orationes has nunc coniunctas iterum edi noluisset auctor, nisi multi, qui olim unam et alteram audiverant, id postulassent.
Non autem edi curasset sua sponte, quod in eis insunt, quae ipsi videantur esse excusanda.
Primum enim quod, quae quoque anno dixit auctor, ea ad huius anni res et condiciones sunt accommodata, tum, quum haberentur orationes, facile, quo quidque spectaret, est intellectum:
nunc multis annis interiectis possunt generatim dicta videri, quae ad praesentem tum rerum statum referebantur.
Deinde auctor vidit, vel ipso invito aliquarum rerum memoriam in his orationibus esse iteratam, quod temporis vel argumenti similitudo ad similia dicenda incitaverat.
Excusavit huiusmodi repetitionem auctor hinc inde, ut p.
217 et et 296, et censet se de eisdem rebus non plane eadem dixisse.
Tertio loco auctor temporibus et rebus commotioribus non sine ira et studio se dixisse confitetur;
quod temporum excusat ratio.

Quae res ad secundam potissimum spectat orationem, in qua quae insunt invidiosius dicta, ea, etsi tum audientibus accepta fuerunt, nunc omisisset vel retractasset auctor, nisi haec immutatio visa esset et delere temporis illius memoriam imaginemque ea oratione expressam, et quasi quaedam esse reprehensio eorum sensuum et contentionum, quibus tum Borussia universa agitabatur.
Ipse orator ultro fatetur , et censet se de eisdem rebus non plane eadem dixisse.

quod temporum excusat ratio.

241, ,
se in his orationibus haud raro indulsisse animo irritatiori et obsecutum esse odiis, quae temporum iubebat ratio;
et ibidem data opera monuit, deponendas esse inimicitias, quum primum fuerit reconciliationis copia facta.

Quapropter sperat auctor, ex eis, quae tum acerbius sunt dicta, neminem aestimaturum, quomodo in hac, qua nunc fruimur, principum et populorum cultissimorum reconciliatione felicissima animatus ipse sit.

Quapropter sperat auctor, ex eis, quae tum acerbius sunt dicta, neminem aestimaturum, quomodo in hac, qua nunc fruimur, principum et populorum cultissimorum reconciliatione felicissima animatus ipse sit.
Genus dicendi non id efficere studuit auctor, quod Ciceroniano esset simile, sed alia quoque exempla sibi proposuit.
Argenteae igitur aetatis usum sequi non dubitavit, neque omnes eas grammaticorum regulas observavit, quae Cicerone potissimum nituntur.
Immo interdum consulto ab eis recessit et rariorem aliquam dicendi formulam vel vocem captavit.
Nonnullis tamen locis vocabulorum delectus et structura et pauca quaedam alia secundis curis sunt mutata, quod generatim indicatum esse sufficiet.

Ceterum facile cognoscetur non omnium orationum dicendi genus esse idem, sed per longam annorum seriem, quibus auctor ex muneris officio orationes has Latinas habuit, paullatim aliquatenus esse mutatum.
Brevi conspectu comprehensa addidi orationum argumenta potissima, instituto, ut opinor, haud inutili.
Scripsi Berolini Nonis Ianuariis a.

div.head: I. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. Aug. a. MDCCCXII. habita.

p.s: When the Senate of this literary community invited some of you and summoned others to hear the speech by which we have resolved to celebrate the birthday of the best King today, not according to custom but from the heart, most distinguished, most noble, most learned men, and most beloved fellow soldiers:
We think that none of you was ignorant of what was to be expected in this document of public joy.
For Frederick William, the most modest and most civil of kings, does not demand to be praised by mouth and words;
rather than merely giving laws to the state, but, as a king ought to appear to the wise Greeks, he himself should be a living law:

He wants the memory of his virtue to be inscribed in the hearts of the citizens, as on tablets, so that, following his example, they may approve, praise, cultivate, and practice moderation, justice, piety, constancy, and finally all the good arts that pertain to the public welfare.
Therefore all panegyrical praise will be absent, the more so because this whole genre, partly from its praisers, partly from those who were praised, has drawn some slight stigma.

For from the time when the republic of the Athenians, by an excellent policy, established that citizens who, fighting bravely against the enemy, had met a glorious death for their fatherland should be publicly praised:

Although the subject was excellent and magnificent, nevertheless even in treating this subject the greatest orators could not escape the appearance of flattery, because they preferred to wander off into praises of the living rather than to dwell on the virtues of the dead in extolling them.
Although the fault was less in this praise of living men, because not one or another, but the whole state was being praised:
But when the supreme power was transferred from many to one man, praise, which had begun from a most noble origin, fell back into base and servile flattery.

For to pass over the Greeks, who, when liberty was extinguished, when that incredible ardor of mind by which they were borne to every most excellent deed was extinguished, and finally when their ancient virtue was extinguished, seemed foolish even to the admirers of the Greek name:
Who would approve the Panegyric of Pliny in every part, although it was spoken to that emperor than whom the earth bore no better?
Who, indeed, a little more liberal, would take delight in Eumenius, Nazarius, Latinus Pacatus, both Mamertini, and others of this school?
You may excuse the shameful flattery of these men by the misfortune of the times;
But as for us, who is there that would not proclaim us blessed, because we obey this King, whom it is both permitted to praise without flattery and not to praise without offense?
But if I had thought that you, listeners, would wait for the King to be praised worthily by my proclamation, whose accumulated benefits to the fatherland are proclaimed by the voice of all;
certainly, conscious of my own weakness, I would never have brought myself to ascend this platform;
but since I know that something lighter is demanded of me, I console myself in some measure with your indulgence for the scantiness of my talent.
Nevertheless, to grant that that which is by far the most difficult is remitted, both in fact and in opinion;
How great it is to speak on this day, before this assembly, from this place, on any subject whatsoever, everyone understands who wishes to measure the dignity of the matter with a just standard:
But I, myself called into the crisis, feel it so strongly that it almost overwhelms my mind.

For, as Cicero made Licinius Crassus say, it is a great burden and duty to undertake and profess that one, while all are silent, is to be heard alone on the greatest matters in a great assembly of men.
But what an assembly this is, and how great!
What a province, and how great, has been entrusted to me!
It seems so great to me, listeners, that when I consider each detail, my hope already fails that I can respond adequately to it.

For first I must speak not in a mediocre town, but in a leading city, which has for a long time been most full of urbanity and learning, and in a certain sense in the very royal court, which has been celebrated not moderately with the praises of learning.

Then I see here seated the most noble and most distinguished men of the state, and among them, both the overseers and presidents of the sacred affairs and of the disciplines of studies throughout the Prussian land, and also of our literary republic, most grave men, who know how to set aside an uncivil and imprudent saying with a witty and wise one most skillfully:
That my speech is approved by them, as I ought most earnestly to desire, so I scarcely dare to hope, and hardly even that.
Moreover, I see gathered here both the fathers of this university and other men distinguished by the fame of their learning and talent:

who, when liberty was extinguished, when that incredible ardor of spirit by which they were borne to every most excellent deed was extinguished, and finally when their former virtue was extinguished, seemed foolish even to the admirers of the Greek name itself:
Who would approve the Panegyric of Pliny in every part, although it was spoken to that emperor than whom the earth bore no better?
But who, being a little more liberal, would take delight in Eumenius, Nazarius, Latinus Pacatus, both Mamertini, and others of this sect?
You may excuse their disgraceful flattery by the unhappiness of the times;
But as for us, who is there that would not call us blessed, because we obey this King, whom it is both permitted to praise without flattery and not to praise without offense?
But if I had thought that you would wait, listeners, for the King to be praised worthily by my proclamation, whose benefits heaped upon the fatherland are proclaimed by the voice of all;
certainly, conscious of my own weakness, I would never have undertaken to ascend here:
but since I know that something lighter is demanded of me, I console myself in some measure with your indulgence for the scantiness of my talent.
Nevertheless, to grant that that which is by far the most difficult both is and is considered to be remitted;
How great it is to speak on this day, before this assembly, from this place, on any subject whatsoever, everyone understands who wishes to measure the dignity of the matter with a just standard.
But I, myself called into the crisis, feel it so strongly that it almost overwhelms my mind.

For, as Tullius made Licinius Crassus say, it is a great burden and duty to undertake and profess that one, while all are silent, is to be heard alone on the greatest matters in a great assembly of men.
But what an extraordinary assembly this is!
What and how great a province has been entrusted to me?
It seems so great to me, listeners, that when I consider each detail, my hope already fails that I can respond adequately to it.

For first I must say that it is not in a mediocre town, but in a leading city, long since most full of refinement and learning, and in a certain sense in the very royal court, celebrated not a little with the praises of learning.

Then I see sitting here the most noble and most distinguished men of the state, and among them, both the overseers and presidents of sacred affairs and of the disciplines of study throughout the Prussian land, and also of our literary republic, most grave men, who know how to set aside an uncivil and imprudent saying with a witty and wise cleverness:
That my speech is approved by them, as I ought to desire greatly, so I scarcely, and not even scarcely, dare to hope.
Moreover, I see gathered here both the fathers of this university and other men distinguished by the fame of their learning and talent:
The more learned each of them is, and the more equipped with sharpness of mind and sense of elegance, the more keenly they must notice faults in the speaker.

Finally, you, fellow soldiers, are present in great number, for whom, that I may narrate something useful for learning, the reason of our affairs seems to demand, but the popularity of the oratorical genre scarcely tolerates it.
Finally, I am not playing my own role, which is indeed a light one.
I am playing the part of the Senate, which is far more weighty, since it has appointed me as the public interpreter of its feelings.
This it did because of the favorable opinion it has conceived of me, not because of my modesty.
When I consider these things, how do you think I am disposed?

Why should I bring forward something worthy in some measure of the celebration of this very day, of the grandeur of this place, of the most crowded assembly of these most distinguished men, and finally of the authority of the most renowned college, which chose me as its orator?
Listen to what I have devised.

Since I despaired that it could happen that I should render any argument so adorned by my diligence that not only the matter but also the talent of the speaker would be approved by you, and since the allurements of oratory and words as if branded with curling irons seemed no less alien to your dignity, to these times of the republic, and especially to the singular gravity of our King, to whom this day is consecrated:
I have chosen a subject that is connected both with our affairs and with my studies, one that would recommend itself by its own weight rather than require any art or eloquence of mine.
I will present to you, however, the images of two cities, which were the most famous among the Greek cities, sketched with first lines:
of which the one was tempered by wise institutions and laws, but was separated by a very long interval from letters and more elegant learning;
The latter, by means of all the best arts, not only flourished itself, but imbued, illuminated, and made gentle and tame the whole world:
When these are compared and contrasted with each other, no one will be found who hesitates in making the calculation, which one was more effective in forming humanity.

When I mention these, who is there that does not understand that I am speaking of Sparta and Athens, the former established divinely by the Apolline laws of Lycurgus, the latter ordered by the liberal institutions of Solon:
Was not each of these states ennobled both by its own splendor and greatness, and by the brilliant talents of the ancient writers, who would not allow the deeds performed by them to remain obscure?
As I adorn this Sparta, as they say, in order to discuss something briefly about these states, grant me this, listeners, that the course of my speech may be aided by the breeze of your favor.
Indeed, when I consider Sparta, no individuals are more learned and more equipped in sharpness of mind and sense of elegance, so they must notice faults in a speaker all the more keenly.

Finally, you, fellow soldiers, are present in great number, for whom, that I should narrate something useful for learning, the reason of our affairs seems to demand, but the popularity of the oratorical genre scarcely tolerates it.
Finally, I do not sustain my own person, which is indeed light.
I am playing the part of the Senate, by far the most important one, which has appointed me as the public interpreter of its feelings.
It did this because of the favorable opinion it has conceived of me, not because of my modesty.
When I consider these things, how do you think I am disposed?

What shall I bring forth that is in some measure worthy of the celebration of this very day, the grandeur of this place, the most crowded assembly of these most distinguished men, and finally the authority of this most renowned college, which has chosen me as its orator?
Listen to what I have devised.

Since I despaired that it could happen that I should render any argument so adorned by my diligence that not only the matter but also the talent of the speaker would be approved by you, and since the allurements of speech and words as if curled with curling irons seemed no less alien to your dignity, to these times of the republic, and especially to the singular gravity of our King, to whom this day is consecrated:
I have chosen a subject that is connected both with our affairs and with my studies, one that would recommend itself by its own weight rather than require any skill or eloquence of mine.
I will, however, present to you the images of two cities, which were the most famous among the Greek cities, sketched with first lines:
of which the one was tempered by wise institutions and laws, but was separated by a very long interval from letters and more elegant learning;
The one, by all the best arts, not only flourished itself, but imbued, illuminated, and made gentle and tame the whole world.
When these are compared and set side by side, no one will be found who hesitates in casting up the accounts, which one was more effective in forming humanity.

When I mention these, who is there that does not understand that I mean Sparta and Athens, the one established divinely by the Apolline laws of Lycurgus, the other ordered by the liberal institutions of Solon:
Was not each of these states ennobled both by its own splendor and greatness, and by the brilliant talents of the ancient writers, who would not allow the deeds performed by them to remain obscure?
As I adorn this Sparta, as they say, in order to discuss something in summary about these states, grant me this, listeners, that the course of my speech may be aided by the breeze of your goodwill.
Indeed, when I consider Sparta, I see no commonwealth ever more firmly established, or more distinguished by the virtue of its citizens, so domestic as well as military, at home and abroad.

This they owed partly to the kindness of nature, which had equipped them with those arts so that they seemed born and made for pure and strict morals, and partly to the wisdom of the lawgiver, by which it was provided that they should never deviate from the simplicity of their former way of life.
Since he understood that nothing contributes so much to the happiness of mortals as if they used those laws which best suited the character of each people,

For the Dorians, a rustic and hardy nation, accustomed to cultivating mountains, hunting, and waging war, he so described a way of life, as it were, to a standard, that he directed their ancient pursuits to good fruit, strengthened their constant and firm character, preserved the frugality of the old age, and tempered their innate ferocity with institutions both sacred and profane, and turned them especially against enemies from the internal discords by which they were previously troubled.

He also perceived very wisely that men could not be restrained from continually attempting new revolutions, unless the law were sanctioned by the majesty of the divine power, which they would fear to violate or diminish, so that it might remain forever:
and therefore he referred to Pythian Apollo those ordinances by which the precepts of public discipline were contained;

And whereas in other states laws were given for a time, so that they could be repealed as soon as it pleased the people, at Sparta he brought it about on such a condition that they should never be without force, and could never be rescinded.
Thus it came about that the ancient form of the republic lasted a very long time, and nowhere were the minds of citizens bound by law more religiously than at Sparta.
But not all had the full rights of citizenship; only the nobles, or Spartans, especially of Dorian stock, who had fixed their abode in the city of Sparta and excelled in prudence and courage:
The rest of the Laconians lived in towns and fields, free in appearance, but in reality subject.
They say that at a certain time the Laconian land was so divided that nine thousand lots were assigned to the Spartans, thirty thousand to the Laconians, one to each.
And it was enacted that no one should ever become richer than another, so that it was not permitted to buy or sell land, nor to give it as a gift, nor to bequeath it, nor to divide it.
The inheritance passed intact to the eldest son;
It was forbidden to give a dowry to daughters;
Whence two or more portions could not in ancient times come to one person.
The power of the kings was circumscribed by the narrowest limits:
The authority of the ephors, guardians of the people, was at first small, but increased with the decay of the times:

I see a senate of twenty-eight men, which before the domination of the Ephors had held the highest power, [and] a republic never more firmly established, or more distinguished by the virtue of its citizens both at home and abroad, both in domestic and military affairs.

This they owed partly to the kindness of nature, which had equipped them with those arts so that they seemed born and made for pure and strict morals, and partly to the wisdom of the lawgiver, by which it was provided that they should never deviate from the simplicity of their former way of life.
And since he understood that nothing contributes so much to the happiness of mortals as if they used those laws which best suited the character of each people;

For the Dorians, a rustic and hardy nation, accustomed to cultivating mountains, hunting, and waging war, he so described a manner of life, as it were, to a rule, that he directed their ancient pursuits to good fruit, confirmed their constant and firm character, preserved the frugality of the old age, tempered their innate ferocity with institutions both sacred and profane, and turned them especially from internal discords, by which they were previously troubled, against the enemy.

He also perceived very wisely that men could not be restrained from continually attempting new things, unless the law were sanctioned by the majesty of the divine power, which they would fear to harm or diminish, so that it might always remain:
and therefore he referred to Pythian Apollo those rhetra, by which the precepts of public discipline were contained;

And whereas in other states laws were given for a time, so that they could be repealed as soon as it pleased the people, at Sparta he proposed them on such a condition that they should never be invalid, and never be rescinded.
Thus it came about that the ancient form of the republic lasted very long, and nowhere were the minds of citizens bound by law more religiously than at Sparta.
However, not all had citizenship with full rights, but the nobles, or Spartans, especially of Dorian stock, who had fixed their abode in the city of Sparta, and excelled in prudence and courage:
The rest of the Laconians lived in towns and fields, free in appearance, but in reality subject.
They say that the Laconian land was divided at a certain time in such a way that nine thousand lots were assigned to the Spartans, thirty thousand to the Laconians, one to each individual:
And it was enacted that no one should ever become richer than another, so that it was not permitted to buy or sell land, nor to give it as a gift, nor to bequeath it, nor to divide it.
The inheritance passed intact to the eldest son.
It was forbidden to give a dowry to daughters.
Hence two or more portions could not in ancient times come to one person.
The power of the kings was circumscribed by the narrowest limits.
The authority of the ephors, guardians of the people, was at first small, but increased with the ruin of the times.
The senate of twenty-eight men, which before the domination of the Ephors had held the highest power, was chosen from the nobles, being at least sixty years old and distinguished by singular probity;
nor was the dignity extinguished except with life.
And no one is ignorant of how much force this equal division of goods and the rule of the best had.

For since it is established that in the states of the ancients very many disturbances and changes of the republic arose from the excessive inequality of wealth, which Phaleas of Chalcedon, Philolaus of Thebes, and Plato in his nearest ideal state, which he founded in his work on laws, earnestly strove to remove;
and since it is equally established that popular domination, as the license of the common people swells, easily declines into the most arrogant tyranny either of the mob or of one man:
So strong were the Dorian institutions of the Spartans that the state, though disturbed by very rare innovations, never experienced the violence of a tyrant before Machanidas and Nabis.

But the fact that the Spartans obeyed their elders, and those holding a perpetual magistracy, gave occasion for Aristotle's criticism, who said that this is to be endured where men are upright and well trained:
Yet he says that the same men were not regarded as such by the lawgiver himself;
And just as there is a certain old age of the body, so he reminds us that there is a certain old age of the mind.
However that may be, I would certainly contend that the stability of the republic could not have been better provided for than by this honor paid to old age.
For who is more tenacious of the old state of affairs than a composed and moderate old age?
Who is more eager for new things than the keen and fiery minds of young men just flying into public life?
And how great is the wisdom of old men?
How great their knowledge of affairs!
What counsels!
How great is the dignity!
How great is the steadfastness!

Therefore the Spartans, since they thought that boldness belongs to the flourishing age and prudence to the aging one, wished the young to excel in bodily strength, in battle and with the sword, and they judged that the things which are administered by reason, judgment, and spirit should be done by the old:
And therefore the highest council of the state, which the Athenians called the Council, at Sparta was both the Senate and was so called.
And just as in a family the highest honor is given to the father of the family, so at Sparta, which the lawgiver strove to make one and undivided family, the greatest reverence was for the elders.

But how they arranged their property and marriages, and with what arts they trained the boys and youths to temperance, prudence, courage, piety, and obedience to the laws, I do not wish to relate to those who know.
But what shall I say, that the legislator kept them away from trade, from maritime business, from agriculture, and from other illiberal occupations?
And indeed, it was not permitted for a Senator to engage in trade even in Rome.
And at Thebes, those who wished to enter public life had to be at least sixty years old, chosen from the nobles, and distinguished by exceptional uprightness.
Nor was dignity extinguished except with life.
And no one is unaware of how much influence this equal division of goods and the rule of the best have had.

For since it is established that in the states of the ancients very many disturbances and changes of the republic arose from excessive inequality of wealth, which Phaleas of Chalcedon, Philolaus of Thebes, and Plato in his most recent ideal state, which he founded in his work on laws, diligently strove to remove;
And since it is equally certain that popular rule easily declines into the most arrogant tyranny of either the mob or a single man, as the license of the common people grows, ...
To such an extent did the Dorian institutions of the Spartans prevail, that the state, disturbed by very rare revolutions, never experienced the violence of any tyrant before Machanidas and Nabis.

But the fact that the Spartans obeyed their elders, and those holding perpetual office, gave occasion to Aristotle's criticism, who said that this was to be endured when the men are upright and well trained:
he nevertheless denies that they were regarded as such by the lawgiver himself;
and he warns that just as there is a certain old age of the body, so there is of the mind.
However that may be, I would certainly contend that the stability of the state could not have been better provided for than by this honor paid to old age.
For who is more tenacious of the old condition of affairs than a composed and moderate old age?
Who is more eager for new things than the sharp and hot minds of young men recently flying into the republic?
And how great is the wisdom of old men?
How great is their knowledge of affairs?
What counsels!
How great is their dignity!
How great is their constancy!

Therefore the Spartans, since they thought that boldness belongs to the flourishing age and prudence to the aging one, wanted the young to excel in bodily strength, in battle and with the sword, and judged that the old should manage those things which are administered by reason, judgment, and spirit:
and therefore the highest council of the state, which the Athenians called the Council, at Sparta was and was called the Senate.

Therefore, when I say that the character of Athens is opposed to Sparta with a contrary front, whether I look at the form and institutions of the state, or at the condition of the citizens, their mode of life and culture as a whole, I think I do not stray very far from the truth.

For the Ionian race, which, after having once inhabited the northern shores of the Peloponnese, was received by the kindred inhabitants of the Attic coast and afterwards occupied the maritime regions of Asia Minor and very many islands, by the very choice of its abodes, most suitable for the landing of ships and for commerce, declared that wonderful agility of mind, a disposition more mobile than firm, and a love of a freer life, which, according to Aristotle's judgment, is generally connected with maritime pursuits:

So far is it from having endured the rule of the best men for a long time, or from having deemed the strict discipline of morals, in which the Spartans delighted, tolerable, that it even considered a life of this kind more suitable for slaves than for free men, and scarcely worth living.

What of the fact that those two famous models of Plato's perfect republic are more similar to no Greek state than to the Laconian?

What of the fact that in Italy the Pythagoreans, the most divine of the wise, in order to make the people truly blessed, established a form of state not at all dissimilar?

But from the time when the Spartans departed from their ancient simplicity, from the time when, after very many of the noblest families had been destroyed in war, the allotments of the suburban lands returned to about a thousand wealthy men, from the time when this iron race began to gape after gold, and all the coins from all Greece and from the barbarian world flowed together into Sparta, whence, like beasts from the lion's den, they would never have gone forth:

From that time onward, corrupted and defiled by luxury, ambition, avarice, and all manner of base arts, they degenerated the more shamefully, the less nature had made them prone to vices of that kind.

But that Athens, splendid and illustrious, the glory and pillar of Greece, as the Theban bard declared, was blessed in its own laws before they migrated from it — why should I undertake to persuade those already persuaded?
Indeed, many vices that plagued other states were unknown to her.

From this it came about that Socrates, Xenophon, Plato, and every most prudent one of the ancients approved the Spartan republic with their votes, to such an extent that they called it most just and most equitable, and judged that it came closest to perfection.
What of the fact that those two models of the perfect republic of Plato are similar to none of the Greek ones more than to the Laconian?

What of the fact that Solon, when he declared that his laws were not the best, but such as could have been enacted, and boasted that he himself knew better ones, seems to have meant none other than the Dorian laws of Pythian Apollo?
What of the fact that in Italy the Pythagoreans, the most divine of the wise, in order to make the people truly blessed, established a form of state not unlike this to a great degree?

But from the time when the Spartans departed from their ancient simplicity, from the time when, after very many of the noblest families had been destroyed in war, the allotments of the suburban lands returned to about a thousand wealthy men, from the time when this iron race began to gape after gold, and all the coins from all Greece and from the barbarian world flowed together into Sparta, whence, like beasts from the lairs of a lion, they would never have gone forth:

From that time onward, corrupted and defiled by luxury, ambition, avarice, and all manner of evil arts, they degenerated the more shamefully in proportion as nature had made them less prone to vices of that kind.

But that Athens, splendid and illustrious, the glory and pillar of Greece, as the Theban bard declared, was blessed in its own laws before they were abandoned — why should I undertake to persuade those already persuaded?

For now the sails must be furled, and many things must be omitted, which I cannot include in the course of a single hour, so that at least I may mention one thing, which does not seem to me foreign either to this place or to these times.
Of course Sparta benefited few citizens:
Athens spread the most abundant fruits of talents throughout the whole world.
That one, great in strength, virtue, and deeds, had no benefits toward outsiders:
These have worked not for themselves alone, but for the human race.
Sparta fell:

The learning of Athens, like runners with a torch, generations handed on to generations, and will hand on henceforth into the everlasting memory of every age, so that from it, as from the sacred flame of the prytaneum, the lights of the mind may be kindled:
And they will never perish, as long as humanity, as long as wisdom, as long as literature and the arts shall be dear to mortals.

But no one will doubt that our age should follow not so much that Spartan discipline as the liberality of Athens, since even our most holy religion has willed that we should be not as slaves, but as free men, and should think freely.
Certainly, what the divine Chrysostom not absurdly declared, that by the cross of Christ all rustics were made philosophers:
This indeed seems to tend to this, that any servitude of minds should be judged by Christian men as most alien.

And indeed, you would in vain today attempt to confine the immensity of the immortal mind by setting limits, since the brightest lights of literature have been so widely diffused and disseminated throughout all lands that, if anyone, employing that force, should have tried to extinguish them and to cover and wrap them in darkness, whether for any nation or any part of learning, nothing would appear sooner than the great misery under which those labor whose mental light, as it were, is being dug out.
The sacred flame of the prytaneum, the lights of the mind, they kindle:
And they will never perish, as long as humanity, as long as wisdom, as long as literature and the arts are dear to mortals.

But no one will doubt that for our age, not so much that Spartan discipline as the liberality of Athens is to be followed, since even our most holy religion willed that we should be not as slaves, but as free men, and that we should think freely.
Certainly, what the Divine Chrysostom not absurdly pronounced, that by the cross of Christ all rustics have been made philosophers:
This indeed seems to tend to this, that any servitude of minds whatsoever should be judged by Christian men as most alien.

And today you would in vain attempt to confine the immensity of the immortal mind by drawing boundaries, since the brightest lights of literature have been so widely diffused and disseminated throughout all lands that, if anyone, using that force, should have tried to extinguish them and to cover and wrap them in darkness any nation or any part of learning, nothing would appear sooner than the great misery suffered by those from whom the light of the mind is, as it were, dug out.

And in our state, indeed, it is well known that literature flourishes not only through the talents of the citizens, but especially through the liberal counsels of the princes, so that few can contend with us for the palm of learning.
For when we review the memory of times, even in that age in which refined learning was quite rare in these lands, we find several of our princes not moderately learned:
Frederick the Great surpassed them in greatness of soul and civic prudence, in the glory of his deeds, and in the extent of his empire, just as he did in the pursuit of literature.
And under that king it came to pass—which had it not come to pass, Plato said the human race could not be happy—that a philosopher ruled and a king philosophized.
But the philosopher, since he wishes to make as many as possible like himself, that Frederick thought nothing more to be promoted than the good arts and the freedom of feeling and speaking:
Where that was suppressed, there you will find even the most wholesome teachings of scholars often condemned because of a vain suspicion of impiety or of any other fault.
However, under his rule this lamentable thing happened, that the sanctity of religion was then for the first time in Germany begun to be undermined by an impious attempt:
From which how many and how great evils have invaded the fatherland, now at last the imprudent equally with the prudent perceive.
A matter most worthy indeed of the solicitous care of wise princes:
Nor has it been neglected in these lands;
but you would with difficulty remedy an evil, against whose beginnings one had to stand;
Nor can you easily keep a limit in restraining a thing that is most impatient of a limit.

But in our age, so many dangers and ruins of public and private fortune are already beginning to call back the minds of mortals from lowly pursuits to the contemplation of heavenly things, and they teach us to look aloft.

Frederick William, indeed, as he fulfills all the duties of a good prince, so he combines both praises: that of letters established with the greatest liberality and munificence, and that of exceptional piety, which he conspicuously displays as a kind of example of ancient religion, faith, and uprightness.

Indeed, to confine myself now to what seems most relevant to us, when I consider in what times, at what expense, in how short a space, with what incredible ardor for advancing studies, and finally with what successes this school of learning was founded, increased, and perfected:

I cannot but be moved, partly by the noble institutions and plans of the wisest King, by which he has most fruitfully provided not only for us alone, but for all Germany, and not only for this age, but for future centuries, and partly by the prudence, goodness, and singular industry of the greatest men, to whom the guardianship of letters among us has been entrusted.
And at this point I must address you, my dearest fellow soldiers.

See how much this city values you, which has opened such a gymnasium for your studies, which has gathered so many teachers of the arts from all sides for your sake, which has provided so great an equipment of all learning for your sake:
See that the hope of the fatherland is placed in you, and lest it fall in vain, the state deigns to care for your education with such great concern:
See the examples of your ancestors, the expectation of your parents, the precepts of your teachers, the reverence for the laws;
Consider these things again and again, and take courage in your minds, so that you may prove yourselves worthy of such great gifts, worthy of such great hope, worthy of your place and rank.
But, I think, I am cheering on those who are running, so that they may run:
I certainly think I know that very many of you burn with praiseworthy zeal for literature, and are distinguished by modesty of character and honesty.

Is it now surprising that, with this king, with these ministers of the royal will, and—if I may say so—with these teachers and students, our affairs have grown most happily, and are being increased and adorned with new increments day by day, and have not yet suffered any loss?
And when I say 'anything,' I except that which could not be avoided by human means.
Who among you does not understand that I am lamenting that funeral, listeners, which we recently conducted not without groaning?
O bitter remembrance of that grief, by which I wish the cheerfulness of this day had not been saddened!
when he was snatched away by an untimely death, he than whom no one could be dearer to us;

But in our age, so many dangers and ruins of public and private fortune are beginning to call back the minds of mortals from humble pursuits to the contemplation of heavenly things, and to teach them to look upward.

But Frederick William, indeed, as he fulfills all the duties of a good prince, so he combines both praises: that of literature established with the greatest liberality and munificence, and that of exceptional piety, which he excellently sets forth as a kind of example of ancient religion, faith, and probity.

Consider these things again and again, and take virtue into your soul, so that you may prove yourselves worthy of such great gifts, worthy of such great hope, worthy of your place and rank.

I certainly think I know that very many of you burn with a praiseworthy zeal for literature, and are distinguished by modesty of character and by honesty.

But when I say 'anything,' I except that which could not be avoided by human means.
