when he was snatched away by an untimely death, he than whom no one could be dearer to us;

Whenever I remember him, whenever I recall his singular candor of mind and his exceptional courtesy joined with such great gifts of talent, so often am I seized with grief, even against my will, and I, who was not a close friend, form a conjecture from these things about you, who had come to know his virtue through long acquaintance.
Farewell, noble soul:
Your memory lives and will live, which you hold stored in our hearts, in the monuments of your genius, and in the esteem of all good men.

Whenever I remember him, whenever I recall his singular candor and extraordinary courtesy joined with such great gifts of mind, so often I am seized with grief even against my will, and I, who was not a close friend, make a conjecture about those of you who had known his virtue through long acquaintance.
Farewell, noble soul!
Your memory lives and will live, which you have stored away in our hearts, in the monuments of genius, and in the esteem of all good people.
In three words I have expressed our feelings:
We must not give in to lamentations today.
Let us turn our step away from the funeral and turn to offering prayers for the perpetual health of the best Prince.

And so we worship God, the Best and Greatest, with a pious mind, so that, since He wills mortals to be as upright and as happy as possible, He may preserve for us Frederick William, the wisest, most just, most merciful King, born to rouse the virtue of citizens and to aid their interests;

may He make His counsels most prosperous for the republic, and imbue the minds of the citizens with that reverence for the laws and love of the fatherland and of the Father of the fatherland, which can either lighten the most burdensome toils of empire or even render them pleasant:
then, that he may form the august Prince, heir of the realm, the hope and delight of the people, after the most noble example of his father, and may one day make him excel in his father's arts:
finally, that he may sustain and preserve the whole Augustan house for all time.

div.head: II. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXIV. habita.

p.s: If I should say that no happier day has existed up to this time for this literary republic, most exalted Princes, most distinguished and illustrious men, beloved fellow soldiers, than the one which today has shone forth not only to the joy of our countrymen, but to the common joy of the Germans, indeed of all Europe;
I do not fear that anyone may think that this was said more in an oratorical manner than from the magnitude and dignity of the matter.

For since the birthday of Frederick William is considered most auspicious both by all citizens throughout the empire and especially by this school, which was most generously founded by him, and is celebrated every year;

Although this is the fourth year in which we publicly venerate from this place the prince born to bless mortals, in the previous three years it was not possible to approach with equal piety, yet not with this uplifted and cheerful mind, with this sweet and grateful affection, and finally with this great confidence and security in our affairs:

But the fear of an impending calamity, which seemed able to utterly overthrow the weakened state, if it did not disturb the joy of the first solemnities, certainly mingled it with the anxieties of the troubled.

The other was then done, when the most just king, lest the public safety be endangered, was compelled to serve the most unjust cause against his own feeling and will, to enter into alliance with the enemy of all, to hand over our fields, cities, and citadels into the power of a treacherous ally, and to send chosen troops against a prince joined in sincere friendship into northern lands:
At that time, no one is unaware of how great grief afflicted the royal mind.

Finally, on the third day returning, the liberty of Prussia, begun indeed in the sacred name of the King, had been achieved by the virtue of Frederick William, but not yet completed, and indeed auspices of a glorious outcome were being shown, but the fierce enemy was five miles away from the City.
But today, when I must speak, how greatly do you think I am moved, if I compare my former poverty, miseries, and contempt with the present greatness of our affairs?

If I take in, as it were in one view, the King's wisdom and generous counsels, by which so great a change of affairs has been effected; the people's loyalty, obedience, and most ardent zeal for advancing the state; the valor of the armies, the prudence of the leaders, so many and so great victories; and finally, the outcome of a most severe and cruel war, so prosperous and glorious?

For now it seems that we must rejoice and exult immortally, now with bended knee, with hands stretched to heaven, the divine power must be adored, by whose benefit such great and now already unusual happiness has come to mortals.
And not otherwise, as I think, are you affected.
And so, since I think that no one has come here with that expectation, that he would be taught any subject whatsoever, but that he would learn our feelings and mingle them with his own;

I have nothing more alien from this day and from the minds of the citizens, who are uniquely intent on the merits of the great King, than an argument drawn, as is customary, from some branch of learning.

I see that what is demanded of me is that which is by far the most difficult: that, having recalled the memory of the deeds accomplished under the auspices of Frederick William with courage and success, I should set forth in weighty and eloquent words how great he proved himself, how great gratitude, how great reverence, how great piety we owe him.

But by Hercules, I do not know whether anyone may seem more unequal to sustaining this most honorable office than I, who have been appointed not by my own counsel but by yours, Fathers, as the herald of royal virtue.
But if to celebrate great matters eloquently is rightly considered difficult, what shall I say about those things which seem to be the greatest in the memory of mankind?

When you would scarcely think that the eloquence of a Demosthenes or a Cicero could suffice for these things, do you think that a man brought forth from the shade of literature into this most brilliant light of the assembly can match the magnitude of deeds with words?

Therefore, since I understand that this indulgence cannot be granted to me, that I should not undertake a most serious matter, and yet I perceive that if I wished to embrace the whole material of praises, my strength would fail me;
In order that my speech may be in some measure adapted to these solemnities, I will keep a certain middle course:

Concerning the happiness of our state, established by the virtues of Frederick William, I will discourse briefly in such a way that I neither enumerate all the goods which the fatherland enjoys, nor omit those through which, recently emerging from the greatest calamity, it has attained immortal glory.

Yet even so I see that I must beg your indulgence, so that if I have not fully satisfied the requirements, you may forgive my intention, and you may judge what I have said more from your kindness than from the importance of the subject.

Shall I embrace in one single view the most ardent courage of the armies, the prudence of the generals, so many and such great victories, and finally the outcome of a most severe and cruel war, so prosperous and glorious?

For now it seems that we must rejoice and exult immortally, now with bended knee, with hands stretched to heaven, we must adore the divine power, by whose benefit such great, new, and now already unusual happiness has come to mortals.
And not otherwise, as I think, are you affected.
And so, since I think that no one has come here with that expectation, that he would be taught any subject whatsoever, but that he would learn our feelings and mingle them with his own;

I have nothing more alien from this day and from the minds of the citizens, who are uniquely intent on the merits of the great King, than an argument drawn, as is customary, from some branch of learning.

I see that what is demanded of me is by far the most difficult thing: that, with the memory of the deeds bravely and successfully accomplished under the auspices of Frederick William recalled, I should set forth in weighty and eloquent words how great he proved himself, how great gratitude, how great reverence, how great piety we owe him.

But, by Hercules, I do not know whether anyone may seem more unequal to sustaining this most honorable office than I, who have been appointed not by my own counsel but by yours, Fathers, as the herald of royal virtue.
But if it is rightly considered difficult to celebrate great matters eloquently, what shall I say about those things which seem to be the greatest in the memory of mankind?

Since you would scarcely think that the eloquence of a Demosthenes or a Cicero could suffice for these things, do you think that a man brought forth from the shade of literature into this most brilliant light of the assembly can match the magnitude of deeds with words?

Therefore, since I understand that this indulgence cannot be granted to me, that I should undertake a most serious matter, but on the other hand I clearly see that if I wished to embrace the whole material of praises, my strength would fail me;
In order that my speech may be in some measure adapted to these solemnities, I shall keep a certain middle course:

Concerning the happiness of our state, established by the virtues of Frederick William, I shall speak briefly in such a way that I neither enumerate all the goods which our fatherland enjoys, nor omit those through which, having recently emerged from the greatest calamity, it has attained immortal glory.

Yet even so I see that I must beg your indulgence, so that, if I have not fully satisfied the requirements, you may forgive my intention, and that you may judge what I have said more by your goodwill than by the importance of the subject.

But as I look around to see where I should turn first, just as those who once praised the Athenian state used to place its chief prosperity in popular government, so the sum of our advantages seems to consist in this, that we obey a king.
But when I say this, if you think that I am speaking of the common advantage of almost all the nations of Europe, as they are now constituted, and not of our own particular advantage;
and although I grant that you judge rightly, yet I maintain that in our state the excellence of royal government has shone forth most clearly and has stood out most eminently.

For when, against the enemy of the human race, who, not content with our money and fortunes, also wanted the freedom of our minds to be taken away, and sought our blood and life, the state being besieged by hostile forces, its resources being diminished, an army had to be equipped not of moderate size, but as great as Prussia had never prepared even in its most flourishing age, and this could not be done step by step and at leisure, but had to be hastened with the utmost speed:

Then, therefore, who is there who would think that such great undertakings could have been brought to completion so vigorously, in so short a time, so peacefully, unless everything had been done by the authority of a beloved king?
What empire is more ready for action than a kingly one?
When do the universal forces and the resources for protecting liberty agree more than when one person governs, who, holding the reins with a strong hand, guides everything?
But where does discord more frequently rage and more fatally break the strength of the republic, than in those states which are governed by the domination of a few or by popular power?

But if the most noble nation of the Spaniards, which could not be deterred by any labor, by no disaster, by no miseries, by no torments, by no atrocity and cruelty of the enemy from the path of liberating the fatherland, had had such a king as we revere, truly you would have seen increased strength, increased concord, increased sinews of doing things.
What about the Helvetians?
What of the Batavi?
Those, harassed by internal troubles, did nothing worthy of their ancestral glory;
These, although they showed minds very inclined to recover liberty, unless they had been left destitute by their leader long since exiled, would without doubt have prepared forces sooner.

Add that by piety toward a kind king, the minds of men are so aroused and inflamed that they fight for his preservation no less than for altar and hearth, and think that nothing by which his name could be diminished, or honor detracted, or power weakened, is to be tolerated as long as they live and breathe.

And indeed, although many disagree, I do not hesitate to affirm that among the greatest benefits with which God has loaded mortals from the very cradle of the Christian faith, this is by no means the least: that whereas formerly the peoples distinguished by refined learning mostly established a popular form of government, but monarchy or rather tyranny suited the rude and barbarous, the sum of advantages seems to be contained in this, that we obey a king.
But when I say this, if you think that I am speaking of the common advantage of almost all European nations, as they are now constituted, not of our own particular one,
Although I grant that you judge rightly, nevertheless I maintain that in our state the excellence of royal government has shone forth most clearly and has stood out most eminently.

For when, against the enemy of the human race, who, not content with our money and fortunes, also wished our freedom of spirit to be taken away and sought our blood and life, the state being besieged by hostile forces, with resources diminished, an army had to be equipped not of moderate size, but as great as even in its most flourishing age Prussia had not prepared, and this could not be done step by step and at leisure, but had to be accelerated with the greatest haste:

Then who is there who would think that such great undertakings could have been brought to completion so vigorously, in so short a time, so peacefully, unless everything had been done by the authority of a beloved king?
What empire is more prompt for action than a royal one?
When do the forces and the resources for protecting liberty agree more than when one person is at the helm, who, holding the reins with a strong hand, guides everything?
But where does discord more frequently rage and more fatally break the strength of the republic, than in those states which are governed by the domination of a few or by popular power?

But if the most noble nation of the Spaniards, which could not be deterred by any labor, by any disaster, by any miseries, by any torments, by any atrocity and cruelty of the enemy from the path of liberating the fatherland, had had such a king as we venerate, truly you would have seen increased strength, increased concord, increased sinews of action.
What about the Helvetians?
What of the Batavi?
Those, harassed by their internal troubles, did nothing worthy of their ancestral glory;
These, although they showed minds very inclined to recover liberty, unless they had been left destitute by their leader long since exiled, would without doubt have prepared forces sooner.

Add that by loyalty toward a kind king the minds of men are so stirred and inflamed that they fight for his preservation no less than for altar and hearth, and think that nothing by which his name can be diminished, or honor impaired, or power weakened, is to be tolerated as long as they live and breathe.

And indeed, although many disagree, I do not hesitate to affirm that among the greatest benefits with which God has from the very cradle of the Christian faith showered mortals, this is by no means the least: that whereas formerly the peoples distinguished by refined learning had for the most part instituted a popular form of government, while monarchy, or rather tyranny, held in its grasp nations that were very rude and covered with the rust of barbarism, he gradually recalled every most civilized people to the primitive simplicity of royal dominion, which, as being nearest to the authority of a father of a family, is agreed to have been the original form, and was soon after overthrown partly by the pride of kings, partly by the impotence of the nobles, partly by the unbridled license of the commons.

I am not the sort of person who would attempt to play the role of a disparager of the ancients, especially the Greeks, to criticize that noble ardor by which they were driven to dare the greatest deeds, their most vehement love of country and liberty, their implacable hatred of tyrants, or to take up the cause of tyrants.

But I see that the splendor of their achievements, which ought to be and have been an example for us ourselves, and the lights of arts and disciplines, with which they have illuminated the world and, I pray, will illuminate the farthest posterity, dazzle the eyesight of some, so that they think that whatever Greece has produced should be extolled by their own proclamation, and, deceived by a false appearance, they exaggerate its happiness more than is fitting.
For surely the countless disturbances by which their states were struck, surely the slaughters, exiles, proscriptions, and almost daily confiscations of property, are not to be regarded as happiness?
Most things were administered according to the desires of individuals:
Rare was justice among citizens, no restraint among the common people.
Those Athenians, the most distinguished of all the Greeks, were daily lending their ears to reason;
but their minds were not obeying.
Wealth unjustly acquired, from the time of Pericles onward, they squander through fickleness, they waste through largesses.
But who indeed was allowed to help the same state notably with impunity?
Did they not punish with exile the leading men, Themistocles, Aristides, Cimon, and Alcibiades, for reasons either trivial or nonexistent?
Indeed, because the common people pursued every excellence of virtue with envy, it was enough to drive out an exceptional man, if he had deserved well of the republic;

This the Ephesians openly confessed, when they expelled Hermodorus, an excellent citizen and a friend of the natural philosopher Heraclitus, to whom, because he was said to have assisted the decemvirs in writing the laws, a statue was publicly dedicated in the comitium at Rome, with these words:

Although it held nations overgrown with rust, it gradually recalled every most civilized people to the primitive simplicity of royal dominion, which, as being nearest to the authority of a father of a family, is known to have been original, and later to have been overthrown partly by the pride of kings, partly by the powerlessness of the nobles, partly by the unbridledness of the common people.

I am not the one who would attempt to play the role of a disparager of the ancients, especially the Greeks, to censure that noble ardor by which they were driven to dare the greatest deeds, their most vehement love of country and liberty, their implacable hatred of tyrants, or to take up the cause of tyrants:

but I see that the eyesight of some is dazzled by the splendor of their achievements, which ought to be and have been an example for us ourselves, and by the lights of arts and sciences, with which they illuminated the world and, I pray, will illuminate posterity to the utmost, so that they think that whatever Greece produced should be extolled by their proclamation, and, deceived by a false appearance, exaggerate its happiness more than is fitting.

For surely the countless disturbances by which their states were struck, surely the slaughters, exiles, proscriptions, and almost daily confiscations of property, are not to be regarded as a state of happiness?
Most things were administered by the desires of individuals:
rare was justice among citizens, no restraint among the common people.
Those Athenians, the most excellent of all Greeks, were lending their ears to reason every day;
but their minds were not obeying.
Wealth unjustly acquired, from the time of Pericles onward, they squander through fickleness, they waste through lavish expenditures.
But who indeed was allowed to help that same city remarkably with impunity?
Did they not punish with exile the leading men, Themistocles, Aristides, Cimon, Alcibiades, for reasons either trivial or nonexistent?
Indeed, because the common people pursued all excellence of virtue with envy, it was enough to drive out an exceptional man, if he had deserved well of the republic;

This the Ephesians openly admitted, when they expelled Hermodorus, an excellent fellow-citizen and a friend of the natural philosopher Heraclitus, to whom, because he was said to have assisted the decemvirs in writing the laws, a statue had been publicly dedicated in the comitium at Rome, with these words:
“Let none of us be the best;
But if anyone should arise, let him be in another place and among other people: for this reason Heraclitus rightly judged that all the Ephesians deserved to be put to death.

These and other things, which the narrowness of this hour excludes, lead me to believe that that singular freedom of Athens and of many Greek states was rather a harsh servitude under a greedy and ungrateful master, and that the rule of the people, a monstrous and changeable beast, was not far from extreme tyranny:
which itself is born from that, and why Heraclitus judged with his own right that all Ephesians should be punished with death.

These and other things, which the narrowness of this hour excludes, lead me to believe that that singular freedom of Athens and of many cities of Greece was rather a harsh servitude under a greedy and ungrateful master, and that the domination of the people, a monstrous and manifold beast, is not far from extreme tyranny:
That very thing was not hidden from the ancient philosophers, and to those who at first admired the recent French liberty, the most sorrowful outcome showed it.

But with a royal government established by salutary laws, there is nothing more calm, nothing more just, nor more inclined to do good, finally nothing more liberal and more suited to promoting arts and letters.
The ancient philosophers were not unaware of it, and to those who at first admired the recent French liberty, the most sorrowful outcome showed it.

But with a royal government established by salutary laws, there is nothing more calm, nothing more just, nor more inclined to doing good, finally nothing more liberal and more suited to promoting the arts and letters.
Perhaps I have lingered too long in the introduction, having made mention of the ancients:
but you will grant that to our studies, in which we all most gladly linger.

Now to return to my subject, I understand by the king I mentioned such a one as we behold Frederick William, divinely given to this people, not such as the common people call a king, who often differs little from a tyrant:
Yet these, if you look at the truth, are found to be separated by a very long interval and completely different.
For the tyrant is unrestrained in spirit, greedy, proud:
He refers everything to his own advantage;
he neglects the interests of the people, whom he hates, and even thinks they are harmful to his own.
And so it abolishes the fairness of law, drains the fortunes of citizens, and suppresses, as much as it can, the freedom of feeling and speaking:
it prefers to act by force rather than by kindness:
it seeks pleasures for itself from the miseries and labors of others.
Whoever devotes himself to such practices must necessarily also suffer the evils with which he has afflicted others.
But all the king's plans are directed to this end, that the people may be as happy as possible, and this does not conflict with that, but harmonizes with it:
He complies with their harmless wishes and pursuits, because he knows the divine voice of the people:
As God's vicar on earth, glowing with heavenly love for the human race, he is a father to all, fair, benevolent, gentle, civil:
As a model of all virtues, he strives to shape everyone according to his own example.
But is this not truly the image of Frederick William?

If anyone should decide to praise him, he will not be able to say anything more excellent than his harmony with his people and the fellowship joined by mutual love, in which all the other virtues of a prince complete in every respect are contained.
And indeed, nothing is more useful for the glory of both, or for their happiness, than this common bond of king and people.

For glory, because a king deprived of the strength of his people is weak, and a people without the wisdom and command of its king is discordant; but when both are united, each one's name is made illustrious by the great deeds of the other.

For happiness, because one fosters the prosperity of the other, and the greatest goods of the people are placed in a kind king, but the royal spirit, amid the most troublesome cares and in the very crisis of the republic, is raised and strengthened by nothing more than by the zeal of the people, whom he had won over by his kindness.
By this most auspicious union, therefore, whatever has been done by us in the recent time with distinction, is partly known to have been accomplished.
But this is owed to the generous, merciful, and wise mind of Frederick William.

He, first yielding to the injustice of fortune, bore adverse circumstances most steadfastly, and meanwhile held nothing more important or more weighty than to bind the minds of the citizens, whom the enemy wished to be as estranged as possible from him, to himself by virtues, and to take care through prudent institutions that they should not become slothful and cowardly:

Soon, when the opportunity for action was offered, a most fierce avenger of liberty, divinely roused, called forth the people, who were hiding in the countryside and in the cities, having encouraged his own men who had long been impatiently waiting, into the sun and the dust;
From farmers, laborers, merchants, scholars, and freeborn youths, he suddenly prepared an army that not only despised enemies but also death, was eager for victory, and was prodigal of life.
Behold a spectacle worthy for later posterity to look back upon!

The best prince, unharmed by the ruin of the republic, and the flower of the whole nation, together with the tyrant and his forces, which were at first far more numerous but were especially gathered by force, were destroyed!

Then for the first time we saw the virtue of the Germans, as if awakened from a deep sleep, when the sacred cohorts of the most noble youth followed Frederick William's voice voluntarily, together with a varied multitude:
You would say that grandfathers and great-grandfathers had returned from the underworld, whose examples our men were emulating.
O great good of the people, which is placed in the memory of deeds clearly done by our ancestors!
The greatness of Frederick the Second, the ancient dignity of the Prussian empire, the bravery of the former armies, were hovering before the minds of all:
When they had all decided that that glory was to be recovered, just as the Spartans of old, so the Prussian youths, equal to them, promised that they would surpass the valor of their grandfathers:
and they stood by their promises.
There were, listeners, those who placed the glory of the Germans in this, that they excelled in the arts and in letters, who sought in these a sweet rest and a consolation for lost freedom:

Indeed there were those who even told foreign nations that the Germans were little suited for action, but were uniquely born for meditation, for philosophizing, for acquiring knowledge of various things, and who praised them especially on this account.
O crafty or foolish praisers of German virtue!
O vain little glory of letters, if freedom is lacking!
Did the Germans hold such plans, commit such disgrace, as to find contentment in literature, forgetful of their fatherland and freedom?
It is not so, listeners, it is not so:

But the learned felt the cruel necessity equally with the unlearned, or even more so; by this most auspicious union, whatever we have recently accomplished gloriously, it is evident that it was in part brought about:
But this is owed to the generous, clement, wise mind of Frederick William.

He, first yielding to the injustice of fortune, bore adverse circumstances most steadfastly, and meanwhile held nothing more important and more weighty than to bind to himself the minds of the citizens, whom the enemy wished to be as alienated as possible from him, and to guard by prudent institutions lest they become slothful and cowardly:

Soon, when the opportunity for action was offered, a most fierce avenger of liberty, divinely roused, called out the people who were hiding in the countryside and in the cities, having encouraged his own men who had long been impatiently waiting, into the sun and dust;
From farmers, laborers, merchants, scholars, and freeborn youths he suddenly prepared an army that despised not only enemies but death, was eager for victory, and was prodigal of life.
Behold a spectacle worthy for later posterity to look back upon!

The best prince, unharmed by the ruin of the state, and the flower of the whole nation, together with the tyrant and his forces, which were at first far more numerous but were especially gathered by force, were destroyed!

Then for the first time we saw the virtue of the Germans, as if awakened from a deep sleep, when the sacred cohorts of the most noble youth followed Frederick William's voice voluntarily, together with a varied multitude:
You would say that grandfathers and great-grandfathers had returned from the underworld, whose examples our men were emulating.
O great good of the people, which is placed in the memory of deeds clearly performed by our ancestors!
The greatness of Frederick the Second, the ancient dignity of the Prussian empire, the bravery of the former armies, were present to the minds of all:
When they had all decided that that glory was to be recovered, just as the Spartans once, so the Prussian youths, equal to them, promised that they would surpass the virtue of their grandfathers:
and they stood by their promises.
There were, listeners, those who placed the glory of the Germans in this, that they excelled in the arts and in letters, who sought in these a sweet rest and a solace for lost liberty:

Indeed, there were those who even told foreign nations that the Germans were little suited for action, but were uniquely born for meditation, for philosophizing, for acquiring knowledge of various things, and who praised them especially on this account.
O crafty or foolish praisers of German virtue!
O vain little glory of letters, if liberty is lacking!
Did the Germans hold those plans, did they commit that disgrace, that they should find contentment in literature, forgetful of their fatherland and of freedom?
It is not so, listeners, it is not so:

but the learned equally with the unlearned, or even those more so, felt the cruel necessity of obeying a most harsh and most atrocious master, and yet they did not see how they could shake off the yoke and be freed from their chains:

at facultate data ii, qui litteris operam dabant, huius inprimis universitatis iuvenes, quin etiam doctores aliquot, quos nobis redditos fausta fortuna gratulamur, spreto, qui hanc urbem tenebat, Gallico milite inter primos arma ceperunt, suoque exemplo commonstrarunt, quanto libertatis patriaeque amore animi flagrarent artibus bonis imbuti, et quanta esset Germanorum, Borussorumque maxime virtus, qui ad disciplinas colendas natura propensi et ingeniorum luminibus clarissimis insignes, ad proelia vitaeque pericula haud essent minus parati, similes prorsus admirandis illis ad Marathonem Salaminemque proeliatoribus, qui quum sub Persico tyranno eruditioni, qua omnibus mortalibus praestabant, in otio segni vacare possent, morti incertae malebant obviam ire, quam certam pati servitutem.
Apage igitur ambiguam istam doctrinae laudem:
arma perinde ac libri tractentur.
Quid enim litterae valent in servitio?
Unless perhaps, like the Greeks, you should perform the duties of learned slaves for a generous victor.
Take away the fatherland, take away liberty:
you will have cut the sinews of literature.
For in liberty literature stirs the noblest feelings:
they teach us to set aside these earthly and perishable goods in favor of eternal and never-dying ones;
They call back the immortal mind from sordid cares:
which is the source of great deeds:
The same [minds], when oppressed, serve; you may see them creeping lowly, which God gave to men, that they might lift them up;
having fallen into the vile flattery of tyrants, they are numb as if they had seen the Gorgon.
And both kings and tyrants know this.
For who has fostered the freedom of studies, from which the most joyful flower of literature has sprung, more than that model of royal dignity and wisdom, Frederick William?

Who has done more harm to the liberal arts, who has confined the cultivation of minds within a narrower limit, who has hated the light of learning more than that most unrestrained of tyrants, whose name I do not wish to diminish the joy of this day by mentioning?
They had to obey a most harsh and most cruel master, and yet they did not see how they could shake off the yoke and be freed from their chains:

at facultate data ii, qui litteris operam dabant, huius inprimis universitatis iuvenes, quin etiam doctores aliquot, quos nobis redditos fausta fortuna gratulamur, spreto, qui hanc urbem tenebat, Gallico milite inter primos arma ceperunt, suoque exemplo commonstrarunt, quanto libertatis patriaeque amore animi flagrarent artibus bonis imbuti, et quanta esset Germanorum, Borussorumque maxime virtus, qui ad disciplinas colendas natura propensi et ingeniorum luminibus clarissimis insignes, ad proelia vitaeque pericula haud essent minus parati, similes prorsus admirandis illis ad Marathonem Salaminemque proeliatoribus, qui quum sub Persico tyranno eruditioni, qua omnibus mortalibus praestabant, in otio segni vacare possent, morti incertae malebant obviam ire, quam certam pati servitutem.
Apage igitur ambiguam istam doctrinae laudem:
arma perinde ac libri tractentur.
Quid enim litterae valent in servitio?
Unless perhaps, like the Greeks, you should perform the duties of a learned slave to a generous conqueror.
Take away the fatherland, take away liberty:
you will have cut the sinews of literature.
For in liberty literature stirs the noblest feelings:
they teach us to subordinate these earthly and perishable goods to eternal and never-perishing ones;
They call back the immortal mind from sordid cares:
which is the source of great deeds:
The same [studies], when oppressed, serve; you may see them, which God gave to men to raise them up, creep humbly;
Having fallen into the vile flattery of tyrants, they are stupefied as if they had seen the Gorgon.
And both kings and tyrants know this.
For who cherished the freedom of studies, from which the most joyful flower of literature has sprung, more than that model of royal dignity and wisdom, Frederick William?

Who has done more harm to the liberal arts, who has confined the cultivation of talents within a narrower limit, who has been more hostile to the light of learning, than that most unbridled of tyrants, whose name I do not wish to diminish the joy of this day by mentioning?
But I return to the path, so that I may pause for a while in the contemplation of our greatness and happiness.
Where then shall I first begin, listeners, or what shall I first celebrate?
The pursuits of the Prussian people?
Or the valor of the armies?
Was it the prudence of the generals?
All were emulating one another, so that each might surpass the other.
Indeed, my speech would have to become grander and more sublime than itself, if everything were to be told as it happened.
But I console myself with the thought that I speak before those who were not only witnesses and spectators of the events, but also their directors and actors.
So that it may suffice to have touched upon individual points and to have recalled them to memory.
For from that most glorious concord between the people and the king there arose so great a contention among the citizens, that I know not whether any age has seen its like.

so all men of every rank conspired, that each one offered to the King and his country whatever was dearest to him, some their money, gold, silver, which was but little left over from much, others their own bodies and those of their children, others consecrating both to the common good:

And although in other places and at another time taxes were paid with difficulty, and contributions were made even more reluctantly, first among us, with the order of things reversed, much more was contributed than was demanded;
Young men leaving their schools, sons leaving their parents, youths leaving their betrothed, husbands leaving their wives, demanded military service:

If anyone was hindered either by ill health or by public duties or by private inconveniences from giving in their names, they bore it with hardly a fair mind, because they saw themselves deprived of the highest honor, which they thought consisted in defending their fatherland.
Yet those who remained were not sluggish.
Even the domestic multitude had taken up arms, with no distinction of ages or ranks:
The same people diligently devoted their labor to providing supplies and tending the wounded:
Noble women, while tending the sick, found death, which, because of the weakness of their sex, only individuals were permitted to meet before the enemy:
No one longed for peace, in order to be relieved of so many and such great burdens, unless peace restored liberty and the dignity, firmness, and security of the empire.
And what shall I say about the armies and the generals?
No praises can equal their merits, no rewards can sufficiently repay them.
How extraordinary, how great were the plans of the generals!
What constancy of the soldiers in enduring hardships!
What bravery of those fighting!
What confidence before the battle, what moderation among the victors!
What a death in battle!
They breathed out their soul joyfully, when with the proclamation of the divine will they venerated the best King.
Indeed, with such great efforts, both ours and those of the allies, success answered.
How many and how great were the defeats of the enemy forces, how many thousands of captives, how many leaders among them, how many captured engines of war, how many citadels:
what allies were estranged, how much territory was brought under our control:
The city of the Parisii was stormed, which, proudly boasting itself to be the chief and mistress of Europe and the whole world, will not, if I see anything, boast any longer hereafter:
The tyrant of Europe was cast down and sent into exile.
The ensuing salutary peace gave a king to France;
As for Germany, whatever in these twenty years — I speak among those who were not only witnesses and spectators of events, but also their directors and actors —
so that it suffices to have touched upon individual points and to have recalled them to memory.
For from that most glorious concord between the people and the king arose so great a strife of citizens, that I know not whether any age has seen its like.

Thus all men of all ranks conspired, so that everyone would offer to the King and the fatherland whatever was dearest to him, some their money, gold, silver, which was but a small remnant of much, others their own bodies and those of their children, others consecrating both to the common good:

And although in other places and at other times taxes were paid reluctantly, and military pay was even more reluctantly provided, first among us, with the order of things reversed, much more was contributed than was demanded;
Young men leaving their schools, sons their parents, youths their betrothed, husbands their wives, demanded military service:

If some were hindered by ill health, or by public duties, or by private misfortunes, from giving in their names, they bore it with no equanimity, because they saw themselves deprived of the highest honor, which they thought was placed in defending their country.
And yet those who remained were not sluggish.
Even the domestic multitude had taken up arms, with no distinction of ages or ranks:
They diligently devoted their efforts to providing supplies and tending to the wounded.
Noble women, while tending the sick, found death, which, because of the weakness of their sex, only a few were permitted to meet before the enemy.
No one longed for peace, in order to be relieved of so many and such great burdens, unless peace restored liberty, and the dignity, firmness, and security of the empire.
And what shall I say about the armies and the generals?
Their merits no praises can equal, no rewards can sufficiently repay.
How extraordinary, how great were the plans of the generals!
What constancy of the soldiers in enduring hardships!
What courage of those fighting!
What confidence before the battle, what moderation among the victors!
What a death in battles!
They breathed out their soul joyfully, when with the proclamation of the divine will they honored the best King.
But to such great efforts, both ours and those of the allies, success responded.
How many and how great were the defeats of the enemy's forces, how many thousands of captives, how many of their leaders, how many captured engines of war, how many citadels!
What allies were alienated, how much territory was brought under our power!
The city of the Parisii was stormed, which, proud, was rashly boasting itself the chief and mistress of Europe and of the whole world; hereafter, if I see anything, it will no longer boast.
The tyrant of Europe was cast down and sent into exile.
A salutary peace followed and gave a king to France;
Whatever Germany had lost through the chances of war in these twenty-two years, it restored:
And after such great slaughters the Gauls could have been afflicted more severely, if we had wished to turn back upon them the things we had suffered from them.

But such was our noble clemency, that we dealt most gently with those who had set out so far from their homes, as once to Rome and Delphi, to ravage and plunder all lands, and who had used fortune immoderately, even within their own borders.
We spared those who had raged against us so fiercely and had threatened even worse things, when they were conquered.
Finally, to those whose faith and religion had been nothing, we showed in actual fact that native integrity of the German nation, most remote from all pretense and deceit.
But those men who accomplished these deeds now return to their homes, so that they may be as good citizens as they were soldiers;
not laden with booty, which a mercenary covets, but content with their own poverty and with the glory of the Prussian name increased beyond measure and with the admiration of the whole world.
Two had been lost through the chances of war; he restored them:
And after such great slaughters, the Gauls could have been more severely afflicted, if we had wished to turn back upon them the very things we had suffered from them.

But such was our generous lenity, that, although they had set out from their own abodes, as once to Rome and Delphi, to harass and plunder all lands, and although they had used fortune immoderately, yet we dealt with them in their own territories with the greatest moderation.
We should spare those who had raged so fiercely against us and had threatened even worse things, once they were defeated.
Finally, to those who had shown no faith and no religion, we would demonstrate in actual fact that native integrity of the German nation, which is most remote from all pretense and deceit.
But those who accomplished those things now return to their household gods, so that they may be citizens as good as they were soldiers.
not laden with booty, at which a mercenary gapes, but content with their own poverty and with the glory of the Prussian name increased to an immense degree and with the admiration of the whole world.
But of so great and so manifold happiness, founded not in riches but in virtue and the goods of the mind, the sole author was Frederick William.

He raised the Prussian people to that height, that it was an example to the other peoples of Germany and of all Europe, just as he himself presents the most perfect model of a king, being adorned, indeed, with all those gifts with which a prince, perfect in every respect, ought to be furnished.
For it befits a king to be brave, so that he may protect the state from external force;
frugal, lest he squander the resources of the republic on expenses and superfluous magnificence, yet neither sordid nor avaricious, but generous and munificent;
moreover, just, and with severity gentle and clement;
the same man religious, pious, wise, energetic, and popular with gravity;
the establisher of literature and the arts;
finally, in private life, upright and pure, and a good father of a family, because it cannot happen that he loves his subjects who does not embrace even his wife and children with sincere love.
But who was braver than Frederick William?
who was more frugal and at the same time more generous?
Who is more just and more gentle?
Who is more religious?
But why do I recall individual things?
For there is no one who does not know that all the things I have said are present in Frederick William in a remarkable way.
I will say one thing, which pertains most closely to our own person, what he was for good letters.
For although the merits of the earlier kings concerning learning of every kind are not small, nevertheless Frederick William surpassed all both in the number of benefits and in their magnitude.

He who, even at that time when the state lay prostrate, afflicted by misfortunes, founded not one or two abodes of learning, but reformed and restored the entire system of studies, using the counsels of those wise men who preside over public education and sacred matters, especially of that most excellent man to whom, on account of his distinguished virtue, the care of all internal affairs was very recently entrusted to the joy of all, because he rightly understood that the weakened forces of the state could not be better aided than by the light of the arts and the cultivation of talents.
He founded our seat of learning with such munificence as no one among earlier men has employed.
In it, the young men, trained not only in letters but excelling in every virtue, have returned greater thanks to the most august King by their deeds than I can express in words.

But since he has done these things amid public dangers and calamities, it is permissible to draw a conjecture from this as to what the studies of the arts may expect from Frederick William now that the strength of the state has been restored and its resources increased.
For will he indeed allow those things to fall apart in favorable fortune, which had been prepared through adversity with many labors?

Will that most constant Frederick William now abandon the institutions which he had set before himself, because he foresaw that they would be most salutary for the republic, after the matter itself has shown how correctly his far-seeing mind had divined?
But I do not want to waste effort in praising the King:
for the deeds done by him do not speak, but they shout;

and he has no need of proclamation or statues and columns, since in the hearts of the citizens so many altars rise for him, on which the feelings of a grateful mind are offered, not incense is burned.
This one thing it will be permitted to add.

The divine investigator of human nature, Plato, when he teaches that the various forms of governing a state arise not from an oak and a rock, as the proverb says, but from the character of the men who constitute it, judges that the minds of some are kingly, of others tyrannical, and likewise that others are formed after the likeness of popular rule or the domination of a few; and he declares so ingeniously what condition of mind corresponds to each state, that I grieve that these things can be only hinted at by me, not expounded more fully in this place.
But what mind does he call kingly, what tyrannical?
Indeed, when he distributes the mind among the three provinces, namely reason, anger, and desire, and accurately defines what they are and of what sort they are,
He teaches that it is characteristic of a tyrannical nature that desire, together with base lust, violently subdues the more excellent gifts of the mind and drags them headlong.
From this source is born discord, intemperance, madness, a restless and inconstant mind, prone to any crimes whatsoever.

We see that such a disposition has founded not one or another seat of learning, but the whole system of studies, having used the counsels of those wise men who preside over public instruction and sacred affairs, and especially of that most excellent man, to whom, on account of his distinguished virtue, the care of all internal affairs has been very recently entrusted to the joy of all, has corrected and restored it, because he well understood that to the weakened forces of the state no better aid could be given than by the light of the arts and the cultivation of minds.
He founded our seat of learning with such munificence as no one among his predecessors ever displayed.
In it, the young men, trained not only in letters but in all virtue, have returned greater thanks to the most august King by their deeds than I can express in words.

But since he has done these things amid public dangers and calamities, it is permitted to take from this a conjecture of what the studies of the arts may expect from Frederick William, now that the strength of the state has been restored and its resources increased.
For will he indeed allow to perish in favorable fortune those things which were prepared through adversity with many labors?

Will that most constant Frederick William now desert the institutions which he had set before himself, because he foresaw that they would be most salutary for the republic, after the matter itself has shown how correctly his penetrating mind had divined?
But I do not want to waste effort in praising the King:
for the deeds done by him do not speak, but they shout;

and he has no need of proclamation or statues and columns, since in the hearts of the citizens so many altars rise for him, on which the feelings of a grateful mind are offered, not incense is burned.
This one thing it will be permitted to add.

The divine investigator of human nature, Plato, when he teaches that the various forms of governing a state arise not from an oak and a rock, as the proverb says, but from the characters of the men who constitute it, judges that the minds of some are kingly, of others tyrannical, and likewise that others are shaped to the likeness of popular rule or the domination of a few; and he declares so ingeniously what condition of mind corresponds to each state, that I grieve that these things can only be hinted at by me here, not set forth more fully.
But what mind does he call kingly, what tyrannical?
Indeed, when he distributes the mind among three provinces, namely reason, anger, and desire, and accurately defines what they are and of what sort they are,
He teaches that it is characteristic of a tyrannical disposition that desire, together with base lust, violently subdues the more excellent gifts of the mind and drags them headlong.
From this source is born civil discord, intemperance, madness, a restless, inconstant mind, prone to any crimes whatsoever.

We see that such is the nature of that man, who, of all tyrants that ever existed, the chief, even against himself exercised this dread tyranny of his passions, in the midst of his greatest power the most powerless and most wretched in mind.
But in the royal mind reason governs the other parts;
the passions obey anger:
From this source come wisdom, equity, and moderation;
from this source comes the greatest harmony under the gentle rule of reason;
Finally, a truly divine serenity and tranquility even in adverse circumstances.
Thus, is not the most blessed soul of Frederick William formed, managing all things by reason, without anger and partiality, and ruling not only his subjects, but also himself and his own desires?

It is the mark of that man, who, of all tyrants that ever existed, the chief, even against himself exercised this dreadful tyranny of desires, in the greatest power once the most powerless and most wretched of mind.
But in the royal mind reason governs the other parts;
the desires obey anger:
from this come wisdom, equity, moderation;
from this comes the greatest harmony under the gentle rule of reason;
finally, a truly divine serenity and tranquility even in adverse circumstances.

Thus, is not the most blessed soul of Frederick William so constituted, that he managed everything with reason, without anger and partiality, and ruled not only his subjects but also himself and his own desires?
O God, best and greatest, with pious veneration we call upon you, to whom we owe such great happiness.
You have not only given us Frederick William, but you have formed him such as he showed himself to his own people and to the world:
You destroyed those fierce and monstrous hordes, which had set out to crush Russia, by cold, hunger, and the sword:
By so great a punishment you called back piety into the hearts of mortals, you roused the noblest feelings, especially love of country, and you strengthened them:
You have won for us such great and so distinguished allies, and you have bent the minds of princes to concord:
You yourself, through these instruments of your clemency, have accomplished such great deeds.
Then hail to you, laureate King, under whose auspices this war was undertaken and brought to a successful conclusion;
Hail, and live among us safe and happy into extreme old age.
Hail to you, soldiers and most brave leaders, by whose labors and blood good things have been bought for us at the highest price with the olive branch of peace;
Hail, fellow soldiers, who, sent forth from this wrestling-school of studies into the broader fields of battles, have now returned adorned with victorious glory.
And those who have breathed their last are blessed.
Let no one honor them with tears:
their bodies rest in peace;
their souls live, their name lives and will live through the mouths of men:
their late descendants will cultivate their sacred memory.

Finally, I pray that God may preserve the King, most wise, most just, most merciful, and the magnanimous Prince, heir of the kingdom, together with the whole August house; may He preserve the strength, glory, and virtues of the Prussian people;
may He preserve peace, the nourishing mother of all good things, and also of the arts and letters.
May the supreme deity make these vows as ratified as they have been religiously made by us.

div.head: III. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXVI. habita.

p.s: Wisely and piously, most excellent men, distinguished, most renowned, most learned, most honorable fellow students, from the very beginning of this school it has been established that a gathering should be held annually in our buildings to celebrate the birthday of the best King, because we not only, like other citizens, venerate him as the common founder, prince, and lord of the state, but as the sole author and founder of our affairs:

So that on the day on which Frederick William was born, to the most auspicious fortune of that day this wrestling-school of studies, this joyful abundance of every kind of literature, may rightly seem to be owed.

But what is more suited to these most sacred solemnities, what more adapted to our feelings, than that a prince be praised in a public speech, to whose zeal for promoting the arts we owe what we teach, to whose munificence we owe that we flourish, and finally to whose virtue we owe that we live?

And indeed, although I understand that I cannot equal the deeds of this king with my words, although I feel that this is by far the most serious of the duties entrusted to me, because I must speak not once or twice, but every year from this place and on this very day:
nevertheless I judge absolutely that I have undertaken a task that is arduous rather than difficult or full of risk;

Since on the one hand such a great and so blessed abundance of praises is at hand and, as it were, overflows, that I must look around more for what I should not say than for what I should say, and on the other hand, with this king, it is permitted to speak the truth without danger of offense:

Hence it happens that, before I come to speak, I am wont to be struck with awe at the sight of the magnitude of the matter, but soon, having collected my courage, although I was neither born nor made for flattering kings, nothing seems to me more pleasant, nothing more excellent, than to interpret openly before so great, so ample, so splendid, so learned an assembly your feelings, Fathers, and the vows undertaken for the best Prince, and to discourse copiously on the royal merits.
But if we wish to recall the deeds of the past year, we shall find that Frederick William was distinguished not only in war, but also in the arts of peace:
I can, if it pleases, recount not a few things done excellently by him:

so many discharges and dismissals of soldiers, by which he restored to the fields their cultivators, to the workshops their laborers, to the schools and letters their students, to wives and children their husbands and fathers of families, to parents their sons;
That most sacred treaty, which he made with the Caesars, most like himself, for firmly pacifying the whole world;
The taxes were lightened for the subjects;
The provinces were recently wisely established;
The church was increased and adorned with magnificent honors;
The splendid works of artists were procured at great expense for the public benefit;
Many other benefits, partly completed, partly begun, partly most kindly promised to their peoples from time to time.
But nevertheless, why I should think that the most abundant material should now be left untouched, there were especially two reasons, listeners.
For first, the modesty of our King is to be regarded:
he scorns to be praised every year with deliberate effort and to be exalted beyond other mortals:
and plainly, what Caecilius [said] about his Trajan, to recount his glorious deeds:

The discharge and dismissal of so many soldiers, by which he restored cultivators to the fields, workers to the workshops, students to the schools and literature, husbands and fathers of families to their wives and children, and sons to their parents;
That most sacred treaty, which he made with Caesars most like himself for firmly pacifying the whole world;
The taxes lightened for the conquered;
The provinces recently wisely established;
The church increased and adorned with magnificent honors;
The splendid works of artists procured at great expense for the public benefit;
There are many other benefits, some completed, some begun, some very kindly promised to their peoples from time to time.
Nevertheless, why I should think that a most abundant subject should now be left untouched, there were chiefly two reasons, my hearers.
For first, the modesty of our King is to be observed:
He refuses to be praised every year deliberately and to be exalted above other mortals:

And plainly, what Caecilius says about his Trajan, 'he considers himself one of us, and for this very reason he excels and stands out all the more, because he thinks himself one of us.' Then, the things that are vigorously done abroad and in war, because they reach the ears and minds of all, can rightly and in proportion to the greatness of the deeds be celebrated even by those who were not present:

What happens at home in peace, what happens in the court, in the councils, either by kings or under royal auspices, can rightly be proclaimed only by one who is either a participant in the deliberations or an administrator of the state, thoroughly trained by experience in affairs.
Hence whatever comes into our knowledge is certainly of such a kind that I would not say it is as well known to you as to me, but it is known to the general public.

There was a time, listeners, when from the oratorical platform even the civic virtue of good princes could be candidly and worthily recognized, when Pliny, when Fronto, when other upright and eloquent men who had touched public affairs, soothed Trajans, Hadrians, Marcus Aureliuses, to whose most holy assembly it is right to add our King, with expressions of gratitude;
but those were great consuls, who had learned to inspect and assess public affairs by experience;
We have often heard that we scholars know too little about these matters.
They were active in the light of the forum and the senate.
Our eloquence is forced to hide in the shade and narrow confines of the schools.
Therefore, restrain your emotions somewhat, which this day justly claims for itself, just as I restrain myself against my own will in praising the King.

May I be allowed to recall the memory of earlier times, and to summon from the ancestors of the royal line one prince, who in his own age similarly earned the favor of literary studies. Then, those things which are carried on abroad and with arms, because they reach the ears and minds of all, can rightly and in proportion to the greatness of the deeds be celebrated even by those who were not present:

What happens at home in peace, what happens in the palace, in the senate-houses, either by kings or under royal auspices, can rightly be proclaimed only by one who is either a participant in the councils or an administrator of the state to be governed, thoroughly trained by experience in affairs.
Therefore, whatever comes into our knowledge, that certainly is of such a kind that I would not say it is as well known to you as to me, but it is known to the general public.

May I be allowed to recall the memory of earlier times, and to summon from the ancestors of the royal line one prince, who in his own age deserved well of literary studies just as our Frederick William did in ours;
so that from the comparison of a most noble example, if it can be done through my insignificance, I may seek some addition, of whatever sort, to the glory of our founder and parent.
and our Frederick William;
so that, from the comparison of a most noble example, if it can be done through my humble ability, I may seek some addition, of whatever sort, to the glory of our founder and parent.
I mean Albert, Margrave of Brandenburg, first Duke of Prussia, who, by founding the University of Königsberg, secured for himself the eternity of his name.

He, the son of Frederick, Margrave of Onolzbach, grandson of Albert Achilles, who was also called Ulysses, a prince most brave and strongest of all his equals, after he had received the dignity of a canon at Cologne of the Agrippinians, at which time, having followed his father in the retinue of Emperor Maximilian, who was then subduing Italy, especially by the urging and authority of Joachim Nestor, Elector of Brandenburg, at the age of twenty, is created Master of the Knights of the Teutonic Order of the Hospital of Blessed Mary of Jerusalem.
A man who, through the envy and favor of authors, experienced the desire for fame, because his deeds were either composed by some with implacable hatred, or celebrated by others with excessive zeal.
Albertus excelled in courage, piety, humanity, and clemency:
vigorous, upright, prudent, modest:
a faithful friend, steadfast in marriage:

Having respected the dignity of the orders of the state, he exacted contributions and taxes only when they had been granted by them, and at the beginning, as Master of the Horse, he shared with the nobility and the towns the rights of war and peace, of treaties, and of embassies.
Moreover, in administering the state and in his counsels he was inconsistent, and he allowed himself to be guided by his intimates, to whom he attributed more influence than a prince ought.
Being more eager to seize the principate and to increase his power, he burdened his subjects, already oppressed by the weight of wars, with tributes.

Amid civil disturbances and the dissensions of factions, especially of the nobles and the farmers, he preserved equity too little, favoring the aristocrats more, so that they would more willingly grant taxes;
He allowed the tranquility of his mind to be disturbed by suspicions and fear:
Finally, religion turned into superstition entangled the weak old man with magical frauds, to be deluded by the tricks of wicked men, especially foreigners.
Indeed, this misfortune of princes is no light one, that if they err ever so little, the more conspicuous they are, the greater it is considered.
And from the things they have done well, honor is taken away, because they are thought to have done them not for the common good but for their own sake.
And Albert's condition indeed was so uncertain and doubtful that he had to do many things for his own sake, which a long and sufficiently established power can scorn with impunity.

He, when as Master of the Horse he had waged war with the Poles for thirteen years, after peace was made and the equestrian order was suppressed, became Duke of Prussia; he was compelled to provide resources by which he might protect a dominion acquired neither by force nor by the finest arts, to win renown for himself, to bind the nobility to himself, to retain the loyalty of the commons, to court the favor of the Roman Emperor and the King of Poland, and to defend himself from the hatred of the order, by concealing from time to time his religion, concerning which he voluntarily offered himself for a conference, and to assume various forms, as circumstances demanded.
Yet he did not so serve the times as to dare nothing, but he exposed himself to not a few dangers:

Indeed, when he was summoned by Caesar through a herald to give an account of his usurped rule and of his abandoned former religion, and to satisfy his creditors, and when an edict was published in the very senate-house at Königsberg, and finally, when the Prussian land had been assigned in the Augustan assembly to Walter von Cronberg, Master of the Order, he was ordered either to withdraw from the principality or to plead his case in the supreme court of the Empire, with the additional threat of proscription; and at last, as had been foretold, being proscribed, he was brought into the utmost peril, had not the loyalty of his subjects prevailed more than Caesar's anger, and had fortune not aided Albert by keeping the imperial forces occupied in more serious wars.

Indeed, although he did not adopt religion as a pretext in order to gain power—since he embraced Luther's salutary doctrine, which at that time was being spread throughout Germany and the neighboring lands, with a sincere mind—
Nevertheless, he was not unaware how much it contributed to establishing a new principate.

And Luther, to whom, when he was seeking aid against the Poles at the Diet of Nuremberg, the office of Master of the Horse was even then being procured through Andrew Osiander, had urged Albert to lay aside the dress of his order, and, with the laws abrogated, to take the principality for himself and to marry a wife;
Philip had held the same opinion:
Albert smiled, but said nothing.

He became the leader of Prussia, and was compelled to provide resources by which he might protect his rule, won neither by force nor by the finest arts, to win renown for himself, to bind the nobility to himself, to retain the loyalty of the common people, to court the favor of the Roman Emperor and the King of Poland, and to defend himself from the envy of the order by concealing his religion, which he had voluntarily offered to discuss, and to assume various forms as circumstances demanded.
Yet he did not so serve the times as to dare nothing, but he exposed himself to not a few dangers:

quin a Caesare per praeconem evocatus, ut regni usurpati religionisque pristinae exutae rationem redderet, et creditoribus suis satisfaceret, edictoque in ipsa curia Regiomonte promulgato, tandem in comitiis Augustanis terra Borussica Gualtero Cronbergio, Magistro ordinis addicta, aut principatu decedere aut in supremo Imperii iudicio causam agere additis proscriptionis minis iussus, postremo, ut praedictum erat, proscriptus in discrimen summum adducebatur, ni fides subiectorum plus quam Caesaris ira valuisset, et fortuna Albertum adiuvisset copias imperatorias bellis gravioribus detinens.

nevertheless, he was not unaware how much it contributed to establishing a new principate.

Philip had thought the same:

Therefore, since Albert's rule was supported by new faith, but this could not be sustained and preserved together with a sounder discipline, unless schools of the arts were founded in Prussia, in which men suitable for teaching the people would be educated;

Moreover, since he was pleasing Sigismund Augustus, then king of Poland and his patron, by fostering his studies, because he needed his help against the Emperor and the knights who were especially preparing arms in Livonia, and since these things were especially dear to him;
finally, since he made the citizens' own inclinations more favorable to himself by this matter:
it is understood that the advantages of literature were not alien to the Duke's advantage.
I do not say this in order to diminish his glory by disparaging it:
For letters, since they make the people happier by cultivating their talents and improving their morals, greatly help every best prince.
They are an obstacle to tyrannical domination.
Finally, that one is to be considered a good prince who has learned that letters strengthen his power, not that it must be protected by military aid.

It was added that Albert, who was at that time devoted to learning and accustomed to cultivate learned and pious men and to follow their advice, ardently desired that the light of literature and religion should be spread most widely because of their own excellence.
He was not only skilled in the Latin language, but he also delighted in it:
In eloquence he is compared with Cicero and Demosthenes by an equal writer with a certainly more generous praise.

But if he advised the senate of the Königsberg academy by letter to use the German language in those things that were to be written to him, he did this not for his own sake, but because, while he was teaching, some of the councilors with whom he deliberated about those matters were so unskilled in the Latin language that time was spent in interpreting documents for their benefit.
A memorable example of a prince far more learned than his band of friends, yet by no means unique in the Brandenburg line:
And in that age solid learning drawn from the sources of antiquity was more common in courts, since French wit and pleasantries had not yet subdued them and made them, as it were, tributary.

The Prussian tables, compiled by Erasmus Reinhold, testify that he cherished the same mathematics; and because Albert provided the expenses, just as the Alphonsine tables once did from the king of Castile, they took their name from him.
But the discipline of the theologians was so beloved by the pious prince that he not only attended public disputations, but also the lectures of the professors together with the students.
Nor should his double library, one Latin, the other German, be omitted, partly prepared for his own use, partly for common use.

Finally, his wife Anna Dorothea, daughter of Frederick, king of the Danes, kindled a most beautiful ardor; that her husband was impelled by her to dedicate the halls to the Muses, and that the pious work was diligently aided, besides John Brissmannus, George Sabinus, the first rector of the university, testifies in an elegiac poem:

She herself built a part of the house of the academy from its own revenues, provided stipends for noble youths, and if she saw any of the young students in worn-out clothing and attire, she ordered them to be called to her and gave them clothes.

Now indeed how wisely, how piously, how liberally Albertus conducted himself in founding the seat of the arts, he himself best indicates in the letters published before the dedication.

For when peace was restored to Prussia, although many civic ornaments had been destroyed or shaken by war, he says that he brought back and fortified the courts, laws, discipline, and moral censorship, and that he embraced the care of divine matters and literature, in which God wished the doctrine of the true religion to be included:
After weighing the matter with learned and pious men, he placed over the churches men well instructed in the knowledge of the gospel and endowed with upright morals:

And because posterity could not have teachers of religion unless literature were cultivated, and without these most civil rights and duties could not be retained, they established schools for boys throughout the towns, where the elements of the Latin language and the Christian faith would be taught, and finally at Königsberg an academy, in which all honorable arts would be explained in order and completely, and the languages, whose knowledge is necessary for the church, would be learned.
He foresaw that many, who care little for divine matters, or who think that empires are to be governed only by force and arms, not by religion, laws, and discipline, would condemn his plan.

Nevertheless, he said that the reason for his plan was perfectly clear to him, since he knew that the first care of all princes in governing the state ought to be that the true knowledge of God be spread widely.

and that, for those who had been subjected to him, whose outstanding courage and loyalty in his own dangers had been proven, this gratitude ought to have been shown, that he should adorn their homeland, as much as he could, with genuine goods.

yet to himself the reason of the institution stands excellently, who knows that the first care of all in governing the state ought to be that the right knowledge of God be widely propagated;

and that, for those who had shown outstanding courage and loyalty in his dangers, this gratitude ought to have been shown, that he should adorn their fatherland, as far as he could, with genuine goods.

Itaque propter publicam et Borussiae et gentium vicinarum utilitatem viros eruditos et insignes, qui partim grammaticen Latinam traderent atque ad puram et nativam sermonis Romani formam in scribendo, quantum fieri posset, iuventutem assuefacerent, partim Graecae Hebraicaeque linguae auctores proponerent, partim philosophiae ac mathematum initia, iusque civile et artem medicam docerent, salariis allectos esse largioribus, quam quae per Germaniam usitata essent.
He even promised additions to those whom he had observed to be more useful to the academy:
He promised the customary exemptions and privileges to be obtained, which, however, were granted not by the Emperor nor by the Roman Pontiff, but by the King of Poland alone:

Finally, he recommends the governance of morals, and declares that he himself will undertake this province, so that those who are unwilling to be bent to virtue may be removed, since in almost all academies examples of this kind are seen, which seem worthy not only of Christian schools, but not even of any civil society.
The dedication of the academy, performed according to custom:
Prudent and humane laws were given;
no small authority of jurisdiction was conferred:

Therefore, for the public benefit both of Prussia and of neighboring nations, I grant that learned and distinguished men were attracted by more generous salaries than those customary throughout Germany, some to teach Latin grammar and to accustom the youth, as far as possible, to the pure and native form of Roman speech in writing, others to present the authors of the Greek and Hebrew languages, and others to teach the beginnings of philosophy and mathematics, as well as civil law and the medical art.

The dedication of the academy, performed according to custom:
Prudent and humane laws were given;
The authority of jurisdiction, not inconsiderable, was conferred:
To those who had completed their studies at Königsberg, not-to-be-despised privileges were granted:
An annual allowance was supplied of four thousand marks, quite generously in that cheapness of provisions;

From this a fourth part was provided for the students' common meals, a praiseworthy institution especially in a city famous for its throng of people, where although for clever young men there is an opportunity of earning a living, nevertheless because the grain supply is not rarely set on fire, certainly one does not live well on little:

As the price of grain was rising, moved by the complaints of the academy, he increased their income, and decided to give them estates, which, however, fearing lawsuits, he allowed to be taken from him.

Moreover, he gave dwellings to the teachers, and adorned them with honors in such a way that he would have aroused the envy of the other parts of the state, if the candor and simplicity of that age could have envied literature.
For in his edicts he placed the Rector and the professors of the University of Königsberg in the first position, after these the lords, the nobility, the knights, the clergy, the towns, and the rest:

Privately he so favored the doctors that, when he heard of the death of Stanislaus Rapagellanus, a leading theologian and one of the few eloquent, although he was outside the city, he returned to attend the funeral, and gave him a place next to his own monument;
He imitated the example, as Sabinus says, of Scipio Africanus, who had honored Ennius with similar honor.
But how dear Sabinus was to him, one may see from many documents;
and indeed he had deserved the friendship of the prince by his distinguished learning:
who, being a native of the March, formed by the instruction of Melanchthon, soon his father-in-law, and refined in Italy, excelled in the knowledge of the liberal arts and of law:
