a moderate number of students had flocked together just at the birth of the school, although there were only eleven professors;
the discord among the teachers, which had arisen at the very beginning in the manner of those times, was happily settled before the senate.
But how much Albertus accomplished for Prussia is evident even without my mentioning it.

For at the time when he invited the inhabitants of the Baltic bay to embrace letters, although Vinricus Kniprodius, Master of the Knights, had established in the town of Culm, at the end of the fourteenth century, a school modeled on the University of Bologna, confirmed by Urban VI, nevertheless because that school was extinguished early, ecclesiastical teachers and instructors had to be summoned either from Poland or from Germany:
There was such a great scarcity of them even when Albert was reigning that Luther could not satisfy the people of Riga and Albert himself when they asked.
Those who were suitable refused;
those who were willing would not be sufficient:
Moreover, the natives in Germany could not devote themselves to literature unless they were either well-off in family property or were provided with more generous stipends.

What of the fact that Sabinus, in a letter to Cardinal Pietro Bembo, by which he attempts to secure the papal privilege for the recently founded academy, complains of the great savagery of the Scythian people, and that scarcely in neighboring regions can a civilized way of life be maintained by laws, discipline, and authority, judging worthy of the highest praise anyone who should endeavor to cultivate these peoples and to lead them, even moderately, to the knowledge of God and the understanding of virtue?

That in these lands the arts and sciences now flourish, that they have produced men distinguished in every kind of learning, poets, philosophers, and the greatest scholars, is owed at least in some part to Albert.
He gradually drove out the former savagery, rubbed off the rust of barbarism, and illuminated minds with the lights of purer learning:
And because he accomplished this in a more difficult time, by so much the more he earned the favor of the people.

Nor do I think that this should be omitted, that he wished the home of the arts to be especially in that city which he himself inhabited, so that teachers and learners might be before his eyes and ears, and that he himself might enjoy their instruction and friendship:
By which indeed he most clearly testified his zeal.

Indeed, those princes seem to care little for literature, who either wish it to be removed as far as possible from their sight, or lend an ear to those who wish it, because in small towns both teachers and students live more comfortably, because liberty—I know not whether it is youthful license—does not suit a palace and the seat of princely power, because young men may be corrupted by bad morals:
Although these arguments are plausible, nevertheless our academic community teaches how little should be attributed to them.
For we have seen that academic life is improved, license is diminished, but true liberty is confirmed:
The other inconveniences can be healed by prudent and benevolent remedies.

And so it was well done that the plan of George Frederick, Margrave of Ansbach, who was administering Prussia on behalf of Albert's son, although it had been confirmed by Urban VI, was nevertheless, because it was extinguished early, a cause truly trivial, arising from the dissensions between the studious youth and the merchants, to establish a school in the town of Culm after the model of the University of Bologna; for that reason, ecclesiastical doctors and teachers had to be summoned either from Poland or from Germany.

Those who were suitable refused;

Nor do I think it should be omitted, that he wished the home of the arts to be especially in that city which he himself inhabited, so that teachers and learners might be before his eyes and ears, and he himself might enjoy their instruction and friendship.
By which indeed he most clearly testified his zeal.

Indeed, those princes seem to cultivate letters but little, who either wish them to be removed as far as possible from their sight, or lend an ear to those who wish it, because in moderate towns both teachers and students live more comfortably, because liberty—I know not whether youthful license—does not suit a palace and the seat of princely power, because young men may be corrupted by bad morals:
Although these arguments are plausible, nevertheless our academic community teaches how little should be attributed to them.
For we have seen academic life improved, license diminished, and true freedom strengthened:
The remaining inconveniences can be healed by prudent and benevolent remedies.

And so it was very well done that the plan of Georg Friedrich, Margrave of Onolzbach, who was administering Prussia in place of Albert's son, to transfer the Albertine school to Velavia, on account of dissensions that had arisen between the studious youth and the merchants, a truly trivial cause, was afterwards abandoned.
But for that wonderful favor toward literature, one would have wished that Albert had received a better return than we find was then the case.
For the pious prince was troubled by the quarrels of theologians, especially those of Osiander, Johannes Funccius, Fridericus Staphylus, and Ioachimus Morlinus:

while the former, certainly ingenious and not unlearned men, reproaching Luther and Melanchthon with Aristotelian theology, disguised the genuine faith with the doctrines of Bonaventura and Pico della Mirandola and other mystical opinions;
the latter, slavishly devoted to Luther's formulas, would pronounce anyone a heretic who had deviated from him even a finger's breadth;

Both were quarrelsome and irascible, so far removed from Christian gentleness and humanity that they not only fought most fiercely with words, but also it was not far from coming to blows with weapons.

And indeed, having fallen completely into madness, they thought that the divine power could not be appeased in any way, nor made favorable to themselves, nor the purity of religion better preserved, than by quarreling about words, by pursuing subtle questions, by inventing accusations, by condemning adversaries, and by persecuting them with more than pontifical hatred.
And so some of the learned were driven out, others left of their own accord;
The leader himself was insolently despised, afflicted with insults, called into suspicion both among his own people and among foreigners:

Finally, disagreements of opinions passed over into civil discords, not without the fault of the prince, who, while he mixed himself in the tumults of the theologians, while he now strove to reconcile the parties and settle the controversies, now punished the refractory, more inflamed and exasperated the excited minds, which were impatient of kindness as well as of severity.

But if the piety of that age, especially when compared with our own sluggishness, seems to deserve the highest reverence, because it placed divine worship above all other things, and dared to uphold it with the greatest effort even against the authority of rulers,

nevertheless, there is reason for us to congratulate our age that such troublesome disputes have been removed from sacred literature, that minds have been freed from that anxiety and sadness, and that the state has been liberated from the evils flowing from them.
The plan of transferring Albertina to Velavia was afterwards abandoned.
But for that wonderful favor toward literature, one would have wished that Albert had received a better return than we find was then the case.
For the pious prince was troubled by the quarrels of the theologians, especially of Osiander, John Funccius, Frederick Staphylus, and Joachim Morlinus:

since the latter, certainly ingenious and not unlearned men, reproaching Luther and Melanchthon with Aristotelian theology, would disguise genuine faith with the doctrines of Bonaventure and Pico della Mirandola and other mystical opinions;
Those who were slavishly devoted to Luther's formulas would declare anyone a heretic who had deviated from him even by a finger's breadth.
Both sides were quarrelsome and irascible, so far removed from Christian gentleness and humanity that they not only fought most bitterly with words, but also came very close to fighting with weapons.

And having completely fallen into madness, they thought that the divine power could not be appeased by anything, nor be rendered favorable to themselves, nor the purity of religion be better preserved, than by contending about words, by pursuing subtle questions, by inventing accusations, by condemning adversaries, and by persecuting them with envy more than pontifical.
And so of the learned, some were driven out, others departed voluntarily;
The leader himself, insolently despised, afflicted with insults, was called into suspicion both among his own and among foreigners:

Finally, the disagreements of opinions passed over into civil discords, not without the fault of the prince, who, while he mixed himself in the tumults of the theologians, while he now strove to reconcile the parties and settle the controversies, now punished the refractory, more inflamed and exasperated the excited minds, which were impatient of kindness as well as of severity.

But if the piety of that age, especially when compared with our own sluggishness, seems to deserve the highest reverence, because it placed divine worship above all other things, and dared to uphold it with the greatest effort even against the authority of rulers,

yet there is reason for us to congratulate our age, because such troublesome disputes have been removed from sacred literature, minds have been freed from that anxiety and sadness, and the state has been liberated from the evils that flow from them.

But I recall myself from the contemplation of the man, who, as my opinion bears, having obtained the principate by divine will, began and completed a most excellent work with such skill, such piety, with a mind so simple, so sincere, that he should never not be adorned with the praise and proclamation of all good men.
Today indeed almost nothing remains of the old and pure custom, which delights and holds the one considering that age:
Time has changed the form and appearance of almost all things:
religion yielded to avarice, grave severity to elegant levity, fidelity to cunning, flattery, and frivolous arts:
nevertheless, the pursuit of literature remained and even increased;
there remained good men, wise, ready, bold for every most beautiful deed, who could restore a better state;
our princes remained, exceptionally favoring the honorable arts:
And amid so many ruins and calamities, nevertheless seeds have been sown that will one day yield more joyful fruits.
Truly, a providence that foresees and is kind governs and guides human affairs;
because it brings forth good things from evils, happiness from destruction, freedom from slavery:
so that we see the Prussian kingdom, which had been compelled to serve a foreign tyranny, restored to its former power by the truly divine counsels of Frederick William.

He indeed not only desires the recovery of the strength of the empire and the glory of arms, but also, which is much greater, he strives to build the happiness of the citizens upon firm foundations, when he intends to grant to the people, whose loyalty he found in his dangers no less than Albert did, whose interests he sees as not separate from his own, the rights to be established by laws, when he undertakes the care of divine matters, when he fosters the arts and sciences with the greatest liberality, not equaling but surpassing his ancestors in emulation.

For to stop now with Albert alone, whose humanity, modesty, piety, courage, and other virtues he displays with dignity and majesty, who does not understand how much he left behind him, when in this city and in these buildings he established our school much more magnificently, and furnished it with the most abundant equipment and furniture, not in flourishing circumstances and with empire confirmed, but with it tottering, broken, diminished?

Let us give thanks to the most merciful King for this benefit, fellow soldiers, not with artificially crafted words, but with that innocence and holiness which we venerate in him, but with concord and obedience to be shown to the laws and with diligently assisting the public interests:

Let us give thanks to God, the Best and Greatest, because He has entrusted the reins of empire to this king, who can both defend the state with arms and temper it with salutary institutions, who is privately an example of uprightness to the citizens, and publicly the best father of the fatherland.

Finally, we direct pious prayers to the supreme deity, that he may preserve Frederick William safe together with the whole Augustan house, and since without divine help nothing can be done rightly, that he may guide all his cares and thoughts, and finally that he may confirm the peace restored to the world and preserve it for our welfare as long as possible.
He changed his appearance:
religion yielded to avarice, stern severity to elegant frivolity, faithfulness to cunning and flattery and frivolous arts:
Nevertheless, the pursuit of literature remained and was increased.
There remained good men, wise, ready, bold for every most beautiful deed, who could restore a better state of affairs;
Our leaders remained, exceptionally favoring the honorable arts:
And amid so many ruins and calamities, nevertheless seeds were sown that would one day yield more joyful fruits.
Indeed, a divine power that provides and is kind cares for and governs human affairs;
that it brings good things out of evils, happiness out of destruction, freedom out of slavery:
as we see the Prussian kingdom, which had been compelled to serve a foreign tyranny, restored to its former power by the truly divine counsels of Frederick William.

He indeed not only desires the recovery of the strength of the empire and the glory of arms, but also—what is much greater—he strives to build the happiness of the citizens upon firm foundations, when he intends to grant to the people, whose loyalty he found in his dangers no less than Albert did, whose interests he sees are not separated from his own, the rights to be established by laws, when he undertakes the care of divine matters, when he fosters the arts and learning with the greatest liberality, emulating his ancestors not by equaling but by surpassing them.

For to stop with Albert alone, whose humanity, modesty, piety, courage, and other virtues he displays with dignity and majesty, who does not understand how much he left behind him, when in this city and in these buildings he established our school much more magnificently, and furnished it with the most abundant equipment and furniture, not in flourishing circumstances and with empire confirmed, but with it tottering, broken, and diminished?

Let us give thanks, fellow soldiers, to the most merciful King for this benefit, not with artificially crafted words, but with that innocence and holiness which we venerate in him, but with concord and obedience to be shown to the laws and with diligently aiding the public interests:

Let us give thanks to God, the Best and Greatest, because He has entrusted the reins of empire to this king, who can both defend the state with arms and temper it with salutary institutions, who privately is an example of uprightness to the citizens, and publicly the best father of the fatherland.

Finally, we direct our pious prayers to the supreme deity, that he may keep Frederick William safe together with his entire August house, and since nothing can be rightly accomplished without divine help, that he may guide all his cares and thoughts, and finally that he may confirm the peace restored to the world and preserve it for our welfare as long as possible.

div.head: IV. Oratio in dedicatione universitatis litterariae Bero- linensis d. XXVI. m. April. a. MDCCCXVII. habita.

p.s: What we had sought with the most burning prayers for a long time and had awaited with the greatest longing, most excellent sir, distinguished and renowned gentlemen, most honored fellow students,

that thing is now being done before our very eyes by most distinguished men; I pray to God Almighty that it may turn out auspiciously, happily, and prosperously for our school and for the whole commonwealth.

For so great is the seriousness of this act, so great the force and power of the law handed down to us, that if that one has been well and with divine help completed, if this one is never not religiously observed and retained, our literary university is firmly established, and is destined to remain unharmed for as long as the fleeting and fragile condition of all human affairs permits.
But if the memory of this day should fade, or the most sacred law be neglected, broken, overthrown, then at last the safety of our affairs would be at stake.
But if this law was established in the presence of God, it cannot be annulled without God.
Today a seat is dedicated to literature, which, having protected its place through seven years amid various vicissitudes, has given proof of itself.

quo die ego huc vocatus, ut quod mihi ex re videretur, paucis dissererem, simul ut Regi augusto beneficii in nos collati grates agerem, quamquam mihi tempus perexiguum concessum et quasi ad aquam dicendum est, ad sollemnium dignitatem argumenti praestantia aliqua ex parte studens accedere, religioni duco de re ulla dicere quam de ipsa instituti gravissimi ratione, qui finis, quod ingenium sit doctrinae disciplinaeque academicae, quid Rex sapientissimus in schola hac artium condenda maxime spectasse videatur, denique quid nobis factum et posthac faciendum sit, quo studii litterarum indoli voluntatique regiae optime respondeamus.

And first, I will not set forth by what beginnings and causes, after the decay of the times and the ruin of states, while a deadly tyranny gradually encroached, by which not only bodies but even minds themselves were held bound and constrained, and soon by the incursions of barbarous peoples the most flourishing flower of literature among the ancients was extinguished, the universities of scholars arose, as I omit the Britons, in Gaul and Italy and then in Germany, and with literature reborn took growth, dispelled the darkness from minds, opened the purer springs of religion, and spread abroad the light, and finally diligently cultivated very many branches of learning.

I think no one will be my opponent, if I say that in our age universities are either the most important schools or ought to be, in which, just as parents transmit life to their children, so teachers, perfect in their own kind, propagate solid learning and knowledge, as complete as possible according to the condition of each age, to the growing offspring.

But the knowledge I mean, I think, is not to be placed in experience sought from without and in the varied cognition of things visible or subject to the senses, not in the traditional knowledge of deeds and opinions, not in the powers of memory or in any arts of acumen and skill;

But although the human race can do nothing without the support and service of the senses, nevertheless knowledge is concerned with reason, which holds the purest notions of all things, and which, being simple and immortal and eternal, uses this perishable dwelling of the body, until, with its bonds loosened and its prison broken, it is carried back to that most holy fountain of wisdom from which it came forth.

There is certainly, there is something divine in the minds of men, which, overshadowed by the mists of corporeal nature and lulled to sleep by inactivity, must be roused and unfolded, so that it may shine with its innate beauty and illuminate the dark regions of the soul.
This divine power can place mortals on the highest step of wisdom:
this is the guide of virtue, this is the helmsman of life:
to this must everything we do be directed.
Rightly, therefore, every most liberal-minded person has set no other end of knowledge than knowledge itself, than which you could find nothing greater or more divine.

But that [philosophy] is separated and set apart from the crafts and the gainful arts by this very thing to an immense degree, because it has its highest end placed within itself, because it traces back each and every thing from a common origin and gathers it from the first beginnings, and finally because, not deceived by the judgment of the senses nor by opinions, it scrutinizes the most remote causes of things with the keenness of mind and intellect.

Therefore we rightly despise those and do not judge them truly learned, who either estimate the dignity of learning solely from the use of daily life, or devote themselves to letters for the sake of bread and of procuring a livelihood, or, neglecting inner knowledge, hand over common things, which you may behold with your eyes or touch with your fingers, as it were, from hand to hand; and when the most joyful flower of a higher [learning] has been extinguished, universities of scholars, to omit the Britons, arose in France and Italy and then in Germany, and with the revival of letters took growth, dispelled darkness from minds, opened the fountains of purer religion, and disseminated light; finally, they diligently cultivated very many branches of learning.

I think no one will be my opponent, if I say that in our age universities are either the most important schools or ought to be, in which, just as parents transmit life to their children, so teachers, perfect in their own kind, transmit solid learning and knowledge, as complete as possible according to the condition of each age, to the growing offspring.

But the knowledge I speak of, I think, is not to be placed in experience sought from without and in the varied cognition of things visible or subject to the senses, not in the traditional knowledge of deeds done and opinions held, not in the powers of memory or in any arts of acuteness and skill whatsoever;

But although the human race can do nothing without the support and service of the senses, nevertheless knowledge is concerned with reason, which holds the purest notions of all things, and which, being simple and immortal and eternal, uses this perishable dwelling of the body until, with its bonds loosened and its prison broken, it is carried back to that most holy fountain of wisdom from which it came forth.

There is certainly, there is something divine in the minds of men, which, obscured by the mists of corporeal nature and lulled to sleep by inactivity, must be roused and unfolded, so that it may shine with its innate beauty and illuminate the dark parts of the soul.
This divine power can place mortals on the highest step of wisdom:
this is the guide of virtue, this is the helmsman of life:
to this must everything we do be directed.
Therefore rightly does every most liberal-minded person set no other end of knowledge than knowledge itself, than which you could find nothing greater or more divine.

But that [philosophy] is separated and set apart from the crafts and the lucrative arts by this very thing to an immense degree, because it has its highest end placed within itself, because it traces back each individual thing whatsoever from a common origin and gathers it from the first beginnings, and finally because, not deceived by the judgment of the senses nor by opinions, it scrutinizes the most remote causes of things with the keenness of mind and intellect.

Therefore we rightly despise those people and do not judge them to be truly learned, who either estimate the dignity of learning solely by its usefulness in everyday life, or devote themselves to literature for the sake of bread and earning a living, or, neglecting deeper knowledge, hand over common things, which you may see with your eyes or touch with your fingers, as it were from hand to hand, and who not only think that every higher and somewhat more recondite investigation of nature, whether divine or human, is vain, but even try to make it suspect.
Since these things are so, it is sufficiently clear what, in my opinion, the method of academic instruction ought to be.
For all genuine culture of the mind must begin with the hearing of philosophers, who teach the method of philosophizing, moral and natural doctrine, mathematics, the humanities, and history:

By dealing with these things, the minds of young men are both best drawn away from that illiberal manner of beginning their studies, which not a few pursue, and are imbued with those notions by which all other things are founded and held together.

Furthermore, no discipline is to be taught or learned in such a way that students receive from the teacher and commit to memory a raw and undigested material, neither arranged in proper order nor illuminated by the lights of thought, nor drawn from a single source in its precepts.

Nor should one rest content with common matters, which you may perceive with no or very slight mental effort, but minds must be kindled and exercised, so that, desiring to quench the most burning thirst for knowledge, they may plunge deeply into profound cognition, and soon dare to approach the sanctuaries of literature, untrodden by anyone before, and to be wise with no guide.

Moreover, since this nature is implanted in men, that they gladly abuse their talent, and turn learning itself into profit, twist their opinions for private advantage or in favor of the powerful, and turn them this way and that, and finally, through base ambition, love to make the worse argument the better:

For a religious teacher, nothing must be provided for before this: that by example and by words he sharpen and strengthen the sense of truth and goodness in tender minds, and turn them far away from pretense, arrogance, greed, and profit.

But now I see that I have been brought to that point, listeners, which I was especially eager to avoid, that I have fallen into an argument so ample, so rich, that if I wished to treat it properly, I would have to say many things that would be trite and stale to you, most distinguished teachers, and even if I said the most numerous and weightiest things, I would still seem to have omitted not fewer nor less important ones.
Therefore, lest I strike upon this rock, I recall myself from my course and draw in my sails.
They consider every investigation of nature, whether divine or human, that is even a little more recondite, not only useless, but they even try to render it suspect.
Since these things are so, it is sufficiently clear what, in my opinion, the principle of academic instruction ought to be.
For indeed all genuine culture of the mind must begin with the hearing of philosophers, who teach the way of philosophizing, moral and natural doctrine, mathematics, the humanities, and history:

By dealing with these, the minds of the young are both excellently drawn away from that illiberal manner of undertaking studies, which not a few follow, and are imbued with those notions by which all other things are founded and held together.

Furthermore, no discipline should be taught or learned in such a way that students receive from the teacher and commit to memory a raw and undigested material, neither arranged in proper order nor illuminated by the lights of thought, nor drawn from a single source of precepts.

Nor should one rest content with common matters, which you may perceive with no or very slight mental effort, but minds must be kindled and exercised, so that, desiring to quench the most burning thirst for knowledge, they may plunge deeply into profound cognition, and soon dare to approach the innermost sanctuaries of literature, untrodden by anyone before, and to be wise with no guide.

Moreover, since this nature is implanted in men, that they gladly abuse their talent, and turn learning itself into profit, twist their opinions for private advantage or in favor of the powerful, and turn them this way and that, and finally, through base ambition, love to make the worse cause the better:

For a religious teacher, nothing must be provided for before this: that by example and words he sharpen and strengthen the sense of truth and goodness in tender minds, and turn them far away from pretense, arrogance, greed, and profit.

But now I see that I have been brought to that point, listeners, which I was most eager to avoid, that I have fallen into an argument so ample, so copious, that if I wished to treat it properly, I would have to say many things which would be trite and stale to you, most distinguished teachers, and even if I had said the most numerous and weightiest things, I would still seem to have omitted things neither fewer nor less important.
Therefore, lest I strike upon this rock, I draw myself back from my course and shorten sail.
But someone will say:
you indeed remove literature as far as possible from all communion with life and business, and relegate it to idle leisure:
although you may have set them forth as good, as becoming;
so you point out no utility, especially no public one:
this certainly, in this place and on this very day, neither cautiously enough nor appropriately.

But I, indeed, to avoid dwelling on the sweetness of the Muses, which countless people have sung and still sing, first maintain that genuine learning is the teacher of virtue and the most powerful producer of tranquility of mind, being separated by an immense distance from that pernicious opinion which separates honesty from knowledge.
For letters, when properly cultivated, rout and eradicate the empty images of things and the errors to which vices owe their origin:
They place those who have been drawn away from sordid cares in the contemplation of the best and immutable things.

Having removed them from anxieties, they lead them to the most limpid springs of divine rites, from which alone you may most fully draw what is beautiful, what is honorable, what is worthy of an immortal human being.
From here are prepared riches, which can be neither snatched away by theft, nor destroyed by fire, nor consumed by any misfortunes.
From here come faith, justice, temperance.

From this come grave and steadfast men, who, because they have learned to despise fortune, are unshaken in adversity, undaunted by the commands of masters, and are not subdued by any force or even by the fear of death, so that they depart from their purpose.

If in our age only a scant supply of such men has been found, if we have seen not a few who were base, timid, ambitious, and flatterers of tyrants, I think that those men have not gathered the best fruit from the study of literature, but have plucked certain dry and barren little flowers of learning.

For to say in one word what I feel, this seems to me the most excellent praise and the greatest usefulness of literature, that they bring freedom of mind, in which the highest goods of the human race are contained.

But it is the task of the learned academics to rouse in well-born youths that most unworthy servitude by which their minds have been taken captive, so that it may be shaken off, so that human life may be improved, so that superstition may flee away, and religion be strengthened:
That this is not peculiar to philosophy, but can and ought to be done equally by theologians, jurists, and physicians, I need not explain.
But just as letters procure the greatest freedom, so if you take away freedom from them and bind teachers to fixed formulas, you will have cut out the eye of the human race:
The Muses, impatient of servitude, will be silent;
great talents will cease;
but flattery will burst forth;
in place of wisdom, folly, and finally crime in place of virtue, will hold sway.

And indeed the flower and freedom of letters is aided by nothing more than by this union of the disciplines, which is set before us in our universities, where, rejoicing in each other's fruit, all are illuminated by the common light of philosophy, and thrive through the bond and kinship that exists among all:
But if the spirit of letters is one, they are best held together in one body.

Therefore, I maintain, at an immense distance from that pernicious opinion which separates virtue from knowledge, that first of all, genuine learning is the teacher of virtue and the most powerful producer of tranquility of mind, a truth which countless people have sung and still sing.
For letters, when properly cultivated, rout and eradicate the empty images of things and the errors to which vices owe their origin:
they draw men away from sordid cares and place them in the contemplation of the best and immutable things:

They lead those who are removed from anxieties to the most limpid springs of divine rites, from which alone you may most fully draw what is beautiful, what is honorable, what is worthy of an immortal human being.
From here are prepared resources that can neither be snatched by theft, nor destroyed by fire, nor consumed by any misfortunes.
From here come faith, justice, temperance.

Hence grave and steadfast men, who, because they have learned to despise fortune, remain unshaken in adversity, undaunted by the commands of their masters, are not subdued by any force or even by the fear of death, so that they depart from their purpose.

If in our age only a scant supply of such men has been found, if we have seen not a few who were base, timid, ambitious, and flatterers of tyrants, I think that those men have not reaped the best fruit from the study of literature, but have plucked certain dry and sterile little flowers of learning.

For to say in one word what I feel, this seems to me the most excellent praise and the greatest utility of literature, that they bring freedom of mind, in which the highest goods of the human race are contained.

But it is the task of the learned academics to rouse in well-born youths that most unworthy servitude by which their minds have been taken captive, so that it may be shaken off, so that human life may be improved, so that superstition may flee away, and religion be strengthened.
That this is not peculiar to philosophy, but can and ought to be done equally by theologians, jurists, and physicians, I need not explain.
But just as letters procure the greatest freedom, so if you take away freedom from them and bind teachers to fixed formulas, you will have cut out the eye of the human race:
The Muses, impatient of servitude, will be silent;
great talents will cease;
but flattery will burst forth;
in place of wisdom, folly, and finally crime in place of virtue, will hold sway.

And indeed the flower and freedom of letters is aided by nothing more than by this union of the disciplines, which is set before us in our universities, where, rejoicing in the fruit of one another, all are illuminated by the common light of philosophy, and they flourish through the bond and kinship that exists among all:
But if the spirit of letters is one, they are best held together in one body.

Therefore, the enemy of the human race, in order to suppress literature and the freedom of minds, which was dangerous to him, not only restrained teachers with strict discipline, but also, in order to rule by dividing, wanted philosophy, theology, the study of law, and the medical art to be separated, just as the weaver's craft is divided from the cobbler's and the smith's;
Hence he divided the university into individual schools in separate places, and set the arts apart as if on islands:
who now himself grows old on the rock of Ocean.
Moreover, since the minds of young men emerge to freedom with difficulty, if whatever is to be learned and done is commanded, and the whole life is restrained by fear of a teacher;
in Germany we see that in the universities a certain freedom of living, which they are accustomed to call academic and interpret variously and sometimes worse, has been granted to the schools:
Each person chooses for himself to what branch of learning he will devote himself, with what he will nourish his mind, and what way of life he will adopt.
Instead of the military obedience that that same tyrant Corsus had imposed on eager young men, they are governed by paternal advice and by authority strengthened by the power of jurisdiction.
Finally, we are in the place of parents.
You, dearest comrades, are not so much pupils as household members and children, who, just as they have derived their name from liberty, so ought to be treated liberally.
But license must be restrained:
If it can be done, by admonition and exhortation;
But if not, the swollen joints or those affected with incurable disease must be cut off with the knife.

Now, when you have been thus trained and refined and have come to the administration of the state and the honorable arts, the fruits of learning must be scattered by you and brought forth for the happiness both of the city itself and of individuals:
The freedom of minds, which a good republic values most highly, because without it not even civil [freedom] can be retained, must be disseminated.
The genuine worship of the divine must be promoted.
The gifts of the mind, to which the strengths of the body serve, must be unfolded.
Justice, equity, and all virtue must be propagated.
The misery of the human race, ignorance, poverty, weakness of bodies, the force of diseases, must be either repelled or alleviated.
From you, recently distinguished even by warlike glory, the ornaments of peace will now be sought.
In these most useful pursuits, may you never, fellow soldiers, deviate from the straight path, on which, unless everything deceives me, you have thoroughly resolved to strive onward.
May ambition, greed, and evil arts never lead anyone astray, forgetful of our exhortation.

Do not forget that a man who was not educated in a life of leisure, not inexperienced in the conduct of affairs, but experienced in public affairs and the vicissitudes of fortune, that Tullius, having traversed a life spent in activity and devoted to occupations, an enemy of the human race, in order to suppress literature and the freedom of minds dangerous to himself, not only restrained teachers with strict discipline, but also, in order to rule by dividing, wanted philosophy, theology, the doctrine of law, and the medical art to be separate, just as the weaver's craft is divided from the cobbler's and the smith's.
Hence he divided the university into individual schools separated by location, and separated the arts as if into islands.
who now himself grows old on a rock in the ocean.
Moreover, since the minds of young men emerge to freedom with difficulty, if whatever must be learned and done is commanded, and the whole life is restrained by the fear of a teacher;
In Germany we see that the universities have granted to the schools a certain freedom of living, which they are accustomed to call academic and interpret variously and sometimes worse.
Each one chooses for himself to what branch of learning he devotes himself, with what he nourishes his mind, what way of life he adopts.
Instead of the military obedience which that same Corsican tyrant had imposed on young students, they are governed by paternal advice and by authority strengthened by the power of jurisdiction.
Finally, we are in the place of parents.
You, my dearest comrades, are not so much disciples as household members and children, who, just as they have derived their name from liberty, so ought they to be treated liberally.
But license must be curbed:
if it can be done, by admonition and exhortation;
if not, swollen joints or limbs affected with incurable disease must be cut off with the knife.

Now, when you have been so trained and refined and have come to the administration of the state and the practice of the honorable arts, the fruits of learning are to be spread abroad by you and to be brought forth for the happiness both of the state itself and of individuals:
the freedom of minds, which a good republic values most highly, because without it not even civil life can be maintained, must be disseminated;
the genuine worship of the deity must be promoted;
the gifts of the mind, to which the strength of the body is subservient, must be unfolded;
Justice, equity, and universal virtue must be propagated;
the misery of the human race, ignorance, poverty, weakness of bodies, the force of diseases either to be repelled or alleviated.
From you, even recently distinguished by martial glory, the ornaments of peace will now be sought.
In these most useful undertakings, would that you never deviate from the straight path, on which, unless everything deceives me, you have thoroughly resolved to strive, fellow soldiers;
Would that ambition, greed, and evil arts might not lead anyone astray, forgetful of our exhortation!

Do not forget that a man who was not educated in a life of leisure, not inexperienced in the conduct of affairs, but who had experienced the state and the vicissitudes of fortune, that Tullius, having traversed a life spent and devoted to occupations, says:
He says: One day spent well and according to the precepts of philosophy is to be preferred to an immortality of sinning.

But we have learned that the wisest king, when he was founding munificently the seat of the arts, which is dedicated today, and was furnishing it with a sufficiently ample equipment, had no other purpose than that, with the strength of arms broken and shattered, with the boundaries of the empire narrowed by half, with the state subjected to a most cruel enemy and harassed and afflicted by countless evils, he might rouse, strengthen, and fortify the powers of the mind, by which all things are overcome:
What more prudent, what more liberal, what more worthy of a king can be devised than this?
Since we were aiming at this end, we directed our efforts almost to the point which I explained a little earlier should be the direction.
that the young men entrusted to our care should not regard the liberal arts as a place for practicing trades for the sake of profit;
that they might be raised to sublime knowledge;
that they might conceive and nurture noble plans;
that they might be imbued with piety, love of country, and respect for the laws;
so that they might be both modest, and, where there was need, brave;
finally, that in his own kind each one should be such as I have indicated he ought to be.
And fortune favored our undertakings;
our discipline attracted a large number of young men even in their earliest years:
those who were soon called away to war proved their valor by distinguished deeds.
The greatest part of them now enjoys renown;

About forty men met an honorable death in battle or through the force of hardships and wounds; for them you annually bring funeral offerings with the greatest honor, and we at last will at some time erect a monument by which a distinguished example may be handed down to posterity.
And we do not mourn only those men:
They do not see this most auspicious day: Willdenow, Fichte, Reil, Klaproth.
These lights of literature, whose name flies through the mouths of men, have been sealed in our hearts; fortune has begrudged us this day, or rather the very men themselves.
But as long as the republic depended on the will of another, we led a precarious life among enemies.
When the liberty of the Germans was begun, then at last our affairs have obtained security.

Therefore, after the wars were finished, they flourished more joyfully, and there is no need to fear that they will fall, as long as we rejoice in this king, the most steadfast champion and preserver of good literature, freedom, and honesty.
While you preside over us, most excellent minister of the king's counsels, who with such kind and prudent care protect and guard our school;
While we ourselves and you, fellow soldiers, will be in our duty.
I know that certain things stand in our way, which, if I wished, I could mention:
Nor do I fear giving offense, since I speak among ourselves, and I think that all pretense is far from the dignity of an orator:
But I do not wish to say anything more serious or sadder on this day.
Our learning, indeed, harms no one;
and in the royal city, for literature to dwell is advantageous both to the city and to literature:
to the city, lest those who are unlearned be considered learned;
to literature, lest they remain hidden.
But surely the powers of the mind are not less effective in peaceful times than in troubled ones?
Should they be put to sleep as useless once the empire has been restored?
On the contrary, they themselves must be sharpened and exercised more keenly.
Why indeed?
Do we not know that very many states have become enfeebled by sluggish peace and have been undermined by indolence?
To prevent this from happening, states must take the greatest care.

Therefore, in order that we may satisfy the most merciful counsels of our Lord, which I think I interpret most correctly, we ought diligently to pursue the path which we have entered upon, and with those arts by which Prussia has always excelled, and by which, setting before its eyes the illustrious example of Frederick the Great, who remarkably protected the freedom of minds, it will excel hereafter, to illuminate the fatherland with their light and to aid the happiness of the citizens.
But you, fellow soldiers, continue to show the obedience to the laws and the diligence in literature that you have shown up to now.
If we make this promise today with the utmost religious scrupulousness, I believe that a most pleasing expression of gratitude has been made to the best of kings.
I think that everything is far from the dignity of an orator:
But I do not wish to say anything more serious or more sorrowful on this day.
Our learning, indeed, harms no one;
and that letters dwell in the royal city is advantageous both to the city and to letters:
to the city, lest those who are unlearned be considered learned;
to letters, lest they lie hidden.
But surely the powers of the mind are not less effective in peaceful times than in troubled ones?
Should they be put to sleep as useless now that the empire has been restored?
On the contrary, they must be sharpened and exercised more keenly.
Why, indeed?
Do we not know that very many states have grown sluggish in languid peace and have been weakened by idleness?
To prevent this from happening, states must take the greatest care.

Therefore, in order that we may satisfy the most merciful counsels of our Lord, which I think I interpret most correctly, we must diligently pursue the path we have entered upon, and with those arts by which Prussia has always excelled, and by which, setting before its eyes the illustrious example of Frederick the Great, who remarkably protects the freedom of minds, it will henceforth excel, we must illuminate the fatherland with their light and promote the happiness of the citizens.
But you, fellow soldiers, continue to show the obedience to the laws and the diligence in literature that you have shown up to now.
If we make these promises most religiously today, I think that a most pleasing expression of thanks has been made to the best King.
But as for the most precious pledge of royal goodwill that we have received handed over through the hands of an outstanding man, it remains for us to see how it was handed over.

In entering upon this matter, it will not be irrelevant to set forth the memory of times, in order that it may be understood with what ceremonies our ancestors inaugurated schools as temples, as cities, as colonies, and in order that things placed in opposition and juxtaposition may shine forth more brightly.

Therefore, that I may not pursue foreign examples, from the now royal family, Frederick the Third, the Elector, who soon became the first king of Prussia, the great-great-grandfather of our King, is the last of the princes who founded a university:

Its dedication was recorded in writing four years later by Christoph Cellarius at the command of the Prince, so that it might be known to posterity with what cares and how great zeal the University of Halle was begun and completed.
While I read these things, I was struck with amazement;
nor can I refrain from drawing some things from it:
But if I should wish to set forth all things in proportion to the magnificence of the matter, I should spend the whole day in speaking.

For after the Elector, although everything resounded with war, having summoned several teachers, established the academy that had once been agitated in the mind of Cardinal Albert, from the equestrian school which his father had founded at Halle:

When, returning from the Carolinian waters to Berlin, he had arrived at the city of Halle, marveling at the number of young men who came to meet him out of respect, and having matured his plan and obtained the imperial privileges, since nothing now seemed to be lacking for the new work except the solemn rite and the religious consecration, he ordered preparations to be made for his splendid inauguration.

It was announced by an edict published in both languages that the Friderician Academy would be dedicated on the Kalends of July, on the very birthday of the Prince, in the ancient manner, with the reasons added which had impelled the Prince to establish a new seat for the arts, and with the suitability of the location commended.
The Magdeburg estates, whose liberality was afterwards outstanding both in founding and in preserving the school, having been admonished by special letters:
The other universities of Brandenburg, invited by the council of professors to send someone who would congratulate the founder, and the newly founded schools, would wish him well.
A triumphal gate was built by the students, with elegant ornament, with statues, insignia, tablets, and inscriptions.

As the day approached, with spectators and witnesses of the solemnities flowing together from all sides, especially from the neighboring academies, some were sent ahead from the court to prepare the apparatus and the military pomp.

Then the Elector, together with the most distinguished of his ministers—among whom I name Paul Fuchs, the prince's orator, Ludolph and Everard Dankelmann, and that distinguished ornament of letters, Ezekiel Spanheim—and with the provincial estates, amid the sounds of the bronze trumpet and the thunder of cannons brought from Magdeburg and the musical harmonies, was met on his entry into the city in splendid procession by a cavalry of about one hundred and fifty noble youths, with drawn swords, so that, as Cellarius's words are, they might prove themselves equally prepared in the discipline of Mars as in that of Apollo, and by the professors together with the urban senate and the priests.
After the day was spent in rejoicing, and the night was given to festivity and to the veneration of the Prince, with symphonic concerts performed for the Elector and his brother Philipp Wilhelm.
The first of July was a Sunday:
early in the morning sacred rites were performed in the temples;
afterwards all were intent on the spectacle.
And at the ninth hour the Elector, having been conveyed from the palace to the college of the academy, was received there by the professors:

Then the immense column, distributed into ten divisions, was splendidly and most magnificently equipped, and with the same number of heralds going before, was led into the temple of the citadel in the space of two hours.
A cohort of soldiers at the front:
Another closed the column.

There the dedication was completed, with the Elector sitting on a most ornate tribunal with his brother and the chief ministers of the court, and with the counts who were to carry the insignia and the professors dressed becomingly and their leaders:

After the sacred rites had been performed by Benjamin Ursinus, the Prince's preacher, Paul Fuchsius, with eloquent speech, after a mature deliberation and after obtaining the imperial privileges, since nothing now seemed to be lacking for the new work except the solemn rite and the religion of consecration, ordered that preparations be made for those things by which it might be splendidly inaugurated.

It was announced by an edict published in both languages that the Friderician Academy would be dedicated on the Calends of July, on the very birthday of the Prince, in the ancient manner, with the reasons added which had impelled the Prince to establish a new seat for the arts, and with the suitability of the location commended.
The Magdeburg estates, whose liberality was afterwards outstanding both in founding and in preserving the school, having been admonished by special letters:
The other universities of Brandenburg, invited by the council of professors to send someone who would thank the founder, and the newly founded schools, would wish him well.
A triumphal gate was built by the students, with elegant ornament, with statues, insignia, tablets, and inscriptions.

As the day approached, with spectators and witnesses of the solemnities flowing together from all sides, especially from the neighboring academies, some were sent ahead from the palace to prepare the apparatus and the military pomp.

Then the Elector, together with the most distinguished of his ministers—among whom I name Paul Fuchs, the prince's orator, Ludolph and Everard Dankelmann, and that illustrious ornament of letters, Ezekiel Spanheim—and with the provincial estates, amid the sounds of the bronze trumpet and the thunder of cannons brought from Magdeburg and the musical harmonies, was met on his entry into the city in splendid procession by a cavalry of about one hundred and fifty noble youths, with drawn swords, so that, as Cellarius's words are, they might prove themselves equally prepared in the discipline of Mars as in that of Apollo, and by the professors together with the urban senate and the priests.
After the day was spent in rejoicing and the night was given to festivity and to reverence for the Prince, with symphonic concerts performed for the Elector and his brother Philipp Wilhelm.
The first of July was a Sunday:
early in the morning sacred rites were performed in the temples;
afterwards all were intent on the spectacle.
And at the ninth hour the Elector, conveyed from the palace to the university hall, was received there by the professors:

Then the immense column, distributed into ten divisions, was led into the temple of the citadel in the space of two hours, with the same number of heralds going before, and it was equipped with extraordinary splendor and magnificence.
A cohort of soldiers at the front:
Another closed the column.

There the dedication was completed, with the Elector sitting on a most ornate tribunal with his brother and the principal ministers of the court, and with the counts who were to carry the insignia and the professors dressed with dignity and their leaders:

After the sacred rites were performed by Beniamine Ursinus, the Prince's preacher, Paulus Fuchsius, with eloquent speech amid various ceremonies, while the insignia were being brought to the companions as each had requested, inaugurated the academy;
He called the Prorector to the chair, clothed him in purple, and adorned him with scepters, after the privileges, keys, album, and seals were handed over, and each insignia was suitably explained.
Then the oath was taken:
The Prorector gave thanks:
The sound of bells and the crash of cannons filled the sky.

In the forum, coins were scattered, struck in three forms in memory of the dedication, and wine was poured out for the common people from a double spring, while they venerated the deity in the temple.

After these things, twelve hundred were dining in the palace: the regular professors with the Elector and his brother and the imperial legate, others with the counts and courtiers, and the Magdeburg orders in their own dining rooms;
But in total, up to three thousand men were received that day by the generosity of the Elector.
On the following day, in the church of Mary, fifty-three doctors and masters were created.
And after the Prince had later departed, in the publication of the privileges Christoph Cellarius again gave thanks.
I say nothing about congratulatory booklets, letters, poems.
He inaugurated the academy, bringing various insignia to the counts, as each had demanded.

He clothed the Prorector, called to the chair, in purple and adorned him with scepters, after the privileges, keys, album, and seals had been handed over, and each insignia had been suitably explained.
Then the oath was taken:
The Prorector gave thanks:
The sound of bells, the crash of cannons filled the sky.

In the forum, coins struck in three forms were scattered in memory of the dedication, and wine was poured out from a double fountain for the common people, while they venerated the deity in the temple.

After these things, one thousand two hundred were feasting in the palace: the ordinary professors with the Elector and his brother and the imperial legate, others with the counts and courtiers, and the Magdeburg Orders in their own dining rooms;
In all, however, about three thousand people were received that day by the Elector's generosity.
On the following day, in the church of Mary, fifty-three doctors and masters were created;
And after the Prince had departed, in the publication of the privileges Christophorus Cellarius again gave thanks.
I say nothing about congratulatory booklets, letters, poems.
For what reason, then, have I mentioned these things?
Or is it so that, by comparison with the most solemn ceremonies, I may belittle these of ours?
Or is it that literature now seems to be despised and looked down upon because of the poverty of these men?
By no means:
For neither can anything of that sort be said without the greatest injustice.

But those things, done at that time according to the genius of that age and the custom of those men, are not to be judged foolish, since they are pious and proper, nor are they to be admired as if uniquely right, which were done by a prince who was good and most devoted to literature, but undoubtedly too lavish in expenditures and shows.
We indeed have seen the most splendid displays quickly pass away:
adversity taught modesty, and to judge the truth of things more important than empty show.
And if any appearance is even today put forward:
although not even the court produces such great gifts:
certainly you would prefer any display of erudition to be absent from the school.
Therefore, if the pure simplicity of these solemnities needs any excuse,

it has it in the dignity of letters and wisdom, it has it in the singular modesty of our Lord, entirely free from all pretense, it has it in the disposition of the most excellent man who manages our affairs, most similar to a royal mind.
May God preserve for them this correct estimation of things:

May God preserve Frederick William, the Father of the Fatherland, the founder of our university, together with the whole Augustan house, and may He grant to us and to the state a perpetual author and preserver of all good things.

div.head: V. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXVII. habita.

p.s: Whenever I have to speak before you on the birthday of Frederick William, the Father of his Country, most excellent men, illustrious, noble, colleagues and most beloved fellow soldiers;
so often do anxieties so great distract my mind, that I rightly think that no one can appreciate the magnitude of this office, unless his condition has been the same as mine.
For although it is easy and pleasant to celebrate the virtues of the King and of the Prussian state, for which matter material never fails;

Nevertheless, necessity, which the religious observance of this most auspicious day imposes, if your feelings and the vows undertaken for the best King are to be explained each year by one and the same interpreter, can easily confuse the speaker, because he is compelled either to omit what has long seemed to him most important, or to repeat more than once what has already been said, and to lose all that charm of speech which is gained by novelty.
When I profess this, no one will take it as said in such a way that I deny that in Frederick William there exists a most abundant supply of many and varied praises:

but we are so constituted by nature that generally different people are more delighted and captivated by different arts, and each one indeed directs his mind more keenly to those things that especially please him, considers and admires those more studiously, and proposes those to be looked at and admired by his listeners:

Hence it happens that, among those who are worthy of manifold praise, the same men return to the same subjects in different years, while different men, each according to his own talent, taking a different part for themselves, at the same time bring forth entirely dissimilar things.

But as for me, to whom the highest honor has fallen, that I should be publicly constituted as the orator of the Senate on this platform, if, having been girded for the fourth time today for celebrating these most sacred solemnities with my voice, I should depart somewhat from the King, who is far superior to our proclamations, in order to avoid that which I have indicated, whether it be a fault or an inconvenience, this one excuse will sufficiently protect me, that Pliny praised Trajan only once.

What of the fact that it seems not inappropriate to this very day and to the Prince, the author both of the divine worship and of the happy establishment of letters, to take possession now of the memory of that greatest matter, notably aided by the most glorious ancestors of our Lord, whose third centenary we are about to celebrate duly in its own time this year:

I mean the restoration and reformation of Christian doctrine, faith, and religion, by which, more than three hundred years ago, a new light shone upon the whole world and especially upon Germany, so great that mortals have not seen such a light since the birth of Christ, and I am confident that all or most will judge that it can never be obscured or extinguished.

In this truly excellent subject, although I perceive that nothing can be said by me either more refined or more recondite, since the industry and skill of so many diligent writers has exhausted it, nevertheless I engage in it the more willingly, because I understand that it is most closely connected not only with my studies, but also with literature itself and the system of public education, and I hope that it will be not at all unwelcome to all of you, even to those who are not devoted to Luther's doctrine.
For I will not stir up this Camarina, so as to descend into the field of controversies and to agitate subtle and thorny disputations;
but, leaving aside the heads of doctrine which are proper and peculiar to theologians, I shall rather endeavor to treat those things which have in themselves the least envy:

Relying on your kindness, which I have experienced more often than I can say, I shall briefly set forth what the liberal arts have contributed to the purification of the church, and what the church, once purified, has accomplished through the arts; and I shall add only so much about the rest as may seem sufficient for an appreciation of the facts.
To take up that matter, which has been notably aided by the most glorious ancestors of our Lord, whose third centennial we are about to celebrate in due time this year:

I mean the restoration and reformation of Christian doctrine, faith, and religion, by which, before these three hundred years, a new light shone upon the whole world and especially upon Germany, so great that mortals have not seen such a light since the birth of Christ, and I think that all or most will judge that it can never be covered or extinguished.

In this truly excellent subject, although I perceive that nothing can be said by me either more refined or more recondite, since the industry and skill of so many diligent writers has exhausted it, nevertheless I engage in it the more willingly, because I understand that it is most closely connected not only with my studies, but also with literature itself and the system of public education, and I hope that it will be not at all unwelcome to all of you, even to those who are not devoted to Luther's doctrine.
For I will not stir up this Camarina, so as to descend into the field of controversies and to agitate subtle and thorny disputes;
but, leaving aside the heads of doctrine which are proper and peculiar to theologians, I shall rather endeavor to treat those things which have the least envy in themselves:

Relying on your kindness, which I have experienced quite often, I will briefly explain how much the good arts have contributed to purifying the church, and what the church, once improved, has accomplished through the arts; I will add only as much about the rest as seems sufficient for evaluating the matters.

Therefore, to state my opinion briefly and clearly at the very outset, listeners, I maintain that the teachings of the Gospel could not have been brought forward day by day without literature, nor could the disciplines and arts have been cultivated as they were later without the correction of sacred institutions.

For when you review with me the earlier times, you will not deny that that age, which I neither despise nor think I measure by a just standard, did not lack great virtues and men as distinguished in other respects as they were remarkable for their exceptional piety;
so you will concede that the ruin and calamity of the church was brought about by nothing more than the encroaching ignorance and barbarism of the best things:

When those who ought to have been the founders and guardians of the learning handed down from antiquity, the priests and ministers of the sacred rites, fell into such great ignorance that they had no judgment at all about either divine or human affairs, that many gradually unlearned the Latin language which was their native tongue, and some were not even imbued with the first rudiments of letters, which six-year-old boys know, nor did they understand the formulas and prayers which they recited:

Not without the fault of the Pontiffs, of whom some not only scorned and despised literature, but, thinking that sanctity agrees better with ignorance than with wisdom, condemned whatever smacked of learning as a crime of impiety and deemed it dangerous and pernicious to religion, just as unlearned princes are wont to fear for the security of their kingdoms from the learned.
And indeed, if religion differs in no way from superstition, it does considerable harm to that cultivation of the mind which dispels and overthrows superstition.
But if genuine piety cannot be separated from a correct knowledge of the divine and human nature, religion will not refuse the light of learning.

But if the ministers of the church had diligently cultivated the liberal arts, had formed, nourished, and exercised their talents with the most excellent studies, then indeed neither would the divine institutions have been adorned with so many human opinions, smeared and burdened with so many tricks, and finally enclosed and constrained by such troublesome formulas, nor would mortals, who were born for freedom and moreover freed from the bonds of superstition by the very discipline of Christ, have undergone a new and intolerable servitude of minds, from which neither the schools already restored by Charlemagne nor the scholastic philosophers, who were largely captured by accepted opinions, were able to release them.

More than is owed to the Turks themselves, the enemies of the Christian name, who, after Greece was captured and Constantinople was stormed, drove the learned men into Italy, for whom the way had been opened by certain men who had gone there beforehand as scouts, as it were.
Then the study of languages, especially Greek, was spread abroad.

And learned Italians dared to speak what they felt, from which Petrarch, Boccaccio, Lorenzo Valla, Leonardo Bruni of Arezzo, Poggio of Florence, Niccolò Perotti, Francesco Filelfo, Angelo Poliziano, and other industrious and talented men partly opened up the sources of antiquity, and partly, by restoring the purity of language, displayed elegance of style and eloquence.

But the Aristotelian theology, to which the scholastic art adhered, was first broken through by the sect of the Platonists, through George Gemistius, Bessarion, Marcus Musurus, John Pico della Mirandola, Marsilio Ficino, and the Platonic Academy, so strengthened and increased that it drew to its side the most brilliant and noble ornaments of Italy.

The recently invented printing press was added, by whose aid every best book was widely disseminated, devised more quickly than by word of mouth, which nevertheless, being called winged, was carried even to remote lands.

Nor was the institution of universities, whose number was not small in the fifteenth century, although obscured by the darkness of the scholastics, entirely useless at that time, because young men, in great numbers, through the fault of the popes, some of whom not only despised and loathed literature, but, thinking that sanctity agreed better with ignorance than with wisdom, condemned whatever smacked of learning as a crime of impiety and judged it dangerous and pernicious to religion, just as unlearned princes are wont to fear learned men for the security of their kingdoms.
And indeed, if religion differs in nothing from superstition, it does considerable harm to that cultivation of the mind which dispels and overthrows superstition.
But if genuine piety cannot be separated from a correct knowledge of divine and human nature, religion will not refuse the light of learning.

But if the ministers of the church had diligently cultivated the liberal arts, had formed, nourished, and exercised their talents with the most excellent studies, then indeed neither would the divine institutions have been adorned with so many human opinions, smeared and burdened with so many tricks, and finally enclosed and constrained by such troublesome formulas, nor would mortals, who were born for freedom and moreover freed from the bonds of superstition by the discipline of Christ himself, have undergone a new and intolerable servitude of minds, from which neither the schools already restored by Charlemagne nor the scholastic philosophers, largely captured by received opinions, were able to release them.

More than is owed to those very enemies of the Christian name, the Turks, who, after Greece was captured and Constantinople was stormed, drove the learned men into Italy, for whom the way had been opened by certain men who had gone there earlier as scouts, as it were.
Then the studies of languages, especially Greek, were spread abroad.

And the learned Italians dared to speak what they felt, from which time Petrarch, Boccaccio, Lorenzo Valla, Leonardo Bruni of Arezzo, Poggio of Florence, Niccolò Perotti, Francesco Filelfo, Angelo Poliziano, and other industrious and talented men partly opened up the sources of antiquity, and partly, by restoring the purity of language, displayed elegance of style and eloquence.

But the Aristotelian theology, to which the scholastic art adhered, was first broken through by the sect of the Platonists, through George Gemistius, Bessarion, Marcus Musurus, John Pico of Mirandola, Marsilio Ficino, and the Platonic Academy, so strengthened and increased that it drew to its side the most brilliant and noble ornaments of Italy.

The recently invented printing press was added, by whose aid every best book was widely disseminated, having been devised more quickly than the voice, which nevertheless, called winged, was carried even to remote lands.

Nor was the institution of universities, whose number not small emerged in the fifteenth century, although obscured by the darkness of the scholastics, entirely useless then, because young men gathered in great numbers, if any more distinguished teacher had arisen, scattered the seeds of better discipline among their own.

How much these things contributed to the correction of sacred doctrine, and how much they prepared favorable outcomes for so great an undertaking, is partly testified by Luther himself, and partly can be gathered from certain arguments and indications.
For he indeed asserts that languages were not cultivated in monasteries and universities, lest the demonic empire should suffer a loss of such a kind that could not easily be repaired;
Whence it came about that they could write neither in Latin nor in German, and with their language and gospel corrupted and with reason itself almost stripped away, they were not far from beasts:

But by divine providence Greece was reduced into the power of the barbarians, so that the Greeks, fugitive and scattered, might spread their native language to foreign nations, so that other languages also might be learned, and finally so that the gospel might be revealed:
For not everything is accomplished by divine inspiration and breath, as some thought.
Certainly, unless he had been equipped with the aid of languages, it would have been permitted to him to be pious and to harangue before a few, but not to subdue the Pontiff and the sophists.
The same man, by refuting Aristotle, sufficiently shows that no small benefit is secured for the church.
But those very restorers of literature had elevated the authority of the pontiff and the priest by chastising the perversity of morals.
He shows the popes' masks, paying the penalties of their crimes, the church foul with filth, buried under the weight of shameful deeds, in the underworld:
That gentle Petrarch first called the papal court by the name of Babylon, which later stuck, as a reproach, and says that he left Rome, the seat of misery and nursery of error, never to return:
Others with not unrefined verses attacked the vices of the priests.

And that the art of printing books was seen as harmful by the Pontiffs themselves, especially in that license of writers then much greater than now, you may see from the edicts by which they attempted to restrain the freedom of speaking and thinking in Germany itself, on account of certain writings published among the Magdeburgers, the people of Cologne, the Treveri, and the people of Mainz, already at the end of the fifteenth century, more cunningly than rightly.
When they had gathered together, if any more distinguished teacher had emerged, they scattered the seeds of a better discipline among their own people.

How much these things contributed to the correction of sacred doctrine, and how they prepared prosperous successes for so great an undertaking, is partly testified by Luther himself, and partly can be gathered from certain arguments and indications.
For he indeed asserts that the languages were formerly not cultivated in the monasteries and universities, lest the demonic empire should suffer a loss of such a kind as would not easily be repaired;
Whence it happened that they could write neither in Latin nor in German, and with their language and gospel corrupted and reason itself almost stripped away, they were not far from beasts.

But by divine providence Greece was reduced into the power of the barbarians, so that the Greeks, fugitive and scattered, might spread their native language to foreign nations, so that other languages also might be learned, and finally so that the gospel might be revealed.
For not everything was accomplished by divine inspiration and breath, as some thought.
Certainly, unless he had been equipped with the protection of languages, it would have been permitted for him to be pious and to harangue before a few, but not to subdue the Pontiff and the sophists.
The same man, by refuting Aristotle, clearly shows that no small benefit is secured for the church.
But those very restorers of literature, by chastising the perversity of morals, had raised the authority of the pontiff and the priest.
He shows at the underworld the popes' masks of those paying the penalties for their crimes, the church filthy with squalor, overwhelmed by the weight of shameful deeds.
That gentle Petrarch first signifies the papal court by the name of Babylon, which later stuck, as a reproach, and says that he left Rome, the seat of misery and nursery of error, never to return.
Others with not unrefined verses used to satirize the vices of the priests.

And that the art of printing books was seen as harmful by the Pontiffs themselves, especially in that much greater license of writers than now, you may see from the edicts by which they attempted to restrain the freedom of speaking and thinking in Germany itself, on account of certain writings published among the Magdeburgers, Cologne, Trier, and Mainz, already at the end of the fifteenth century, more cunningly than rightly.

Sed apud populares nostros litterae, quae per viros in Italia excultos, et maxime per Rudolphum Agricolam olim erant stabilitae, ad fontium sacrorum intelligentiam accommodatae a Reuchlino et Erasmo sunt, quorum alter Hebraica docuit, alter non solum de libris novi foederis pro illius aetatis habitu optime meritus est, verum etiam scholasticas tricas multis pridem invisas
sensim et pedetentim removit, ac stultitiam temporum sale perfricuit, ipse magnus sine dubio ut studiorum, sic rerum sacrarum reformator futurus, nisi iocari quam serio agere, et prae ambitione ac timiditate gratiam potentum aucupari suaque consilia ad aliena componere, quam simplici ac forti animo, quae sibi recta viderentur, dicere praetulisset:
Hence it happened that he pleased neither side.

Now, since the idleness, luxury, avarice, and lust of the priests and monks lay open to the view of all, being vividly described in the very Lateran Council in the speech of Giovanni Francesco Pico; and since, moreover, the German princes bore with the greatest indignation the tributes exacted by the Pope, and it was established by abundant testimonies that the supreme magistrates of the Church did not hold the God of the Christians in higher regard than Jupiter, Christ than Apollo and Aesculapius, and the Virgin Mother than Diana:

For the successful undertaking of new enterprises, almost nothing was lacking except a favorable opportunity, which the quaestors of Leo and Cardinal Albert provided by establishing treasuries throughout all provinces and by most shameless harangues, and a bold man, divinely roused, who did not fear to throw himself into this crisis.

That man was Luther, a man not brought up in luxury, but one who experienced a hard boyhood and a disciplined youth; content with little, free from ambition, wonderfully steadfast, and likewise diligent, energetic, and ready, because he coveted neither honors nor wealth; he could be moved from his undertaken labor by no allurements, no threats, and no danger:
In sanctity and justice similar to Socrates and Aristides, a friend of so many princes, he died poor, he who had been born poor.
But his power of speaking, combined with richness and charm, equaled his piety.

His oratory, especially in his native language, was sharp, vehement, unrestrained, full of spirit and terror; the feeble and delicate elegance and modesty of our age can scarcely endure it, and you should not be surprised that there are people today who criticize him.
And there was as much learning in him as seemed sufficient.
And he learned something every day, and whatever was lacking Philip supplied.
When someone had reproached him with grammar, Luther openly declared that he would not be reluctant to depart from his opinion if that grammarian had judged otherwise.
