It is remarkable how much he differs from Gregory the Great, the establisher of ceremonies, who charges Desiderius, bishop of Gaul, with this abominable crime, because he, a priest, had taught some people grammar.

By these arts, one man, a master of philosophy and theology, trusting in divine aid, not only removed the Emperor Charles, in whose territories the sun never set, whom Francis, king of the French, then the most powerful of princes, could not oppose in arms, but also, with a sharp wit, ridiculed the folly of the times; he himself would undoubtedly have been a great reformer of sacred affairs as well as of studies, had he not preferred to jest rather than to act seriously, and, out of ambition and timidity, to court the favor of the powerful and to adapt his plans to those of others, rather than to speak with a simple and strong mind what seemed right to him.
Hence it happened that he pleased neither party.

Now, since the idleness, luxury, avarice, and lust of the priests and monks were exposed to the view of all, as was vividly described in the speech of Giovanni Francesco Pico at the Lateran Council itself; and since, moreover, the German princes bore with the greatest indignation the tributes exacted by the Pope, and it was established by abundant testimonies that the Christians did not hold God in higher regard than Jupiter, Christ than Apollo and Aesculapius, and the Virgin Mother than Diana:

For the successful undertaking of new enterprises, almost nothing was lacking except a favorable opportunity, which the quaestors of Leo and Cardinal Albert provided by establishing treasuries throughout all provinces and by most shameless harangues, and a bold man, divinely roused, who did not fear to expose himself to this crisis.

He was Luther, a man not brought up in luxury, but one who experienced a hard boyhood and a disciplined youth; content with little, free from ambition, wonderfully steadfast, likewise diligent, energetic, ready, because he coveted neither honors nor wealth; he could be moved from his undertaken work by no allurements, no threats, no danger.
In holiness and justice similar to Socrates and Aristides, a friend of so many princes, he died poor, he who had been born poor.
But his eloquence, combined with richness and charm, equaled his piety.

His oratory, especially in his native tongue, was sharp, vehement, unrestrained, full of spirit and terror; the feeble and delicate elegance and modesty of our age can scarcely contain it, and you should not be surprised that there are those today who criticize it.
And there was as much learning in him as seemed sufficient.
And he learned something every day, and whatever was lacking Philip supplied.
When someone had reproached him with grammar, Luther openly declared that he would not be reluctant to depart from his opinion if that grammarian had judged otherwise.

It is remarkable how much he differs from Gregory the Great, the establisher of ceremonies, who reproaches Desiderius, bishop of Gaul, with this abominable crime, because he, a priest, had taught some people grammar.

By these arts, one man, a master of philosophy and theology, trusting in divine aid, not only resisted the unbridled desire of Emperor Charles, in whose territories the sun never set, whom Francis, king of the French, then the most powerful of princes, had been unable to oppose by arms, but also broke the power of the Pope, who seemed to himself to be the vicar of God himself, and first inspired, as it were, his own soul into a great part of Germany, soon into Europe, and changed the face of all things.
He set before all who with the strength of their minds undertake a difficult task an admirable example of persistent virtue;

But if one has looked at this, who would not be moved by such greatness, and who would think that any statue or column could be erected for him that would match the magnitude and fruits of the deeds accomplished by him?

Who, I ask, does not understand that for a brave spirit nothing is impassable, and that its onslaught is not checked or broken by worn-out terrors, but is rather strengthened and increased by the very obstacles?

For from the time when Luther began to be exposed to dangers and was condemned, he had a more certain refuge in his friends, since several princes, many nobles, and almost the whole people understood that the matter concerned not one man alone, but the Germans, for whom he very rightly proclaimed that he was born for their advantage.
since he had undertaken a struggle for liberty against papal domination, if not greater, certainly more fruitful, than that which in our century freed Germany from the dominion of the French:
Nor is there any doubt that the new doctrine would have taken possession of the whole fatherland, had not punishment been inflicted in many places upon pious men by sword and flame.
Yet in this respect that age excelled, that if anyone had been afflicted in one state, refuge lay open in another:
By this just liberty was strengthened, and this was brought about, that princes dared less than the kings of Asia, who exercise their power carelessly among slaves.
No one fails to see how much this matter benefited Luther.
For if, as my opinion holds, so great a revolution could not be accomplished by a man who was lowly and humble, or who timidly watched the nods of the powerful;

If some fierceness was needed, which in Luther is known to have been so great that, thinking he owed more to God than to mortals, he would not spare even kings, and would not obey even Frederick the Wise himself, a prince who in sacred matters claimed very little for himself but referred almost everything to learned theologians, especially those of the University of Wittenberg, in all things:
Indeed, he would have been crushed before he had accomplished anything, if any word spoken more severely or more freely had been maliciously twisted into an offense against majesty.
And there were indeed, and there are even today, those who have attributed something seditious to Luther and his teaching.
I see clearly what displeases them.

Indeed, it stings them that he admonished the masters with a somewhat harsher pen, lest they mistreat their subjects, and that he could have, and did, constantly oppose unbridled desire, but also that he broke the power of the Pope, who seemed to himself to be the vicar of God himself, and first inspired, as it were, his own soul into a great part of Germany, and soon into Europe, and changed the face of all things.
He set before all who undertake a difficult work with the powers of the mind an admirable example of persistent virtue;

But if he should consider this, who would not be moved by such greatness, and who would think that no statue, no column could be erected for him that would correspond to the magnitude and fruits of the deeds accomplished by him?

Who is there, I ask, that does not understand that for a brave spirit nothing is not passable, and that its onslaught is not checked or broken by obsolete terrors, but is rather strengthened and increased by the very obstacles?

For from the time when Luther began to be exposed to dangers and was condemned, he had a more certain refuge in his friends, since several princes, many nobles, and almost the whole people understood that the matter concerned not one man alone, but the Germans, for whose advantage he most rightly proclaimed himself to have been born.

since he had undertaken a struggle for freedom against papal domination, if not greater, certainly more fruitful, than that by which in our century Germany was delivered from the dominion of the French:
Nor is there any doubt that the new doctrine would have taken possession of the whole fatherland, had not punishment been inflicted in many places upon pious men by sword and flame.
Yet in this respect that age excelled, that if anyone had been afflicted in one state, refuge lay open in another:
by which just liberty was confirmed and this was brought about, that princes dared less than the kings of Asia, who exercise their rule carelessly among slaves.
No one fails to see how much this matter benefited Luther.
For if, as my opinion holds, so great a revolution could not be accomplished by a man who was lowly and humble, or who timidly looked at the nods of the powerful;

If some fierceness was needed, which in Luther is known to have been so great that, thinking he owed more to God than to mortals, even to the point of giving a diadem, he would not spare even kings, and would not obey even Frederick the Wise himself, a prince who in sacred matters claimed very little for himself, but referred almost everything to learned theologians, especially those of the University of Wittenberg, in all things:
Indeed, he would have been crushed before he had accomplished anything, if any word spoken too harshly or too freely had been maliciously construed as an offense against the majesty of the people.
And there were indeed, and there are even today, those who have attributed to Luther and his teaching something seditious.
I see clearly what displeases them.

Surely it stings them that he admonished their masters with a somewhat harsher pen, lest they harass their subjects, that he undertook to protect the rights of the people, that he undertook to shake off the servitude of souls.

But how much he urged the people to render obedience to the magistrates, how he rebuked the turbulent movements and the license of the plowmen, how he censured the popular government, I need not explain to those who have read his writings.
because he undertook to protect the rights of the people, because he undertook to shake off the slavery of their minds.

But how much he urged the people to obey the magistrates, how he rebuked the turbulent movements and the license of the plowmen, and how he criticized the popular government, there is no need for me to explain to those who have read his writings.
Now when you ask, listeners, what it is that I have judged that great utility was brought to the cultivation of talents by the correction of the church;

To say nothing of the vernacular language admirably shaped by Luther, I think I shall have given a sufficient answer by this one reply, if I say that with the restoration of the purity of religion, superstition was driven out and free inquiry into the most important matters was restored to the human race.
For what is more hostile to literature than superstition?

What retards the eagerness of study more, what dulls the edge of the mind more, than an imperious authority, in which if you have become accustomed to acquiesce, then there is no need for you to inquire for yourself?
Superstition killed Socrates, whom none of the ancients had approached more closely to the true knowledge of God, accused of impiety, by poison;

It drove Anaxagoras into exile, who was among the first to philosophize about the mind that governs the world, because he had held a different opinion about the sun than the Athenians, having been ensnared by the same charge.
It condemned the order of the celestial spheres discovered by Copernicus by a decree of the Roman curia.
It condemned Galileo Galilei, who had deeply investigated the secrets of nature, to prison and relegated him to a retreat.
Finally, it handed over so many wise and innocent men of every kind to tortures and punishments.
But what about the authority of men?
Do we not see that those who allow themselves to be bound and held by it are either frivolous and weak-minded, or unskilled and ignorant, or pretenders?

Since these things are so, that constitution of the church must necessarily be beneficial to literature, in which it is permitted to escape the authority of men with impunity, to approach and examine the sacred sources, and finally to think freely about the nature of divine and human things.

How much more earnest care for the education of youth is connected with this kind of discipline is evident not only from the matter itself, but is also confirmed by the experience of the time that followed.
Therefore Luther considered nothing more important than to urge princes and cities to found schools:

For he thought that the strength and safety of the state lay not so much in amassing wealth, in elegant buildings, in roads, bridges, and embankments constructed at great expense, in forts and walls, in arsenals filled with weapons, artillery, and breastplates—resources which, if bad or foolish men should use them, would bring greater destruction than benefit—but much more in the honesty, prudence, and learning of well-educated citizens, by whom wealth could be acquired and properly invested.

When the Romans understood this, they took care that boys should be educated in Greek and Latin letters and liberal arts in such a way that a great crop of most skillful men, equipped with varied learning, would arise, and that in a single soldier more learning would be found than in all the monks, priests, and bishops of Germany gathered together.

And so, that which is in no way to be endured, that the state should obey logs and blocks, especially in that felicity of the age, in which it has already been brought about that eighteen-year-old youths can turn out more learned than those who once spent twenty or forty years in the discipline of monasteries or universities with the greatest detriment to their morals:
He wisely recommends liberal studies, the reading of poets, the knowledge of history and of languages, both Latin and Greek and Hebrew.
If these are neglected, not only can the Gospel be lost and ruined, but it can even come to such a pass that no ability to speak and write either in Latin or in German remains.

The judgment of these most prudent men seems to be the more necessary to be recalled to the memory of our contemporaries, the more numerous are those in our age who either neglect or despise ancient literature, and think that nothing is more foolish than if anyone should speak or write in Latin.
Indeed, when Luther, a truly German man, plainly declares that he does not at all approve of those who think that effort should be given to only one language:

In this age I fear that those most weighty words of the same man will soon fall, since the Latin language even now so becomes obsolete in these lands that the age seems to incline almost to barbarism.

But to return to the point from which I digressed: since it had happened through the correction of sacred matters that the immense wealth of the monasteries, abandoned by those who had lurked there, was without a master, lest such great resources, once bequeathed by the kindness of pious men, should be dissipated by the princes and nobles who coveted them, and should be assigned to those to whom they least pertained:

Luther wished that they should be restored partly to the needy heirs of those who had given them, partly be destined for relieving the poverty of the citizens, and partly for administering sacred rites and especially for founding and equipping schools:
than which nothing more just nor more useful could be done.

If this plan had been religiously obeyed in all places and at all times, there would not be so many schools with such poverty, but much more would be placed in the honesty, prudence, and learning of well-educated citizens, by which wealth could be both acquired and properly invested:

When the Romans understood this, they took care that the boys should be educated in Greek and Latin letters and liberal arts in such a way that a great crop of most skillful men, equipped with varied learning, would spring up, and that in a single soldier more learning would be found than in all the monks, priests, and bishops of Germany gathered together in one place.

And so, what is in no way to be endured, that the state should obey logs and blocks of wood, especially in that felicity of the age, in which it has already been brought about that eighteen-year-old youths can turn out more learned than those who once spent twenty or forty years in the discipline of monasteries or universities with the greatest detriment to their morals:
He wisely recommends liberal studies, the reading of poets, the knowledge of history and of languages, both Latin and Greek and Hebrew.
If these are neglected, not only is the gospel lost and ruined, but it can come to such a point that no ability to speak and write either in Latin or in German remains.

That judgment of the most prudent men seems to be the more necessary to be recalled to the memory of our contemporaries, the more there are in our age who either neglect or despise ancient literature, and think that nothing is more foolish than if anyone should speak or write in Latin.
Indeed, when Luther, a truly German man, plainly declares that those who think that one should devote effort to only one language are not at all approved by him:

In this age I fear that those most weighty words of the same man will soon fall, since the Latin language is already now so much becoming obsolete in these lands that the age seems to be inclining almost to barbarism.

But to return to the point from which I digressed: since it had happened through the correction of sacred matters that the immense wealth of the monasteries, abandoned by those who had lurked there, was without a master, lest such great resources, once bequeathed by the kindness of pious men, should be dissipated by the princes and nobles who coveted them, and should be assigned to those to whom they least pertained:

Luther wanted that they should be restored partly to the needy heirs of those who had donated them, partly be destined for relieving the poverty of the citizens, partly for administering sacred rites and especially for founding and equipping schools:
than which nothing more just nor more useful could be done.
If this plan had been religiously obeyed in all places and times, not so many schools would suffer from such great poverty.
Indeed, I recall with no small joy that Frederick William, that most just prince, did this very recently.
They were working.
Indeed, I recall with no small joy that Frederick William, that most just prince, did this very recently.
But lest I seem to anyone to be overdoing the role of a eulogist, I will not conceal what evils after Luther invaded our common fatherland from that movement.
I shall speak truthfully, listeners.
The division of opinion was the cause of the most atrocious wars, by which all Germany was laid waste, and literature itself, recently born, was severely afflicted:
quarrels and enmities arose among citizens of one republic, one city, one town:
irreparable damage was inflicted on the empire of the Germans, who from that time almost never coalesced in harmony with firm faith:
to foreign nations, whether enemies or under the pretext of friendship, our land was given as prey.
But when you have weighed the matter without anger and partiality, you will not cast the blame upon the followers of Luther, who had no advantage in the civil discord:
but upon the obstinacy of the Popes and Emperors, who with a nefarious endeavor strove to extirpate the new doctrine utterly with sword and fire.
They fought for their altars and hearths:
for these it was superfluous to fight for excessive power.
They demanded equal liberty for all:
They were not yielding anything regarding the most unjust conditions.

For although at the beginning of the disturbances Leo himself, with his characteristic gentleness, had even praised Luther, afterwards they all proscribed the followers of this sect and cursed them with the most bitter imprecations:

And without considering what should be granted to the times, what the new disposition of minds demanded, but despising the Germans, whom the Italians then, as recently the French, regarded as beasts, they resolved to resist the course of the human spirit and to overthrow with force those who opposed them.
But those are greatly mistaken who think that the onslaught of new things is to be eluded by punishments or by throwing obstacles in its way.
It is better restrained by gentle measures.
History teaches this, the best teacher of political prudence and a truthful prophetess, provided only that the lust and desire of men do not take away trust from her, as Apollo did from Cassandra.

But these things, which were then so done, it is now vain to deplore with womanish lamentation, and that does not befit those who obey the Brandenburg house, of which a not small part from the beginning greatly favored Luther's undertakings.
For although that very man, who had roused the reformer of religions by the selling of indulgences through Tetzel, was from this same family;
although Elector Joachim the First opposed Luther's doctrine so bitterly that his wife, devoted to the evangelical discipline, was forced to avoid danger to her life by exile:

nevertheless, those who reigned in Franconia, the Brandenburgers, together with Albert, Master of the Knights, chose this sect for themselves early, whose example Elector Joachim the Second later followed:
And it seems to have happened not by human means, but by divine plan, that the Brandenburg dominion was greatly increased by the reformation of the church.
I will say something a bit more blunt, but perhaps not far from the truth:

the name of Brandenburg owes no less to Luther and the fall of the papal power in Germany than to its armies and most valiant leaders, since a great part of the lands subject to it was formerly under the power of bishops and other lords connected with the church;

Since Prussia itself, not long after the beginning of the restoration of sacred affairs, passed to the Brandenburg prince, since Halberstadt, Magdeburg, and many other territories were in due time transferred from the priests to the Elector:
not to mention those lands that have been acquired in our age.
Finally, as if by some fate of the place, almost all those whom Luther's life made famous are now ours:
Islebia, where he was born, Erfordia, where he was educated, and Viteberga itself, where he taught, from which he illuminated the whole world with the brightest lights.

But in this century, after those most bitter quarrels have now cooled down, and the suspicions have been removed by which the different sects persecuted one another, under the most gentle rule of Frederick William the peoples of both religions are held together joined in brotherly spirits.

Since he, with the republic restored by the strength of arms, embraces sacred matters with the greatest care, and is himself an outstanding example and model of piety, this is not, as with many, sluggishness, but fairness and reason, because he loves neither side more, thinks that neither side has greater trustworthiness, and does not bind the feelings of minds with any bonds.

What of the fact that he has earned the favor of the Pontiff himself, who has not obscurely testified how much he would grant to Frederick William, by restoring the Palatine troops to their former seat?

Nor, however, does our King allow the advantages gained by the improvement of the church to slip away or be diminished, who adds this to his other virtues, that he promotes and strengthens the pursuit of letters by cultivating arts and disciplines, and by founding schools of every kind partly and partly by enlarging them with more splendid equipment.
To whom, I ask, have the greater fruits of this liberality flowed, than to our seat of learning?
Therefore, although the birthday of Frederick William is common to the whole fatherland, nevertheless it ought to seem in a certain way proper to this university;

Nor will it ever cease to recall with grateful mind the merits of its parent and to proclaim its praises, but every year on this most joyful day, in the words and laws of the most clement Prince, which they chose in good time from him, whose example Joachim the Second, the Elector, afterwards followed:
Nor does it seem to have happened by human means, but by divine counsel, that the Brandenburg state was greatly increased by the reformation of the church.
I will say something a bit more rich, but perhaps not unlike the truth:

The name of Brandenburg owes no less to Luther and to the fall of the papal power in Germany than to its armies and most valiant leaders, since a great part of the lands that obeyed it had formerly been under the power of bishops and other lords connected with the church.

Since Prussia itself, not long after the beginning of the restoration of sacred things, passed into the hands of a Brandenburg prince; since Halberstadt, Magdeburg, and many other territories were transferred from the priests to the Elector at an early date:
Not to mention those lands that have been acquired in our age.
Finally, as if by some fate of the place, almost all those whom Luther's life made famous are now ours:
Eisleben, where he was born, Erfurt, where he was educated, and Wittenberg itself, where he taught, from which he illuminated the world with the brightest lights.

But in this age, after those most bitter angers have now already cooled down, and the suspicions have been removed, with which the different sects were persecuting each other in turn, under the most gentle rule of Frederick William, the peoples of both religions are held together joined by brotherly spirits.

Since he, after the republic was restored by the strength of arms, embraces sacred matters with the greatest care, and is himself an outstanding example and model of piety, this is not, as with many, sluggishness, but fairness and reason, because he loves neither side more, thinks that neither side has greater trustworthiness, and does not bind the feelings of minds with any bonds.

What of the fact that he has earned the favor of the Pontiff himself, who has not obscurely testified how much he attributed to Frederick William by restoring the Palatine troops to their former seat?

Nor, however, does our King suffer that the advantages gained by the improvement of the church be lost or diminished, who adds this to his other virtues, that he excites and strengthens the pursuit of letters by cultivating arts and disciplines, and by founding schools of every kind partly and partly by enlarging them with more splendid equipment.
To whom, I ask, have the greater fruits of this liberality flowed, than to our seat of learning?
Therefore, although the birthday of Frederick William is common to the whole fatherland, nevertheless it ought to seem in some way proper to this university;

And it will never cease to recall with grateful mind the merits of its parent and to proclaim his praises, but every year on this most joyful day it will most solemnly bind itself to the words of the most clement Prince and to the laws most recently and kindly given by him, and it will implore the supreme deity with the most earnest prayer that it may add perpetuity to the welfare of the best King, of the royal house, and of the Prussian state.
I have spoken.

Recently, having been kindly given, he will bind himself most religiously, and he will implore the supreme deity with the most earnest prayer that he may add perpetuity to the welfare of the best King, of the royal house, and of the Prussian state.
I have spoken.

div.head: VI. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXVIII. habita.

p.s: As this day, most longed-for by me and by all of you, most excellent men, illustrious, noble, most weighty colleagues, and especially dear fellow students, returns, it cannot happen more pleasantly to any state of this kingdom than to our school of learning, that this whole day is accustomed to be given and dedicated to the solemnities by which we celebrate with the greatest joy the most powerful King given to us by divine providence, proclaim the benefits conferred by him upon the commonwealth, and finally offer up pious vows for his safety and future reign.

Because our university of letters, founded eight years ago by the wisest counsels of that man, as often before, so especially in this year, has experienced the greatest proofs of royal kindness, munificence, and clemency.

And indeed, not to mention lesser matters, although in these too there is no doubtful indication of goodwill, will anyone doubt that this was a distinguished mark of the King's favor, that several teachers have been very recently added to our university, and these partly summoned here from other academies, so that they might take up offices not without detriment to our affairs?
that our institutions, especially the medical ones, have been enlarged and strengthened in this very year?

What? The most wise king, by laws promulgated in the previous year, has added these scepters, which are now seen for the first time, the most ample and most splendid insignia of our power, with the greatest liberality?

Iam vero quum hic annus rei publicae quum universae tum maxime litterariae mutatione ministrorum regiorum, qui summae rerum praepositi sunt, memorabilis fuerit, quis est quin intelligat, huic universitati Regem optime consuluisse, quod, quum ille nobis eriperetur, qui tot per annos res nostras bene, diligenter,
strenue, integre curaverat, cui multa et praeclara iam debebamus, plura sine dubio debituri eramus, postremo quocum diuturno usu quandam quasi familiaritatem contraxeramus, quique in ipso abdicationis momento, quam ipsi cari essemus, candide declaravit, vir nobis praefectus est, quo neque digniorem consensus hominum monstrare, nec peritiorem eruditio comprobare, neque promptiorem, liberaliorem, humaniorem experientia edocti desiderare et expetere queant:

I mean a man distinguished by exceptional skills and equal reputation publicly, and finally excelling in all endowments of mind and talent, which you would not demand as necessary in a leader of literature, but would wish that each excellent one could rarely occur.

For what greater advantage can there be for the flourishing of learning than a prefect of such a kind, who seems to devote all his strength and all his care, so that the studies of letters, taken up from their foundations, may be nourished and spread more widely, and may enjoy that dignity and honor which they deserve?
I say these things at the very beginning of my speech, not because I praise that most excellent man as he deserves:
For this place does not admit this argument:
but so that I may proclaim and extol the judgment of the most merciful king.

A man was placed over us who had managed affairs with energy and integrity, to whom we already owed much and excellent service, and to whom we would undoubtedly owe more in the future; finally, with whom through long use we had contracted a certain kind of familiarity, and who at the very moment of his abdication candidly declared how dear we were to him; a man than whom neither the consensus of men could point out a more worthy one, nor learning approve a more skilled one, nor those taught by experience desire and seek a more ready, more generous, more humane one.

A man, I say, distinguished by exceptional skills and equal fame publicly, and finally excelling in all the endowments of mind and talent, which you would not demand as necessary in a leader of literature, but would wish that each excellent one might rarely occur.

For what greater advantage can there be for the flourishing of learning than a prefect of such a kind, who seems to devote all his strength and all his care to the end that the studies of letters, taken up from their very beginnings, may be nourished and spread more widely, and that they may enjoy the dignity and honor they deserve?
I say these things at the very beginning of my speech, not because I would praise a most excellent man as he deserves:
for this place does not admit of this argument:
but in order that I may proclaim and extol the judgment of the most merciful King.
Another matter remains, which, even at the risk of giving offense, if not to be explained, certainly seems to need touching upon.

For from a most honorable beginning, from the memory of the church restored by Martin Luther, celebrated at the beginning of this academic year by the alumni of the German universities, because in those solemnities certain things had happened which would incur censure, a great envy of the schools was stirred up against the universities, and among us indeed it was increased by a certain disturbance, which had turned the keen mind of the King himself to attention.

Then indeed those who in this royal city either thought that the license of some young men, which can be restrained by the easiest remedies, was a greater evil than literature was a good, or for some unknown reasons judged that this palaestra of learning, still unfamiliar to many, was not to be endured, most eagerly spread the rumor about transferring or abolishing our school, not even observing the reverence which is owed to the Prince, when they accused the most steadfast King of manifest inconstancy, while they falsely claimed that he was thinking about rescinding the things he had decreed the year before.

But in that matter, about which I have begun to speak, the best of princes not only approved of his customary fairness and leniency, but also showed most clearly how skilled an assessor of young men he was, since he thought that action should not be taken against them as if they were conspirators, but that something should be remitted and indulged to the youthful ardor of their talents.
But someone may think that I, in praising the King, am using these matters inappropriately, since greater things, and things far removed from any suspicion of envy, could be brought forward.

I indeed do not consider this a small matter, if a leader, especially one educated and formed in military command, among such great agitations of minds as now either exist or are regarded, acts gently, and prefers to compose and pacify minds with milder counsels rather than to subdue them by force and at the same time exasperate them:

Nor do I think that a discussion of those matters which pertain not to the schools of literature but to the whole commonwealth is sufficiently safe, because concerning the greatest affairs, since they are generally conducted in secret, not everyone has a settled judgment, and whatever you may say, you will have given occasion for the charge of either flattery or detraction.
Therefore I keep myself away from this most spacious field, and I prefer not to attain what is highest rather than to risk myself in that which I feel myself unequal to.

Therefore, in such a great struggle to establish the good arts, it is helpful to know what it is especially that the studies of literature bring to the utility of the republic, and why they seem to be nourished and fostered with more intense care by the wise moderators of states, among whom Frederick William holds a particularly distinguished place.

For although I myself do not greatly disagree with those who say that in literature one should not at all look to utility, but that it should be cultivated and practiced for its own sake, like everything that is best and virtue itself;
Nevertheless, if I consider that true utility cannot be separated from those things which are truly good, I readily concede that literature also ought to be useful.

Nor indeed do I call that utility by which learning is commonly recommended to some, namely that it provides to the state servants fit for rightly performing commands and for managing public affairs like slaves without reason or any feeling, and that it increases crafts, by which the fortunes of citizens are aided, by supplying inventions:
although not even this is to be despised:
but I judge quite the opposite, that letters can neither provide that nor ought to be directed to this.

And indeed, that letters are not subservient to that thing which I placed first, is understood even from this: that each person cannot learn knowledge from outside, but can only draw it from his own mind and, as it were, unfold it with a skilled teacher as guide, and that the force and power of knowledge and letters is not placed in the memory and tradition of everyday things, nor in a certain faculty of acting according to prescribed laws, but in a liberal and inner cognition of divine and human things, to be deduced from the very principles.
And certainly, if the disciplines had been born and prepared for that use of rulers which I mentioned, they could not and should not be carried to a greater perfection day by day;

But philosophy, which by no means allows itself to be reduced to these narrow limits, had to be driven out and proscribed.

But to me and to you all, I am quite sure, all those things that make life easier and more pleasant seem to be sought not for their own sake, but so that the mind, freed from the cares that the necessity of nature imposes, may more freely follow its divine nature, that is, may cultivate virtue and acquire the deepest knowledge and learning for itself:

This indeed we will bear easily, and we will not demand what is unfair, that unskilled men should judge accurately about a matter foreign to them;

after Plato, indignant, reproached them because they diverted geometry from the pure notions of the intellect to the considerations of corporeal nature and illiberal handicraft, the mechanical art was separated from geometry and philosophy, and was added to the military disciplines:
Nor did anyone who wished to be regarded as a mathematician think that he could excel by mechanical inventions, even the most useful and most admirable ones.

Therefore Archimedes, who so greatly excelled in that art that he said he could move the earth if another earth were given to him on which to stand, and not only boasted such things, but in the siege of Syracuse defeated Marcellus and the most powerful forces by the force of his machines and engines, like a hundred-handed Briareus or Typhoeus, and prevailing beyond human strength;

Nevertheless, he did not attribute much to his instruments, but he did these things almost playfully, intending to gratify King Hiero, who had asked him to bring forth demonstrations of his knowledge adapted to the comprehension of the common people.

And he was of such liberality and greatness of mind that he did not think the things by which he had gained the reputation of a wisdom not mortal but altogether divine worthy to be committed to writing, but sought his chief praise and remembrance among posterity in a clear and elegant exposition of theorems.
Therefore he ordered that not a wolf, not a crane, not a scorpion, not any engine or torment, but a sphere with a cylinder be carved on the tomb.

And I have discussed these matters to this end, that from the memory of earlier times it might be evident that letters, when they were connected with sacred things, were not nourished from some illiberal and sordid cause, nor, when they were separated from the state and entrusted to themselves, were they neglected by the leaders of states, but were especially cultivated by them.

But to those who consider either of those conditions, this immediately presents itself: that a certain greater utility of learning was observed by earlier men, who understood in their science that the vital force and, as it were, the soul and mind of the republic is placed, which penetrates and moves the body that is by itself inert;

And just as, according to the doctrine of the Pythagoreans, the soul of the world is stretched out and extended from the central fire, which holds the place of Vesta and the hearth, through the whole nature of things, and is wrapped around the sky from outside, so from the schools of literature reason is diffused through the state, containing all things and illuminating and rousing them with its light.
But to minds, as the natural philosopher Heraclitus says, nothing is more hostile than rest.
And so knowledge, not all knowledge, but that which is worthy of this name, of its own accord strives toward perfection:
Hence it happens that it, having thoroughly insinuated itself into the state, of its own accord carries it along and advances it to a better condition.
Now what greater advantage, I ask, can be procured for the state?
For it, unless it is advanced, while it stands still, may be corrupted by idleness and sluggishness.
Yet those kingdoms, which are more firmly supported by their own mass, can lack literature, if not with impunity, at least more securely.
Those states, like Prussia, like almost all of Germany, which are unequal in strength to their neighbors, must make up for what is lacking in resources by the vigor of their intellects.

From whom I am so far from thinking that I should yield, that I judge no part of knowledge to be more useful to the state than philosophy.

For although philosophy alone cannot govern states, since there is need of much practical experience and of an accurate knowledge both of the peoples and of all institutions in the state, which history supplies,

nevertheless philosophy not only sharpens and exercises the mind excellently, corrects morals, explains the reasons of the most important matters, and frees minds from superstition and from preconceived opinions;

which thing, as it can sometimes be useful, if those who have the power of choosing are far from anger and partiality, and do not regard private advantages more than public ones;

Thus it seems to me that the welfare of literature is better provided for when schools obey the gentle governance of the state, which takes care with prudent and attentive concern that laws are not violated, that well-established institutions do not become obsolete through negligence, and that the literary enterprise suffers no other harm, and whatever benefits the pursuit of learning, it recommends, advises, and commands with greater authority.

I say, to such a governance as we rejoice has fallen to our literary university, a governance that combines counsel in planning, industry in acting, and speed in completing with courtesy, affability, and goodwill.

But I consider this to be the chief sign of external liberty, without which even that greater and inner liberty cannot be preserved, namely that each university be administered in the manner of a college or of a common and public body, and that, exempt from the will, caprice, and envy of the most powerful, it have security and sanctity through the force of laws and privileges.

In this regard, observe the wisdom of our ancestors, who founded schools of learning in the very likeness of municipalities, and granted them two most important things on which they could most firmly rely: jurisdiction over their own members and ownership of lands and revenues.

Of these, the latter has persisted in almost all the academies of Germany, certainly in those that are in Protestant lands, through all the vicissitudes of civil affairs, in various ways, although limited, because the rulers of the states perceived that judgments must be exercised in one way among young students, in another among other men.
except that in a few places the domination of the French had, for some years, driven out the ancient institution.

The other [kind] involved the teachers of the universities founded long ago in various affairs, perhaps not very compatible with the more diligent cultivation of the arts and disciplines and with more recondite knowledge.

But just as it kept the church, so it kept the schools connected to it, for the most part safe from greed and desire, and it secured for them that stability which, as we have proposed, must be free in order to attract both teachers and students.

But it is agreed that liberty is twofold: one kind is of lesser value, which is concerned with external matters; the other is far greater, which, when you have called it inner, you will name by its own proper name.

Nor, however, do I seek the former kind of liberty in this, that the schools of the liberal arts, being immune from all authority of the prince and his magistrates, should govern themselves, and indeed elect and appoint public teachers by their own votes.
This matter, as it can sometimes be useful, if those who have the power of choosing are far from anger and partiality, and do not regard private advantages more than public ones;

In this regard, observe the wisdom of our ancestors, who founded schools of learning exactly in the form of municipalities, and granted them two very important things on which they could most firmly rely: jurisdiction over their own members and ownership of lands and revenues.

Of these, the latter has persisted in almost all German academies, certainly in those that are in Protestant lands, through all the vicissitudes of civil affairs, albeit limited in various ways, because the rulers of the states perceived that judgments must be exercised in one way among young students and in another among other men.

But just as it kept the church, so it kept the schools connected to it, for the most part safe from avarice and desire, and it secured for them that stability which could attract both teachers and students, whereas unstable and tottering things deter them.
Moreover, the possession of lands assigned to the literary colleges, among the ambassadors who protect the rights of the people, a place honorable and worthy of learning.
And because the public schools, supported by their own resources, seemed inviolable, the private generosity of pious and learned men was also stirred to enrich them with gifts and benefits.
until the powerful showed that neither shame nor faith nor religion stood in their way, so that they dared commit sacrilege.
Which things when I candidly profess:
For true history proves that it is not fitting for this place or for my person to put on a painted and deceitful appearance on things.

I am not afraid that I may seem to anyone to slander our state, which in such great evils and difficulties has acted most temperately, and while it especially does this, that the flower and honor of the church and of letters may be preserved and grow, it is so far from filth and avarice that it is deservedly considered most kind and most generous.

Nor did I begin to speak about lands and fields, so that I might reproach anyone with what would be the utmost shamelessness, namely that our school of letters does not enjoy this, as it were, pledge of permanence;
But where the course of my speech has carried me, that I did not want to anxiously avoid.
On the contrary, in a plainly different condition, such as ours is, I see no small advantages.

Among these it happens that schools that are so fortified on every side that they seem unable to be attacked or destroyed by any chance, by any moderate force, by any cause either legitimate or at least plausible, easily languish in idleness.

While in those matters which depend entirely on the judgment of the state, we vary according to the plans and institutions of the powerful, all the powers of our minds must be exercised more keenly, and all must advance as if intent and prepared, so that nothing loose or remiss may appear anywhere:
Moreover, because these very things can be more easily corrected, adapted to the genius and needs of the age, and finally brought to greater perfection;
And since their safety depends more on the state or the prince, they are generally cultivated, aided, and cherished by them more than those which are endowed with greater freedom.
And there are indeed two excellent pledges in which academies can trust, one placed in the state, the other in their own virtue.

But if that virtue should perish, to which the preservation and advancement of learning are especially devoted, then letters may fall together with the state, as they fell among the Greeks and Romans.

But if the schools of the arts, already through their own indolence, cannot maintain their dignity and procure esteem for themselves, then the decrepit bodies could die, while the uncertain and tottering ones deter the students;

And since their safety depends more on the state or the prince, they are generally cultivated, aided, and cherished by them more than those which are endowed with greater freedom.
And there are indeed two excellent pledges in which academies can trust, one placed in the state, the other in their own virtue.

But if that virtue should perish, to which the preservation and advancement of learning are especially devoted, then letters may fall together with the state, as they fell among the Greeks and Romans.

But if the schools of the arts cannot now maintain their dignity and win esteem for themselves by their own merit, it is better for their decrepit bodies to die than to lead a precarious and miserable life, and one most harmful to the states themselves.

For nothing, in my judgment, infects the state with a more pestilential corruption than a depraved and corrupt university system, which, instead of learned, wise, and upright men, sends forth ignorant, stupid, and morally perverted individuals.
To this evil, when it has been fixed deeply, as they say, in the very marrow of the schools, you would with difficulty remedy it by correction, but most certainly by eradication.

Finally, for those who prudently weigh the importance of things, the other kind of freedom in literature will seem much more serious, which I have called inner freedom, and I think it should be placed in the method of teaching and writing, unconstrained and unimpeded by any illiberal laws.

Since this school also has been confirmed by the most sacred statutes, and since, beyond the other advantages, all things seem to have been provided for, so that our teaching may not deviate from the correct goal of knowledge, nor fail to render to the state the benefits which I have mentioned:

The wisdom of Frederick William can never be sufficiently proclaimed, who established the seat of learning in this city, the capital of the empire, where the scattered seeds of letters could bear more abundant fruit than in a less distinguished place.

We pray today, with all our heart and with the deepest feeling of gratitude and of the devotion owed to the best of kings, that He, the Best and Greatest God, may add to this life many years that are favorable, happy, and prosperous for us and for the whole state.
I have spoken.
It is better than to lead a precarious and wretched life, and one most destructive to the very states themselves.

For nothing, in my judgment, infects the state with a more pestilential corruption than a depraved and corrupt university system, which, instead of learned, wise, and upright men, sends forth ignorant, stupid, and morally perverse individuals.

Since this school also has been confirmed by the most sacred constitutions, and since, besides the other advantages, all things seem to have been provided for, so that our teaching may not deviate from the right end of knowledge, nor fail to render to the state those utilities which I have mentioned:

The wisdom of Frederick William can never be sufficiently praised, who established the seat of learning in this city, the capital of the empire, where the scattered seeds of letters could bear more abundant fruit than in a less distinguished place.

We pray today, with all our heart and with the deepest feeling of gratitude and of the devotion owed to the best of kings, that the Best and Greatest God may add to this life of his many years that are favorable, happy, and prosperous for us and for the whole state.
I have spoken.

div.head: VII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXIX. habita.

p.s: In these most sacred solemnities, dedicated to the name of Frederick William, the founder of letters, about whom I shall speak, nothing is offered, auditors, that is at once more suitable to this day and to my and your person and to these times, than an argument, of whatever kind, drawn from letters themselves.

For while I look around to see what I should especially narrate, I understand that our speech will have very much gratitude and delight, when I have spoken about the state, which has been brought from a ruined condition into this moderate flower of happiness by the cares and occupations of a most powerful prince, and about those matters especially which have been publicly done and instituted this year;
But if I have set forth the nature of our academy, such as it has been in these recent times, I see that this lecture will be a most honorable discussion.
But what things have happened to the university each year, whether prosperous or adverse, these must be left to the Rector when he speaks at the abdication of his office.
But although I do not now for the first time avoid public affairs, nevertheless, because envy grows more fierce day by day, it now dissuades me even more sharply than before from treating of it.

Therefore, having set aside the greatest matters, which might draw us into the fields of public life, and having removed the shining lights from afar, by which you could distinguish and illuminate words, you will hear a slender discussion, not sufficiently oratorical for hearing, and, because this place excludes a more subtle doctrine, a little less accurate for reading.
I am about to speak about shaping a person to perfect humanity, and indeed in such a way that, leaving present circumstances behind from time to time, I take refuge in more remote antiquity:

In this matter, if I have departed somewhat further from the praises of the King, this can be some consolation to me, because not only, since I must deal with the same material every year, is the inconvenience compensated by the variety of the subject, but also the matter which I am about to treat ought to seem altogether most worthy of being considered on the birthday festival of a King who exceptionally promotes the humane culture and learning of his citizens.
Therefore, when you ask to what cultivation men are to be formed and educated, I answer that it is twofold:
one is peculiar and proper to each individual, by which each person is made fit for the art or trade by which he seeks to earn his living;

The other kind, which is common to all those whom nature has equipped with the talents needed for it and fortune has placed in a position where they can aspire to a more refined education through their private means, is not pursued for profit or for the sake of sustaining life, but, having its end placed within itself, it neither accomplishes nor attempts to accomplish anything other than that the entire powers of each individual should be unfolded and exercised as perfectly as possible:
They are accustomed to call him either liberal for that very reason which we have mentioned, or humane because he regards nothing beyond humanity.
For if we say 'human learning,' we do not intend by the meaning of this word to separate the human from the animal or from the divine nature.

Indeed, since it is understood that it is placed between the two and partakes of both, the principle of human culture is so constituted that it cultivates, by sowing the seeds of religion, and by awakening the knowledge of the divine nature, insofar as we can attain it by thought, and altogether by shaping and strengthening the powers of the mind and intellect, that which is akin to the divine in human beings.

Then, as for that part which we share with the beasts, I mean the bodily nature, let it be so formed that it is as little troublesome as possible to the mind and obeys and serves the mind's plans as well as can be done.
Since these things are so, neither is the cultivation of the mind to be regarded as entirely liberal, nor that of the body as illiberal.
But although the pursuit of forming the mind and intellect is, for the most part, liberal and truly humane, yet it is well known that this too can be turned to profit:
so that those who profess arts and doctrines are accustomed both to derive and to seek profit from these very things:

And indeed, on the other hand, no one will doubt that he who seeks nothing but the perfection of the body itself, removed from all the filth of manual labor, in exercising the body's strength, is performing a liberal service.

But if the liberal arts have profit attached to them, they are not practiced by those who handle them correctly for the sake of that profit itself, but because they are held and delighted by the charm and excellence of those arts, because they greatly desire to spread more widely what seems pleasing and useful to themselves, and finally because they have persuaded themselves that no greater benefit can be brought to mortals by anything than by the cultivation of minds and universal human learning:
But whatever profit comes to them from this, they accept with this intention: Therefore, when you ask to what cultivation men are to be formed and educated, I answer that it is twofold:
one peculiar and proper to each individual, by which each person is made fit for the art or trade by which he seeks to earn his living;

The other kind, which is common to all those whom nature has equipped with the talents needed for it and fortune has placed in a position where they can aspire to a more refined education through their family means, is not acquired for profit or for the sake of sustaining life, but, having its end placed within itself, it neither accomplishes nor attempts to accomplish anything other than that the entire powers of each individual be unfolded and exercised as perfectly as possible:
Whom they are accustomed to call either liberal for that very reason which we have mentioned, or humane because he regards nothing beyond humanity.
For if we say human learning, we do not intend by the meaning of this word to separate the human from the animal or from the divine nature:

Indeed, since it is understood that [philosophy] is placed between the two and partakes of both, the principle of human culture is so constituted that it is cultivated by scattering the seeds of religion, by awakening the knowledge of the divine nature, insofar as we can attain it by thought, and altogether by shaping and strengthening the powers of the mind and intellect.

Then, as for that part which we share with the beasts, I mean the bodily nature, let it be so formed that it is as little troublesome as possible to the mind and that it obeys and serves the mind's plans as well as can be done.
Since these things are so, neither is the cultivation of the mind to be regarded as altogether liberal, nor that of the body as illiberal;
But although the pursuit of forming the mind and character is, for the most part, liberal and truly humane, yet it is well known that this too can be turned to profit:
so that those who profess arts and doctrines both derive and are accustomed to seek gain from these very things:

And indeed, on the other hand, with regard to exercising the body's strength, no one will doubt that he who seeks nothing but the very perfection of the body, removed from all the filth of handicraft, performs liberal work.

Yet if the liberal arts have profit attached to them, they are not practiced by those who treat them correctly for the sake of that profit itself, but because they are held and delighted by the charm and excellence of those arts, because they greatly desire to spread more widely what seems to them pleasing and useful, and finally because they have persuaded themselves that no greater benefit can be brought to mortals by anything than by the cultivation of minds and universal human learning:

But whatever profit comes to them from that, they accept with this intention: not that they have resolved to gather wealth from the pursuit of the arts, with which, once acquired, they might be released from those occupations, but that, having provided for what they themselves and their families need, they may lead a freer and more secure life in letters.

not that they have resolved to gather wealth from the pursuit of the arts, with which once obtained they may be released from those occupations, but that, having provided for what they themselves with their families need, they may lead a freer and more secure life in letters.

But to dwell now on that which I have proposed to treat, having set aside those arts and disciplines or rather occupations, which individuals may have undertaken for themselves to practice for the sake of a livelihood:

The Greeks, the teachers of all learning and of humanity itself, embraced humane and liberal culture in two things, music and gymnastics, of which no one is ignorant that the one comprehends the exercise of the body, the other of the mind, since by the name of music they were accustomed to call not only the faculty of singing with lyre or flute or voice, but every culture proceeding from the Muses.

Because this kind of learning ought to be common to all who are properly educated, just as Aristotle judged concerning the study of music, so it must be determined concerning almost all parts of liberal education, that a liberally educated person, unless he has decided to practice an art professionally, should not excel in any one of them and surpass others to the same extent as one who professes that discipline, but should be imbued with all of them in a certain uniform measure and formed into a certain pleasant and beautiful harmony of the mind and of all the powers of the body.

Whoever has attained this, whatever path of life or doctrine he is afterwards going to enter, in which he will fix his abode, he will pursue it with greater profit, and will not, like artisans their sedentary trades, or servants their commanded services, refer it to the common use of life, but in all things will regard a more sublime and humane reason:

And because he has embraced not only one discipline, but a certain cycle of notions, when he has devoted himself to letters, he will not, as many do to the great detriment of sound learning, neglect or despise all others in comparison with his own art, but, performing the duty of a fair judge, he will assign to each thing its own praise.

Now indeed, to descend to particulars, musical education included partly music itself and partly the instruction of letters, from the very first rudiments all the way to poetry, oratory, and philosophy:

And music itself, especially that ancient and severe music, which was not only publicly established and guarded at Sparta but also in other places, used to form the tender feelings of the mind to the legitimate sounds of rhythm and harmony, and by teaching magnificent modes to be learned by heart, accustomed the young offspring to seriousness of character;
With the movement of the body agreeing with these, it produced a pleasing and at the same time honorable grace of bearing and of countenance:

Indeed, literature, and especially poetry, provided refined and polished judges of all the works of genius, and together with the study of wisdom and eloquence enriched the abundance of words and thoughts, and finally set before the minds great precepts of virtue and knowledge, and great counsels.

We know that not only assemblies and courts of law were openly exercised for this purpose, but even the theaters themselves served it, in which, at least in the earlier age, not as is usually the case today to a great extent, were heard the uncultivated witticisms of rude and unpolished writers, hateful to the Muses, attracting the unrefined populace, or frivolous dances were witnessed, but poems of the most excellent poets elaborated with the greatest art.
But just as by musical education, after savagery, cruelty, and ignorance had been driven away, the principal virtues—I mean temperance, prudence, and even justice—were remarkably cultivated;
so bodily exercise called forth courage and steadfastness, and drove out softness and cowardice:

Hence it came about that liberty, which you could hardly defend without boldness, was remarkably strengthened, and that the Greeks were separated by an extraordinary distance from the barbarians, whether from their priestly tricks or from the utterly inhuman worship of savage masters who obeyed slavishly, and that the huge assaults of the Persian mass were checked by the most noble deeds.

What of the fact that no kind of learning is more suited than that liberal one, which was accepted in practice among the Greeks, for arousing the feelings of liberty, and, since without these upright men cannot exist, for developing the whole of virtue?

For in the first place, unless literature is cultivated with liberal studies, but with that end, that from the acquired ability either of teaching or of acting we may gain profit, may attain to public offices, may be increased with honors, they serve rather to base desire and insane ambition, which cast men down into the state of slaves.

Indeed, we have seen that those for whom the highest happiness is placed in wealth, as very many seem to determine today, are altogether careless of liberty, and either love or endure even the harshest domination, and do not even bear with difficulty the change of masters, if only some little profit can flow from it to themselves;

Indeed, the memory of past deeds declares clearly enough that nothing is more destructive to states than ambition, and that it is so far from being the case that it should be nourished and encouraged, as some advise, by devising and granting various kinds of honors, that even by these the morals of citizens are thoroughly corrupted and infected with an incurable disease, if anyone is willing to listen to history.
Finally, nothing was adorning liberty, which the ancients judged to be the highest good:

Indeed, literature, and especially poetry, provided refined and polished judges of all works of genius, and together with the study of wisdom and eloquence enriched the abundance of words and thoughts, and finally set before the mind great precepts of virtue and knowledge, and great counsels.

We know that not only assemblies and courts of law were openly exercised for this purpose, but even the theaters themselves served it, in which, at least in the older age, not as is usually the case today for the most part, were heard the unpolished witticisms of rude and unlearned and inept writers, or frivolous dances were witnessed, attracting the uncultivated common people, but poems of the most excellent poets elaborated with the greatest art.
But just as by musical education, when savagery, cruelty, and ignorance were banished, the principal virtues—I mean temperance, prudence, and indeed justice—were remarkably cultivated;
so bodily exercise called forth courage and steadfastness, and drove out softness and cowardice:

Hence it came about that liberty, which you could hardly defend without boldness, was remarkably strengthened, and that the Greeks were separated by an enormous distance from the barbarians, whether from their priestly tricks or from the utterly inhuman worship of savage masters who obeyed slavishly, and that the huge assaults of the Persian mass were checked by the most noble deeds.

What of the fact that no kind of learning is more suited to rousing the feelings of liberty, and, since without these upright men cannot exist, to developing virtue as a whole, than that liberal one which had been adopted by usage among the Greeks?

For in the first place, unless letters are cultivated with liberal studies, but with that end, that from the acquired ability of teaching or acting we may gain profit, we may attain to public offices, we may be increased with honors, they serve rather to base desire and insane ambition, which cast men down into the state of slaves.

Indeed, we have seen that those for whom the highest happiness is placed in wealth, as very many seem to determine today, are altogether careless of liberty, and either love or endure even the harshest domination, and do not even bear with difficulty the change of masters, if only some little profit can flow from it to them;

But that nothing is more pernicious to states than ambition, and that it is so far from being the case that it should be nourished and increased by devising and granting various kinds of honors, as some advise, that even by these the morals of citizens are thoroughly corrupted and infected with an incurable disease, the memory of deeds done, if anyone is willing to listen to history, declares clearly enough.

Finally, nothing was so closely connected with liberty, which the ancients judged to be the highest good, as bodily exercise, which they had forbidden to slaves much more than literature, lest they should ever be able to attain to the honor and virtue of citizens.
And such was the gymnastic art of the Greeks, that it was entirely liberal and was directed to no use of life or to any definite end beyond the cultivation of humanity.

For although young men were made more fit for the labors of war and for handling arms by exercising the strength of the body, nevertheless that training differed greatly from military exercise, being adapted to a certain particular kind of utility:
This itself, however necessary it is, since in military command there is need of severity of discipline and obedience, is considered by no means suitable for attaining a liberal education.
Therefore, to return to what I said above, those states of the Greeks which most regarded the liberty of their citizens especially cultivated that humane education of youth:
On the contrary, states opposed to liberty, such as the empires of the East, if they were not so from the beginning, certainly became so in the course of time, neglected it.
Nor was this unjustly:
For no people bears unjust tyranny more easily than the brutish, barbarous, effeminate.
It was as closely connected as bodily exercise, which they had forbidden to slaves much more than literature, lest they should ever be able to attain to the honor and virtue of citizens.
And such was the gymnastic art of the Greeks, that it was entirely liberal and was directed to no use of life or any definite end beyond the cultivation of humanity.

For although young men were made more fit for the labors of war and for handling arms by exercising the strength of the body, nevertheless that training differed greatly from military exercise, being adapted to a certain particular kind of usefulness:
This itself, however necessary it is, since in military command there is need of severity of discipline and obedience, is considered by no means suitable for attaining a liberal education.
Therefore, to return to what I said above, those republics of the Greeks which most regarded the liberty of their citizens especially cultivated that humane education of youth:
on the other hand, states opposed to liberty, such as the empires of the East, if they were not so from the beginning, certainly became so in the course of time, neglected it.
Nor was this unjustly:
for no people bears an unjust tyranny more easily than the brutish, barbarous, effeminate.
Thus far I have spoken about the ancients.

But in our age, although we can scarcely equal antiquity, let alone surpass it, since it has produced the most perfect image of human learning, nevertheless because our entire culture is supported partly by the Christian faith and partly by the study of ancient literature, a different world of arts and sciences embraces the parts of human learning.

For just as in this matter both ages agree, because the highest goal of a liberal education is placed in this, that youth is formed to that virtue which is most closely connected with knowledge and science of things, nevertheless that is peculiar to us, that we have the beginning of cultivating the intellect from a correct understanding of divine things under the leadership of Christ.

Now, since the Christian religion and philosophy alike demand freedom of mind, which is bound to civil liberty by the closest ties, and are so hostile to every kind of servitude that, as this faith spread more widely and was implanted in the depths of hearts, the yoke of slavery, under which among the ancient Greeks and Romans a great part of mortals had lain oppressed to the disgrace of human nature, was shaken off—although the unworthy condition has been retained, if not entirely, at least in some measure, by certain barbarous nations, and indeed in the New World has been restored through the greatest impiety and avarice—
This very thing is contained in the most sacred precepts of our religion, that, whatever government we obey, men should be trained for just freedom.
With this word, although ambiguous, it will be permissible to use it with impunity.

But the study of literature, which has already grown to such great extent, in our age, after we have been strengthened by so many aids for learning and teaching, pertains more varied and manifold even to liberal education.
Among these matters, the native language must be placed in the first place.
For although in the most ancient times our nation produced poems not to be despised, which were brought into more celebrated notice recently by the labor of some learned and patriotic men;

although before these three hundred years, through that teacher not only of Germany, but of Europe, Luther, the native speech was so cultivated that it lacked neither clarity nor wit nor vigor and strength:

However, since the flower of German learning was soon extinguished by the atrocity of wars, and afterwards learned men used either an uncultivated and barbarous style or the diction of foreigners in writing, and courtiers and more refined men, with the introduction of French literature, had infected the native simplicity of the Germans with a foreign poison:
The manly speech of the Germans was long neglected and was brought into the light of literature only late.
And so in earlier centuries it scarcely, or not even scarcely, looked to human culture:
now, however, it shines so that in almost any genre and especially in poetry not a few examples of excellent diction are held:

except that we limp in history and eloquence, of which the former demands a freer state of affairs than can be accomplished among us, while the latter, if you set aside sacred assemblies, has scarcely found any ground granted to it up to now where it could flourish.

Therefore, in a liberal education, the principal poets among the native writers seem especially to be recommended, by whom one may be raised from this low and wretched condition of life to higher and more joyful things, and, filled with noble thoughts, may be kept safe from the contagion of this common depravity.

Moreover, although I think that music should by no means be excluded from liberal culture, yet I do not know whether poetry now holds more of that power which music had among the ancients in education, especially since the nature of ancient and modern music is entirely different, and among our duller ears the force and efficacy of musical sounds does not seem so great that they insinuate themselves into our hearts as much as they did into those of the ancients.
And indeed, although the art of oratory among us lies especially neglected, I do not judge that the faculty of speaking is to be entirely disregarded in the studies of humanity.
But since nothing is more worthy of a free man than that, under whatever authority we serve, men be trained for just liberty:
with which word, although ambiguous, it will be permitted to use without penalty.

But in our age, after we have been strengthened by so many aids for learning and teaching, the study of literature, which has already grown to such great extent, pertains more variously and multifariously even to liberal education.
Among these matters, the native language must be placed first.
For although in the most ancient times our nation produced poems not to be despised, which have recently been brought into more celebrated notice by the labor of some learned and patriotic men;

Although before these three hundred years, through that teacher not only of Germany but of Europe, Luther, the vernacular speech was so cultivated that it lacked neither clarity nor wit nor vigor and strength:

Nevertheless, since the flower of German learning was soon extinguished by the atrocity of wars, and afterwards the learned used either an uncultivated and barbarous style or the diction of foreigners in writing, and the courtiers and more refined men, with the introduction of French literature, had infected the native simplicity of the Germans with a foreign poison:
The manly speech of the Germans was long neglected and was brought into the light of literature only late.
And so in earlier centuries it scarcely, and not even scarcely, looked to human culture:
now, however, it shines so that in almost any genre and especially in poetry, not a few examples of excellent diction are held:

Except that we limp in history and eloquence, of which the former demands a freer state of affairs than can be accomplished among us, while the latter, if you set aside sacred orations, has scarcely found any ground conceded to it up to now where it could flourish.

Therefore, in a liberal education, the principal poets among the native writers seem especially to be recommended, by whom one may be raised from this low and wretched condition of life to higher and more joyful things, and, filled with noble thoughts, may be kept safe from the contagion of this common depravity.

Indeed, even that power which music had among the ancients in education, although I think that music is by no means to be excluded from liberal culture, nevertheless I do not know whether poetry now holds it more, especially since the nature of ancient and modern music is clearly different, and among the duller ears of our people the force and efficacy of musical sounds does not seem to be so great that they insinuate themselves into our hearts as much as into those of the ancients.
Nor indeed, although oratory may lie especially neglected among us, do I judge that the faculty of speaking is to be entirely postponed in the studies of humanity.

But since nothing is more worthy of a free man than to be able to speak what he thinks, the less public life contributes to forming eloquent men, the more effort and diligence must be placed on that matter, lest when one must speak openly, you hear them stammering who have accomplished the greatest things in secret.
Moreover, in this age, this is demanded of a liberally educated man: that he have some knowledge both of mathematical sciences and of history.

For mathematics, whose immense usefulness for the conveniences of life is evident, supplies this much more excellent fruit, that it sharpens the mind and renders it apt for subtle treatment of things:
whence I seem to myself rightly to wonder, what it is that impelled Socrates in Xenophon to that perverse saying about geometry, that he thought it should not be practiced beyond common utility:

Unless this should rather be attributed to Xenophon's not sufficiently refined judgment, and Plato came closer to the master's opinion, for whom it is well known that the study of mathematical disciplines is considered a meditation on philosophy:
For, when rightly cultivated, it prepares the mind for the understanding of pure notions.
