But the knowledge of history, besides being absolutely necessary for one who has decided to enter public life or to dwell in any branch of literature, is more closely connected with human culture, because it shows the vicissitudes of the human race and the causes and origins of prosperous and adverse fortune, because it teaches the greatest examples of virtue and vice, because it declares, with experience as guide, the correct estimation of things and what is to be judged good or bad, and finally because whatever the philosophy of morals embraces in its precepts, that it presents as if placed before the eyes by opening the broadest field of history.
With these things explained, it remains for me to speak about the study of ancient literature and wisdom.

And concerning the former, although I wish to speak modestly, lest anyone think that I want to heap praises upon my own art, I cannot but say that the study of antiquity can in no way be separated from human learning.

For first, since nearly all the learning of modern peoples has proceeded from Roman, and partly also from Greek, literature, who in our age can be even moderately learned, if he is utterly ignorant of the sources of our learning?

Who, since all branches of learning are held together by this common bond, and none can be rightly handled unless you are learned in Greek and Latin, would have excluded the knowledge of these languages and of these peoples from human literature, on which account the study of antiquity has been especially celebrated?

Indeed, whatever is not the property of a single art, but is the foundation of all arts, namely the ability to speak what one thinks, the less public life contributes to forming eloquent speakers, the more effort and diligence must be placed in that matter, lest where one must speak openly, you hear them stammering who have accomplished the greatest things in secret.
Moreover, in this age, this is demanded of a liberally educated man, that he have some acquaintance with both the mathematical sciences and history.
For mathematics, whose immense use for the conveniences of life is well known, supplies this much more excellent fruit, that it sharpens the mind and renders it apt for subtle treatment of things:
Whence I seem to myself rightly to wonder what it is that drove Socrates in Xenophon to that perverse saying about geometry, that he thought it should not be practiced beyond common utility:

unless rather this is to be attributed to Xenophon's not sufficiently refined judgment, and Plato came closer to the master's opinion, for whom it is well known that the study of mathematical disciplines is held to be the meditation of philosophy:
For indeed, when properly cultivated, it prepares the mind for the understanding of pure concepts.

But the knowledge of history, besides being absolutely necessary for one who has decided to enter public life or to dwell in any branch of literature, is more closely connected with human culture, because it shows the vicissitudes of the human race and the causes and origins of prosperous and adverse fortune, because it teaches the greatest examples of virtue and vice, because it declares, with experience as guide, the correct estimation of things and what is to be judged good or bad, and finally because whatever the philosophy of morals embraces in its precepts, that it presents as if placed before the eyes by opening the broadest field of history.
With these things explained, it remains for me to speak about the study of ancient literature and wisdom.

And concerning the former, although I wish to speak more modestly, lest anyone think that I want to heap praises upon my own art, I cannot but say that the study of antiquity can in no way be separated from human learning.

For first, since the entire learning of modern peoples has proceeded almost entirely from Roman, and partly also from Greek, literature, who in our age can be even moderately learned, if he is utterly ignorant of the sources of our learning?

Who, since all branches of learning are held together by this common bond, and since nothing can be rightly handled unless you are learned in Greek and Latin, would have excluded the knowledge of these languages and of these peoples from humane letters, under which name the study of antiquity has especially been celebrated?
Indeed, whatever is not the property of a single art, but is the foundation of all arts, that must be reckoned among the disciplines of humanity.
It is added that, the more remote ancient literature is from common use, the more liberal it is to be considered.
if, however, their excellence is as great as it is thought to be.
But of which discipline, I ask, are the fruits greater for rousing the powers of the mind?

What discipline sets forth more clearly described examples of self-restraint in great matters, of constancy in adversity, then of courage, love of country, equity, dignity, finally of any virtue whatsoever?

Quibus quod non omnes, qui antiquis litteris operam dant, ita ut par est commoventur, atque ad illa mores suos formant et componunt, partim in certorum quorundam ingeniorum innata et insanabili perversitate causa quaerenda est, partim in eo, quod ratione non liberali utuntur, sed vel ad quaestum faciendum vel ad famam doctrina et acumine comparandam re praestantissima abutuntur, aut quod minuta quaedam et exilia huius disciplinae frustula decerpunt, aut omnino non ut homines, sed ut animalia condocefacta nullo animi affectu non nisi sollertiam aliquam sibi compararunt, nec quid agant considerant, quid didicerint perspiciunt.

Moreover, since the Greeks and Romans cultivated especially those arts by which the highest degree of culture is comprehended, and above all taught the most perfect form of oratory by examples that will never perish, anyone will readily grant that by these models, as the poet says, to be turned over by night and day in hand, a man is exceptionally formed.
I do not say this in the sense that I would recommend a servile imitation of the ancients:

Indeed, in the case of the Greeks, this especially holds me: that in them we see an image of culture, born from the very character of the people without any external aid brought in, complete in all its parts, which we should not imitate, but emulate as far as it can be done according to our own principles.

And indeed, since the Germans, whose language is most similar to the speech of the Greeks, began to devote greater attention to Greek literature, we too have made progress by observing their excellence, and we have been recalled especially from the imitation of the Gauls, by which the love of one's country could have been overthrown together with the ancestral culture.

For nothing seems to alienate us more from the piety owed to our fatherland than if we are too devoted to the literature of another nation, not one that once flourished, but one that now thrives, and, weary of our own goods, we gaze at foreign things.

Moreover, that I do not mean that all should be as versed in the study of antiquity as those who are especially devoted to it, is sufficiently understood from what I said at the beginning about liberal culture.
For indeed, since I demand more, this must be considered among the disciplines of humanity.
It is added that, the more remote ancient literature is from common use, the more liberal it must be considered:
if, however, their excellence is as great as it is thought to be.
But of which discipline, I ask, are the fruits greater for rousing the powers of the mind?

What discipline sets forth clearer examples of self-control in great matters, of constancy in adversity, then of courage, love of country, fairness, dignity, and finally of any virtue, more brilliantly described?

Quibus quod non omnes, qui antiquis litteris operam dant, ita ut par est commoventur, atque ad illa mores suos formant et componunt, partim in certorum quorundam ingeniorum innata et insanabili perversitate causa quaerenda est, partim in eo, quod ratione non liberali utuntur, sed vel ad quaestum faciendum vel ad famam doctrina et acumine comparandam re praestantissima abutuntur, aut quod minuta quaedam et exilia huius disciplinae frustula decerpunt, aut omnino non ut homines, sed ut animalia condocefacta nullo animi affectu non nisi sollertiam aliquam sibi compararunt, nec quid agant considerant, quid didicerint perspiciunt.

Moreover, since the Greeks and Romans cultivated especially those arts by which the highest degree of culture is comprehended, and above all taught the most perfect form of oratory by examples that will never perish, anyone will readily grant that by these models, as the poet says, which are to be turned over by night and day, a man is exceptionally formed.
I do not say this in the sense that I would recommend a servile imitation of the ancients:

Indeed, in the case of the Greeks, this especially holds me: that in them, with no external aid brought in, an image of culture born from the very character of the people is seen complete in all its parts, which we should not imitate, but, as far as it can be done according to our own reason, we should emulate.

And indeed, since the Germans, whose language is most similar to the speech of the Greeks, began to devote greater attention to Greek literature, we ourselves have also made progress through the observed excellence of those [letters], and we have been recalled especially from the imitation of the Gauls, by which, together with the ancestral culture, love of the fatherland could have been overthrown.

For nothing seems to alienate us more from the piety owed to our fatherland than if we are too devoted to the literature of another nation, not one that once flourished, but one that now thrives, and, disgusted with our own goods, we gaze at foreign things.

Moreover, that I do not mean that all should be as versed in the study of antiquity as those who are especially devoted to it, is sufficiently understood from what I said at the beginning about liberal culture:
Since I rather demand that no educated person be ignorant of what it is shameful to be ignorant of, than that he thoroughly know what it is honorable to know in each field.
Finally, that philosophy completes the liberal education, since it has been believed by many both formerly and certainly among you, there is no need for me to explain at length.

Indeed, what I have just said about ancient literature can be asserted to a large extent with a few words changed, and besides other things no less important, which, excluded by the abundance of the subject, I now omit.
So that no learned person may be ignorant of what it is shameful to be ignorant of, but rather that he may thoroughly know what it is honorable to know in each kind.
Finally, since it has long been believed by very many and certainly is believed among you that philosophy completes the liberal education, I need not explain at length.

Concerning this, indeed, what I have just said about ancient literature can for the most part be proclaimed with a few words changed, and other things besides no less important, which, excluded by the abundance of the subject, I now omit.
I turn to the exercise of the body, that is, to a matter which in this age has been agitated by the fiercest not only contentions but also hatreds.
I, led by no partisan zeal, will speak simply what I feel.

Indeed, I think all will agree on this point, that today no less than among the ancients, bodily strength, agility, swiftness, and finally the flourishing of health must be especially cultivated, because the body itself, both when without these virtues it will perform many things less conveniently, and when it will burden the mind, which even a strong body disturbs with the force of desires arising from it, even more with its weakness, unless someone, which is the case of few men and not altogether commendable, has learned to rule the body so imperiously that he keeps it not so much subdued as exhausted.
Moreover, as I indicated above, physical exercise, in such a harmony of both parts of human nature, also arouses, assists, and strengthens those virtues of the mind that pertain to courage.
Therefore, that certain games should be established, by which the body may be best exercised, seems to me hardly doubtful.
Although it may be asked, which arts those games ought to include.

And first, dancing, which produces only grace of movement, although it should not be rejected, nevertheless has very little of the force that we demand from bodily exercise; but partly it approaches more to musical education, and partly, if one may apply the words of ancient philosophy to this matter, it seems to belong less to gymnastics than to the art of adornment, being an ape of gymnastics.

Then riding and the handling of arms, which I by no means despise, are indeed too military, and they do not so much exercise the body itself as teach the use of the instruments which the body governs.
There remain those exercises which were especially cultivated by the ancients: running, jumping, which was also remarkably pleasing to our ancestors, likewise wrestling and things similar to these.
By these the skill and strength of the limbs are remarkably increased.
Nor are the gymnastic associations to be blamed, by which, when properly directed, youthful grace and modesty are formed together with manly seriousness of character.
These societies, organized in the manner of guilds, were open very widely throughout the ancient states.

Finally, I do not recall having read among the ancients, what even in our times, with the form of all things changed, does not seem to be rightly inferred from the consideration of these arts, that gymnastic games support popular government.

But among them, neglect of the gymnasia seemed not only to corrupt morals, but also to bring about the domination of an uncultivated mob, while a perfect cultivation of both body and mind seemed to hand over the reins of the state to the best citizens.

But I also concede that foreign elements can be mixed into the gymnastic games, which must be kept out, and I do not want all perfected wrestlers and boxers to be liberally educated, nor, if I judge that softness must be expelled, do I recommend the harsh way of life of the Cynics or the contempt of a more refined culture.
The associations established by the ancient states were opened very widely.

Finally, I do not remember reading among the ancients—nor does it seem that even in our own times, when the form of all things has changed, it can rightly be inferred from the principles of these arts—that gymnastic games support popular government.

But among them, the neglect of gymnasia seemed not only to corrupt morals, but also to bring about the domination of an uncultivated mob, while the perfect cultivation of both body and mind seemed to hand over the reins of the state to the best men.

But I also concede that foreign elements can be mixed into gymnastic games, which must be kept out, and I do not want all perfect wrestlers and boxers to be liberally educated, nor, if I judge that softness must be expelled, do I recommend the rough way of life of the Cynics or contempt for a more refined culture.
Now I have finished what I had proposed to say about perfecting man.

And since universities serve this purpose, besides scholastic discipline, except that they embrace not only humanistic learning but also other branches of knowledge, it behooves us to strive with all our might to excite and confirm in the young men committed to our care the love of liberal culture.

By doing this, we will best comply with the counsels of the wisest king, who, it is certain, aims at nothing other than the humanity, virtue, and happiness of his citizens, and wishes to command not slaves but free men.
And that he may forever retain this goodwill with his accustomed constancy, we pray with pious mind to God, the ruler of human souls:

To these we add the greatest prayers, that the supreme deity may direct the counselors of the Prince and all the magistrates of this empire to increase the happiness of the people, to equity, justice, and to bringing aid to the oppressed; may preserve harmony in the commonwealth composed of various orders and nations, and tranquility in troubled affairs; may settle disturbances and avert evil counsels:
Finally, that he may protect the safety of the Prince and of the whole Augustan house as long as possible.

div.head: VIII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXX. habita.

p.s: In the solemn birthday celebrations of Frederick William, being appointed as orator every year, listeners, I do not think that this task alone is imposed on me, that I should perpetually and deliberately celebrate the praises of the most beloved King, which I see are less placed in the flattery and proclamation of contemporaries than in the memory of deeds propagated to posterity and in the judgment and estimation of the wise after several ages;

But the sum of this most delightful business seems to me to be this, that it should be declared by a public document that we too are notably imbued with the public joy with which the whole Prussian empire resounds today.

Although this ought to be believed even without this testimony of our senses, since it is rightly considered impious not to venerate the founder, especially that founder who established this school of letters in the very seat of the kingdom and, as it were, in the royal abode, so that the arts might be closer to him;

Nevertheless, to make this clear, both the duty of gratitude demands it and the custom handed down from antiquity, which it is the less proper to omit, the more the ancient customs in literary universities are already gradually becoming obsolete.

But at the same time, since I must perform the office of an orator, I think that nothing should be avoided more than the appearance of a declaimer, who does not direct his speech to some definite end and to the reason of things, but for the sake of tickling ears composes words and in an argument either fictitious or foreign displays eloquence for the sake of speaking:
For I judge that this is unworthy both of your character and of the solemnity of this day:

Indeed, since it is especially the orator's role to give counsel and to explain what is right, excellent, and useful, we must approach the state of affairs that now exist and choose something in which, if we cannot instruct you, most excellent and distinguished men, who understand such matters much better than I, at least we may remind you of one or two things about the condition of our affairs.

Therefore on this day, which is sacred to the name of our founder, at this time, in this crisis of the literary states, when not only are very different opinions of men of various kinds put forward about their character, but also the supreme council of the princes of Germany has zealously turned its mind to the improvement and more careful governance of the universities, and has set over each one its own procurators, who were to observe both teachers and learners, and above all to take care that nothing should take root in them that would be contrary to the purpose and spirit of these schools, as it ought to be:
It seems especially fitting to explain modestly what, in my opinion, is the power of universities, and what the end of teaching in them is.
From my opinion, I say:
Yet since I have learned by long experience and intimacy that it is also yours, dearest colleagues, if I have set it forth, I will perhaps have done something not unpleasant to you.

Moreover, that the judgment of the king, who is most wise, and of those ministers and counselors who have been placed over us, is not unlike, is gathered by a sure path from this, that they especially chose and summoned you, to whom the education of youth should be entrusted.

Let the most diverse opinions be brought forward, but also the supreme council of the princes of Germany has diligently turned its mind to the improvement and more careful governance of universities, and has placed over each its own procurators, who should observe both teachers and students, and especially take care that nothing should take root in them that would be contrary to the plan and character of these schools, as it ought to be:
It seems especially fitting to set forth plainly what, in my opinion, is the power of universities, and what the end of teaching in them is.
From my opinion, I say:
Yet since I have learned by long experience and intimacy that yours is the same, dearest colleagues, if I have set it forth, perhaps I shall have done something not unpleasant to you.

Moreover, it is gathered by a sure path that the judgment of the wisest king and of those ministers and counselors who have been placed over us is not dissimilar, because they especially chose and summoned you, to whom the education of youth would be entrusted.

Sed materiam amplissimam, ex qua, quod nihil ad nos magis pertinet, capita quaedam iam olim decerpsi, quum integram ac pro argumenti et dignitate et ubertate tractare in his temporis mihi concessi angustiis nequeam, omissis ceteris locis in hoc uno nunc consistam, de quo minime omnibus constare videtur, utrum quod nonnulli contendunt, universitates litterariae eo consilio conditae condendaeve sint, ut futuri rei publicae magistratus et ministri formentur, atque universa doctoris academici disciplina huic sit fini accommodanda, an illae non ad hunc civitatis usum, sed liberaliore aliqua ratione ad propagandam litterarum doctrinam factae et institutae sint:
I do not wonder that there is the greatest doubt about this at the present time, since in our age the most serious matters are partly consigned to oblivion and partly called into question;
since even about the condition and power of the state itself, within whose boundaries we are all contained, there is no agreement;

Finally, since only those seem able to understand what the power and nature of universities ought to be, who have been not moderately versed in letters and have learned from the memory of earlier times what sort these schools have been from the beginning.

Indeed, for me, whether I look at the origins of the academies or the present state of learning, it is clear that their purpose is none other than that in them young students, with skilled teachers as guides, should thoroughly learn the very doctrine of letters:

But if by this means it is at the same time brought about that skilled ministers are provided for the states, this both increases the usefulness of those schools and brings a notable advantage to the state; nevertheless, this is not to be regarded as the highest and primary end of academic instruction.
It increases the usefulness of the schools and brings a notable advantage to the state; nevertheless, this is not to be regarded as the highest and primary end of academic instruction.

For first, if we may go back to the most remote times and consider what among the ancients, the wisest teachers of all human culture, was in some degree similar to the institution of universities, we find that the schools of the philosophers in Greece were not altogether unlike.
This they understood who wished that literary universities and the lower gymnasia of scholastic youth should be called by names derived from those, academies and lyceums.
To the philosophers, who embraced the nature of things and the precepts of morals, there were added the rhetoricians, who taught the ability of speaking eloquently on any subject;
There were added the grammarians, who together with the philosophers and rhetoricians handed on the circle of liberal learning:
Soon, with many teachers of the arts established in one city, they provided the young men with the opportunity of acquiring varied learning;

And indeed at Athens, Alexandria, Apollonia, and in several other cities, so many men gradually flocked together for the sake of study that those places seem not badly comparable to literary universities.

Although, moreover, the pursuit of wisdom and eloquence made men fit for conducting public affairs, and the sophists, professing either both or one of the two disciplines, promised that they would bring about this very thing, that their pupils would be equal to public business;

tamen tantum abest, ut in hoc studiorum fuerit summa posita, ut etiam multi discipulos a re publica, qualis tum fuit, attingenda revocaverint, et ii potissimum, qui studia lucri vel vanae gloriolae causa tractarent, sophistae usum rei publicae praetexuerint, denique civitates ipsae nihil ad sese illas litteras pertinere arbitratae sint, nisi quod eruditionis splendore captae philosophos, rhetores, grammaticos reveritae sunt summisque honoribus dignos ut plurimum habuerunt, et longe rarius doctrinae lumina reformidantes, sapientes doctosque viros calumniis circumventos exsilio vel morte affecerunt, aut labante rei publicae flore, quod Athenis auctore Sophocle evenit, libertatem docendi sustulerunt.

Then, not to speak of the not very good times of the Roman Empire, even before the revival of letters in the West, universities were founded at that age in which that order of civil ministers, which now flourishes, was not yet established;
so that from the beginning it may easily appear that academies did not serve for forming those;

Since knowledge of Roman law, which shone forth at the University of Bologna, was not at all necessary for the magistrates of the republic, although the doctors of law were both frequently consulted and possessed the highest authority;
Nor were those who practiced medicine ministers of the state, in which class they are not counted even now, but just like other artisans they practiced a private art;

And to say nothing of the philosophers and teachers of the arts, the theologians and priests of the church would obey the command, which in those times, exempt from civil power, constituted a distinct and peculiar state throughout all Christian lands.

And so, when the literary universities, with this class of civil servants widely spread, which existed in the immediately preceding centuries, are found to be far earlier, if you consider the origins of things, in which the right principle of each institution is wont to shine most clearly, because it is as it were overshadowed by no additions;
you will understand that they err who judge that the highest and primitive end of academic discipline is placed in educating public servants:
This is no more true than if someone should say that schools were established with that intention.
When Charlemagne was laying the foundations of these schools in his kingdom, who would have thought that he was thinking of equipping the state with skilled ministers?

Indeed, it is well known that in earlier centuries schools and universities were not attributed to that civic advantage, which is by no means to be despised, but, like temples and monasteries, to the piety of a single prince or of states, and to their love of literature, which they wished to be spread more widely.
and they were frequently consulted and held the highest authority;

And those who practiced medicine were not to be ministers of the state, in which class they are not even now counted, but just like other craftsmen they would practice their art as a private occupation.

And to say nothing of philosophers and teachers of the arts, theologians and priests of the church were subject to the empire, which in those times, exempt from civil power, constituted a distinct and peculiar state throughout all Christian lands.

And so, when literary universities are found to be far earlier than this widely extending class of civil servants, which existed in the immediately preceding centuries, if you consider the origins of things, in which the correct principle of each institution is wont to shine forth most clearly, because it is as it were overshadowed by no additions;
you will understand that they err who judge that the highest and original end of academic discipline is placed in educating public servants:
This is no more true than if someone should say that schools were established with that intention.
When Charlemagne was laying the foundations of these schools in his kingdom, who would have thought that he was thinking about equipping the state with skilled ministers?

Indeed, it is well known that in earlier centuries both schools and universities were not attributed to that civil advantage, which is by no means to be despised, but, like temples and monasteries, to the piety of a single prince or of states, and to their love of literature, which they wished to be disseminated more widely.

Moreover, if literary universities had been founded for the education of public ministers, that institution, which survives from ancient times along with a few others, and which is even now regarded as peculiar to universities alone—I mean academic honors—would certainly have had to be regulated by far different laws;

For then those who seemed fit to discharge the civic duty would have to be appointed as teachers and instructors, not those who had been so approved in some branch of learning that they could cultivate, advance, and profess it:

Since even those who have been engaged in public affairs with the highest praise and skill cannot in any way seek academic honors unless they have acquired a more distinguished knowledge of letters, and on the other hand those who, although unequal to public business, excel in learning are judged uniquely worthy of obtaining those honors, it is clear that the essence of academic discipline is to be placed in the pursuit of arts and sciences, not in shaping men for conducting business.

Nor if the leading men and the state have advanced and honored the teachers and masters created in the academies with certain prerogatives, and have even made them splendid with a certain nobility of old, did they do this because they saw that their servants were being trained in the universities;

But because they thought that those who had been cultivated in these schools up to this degree of perfection, so that they had attained academic honor, were equipped with such great learning that a certain remarkable authority of theirs ought to exist among all men and in the state itself.

And indeed that so great a benefit, formerly conferred upon the academies, has gradually been so diminished that, except for empty words, almost no trace of its former dignity remains, is truly the more to be lamented, because not those who broke the force of such great privileges are to be accused, but those who, partly by treating a matter once regarded as most serious lightly and negligently, partly led by desire for gain, have raised ignorant and uncultivated men to academic honors.

Finally, where literary universities have most retained their ancient character, it is most clearly seen in Britain that the purpose of those colleges is not to produce skill in public service, but to be confined to the teaching of the liberal arts and to the formation of teachers of religion.

I do not say this in order to prefer the old universities to the new ones, or the English universities, which are perhaps too tenacious of the old system, to the German ones, which are rightly considered much more perfect, but in order that it may be understood from this very argument what the origin of universities was:
Moreover, although I am not unaware that not all have been established according to the same standard, I know nevertheless that none has been founded except for the sake of spreading literature.
they seemed to have been established;

But because they thought that those who had been cultivated in these schools up to this degree of perfection, so that they had attained academic honor, were equipped with such great learning that a certain remarkable authority of theirs ought to exist among all men and in the state itself.

And that great benefit, indeed, formerly conferred upon the academies, has gradually been so diminished that, except for empty names, scarcely any trace of their former dignity remains; and this is certainly the more to be lamented, because not those who broke the force of such great privileges are to be accused, but those who, partly by treating a matter once regarded as most serious lightly and negligently, and partly led by desire for gain, have raised ignorant and uncultivated men to academic honors.

Finally, where literary universities have most retained their ancient character, it is most clearly seen in Britain that the purpose of those colleges is not to produce skill in public service, but to be contained in the teaching of the liberal arts and in the formation of teachers of religion.

I do not say this in order to prefer the old universities to the new ones, or the English universities, which are perhaps too tenacious of the old system, to the German ones, which are rightly considered much more perfect, but in order that it may be understood from this argument too what the origin of the universities was:
Moreover, although I am not unaware that not all were established according to the same standard, I know nevertheless that none was founded except for the purpose of spreading learning.

Now, since the limits of this speech exclude a more careful treatment of this matter, which would be strengthened by more accurate arguments to be drawn from the storehouse of history, I turn to the present state of letters and the condition of public education, in order that I may briefly set forth what place, in my judgment, universities occupy among the other institutions of this kind.

For, with the light of letters and religion having gradually spread to men of all ranks, especially since the reformation and restoration of the church in Germany, various schools and colleges of learned men have arisen down to our own days, which seem to me to be best divided into five classes.

The first kind includes the schools that are called popular, in which the infantile and childish age is imbued with the first elements of letters, which are most necessary for every person for the use of life, and likewise with the precepts of the Christian faith and of morals, and with certain very small particles plucked from the circle of learning, such as it is fitting that no one should be ignorant of and that even tender or uncultivated minds can grasp, and is nourished, as it were, with the milk of common notions:
For if schools had not been established in almost every village, there would hardly be any way to distinguish a human being from a beast.
Therefore the zeal of our age and of our state is all the more to be praised, because it is directed toward founding and improving those schools.
Nor indeed do I judge those schools, which some have called civic, to be very different from these.
except that they ought to include somewhat more subjects, and among them certain arts useful for the practice of trades.
if they were not, there would hardly be a way to distinguish man from beast.
Therefore the zeal of our age and of our state is all the more to be praised, because it is directed to founding and improving those games.
Nor indeed do I judge those games, which some have called civic, to be very different from these.
except that they ought to include somewhat more subjects, and among them certain arts useful for handling crafts.
The other kind is that of the so-called learned schools, gymnasiums, and lyceums;

In these [studies] both those are cultivated, whom parents have wished to pass over to the business of common life, but to be distinguished from the rude multitude by a certain more elegant culture, and especially those who desire to devote themselves to letters and doctrines with diligence, and among these also those who, because they were born in a higher place, or for the sake of seeking a livelihood, have conceived with immature counsel, not suited to that age, [the intention] to approach public affairs and to perform civil duties:
In these schools, by the agreement of the wise, the whole course of instruction ought to be directed toward liberal learning, by which minds are made fit for undertaking higher studies.

In the third place come the universities, which, because of the immense abundance of subjects, are divided into four parts; and these are now so constituted that students can pursue the course of learning begun in the gymnasia, and whatever art they have chosen, in it they can, by the instruction of their teachers, arrive at a certain degree of perfection.

For those studies, which are pursued in universities, although they are especially suited for training the ministers of the state, yet are found by the very presidents of the republics to be so equipped, that you may understand that the purpose of the institution is not even now placed in that matter, but in the transmission of universal learning:

Whence also teachers have been given to those arts which, being very far removed from common use, are wholly engaged in the knowledge of hidden and abstruse things, and the explanation of no doctrine has been confined within very narrow limits of public utility.

Therefore, the universities are separated from the lower gymnasia by no distinction, except that they both teach a higher science and embrace a wider circle of doctrines, with those arts added which young men not yet strengthened, who are educated in those schools, cannot rightly perceive;
In this class are counted not only the deeper knowledge of divine things, of law, and of medicine, but also the various parts of philosophy:

All these things must be learned in universities in such a way that not only those things which pertain to the skill of public service are picked out, but whatever in each discipline is true or false, whatever is useful or harmful to the human race, whatever history and right reason teach, and finally whatever opinions, precepts, and doctrines you can hammer out with the strength and effort of your mind, should be set forth according to the capacity of the students, even if those things cannot be adapted to the conduct of public affairs in the condition of things that prevails.
Although I would not readily concede that any discipline is so useless that some benefit could not at some time flow from it even into the state and common life.

And so these schools, to which the name of universities was once given because they were regarded as bodies of teachers and learners endowed with certain rights and privileges, just as the guilds of artisans were, now deserve that designation even for this reason, that they embrace the whole field of learning with a very wide compass, and one bounded by no other limits than those of what is honorable, upright, and true:
Whence in some princely edicts already in earlier centuries they are called General Studies.
But if the nature of universities were different, the highest rank would be missed in the most wisely arranged order of public instruction;

If anyone should try to claim that place for the learned societies, which are also called by the common name of academies along with universities, he will certainly not have me as an assenting supporter.

Let it be set forth according to the capacity of the pupils what is useful, what is harmful, what history and right reason teach, and finally whatever of opinions, precepts, and doctrines you can hammer out by the strength and exertion of your intellect, even if those things cannot be adapted to the conduct of public affairs in the condition of things that prevails.
Although I would not readily concede that any discipline is so useless that some benefit from it could not at some time also flow into the state and common life.

And so these schools, to which the name of universities was once given because they were regarded as bodies of teachers and learners endowed with certain rights and privileges, just as the guilds of artisans were, now deserve that designation even for this reason, that they embrace the whole field of learning with a very wide compass, and one not circumscribed by any limits except those of what is honorable, upright, and true:
Whence in some edicts of princes in earlier centuries they are called general studies.
But if the nature of universities were different, in the order of public instruction, most wisely arranged, the highest grade would be lacking;

If anyone should contend that learned societies, which are also called by the common name of academies along with universities, should occupy that place, he will certainly not have me as an assenting supporter.

For these, being most closely connected to universities by the liberality of their studies, constitute in the fourth place a particular community of learned men, differing from the character of universities to the extent that it is not the role of those associations to teach less experienced youths;

But colleagues should share with colleagues whatever each has discovered, when they are equal or nearly equal in learning and talent, and each should help the other with his own understanding and in turn be helped, and all together, with united strength, ought to accomplish in literature those things which cannot be completed by individual scholars, either because many see more, or because a greater apparatus is needed than the industry and resources of one man can provide.

especially where most of the members have been granted that leisure, that, freed from other occupations and cares, or at least burdened with not so many, they may be able to devote either all their time or the greatest part to the advancement of letters.

Finally, in the most recent times especially, a fifth institution of the discipline has been added, which has been devoted either wholly or to a great extent to the exercises that are usually called practical, and this is varied according to the nature of the art and of the students and according to the end toward which it tends:

Since some institutions of this kind are intended for ecclesiastical orators and ministers of the divine word, others for teachers of schools, whether elementary or higher, others for future judges, others for physicians or surgeons, especially military ones, others for agriculture, forestry, veterinary science, and other affairs of this sort.
But these things are partly such that they seem necessary for completing higher studies;
This is the point to which a great part of medical, theological, and philological exercise pertains, and to which a place has rightly been given in the universities themselves:

In part, in those schools, the empiricists are trained not for liberal and profound science and genuine erudition, but for a certain skill to be exercised as if from commands and from experience acquired by use, but for the most part destitute of reasons;
This method of instruction is inferior to academic schools:

Partly by the institutions which I have mentioned, young men, after completing their studies at the university in due course, are trained for the proper conduct of business and the discharge of duties;
To this end, to use examples drawn from our own state, candidates are trained in the courts and in the boards placed over the administration of the provinces in a most useful manner;
To this end among us seminaries for schoolmasters have been established, and at Wittenberg the most wise King recently founded with notable piety a seminary for clergymen.

Although these things have been explained briefly, I think it is evident even without my pointing it out, that in this fifth class of institutions alone, and not in the whole of it, but in only one or another of those forms which I have described, the public ministers of the state are deliberately trained.

And that these things have been established by me not arbitrarily, but according to the truth of the matter, you may also understand from this, that for the benefit of the universities and other schools all are admitted who wish to apply their mind to letters, but to those parts of exercises which I mentioned last, access is open almost only to those who have declared that they seek public offices.
They may be intended for agriculture, forestry, veterinary medicine, and other occupations of this kind.
But these things are partly such that they seem necessary for completing higher studies;
to which a large part of medical, theological, and philological exercise belongs, to which in the universities themselves a place has rightly been given:

In some of those schools, the empiricists are trained not for liberal and profound science and genuine learning, but for a certain skill to be exercised according to precepts as if commanded and experience acquired by use, but for the most part destitute of reason.
This method of instruction is inferior to academic schools.

Partly by those institutions which I have mentioned, young men, after completing their studies at the university in due form, are trained for the proper handling of business and the discharge of duties.
To this end, to use examples drawn from our own state, candidates are trained in the courts and in the colleges of those set over the administration of provinces, in a most useful manner;
To this end, among us seminaries of scholarly teachers have been established, and at Wittenberg the most wise king recently founded a seminary for churchmen with remarkable piety.

Although these things have been explained briefly, even without my pointing it out, I think it is clear that in this fifth class of institutions alone, and not in the whole of it, but in only one or another of those forms which I have described, the public ministers of the state are deliberately trained.

And that these things have been established by me not arbitrarily, but according to the truth of the matter, you may also understand from this, that for the benefit of the universities and other schools all are admitted who wish to apply their mind to letters, but to those parts of the exercises which I mentioned last, access is open almost only to those who have declared that they are seeking public offices.

Indeed, who among you, listeners, would not rejoice that a more correct opinion concerning the system of universities is so firmly implanted in the most wise King and his counselors, that all the academies of the Prussian state are exclusively adapted to that form which we demand?

Nam ne nunc a nostris rebus discedam, quis non intelligat magnificos hos apparatus et cuiusvis generis doctrinarum subsidia amplissima et splendidissima, quae non modo huic universitati litterariae, sed ipsi regiae urbi ornamento sunt, et quae Regis benignissimi munificentia et viri illius excellentissimi, qui institutioni publicae in hoc imperio praeest, prudenti et liberali cura magis in dies augentur, haec inquam non alio consilio comparata esse, nisi ut rerum optimarum disciplina non sordida aliqua de causa, sed ob insitam praestantiam pertractetur
latiusque et altius excolatur?
Who does not see that the same institutions have been observed and are still observed in the selection of the teachers themselves, whether one considers their talents and learning or their number?

For as soon as that opinion, against which we have been arguing, was given a place, because it seemed that the necessities of the state could be satisfied with small resources, and the greatest part both of those things and of these men was scattered as if superfluous, and, with the common bond of learning dissolved, which certainly is least needed for forming only the servants of the state, separate schools of some disciplines were established in place of the universities:
Therefore, in the present state of literature, since the individual disciplines have already been too much separated, nothing would be more pernicious.

Then not only the students, many of whom even now, when another end of academic instruction is held, hastening to public offices, to the great detriment of both literature and the republic itself, are estranged from accurate learning and liberal studies, would also be content with a more slender and meager knowledge of things;

But also to the doctrines themselves, if the universities were to be reshaped into another form, the ultimate harm would be done, since besides the learned societies, whose effectiveness cannot, given the circumstances, be as great as that of universities among all people, no seat would be left for the higher sciences.

Nor would men distinguished by learning, but skilled pragmatics, who now, unless endowed with exceptional talent and learning, are considered insufficiently suited for this matter, be about to occupy the chairs.
Finally, with the freedom of teaching removed, not what is right and true would have to be handed over to learners, but what was acceptable and approved by the powerful, the rulers of states.
What can be found more unworthy than this for learned men?
And should it be cultivated more widely and more deeply?
Who does not see that in the very selection of teachers, whether one considers their talents and learning or their number, the same institutions have been preserved and are still preserved?

For as soon as that opinion, against which we have been arguing, was given a place, because it seemed that the needs of the state could be satisfied with small resources, and by far the greatest part both of those things and of these men was scattered as superfluous, and with the common bond of learning dissolved, which certainly is least needed for forming only the servants of the state, separate schools of some disciplines were established in place of the universities:
Therefore, in the present state of literature, since the individual disciplines have already been too much separated, nothing would be more pernicious.

Then not only the students, many of whom even now, when another end of academic instruction is held, hastening to public offices, to the great detriment of both literature and the republic itself, are estranged from accurate learning and liberal studies, would also be content with a more slender and meager knowledge of things;

But also to the doctrines themselves, if the universities were to be reduced to another form, the greatest harm would be done, since besides the learned societies, whose effectiveness cannot be as great as that of universities among all people, no seat would be left for the more sublime science:

Nor would men distinguished by learning, but rather skilled practical men, who now, unless they are endowed with exceptional talent and learning, are considered insufficiently suited for this task, be about to occupy the chairs.
Finally, with the freedom of teaching removed, not what is right and true would have to be handed over to learners, but what was acceptable and approved by the powerful, the rulers of states.
What can be found more unworthy than this for learned men?
But indeed there is another reason why every most civilized state, and especially ours, supports the study of literature in universities and spends no small sums on it;
for it is exactly the same reason that brings it about that the church is supported by public expenditures.

For since it is understood that not only is the human race, not illuminated by the light of religion, utterly ruined, but that the sense of the divine is so implanted in human minds that not even any barbarians, unless utterly brutish, lack it:

The state takes care that the natural disposition of the human mind is cultivated and nourished; it is the state's role to provide the opportunity for developing and advancing the highest talents and goods of mortals, not to tolerate or foster them only insofar as they seem useful to rulers for governing their subjects.

And since the system of letters is equal, the state also founded its own temples for them, lest, being entrusted to the judgment of private individuals, they should be neglected by chance or human carelessness.
Among these, universities hold almost the foremost place.
And it has been well done that these schools have been scattered especially in Germany through all provinces, so that scarcely any is bereft of literary renown;

but the most wise King has done excellently in adorning the principal cities of the realm with universities, where, to say nothing of other advantages, literature may conveniently exert the most powerful influence upon men of various ranks.
Nor should expenses be anxiously calculated according to the number of students who are to be educated.
This is what a certain person recently dared to do, in the manner of money-changers or bankers rather than of learned men.
For these literary colleges were not granted revenues so that the fee for instruction might be paid publicly to the teachers, but so that the flower and honor of studies might be firmly established.

Finally, when the state saw that those whose minds had been properly refined by education were governing the city most wisely, and that neither those who had been cultivated by private industry nor those who had been trained in other schools were equipped with such great skill in letters as the students of universities are accustomed to have;

It gradually prevailed, so that almost no one was entrusted with a magistracy or any more serious public office, unless he had devoted himself for several years to studies at universities, and those who wished to prepare themselves for civil affairs embraced exclusively the discipline of universities:
Hence some, deceived by the empty appearance of things, think that universities were founded for the purpose of forming public officials.
Moreover, that honorable judgment concerning the discipline of universities was beneficial both to the state and to literature:
For the republic, because nothing can be more useful to it than the light of arts and sciences, which, like the life-giving and guiding soul, pervades all the members of the state;

For literature, because those who have thoroughly learned its power through good education, when they have been placed in charge of the highest affairs, support the pursuits of the arts with greater kindness and generosity:
When the governors of states, either unskilled in literature or imbued only with the first rudiments, especially if, as usually happens, arrogance has been added, despise learning or hold it suspect.
If they were neglected by the judgment of private individuals, by chance or by the carelessness of men, the state founded its own temples:
Among these, the universities hold nearly the foremost place.
And it is well done, that these schools in Germany especially are so spread through all provinces, that scarcely any is deprived of literary fame;

but the most wise king has done well, that he adorned the chief cities of the kingdom with universities, where, that I may pass over other advantages, literature may conveniently exercise the most weighty influence upon men of various ranks.
Nor are the expenses to be anxiously compared with the number of pupils who are to be educated:
This is what a certain person recently dared to do, more in the manner of money-changers or bankers than of learned men.

For revenues were not granted to these literary associations so that the wages of teaching might be paid publicly to the teachers, but so that the flower and honor of studies might be firmly established.

Finally, when the state saw that those whose minds had been properly refined by education were governing the city most wisely, and that neither those who had been trained by private industry nor those who had been cultivated in other schools were equipped with such great skill in letters as the alumni of universities are accustomed to have;

It gradually gained strength, so that almost no one was entrusted with a magistracy or any more serious public office unless he had devoted several years to studies at universities, and those who wished to prepare themselves for civil affairs embraced exclusively the discipline of universities:
Hence some, deceived by the empty appearance of things, think that universities were founded for the purpose of forming public officials.
Moreover, that honorable judgment concerning the discipline of universities was beneficial both to the state and to literature:
For the republic, because nothing can be more useful to it than the light of arts and sciences, which, like the life-giving and guiding soul, pervades all the members of the state;

For literature, because those who have thoroughly learned its power from a good education, when they have been placed at the head of affairs, support the pursuits of the arts with greater kindness and generosity:

Since the governors of states, whether unskilled in literature or only imbued with its first rudiments, especially if, as usually happens, arrogance has been added, despise learning or hold it suspect.

And from this it is at the same time understood, how much the states must beware, lest the universities suffer any loss, or their dignity be harmed by unworthy words or deeds, or be corrupted by internal vices;
Since it is reasonable that such things should arise from time to time among such a great multitude of young men, care must be taken that they do not grow.
But a skillful hand must be applied, lest the wounds become ulcerated.

And wise physicians will treat the present evils in such a way that neither the old ones, which the opportunity of the times, although inveterate, has almost removed by divine rather than human counsel, return with greater force, nor new and deadly ones arise.
Which indeed we need not fear at all.
Trusting in the kindness of a most merciful king, we sail in the harbor;
And God, who brings forth the best from the worst beyond expectation, will calm the present disturbances.
We, colleagues, seem to ourselves to know what our duty is;
I urge you, fellow soldiers, never to forget what the end of academic discipline is, which I have shown to be placed in the cultivation of the good arts with the greatest assiduity and diligence;
Therefore, turn your minds to those things, and eagerly seize these immortal blessings, which the kindness of the most wise King offers to you.
Our affairs this year, if not cut down, have certainly been diminished by certain accidental losses:
Death has carried off two most distinguished teachers, most dear to us, and them placed in the flower of age:
But no republic applies a more prudent and more fortunate care to repairing the losses of literature than ours under the auspices of Frederick William.
May God, the Best and Greatest, preserve this king, adorned with the virtues of peace and war, for us and for the whole state, to extreme old age;
may He preserve the royal Augustan house, supported by so many most upright and most brave young men.
These are not our prayers, but the prayers of all citizens;
they are perpetual, not of today;
but on this day they are so much more sacred, as this day is considered more sacred.
I have spoken.

so that neither the old troubles, which although long-standing the opportunity of the times has almost removed by divine rather than human counsel, may return with greater force, nor new and deadly ones arise.
But this is by no means to be feared by us.
Trusting in the kindness of the most merciful king, we sail in the harbor;
and God, who brings forth the best from the worst beyond expectation, will settle the present disturbances.
We, colleagues, seem to ourselves to know what is our duty;
I urge you, fellow soldiers, never to forget what the goal of academic discipline is, which I have shown to be placed in the zealous and diligent pursuit of the liberal arts;
Therefore apply your mind to those things, and eagerly seize these immortal goods, which the kindness of the most wise King offers to you.
Our affairs this year, if not ruined, have certainly been diminished by certain accidental losses:
Death has carried off two most distinguished teachers, most dear to us, and both in the flower of their age.
But no state applies a more prudent and more fortunate care to repairing the losses of literature than ours, under the auspices of Frederick William.
May God, the Best and Greatest, preserve this king, adorned with the virtues of peace and war, for us and for the whole state to the utmost old age;
may he preserve the royal August house, supported by so many most upright and most brave young men.
These are not our prayers, but the prayers of all citizens;
they are perpetual, not of today;
but on this day they are so much more sacred, as this day is considered more sacred.
I have spoken.

div.head: IX. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXI. habita.

p.s: It seems to me a great task, even after frequent practice, to speak on the King, the delight of the people, on that day on which the whole city rejoices that he was given to it by divine providence, that is, on that day on which, since it is difficult to equal the feelings of the mind with words, however much you may say, you will think that not only the listeners but even yourself have not been satisfied.

I judge it to be a greater matter when, although a rich subject matter is set before the orator, a limit of speaking must be sought and care must be taken, lest you speak in such a way that the speech seems to be less fitting to the king's own singular modesty.
For we are not unaware that he wishes not so much to be praised as to do praiseworthy deeds.

It is a very great thing to speak about him before those whom, if anything either somewhat unrefined or less appropriately or rather coarsely has slipped out, you know to be sharply stung and rebuked.
But again, in those matters in which the greatest difficulty is placed, in the same I see consolation and remedy to be present.
For first, because I speak in the presence of those who have come with minds most ready and exceptionally well-disposed to revere the King;

If I have not set forth the virtues of Frederick William according to their abundance, but have run through them as if doing something else, whatever I have touched upon lightly will be taken by you in a greater sense and will grow in your minds, which cherish them.
so that a tiny spark, as it were, thrown into your breasts, may kindle a most ardent flame of love and admiration;
then, by the King's well-known modesty, I shall escape the appearance of an importunate panegyrist;

Finally, among the learned or those eager for learning, it is permissible, from the memory of earlier events, to mix in such things which, even if they seem not to pertain to this matter, they should not reject as foreign, but with which they may even delight themselves, while they consider and compare how, at various times and in different states of affairs, distinguished men have deserved well of the human race.

For this brings almost the greatest pleasure to thoughtful men, not if someone tells them things in which nothing is left to their own intelligence, but if you have set before them ample material for inquiry, which they can survey, weigh, and judge, from which they may draw richer thoughts, opinions, and feelings than those contained in the speaker's words.
Therefore today I have decided to return to more remote times and to say a few words about a man once most great, whose merits and fame, although he was not a king, scarcely any king has equaled:
I shall bring forward Pericles, the founder of arts and letters, so fortunate that no age has produced his equal;
but from the deeds of so great a man I shall especially select those things which seem to me suited to the solemnity of this day.
They are contained in the speaker's words, and they draw out his thoughts, opinions, and feelings.
Therefore today I have decided to return to more remote times and to say a few things about a man once most great, whose merits and fame, although he was not a king, scarcely any king has equaled:
I shall bring forward Pericles, the founder of arts and letters, so fortunate that no age has produced his equal;
But from the deeds of so great a man I will especially select those which seem to me to be suited to the solemnity of this day.

Therefore, concerning Pericles, so that, before I come to those matters for the sake of which I have decided to speak about him, I may first say a few things, it is agreed that he did not suddenly creep into the commonwealth as a new man, but that he was born of most noble parents, who had held no small part in the state.
For he had as his father Xanthippus, under whose command as general the Greeks had defeated the Persian fleet at Mycale;
he had as his mother Agariste, an Alcmaeonid, from that family which traced its origin back to Nestor, son of Neleus, and was closely related to the ancient royal line at Athens:
his maternal grandmother was the daughter of Clisthenes, tyrant of the Sicyonians:
his mother's uncle was Clisthenes, son of Megacles, the Athenian lawgiver, under whose leadership especially the state had shaken off the rule of the Pisistratids.
But Pericles, emulating his great parents, proved himself even greater than they.

After the aristocratic party had been defeated and he had won the favor of the people, when he saw that the liberty and power of the Athenians could not be supported except by naval forces, following in the footsteps of Themistocles, who had attributed much to the sea, he partly preserved and partly acquired so many and such great allies and revenues of his country that no state was stronger than Athens, and that Athens herself was the wealthiest of all.

But when he accomplished this, if he seems to have admitted many things that cannot be approved, one must consider that the state of affairs was such that he had to do many harsher things not of his own accord, but unwillingly, because nearly perpetual discords troubled both all Greece and individual states, and the power of the Lacedaemonians, who were especially hostile to the Athenians, had to be restrained, since they, though as desirous of supremacy as the Athenians, were nevertheless unequal to maintaining the same.
But even in those matters which you might justly criticize, Pericles did not pursue private advantage, nor did he ever do anything base or contemptible:
Whatever he did, they are evidences of a great mind;
Greater were those things which he attempted but did not complete:

Indeed, it is not obscure that a common league of all the Greeks in Asia and Europe agitated for this, by which, besides the restoration of the temples destroyed by the barbarians and the celebration of the common religious rites, the duration of peace and free and secure navigation would be ensured.
The Lacedaemonians were the greatest obstacle to this league being made.

Nevertheless, the same man, although he omitted nothing that would be magnificent for the fatherland, accurately discerning what could or could not be done according to the state of affairs, preferred to preserve the empire he had acquired with singular moderation rather than to undertake long and dangerous expeditions.

And although others thought that Egypt, which had already been destructive to the Athenians before, Sicily, which after Pericles was ruinous to the Attic forces, Etruria, and Carthage should be attempted, he was unwilling to put the citizens at risk, but sought glory as a war leader especially in this, that he should undertake nothing too difficult or uncertain, and that the soldiers, as he himself said, as far as it lay in his power, could be immortal.

But although he earned a great name among posterity either by the counsels of the wise alone in governing the state and by deeds bravely done, by which he raised the Athenians above all the other peoples of Greece, yet you might doubt whether he wished to acquire such great power for his fatherland that the arts and letters and the whole culture of humanity could be more generously fostered and flourish more joyfully, or whether he strove for these very things more notably, in order to increase the glory and splendor of Athens.
Concerning this I judge thus: that Pericles did not act with the exclusion of the one or the other;

but since he saw that the Attic state could not be the leader unless it excelled in commerce, wealth, army, and fleets, he likewise perceived that, even when strengthened by these very resources, unless the distinction of the arts and the light of literature were added, it would be a rude and unformed mass:
therefore he thought that not one of the two for the sake of the other, but each for its own sake, was to be sought as a good.
The long duration of peace and free and secure navigation were to be celebrated.
The Lacedaemonians were the greatest obstacle to the making of that treaty.

Yet the same man, although he omitted nothing that was magnificent for his country, accurately discerning what could or could not be done according to the state of affairs, preferred to guard with singular moderation the empire he had acquired rather than to undertake long and dangerous expeditions.

And although others thought that Egypt, which had already been destructive to the Athenians before, Sicily, which after Pericles was the ruin of the Attic forces, Etruria, and Carthage should be attacked, he was unwilling to put the citizens at risk, but sought glory as a war leader especially in this, that he would undertake nothing too difficult or uncertain, and that the soldiers, as he himself used to say, could be immortal as far as it depended on him.

But although he earned a great name among posterity either by his counsels alone, which were prudent in governing the state, and by his deeds bravely done, by which he raised the Athenians above all the other peoples of Greece, nevertheless you might doubt whether he wished to acquire for his fatherland so great a power that arts and letters and the whole culture of humanity could be more generously fostered and flourish more joyfully, or whether he strove for these very things more notably, in order to increase the glory and splendor of Athens.
Concerning this I judge thus: that Pericles did not act with the exclusion of the one or the other;

but since he saw that the Attic state could not be the leader unless it excelled in commerce, wealth, army, and fleets, he likewise perceived that, even when strengthened by these very resources, unless the distinction of the arts and the light of literature were added, it would be a rude and unformed mass:
therefore he thought that not one for the sake of the other, but each for its own sake, was to be procured as a good.

For to confine myself now to literature and the arts, Pericles embraced them neither for the sake of display nor for the sake of the cheap conveniences of common life, but because he understood that nothing was more honorable or more glorious than they.

For his talent was formed and polished not only by boyhood education, but also in his adult years by the instruction and intimacy of the most learned men, and equipped with the knowledge of the most important studies.

For first, in that one art by which states were then governed, he so possessed eloquence that it was said that the most powerful thunderbolt of that language was in it, and the imperial voice in the forum was compared to the thunderbolts of Olympian Jove:
Whence he alone reigned in the assemblies, and no one easily resisted his prudence and strength, with which he was powerful in speaking.
But that man nourished a full, weighty, magnificent, sharp, and precise oration with the doctrine of the philosophers, which strengthened the innate greatness of the mind with excellent precepts.
But at that age, when two philosophical schools especially flourished, the Eleatic and the Ionian, he associated familiarly with the leaders of both.
For he heard Zeno of Elea, the disciple and friend of the great Parmenides, when he was staying at Athens, along with other nobles.

His dialectical and abstruse method of philosophizing, although something could even be derived from it for speaking well, yet being chiefly concerned with understanding the nature of things and very far removed from visible objects, can serve as evidence that Pericles did not seek only those things which he could use on the platform, but was led by a liberal and genuine pursuit of wisdom.
Indeed, that age is worthy of the greatest admiration, in which men educated in philosophy commanded great public affairs and armies;

a spectacle worthy of admiration: Pericles, a disciple of Zeno of Elea, fighting with his fleet at Samos against Melissus, son of Ithagenes, who, in nearly the same times as Zeno, having written a book on being and nature, became famous among the leaders of the Eleatic school.

And he was not devoted to this one class of opinions alone, which you would especially praise in a man placed at the head of a state, whom it behooves to know and tolerate various systems of philosophy, not to despise or exclude one in preference to another's pursuit; but Pericles was especially devoted to a wise man of a quite different school, Anaxagoras the natural philosopher, a man of great spirit, who, led by a divine impulse of philosophizing, had left his house and fields, and he admired him remarkably.

Plutarch reports that Protagoras the sophist was a companion of Pericles and that he had long discussions with him, and these about arguments of such a kind that it may seem ridiculous to us, just as it seemed to Pericles' son, to be stuck on them.

This he must be thought to have done either for the sake of exercise and of the mind, or because it was in his interest to investigate more carefully, for some reason that is not of this place, things that to one considering them more lightly are thought to be of no use.
Now indeed, to speak of the artists, it is established by reliable authorities that Damon the musician was a companion of Pericles:

Since he was both most skilled in civil affairs and of such great authority in the state that he was banished from his country by votes of ostracism, and since he practiced music not only with hand and voice, but also embraced the power and force of numbers and modes with philosophical and mathematical reasoning, it is probable that that Pericles had him as an assistant and friend and counselor both in the affairs of the state and in judging poems and music.

But whatever pertained to the construction and adornment of buildings and to sculpture and related arts, in that no one is ignorant that Phidias, an immortal man, who, when two schools of philosophers especially flourished, the Eleatic and the Ionic, enjoyed the friendship of the leaders of both, was preeminent in the majesty of the gods through his statues.

But whatever pertained to building and adorning edifices and to sculpture and related arts, in that no one is unaware that Phidias, an immortal man, who did not attain but enhanced the majesty of the gods with images made by himself, was not only an adviser to Pericles but also a supervisor of the works.
