Thus he, as befits a ruler of a state, measured with his mind nearly the whole circle of arts and letters:
and just as he himself neglected no part of them, so all of them then flowed together to Athens, and there fixed their seat:

Not because the state, with Pericles urging, spent money on maintaining everyone, but because the elegant and splendid administration of the city and the remarkable freedom granted to literature and the honor paid to the good arts invited outstanding talents more than other places, and because the minds of the Athenians were so raised to every best pursuit that among them every most cultivated person wished to be heard, seen, and approved.

Therefore, to begin with poetry, among the epic poets, whose art was then languishing, the one who is thought to have excelled alone, Choerilus of Samos, the most distinguished herald of the Persian wars, he seems to have been especially approved and cultivated at Athens;
Moreover, the genre of lyric poetry, which especially survived at that age, the dithyrambic, was especially practiced in the cyclic choruses of the Athenians.
But no part of poetry was flourishing more joyfully at that time than the scenic, which was formed and perfected almost nowhere except at Athens;

And tragedy indeed, after Aeschylus, Pericles the elder, and, because he was a lover of the old discipline, more alien to him than devoted to him, Sophocles perfected, who, when the play Antigone was produced, was elected colleague of Pericles by the Athenian people in the Samian praetorship;
Euripides succeeded him, and I infer from a certain indication that he too was remarkably devoted to Pericles.
And although enormous sums were spent on lyric and tragic competitions, comedy too was not neglected, although it was hostile to the leading men of the state:

for such was Pericles, who could easily bear the insults and reproaches of the envious and much more of scurrilous and witty men, and did not think that the freedom of jesting should be restricted by plebiscites:
But if the license of old comedy was once checked under this very law, that law did not remain in force for more than four years.

At that time also the writer of history became famous, whom they are accustomed to call the father of history, Herodotus, who is said to have recited his work or part of his work at Athens, and was undoubtedly connected with Pericles, whether he became a citizen of Thurii, a colony founded by him, before or after that time;
Nor would anyone who has read his books more carefully deny that more was written in favor of the Athenians and especially of Pericles.
Thucydides himself, indeed, than whom no age has produced nor will produce a more excellent historian, owes to that age the force of his oratory and his political wisdom.
What shall I say about eloquence?

When Gorgias and other sophists, and among the Athenians Antiphon of Rhamnus, were reducing it to the form of an art, Pericles himself, although he left nothing in writing except decrees, perfected that grand style of speaking, of which Thucydides gives examples, together with his contemporaries.

After them, Lysias, although he was of a later age, would nevertheless, had Pericles not existed, have cultivated the subtle form of oratory at Athens, since his father Cephalus of Syracuse had been persuaded by Pericles to move to Athens.

In philosophy, moreover, besides those schools which I mentioned above, the sophists, tolerated in the Attic state and attracted by the gifts of wealthy men, excited a zeal for discussing all things on opposite sides.

In these discussions, Socrates, eminent, laid the foundations of Attic philosophy with that dialectical and critical method of inquiry and with the most sacred precepts of morals, whose splendor shines most brightly down to our times.

But when in that age too there were those who, subdued by vain superstition, shrank from the light of philosophy as owls do from the sun, or with cunning pretense used religion as a screen for private interests or enmities, Pericles, freed from anxieties of that sort by the physical doctrine of Anaxagoras, protected the philosophers as long as he could;

And after the parties of the adversaries had grown strong, so that they themselves might be especially troublesome, they accused Aspasia and Anaxagoras—who nevertheless, thinking most worthily about divine matters, said that mind adorns and governs all things—of impiety; but by the authority and prudence of Pericles it was brought about that, while he himself was still alive, no one of the philosophers was punished too severely.
Aspasia certainly he rescued from danger by his entreaties, and Anaxagoras, sent away secretly, he rescued from danger.

But afterwards, through the arts of wicked and fanatical men, not only was Protagoras reduced to such a state that he avoided destruction only by flight and his books were publicly burned, but Socrates himself, the most upright of philosophers, was punished as a despiser of the divine and a corrupter of youth.

But the arts surpassed the great flower of literature that then existed, if that is possible.

For after it had been sufficiently provided for the collection of resources and the filling of the treasury, Pericles did not want the Athenian people to lie in wait for wealth like a greedy person, nor that gold and silver should be hidden away in the treasury, but he decided that as much as could be spent without public loss should be expended, so that the city and the shrines of the gods might be magnificently adorned, and that part of the people which would not disdain labor might be supported by an honorable gain:

Moreover, since he saw that the Athenians could not live on their own produce and be, as it were, bound to their fields like the Spartans or Boeotians, but that a state enjoying popular government and maritime power ought to excel in the excellence and renown of its manufactures and in the commerce thereby increased.

Therefore he persuaded the people to undertake such works, by which everlasting glory would accrue to the state, and all arts and all hands would be set in motion, and almost the whole city would at the same time be adorned and nourished from itself.

Those who worked marble, bronze, gold, ivory, cypress, and ebony, craftsmen of every kind, stonecutters, sculptors, goldsmiths, painters, embroiderers, dyers, and finally those who brought material by ships or wagons, were so employed by Pericles' plan that at that time there was the greatest industry of workshops and craftsmanship in Athens.

And what you may especially wonder at, in a very short space of time he completed not one or two buildings, but very many and especially lofty works: the Parthenon, the Eleusinium, the sanctuary of the initiates, the Odeum, the Long Walls, the Propylaea, and others.
not those that would soon fall, but such as could withstand, I will not say the injury of time, but the devastations of savage barbarians.

For those who, after the people had gradually degenerated from the virtue of their ancestors through various misfortunes, reduced it to the most unjust slavery, from which may it now be delivered forever by the magnanimous struggles worthy of the fame of their fathers, could not entirely destroy the monuments of its former splendor;

But just as all the more refined culture throughout Europe originated from the Greeks, so those works are still an example to our artists, and in this very city the remains of the statues preserved in the pediments of the Parthenon, reproduced in images through the kindness of our King, are to be seen.

Now indeed, to pass to the other part of the arts, which is especially concerned with music, under Pericles, in the festivals of the gods, scenic performances and choruses of every kind and solemn processions were celebrated with such great splendor, not indeed rude and barbarous, but magnificent and elegant, so that it may be thought that more expense was spent on these things than on the military expeditions for freedom and supremacy:
Actors, singers, dancers, flute-players, and lyre-players of the highest distinction flourished at Athens.

Although their perfection cannot be perceived today by eyes and ears, nevertheless anyone who is not ignorant of antiquity would deny that those who could please the most cultivated men, who could please Pericles or Sophocles, were not each supreme in their own art.

But perhaps I have lingered too long in contemplating Pericles, my hearers;
nor have I accomplished that which someone might have expected me to accomplish;
I cannot equal such great matters with meager words, nor is it permitted, confined within these limits, to run out into individual points in such a way that one could satisfy by speaking;

Finally, I have not undertaken to delineate the whole image of Pericles, nor to speak about him for his own sake, but I wished to set forth the leader of the state, who had especially aided literature and the arts.
In which I chose him, whom it would not repent to have set forth as a most polished exemplar and complete in all respects;
If you had tried to adorn him with words, you would have achieved this one thing, that he would seem greater by praise.
But if I had spoken about the princes of the Medici family before him, I could rightly be reproached for neglecting the greatest things and aiming at lesser ones;
although I would by no means deny that these are worthy of the highest praise:
but if I had brought forward Louis, king of the French, whom the flattery of his contemporaries wished to be called Great, I would fear that my speech would be despised;
I understand that Octavianus Augustus, who was certainly kind to literature, follows Pericles at a long interval.

With what face should I have brought the Egyptian kings, the Ptolemies, who were most devoted to learning, but for the most part foul in depravity of character or luxury, to this assembly which is now being held?
Yet I readily concede that our times are much more similar to those which I have just mentioned than to the age of Pericles;
And just as those ages, so this age of ours can emulate, but not attain, the age of Pericles.
For the culture of each age arises and is completed by the confluence of many and various causes.

But our age, if any other, is separated by a very long interval from the native simplicity of the Periclean age and from the other virtues by which Greece then excelled, which it would be long to set forth and not suited to this place.
Therefore, whoever today has set before himself to become a Pericles as much as possible, by attempting and by lavishing anything, will not accomplish much.

For no one will bring that state of affairs to pass by his own counsels, which has its foundations laid in the whole nature and character of the people, in the course of earlier times, in the condition of the present, and, to embrace everything in one word, in the fate of the nation divinely predetermined.

Nor, however much one may attribute to Pericles, will anyone deny that Pericles did not provoke all those talents, but fostered them and equipped them with resources, and used them liberally and munificently.
In our age, indeed, it is agreed that the face of all things is entirely different;
the field of letters is wider than of old:
letters themselves are manifold:
of these, some kinds are liberal, others are either turned to the use of life or invented for it:
the use of the arts which they call beautiful extends less widely:
others, indeed, are equally celebrated as in antiquity and, according to the judgment of our men, which is especially held concerning music, more perfect;
Others, in many lands even of more civilized Europe, after splendid beginnings long ago, have become almost obsolete.
Reverence for the divine in minds, ceremonies for the most part without splendid display:

Nor have they learned to separate learning from utility.

Therefore, today, whoever has been placed in charge of the state and has decided to care for the arts and letters, given the present state of affairs, will have to follow institutions far different from those of that Pericles, at least in part.

And certainly Frederick William, a most wise king, does diligently what can be done.

For first, to speak of those arts which are employed in working out statues and images, in engraving and carving, and finally in drawing and painting, their task of assisting, which was once simple, if you set aside the instruction of schools, which I will omit here, is now found to be especially twofold.

For indeed, after the Greeks for the most part, and then also those of the more recent ones who, from the time when letters were restored, especially became famous in painting, taught the correct method by outstanding examples, and different schools of artists arose, from which various things were attempted and accomplished;

Since it has been understood that, by means of examples, which are not found everywhere, both artists are to be instructed and the minds of spectators are to be formed, it is necessary to collect monuments and to set forth the best models, in which the origins, progress, and decline of the arts, and what was excellent and what was to be avoided, might be recognized.

But by collecting fragments of marbles and painted panels, however splendid, the arts are not revived, unless worthy and abundant material is provided for the talents, which are never entirely lacking, in which they may not only test their strength once or twice, but by continuous use and frequent practice may attain perfection.
Frederick William provides both kinds of support especially from that time when the power and dignity of the empire were restored by his most prudent counsels and the valor of his armies.

After he recovered the most precious treasures of elegant works, which had been magnificently furnished by the generous care of his ancestors, from the spoils of the enemy, he increased them at his own expense with new and distinguished additions, and he will increase them.

And since this apparatus, scattered through the royal houses, cannot serve the conveniences that are desired, he ordered a museum to be founded by the arts, which, when it has been completed and adorned, will offer to students no less delight, and to artists utility, than several already leading cities offer.
But Frederick William does not confine himself to this.
For just as the kings of Prussia long ago wished that even workshops and common trades should be brought to a higher perfection, so that we might rival foreigners;

so Frederick William, under whose rule the state has obtained distinguished artists, supplies to architects, sculptors, statuaries, and painters abundant material for undertaking most famous works, which seem able to endure for ages:
the pious king adorns temples, builds monuments, places statues, grateful toward the people, the army, the leaders; the commander [does so].
The prince, indulging in the delights of the city and of the citizens, restored the theater that had been consumed by flames.
Nor should I fear to say those things which the morose may have considered trifling, the scenic and musical arts.

To these, so much the more earnest attention must be paid, because the more, if they are viewed as charming, the minds of the citizens are daily molded by hearing them; if as perverse or less decorous, judgment and morals are corrupted.
For who is there who thinks that anything is detracted from the severity of Pericles because he adorned his fatherland with scenic performances?
Who does not understand that it is fitting for the leader of the people to be involved in pleasures?

Who is unaware that the Athenians were made more refined by nothing so much as by the art of the stage, which was, as it were, their own, and that from all Greek literature nothing has come down to us more serious or more magnificent than the stage plays and the songs written for the musical contests?
Therefore, it is entirely Periclean that a splendor worthy of this kingdom should be established in these things.
The more so because the private manner of life and dress of Frederick William is seen to be simpler.
So that you may see that he aims not at ostentation and pomp but at public dignity.

But having dismissed these matters, in order that I may come to those things which are nearest to us, that we must also come to the aid of literature in a different way than in antiquity, there is no need for me to explain at length.

Since these studies once had almost only security from the state and honorable esteem to be sought, because those who taught them either by writings or by voice were themselves sufficiently equipped with domestic means, or demanded a huge fee from their students, it has long been the case that they need the care of princes and states, and they must be increased by founding schools and by salaries of teachers.
In this matter, what Frederick William proved himself to be, this very literary university, this very assembly is evidence, which, unless we had been summoned by him, would not be held in this place.

Nor indeed does he, led by some partiality, as princes are wont, favor one kind of schools or one kind of discipline and disregard the rest, but what is by far the best, he treats all with a certain equal benevolence.
Therefore, to say nothing of the lesser games, in the whole Prussian empire the gymnasia and lycea are furnished with suitable teachers quite lavishly;
for those things which pertain to the common life and the advantages of the state, special schools are established;

but the universities, in which a higher knowledge of the sciences is handed down, none of those princes who have existed for a long time has preserved, restored, and founded more munificently and wisely.
I need not explain at length that we must come to the aid of those things which are nearest to us, also in writing, and in a manner different from that of antiquity.

Although these studies once sought almost only security from the state and honorable esteem, since those who taught them either by writings or by voice were themselves sufficiently equipped with domestic resources, or demanded a huge fee from their students, it has long been the case that they need the care of princes and states, and they must be increased by founding schools and by stipends for teachers.

In this matter, what sort of man Frederick William has shown himself to be, this very university, this very assembly is evidence, which, unless we had been summoned by him, would not be taking place in this place.

Nor indeed does he, led by some partiality, as princes are wont, favor one kind of schools or one kind of discipline and hold the rest in lower regard, but, which is by far the best, he treats all with a certain equal benevolence.
Therefore, to say nothing of the lesser games, in the whole Prussian empire the gymnasia and lycea are furnished with suitable teachers quite lavishly;
for those things that pertain to the common life and the advantages of the state, special schools are established;

but the universities, in which a higher knowledge of the sciences may be handed down, none of those princes who have been for a long time has preserved, restored, founded more munificently and wisely.

While I run through these things as briefly as possible and do not embellish them with many words, nevertheless I seem to myself to have accomplished this, that the mention of Pericles, thrown in, should not be considered entirely empty nor foreign to these solemnities.

Therefore, just as that age brought forth a rich harvest of the best things, with the remnants of which we still delight and are instructed, so, I pray, may the reign of Frederick William be more conspicuous day by day in the flower of arts and letters, and may it produce such things as may transmit to future ages a similar fame and fruit of learning:

So that he for whose name provision has been made sufficiently for posterity by the integrity of his life, the goodness of his rule, and the greatness of his deeds, may also be honored with that glory.
By these qualities Frederick William has gained and maintains the affection and veneration of his citizens.

And what Pericles, when dying, is said to have said, while some of those standing around were praising different things in his life, that these things had also happened to others and were common to him with fortune, but that this was by far the greatest and most beautiful thing for him, that no Athenian had put on a black garment because of him — this Frederick William surpasses:
We have seen him wrestling with fortune, through whom not only has no one ever put on a black garment, but on whose birthday citizens use a festive and joyful garment.

Therefore may God, the Best and Greatest, keep such a king safe with the Augustan house, and lead him and the republic, which he wisely governs, on a tranquil, happy course proceeding toward all good and prosperous things.

May God, the Best and Greatest, keep the king safe and sound with his August house, and may He lead for him and for the state, which he governs wisely, a calm, happy course proceeding toward all good and prosperous things.

div.head: X. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXII. habita.

p.s: Of all the assemblies that are held in our buildings and especially in this hall throughout the year, none is more frequented, nor more distinguished by the nobility and dignity of those present, nor more sacred by the gravity of the matters transacted, than these solemn rites instituted annually and to be instituted hereafter for piously honoring the name of Frederick William, our most beloved King.
The more I understand this, the less I ever satisfy myself not only in speaking, but even in choosing the subject itself.

And although the treatment of almost all things is made easier by use and practice, this one duty, the more often I undertake it, the more clearly I see that it is so difficult that it far, far exceeds my strength.

To the other difficulties is added this not least one, that since those things which are most distinguished in a king pertain to the state, and the material sought from that source seems most worthy, which we might set forth before such and so great an assembly, I scarcely dare to touch that most abundant matter;
because my mind, estranged from public affairs, is occupied only in literature:
This we know to be especially in accordance with the will of our most wise King.

Therefore, with the greatest things snatched away, what remains, listeners, except that, withdrawing a little longer from the proclamation of the King's praises—who neither desires nor demands them—I should take refuge in an argument drawn from school, lest I engage in those things for which I seem less fit?

When you have granted me this, since it is probable that each one of those about whom I shall speak will speak, if not excellently, at least moderately well, you will also have granted me this, that I speak about the discipline of ancient literature.
But do not fear that by setting forth those things which seem to me more than to you, and to any other day more than to the birthday of the most deserving King, I shall be troublesome to you today.

I am not so foolish as to try, by immoderately boasting of those studies, as some do, to detract from the rest, intending by an illiberal and arrogant discussion to produce nothing but nausea in my hearers.
Nor will I wander so far that my speech may not find its way back.
I will confine myself to those things which I think are not entirely foreign to any of you, who are all furnished with this most important part of public education.

And since nothing can be entirely separated from the state's affairs, I will conveniently arrive even at that point, which perhaps you hoped I would reach earlier, namely, to seek praise for the ruling house and the most gracious Prince from those things that have been well established in this empire.
Finally, I do not ask that you be fair judges to me, unless you will recognize that I am not an unfair orator.
which seem to be fitting for the birthday of a most deserving king, today I shall be troublesome to you.

I am not so foolish as to try to detract from others by immoderately boasting of those letters, as some do, intending by an illiberal and arrogant discussion to do nothing else but cause nausea to the listeners.
nor will I wander so far that my speech may not find a way back.
I will confine myself to those things which I think are not entirely foreign to any of you, since you are all equipped with this most important part of public education.

And since nothing can be entirely separated from the state's affairs, I will conveniently arrive even at that point, to which perhaps you hoped I would come sooner, so that from those things which are well established in this empire, I may seek praise for the ruling house and the most gracious Prince.
Finally, I do not seek that you be fair judges to me, unless you will recognize that I am not a wholly unworthy orator.
For, to begin with this, those who have labored longer in some field and have deeply buried their mind in it, I do not consider it unworthy if they attribute the most to the same field:
For if they did not value it most highly, it would be a wonder if they did not leave it entirely and transfer their zeal and industry to all other things:

But if anyone has not yet understood that, according as each person is carried by his natural talent, different people excel in different things, and that in the whole circle of learning there is no province that rules, none that is somewhat more extensive and serves, none that excels alone, so that the colonists of the rest are, as it were, counted by their capitation;
let him know that he has made little progress, and that he measures literature not by a just measure, but by the very narrow measure of his own petty mind.

I know that there have been and are theologians, jurists, physicians, philosophers, philologists, physicists, poets, who think that they alone know what is worth the effort, and that others know nothing or only trifles, and that all the other arts are to be valued at nothing.
who seem to me, by this very pride of judgment, to confess that they do not know very many things.

For if they did not completely ignore whatever lies beyond the boundaries of that discipline which they have embraced, even if they had only lightly touched those external matters and tasted them with the tips of their lips, they would have recognized that in the individual arts, when properly handled, there is the deepest knowledge.
But as in those schools in which one or another doctrine is taught separately, let us allow this one to pride itself in its own separate place;

Certainly in a university, where distinguished teachers are appointed for each discipline, if anyone among the teachers should despise the other subjects, he is the less to be tolerated, the more easily he can correct his error from the association of his colleagues, and the more harmful he can be to his students.
For he who lives in solitude, because he rarely compares what is foreign with his own, will the more often be led to value his own more highly than is right;
On the other hand, nothing learned can more effectively compel one to modesty than the daily, almost visual encounter with the various arts.
And he who, by disparaging others, draws learners away from getting to know them, takes from them a great part of those things by which they nourish their minds.

Therefore, intending to speak about the study of antiquity, I will especially take care to remove carefully what is falsely wont to be proclaimed about it to the detriment of other disciplines, especially since I understand that something is commonly attributed to it which seems to be common to all good arts rather.
For it has become established that the things which are comprehended in this discipline are called studies of humanity:
from which some, having set out, thought that humanity is proper and peculiar to this kind of literature:
This is so far from being my true opinion, that I think no science worthy of this name can be without humanity.
For first, if you should think that humanity consists in elegance of manners, in courtesy, gentleness, and charm,
everyone understands that letters of any kind contribute something, but only something, to these, because by them all manners are softened and desires are tempered:
Indeed, many have complained that those who are occupied with the study of antiquity are not always found to be the most humane when compared to that power of the voice.
Although I myself would hardly concede that severity, and in its proper place even harshness, conflicts with genuine humanity;
For who would approve of compliance in all matters and toward all people?
Who would not rather judge that vices, malice, and corrupt morals must be pursued and censured with the greatest force?
For truly, one who shows himself obliging to everyone, I would call him not so much humane as cowardly, or cunning and feigned like a little fox;
And no one would deny that Cicero and Demosthenes, although they rush against their adversaries with great force, were nevertheless most cultivated men.

But I judge that something greater and more serious is comprehended by humanitas, I mean the faculty of acting rightly and according to the precepts of virtue, of conceiving in the mind universal notions of things, which they call ideas, and finally of explaining aptly what you feel:
Since these things are peculiar to man, they alone seem to contain the force of humanitas.
But who is so foolish as to think, especially in the present state of learning, that those things are founded solely on ancient literature, or chiefly on it?

For I will not speak of shaping life according to virtue, that each discipline has innate in it the purest notions, and that philosophy excels in these very things, unless it lives, because it rarely combines what is foreign with its own, it will more often be led to value its own more highly than is right;
On the contrary, nothing learned can more effectively compel one to modesty than the daily, as it were, sight of the various arts:
And he who, while learning, by disparaging the works of others, draws back from getting to know them, takes away from them a great part of those things by which they might nourish their minds.

Therefore, about to speak about the study of antiquity, I will especially take care to remove diligently what is falsely wont to be said about it to the detriment of other disciplines, especially since I understand that something is commonly attributed to it which seems rather to be common to all good arts.
For indeed it has become established that the studies which are embraced by this discipline are called the humanities.
From this some have concluded that humanity is proper and peculiar to this kind of literature.
This is so far from being true in my judgment, that I think humanity cannot be absent from any science worthy of this name.
For first, if you should think that humanity consists in elegance of manners, in courtesy, gentleness, and charm;
Everyone understands something, but only something, to bring any letters whatsoever to these things, because for all people morals are softened and desires are tempered:
Indeed, many have complained that those who are occupied in the knowledge of antiquity, when compared to that power of the voice, are not always found to be most humane.
Although I would hardly concede that severity and, in its own place, even harshness itself fight with genuine humanity;
For who would approve of obsequiousness in all matters and toward all people?
Who would not rather judge that vices, malice, and corrupt morals must be pursued and censured with the greatest force?
For truly, if someone presents himself as obliging to everyone, I would call him not so much humane as cowardly, or, like a little fox, cunning and feigned;
And no one would deny that Cicero and Demosthenes, although they rushed against their adversaries with great force, were nevertheless most cultivated men.

But I judge that something greater and more serious is comprehended by humanitas, I mean the faculty of acting rightly and according to the precepts of virtue, of conceiving in the mind universal notions of things, which they call ideas, and finally of explaining aptly what you feel:
Since these things are proper to man, they alone seem to contain the force of humanitas.
But indeed, who is so stupid as to think that those things are founded solely on ancient literature, or especially on these, particularly in the present state of learning that now prevails?

For not to mention that I might speak of life being conformed to virtue, that the purest notions are innate in every discipline, and that philosophy excels in these very things unless it is ruined by vain fancies, there is no need for us to demonstrate.
And who would dare to exclude theology from humane learning, unless one who has ordered God to be banished from humanity?
But the science of law and the medical art, just as they rest on use and experience, so they are based on the deepest notions.

And although we may concede that perfect philology could have seemed to some especially humane, which in the most perfect works of the human mind experiences the immense depth of the human spirit, and comprehends through inner knowledge whatever is magnificent, noble, sweet, and pleasant, whatever moves, strikes, calms, and uplifts the minds of men:
yet those written Muses do not alone breathe sweetness;
even the cups and corollas of flowers are inhabited by Venus and Grace:
Those Empedoclean principles, love and strife, by which human beings are driven, also govern the nature of things, gather and separate inanimate matter, unite and disunite them;
And reason, diffused throughout the whole world, pours over the forms and images of notions upon the mind intent on those greatest and smallest works of the divine maker.
Nor, if I wished, could I say by what right the most subtle grammatical questions could be considered more human than the microscopic observations of physicists.
What of the fact that the whole material of ancient studies, if you except the ancient languages, is contained in the other disciplines themselves?
If these did not pertain to humanity, that study which is composed from them could not be called humane.
Unless perhaps you have sought humanity in this, that in the writings of philologists only the slender beginnings of individual things are handed down, while the more abstruse matters are neglected:
Just as Aristotle did not want the liberally educated to be trained in the arts in such a way that they become perfect in them, but that they be imbued with the rudiments:
And although this was well said about liberal education, it should not be transferred to the method of judging doctrines.
For my part, as I have sufficiently indicated, humanity seems to consist especially in the understanding of concepts:
and where these fail, there I think the trade of a petty craftsman begins;
I see that not a few of those very men who devote themselves to ancient literature are held by this.
I mean all those who, unequal to their predecessors, pile up a rough, unpolished, and gloomy mass of matter and words.
But let us also consider that part of culture which I said consists in being able to speak what you think.

I do not deny that the study of ancient literature can be of great service to it, since it examines and scrutinizes the words, thoughts, style, and speech in the most perfect examples of the most distinguished writers;
Nevertheless, that it is not so great as is commonly thought, and that it is not ruined by vain fancies, we do not need to demonstrate.
And who would dare to separate theology from humanity, unless he who has ordered God to be exiled from man?
But the science of law and the medical art, just as they rest on use and experience, so they are based on the deepest notions.

And even if we grant that perfect philology could have seemed to some especially humane, which in the most perfect works of genius experiences the immense depth of the human mind, and comprehends with inner knowledge whatever is magnificent, generous, sweet, pleasant, whatever moves, strikes, calms, and uplifts human minds:
Nevertheless, those written Muses do not alone breathe delight;
Venus and Grace also dwell in the cups and garlands of flowers.
Those Empedoclean principles, love and hate, by which men are led, also govern the nature of things, gather and separate, unite and disunite inanimate materials;
And reason, diffused throughout the whole world, pours the forms and images of notions upon the mind intent upon those works of the divine craftsman, in the greatest and smallest things alike.
Nor, even if I wished, could I say by what right the most subtle grammatical investigations could be considered more humane than the microscopic observations of physicists.
What of the fact that the entire material of ancient studies, if you except the ancient languages, is contained in the other disciplines themselves?
If these did not pertain to humanity, that study which is composed from them could not be called humane.
Unless perhaps you should seek humanity in this, that in the writings of philologists only the slender beginnings of individual things are handed down, and the more abstruse matters are neglected:
just as Aristotle wished that those who are to be liberally educated should not be so trained in the arts that they are perfect in them, but that they should be imbued with the rudiments:
And although this was not badly said concerning liberal education, it ought not to be transferred to the judging of the system of learning.
For my part, as I have sufficiently indicated, culture seems to me to consist especially in the understanding of concepts.
Where these are lacking, there, I think, the trade of the petty craftsman begins;
By which I see that not a few of those very persons who devote themselves to ancient literature are held;
I mean all who, unequal to their betters, heap up a rough, unformed, and dark mass of things and words.
But let us also consider that part of culture which I said is placed in this, that you can say what you feel.

To which I do not deny that the study of ancient literature can be of outstanding benefit, since it looks at and examines in the most perfect examples of the most excellent writers the words, thoughts, style, and speech;
yet this usefulness is not as great as is commonly thought.
For first, it is agreed that people become eloquent chiefly by the benefit of nature;
But practice must be added, which among students of antiquity is usually very slight.
Then criticism and grammatical discipline indeed form and shape judgment, but they rather draw it back from speaking readily than supply that faculty.

Indeed, we see that very many who are more diligently engaged in that kind of study (and I do not except myself) are not greatly practiced in speaking, but are reduced to such a state by the accurate and subtle investigation of discourse, that both a supply of thoughts fails them, and their very speech, because they perceive faults more keenly and guard against them more fearfully, flows less freely, as if distrusting itself:

Just as Aristarchus, the father of grammarians, when asked, as it seems, why he did not himself compose a poem, since he had the best knowledge of the faults and virtues of poems, is said to have replied that he could not write as he wished, and did not wish to write as he could.

Others, by constantly turning over the best models, have achieved this one thing: that, as is especially charged against Latin orators, they say nothing in many words, or, like the Emperor Claudius, they write elegantly but ineptly.

Finally, if you wish to call by the name of humanity that even cultivation of the powers of the mind which the study of ancient literature is said to provide, and yet has not provided to many, that very even cultivation depends more on the goodness of natural talent, and will be the more perfect the more things the mind, properly refined and ordered, can embrace in thought;

In this matter the greatest philosophers will be those who, if any, having traversed the whole circle of learning, have shown the same magnitude of talent that we know existed in Aristotle and Leibniz.
This is the usefulness.
For first, it is established that men become eloquent chiefly by the benefit of nature;
but practice must be added, which among students of antiquity is usually very slight.
Then critical and grammatical discipline indeed forms and shapes judgment, but it rather calls one back from speaking readily than brings that faculty.

Indeed, we see that very many who are more diligently engaged in that kind of study (and I do not except myself) are not greatly practiced in speaking, but are reduced by the careful and subtle investigation of language to such a point that both an abundance of thoughts fails them, and their very speech, because they perceive faults more keenly and guard against them more fearfully, as if distrusting itself, flows less freely:

Almost as Aristarchus, the father of grammarians, when asked, as it seems, why he did not himself compose a poem, since he had the faults and virtues of poems very well known, is said to have replied that he could not write as he would wish, nor would he wish to write as he could.

Others, by turning over the best models, have achieved this one thing, that, as is especially reproached to Latin orators, they say nothing in many words, or, like the Emperor Claudius, they write elegantly but ineptly.

Finally, if you wish to call by the name of humanity that balanced cultivation of the mind's powers, which the study of ancient literature is said to provide—though it has not provided it for many—that very balanced learning depends more on the goodness of one's natural talent, and will be the more perfect the more things the mind, properly worked over and arranged, can embrace in thought.

In this, the greatest philosophers will be those who, if any, having traversed the whole circle of learning with the greatness of talent that we know existed in Aristotle and Leibniz, will have done so.

Since these things are so, I pass over that distinguished title imposed upon our literature, and I refer it back to the age from which it was propagated, in which the European nations, emerging from the filth of inveterate barbarism and growing warm in the contemplation of the ancient authors, sought from there the seeds of all better culture; in which the supreme poet Dante Alighieri looked up to Virgil as a specimen of his art complete in all respects, and Francesco Petrarca thought about restoring the Latin language to common use; in which in the books of Plato and Aristotle the only sources of sounder philosophy gushed forth.
Finally, the best minds were rightly turning to imitating the elegance of the ancient writers in the Latin language:
Now, with literature grown up, it seems that a different decision must be made.

Therefore, when you ask what and what kind of philology is in my judgment, I answer in the simplest way, if it is taken not in the broader sense that lies in the word itself, but as it is usually referred to ancient literature, that it is the historical and philosophical knowledge of all antiquity.
Of all antiquity, I say:

In this respect it differs in some measure from history, which chiefly teaches events in chronological order, whereas philology comprehends the whole life of ancient peoples and tries to know it in all its parts.
However, whoever examines the matter more keenly will find no part of philology that cannot become a subject for history.

Therefore, those who restrict the boundaries of this discipline to the arts of the interpreter and the critic seem to me to err greatly, for it is clear that these arts contain not the highest limits of learning, but the instruments for discovering truth:

I say this not in contempt of those arts, but because the matter itself demands it, since I understand that there is in them something more recondite than most people see, provided that they do not think that criticism consists solely in correcting the errors of copyists, while they call it divine, thereby of their own accord ridiculing and prostituting its divinity by that paltry use of it.
And I judge it no less disgraceful if anyone should offer a rude heap of various things as philology.

When I attribute philosophical cognition to it, I mean this: that the highest notions are to be sought out, implanted by nature in ancient nations and expressed, as it were, in visible images in the individual parts of ancient culture.
These notions are not to be established arbitrarily; how they can be found by the right path, I will not now explain.

Now, lest I linger too long on this matter, which is indeed great, and which I would call the head of all learning, when you have come to the individual parts, an exposition of each one must be given, not only well arranged and confirmed by suitable witnesses, but also consistent with those highest notions, so that, while each thing is spread before our eyes, we may understand that it is so formed and has undergone these changes in the course of time, not by chance, but by inner necessity, as far as this can exist in human affairs.
The word is taken in its meaning, but as is customary it is referred to ancient literature, that it is the historical and philosophical knowledge of all antiquity.
Of all antiquity, I say:

by which it differs in some way from history, which chiefly teaches events in the order of times, whereas philology comprehends the whole life of ancient peoples and tries to know it in each of its parts:
However, whoever examines the matter more keenly will find no part of philology that cannot become a subject for history.

Therefore, those who restrict the boundaries of this discipline to the arts of the interpreter and critic seem to me to err greatly, for it is clear that these arts contain not the highest limits of learning, but the instruments for discovering truth.

I say this not in contempt of those arts, but because the matter itself demands it, since I understand that there is in them something more recondite than most people see, provided that they do not think that criticism is confined to correcting the errors of copyists, while they call it divine, thereby of their own accord ridiculing and prostituting its divinity by that paltry use of it.
Nor do I judge it less disgraceful if someone should offer a rude heap of various things as philology.

When I attribute philosophical cognition to it, I mean that the highest notions are to be sought out, implanted by nature in ancient nations and expressed, as it were, in visible images in the individual parts of ancient culture:
These notions are not to be established arbitrarily; how they can be found by the right path, I will not now explain.

Now, lest I linger too long on this matter, which is indeed great, and which I would call the head of all learning, when you have come to the individual parts, an exposition of each one must be given, not only well arranged and confirmed by suitable witnesses, but also consistent with those highest notions, so that, while each thing is spread out before our eyes, we may understand that it is so formed and has experienced these changes in the course of time, not by chance, but by inner necessity, as far as this can exist in human affairs.
But I indicate the parts themselves, which are to be divided again into their own subdivisions, in three words:
first, the knowledge of public affairs, with the notice of times and places, and of civil institutions, and also of law;
second, the demonstration of private affairs; third, that of religions and arts;

fourth, the history of all doctrines, of philosophy, of moral and natural disciplines, of styles and literary genres, and finally the perfect explanation of the language, to which the primitive knowledge of the nation is innate:
Why I have so composed and separated these parts, which embrace the whole subject matter of philology, demands a more extensive investigation.

But if you have delineated the study of antiquity in this manner, you will concede that not only is the deepest and broadest learning exercised in those studies, but that, as for many arts, so also for this one no single person suffices:

Indeed, it is well known that he who has striven to become perfect in all parts cannot attain the highest in any, just as Eratosthenes, who first used the name of philologist, was considered not first in any field, but second in all.
By dividing the tasks, much progress will also be made here, since, as Hesiod says, the half is more than the whole.

But in whatever particular field they each display more distinguished industry, they ought to be equipped with the most important concepts of the whole discipline, lest they occupy the place of mere craftsmen.

Finally, since it seems certain that, just as the Greeks traced the beginnings of all arts back to Homer as their author, so all the arts that have been cultivated in our times have their roots in antiquity;
It is clear to all learned men that philology is common, not peculiar to those who are called philologists, and that it cannot be completed without the support of the other disciplines.

If you have sketched the study of antiquity in this manner, you will concede that not only is the deepest and broadest learning exercised in it, but that just as many arts, so also for this one no single person suffices.

Indeed, it is evident that he who strives to become perfect in all parts cannot attain the highest in any, just as Eratosthenes, who first used the name of philologist, was considered not first in any field, but second in all.
By dividing the tasks, much will also be gained here, since, as Hesiod says, the half is more than the whole.
But in whatever particular part they place a more distinguished industry, they ought to be equipped with the most important notions of the whole discipline, lest they occupy the place of artisans.

Finally, since it seems certain that, just as the Greeks traced the beginnings of all arts back to Homer as their author, so all the arts that have been cultivated in our times have their roots in antiquity;
It is clear that philology is common to all learned people, not peculiar to those who are called philologists, and that it cannot be completed without the support of the other disciplines.

I seem to myself to have accomplished what I wanted, listeners, namely to show that I do not wish to adorn my studies with words beyond measure, but that I am conducting the common business of all learned men, as is fitting in such great harmony of various disciplines among us, of which none is judged by those most distinguished men, whom the Father of the Fatherland wished to be placed over us for our greatest advantage, to be either more excellent or more useful than the others;
At the same time, I think it can be gathered from my discussion that the study of antiquity is not unworthy to be cultivated by the efforts of many scholars.
And yet not even this is perfect, if someone, despising the arts of our age, has known nothing but ancient things.
But since I have spoken thus far about the science of antiquity itself, I now pass on to that which may be referred especially to public utility.
For since it is found that, in the study of ancient literature, by a custom handed down from an earlier age, a special place was given in the instruction of the schools;
it was asked whether this practice was rightly retained up to the present or not:
for it had been understood, as I explained above, that even the other disciplines of humanity scatter seeds.

But I will not descend to the arguments with which the two sides have contended, nor will I explain how one who learns a language correctly in childhood not only exercises the powers of his mind most keenly, but also, as it were without knowing it, imbibes an immense store of notions:

The prerogative that is attributed to ancient literature in the education of youth seems to rest especially on this foundation, that, whatever excellent thing the recent age has produced, the old classical writers have not ceased to be the most important, and the tender minds ought to be imbued with those things which are best, so that they may be filled with the most beautiful forms.
I see indeed that it can be doubted who are the classical writers;
But to cut short a long discussion, I call that classic which, the more you consider it, the more it pleases, not that which, even if it pleased at first, grows stale with constant contemplation.
Nor do I speak of the judgment of only one man or of a few:
What is classic grows with the agreement of succeeding ages as it ages, if indeed what always flourishes ages;
We measure the charm of other things by their novelty.
Time tests everything;
In time those old writers were approved;
and the judgment of centuries, especially in those things that are publicly established, is not to be made of the least importance, nor is anything to be rashly innovated.

It has brought forth excellent [writers]; the old classical writers have not ceased to be the most important, and the minds of the young ought to be imbued with those things which are best, so that they may be filled with the most beautiful forms.
I see indeed that it can be doubted who are classical;

But to cut short a long discussion, I call that classic which, the more you consider it, the more it pleases, not classic that which, even if it pleased at first, grows stale by constant contemplation.
Nor do I speak of the judgment of only one man or of a few:
what is classic grows with the consensus of succeeding ages, growing old, if indeed what always flourishes grows old;
We measure the charm of other things by their novelty.
Time tests all things;
In time, those ancient writers were approved;
and the judgment of centuries, especially in those things which are publicly established, is not to be made of the least importance, nor is anything to be rashly innovated.
But I conjecture from certain indications that our ancestors, most prudent in handing down ancient authors to youth, also had another aim.
For although to scrutinize the nature of things is rightly held to be excellent, nevertheless human affairs are nearest to man;

But among human things, nothing is more common to men, nothing ought to be dearer, than that society established by nature itself, which contains all the goods of man, the state, the fatherland of each one.
And indeed the love of one's fatherland is so diffused through nearly all the ancient writers that I would call it, as it were, the vital breath of antiquity:
Unfold the poets, philosophers, orators, and historians of events;
You will find that the love of one's country, and of liberty, without which no country can exist, is implanted in the innermost hearts of all.

When I consider this, I do not hesitate to affirm that no explanation of the history of the fatherland, in which we altogether limp, because excellent writers of this kind rarely arise among our countrymen for certain reasons, no knowledge of the laws and institutions of the fathers, no public solemnities so foster the love of the fatherland and the sense of just liberty as the reading of the ancient writers, and that boys rightly instructed in that discipline, with the very first rudiments, by reading Nepos himself, by other excellent examples, [are so fostered].
Indeed, since no better teachers of political wisdom than the ancients can be found, not only will boys be trained from them for love of country, but also men for conducting affairs.
But about this, although it can be approved by the authority of the greatest men and by the matter itself, I think it better to be silent, lest I exceed what befits my person:
What I placed in the first position, it pleases me to illustrate with conspicuous examples.
Let Frederick the Great and the Emperor Napoleon serve as examples.
Of these two, when the latter, with his characteristic shrewdness, understood that the treatment of the ancient writers was hostile to unjust tyranny, that treatment greatly displeased him;

That Frederick the Great, the principal founder of this empire, so that everything that could nourish the mind and free it from servitude, thus especially the Greek and Latin authors pleased him and seemed most suitable for scholastic instruction, is a very well-known fact.

He who, on the threshold of old age, with the strength of his body worn down but with his mind intact, when he had ordered the best Greek authors to be read to him constantly, although he had been educated especially in French literature, which is most alien to the Greek character, and knew those very Greek authors themselves, deprived of their force, only from French translations;

Nevertheless, having been exceedingly delighted with them, and, to dwell on this one point, having admired the excellence of his genius in Demosthenes' speech On the Crown, which is filled with great thoughts and with the dearest affection toward his country.

We know that the same man, led by his own counsels, not by those of his friends, ordered that the principal Greek and Latin writers should be read most diligently in the schools, and that not only the words of the young men should be entrusted to memory, but also the method of treating subjects and the subjects themselves and the opinions should be explained.
Thus, while Frederick the Great was reigning, in this empire and especially in this city, the foundations of a better discipline were laid more securely.
These institutions, which Frederick William, our most wise king, not only retained but strengthened,
He, having conquered the common enemy of Europe, warded off that barbarism which threatened from him.
Therefore I cannot but praise that institution of which I have spoken:
For this is the pledge of liberty.
Those who feared it for any reason, lest those writers be handed over intact to the youth, took care
so that even minds might be mutilated, lest limbs be able to move:
Although those men rarely attained what they desired, because, to adapt the words of a most distinguished writer to this matter, the memory of a following age cannot be extinguished by present power.

Nor indeed, when the young offspring is nourished with those foods, is it mixed into the conduct of affairs, for which the ancients themselves, with their years set for this matter, deemed it unequal;
But, far removed from the contagion of present circumstances, it moves in pure air, which the youthful mind ought to draw in with its breath.

Therefore they seem to me to have erred greatly, who, when they wished to portray genuine Germans, being for the most part almost hostile to the study of ancient literature, thought that those studies should either be banished or confined within very narrow limits.
he would understand, in accordance with his own keenness, the treatment of the ancient writers; that very thing greatly displeased him;

Nevertheless, he was exceedingly delighted with them, and, to dwell on this one point, in Demosthenes' speech On the Crown, which is filled with great thoughts and the most affectionate feeling toward his country, he admired the excellence of his genius.
