Thus, while Frederick the Great reigned, in this empire and especially in this city, the foundations of a better discipline were laid more firmly.
These institutions, which Frederick William, our most wise king, not only retained but also strengthened,
He, having conquered the common enemy of Europe, warded off that barbarism which threatened from him.
Therefore I cannot but praise that institution of which I have spoken:
For this is the pledge of liberty.
Those who feared it for any reason, lest those writers be handed over intact to the youth, took care;
so that even minds might be mutilated, lest limbs be able to move:
Although those men rarely attained what they desired, because, to adapt the words of a most distinguished writer to this matter, the memory of a following age cannot be extinguished by present power.

Nor indeed, when the young offspring is nourished by those means, is it mixed up in the conduct of affairs, for which the ancients themselves, with their years set apart for this matter, were not equal.
But, far removed from the contagion of present affairs, it moves in pure air, which the youthful mind ought to draw in with its breath.

Therefore they seem to me to have erred greatly, who, when they wished to portray genuine Germans, being for the most part almost hostile to the study of ancient literature, thought that those studies should either be banished or confined within very narrow limits.
Let us therefore preserve this common good of the human race, by which all ages have been nourished:

But let us also give thanks to the most merciful Prince, whom we indeed always venerate silently, but today openly, under whose auspices the discipline of the schools is aided with the most favorable success by those most distinguished men who have been placed over us as well.
From this it is understood that they have a clear view of the things on which the true safety of the people rests.
For I may seem to say something ridiculous;
Nevertheless, I will say that neither armies, nor resources, nor the most distinguished men are as great a defense to the state as good teachers of youth.

Among these, we indeed are the first, but as schoolteachers, of whom not a few are equipped with such an abundance of learning that they would even suffice for greater duties, they seem to me all the more worthy of remuneration, the greater their burden is and the less splendid their position.

In the more ample establishment of universities, the rulers of states do not always seem to have been strangers to ostentation, because such great authority was once attributed to them, and is partly still attributed, that a whole kingdom can boast of one university.
Where the institutions of schools, being less conspicuous, are deemed worthy of the same care, it is evident that not a vain show, but the very truth of things is exclusively regarded.

But Frederick William was adorned with both kinds of glory: on the one hand, with the greatest munificence towards the universities, which he established and furnished with the most ample equipment, a munificence entirely free from all ostentation, and which we especially owe to him; and on the other hand, also with the glory of the schools, which were more and more increased.

We venerate him, the most merciful one, silently indeed always, but today openly; under his auspices the discipline of the schools is aided with the most favorable success by those most distinguished men who have also been placed over us.
From this it is understood that they have clearly perceived on what things the true safety of the people rests.
For although I may seem to say something ridiculous,
nevertheless I will say that not armies, not resources, not most illustrious men are so great a defense to the state as good teachers of youth.

Among these, we indeed are the first, but the scholastic teachers, among whom not a few are equipped with such an abundance of learning that they would even suffice for greater offices, seem to me all the more worthy of remuneration, the greater their burden is and the less splendid their position.

In the more generous endowment of universities, the rulers of states do not always seem to have been strangers to ostentation, because such great authority was once attributed to them, and is partly still attributed, that a whole kingdom could boast of one university:
Where the institutions of schools, being less conspicuous, are deemed worthy of the same care, it is evident that not empty show, but the very truth of things is exclusively regarded.

But Frederick William was adorned with both kinds of glory, both by the universities, which he established with the greatest munificence and with that munificence free from all ostentation, and which he furnished with the most ample equipment, for which we especially owe him thanks, and also by the schools, which were more and more increased.

But for us, while the other ministers of the state are to be formed, especially the scholastic and ecclesiastical teachers, who can satisfy the needs of the republic and the desires of the most gracious King.
How great this duty is, none of you does not understand.

My mind is stirred, listeners, when I think how much, especially in these times, when the eyes of all are cast upon us, we must strive to respond to the wishes of our founder, who desires the best of everything:
But when he has seen our goodwill, since nothing perfect can be accomplished by human strength, he will calmly grant pardon for those things that are left unfinished.
My mind is stirred when I see in one view how much we owe him;
My mouth is stopped while I hesitate what to say first, what second, what third.
Therefore, to embrace much in few words, whatever I have said over so many years about our dearest King on this day and from this very platform:
For I have said many things, with you as witnesses, which I do not think have been consigned to oblivion by any of you, whom I know have always been attentive listeners to me:
Therefore, whatever I have said so often in previous years, know that it all now fills my mind at this critical moment;
Recall it in your mind, and from that make a conjecture how great is what I feel.

Filled with these feelings, pray with me to God, the author and preserver of all good things, that He may preserve that most holy head for us and for the state into extreme old age, and that He may keep the entire royal house whole, safe, and unharmed forever.
to fulfill mine;
Recall this in your mind, and from that make a conjecture of how great is what I feel.

Filled with these feelings, you also pray with me to God, the author and preserver of all good things, that He may preserve that most sacred head for us and for the state into extreme old age, and that He may keep the entire royal house whole, safe, and unharmed forever.

div.head: XI. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXIII. habita.

p.s: Since, from that time, listeners, when our seat of learning was founded under the most auspicious patronage of Frederick William, you have heard, once every year and on this very day, from this place, the praises of the most beloved King set forth;
in this academic year which we are now passing through, it has happened by a remarkable gift of God, that on today's solemnities we venerate the best Prince not for the first time but for the second:

After we saw that most joyful day, on which the whole state, with the greatest feeling of devotion, congratulated us together with the Father of his country on the twenty-five years of his reign completed through virtues and benefits.

There had then gathered a truly splendid circle of distinguished men engaged in public affairs, and in the first place had taken his seat the King's son, heir to the throne, the hope and delight of the people:

Before them, our highest magistrate, when he understood that a more magnificent and more abundant speech was fitting for the special solemnities, which we pray with all our might may not remain special, and since he himself had formerly conducted the state, and had judged an argument drawn in large part from a more intimate knowledge of affairs to be suited to his own person and to those who were present,

These things, I say, since they were so, he then spoke in such a way that he would set forth at length whatever had been excellently done by Frederick William through so many periods of five years at home and in war, whatever was prudent, pious, civil, generous, and finally would praise the Prince extraordinarily through all parts of public and private life, and would snatch away from himself—forgive the speaker—and from his successors, being more favorable, all material however ample for a secondary orator before mindful ears.

Therefore, what I did in previous years, namely, not to set forth the King's entire merits with deliberate effort, but to treat some matter that was in a way external, and to adapt it to the present state of affairs, and from that to derive the King's singular praise, that one thing I now see is left for me.
Although you will understand that even so the path of speaking is not clear for me, if you consider that today I am delivering the tenth oration in these very solemnities;
If my talent has any power either in celebrating the name of the King or in unfolding the theme that befits this day and you, I have long since exhausted all of it.
Finally, since I judge it unworthy both of me and of you to repeat what has been said before, the material must now be sought from afar.
So that he is unfair who charges me with a fault that is an inconvenience of my condition.

But as I reflect how often I have proclaimed the distinguished services of Frederick William to literature, this thought has occurred to me, that it is especially excellent for a prince to come to the aid of literature, particularly in this age, when learning has been brought into suspicion, and the age, raised up to liberal and profound knowledge, is attempted by the obscure contentions of certain men to be reduced back into darkness;

However, that is not an unqualified praise of the king, because it is well known that many princes have combined both learning and the pursuit of learning with the utmost depravity of morals and with savage and unbridled tyranny.
Therefore, little is to be attributed to that kindness toward the arts, unless it has flowed from a soul free from all depravity.
When we compare Frederick William to this standard, what in him delights us more than that great harmony of virtues?
For while he fosters literature and the arts, he is also pious and religious without superstition;
while he nourishes the reverence for the divine power both most sacredly in his own heart and spreads it in the minds of his citizens, he is also a vigorous leader of the army;
And, equating the honors of public virtues with private morals, he tempers severity with affability.

Therefore, since our excellent king is such not by my opinion but by the consensus of all, what wonder if he demands from the learned, especially from those to whom he himself entrusted public instruction, not only learning and skill, but also integrity?
Hence my plan to discuss now a few things about those matters in which the virtue of the learned seems to me to be discerned:
I will explain how, in my opinion, we may most correctly satisfy the expectation of the wisest king in our conduct, as far as can be done in this brief time.

Although I scarcely hope, and indeed not even scarcely, that I will be equal to this task, I who am fully conscious of my own weakness, therefore, because in previous years I did this, that I did not set forth the entire merits of the King with deliberate effort, but I treated some matter that was in a way external, and I adapted it to the present state of affairs, and from that I derived the King's singular praise, that one thing I now see is left to me.
However, you will understand that even in this way the path of speaking is not made easy for me, if you consider that today I am delivering the tenth oration in these very solemnities;
if my talent has any value either in celebrating the name of the King or in explaining the theme that suits this day and you, I have long since exhausted all of it;
Finally, since I judge it unworthy of both you and me to repeat what has already been said, the material must now be sought from afar.
So that he is unfair who would blame me for what is a disadvantage of my condition.

But as I reflect how often I have proclaimed the distinguished services of Frederick William to literature, this thought has occurred to me: that it is especially excellent for a prince to come to the aid of literature, particularly in this age, when learning has been brought under suspicion, and the age, raised up to a liberal and profound science, is attempted by the obscure contentions of certain men to be reduced back into darkness;

However, that is not an absolute praise of the king, because it is well known that many princes have combined both learning and the pursuit of learning with the utmost depravity of morals and with savage and unbridled tyranny.
Therefore, little is to be attributed to that kindness toward the arts, unless it has flowed from a soul free from all depravity.
When we compare Frederick William to this standard, what in him delights us more than that great harmony of virtues?
For while he fosters literature and the arts, he is also pious and religious without superstition;
while he nourishes reverence for the divine power both most sacredly in his own heart and spreads it in the minds of his citizens, he is also a vigorous leader of the army;
And, equating the honors of public virtues with private morals, he tempers severity with courtesy.

Therefore, since our excellent king is such, not by my opinion but by the consensus of all, what wonder if he demands from the learned, especially from those to whom he himself entrusted public instruction, not only learning and skill, but also integrity?
Hence it is my plan to discuss briefly now some of those things in which the virtue of the learned seems to me to be discerned:
So that I may set forth, as best I can in this brief time, how we may most rightly satisfy the expectation of the most wise King, in my opinion at least, by our action.

Although I scarcely hope, and not even scarcely, that I will be equal to this task, I who am fully conscious of my own weakness, nevertheless, in accordance with your indulgence, which I have experienced so often, you will forgive my intention the more willingly because I have come here not trusting in my strength, but through the duty of my office.

Nevertheless, I ask that you, in your indulgence, which I have so often experienced, forgive my intention the more willingly because I have come here not trusting in my own strength, but through the duty of my office.
But someone may ask me, who am about to speak about the virtue of the learned:
Do you think that there is a certain and peculiar virtue of the learned, removed from the customs of other mortals?
By no means, I reply.
Those things which are good and beautiful in all men, which are considered the human or civil, private or public duties of each one, these also belong to the learned:
nay, the more these have cultivated their mind, the more they ought to surpass others in the common virtues of all, so that others may be formed according to their example;
And even the most learned man is to be despised, who, as some formerly especially did, denies that he is bound by those precepts of an honorable life which are commonly prescribed.

Nevertheless, since there is a certain special business of the learned, by which their occupations differ from those of other men, the one virtue of the human race seems to be contained in the learned, insofar as they are learned, in one way, and in another way among those who are engaged in a different kind of life.
For although science may also be useful for the state, for private and domestic affairs, for trades, and for lucrative arts, its end is certainly not to be found anywhere except in science itself.
And since the learned man is occupied with science, his proper virtue is to be regarded only in this.
But since the notion of science cannot be separated from truth,
unless the learned man has attained true knowledge, he will be deprived of his virtue:

And so, just as all virtue is comprehended in knowledge according to the opinion of the greatest philosopher of antiquity, so in the virtues of learned men I think wisdom and correct knowledge of things is most important, and that they have departed from their genuine virtue by as much as they are entangled in more numerous and more serious errors:
When I say this, I do not fear the criticism of those who refer virtue solely to the will.
For since the intellect moves the will, from defects of notions evil plans arise.
And by excusing any errors whatsoever through sincerity of will, you would have removed virtue itself.

But if nevertheless many disagree about the greatest matters, I do not therefore think that either party is to be judged depraved, because very different opinions have not rarely flowed from the same eternal truth, which the weakness implanted in our nature hinders from perceiving pure and undefiled, while one person by mixing in something else obscures the divine form, and perfect knowledge follows at a distance.

But whoever does not combine the study of wisdom with self-knowledge will follow it after a very long interval, for only by self-knowledge can one understand how much progress one has made, what one knows, and what one does not know.
so that, being temperate, he may keep himself within his own limits, and not meddle with those of others, to which he is unequal.
Opposed to this is the vice of arrogance, by which some are oppressed, even those who seem modest.
I mean those who, although they themselves do not sufficiently master the disciplines, undertake to hand them on to others.

For this reason the opinion of those who say that the education of youth should be entrusted not to the most learned but to the most upright men seems to me the less to be approved, since one who takes upon himself a task of which he is in no way capable cannot be regarded as most upright.
unless he has joined to it the knowledge of the thing itself, by which alone he can understand how much he has accomplished, and what he knows and what he does not know;
so that, being temperate, he may keep himself within his own bounds, and not mix himself with those of others, to which he is unequal.
contrary to which is the vice of arrogance, by which some are oppressed, even those who seem modest;
I mean those who undertake to teach others the disciplines which they themselves do not sufficiently hold.

Therefore, the opinion of those who say that the education of youth should be entrusted not to the most learned but to the most upright men seems to me less to be approved, since he who takes upon himself a task of which he is in no way capable cannot be regarded as most upright.

Now indeed, to pass from those things which pertain more to knowledge to that which belongs to the will, just as the health of the body seems to consist in the complete harmony of all its parts and powers, so the concord and agreement of the mind makes a just man, and without this concord no virtue of the soul exists;
But what greater discord can there be, than if someone should think one thing and say another?
But the force of ill-restrained desires also drives even learned men to become false, and teaches them, as he says, to keep one thing hidden in the breast and another ready on the tongue.

Among these there are few, but there are nevertheless some, who, especially when they have acquired some fame for themselves, puffed up with immense pride, despise all others in comparison with themselves, and if anyone else excels, cannot bear it without envy;

who try to persuade others that they know everything best, and although they themselves understand that others have deserved well, nevertheless they disparage them, wish to detract from their praises, and to obstruct their undertakings;
for no other reason, indeed, than that since they wish to be regarded as the only wise men, they take another's glory as a diminution of their own eminence.

This wicked desire for glory, just as it cannot arise except from a corrupt mind, so whoever is possessed by it no longer seeks the truth in order that it may be understood as true, but, referring everything to his own name, attempts either to attack the truth itself or to envelop it in darkness, whenever he has judged that it serves his own cause.

To me indeed, although I know that many think otherwise, ambition seems not only not a great force for virtue, but also in public affairs and in literature to be a most pernicious evil, and that not consisting in the fault which I have just now set forth, but spreading much more widely still.

For in those disciplines which it is valuable for all to know, for those who think that the knowledge of things divine and human is not foreign to them, especially in philosophy and history and the doctrine of civil affairs, and finally in the science of theologians, according to the character of the ages, different things at different times please both the common people and the powerful;
Seeking their favor, ambitious scholars adapt their opinions to those by whom they wish to be approved, and thus creep into their minds:
Therefore they bend and twist their opinions this way and that, and first they deceive others, then soon themselves.
The same men, according as it has seemed convenient, change what they had previously embraced;
Such men the Greeks used to call cothurni.
Indeed, the divinity of learning does not allow that those (doctrines) be fitted to the palates of cooks, as it were, or to the opinions of patrons;
Nor, if we have resolved to proceed along the pure path of knowledge, can we look around in every direction to see what will please each person in each period of five years, and what will displease.
But if, according to the various institutions of rulers, even letters would have to change, some would be such in a popular government, others under aristocracies, others in kingdoms:
although nevertheless their condition is such that they obey reason alone, which is one and simple.
But since reason is indeed diffused and disseminated through all the parts of every best state, rightly pursued learning cannot conflict with a well-constituted republic:
If they disagree with each other, it is necessary that either the letters or the states be corrupt.

But in literature, since not a few manage everything at their own discretion, but rather with the combined talents and efforts of many learned men, since one corrects another, corrects errors, teaches truer things, and so many learned men cannot be subjected to the authority and, as it were, tyranny of one, being accustomed to freedom of thought and solely intent on searching out the truth;
Unless, perhaps, by the fault of the state itself certain fixed opinions, not the best, are cherished, and better ones are prohibited, the whole republic of letters cannot easily rush into ruin.
When a well-cultivated governor of the state has understood that individuals have erred by misusing letters, scarcely anyone will deny that it is his power to restrain those men.

Only let not the fault of one be transferred to all, and let not the art itself be considered harmful because of the error of an artist, and let not liberty be taken away from literature, which, once you have removed it, even the most diligent care will not be able to restore.
But he who has reviewed the memory of times will find that ruined states or their leaders have not infrequently been hostile to learning.
For not only on account of confession of faith and religion have pious men experienced sword and fire;
But because philosophy seemed to censure unjust power, it also had those by whom it was harassed.

Thus at Rome, when Junius Rusticus had published the praises of Paetus Thrasea and Helvidius Priscus and had called them most holy men, on the occasion of that crime all philosophers, just as formerly actors and Chaldaeans, were banished by a decree of the senate and were forbidden from the city and Italy.
How ambitious learned men accommodate their opinions to those by whom they wish to be approved, and thus creep into their minds:
therefore they bend and twist their opinions this way and that, and first deceive others, then themselves:
the same men, according as it has seemed convenient, change what they had previously embraced;
such men the Greeks used to call 'cothurni' (buskins).
But indeed the divinity of learning does not allow that those [doctrines] be fitted, like the dishes of cooks to palates, to the opinions of patrons;
Nor, if we have decided to proceed along the pure path of knowledge, can we look around in every direction to see what will please each person in each period of five years, and what will displease.
But if, according to the various institutions of rulers, even letters would have to change, these would be one kind in a popular government, another under aristocracies, another in kingdoms:
although nevertheless their condition is such that they obey reason alone, which is one and simple.
Indeed, since reason is also diffused and disseminated through all the parts of every best state, rightly pursued learning cannot conflict with a well-constituted republic:
If they disagree with each other, it is necessary that either the letters or the states be corrupt.

But in literature, since not a few manage everything according to their own judgment, but rather with the combined talents and efforts of many scholars, since one corrects another, corrects errors, teaches truer things, and so many learned men, accustomed to freedom of thought and solely intent on searching out the truth, cannot be subjected to the authority and, as it were, tyranny of a single individual;

Unless, perhaps, by the fault of the state itself certain fixed resolutions that are not the best are fostered, better ones are prohibited, the whole commonwealth of letters cannot easily rush into ruin.
When a well-cultivated governor of the state has understood that individuals have erred by misusing letters, scarcely anyone will deny that it is his power to restrain those men.

Only let not the fault of one be transferred to all, and on account of the error of an artisan let the art itself be considered pernicious, and let liberty be taken away from literature, which, when you have removed it, even the most diligent care will not be able to restore.
But he who has reviewed the memory of times will find that ruined states or their leaders have not infrequently been hostile to learning.
For not only on account of confession of faith and religion have pious men experienced iron and fire;
But because philosophy seemed to censure unjust power, it also had those by whom it was harassed.

As once at Rome, when Junius Rusticus had published the praises of Paetus Thrasea and Helvidius Priscus, and had called them most holy men, on the occasion of that crime all philosophers, just as formerly actors and Chaldaeans, were removed by a decree of the senate and were banished from the city and Italy.
Everyone concedes that this was not the fault of the philosophers, among whom were most upright men and Epictetus himself, but of the Emperor and the Senate.

And indeed, who would not think that those who, being learned, have shaped their teachings to the agreement of such masters, become participants in the impiety of tyrants and are to be regarded as parricides in the republic of letters?
Then everyone concedes that the fault was not of the philosophers, among whom there were most upright men and Epictetus himself, but of the Prince and the Senate.

And indeed, who would not think that those who, being learned, have shaped their opinions to the consensus of such masters, become participants in the impiety of tyrants and should be regarded as being in the place of parricides in the literary republic?

Therefore, to return to the point from which I digressed, if any apply their learning to this end, that they may flatter either the common people or the powerful, in order to win favor for themselves or procure honors, I call them not truly learned, but sophists:

For it is the mark of a sophist not to devote himself to eternal truth and genuine knowledge, but, by putting on the appearance of a philosopher, to serve the pleasure of those whose approval he eagerly seeks, and to accustom his mind to their opinions, so that he thinks and says nothing other than what they approve, and judges the same things as they do to be good or bad, beautiful or ugly:
For he does this in order to gain a little glory, to satisfy his ambition, and finally to make a profit.
You see, listeners, that I in speaking spontaneously arrive at a fault, which among the learned I consider not the least, namely the desire for gain.
For not a few seem to be those who, considering learning as a trade, devote mercenary labor to it;
which both the Greek sophists once did and many in our age, especially since payment began to be given to writers:
I do not say this in such a way as to deny that those who devote all their leisure to literature should be rewarded with prizes;
while they are intent on these things, they cannot seek by another way what is necessary for maintaining honorably their livelihood and culture;

But the pursuits of learning ought to spring from the impulse of a mind inclined to the practice of the good arts and, as it were, by a divine instinct, and ought to be directed to the propagation of truth; they ought not to arise from the desire of acquiring wealth, nor to be turned to profit.

And the fruits that are derived from these, whether they are to be held in second or in no place, are to be done either nothing or very little for their sake, which you would not do unless a reward had been set before you.

But I turn my speech away from the vices, which the rule hostile to justice begets from evil desires, and I refresh myself with the contemplation of that virtue, by which, since no single virtue can be held without the others, the rest are perfected;
I mean courage of spirit.
For courage is not only a military virtue:
although all mortals, each in his own way, in a certain sense serve as soldiers:
but wherever there are things that frighten a man, the terrors must be overcome by courage.

For first, no one who has been more keenly engaged in these matters fails to understand with what difficulties the path of wisdom is hedged about, how steep, how obstructed it is, and with how many labors and vigils the inner entrance of the sciences is opened.
Therefore no one can become learned through laziness and torpor.

Although there are certain indolent minds which, spurning solid knowledge and relying on the goodness of the talent they boast of, imagine that the deepest knowledge is revealed to them as if they were dreaming.
On the contrary, if you wish to make progress, there is need of strenuous effort, and impatience of toil, sloth, and distrust of one's powers must be overcome with a brave spirit.
Then, the learned man, in whatever discipline he has undertaken to teach, should not spare his strength in both thoroughly learning it and diligently transmitting it.
Let him boldly defend the truth with the weapons of his intellect; finally, when there is need and it is necessary, let him profess it even at the risk of giving offense.
For as I praise obedience and modesty, unless hypocrisy is present,
As I prefer prudent silence to untimely license in speaking, so I will not approve the man who, without any compelling necessity, has thrown himself headlong into danger.
Thus I think that a learned man can be brought to such a point that, unless he prefers to admit wickedness or hypocrisy in himself, he cannot avoid the crisis.
Therefore, if anyone has been reduced to that state, a constant and resolute mind will hold him back, so that he does not timidly abandon his opinion.

And rightly judging what is truly fearful and what should not be feared, he will not so much dread threats and terrors, by which the immortal mind cannot be subdued, as the sharpest stings of conscience, which burn and prick late.
For, to speak with the poet, the ardor of citizens commanding base things does not shake the just man firm of purpose, nor the face of a threatening tyrant, his mind being solid;
He, since he wishes not to seem good but to be good, will not fear the appearance of wickedness in the midst of the highest justice.
By this greatness of soul Socrates became famous, by this John Huss;
this led Luther through so many dangers of circumstances unshaken:
by this, if it is permitted to compare a heavenly man with mortals, the most holy author of our faith testified to and sealed the divinity of his teaching;
And those whom the madness of their contemporaries condemned, the judgment of centuries acquits and crowns with garlands.
Let the entrance to learning be opened; there is no one who has been engaged in them more keenly but understands:
Therefore, through laziness and sluggishness no one can become learned;

Although there are certain sluggish minds, which, spurning solid knowledge and relying on the goodness of the talent they boast of, think that, as if dreaming, the deepest knowledge is revealed to them.
On the contrary, if you wish to make progress, there is need of strenuous effort, and impatience of toil, sloth, and distrust of one's powers must be overcome with a brave spirit.
Then, the learned man, in whatever discipline he has undertaken to teach, should not spare his strength in both thoroughly learning it and diligently transmitting it.
Let him boldly defend the truth with the weapons of his intellect; finally, when it shall be necessary and essential, let him profess it even at the risk of giving offense.
For just as I praise obedience and modesty, unless hypocrisy lies beneath,
As I prefer prudent silence to untimely license in speaking, I will not approve of the man who, without any compelling necessity, has thrown himself headlong into danger:
Thus I think that a learned man can be brought to such a point that, unless he prefers to admit wickedness or hypocrisy in himself, he cannot avoid the crisis.
Therefore, if anyone has been reduced to that state, a constant and resolute mind will keep him from timidly abandoning his opinion;

And rightly judging what is truly fearful and what should not be feared, he will not so much dread threats and terrors, by which the immortal mind cannot be subdued, as the sharpest stings of conscience, which burn and prick late.
For, to speak with the poet, the ardor of citizens commanding base things does not shake the just man firm of purpose, nor the face of a threatening tyrant, in his solid mind;
The same man, since he wishes not to seem good but to be good, will not fear the appearance of wickedness in the midst of the highest justice.
By this greatness of soul Socrates became famous, by this John Huss;
this led Luther unconquered through so many crises of dangers:
by this, if it is permitted to compare a heavenly man with mortals, the most holy author of our faith testified to and sealed the divinity of his teaching;
And those whom the madness of their contemporaries condemned, the judgment of centuries has acquitted and adorns with crowns.
This seems to me to be the highest virtue of the learned, listeners, and whoever follows it will also hold the other virtues, which it is long and unnecessary to set forth.
For although virtue is one, though divided into its parts, I do not think it necessary to descend to each secondary particle, because he who holds the most important ones has possessed all the rest.

And your role, too, must be considered by me, my dearest colleagues, that is, of men most distinguished in letters, who seem to have known even better what I can set forth according to my own capacity.

Indeed, whoever has entered upon the plan which I have proposed will have great influence for living well in tranquility of mind, in good conscience, and in the consciousness of duty, and anxious cares about the past life will not come upon him on the threshold of old age, but he will live with good hope in whatever fortune.
Of the most distinguished men, who seem to have known even better what I can set forth according to my capacity.

Now indeed, whoever has entered upon the plan which I have proposed will have great influence for living happily in tranquility of mind, in good conscience, and in the awareness of duty, and anxieties about the past life will not assail him on the threshold of old age, but he will live with good hope in whatever fortune.

But we, whom Frederick William, a most upright prince, has assembled for the purpose of educating the youth, ought especially to do this: that we ourselves be upright and honest, and that we make our pupils such by our instruction.

If they have become accustomed in their studies to look exclusively at and admire what is true and right, and to restrain their minds from the base desires that drive mortals astray, then even in the other walks of life and in business, and in the state itself, they will show themselves such as Frederick William demands, and they will excel in purity of morals, obedience to the laws, loyalty, and piety, and they will spread these same arts more and more widely throughout the whole commonwealth.

Nor do I think that in our state anything is to be feared for literature, since Frederick William demands not slavery of minds, but liberal obedience, and we do not live in a corrupt republic, but in one whose citizens, distinguished by love of country proven by deeds, the love of a good king, the strongest bond of concord, joins together as it were into one family:

Although they differ in the situation of their lands, the nature of their climate, their customs, and their institutions, yet they unanimously agree in loving and esteeming the king with affection and judgment.
When this feeling of affection has failed, we must fear that the state, however well constituted, may be overthrown or fall apart.
Hence the greater is the praise of the king, who by justice, moderation, and clemency attracts and fosters the zeal of the people.
For just as these things are acquired and retained by good arts, so when they have been relaxed, they can hardly be recovered.
And when mutual trust between prince and people has been removed, suspicions, hatreds, factional discord, and finally seditions begin to rage.

Since so many kingdoms have been troubled and torn by these, and are still being torn, it can be understood how much we owe to the wise moderation of Frederick William, who provides a tranquil state to this city and happiness to its citizens.

But returning to the praises of the dearest Prince, as I said at the beginning, I have not undertaken to repeat what has already been done and to explain each and every one of his virtues at length by discussing them.
Nevertheless, I will not pass over one thing in silence, to which the theme of my speech leads me of its own accord.
For, as I indicated above, a truly just man is free from every kind of ambition, and ambition itself, since it is to be counted among the desires, harms virtue more than it helps it.
But many princes give much to fame;

Brought up in great affairs, in a court that shows a more splendid appearance than the truth of things, they are accustomed to become used to certain empty images of magnificence, liberality, and glory.
But what of Frederick William?
He, alien to empty show, wishes not to seem good but to be good:
he practices virtue for the sake of virtue:
he will indeed have eternity of name, but he does not seek it ambitiously.
And since I have mentioned liberality, everyone agrees with one voice that no one shows himself more munificent to letters and arts than Frederick William.

Of this praise there exist so many proofs, so many indeed begun, but because great undertakings cannot be completed in a short time, not yet finished, they will exist in the future, so that even if I should wish to enumerate them, my time would not now suffice.
But are these things boasted of?
Did Frederick William undertake these plans for the sake of his name?
Indeed, the King's modesty in conducting these matters is so great that I can scarcely dare to praise them myself.
Therefore, Frederick William's kindness toward literature is found to be such as it ought to be.
Acknowledging this with a grateful mind, I also urge you, fellow soldiers, to show yourselves grateful to your excellent Prince:
This will be done most correctly when you satisfy his expectation.
But what does it expect and demand from you?
Nothing indeed else, except that as in the other institutions of life, so in the pursuit of letters, you be upright and honest.
that each one in his own kind of knowledge may turn out so perfect, as the weakness of the human mind and the disposition of each one may allow;
which cannot happen without diligence and industry;
Finally, so that you may attain that virtue which, unless a learned man possesses it, he must be considered to have lost all the fruit of his labors.
And yet I have taught that continence and temperance are also included, which should admonish us not to meddle with others' affairs.

Indeed, nothing seems more alien to the knowledge of learning than the plans of societies forbidden by laws, such as are accustomed to be established in academies, which have called back not a few not only from the eagerness for studies, but also have entangled them in greater evils, which would have been more serious in the future, had not the King's clemency pardoned those who had lapsed.
Therefore consider with what purpose Frederick William founded this home of letters:
Strive to satisfy this end, and carefully beware of whatever is opposed to his wise plans.
Consider what gifts he has bestowed upon you and bestows daily, with such great opportunity for learning offered, which, being abundant on all sides, harms virtue more than it helps.
But many princes give much to fame;

Those brought up in great affairs, in a court that displays a more splendid appearance than the truth of things, are accustomed to become used to certain empty images of magnificence, liberality, and glory.
But what of Frederick William?
He, far from empty appearance, wishes not to seem good but to be good:
He practices virtue for the sake of virtue:
He will indeed have eternity of name, but he does not seek it ambitiously.
And since I have mentioned liberality, everyone agrees with one voice that no one shows himself more munificent to letters and arts than Frederick William.

Of this praise there exist so many proofs, so many begun indeed, but because great undertakings cannot be completed in a short time, not yet finished, they will exist in the future, so that even if I should wish to enumerate them, my time would not now suffice.
But are these things boasted of?
Did Frederick William undertake these plans for the sake of his own name?
On the contrary, the King's modesty in conducting these matters as well is so great that I can scarcely venture to praise them myself.
Therefore Frederick William's kindness toward literature is found to be such as it ought to be;
Acknowledging this with a grateful mind, I also urge you, fellow soldiers, to show yourselves grateful to your excellent Prince:
This will be done most correctly when you satisfy his expectation.
But what does it expect and demand from you?
Nothing indeed else, except that as in the other institutions of life, so in the pursuit of letters, you be upright and honest:
that each one in his own kind of knowledge may turn out so perfect, as the weakness of the human mind and the nature of each one may allow;
which cannot happen without diligence and industry;
Finally, so that you may attain that virtue which, unless a learned man possesses it, he must be considered to have lost all the fruit of his labors.
And yet I have taught that continence and temperance are also included in that (virtue), which should admonish us not to handle others' affairs.

Indeed, nothing seems more alien to the knowledge of learning than the plans of societies forbidden by laws, such as are accustomed to be established in academies, which have recalled not a few not only from the eagerness for studies, but also have entangled them in greater evils, which would have been more serious in the future, had not the King's clemency pardoned those who had lapsed.
Therefore consider with what purpose Frederick William founded this home of letters:
To satisfy that end, give your effort, and whatever is opposed to his wise counsels, guard against it diligently:
Consider what gifts he has bestowed upon you and bestows daily, with such great opportunity for learning offered to you, which is increased day by day by gathering resources from all sides;

And you testify to minds mindful of benefits, our countrymen by piety towards the Father of the fatherland, foreigners by recollection of the discipline, which you enjoy liberally from his institution, both by reverence for the laws and royal virtue.
It is increased by being gathered daily;

And you testify to minds mindful of benefits, our countrymen by piety towards the Father of the fatherland, foreigners by recollection of the discipline, which you enjoy liberally from his institution, both by reverence for the laws and royal virtue.
But for us, dearest colleagues, what must be done, I would be arrogant if I wanted to say.
We have been taught, we know well enough.
Nevertheless, let us confirm in these solemn and most sacred rites the oath sworn to the best Prince:
Let us pledge that we will propagate the light of literature, love of country, safety of the empire, piety, and virtue by example and instruction.

Finally, let us all who are present invoke the aid and kindness of the divine power, that it may add very many years to the life of Frederick William, that it may protect the good minds of him and of the ministers and of all the citizens, and finally that it may preserve forever the ruling house, the harmony of the republic, and all the dearest goods which it has bestowed upon us.

div.head: XII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXIV. habita.

p.s: About to celebrate the birthday of Frederick William, the best of kings, this year, listeners, I do not think I can take a more serious beginning from anything than from the memory of that day on which the whole state with the greatest zeal prayed for a happy, fortunate, and prosperous marriage for the king's son, heir to the empire, and for the august wife, and rendered the entry of the royal bride distinguished not only by such great pomp, which indeed we had not seen before in this city, but also by that ardor of minds which would provide the surest proof of inner affection.
For whatever was given to the son in honor on that day, it is established by this, how greatly the father was loved by the citizens, at the same time having been approved.
And indeed this is not small.
For the offices of reverence and affection that are offered to princes, you may rarely distinguish whether they are true or feigned:

Indeed, such is the unhappiness of those who rule in the highest fortune, that there are found people who, the closer they are to them or wish to be, the less sincere, less simple and open they tend to be; moreover, they say and do everything more intently, by which they either preserve or procure their favor for themselves, concealing servile obedience under the pretense of goodwill for the sake of private advantage:
Ambition creeps in from every side, and especially in great disturbances, the more hateful those who disparage are, the easier is the approach for the flatterer.

But when the people are numerous, and what happens joyfully for the imperial house they accompany not with their own joy but with exultation, the impulse of loyal devotion bursts forth without hope of rewards;
In public joys each one sets aside his own gains, losses, advantages, and adversities.

Now indeed, if we inquire what things excite so great a fervor of the people, although I do not deny that the duties owed to the head of the state claim something for themselves from that, because the uncorrupted citizens and the very plebs, if they do not perceive, at least they feel that the king sustains the person of the whole state;

nevertheless, by far the greatest part of the virtues that stand out in princes — of justice, kindness, clemency — seems to be attributed to the silent esteem and to the memory of a gloriously administered empire:

Since even those whom the prince has not distinguished by any more notable favor are found to be filled with these feelings, it is evident that those popular demonstrations are very far removed from private advantage.
Therefore nothing can happen to the prince more desirable than that most beautiful spectacle of public joy.
Since we too have been especially allowed to share in this, a greater opportunity has then been given to testify our goodwill than that which recurs every year on this very day.
On the day on which you seem to be compelled, not without your detriment, to use my poor speech repeatedly.
And then the courtesy of the king as well as of the king's son was a great consolation to us;
and it was understood that a youth faithful to its prince was being raised by us:
What could have been more acceptable to us than this, especially at these times, when literary universities, once held in the honors of Germany, are subject to the gravest accusations?

Therefore let us give thanks to the wisest king and to the interpreters of royal counsels, because we seem to be freed at the same time from the blame and suspicion of those evils which have been eradicated among us.

to be sincere, less simple and open, and indeed to say and do everything all the more intently, by which they may either preserve or acquire for themselves the favor of those, covering servile obedience with a pretense of goodwill for the sake of private advantage:
Ambition creeps in from every side, and especially in great upheavals, the more hateful those who disparage are, the easier is the approach for the flatterer.

But when the people in great numbers accompany with their own exultation, not joy, the events that are favorable to the imperial house, the impulse of loyal devotion breaks forth without hope of rewards;
In public joys each person sets aside his own gains, losses, advantages, and adversities.

Now indeed, if we inquire what things excite so great a fervor of the people, although I do not deny that the duties owed to the head of the state claim something for themselves from that source, because the uncorrupted citizens and the very plebs, if they do not perceive, certainly feel that the king sustains the person of the whole state;

nevertheless, by far the greatest part of the virtues that stand out in princes — of justice, of kindness, of clemency — seems to be attributed to the silent esteem and to the memory of a state gloriously administered:

Since even those whom the prince has not distinguished by any notable favor are found to be filled with these feelings, it is clear that those popular demonstrations are far removed from private advantage.
Therefore nothing can happen to the prince more desirable than that most beautiful spectacle of public joy.
Since we too have been allowed to participate in this especially, a greater opportunity has then been given to testify our goodwill than that which recurs every year on this very day:
On the day on which you seem to be compelled, not without your detriment, to use my poor speech repeatedly.
And then the courtesy of the king as well as of the king's son was a great consolation to us;
and it was understood that a youth faithful to its prince is nourished by us:
What could be more acceptable to us than this, especially in these times, when literary universities, once held among the ornaments of Germany, are subject to the gravest accusations?

Therefore let us give thanks to the most wise King and to the interpreters of royal counsels, because we seem at the same time to be freed from the blame and suspicion of those evils which have been eradicated among us.
Indeed, it is a great thing, dearest colleagues, to undertake the education of youth, a great thing at any time:
for the discipline of the present age shapes the fortune of the future one:
it is greater in a precarious state of the republic and in a great crisis, such as foreign power has stirred up for almost all of Europe a few decades ago;
But it seems to me most important, since the shaken world has not yet settled into complete quiet.
For letters lift up minds, they drive away sleep:
or at least, when they first begin to shape sleepy pupils, let them be strong.
And so it can happen that they apply minds roused by letters to a bad purpose, those whose nature is inclined to worse:
yet it is not the fault of letters, if someone abuses the ability acquired by letters.
Indeed, it seems to me that the supreme deity can scarcely bestow upon mortals a more excellent gift than a vigorous and sound knowledge:
In place of which, when they take up a dead one, the loss in this is so much the greater, as the salvation in that is more effective.
Or at least, when they first begin to form sleepy students, let them be strong.
And so it can happen that they apply minds roused by literature to the wrong side, for whom the disposition is prone to worse:
However, it is not the fault of literature if someone, having acquired the ability through literature, abuses it.
Indeed, to me it seems that the supreme deity has scarcely granted a more excellent gift to mortals than vigorous and sound knowledge:
In place of which, when they take up a lifeless one, the loss in this is so much greater, as the salvation in that is more effective.
But what exactly do I call vigorous and sound knowledge?
Not that which stirs up crowds, which would attempt revolutions:
This is not even knowledge, nor will it be called by that name by anyone.
I mean something conceived in the mind, which, especially before you, I hardly feel myself equal to explaining eloquently.
I therefore ask pardon from you, if the outcome does not match so great an undertaking.

For just as nature has given to each living being a life separated to some extent from other things, and endowed with its own powers, which our people call organic, and has comprehended it in an inseparable union of body and soul—of soul, I say, which, as it were, penetrates the whole structure of the body, communicates form and motion to the limbs, and unites the dissociated and inert particles of matter into one whole and fills them with vigor—
so also the vigorous science seems to have been constituted.
Of course, the beginning of its life lies within itself.

And even if it is nourished from without, especially by the state, and is connected with the relations of other human affairs, nevertheless it does not receive its power from them, nor is it their servant, and therefore, unless you wish to corrupt its excellence and beauty, it cannot be cultivated to such an end as to serve alien uses or the pursuit of livelihood:
But those who devote themselves to literature ought to be warmed and stirred by the divine sparks that are within us.

Therefore, the rulers of states who wish well for literature ought to take care and look ahead that men do not occupy public chairs who practice the good arts without being inspired by any nobler impulse, but treat them like hired servants in the place of common duties.
For what will more readily deliver students to idleness than the daily sight of a teacher who teaches his doctrines not in accordance with their worth nor with the ardor with which he ought?
Again, only that knowledge will be vital and strong which you yourself have hammered out with the generative force of your own mind:

so that the ability to teach seems to be placed much less in transmitting doctrines than in stirring minds, and in inciting them to reproduce, according to the disposition of their nature, what the teacher demonstrates.

But if you should try to compel and drive anyone, as if by laying hold of him, to the knowledge of any matter from which his nature recoils, you will accomplish either nothing or this: that, since nothing can be transferred into anyone against his natural disposition, he will not grasp the knowledge with his mind, but only the mere information with his memory.
as if you had made Apollo's form out of a wooden block;
from a person's mind cannot be drawn out those things whose seeds are not placed in it.
Now, since we see that very few mortals have been given so favorable a vein of talent that, whatever object they have applied their mind to, they accomplish it with equal success;

It is understood that the universities of Germany provide a great advantage to learners, because in them free power of choosing various disciplines has been left to them, and they can themselves find out by experience in which they may place their study either against Minerva's will or with her favor:
On this matter we are so much in agreement that anyone who calls it into doubt would be judged to be bound by a heavy stupor.
But I pass over this;
so that I, who think that these commonplaces should be run through briefly, lest your learning disdain my words.

If you should try to compel and force it to be learned, as if by laying hold of it, you will achieve either nothing or this: that, since nothing can be transferred into any mind against its nature, he will not grasp the knowledge with his mind, but the mere acquaintance with his memory.
as if you had made the form of Apollo out of a wooden stump;
they cannot be drawn out of a man's mind, whose seeds are not placed in it.
Now, since we see that very few mortals have been given so generous a vein of talent that, whatever object they have applied their mind to, they accomplish it with equal success;

The universities of Germany are understood to provide a great advantage to learners, because in them free power of choosing various disciplines has been left to them, and they can themselves find out by experience in which they may place their study either against Minerva's will or with her favor:
On this matter we are so agreed among ourselves that anyone who calls it into doubt is judged to be bound by a heavy stupor.
But I pass over this;
so that I, who think these commonplaces should be run through briefly, may not have your learning disdain my words.
But from that generative power of the mind, the mother of all, notions abound, by which matter is governed:
But just as this is indistinct and confused without those, so those are deprived of their body without this.

Both must be so adapted to each other that the mind rightly arranges the abundance of matter, that the abundance of things fills the forms of notions, and finally that there is an indissoluble bond between both; this is what scholars must strive for.
But this is accomplished with more difficulty than very many think.

Since, among those who strive with the greatest force to know pure notions, some not infrequently fall into this fault, that they both hold and hawk about the empty designation of empty places or empty formulas as if they were science itself, and indeed, puffed up with these very things, think themselves by far the wisest; while others, by dividing and distinguishing too much, so cut up and mangle the elements of knowledge that neither juice nor blood remains, but a certain thin appearance and shadow of learning, scarcely clinging to the bones.

On the other hand, there have been and still are those who are busy piling up a rough heap, in which, as Anaxagoras said, all things are mixed together, and intelligence has not yet permeated the mass.
These men, too, from time to time seem to themselves to be the only learned ones, and they despise all others before them as illiterate.

Just as each person will find examples of these faults in his own discipline, so in my studies I see others, endowed with remarkable acumen, but aided too little by sufficient learning, err through that very subtlety; others have their mental vision dimmed and hindered by the mass of material, because they have either insufficient intellectual powers, or they do not cultivate the powers they have.

But even if each of the two methods can bring some benefit to literature, yet it is clear that neither contains the truly vital force of science, but that force is seen in that alone, the agreement of concepts and things.
can, yet it is clear that neither contains the truly vital force of science, but that force is seen in that alone, the agreement of concepts and things.
But when you ask how it can best be aroused and unfolded in the minds of learners, I answer that nothing can accomplish this more surely than the living voice of the teacher:
because he who draws knowledge from books must himself, as it were, restore to what is written there the life and motion that they have lost;
Words that flow from the mouth of a teacher, if only the teacher is suitable, insinuate themselves more easily into the minds of eager students by their own enthusiasm.

And yet I would not call that a living voice, which, as I am now doing according to the custom received in solemn orations, recites what is written and hands it over to be written down and carried home.

But although in the immense apparatus of literature, for comprehending which no single person is sufficient, not every smallest detail can be held in mind and memory, so that accordingly some moderation is needed in this matter;

nevertheless it would be a wonder, if even an average teacher, while teaching, were carried along by a free course of thoughts, and expressed those very things, which he had meditated, distinguished by clearer lights, than when he sat in his study.
The very presence of the learners adds a spur to the one who is discoursing and kindles the sparks of his talent.
Indeed, that saying which has become a proverb, that one learns by teaching, seems to me to be referred especially to this point, not to be interpreted as an excuse for unskilled teachers.

Therefore, not indeed an ornate and copious diction of an orator or declaimer, which is somewhat alien to accurate learning, but an elevated and ready and, as I may say, spirited exposition of thoughts is demanded.
I have not set this before you, most beloved colleagues, in order that you might be taught what you ought to do:
but I judge that in this especially, while nearly all the German universities, then your schools (for let it be allowed me to praise you) excel:
whence it happens that this discipline forms young men for the most part not sluggish and torpid, but inflamed with the most keen desire of propagating the good arts:
This very thing, the more it may blaze forth, can recall them from foreign matters and from things not suitable for this age, by the practice of such things.
Thus, having been cultivated, the young men will hold the learning they have acquired not by memory alone but by understanding.

For just as without memory nothing, not even philosophy, can be learned, because he who lacks it will retain neither things nor notions, but everything will flow out of him as from a perforated vessel;
so that it may even bring great weight to the learned man, namely to be mindful:
nevertheless, whatever knowledge is supported only by the powers of memory and recollection is not living but dead.

From this it is at the same time understood that letters cannot flourish, if a certain fixed and perpetual discipline, which is handed over to memory rather than to the mind, is to be followed, not to mention if a prescribed course is to be followed:
As this itself will grow old more and more day by day, so it will give even fervid minds to languor, unless they resist with innate force.
Certainly there are constant and eternal notions of the human mind, which, because truth is immortal, are never abolished nor obliterated;
but these also are regenerated by free thought, not according to a prescription:
you may command what is to be done, you may forbid what is to be avoided;

And if any pernicious opinions are spread abroad (although in this state, tempered by good morals and institutions, they rarely creep further), lest the republic suffer harm, we must undoubtedly take precautions with milder remedies, or, where necessary, even with harsh ones.
But what is true, what you think, what you are convinced of, cannot be commanded.

Therefore, by prescribing fixed doctrines, you will accomplish nothing, except that both teachers and learners are dulled, indeed become stupid and foolish, or pretend one thing while keeping another hidden in their hearts.
Or should we think that letters, which are constrained by boundaries drawn at will, can grow more than a tree, to which light is blocked and a wall is drawn around?
Those bonds, indeed, which were once most strongly imposed upon literature, were chiefly woven by superstition, lest, with the darkness dispelled, minds should be set free.
But it has died out.

From this it is at the same time understood that literature cannot flourish, if a certain fixed and perpetual discipline, which is handed down to memory rather than to the mind, is to be followed, not to mention if prescribed rules are to be followed:
As this itself will grow old more and more day by day, so it will give even fervid minds to languor, unless they resist with innate force.
Certainly there are constant and eternal notions of the human mind, which, because truth is immortal, are never abolished nor obliterated;
but these also are regenerated by free thought, not according to a prescription:
you may command what should be done, you may forbid what should be avoided;

And if any pernicious doctrines are propagated (although these in a state tempered by good morals and institutions rarely spread more widely), lest the republic suffer any harm, it must undoubtedly be guarded against by milder remedies, or, where there is need, even by harsh ones:
But what is true, what you think, what you are convinced of, cannot be commanded.

Therefore, by prescribing fixed doctrines, you will accomplish nothing, except that both teachers and learners are dulled, indeed become stupid and foolish, or pretend one thing while keeping another hidden in their breast.
Or should we think that letters, which are constrained by boundaries drawn at will, can grow more than a tree, to which light is blocked and a wall is drawn around?
Those bonds, indeed, which were once especially imposed upon literature, were woven chiefly by superstition, lest, with the darkness dispelled, minds should be set free.

Indeed, the governors of states, the wiser they are, the more they desire the light of literature to be spread abroad, because the more intelligent their subjects become, the more their industry, agility, and even their modesty and universal virtue are strengthened.
Thus the state flourishes, and in the midst of the citizens' happiness the house of the princes is firmly established.

On the other hand, just as the unskilled common people, so also the peoples held in the slavery of their minds, rush headlong by a chance impulse into new things and into any crimes whatsoever that must be dared;
Sometimes even the states themselves perish together with their literature, which is withering away, by a long decay.
For although by the hidden counsel of fate divinely established, at different times different nations are increased or diminished, nevertheless the nations themselves accelerate their fates:
And the neglect of literature, which had previously flourished, seems to be a sign of a decrepit state and, as it were, a foreboding of impending ruin.
And indeed that neglect has not been brought about in all places or times by the fault of the state;

On the contrary, the idleness and laziness of private individuals can bring greater harm to literature than the wicked laws and decrees of states, especially when corruption of morals and an insane desire for gain, together with illiberality, grows strong.

For indeed in the Greek states especially, in which literature and the arts reached that flower which up to this very day has nowhere yet been restored, learning was born and took its growth not from public institution, but from the innate character of the race and the common pursuits of private individuals;
so that if you should make a conjecture from the Greeks, you would judge public aid to be not at all necessary for literature:
Indeed, by the time money began to be spent by the states on literature, literature had already long since contracted a stain.
Therefore, the negligence of those whose virtue and talent nourished the doctrines can hasten their destruction.
Nevertheless, for the good arts, it matters very much what the condition of the republic is.

For not to mention how much the savage tyranny of tyrants impedes the investigation of human and divine affairs, and with how great anxiety it disturbs and breaks the minds, which has been proved at Rome by the rule of the most atrocious men and those hostile to the whole human race;

Therefore, to omit this, is there not a great importance in the cultivation of the arts, in what may be expected or demanded from those who are to handle public affairs, who are to execute laws, who are to administer sacred rites?

Would the eloquence of Pericles or of Demosthenes have stood out in Greece, if the Athenian assembly had tolerated a rough and unpolished speech, and if access to public affairs had been open equally to uncultivated men as to the most elegant and learned?
Would Marcus
Tullius Cicero, Gaius

Would Julius Caesar and Octavian Augustus have been about to acquire that abundance of varied learning, if the wisest of their contemporaries had judged that anyone could be distinguished in public life who had barely been imbued with letters?
What of the fact that the ancient Greeks and Romans excelled especially in those disciplines which seemed to make men most fit for conducting public affairs?
Therefore among them no part of the more liberal education was more cultivated than oratory, in which we are especially deficient, because all things were governed by the power of speaking:

And although we may grant that the Greeks were born for the fashioning of oratory, nevertheless, unless that form of state had come to them which favored the more vigorous exercise of this faculty, they would not have made much progress, as Sparta shows, which never produced any orator.
Nor indeed did philosophy seem alien to the Greeks from the management of public affairs;
for which reason philosophy was the more celebrated among them:
whose place at Rome the skill of law in a certain way occupied.

Since these things were so, we do not wonder that very many who excelled in learning among the ancients were not born in a humble station, nor were they versed in the shadow of schools, but each in his own city was either powerful or illustrious.

Just as among the Romans themselves, although they are not to be compared with the Greeks, if we consider especially some poets, they reached such a flower of excellence that up to this very day it has nowhere been restored, not by public institution, but by an innate disposition of the people and by the common pursuits of private individuals, learning was born and took its growth;
so that if you should make a conjecture from the Greeks, you would judge that public assistance is not at all necessary for literature:
