Would Julius Caesar and Octavian Augustus have been about to acquire that abundance of varied learning, if the wisest of their contemporaries had judged that no one could be distinguished in the state who had been barely imbued with letters?
What of the fact that the ancient Greeks and Romans excelled especially in those disciplines which seemed most suitable for conducting public affairs?
Therefore among them no part of the more liberal education was more cultivated than oratory, in which we are most deficient, because all things were governed by the power of speaking:

And although we may concede that the Greeks were born for the fashioning of oratory, nevertheless, unless that form of state had come to them which favored the more vigorous exercise of this faculty, they would not have made much progress, as Sparta shows, which never produced any orator.
Nor indeed did philosophy seem alien to the Greeks from the management of public affairs;
the more philosophy was celebrated among them:
whose place at Rome the skill of law in a certain way occupied.

Since these things were so, we do not wonder that very many who excelled in learning among the ancients were not born in a humble place, nor were they versed in the shadow of schools, but each in his own city was either powerful or illustrious.

In the same way, among the Romans themselves, although they are not to be compared with the Greeks, if you should except some poets especially and certain rhetoricians and grammarians who were freedmen or plebeians, almost all the best authors were knights, senators, praetorians, and consulars.
If you should except the rhetoricians and grammarians who were freedmen or plebeians, almost all the best authors were knights, senators, praetorians, and consulars.

And although it may rightly be judged unfair that the path to literature is closed to gifted minds, which lie hidden even among the rustic common people and among the shopkeepers' apprentices, the assistants in the shops,

nevertheless, I do not know whether in ancient literature this had great force, that men distinguished by nobility of birth, wealth, and honors strove to become famous for the reputation of literature retained from a good education, and did not leave it to little men of humble condition or even to those oppressed by hunger:
Therefore it cannot happen that they become cheap.
And we see that in our own age and in our own republic the pursuits of leading men are being revived.

But in the different disposition of our people, who are less inclined to the liberal arts, and in that rust which they seem to have retained from their former barbarism, the greater part of the nobility as well as the common people, since, unless the state had founded and maintained public games of every kind of literature, letters would soon have fallen.
The state had to take upon itself this excellent burden of nurturing the good arts, and it was taken up.

She will bear this best, if she will provide not only buildings and equipment for literature and a livelihood for those teaching, but also will grant to literature its just freedom, so that it can flourish, and will indeed restrain wantonness, immodesty, and fierceness, but will allow you to feel what you wish and to say what you feel, and indeed will praise the open profession of one's opinion:

Finally, if he will demand a more distinguished skill in letters and a strong and vigorous knowledge from those who have wished to approach the state and to perform its duties, he will indeed reject those mercenaries, who seek nothing from letters except a slight practice, which would scarcely suffice for their duties, and this very practice for the sake of bread.
But if this does not happen, both public and literary affairs will rush to ruin, and in vain will it be labored to prolong a life that is no longer vital to a dead body.

Thus, however many schools were founded by the Roman emperors as the empire was declining, however many salaries were paid to rhetoricians, grammarians, philosophers, physicians, and professors of law, partly much more ample than in our century, however many prerogatives and honors were conferred—

Those benefits could not hold back the impending ruin, because, with spirits broken by servitude and vigor lost, literature had become numb, and those who devoted themselves to it, for the most part, sought not refined and liberal learning, but handsome returns from public offices.
But what did the discipline prescribed through the seven arts profit in the Middle Ages?
With what rudiments did the sad and severe discipline of the monasteries nourish the mind?
Of course, the less exact learning could be imposed on the clergy in barbarous kingdoms, the more it happened that they did not even attain to that which had been commanded.

so that we should be proclaimed blessed, because that age did not consume all the best monuments of a more refined life, but certainly handed them down to posterity, in whom those who, having broken their bonds, dared to be wise themselves might grow warm.
Was it the severe discipline of the monasteries?
Of course, the less exact learning could be imposed on the clergy in barbarous kingdoms, the more it happened that they did not even attain to that which had been commanded.

So that we should be proclaimed blessed, because that age did not destroy all the best monuments of a more refined life, but certainly handed them down to posterity, in which those who, having broken their bonds, dared to think for themselves might grow warm.
But I return from the contemplation of these things, which perhaps led me a little too far astray;
Let us consider the plans of our most beloved king.
For the Prussian state has for a long time enjoyed the praise of vigorous science and of intellect diffused through all parts of the commonwealth;
to this, not to its bulk, its force is to be attributed.
This most excellent reputation, as long as we obey these kings, does not seem to be feared lest it perish.
In our own affairs, whatever has been changed in these recent years was not done with the intention of detracting anything from literature.
Nor has anything been detracted.
Why should we not also in the future be confident, since the King attempts nothing immoderate, and has been observed with the most brilliant proofs of clemency?
This confidence is increased by the affection with which the whole people embraces him, as Germans are devoted with their whole soul to their princes.
For he feels secure and beloved, no less than a father of a family among good children, and he understands that his own safety and that of the people are the same.
The same man is stern, energetic, modest, averse to luxury and pleasures:
but he tempers private and public frugality with that generosity which is fitting.
But although munificence is also seen in giving and in rewarding merits, nevertheless that one is much more excellent and useful which spends wealth on the liberal arts and letters:
from which lasting honors are prepared for the state.
How much Frederick William excelled in both, both in arts and in letters, I have proclaimed not only on many other occasions but especially in a certain Periclean oration long ago:
Now I may add this one thing: the King did not consider the education of youth and the literary enterprise to be that part of the state in which one should spare expenses.
That time is evidence, when this kingdom was fined more than half of its borders; this very literary university, which was then founded, is evidence.
And afterwards nothing was relaxed, but we have experienced the King's perpetual kindness.

Finally, how much the public care for this entire class of things has grown can be understood even from this, that it seemed to be separated from the other affairs of the internal state and worthy of a special administration, entrusted to the best and most experienced men, and if one may judge from the distribution of the supreme government, it claimed for itself the same importance which is held to belong to all revenues and taxes and to military and foreign affairs.
Therefore, concerning what I have discussed above, we see that even from those who seek public offices, no ordinary learning is demanded;

and not only do letters flourish, but also, whatever disturbances the ruinous clubs have produced, academic morals have been eminently corrected, and the former savagery indeed has been so expelled among us that it seems scarcely likely to return.
It has claimed, which is held concerning the revenues and all taxes and military and foreign affairs.
Therefore, concerning what I have discussed above, we see that even from those who seek public offices, no ordinary learning is demanded;

and not only do letters flourish, but also, whatever disturbances the ruinous clubs have produced, academic morals have been eminently corrected, and the former savagery has certainly been so driven out among us that it seems scarcely likely to return.

Since the course of my speech has turned aside to this point, I must warn you in a word, fellow soldiers, that you should persevere in this moderation, in this liberal obedience, and that you should never forget that, although this is proper for the citizens of all universities, yet to you it ought to seem a more sacred duty, who live not only in the royal city, but in the nearest neighborhood of the royal house, nay, in the very eyes and sight of the King.
Nor is it only that Frederick William is a witness to your character, that he ought to serve you as an incentive to virtue;
but this also, both yours and ours, inflames the love of the best Prince, that we enjoy his very sight.
For what is commonly said, that princes are thought greater by those who see them from afar, that indeed you may judge true in the case of those who wrap their head in the splendor of majesty:
That splendor, which strikes unaccustomed eyes more violently, ceases to be venerable through daily habit.

But Frederick William, a popular king, since he possesses those virtues which, the closer you approach, the more distinguished they appear, I understand that he is indeed equally dear to all citizens, but I declare that he is so loved by those who are nearest to him that they at the same time deeply feel and most exactly know why they love him.
You therefore, listeners, both feel and know this best, and indeed with my mouth but with your minds you pray for the help of the highest deity for the Father of the Fatherland.
May the propitious God assent to our prayers, and may he add many glorious and prosperous years both to himself and to the state to his pious worshiper.

div.head: XIII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXV. habita.

p.s: Since this is the fifteenth year, listeners, since this literary university of the dearest King, whose birthday we today piously celebrate, was founded by wise counsels, and the ninth year since, by his command, it was dedicated with solemn rite;

Although during this period of time, for almost a whole year, the pursuits of the arts have been relaxed because of the turmoil of war, and after laying down arms our school has been, as it were, begun anew, nevertheless this school, not indeed by our own merits, but by the kindnesses of our excellent Prince, has in a short time grown to such a degree of splendor and attendance, that, not to say anything too arrogant, it yields to no academy of Germany, and surpasses very many by far.

For what we proclaim with grateful mind and posterity will remember and recall, the flower of letters and the education of every kind, by which the people might be made more refined, no one of our ancestors nor of contemporary princes fostered more lavishly than Frederick William.

Nor is it surprising that in this matter he himself accomplished something greater than the most glorious kings who formerly ruled Prussia, greater than Frederick the First, truly the splendid founder of the University of Halle, greater than that great Frederick, the eternal star of the Prussians;
and not only greater, but also different in many respects from the earlier institutions.
For all other things are of the same form.
Consider this state of the empire, compare the former one:

You will find not only the borders extended, but also the condition of the republic so changed that, just as formerly the Great Elector and soon Frederick the Second were the founders of the kingdom, so Frederick William seems in a certain way to have restored it.
We owe to him so many excellent institutions, he adorned the city with so many ornaments, he heaped the people with so many benefits.
Indeed, a few decades ago we saw the fatherland struck and prostrated by a great calamity.
Then the envious exulted.
They mourned, who had learned to appreciate the virtues of this kingdom;
They endured and hoped with their Prince, the best and bravest:

And soon, by the auspicious counsels of Frederick William, the vital force of the empire, which to some already seemed to be languishing, already seemed to be extinguished, was restored and overflowed, and, pervading the whole body of the state with most joyful vigor, what fruits of health did it not produce?
I am not the one who could precisely point out how each and every part of the state was gradually changed for the better under King Frederick William.
This cannot be done without the greatest experience in affairs.
What lies in everyone's sight, I mention briefly.
For the arrangement of affairs among the king's highest ministers is different from what it once was.
Another division of provinces and form of government, both sacred and profane;
Different constitution of urban affairs and most pleasing to the citizens;
The crafts freed from the bonds of the guilds;
The condition of the rural multitude, freed from servile burdens, was alleviated;
The land itself, by division, more cultivated and more fertile;
The system of military service, revenues, taxes, and commerce was changed.
The army, once not cowardly, indeed ennobled by immortal victories;

But a large part was gathered from mercenaries, who guarded no more than they were guarded, or was enlisted from country folk and common people, who, after being kept for many years at the standards, returned to their own people more corrupt and scarcely fit for civil affairs, or grew old in military service;
The wealthier and more educated youth was exempt from military service and unwarlike:
whence the soldier was more unskilled and had to be restrained by severe punishments, and was more estranged from the citizens:
Finally, in place of the right of military service, which was regarded as honorable by the ancients, there is the most burdensome servitude.

Now all are trained in the exercise of arms, but in this city, which nevertheless is accustomed to be called military, they are discharged earlier than in any other, and are returned to their households, fields, trades, and good arts;
Indeed, what especially concerns us, while they serve in the military, they devote themselves to literature in the universities:
How few in the previous generation were there who thought that these things, which seemed impossible to be united, could be joined together?
Hence the cohorts are full of young men liberally educated, whom a gentle discipline, if indeed there is need, corrects and composes to modesty;
the soldiers themselves, with pride removed, are most honorable and most temperate:
and the number of soldiers is smaller, but the number of warriors is greater.
Nor is a certain order placed before the rest more in military service than in a peaceful state;
The path to higher ranks is open, and to every merit its due honors.
Taxes and tributes, if not reduced, were at least more equitably distributed and more conveniently arranged:

No longer is internal commerce hindered by any obstacles, whereas formerly individual cities were so fenced and closed that whoever set out from one to another seemed to himself to have reached the borders of another kingdom, and all were daily subject to tax collectors:
Now, with the guards removed and with the most joyful vigor permeating the whole body of the state, what fruits of healthful things has it not produced?
I am not the one who could precisely point out, by weighing each and every part of the state, how they were gradually changed for the better under King Frederick William:
which cannot be done without the greatest experience of affairs:
what lies in the sight of all, I mention briefly.
For the arrangement of affairs among the highest ministers of the King is different from what it was formerly;
another is the division of provinces and the form of government, both sacred and profane;
the constitution of urban affairs is different and most pleasing to the citizens;
the workshops are freed from the bonds of the guilds;
the condition of the rural multitude, freed from servile burdens, has been alleviated;
the land itself, by division, is more cultivated and more fertile;
the system of military service, revenues, taxes, and commerce has been changed.
The army, formerly not cowardly, indeed ennobled by immortal victories,

But a large part was gathered from mercenaries, who guarded no more than they were guarded, or was enlisted from country folk and common people, who, after being kept for many years at the standards, returned to their own people corrupted and hardly fit for civil affairs, or grew old in military service.
The wealthier and more educated youth was exempt from military service and unwarlike.
Hence the soldier was more unskilled and had to be restrained by severe punishments, and was more estranged from his fellow citizens.
Finally, in place of the right of military service, which was considered honorable among the ancients, there is the most burdensome servitude.

Now all are trained in the exercise of arms, but in this city, which nevertheless is accustomed to be called military, they are discharged earlier than in any other, and are returned to their households, fields, trades, and good arts;
Indeed, what especially pertains to us, while they serve in the military, they devote themselves to literature in the universities:
How few in the previous generation were there who thought that these things, which seemed impossible to be united, could be joined together?
Hence come cohorts full of young men liberally educated, whom a gentle discipline, if indeed there is need, corrects and composes to modesty;
the soldiers themselves, with pride removed, are most honorable and most temperate:
and the number of soldiers is smaller, but the number of warriors is greater.
Nor is a certain order placed before the rest more in military service than in a peaceful state;
The path to higher ranks is open, and to every merit its due honors.
Taxes and tributes, if not reduced, at least are more equitably distributed and more conveniently arranged:

No longer is internal commerce hindered by any obstacles, whereas formerly individual cities were so fenced and closed that whoever set out from one to another seemed to himself to have arrived at the borders of another kingdom, and all were daily subject to tax collectors:

Now, with guards removed, cities are open day and night, and the gates of many towns have been demolished so that they cannot be closed, and commerce, previously very slow, is accelerated by paving roads and other useful institutions.

Nor indeed did the King order these and other things that differ from the previous form out of a desire for novelty, who, as the ruler of the state ought, especially favors preserving the ancient custom where it is good and useful;
But he understands that a new age must be tempered by new laws and institutions;
that the republic, like all mortal things, being changeable, ought to advance, lest it fail;
and lest it languish through sloth, fresh and vigorous juices must be poured in.
But, although I have selected very few out of very many, are not even these alone such great benefits as only the best princes could confer upon their peoples through many years of rule?

But if those great upheavals that convulsed the world brought no slight distress, from which the states still suffer; if the changed condition of very many things has entangled one or another class of citizens in various difficulties; if the very fertility and kindness of the soil afflicts the farmers:

let us consider that not even the times of the most praised emperors, not even the age of the Antonines, were free from miseries, and that the calamities themselves are relieved munificently by a most merciful king.

Therefore, accidental evils or unavoidable ones, and if anything else of good things seems to be lacking to one or another, will not deter us from proclaiming the fortunate reign of Frederick William, who provides for the state gloriously restored and wisely administered, at home justice, equity, concord, and from foreigners security.

Of this happiness, not the least part is also this, that public and private morals seem to have been corrected, partly because the contemplation of the saddest events has filled the minds of mortals with the religion of the divine deity, and with the more widely disseminated understanding of truth, men are also rendered more upright, partly because the life of the rest is accustomed to be composed according to the example of the king.

For Frederick William combines with royal arts the virtues of a private citizen, an excellent father of a family, moderate in food and dress and averse to the delights of the court, finally temperate in all his life and so modest that after so many victories he does not even allow a laurel to be inserted in his hair.
But what is dearer to the state than good morals?
Take away these:
so that although it abounds in resources, in arms and men, it will fall with a ruin the more disastrous, the greater its appearance had been.
But I return to the point from which I began my speech.

For just as in other matters we see Frederick William entering upon a new path, so in founding seats of learning, new cities open day and night, and the gates of many towns are demolished so that they cannot be closed, and by paving roads and other useful institutions, commerce, previously very slow, is accelerated.

Nor indeed did the King order these and other things that differ from the earlier form out of a desire for novelty, he who, as the ruler of the state ought, especially favors the ancient custom by retaining it, where it is good and useful;
but he understands that a new age must be tempered with new laws and institutions;
that the republic, like all mortal things, being changeable, must advance lest it fail;
and lest it languish through sloth, fresh and vigorous juices must be poured in.
But are not these benefits, even if I have selected only a very few out of very many, so great by themselves that only the best princes could confer them upon their peoples over many years of rule?

let us consider that not even the times of the most praised emperors, not even the age of the Antonines, were free from miseries, and that the calamities themselves are relieved munificently by a most merciful king.

Therefore, accidental evils or unavoidable ones, and if anything else of good things seems to be lacking to one or another, will not deter us from proclaiming the fortunate reign of Frederick William, who provides for the state gloriously restored and prudently administered, at home justice, equity, concord, and from foreigners security.

Of this happiness, not the least part is also this, that public and private morals seem to have been corrected, partly because the contemplation of the saddest events has filled the minds of mortals with the religion of the divine deity, and, with the understanding of truth spread more widely, men are also rendered more upright, partly because the life of the rest is accustomed to be regulated according to the example of the king.

For Frederick William combines with royal arts the virtues of a private citizen, an excellent father of a family, moderate in food and dress, and averse to the delights of the court, finally temperate in all his life and so modest that after so many victories he does not even allow a laurel to be inserted in his hair.
But to the state, what is dearer than good morals?
Take away these:
so that, although it abounds in resources, arms, and men, it will fall with a ruin the more disastrous, the greater its appearance had been.
But I return to the point from which I began my speech.
For just as in other matters we see Frederick William entering upon a new path, so in founding the seats of learning he has followed new plans.
For not only has the whole care of public instruction been greatly exerted, and the lower schools of every kind been excellently supported, partly even established for the first time;

Not only have the slender revenues of most old universities, as is often the case, been increased to a wonderful degree, but also new ones have been founded, and old ones have been completely restored.
Nor can the equipment that these had in ancient times be compared in any way with that furniture with which Frederick William equipped them all.
Finally, what I said about the face of almost all things having been changed under this king, that is seen especially in the universities.
This city is a witness, the seat of the court, of the empire, the camp of many armies of soldiers;
Although this city was already distinguished by arts and letters before, nevertheless Frederick William adorned it with a new kind of beauty of these same arts and letters.
Even before Frederick the Great, Berlin had flourished with the praise of learning and the arts, and had possessed Leibniz himself and the royal society of sciences:
And that king, although he was devoted to foreign literature, nevertheless encouraged the studies of the natives:
And there were at that time in this city most refined intellects, whose memory will not perish.
Afterward, even the more sublime philosophy took root here, and Fichte, who was soon given to the university, taught the city dwellers beyond others.
Mixed were the gatherings of men and freeborn women, whom those most learned men used to teach:

Scarcely anyone could conceive in his mind that a rather unrestrained crowd of young men, who are educated in the universities, streaming together from all sides, could be borne into the royal city and into the royal house.
Indeed, the cradles of the universities were the primary cities, Paris of the Parisians and, closer to us, Prague:

But afterwards, with a change in the manner of life, the universities that were established in large cities were generally less famous, if you except the Königsberg one, which for some time was illuminated by the lights of Kant and others.
Therefore it was a new thing that Frederick William resolved to found a literary university in this city:
This matter, although at first it seemed doubtful, the outcome approved.

For although the most beloved king fosters all schools of the arts with equal kindness, nevertheless it would be surprising if the one that is nearest to him were not regarded as especially worthy of the city, the capital of the nation.
Hence it happens that it is exceptionally enriched with all things.
Then the city contains most precious equipment of every kind, partly collected by earlier kings, partly acquired by Frederick William, by which our studies are greatly aided.
The King opened his royal library to the doctors and students of the university.
Although it is not perfect, nevertheless it has followed his plans.
For not only has the whole care of public instruction been greatly directed, and the lower schools of every kind been excellently aided, partly also been established for the first time;
not only have the slender revenues of the old universities, for the most part, been wonderfully increased, but also new ones have been founded, and old ones completely restored:
Nor can the equipment which these had in ancient times be compared in any way with that furniture with which Frederick William furnished all.
Finally, that I said that the face of almost all things was changed by this king, that is seen especially in the universities.
This city is a witness, the seat of the court, of the empire, the camp of many troops of soldiers;
Although this city was already distinguished by arts and letters before, nevertheless Frederick William adorned it in a new way with the beauty of these same arts and letters.

And there were then in this city most elegant talents, whose memory will not perish.
Afterward also the more sublime philosophy took root here, and Fichte, who was soon given to the university, taught the city dwellers beyond others.
There were mixed gatherings of freeborn men and women, whom those most learned men used to teach.

That a rather licentious crowd of young men, who are formed in literary universities, flowing together from all sides, could be brought into the royal city and into the royal house, scarcely anyone could conceive in his mind.
Indeed, the primary cradles of universities were cities, Paris of the Lutetians and, closer to us, Prague.

But afterwards, with a change in the manner of life, the universities which were established in great cities were generally less famous, if you except the Königsberg one, which was for some time illuminated by the lights of Kant and others.
Therefore it was a new thing that Frederick William resolved to found a literary university in this city:
This matter, although it seemed doubtful at first, the outcome approved.

For although the most beloved King fosters all schools of the arts with equal kindness, nevertheless it would be surprising if the one that is nearest to him were not so regarded as to seem especially worthy of the city, the head of the nation.
Hence it happens that it is exceptionally enriched with all things.
Then the city contains most precious equipment of every kind, partly collected by earlier kings, partly acquired by Frederick William, by which our studies are greatly aided.
The King opened his royal library to the doctors and students of the university.
Although it is not perfect, it is nevertheless so rich that, except for Göttingen, no university in Germany is furnished with so great a treasure.
And since the university was founded, it has been increased at great expense every year, better equipped, and adapted to common use.

Whatever nature produces, whatever the mountains conceal in darkness, whatever the most remote regions of the earth nourish in the way of herbs, shrubs, and trees, whatever animals walk, crawl, fly, or swim on the ground, the museums and well-arranged gardens present to the eyes with admirable abundance and beauty:
The inner structure of the human and animal body, nature's norms and monsters, lie open to the viewer.
I would not mention these things, if they were common;
But they are so constituted that they are an ornament not only to the university, but also to the city and the kingdom.
What shall I say of the many and ample medical institutions?
Nor are there lacking seminaries for training theologians and philologists.

Now that is excellent, that although very many universities excel indeed in letters, but the works of the arts, especially of sculpture and painting, students can contemplate there either few or none, this city also abounds in these:
We already have now museums not to be despised, but the best things lie hidden.

But the magnificent buildings of the King, who is undertaking everything extraordinary and not attempted by his predecessors at enormous expense, now rise up themselves; and when, after a few years, they have been completed, the statues, the paintings, of which there is a huge number and value, the engraved gems long celebrated in fame, the coins, and other monuments, now scattered through many palaces and houses, will be so arranged that a new splendor may accrue to this city from them, and that by the daily sight of the most beautiful images the minds may be educated along with the eyes.

What of the fact that our own artists have given splendid examples of the revived art, with which the buildings and streets of the city are adorned, examples truly unlike the vulgar and monstrous fictions of earlier centuries?
Thus young people, beholding more perfect works, become accustomed to nobler feelings, which, in my judgment, magnificent statues form no less than admonitions.
Moreover, the very magnitude of the city and the seriousness and variety of the affairs that are carried on in it accustom the mind to a greater measure;

Hence it comes about that academic teachers are called away from lawsuits and quarrels, which they would otherwise engage in with mutual spite, and students are called away from that arrogance by which, while they are carried away by empty disputes, they seem to themselves to be the first of all men.
Finally, these men, instead of that sordid and fierce habit and dress, put on an elegance of manners without silliness, and draw a certain silent color of urbanity.
Therefore the academic manners in our state have been eminently corrected;
From this the collection is so rich that, apart from Göttingen, no university in Germany is equipped with such a great treasure.
And this collection, since the university was founded, has been increased at great expense every year, better furnished, and adapted to common use.

Whatever nature produces, whatever the mountains conceal in darkness, whatever the most remote regions of the earth nourish in the way of herbs, shrubs, and trees, whatever animals walk, crawl, fly, or swim on the ground, the museums and well-arranged gardens present to the eyes with admirable abundance and beauty:
The inner structure of the human and animal body, nature's norms and monsters, lie open to the viewer.
I would not bring these up, if they were common;
But they are so constituted that they are an ornament not only to the university, but also to the city and the kingdom.
What shall I say of the many and ample medical institutions?
Nor are there lacking seminaries for training theologians and philologists.

Now that is excellent, that although very many universities excel indeed in letters, yet students can contemplate there either few or no works of the arts, especially of sculpture and painting, this city also abounds in these.
We already have now museums not to be despised, but the best things lie hidden.

But the king's magnificent buildings, which are now rising at enormous expense, are of a kind that surpasses anything previously attempted; and when, after a few years, they shall have been completed, the statues, the paintings, of which there is a vast number and value, the engraved gems, long celebrated for their fame, the coins, and other monuments, now scattered through many palaces and houses, will be so arranged that a new splendor will hence accrue to this city, and the minds of men will be cultivated by the daily sight of the most beautiful images.

What of the fact that our own artists have given splendid examples of revived art, by which the buildings and streets of the city are adorned, examples truly unlike the vulgar and monstrous fictions of earlier centuries?
Thus young people, beholding more perfect works, become accustomed to nobler feelings, which, in my judgment, magnificent statues form no less than admonitions.
Moreover, the very magnitude of the city and the seriousness and variety of the affairs that are transacted in it accustom the mind to a greater measure;

Hence it comes about that academic teachers are called away from lawsuits and quarrels, which they would otherwise engage in with mutual envy, and students are called away from that arrogance by which they seem to themselves, while they are carried away by empty disputes, to be the first of all men.
Finally, these men, instead of that sordid and fierce habit and dress, put on an elegance of manners without silliness, and draw a certain silent color of urbanity.
Therefore the academic manners in our state have been eminently corrected;
Hence there are very few censures and marks of blame, and hardly any except against those who had come here already corrupted.
And let no one think that young men attracted by the allurements of a great city devote less effort to their studies:
Even small towns have their own delights and an abundance of wantonness;
and one may enjoy innocent pleasures in the city itself with less expense and loss of leisure than when neighboring cities are sought for their sake, as is customary:
Finally, in a larger city, academic citizens, the more safely they hide, the less they are subject to the insolent power of clubs, which lay snares most pernicious to the severity of studies.

Nor, if suitable discipline fills young minds with the ardor of learning, is it to be feared that the sight of other things, whatever the frequency of the city brings, will call them away from the handling of literature.

Finally, you yourselves, dearest fellow soldiers, if we except very few out of so great a number, have up to this point shown such great eagerness for studies, that by this success also the judgment of the most wise king has been approved:
And that you will use the same diligence hereafter, former examples promise.

But if nature has granted to this place less fertility of soil, and not the pleasantness of valleys, let us console ourselves with the saying of Socrates, who thought that a man is taught by a man, not by trees:
The very soil of Athens was barren and rocky;
but necessity itself, the mother of the arts, spurred on their talents:
and our city has been endowed with so many internal goods that external ones are less missed.

Therefore let us celebrate this institution of Frederick William, which in his own seat, especially suited for nurturing letters, founded this school of ours, and equipped it with all the endowments that can increase the flower of learning.

Indeed, since the same has also been granted by the most gracious King to the other universities of this realm, and all of them have been adorned both with the most distinguished teachers summoned from everywhere and with whatever subsidies;
so that provision may be made for the renown of these, there is no need to forbid citizens the use of foreign ones:

And this very thing Frederick William established newly and liberally, that whereas formerly our countrymen had to devote themselves to letters in our universities, now all schools of Germany are open indiscriminately to them, unless something particular seems to stand in the way, and each one can choose for himself that one which seems most suitable to him either according to the nature of his studies or of his domestic circumstances.

This law is so firm that not even the corporations of those states are excluded, whose citizens are not allowed to come to our [universities], and that, if any school has been excepted for a particular reason, as soon as the reason has ceased, the exception ceases:

This is what happened in this very year, when the freedom of approaching the University of Jena was restored, and a very small mark [of exception] was made, and hardly except against those who had come here more corrupted.
And let no one think that young men, attracted by the allurements of a great city, devote less effort to their studies:
Even small towns have their own delights and an abundance of wantonness;

And that you will hereafter use the same diligence, former examples promise.

The soil of Athens itself was barren and rocky;

and our city has been endowed with so many internal goods that external ones are less missed.

so that provision may be made for the renown of these, there is no need to forbid citizens the use of foreign ones:

This law is so firm that not even the corporations of those states are excluded, whose citizens are not permitted to approach our [universities], and that, if any school has been excepted for a particular reason, as soon as the reason has ceased, the exception ceases:
This has been demonstrated in this very year by restoring the freedom of approaching the University of Jena.
Surely, if someone has freed the commerce of goods from the bonds by which it was constrained, why should he confine the commerce of minds within narrower limits?
Nor does Frederick William wish that the wills of private individuals be so constrained by laws that whatever they undertake, the law should be an obstacle.

But he thinks that these are the duties of the laws: to restrain the wicked, to protect the good, and, as far as can be done without harm to the state, to provide to each person so much opportunity of managing his own affairs securely, freely, and according to his own judgment.
It has been pointed out.
Surely, he who has freed the commerce of goods from the bonds by which it was constrained, why should he confine the commerce of minds within narrower limits?
Nor does Frederick William wish that the wills of private individuals be so restrained by laws that whatever they undertake, the law should be an obstacle.

But he thinks that these are the duties of the laws: to restrain the wicked, to protect the good, and, as far as can be done without detriment to the republic, to provide to each one so great a faculty of settling his own affairs securely and freely and according to his own judgment.

But to return to our own affairs, although they have long been brought to such a degree of perfection that if nothing new were added, but the most excellent minister of the king and his most prudent counselors, who govern public education with zealous care, were to maintain the former state, the wishes and desires would have been satisfied:

Nevertheless, every year not a few good things are added, which, if our piety can be increased, may bind our hearts more and more wholly to the most clement King, and may testify to the benevolence of the prefects, in whom we have trusted with the greatest confidence.
Many things indeed this year have been instituted usefully and splendidly;
which I would relate, were they not to be reserved for the speech of the highest magistrate in resigning his office:
Nevertheless, this very day demands that I speak about one example of royal munificence and of the generous care of the prefects.
I mean the prizes which today are for the first time publicly awarded to academic citizens, and hereafter, as often as these most auspicious solemnities return, will be awarded.

You might say that one who burns with genuine love of literature neither needs the spur of industry nor is led by ambition or gain, but is held by the excellence of the subject in which he is engaged, and with some divine impulse, without any additional goads, runs to the goal;
The rest, even if enticed by rewards, will not do the work worth the effort.
Although I think this must by no means be denied, yet it is certain that literature and the arts reach the highest point through rivalry:
This is contained in the fact that we strive to attain what seems best to the best, not so much to satisfy any desire for glory or anything else, but rather to attain what seems best to the best.

Therefore among the Greeks, from the most ancient times, prizes were set for running, wrestling, boxing, and other bodily exercises, in which they thought virtue resided, partly monetary and partly crowns, of which the greater authority is that apart from honor they have no utility.
And poets of every kind, especially lyric, dithyrambic, and scenic poets, as well as musicians and even actors themselves, competed with one another for the palm.
And at Corinth and Delphi a contest in painting was also established.
But in a more recent age, literary contests especially began to be held, and these of various kinds.
There is a certain kind of literary contest, a little more remote from the young men who are engaged in the discipline of the universities:

This is what learned societies, or academies, strive to achieve: that the studies and efforts of scholars be directed toward the most difficult questions, for the successful treatment of which either a very ample store of knowledge or the greatest power of intellect and a judgment refined by long practice must be brought to bear.

When their arguments are selected in such a way that what is most suitable to the present needs of each discipline is set forth, if competent authors work on them, it cannot happen but that no small benefit accrues to literature from them.
There is another kind of commissions, which has been received in our university for a long time:
Since this is rather slight and not to be compared with the former, I would not mention it, unless we had also experienced its usefulness.
For since almost every year a certain sum of money was handed over to the Senate, by which the need of honorable and industrious young men might be relieved;
From it, several orders of the university paid rewards to those who had offered suitable proofs of their skill.
From this it is understood that these rewards were indeed awarded to the worthy, but not for the sake of honor, but for relieving need.

Since these things are so, these honorary prizes are different and new among us, to be distributed from the gift of the most merciful King to those citizens who have come out superior in the literary contests of the university.

But since the Prorector of this school has explained the reason for these commissions in the transfer of the fasces, I will not say how they have now been established, but why they were not established before, after they were propagated from the University of Göttingen to others.

For as far as I remember having once learned, at the time when this seat of letters was founded by Frederick William, since he wanted it adorned with whatever decorations, this institution was therefore omitted, because the strength of young men, not yet confirmed, does not seem sufficient for explaining somewhat more abstruse questions:
whence you may fear, lest by rewards you draw out little books of little use, of which in this age, most fertile in books, the supply is not dear.
It may be added that the desire of attaining praise can invite one or another to the treatment of a subject, from which if he abstained, he would better consult his own studies:
another can be puffed up by success itself with the pride of learning, than which nothing is more pernicious to him.
But these disadvantages are easily overcome by advantages:
nor are good things to be let go, because the contest has not been rightly instituted for those who use them.
In more recent times, however, literary commissions in particular have been established, and these of various kinds.
There is a certain kind of literary contest, somewhat removed from the young men who enjoy the discipline of universities:

by which learned societies or academies strive to bring it about that the studies and contentions of scholars are turned to the most difficult questions, for the successful treatment of which either a very ample abundance of knowledge or the greatest force of intellect and a judgment refined by long practice must be employed:

When their arguments are selected in such a way that what is most suitable for the present needs of each discipline is presented, if competent authors work on them, it cannot happen but that no small benefit accrues to literature from them.
There is another kind of commissions, which has been received in our university for a long time:
Since this is rather slight and not to be compared with the former, I would not mention it, unless we had also experienced its usefulness.
For since almost every year a certain sum of money was handed over to the Senate, by which the neediness of honorable and industrious young men might be relieved;
From it, several orders of the university paid out rewards to those who had presented suitable proofs of their skill.
From this it is understood that these rewards were indeed awarded to the worthy, but not for the sake of honor, but for relieving need.

Since these things are so, these honorary prizes are different and new among us, to be distributed from the gift of the most merciful King to those citizens who have come out superior in the literary contests of the university.

But since the Prorector of this school has explained the reason for these commissions in the transfer of the fasces, I will not say how they are now instituted, but why they were not instituted before, after they were propagated from the University of Göttingen to others.

For as far as I remember having once discovered, at the time when this seat of learning was founded by Frederick William, since he wished it to be adorned with any decorations whatsoever, this institution was therefore omitted, because the strength of young men, not yet confirmed, does not seem sufficient for explaining questions a little more abstruse:
whence you may fear, lest by rewards you entice out pamphlets of little use, of which in this age, most fertile in books, the supply is not cheap.
It may be added that the desire of attaining praise can invite one or another to the treatment of a subject, from which if he abstained, he would better consult his own studies:
another, success itself can puff up with the pride of learning, than which nothing is more pernicious to him.
But these disadvantages are easily overcome by advantages:
nor should good things be let go, because he who will not use them rightly will do damage.

For although from young men one would scarcely expect a complete explanation of learned questions, nevertheless they must be encouraged in every way, so that they may make trial of what they themselves can do and learn by the judgment of those more experienced:
nor would you say how much each one is worth, unless you have tested him:
and it is well known that the first attempts of talented young men, full of vigor, not rarely surpass a late and elderly production.
Finally, talents must be known, and those that are outstanding must be brought forth into the light:
which is accomplished best by this institution.
But with a certain moderation applied, suitable material for youthful industry and diligence must be chosen, in which one who has spent several years in academic studies may engage with profit.

Wherefore it seems to me especially pertinent that, since this age is midway between those who are being shaped by the discipline of the gymnasia and those who are approaching the conduct of affairs, we should abstain from arguments of that kind which demand not only an abundance of learning but also that experience of affairs which is proper to practical men.

For indeed, when the young men in the gymnasia are so cultivated by a certain general and elementary circle of learning that, whatever part of knowledge they are about to embrace, they approach it prepared and imbued with the necessary preliminary knowledge:

now the schools of the universities open up the very broad fields of the individual disciplines, and they hand down the teachings of each one by a loftier and more subtle investigation to those who have devoted themselves wholly to it.
But it is not beneficial to approach practical exercise unless you have thoroughly formed your mind with knowledge over many years;

Indeed, whoever approaches it before he has thoroughly grasped the doctrines through long study, he will neither excel in knowledge, nor will he conduct affairs or practice an art with not only somewhat more remarkable skill but also experience:

And we do not see anyone except those who, with a sluggish disposition toward studies and without a more sacred inspiration, but for the sake of bread devote themselves to literature, and, having spurned more accurate knowledge, hasten to betake themselves to those things which they themselves or insufficiently qualified advisers may deem suited to the use of life.
Therefore, for the plan of these disputations, only those arguments are suitable which are derived from the science itself.
especially since the things that pertain to conducting business and practicing an art cannot be handled correctly except by those who have been engaged in action for a longer time.
Now indeed, since it is clear that no one can expect from the alumni of universities that practical skill which would suffice for setting forth practical matters more distinctly:

We also understand that for those who established this literary contest of theirs, the highest thing that academic citizens can and should attain is not in the conduct of affairs, but it will cause harm.

For although from young men you would hardly expect a complete explanation of learned questions, nevertheless they must be encouraged in every way, so that they may make trial of what they themselves can do and learn by the judgment of the more experienced:
nor will you say how much each one is worth, unless you have tested it:

Finally, talents must be known, and the excellent ones must be brought forth into the light:
which is accomplished best by this institution.

But with a certain moderation applied, suitable material for youthful industry and diligence must be chosen, in which one who has spent several years in academic studies may be able to engage with profit.
