now the schools of the universities open up the very broad fields of the individual disciplines, and they hand down the teachings of each one by a loftier and more subtle investigation to those who have applied themselves wholly to it.
But it is not advantageous to approach practical exercise unless you have thoroughly formed your mind with knowledge over many years;

indeed, whoever approaches it before he has thoroughly grasped the doctrines through long study, he will neither excel in knowledge, nor will he conduct affairs or practice an art with not only somewhat more notable skill but also experience:

And we do not see anyone except those who, with a sluggish disposition toward studies, and without a more sacred inspiration, but for the sake of bread, devote themselves to literature, and, despising more accurate knowledge, hasten to betake themselves to those things which they themselves or insufficiently qualified advisers may think suited to the use of life.
Therefore, for the rationale of these disputations, only those arguments are suitable which are derived from the science itself.
especially since the things that pertain to conducting business and practicing an art cannot be handled correctly except by those who have been engaged in action for a longer time.
Now indeed, since it is clear that no one can expect from the alumni of universities that skill in acting which would suffice for setting forth practical matters with sufficient distinctness:

We also understand that, for those who established this literary contest of theirs, the highest thing that academic citizens can and ought to attain is seen to be placed not in the ability to manage affairs and handle business, but in the acquisition of knowledge itself.
This we rejoice at very much.

Therefore, thanks must be given to the most merciful King, both by us, because with such a liberal plan he both enlarged and adorned this seat of the liberal arts, and by you, fellow soldiers, to whom he gives ample opportunity for displaying talent and attaining praise.

Never forget that Frederick William, if any prince, has deserved the name of Father of his Country by the most prosperous constitution of the state, and that he shows himself especially kind and courteous to the young, and omits nothing by which he may look after your interests and your welfare.
Confirm every year on this most auspicious day the covenant of piety owed to the best King.

By your reverence for the laws, integrity of life, and seriousness of studies, you have shown that your minds respond to the plans and expectations of Frederick William, and what he has done and does for you;
feel in your hearts;
finally, join with us in sending most holy prayers to the supreme deity, that he may protect and preserve Frederick William, beneficent to the state, to letters, and to youth.
and it seems to be placed not in the ability to handle affairs, but in the acquisition of knowledge itself;
which we rejoice at very much.

Therefore, thanks must be given to the most merciful King, both by us, because with such a liberal plan he has both enlarged and adorned this seat of the good arts, and by you, fellow soldiers, to whom he gives ample opportunity of showing your talent and of attaining praise.

Never forget that Frederick William, if any prince, has deserved the name of Father of his Country by the most prosperous constitution of the state, and also shows himself especially kind and courteous to the young, and omits nothing by which he may look after your interests and your safety.
Confirm every year on this most auspicious day the covenant of loyalty owed to the best King.

Declared by your reverence for the laws, the integrity of your lives, and the seriousness of your studies, may your minds respond to the plans and expectations of Frederick William, and [may you feel] what he has done and does for you;
may your hearts feel [it];
finally, join with us in sending most holy prayers to the supreme deity, that he may protect and preserve Frederick William, who is beneficent to the state, to letters, and to youth.

div.head: XIV. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXVI. habita.

p.s: On the birthday of Frederick William, when I am about to speak today, what else, listeners, should be offered first than those truly divine blessings, which the best King has brought about and brings about for us, of public happiness, peace, and harmony?

Those blessings, I say, which, while they refresh all Germany and especially Prussia after the many calamities of warlike turmoil, and draw forth the most joyful fruits of literature and the arts placed under the protection of an excellent Prince?

By this thought I am moved the more vehemently, the more I see that some kingdoms, which have been shaken by the same wars, are not yet able to return to tranquility, because they are postponed while the immoderate and unbridled desires of men contend among themselves.
Among us all things are tranquil and moderate:
and these things remain.
And this very moderation in our state, the highest of civil goods, is owed especially to Frederick William, whom nature herself, because of his equal M.
Cicero says that Cato, with regard to honesty, seriousness, greatness of soul, justice, and finally all virtues, was a great and lofty man, and he fashioned him as such.

With this same self-control, no doubt, he governs himself, with it he equips the state, he transfers it, as far as possible, into the minds of friends, magistrates, and citizens, and spreads it through the whole empire like abundant streams.
It can hardly be said how much this also benefits literature.
For in a state undisturbed by any storms of passions, the mind traverses the straight and pure path of knowledge on a quiet journey.
The partisan zeal and madness of those who disagree—whether in civil affairs or in religious matters, which are not alien to the state—turn the clouded minds away from the truth.
They force knowledge—than which the supreme deity has bestowed no holier gift upon mortals—to serve the counsels and wishes of men.
They arm the sophists with captious arts, who may protect the utilities of these very things.

Moreover, although literature both can and ought to contribute much to the conduct of life, nevertheless, whoever rashly adapts it to the present state of affairs and to the often deceptive appearance, it cannot happen but that he is entangled in the gravest errors:
Which, since it is evident in the authors of all disciplines, then especially in historians and philosophers.
For although there is a great abundance of examples available, I will dwell on this one alone, since both parties are accustomed to argue about the character of the age, as it is called;

They think that the character of the age is generally seen in those things to which each person has directed his mind more, and which part of present circumstances has been especially presented to them, or what struggles, what plans they themselves pursue;
so that the wise poet rightly said that they sell their own nature for the nature of the age;

which seems scarcely able to be sufficiently known, unless, being separated by divine influence from the contagion of the age, you have thoroughly discerned, as from on high, all things that are done, and by what causes, and with what outcome.

Indeed, how uncertain, how subject to the passions of men, especially amid great upheavals, this whole divination concerning the character of the present age is, not unlike the Etruscan art, seems to me to be better demonstrated by no example than by that of the greatest among the Germans as a writer of history, who for some time even lived in this city, and was distinguished among few for the elegance of his learning, the immense abundance of his erudition, and the candor of his mind.

He who was at first the fiercest adversary of the French Emperor, soon reconciled to him by a friendly address, prophesied that he would bring a new and almost golden age, whose power was abolished after another five-year period, not without the universal exultation of all mortals, so that, as Cicero says, he formed a great and lofty man for honor, gravity, greatness of soul, justice, and finally for all virtues:

With the same self-restraint with which he rules himself, he equips the state, and transfers it to the minds of friends, magistrates, and citizens, as far as possible, and spreads it through the whole empire like abundant streams.
It can hardly be said how much this benefits even literature.
For in a state undisturbed by any storms of passions, the mind traverses the straight and pure path of knowledge with a quiet journey.
The zeal and madness of factions, whether in civil affairs or in religious matters, which are not alien to the state, turn aside from the truth minds that are clouded.
They force science, than which no holier gift has been bestowed on mortals by the supreme deity, to serve the counsels and wills of men.
They arm sophists with captious arts, who may defend the interests of these very things.

Moreover, although literature can and ought to contribute much to the conduct of life, nevertheless, whoever rashly adapts it to the present state of affairs and to the often deceptive appearance of things, it cannot happen but that he becomes entangled in the gravest errors:
This may be understood both in the authors of all disciplines and especially in historians and philosophers.
For although there is a great abundance of examples, I will confine myself to this one, since both parties are accustomed to dispute about the character of the age, as it is called;

they think that the character of the age is generally seen in those things to which each person has directed his mind more, and which part of present circumstances has been especially presented to them, or what contests, what plans they themselves pursue;
so that the wise poet rightly said that they sell their own nature for the nature of the age;

which seems scarcely able to be known, unless, being separated by divine influence from the contagion of the age, you have thoroughly examined, as from on high, all things that are done, and by what causes, and with what outcome.

Indeed, how uncertain, how subject to the passions of men, especially amid great disturbances, this whole divination about the character of the present age, not unlike the Etruscan, is, seems to me to be proved by no better example than that of the greatest among the Germans as a writer of history, who for some time also lived in this city, and was distinguished among the few for the elegance of his learning, the immense abundance of his erudition, and the candor of his mind:

He who was at first the fiercest adversary of the French Emperor, soon reconciled to him by a courteous address, prophesied that he would bring a new and almost golden age, whose power was abolished after another five-year period, not without the common exultation of all mortals, so that scarcely any traces remain.

I recall this matter to memory, not to reproach the shade of that distinguished man, but to show that even the best of scholars, when caught up and disturbed by the waves of political upheaval, are deceived, and that only in a calm condition of the state is judgment on the greatest matters sound.
so that traces remain.

I recall this matter to memory, not to reproach the shade of that excellent man, but to show that even the best of scholars are deceived and thrown into confusion when caught up in the storms of political upheaval, and that only in a tranquil condition of the state is there sound judgment on the greatest matters.
Now if history and the pursuit of wisdom are subject to those dangers, will it not be permissible to say the same about all knowledge and every discipline?
For all these take root in philosophy and history;
these seek nourishment from those, and when those are removed or neglected, they themselves perish.
Although this seems hardly fitting to set forth in this assembly of most distinguished and most learned men;

Nevertheless, since I understand that from this distinguished assembly, which sits nearest to me, what is expected is not those things which might be suited to it either by their novelty or by their weight of speech, but rather what it is, if not necessary, certainly useful to remind fellow students of, and what can at the same time be referred to the praise of the undertakings instituted under the auspices of Frederick William, because in explaining this conjunction of philosophy and history with the other disciplines both advantages are present, I have decided to set forth a few things about this matter, not with dialectical subtlety, which is proper to the schools, but in an oratorical manner, and then to return to the point from which I have digressed.

Therefore I maintain that philosophy and history, together with the parts dependent on them, to which not without reason natural science, mathematics, and philology are usually added, contain the whole of human knowledge, which has its highest end placed in itself:

from which at an early stage certain branches of learning were separated like branches and joined into specific disciplines, and these, turning historical and philosophical knowledge to the far most beneficial fruit of the human race.

And of these disciplines, indeed, one especially comes to the aid of and heals the corporeal nature of men, two strive to rule the minds with the precepts of laws and justice, to correct and raise them with the most holy religions, to unite them with the dearest bonds of the state and the church, and finally to console them with the better hope of dying.

But who would deny that these same disciplines are supported by the historical and philosophical doctrines I have mentioned, and that they themselves are partly developed by philosophizing, partly by historical inquiry?

For indeed, to begin with jurisprudence, just as all its sources, whether domestic or foreign, cannot be opened and explained except by the historical method, even up to the Romans and beyond them, so from the Greeks, the teachers and leaders of all arts, philosophy also undertook the treatment of law and of all civil affairs.
And indeed the principle of legislation itself seems to be this, that it is mixed and composed from historical and philosophical knowledge.
But what about theology?
Is there any discipline that by its very nature more needs the light of history than that one?
For those things which have been divinely revealed to the human race, we have not experienced ourselves, but we have received them handed down from remote times;
and in these things, which have been handed down, the religious mind finds rest:

except that it strives to strip off the sacred stain which they have contracted from the additions of mortals and especially from superstition, and to restore it to the pure and genuine form of doctrine, which cannot be done without historical knowledge, and to rub off the rust that has been acquired;
after the most holy ceremonies have been corrupted, with divine providence bringing a remedy and rousing noble men, who dare to go against inveterate errors:

That which Luther did, when he recalled Christian doctrine to the faith of the sacred books, in which alone we have long since, and especially in this very year, recognized with singular gratitude that our King, distinguished for piety, finds both Christian truth and the solace and salvation of souls.

Again, because divine literature has handed down the deepest and most serious opinions about those matters which are of the greatest importance to mortals, in which even philosophy itself is engaged; indeed, because the religions of almost every nation contain its primitive wisdom as if enclosed in a seed;

Whoever dares to aspire to the innermost sanctuaries of learning, to open and unfold the seeds of the most sacred doctrines, and to unite the scattered elements into one body of discipline, will not accomplish this without the meditation of a philosopher.

What of the fact that the deeper familiarity with sacred and profane literature was both confirmed long ago by the laws for the directors of public education and very recently increased in this republic, since from that time certain parts of theological study have also been recommended to those who embrace the disciplines that serve the instruction of scholastic youth?

This matter will have a very favorable outcome, if the necessary balance is maintained in it, which one may safely expect in a most temperate state, and it will not seem that piety, which we need not fear, whether true or feigned, can supply the lack of thorough learning, or those advantages will be removed which, from the separation of the two studies, have undoubtedly flowed to the schools in this very empire.
Finally, that the study of medicine without natural science is nothing, there is no need for me to set forth.

And this is also proved by usage and authority, so that in many academies and even among us several professors of medicine are separated from the healing art, and the very principle of legislation seems to be such that it is mixed and composed of historical and philosophical knowledge.
But what of theology?
Or does any discipline by its very nature need the light of history more than that one?
For the things that have been revealed divinely to the human race, we have not experienced ourselves, but we have received them handed down from remote times;
and in these things, which have been handed down, the religious mind finds rest:

except that it strives to strip off the sacred stain which they have contracted from the additions of mortals and especially from superstition, and to restore it to the pure and genuine form of doctrine, which cannot be done without historical knowledge, and to rub off the rust that has been acquired;
after the most sacred ceremonies were corrupted, divine providence bringing a remedy and rousing generous men, who dare to go against inveterate errors:

We have long since, and especially in this very year, recognized with singular gratitude and with a notable proof that our King, distinguished for piety, finds both Christian truth and the solace and salvation of souls in that faith alone to which Luther, when he recalled Christian doctrine to the authority of the sacred books, referred it.

Again, because divine literature has handed down the deepest and most serious opinions about those matters which are of the greatest importance to mortals, in which even philosophy itself is engaged; indeed, because the religions of almost every nation contain its primitive wisdom as if enclosed in a seed;

Whoever dares to aspire to the innermost sanctuaries of learning, to open and unfold the seeds of the most sacred doctrines, to unite the scattered elements into one body of discipline, will not accomplish this without the meditation of a philosopher.

What of the fact that the deeper familiarity with sacred and profane literature was both confirmed long ago by the laws for the directors of public education and very recently increased in this republic, from which time certain parts of theological study have also been recommended to those who embrace the disciplines serving the education of scholastic youth?

This matter will have a most favorable outcome, if the necessary balance is maintained in it, which one may safely expect in a most temperate state, and it will not seem that piety, which we need not fear, whether true or feigned, can supply the lack of thorough learning, nor will those advantages be removed, which from the separation of both studies in this very empire have undoubtedly flowed to the schools.
Finally, I need not explain that the study of medicine without natural science is nothing.

And this is even proved by usage and authority, so that in many universities, and even among us, several professors of medicine, far removed from the practice of the healing art, are occupied solely in investigating nature, and very recently it was wisely established by the most excellent and most distinguished men, to whom Frederick William entrusted this part of the state, that no one should be admitted to seeking the highest honors in medicine unless he had proved a sufficient knowledge of natural things by undergoing a special examination for this purpose.

But who does not understand that this is most beautifully established by physicians and students of medicine, that they investigate the origins of their art from the most remote age, that they do not deem worthy of their care only those things which were proposed or invented yesterday and the day before, but in the treatment of individual diseases, returning with a thoroughly historical method through the spaces of all ages up to Hippocrates, the parent of their art, they diligently repeat from there whatever is either useful or memorable?

Who does not know that these same men, both in former times and especially in our own memory, have followed the doctrines of the philosophers more zealously than any other learned group, in order that they might thoroughly understand the causes of nature and the vital forces by which the inner structure of the body is held together and set in motion?

Therefore, since it is agreed that all disciplines partly draw their material from philosophy and history, and partly use their method and reasoning in discovering, explaining, and confirming their own subjects, let it be permitted to say a few words about the study of antiquity.
From this, because in the age of the rebirth of letters almost all branches of learning had their beginnings, rightly in the education of youth the first place was given to it.
But with the mature literatures of more recent peoples, the dignity of Greek and Roman antiquity no longer seemed to be such that the beginnings of learning had to be derived from it.

Therefore those who, captivated by their excellence, wished to retain those studies, which had been received into the schools for the reason I mentioned, when they wanted to teach why this ought to be done, after the earlier use and fruit of them had been abolished;
Looking around keenly, they could not find anything else than that, for the sake of what is called formal education, Greek and Roman literature and especially languages must be studied.

Hoc ego tantum abest ut mihi persuadeam, qui praesertim non videam homines Graecam Latinamque grammaticam imprimis tenentes ceteris mortalibus animo bene conformato longe praestare, ut quamvis mentibus formandis idonea materia sit, expellendas ex scholis antiquas litteras censeam, et ingenia puerorum et adolescentium, veterum ipsorum exemplo in aliis rebus, quae nobis propiores sint, exercenda, nisi potior causa supersit, quamobrem
factitanda procul remoti in sola rerum natura perscrutanda occupati sint, et nuperrime a viris excellentissimis et illustrissimis, quibus Fridericus Guilelmus hanc rei publicae partem mandavit, constitutum sapienter sit, ne quis ad summos in medicina honores capessendos admitteretur, nisi rerum naturalium cognitionem sufficientem peculiari tentamine in hunc finem subeundo probasset.

But who does not understand that this is most beautifully established by physicians and their students, that they investigate the origins of their art from the most remote age, that they do not deem worthy of their attention only those things which were proposed or invented yesterday and the day before, but in the treatment of individual diseases, returning with a truly historical method through the spaces of all ages up to Hippocrates, the father of their art, they diligently repeat from there whatever is either useful or memorable?

Who does not know that they, both in former times and especially in our memory, have followed the doctrines of the philosophers more diligently than any other family of learned men, in order that they might thoroughly understand the causes of nature and the vital forces by which the inner structure of the body is held together and set in motion?

Therefore, since it is agreed that all disciplines partly draw their material from philosophy and history, and partly use their method and reasoning in discovering, explaining, and confirming their own subjects, let it be permitted to say a few words about the study of antiquity.
From this, because in the age of the rebirth of letters almost all branches of learning had their beginnings, rightly in the education of youth the first place has been given to it.
But with the mature literatures of more recent peoples, the dignity of Greek and Roman antiquity no longer seemed to be such that the beginnings of learning had to be derived from it.

Therefore those who, captivated by their excellence, wished to retain those studies, which had been received into the schools for the reason I mentioned, when they wanted to teach why this ought to be done, after the earlier use and fruit of them had been abolished;
Looking about keenly, they could not find anything else than that Greek and Roman literature, and especially the languages, should be treated for the sake of what is called formal education.

I am so far from being persuaded of this, especially since I do not see that men who are particularly well versed in Greek and Latin grammar far surpass other mortals in a well-formed mind, that although this material is suitable for shaping minds, I would not think that ancient literature should be expelled from the schools, and that the talents of boys and adolescents should be exercised, following the example of the ancients themselves, in other subjects that are closer to us, unless there is a stronger reason why those [ancient letters] should be chosen.
Indeed, that whole line of reasoning is deceptive, and it was devised for this very reason, because the way in which ancient and modern literature are still connected was not correctly assessed.
Even now a large part of history must be drawn from the monuments of antiquity;

even now there is no philosopher of somewhat greater distinction who does not consider the doctrines of the ancient philosophers, which he examines, most worthy, who does not admire the great geniuses of Pythagoras, Plato, and Aristotle:
Finally, not to mention the most accomplished poets and writers, if you except a few particular branches, especially of natural science, the sources of all disciplines flow from antiquity.
Where did the Christian faith take its origin and growth?
Where has law been made perfect to some extent?
What physician, unless unlearned, despises the ancient authors of the art?

Finally, what is this wisdom, by which, after we have, following in the footsteps of the ancients, acquired a moderate education, you would order the foundations to be torn down, because you are busy with building a roof?

Since these things are so, we are instructed in Greek and Latin literature from childhood, because our own cannot be thoroughly learned without them, and those, as it were, by manifold offshoots, permeate our entire education and are diffused through it:

Since in this state, if anywhere, those who are at the head of public affairs understand this very well, from those who, after completing their academic studies, approach the business of taking up offices, some knowledge of ancient literature is also demanded.
Hence, as I hear, Latin examinations will be established for candidates in law in the future;
whence for future doctors of medicine a moderate degree of scholastic learning, which is for the most part acquired through ancient literature, has been judged necessary;
From this it is provided that those who have too much neglected the letters of the schools are not admitted to academic studies unprepared.
For in general in the Prussian state, and especially under King Frederick William, public discipline is tempered by the wisest institutions and laws, by which the flower of letters is aided:
And what seems to me not to be passed over, we are devoted to a liberal education, not a shadowy one;

Nor are we so blind as to form students who are most learned in speaking Latin and Greek, but in almost all other things infants, but we have also introduced other kinds of literature into the schools, and especially we have equipped them with the study of mathematics, whose power is rightly considered not the least in exercising young minds.
Let those be chosen.
Indeed, that whole line of reasoning is deceptive, and it was devised for this very reason, because the way in which ancient and modern literature are still connected was not correctly assessed.
Even now a great part of history must be drawn from the monuments of antiquity;

even now there is no philosopher of somewhat greater distinction who does not consider the doctrines of the ancient philosophers worthy of examination, who does not admire the great geniuses of Pythagoras, Plato, and Aristotle:
Finally, not to mention the most accomplished poets and writers, if you except a few particular parts of natural science especially, the sources of all disciplines flow from antiquity.
Where did the Christian faith take its origin and growth?
Where has law been perfected to some extent?
What physician, unless unlearned, despises the ancient authors of the art?

Finally, what is this wisdom, by which, after we have, following in the footsteps of the ancients, acquired a moderate amount of learning, you order the foundations to be destroyed, because you are busy building the roof?

Since these things are so, we are instructed from childhood in Greek and Latin literature, because our own cannot be thoroughly learned without them, and they, as it were, permeate our entire education through many offshoots and are diffused through it:

Since in this state, if anywhere, those who are at the head of public affairs understand this very well, from those who, after completing their academic studies, proceed to the conduct of business, some knowledge of ancient literature is also required.
Hence, as I hear, Latin examinations will be established for candidates in law in the future.
Hence, for future doctors of medicine, a moderate degree of scholastic learning, which is for the most part acquired through ancient literature, has been judged necessary.
Hence it is provided that those who have too much neglected the letters of the schools should not be admitted to academic studies unprepared.
For in general in the Prussian state, and especially under King Frederick William, public discipline is tempered by the wisest institutions and laws, by which the flower of letters is aided:
and what seems to me not to be passed over, we are devoted to a liberal education, not a shadowy one;

Nor are we so blind as to form students who are most learned in speaking Latin and Greek, but in almost all other things infants, but we have also introduced other kinds of literature into the schools, and especially we have equipped them with the study of mathematics, whose power is rightly considered not the least in exercising young minds.
So much for this.

You understand, however, listeners, that while I briefly run through the individual heads of that argument which I had undertaken to treat, I have in almost every one pointed my finger at those things with which our state, governed by the will of the wisest king, has been especially furnished in this very year, so that, according to the measure of my strength, with a speech indeed meager but sincere, I might connect in a certain continuous thread, as it were in a garland, the prudent decrees concerning the direction of literary studies.
Now someone might say:
But these are trivial things;
Why did you not, with the overflowing horn of plenty that is at hand, bring forth the very many and very great merits of the most kind King concerning this empire?
I indeed, having so often performed the praises of Frederick William from this platform, do not act so as one who turns over a barren subject;
I do not think that the same things must be repeated every year:
Just now, as I did in the previous year, I am deliberately setting forth what Frederick William accomplished for the whole commonwealth.

Just now, in accordance with the opportunity of the times, having selected the more important parts for myself, I celebrate his martial valor, or the patronage of arts or letters undertaken by him, in a fuller discussion.

Finally, I am not satisfied with myself, because I have shown the great plans of Frederick William in great matters, unless I have also shown him to be provident, and his ministers to be provident, in those things which seem smaller.
Although I do not know whether those things, in which I have taken my stand, are not small.

For is this a small matter, to establish institutions, to write laws for cultivating their pursuits, from whose learning, skill, and integrity the honor of letters, the safety of the state, and the goods, bodies, and minds of all citizens will depend?

who will spread the light of knowledge not only throughout the whole state, but will hand down what they have received from their predecessors to later generations, as parents hand on the vital fire to their children?

This most sacred duty ought to be kept perpetually before the eyes both of teachers and of learners, so that they never, led by profit or ambition, decide anything in literature contrary to a good conscience, and so that they do not adapt their opinions—to return to where I began—to the changeable spirit of the age, to the passions of men that rage at a certain time, and finally to any passing intemperance, which is observed in human life just as in the air and sky.
I am speaking of a great and difficult matter:
and it is not approved by all:
but it seems to me that knowledge ought to serve no one, should court neither popular favor nor princely favor nor any other, but should pursue only that which right reason prescribes.
And yet this does not always happen:

Just as philosophy and history—which, however, an ancient precept proclaims should not be bound to any sect—so the other disciplines, connected with them, are driven here and there by fortuitous or external impulses.

I run through these very laws, and I point out that in almost every one of them I have directed my finger to those things by which our state, governed by the will of the wisest King, has been especially equipped in this very year, so that, to the extent of my strength, with a slender but sincere speech, I might connect the decrees concerning the governance of literary studies in a continuous thread, as it were, into a garland.
Now someone might say:
But these things are trivial;
Why should you not have poured out, from the overflowing horn of plenty that is at hand, the very many and very great services of the most kind king to this state?
But I, having so often performed the praises of Frederick William from this platform, do not act so as one who turns over barren material;
I do not think that the same things should be repeated every year:
only, as I did last year, I set forth with deliberate effort what Frederick William has accomplished for the whole state;

Only recently, having selected the more important parts according to the opportunity of the times, I celebrate his military virtue, or the patronage of arts and letters undertaken by him, in a fuller discussion;

Finally, I am not satisfied with myself, because I have shown the great plans of Frederick William in great matters, unless I have also demonstrated that he himself was provident, and his ministers provident, in those things which seem smaller.
Although I do not know whether those things in which I have taken my stand are not insignificant.

For is this a small matter, to establish institutions, to write laws for the cultivation of the studies of those from whose learning, skill, and integrity the honor of letters, the safety of the state, and the goods, bodies, and minds of all citizens will depend?

who will spread the light of knowledge not only throughout the whole state, but will hand down to posterity what they received from their ancestors, as parents hand on the vital fire to their children?

This most sacred duty ought to be constantly kept before the eyes both of teachers and of learners, so that they may never, led by gain or ambition, decide anything in literature contrary to a good conscience, and so that they may not, to return to the point from which I started, adapt their opinions to the changeable spirit of the age, to the passions of men that rage at a certain time, and finally to some passing intemperance, which is observed in the air and sky as well as in human life.
I am speaking of a great and difficult matter:
and it is not approved by all:
but it seems to me that knowledge ought to serve no one, neither to court popular favor nor princely favor nor any other, but to pursue only that which right reason prescribes.
And yet this does not always happen:

Just as philosophy, just as history—which, however, the ancient precept proclaims should be bound to no sect—so the other disciplines, connected with them, are carried here and there by chance or external impulses;
These the very precepts of law and sacred matters follow not rarely.

But if, as an ancient writer says from the sound teachings of the Stoics, law is the highest reason, implanted in nature, which commands what must be done and forbids the contrary, and this reason is established and perfected in the human mind;
to that reason all law, both civil and public, ought to be directed:
but we see that it has been diverted from that to all other things from time to time.

We have received, under the principate of Octavian Augustus, two ornaments of peace, Antistius Labeo and Ateius Capito, who followed different paths: the one favored the old liberty, the other, by wonderful obsequiousness and by bending his opinions to the nod of the masters, so crept into favor that, in the judgment of Tacitus, though skilled in human and divine law, he disgraced an excellent public character and good domestic arts.
These things, once begun, recur in almost all ages in those republics which foster the zeal of factions.

If nothing of this kind is detected among us, thanks must be given to the moderation of the best King, which brings it about that no suitable material for factions is left in this empire, nor must the power of the principate be supported by cunning aids, and how great the healthfulness of this is, all citizens learn daily by experience.
But you perhaps wonder, listeners, that in our republic I maintain that no material for factions is left:

For will not someone say that we have seen those young men, especially the students of universities, rush headlong into the abyss through a deadly conspiracy, almost all of whom, twenty-eight in number, the supreme court of Breslau recently condemned for attempted treason and punished with the severest penalties?
Indeed, those offenses, in which I will not dwell, because the sanctity of this day and the common joy prevent it, can never be sufficiently lamented.
But that was the impulse and madness of a few, and it was not born from a faction that had spread more widely, but was eager to bring about a faction:
And moreover those wicked contentions have been almost entirely extinguished in this empire:

Indeed, even those who govern our affairs, most excellent and most distinguished men, with their characteristic kindness, wish that it be publicly proclaimed today how grateful and pleasing this is to them, that we all, both teachers and students, abhor those mad attempts of some rash young men, and are devoted with our whole heart to the laws of this state and to the best Prince.
These things indeed about public affairs.
But perhaps that is even greater, that greedy and ambitious men abuse divine religion to pursue their own plans.

For after minds, moved as once by prodigies and portents, so in our memory by great changes of affairs and by the enormous mass of public and private evils, not rarely follow teachings and sacred things.

But if, as an ancient writer says, following the sound doctrines of the Stoics, law is the highest reason, implanted in nature, which commands what must be done and forbids the contrary, and this reason is confirmed and perfected in the human mind;
to that reason all law, both civil and public, ought to be directed:
but we see that all these things have been diverted from that reason at various times.

We have received, under the principate of Octavian Augustus, two ornaments of peace, Antistius Labeo and Ateius Capito, who followed different paths, the one having favored the old liberty, the other having crept up to the masters with such wonderful obsequiousness and with opinions to be twisted at their nod, that, in the judgment of Tacitus, though skilled in human and divine law, he disgraced an excellent public life and good domestic arts.
These things, once begun, recur in almost all ages in those republics which nourish the zeal of factions.

Among us, if nothing of this sort is detected, thanks must be given to the temperance of the best King, which brings it about that in this empire no suitable material is left for factions, nor must the power of the principate be supported by cunning aids; and how great the healthfulness of this is, all citizens learn daily by experience.
But perhaps you wonder, listeners, that in our republic I maintain that no material is left for factions:

For will not someone say that we have seen those young men, especially the students of universities, rush headlong into the abyss through a deadly conspiracy, whom the supreme court of Breslau recently condemned almost all, to the number of twenty-eight, for attempted treason, and punished with the severest penalties?
Certainly those offenses, in which, that I may not dwell on them, the sanctity of this day and the common joy prevent me from dwelling, can never be sufficiently deplored;
But that was the impulse and madness of a few, and it was not born from a faction that had spread more widely, but was eager to create a faction:
And moreover those wicked contentions have been almost entirely extinguished in this empire:

Indeed, even those who govern our affairs, most excellent and most distinguished men, with their characteristic kindness, wish that it be publicly proclaimed today how grateful and pleasing this is to them, that we all, both teachers and students, abhor those mad attempts of some rash young men, and that we are devoted with our whole heart to the laws of this state and to our excellent Prince.
So much for public affairs.
But perhaps that is even greater, that greedy and ambitious men abuse divine religion to pursue their own plans.

For after minds, moved as once by prodigies and portents, so in our memory by great changes of affairs and by the immense mass of public and private evils, understood that rest from earthly cares and a harbor, into which you may safely betake yourself, are provided only by reverence for and piety toward the supreme deity:
There are certainly those who try whether, cleverly using that inclination, they can bind peoples with new chains of servitude, so that a few may rule more licentiously:
But if that should succeed for them, a most pernicious superstition would be recalled, the marrows of minds would be infected with corruption.
But from this empire, which for a long time has been fostering the freedom of minds with distinguished protection, that poison is defended;
piety grows, vices are gently opposed:
The best king is an outstanding example of piety, but devoted to no superstition, and finally, in these matters also, by far the greatest, as in all others, he is the firmest pillar.
I will not delay you longer, listeners, and the announcement of the literary commission urges me, which compels me to be briefer than I usually am and wish to be:
Therefore I will embrace in few words what remains.

Indeed, wherever I turn myself (and in the course of years I have traversed in thought almost all parts of the state, occupied with the praise of the best King), wherever, I say, I look around, although nothing human is perfect, nevertheless our city, composed by Frederick William as its guide to tranquility and concord, seems to me to seek solely what is right and good, and to wish to attain it not by a turbulent path nor by a tumultuous struggle, but by a slow and quiet progress, which is very far from sluggishness and lethargy.

By what path we have already attained the good things, when all citizens joyfully acknowledge, bound with us in one mind and with most ardent vows to the most beloved Prince, I demonstrated last year on this very day:
which will ripen in future time and will increase with new growths.
And these things are owed and will be owed first to God, the supreme arbiter of empires, then to Frederick William, whom may the grace of God protect.
I have spoken.
They understood that rest from earthly cares and a harbor into which you may safely retreat are provided only by reverence for and piety toward the supreme deity.
There are indeed some who try whether, cleverly exploiting that disposition, they can bind peoples with new chains of servitude, so that a few may rule more licentiously:
But if that succeeded for them, a most pernicious superstition would be recalled, and the marrow of minds would be infected with decay.
But from this empire, which for a long time has been fostering the freedom of minds with its remarkable protection, that poison is warded off;
piety grows, vices are gently countered:
The best king is an outstanding example of piety, but devoted to no superstition, and finally, of these also, by far the greatest matters, as of all others, he is the firmest pillar.
I will not detain you longer, listeners, and the announcement of the literary commission urges me, which compels me to be briefer than I usually am and wish to be:
Therefore I will embrace in a few words what remains.

Indeed, wherever I turn (and in the course of years I have traversed in thought almost all parts of the state, occupied with the praise of the best King), wherever, I say, I look around, although nothing human is perfect, nevertheless our state, composed by Frederick William as its guide for tranquility and harmony, seems to me to strive solely for what is right and good, and to wish to attain it not by a turbulent path nor by a disorderly struggle, but by a slow and quiet progress, which is very far from sluggishness and lethargy.

By what path we have already attained the good things, when all citizens joyfully acknowledge it, bound together with us in one spirit and with most ardent prayers to the most beloved Prince, that I demonstrated last year on this very day:
which will ripen in the future time and will increase with new growths.
And these things are owed and will be owed first to God, the supreme arbiter of empires, then to Frederick William, whom may the grace of God protect.
I have spoken.

div.head: XV. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXVII. habita.

p.s: Since this duty, both most splendid and most weighty, has been conferred upon me, that I should speak annually in these solemn assemblies before you, hearers,

I have understood that nothing is more to be avoided by me than the noise of empty proclamation and the disgrace of flattery, which that kind of speech would be not only foreign to your and my character, but would not suit the virtues of Frederick William:
For flattery applied to a prince is, as it were, a reproach of him:

Indeed, I have even been accustomed to treat the just praise itself in a condensed manner, since it was too arduous and demanded such an abundance of eloquence and such maturity of judgment as I did not trust to be in me.

Nor, approaching directly at once in a straight course to proclaim the King, did I treat this and that argument somewhat more fully, from which I then strove to draw out those things that you desired and that were suited to this day.

But the more often I speak before you, the more confident I become, partly because I judge that you know me well enough, and partly because I know your indulgence, which will grant me pardon if anything falls out more imprudently:
and so I now almost dare to pursue the praise of Frederick William with no other argument added from outside, deliberately;

The longer I have been engaged in this matter, the more ardently I have desired, repeatedly reflecting and looking more deeply into the noble mind of Frederick William, that the best things, the more they are observed and examined, delight and move us all the more, while those things that shine only with a showy brilliance become cheap when considered more frequently.

And I seem to see, although you would always have been most willing to hear me discoursing about the best king alone, nevertheless that you would bear with the greatest difficulty my turning aside elsewhere especially in this year.

There is no one, not only in this empire, but also among foreigners, whom the health of Frederick William, impaired by an unfortunate accident, has not made anxious, to whom it has not been a grief, that a man, tried before by great public and great private calamities, as gold by fire, now nearer to old age, should be beset by this additional misfortune, if anything is fortuitous:
What vows were undertaken for his safety, and with what joy did his restoration affect everyone!
Why say more?
The King himself testified by a public edict how greatly the zeal of the people and of all the provinces had pleased him;
Not a few cities have testified, not by a pretense of affection but by heartfelt emotion, by festivals appointed on account of the health of the most beloved Prince.
In declaring these feelings, although perhaps we are among the most recent, yet you do not wish us to be the last.
Therefore I think that today we must not depart from the person of Frederick William.
They were undertaken for his safety, but with what joy did his restoration affect everyone!
Why say more?
The King himself testified by a public edict how greatly the zeal of the people and of all provinces had pleased him;
Not a few cities testified, not by a pretense of affection but by heartfelt emotion, by proclaiming festive days for the safety of the most beloved Prince.
In declaring these feelings, although perhaps we are the most recent, yet you do not wish us to be the last.
Therefore, today I am of the opinion that we must not depart from the person of Frederick William.
But if you should ask what it is that Frederick William is so greatly loved by all, I do not find the cause in his private virtues, which abound in him excellently:
For they do not love him as a private person, but as a prince;

Although even domestic customs are admired both by those nearby and by those farther away through reputation, so that generally the people do not only observe those things which the rulers of states publicly say and do, but they also scrutinize private life and habits, friendships, marriages, residences, dinners, and amusements along with serious matters:

Nor is it because he is king by birth that this wins Frederick William such great favor, although princes born to the throne, since they are wont to be gentler and are bound by less necessity of harming their own people, and since the bond of mutual concord has been handed down from their ancestors, are generally dearer to their citizens;
Yet it is not for that reason alone that he is beloved by his people;
For even those, over whom he has recently gained power, love him:
Finally, even this does not seem to me to be the true reason, that we are happy under this king;
For even those who are less blessed love him equally, and the people's enthusiasm was not provoked only by favorable circumstances, but was extraordinarily increased by the very adversities.
Therefore, to comprehend everything in three words, Frederick William is most dear to all, because they either feel or understand that all royal virtue resides in him.
I have said something great, listeners, and perhaps more than my own judgment can approve.
Why, indeed?
Am I the one who can discern, weigh, and examine royal virtue?
What of the fact that no one can know it thoroughly except a king?
We will not, I think, tolerate an unlearned man who judges about learned men:
Will it be permitted for anyone to judge kings, even one who has not approached public affairs?

Indeed, I could defend myself against these words of Niccolò Machiavelli, who in the dedication of his Prince, a most ingenious book, written to Lorenzo de' Medici, contends that just as those who are about to delineate regions are accustomed to stand on some plain in order to consider the nature of mountains and elevated places, but in order to know low and depressed places they are placed on mountains, so, in order that you may better perceive the character of peoples, you ought to be a prince, and in order that you may understand the policy of princes, you ought to be a popular man.

But to that excuse of his, which is more ambitious than befits my mediocrity, this somewhat more modest one seems preferable: that I shall not explain, by a profound discussion worthy of a man who has had experience of public affairs, from which I am by my own right absent, what sort of a prince one ought to be, but in a popular way, as one who has now resolved to set forth why the people is so greatly bound to the best King;
Finally, to speak of the King, since I am bound to him, it will be permitted to me, even if I am unskilled, to speak of him in such a way as if I were not unskilled.
You may better discern the character of peoples, and the prince, by which you may understand the principle of princes, you ought to be a popular man.

But to that excuse of his, which is more ambitious than befits my mediocrity, this somewhat more modest one seems preferable: that I have not undertaken to explain, in a profound discussion worthy of a man experienced in public affairs, from which I am by my own right absent, what sort of prince one ought to be, but rather, in a popular manner, as one who has now resolved to set forth why the people are so greatly bound to the best King.
Finally, to speak of the King, although I am bound, it will be permitted to me, even though unskilled, to speak of him in such a way as if I were not unskilled.

Indeed, intending to define royal virtue, I will not recite to you a list of all the gifts of talent, which, as they ought to be present in other good men, so also in princes, but I say that it is contained in a twofold character of mind: vigorous courage and gentle wisdom, which, although they can seem contrary to each other, nevertheless in a good man entirely conspire.

And indeed courage is needed, so that a prince may defend his empire against any enemy, both foreign and domestic, not only by the strength of arms, but also by the boldness of plans to be undertaken promptly and in time; and when these are postponed through fear or through avoidance of danger, the neglected opportunity often cannot be restored even by the strongest armies:

Then, besides war, in peaceful affairs themselves a brave and steadfast spirit is required, so that in difficult matters that demand keen mental concentration you may persevere diligently and harden yourself against everything by which you could be broken.

If such is the king, with the other good qualities besides, which I shall mention immediately, the people will safely entrust to him themselves and all their fortunes, because they know that he will not neglect anything through softness or weariness of occupations, but will do everything most vigorously:

and the citizens will admire him the more, the more prone to pleasures kingdoms are, the more difficult it is to maintain perpetually in the abundance of all things the severity necessary for a prince;
He can scarcely avoid the rocks to which the sweetest Sirens lure him, unless he is a man endowed with the best nature and educated and formed with care.
Whoever has stuck fast among these, although he may be received with courtesy, yet soon idleness and sloth will bring him into contempt.
But the duty of a prince is not fulfilled by courage alone;

And easily, unless, as the harmonicists temper grave sounds with acute ones and harsh with sweet, the spirited impulse of the breast is mingled with a gentler virtue, it rushes more fiercely into the slaughter of nations, especially when princes have devoted themselves to soldiery alone, to whom that precept of the Etruscan teacher has been too often chanted, that a ruler should have nothing else before his eyes, should practice no other art than the warlike, which alone is princely, and finally should care for nothing else than military discipline and military institutions.

This is so far from being true that he who regards only the army as his concern seems hardly half a prince, and does not understand that the army is raised and maintained for the sake of the state, not the state for the sake of the army.
Not to mention that the authors of that opinion established a tyrant rather than a prince, or, what is even more harmful, confused the one with the other.
But indeed, that temperament which I mentioned, wisdom provides to a royal mind, driving away any fierceness, and especially moderating the reins of civil government:

just as we have known the most celebrated and most beneficent founders and legislators of their own citizens, among whom it will suffice to have named Solon, to have been distinguished by the praise of wisdom:
But that, as I think, comprehends almost all the rest, which must be added to courage.
I do not speak of the shadowy wisdom of schools and sects, which no one will deny that a king can do without with impunity:
Indeed, that an abundance of learning does not form good princes, Tiberius demonstrated by his own example, along with other most learned Roman emperors;
and the excessive learning of Hadrian, in other respects an excellent prince, although it was useful to many, harmed both himself and not a few others:
as M.

If Antoninus and Frederick the Great had been less philosophers, less adorned with the little glory of literature, they would not, with their excellent natural abilities, have been destined to rule worse.
Indeed, the beginning and sum of wisdom is the consciousness of the divine power, which holds the world together by reason and governs it by providence;
just as that same Antoninus writes that God is a mind permeating all things and ruling the universe throughout all time according to the ordered cycles of the ages:
He whose mind is filled with that wisdom will religiously examine whatever he is about to do.

He will be pious without superstition, and will strive to direct his actions according to the divine model, since that evil, which in princes is by far the most deadly, has not infrequently raged with madness against peoples, or at least cast unworthy chains upon their minds.

He will not wish to be regarded by the citizens as a minister of God, so that greater authority and servile reverence may accrue to him, but he will be held in his own estimation, who has been set over free men to care for the salvation of men.

Nor must the king necessarily be equipped with that prudence in all parts of administering the state which we demand from those who handle each individual part, but just as those who once, by the power of intellect and eloquence, taught the teacher's precept that the ruler should have nothing else before his eyes, should practice no other art than the art of war, which alone is the principal one, and finally should care for nothing else than military discipline and military institutions:

This is so far from being true that he who regards only the army as his concern seems hardly half a prince, and does not understand that the army is established and maintained for the sake of the state, not the state for the sake of the army.
Not to mention that the authors of that opinion established a tyrant rather than a prince, or, what is even more harmful, confused the one with the other.
But indeed, that tempering which I mentioned is provided to the royal mind by wisdom, which drives away any fierceness, and especially guides the reins of civil government:
just as we have learned that the most celebrated and most beneficent founders and legislators of their states, of whom it will suffice to have named Solon, were distinguished by the praise of wisdom:
but that, as I think, comprehends almost all the rest, which must be added to courage.

Antoninus, even if Frederick the Great had been less of a philosopher, less adorned with the glory of literature, they would not have been destined to rule worse, given the excellent arts implanted in their nature.
Indeed, the beginning and the sum of wisdom is the consciousness of the divine power, which holds the world together by reason and governs it by providence;
just as that same Antoninus writes that God is a mind permeating all things and ruling the universe through all time according to the ordered cycles of the ages:
That wisdom with which the mind is filled, he will religiously examine whatever he is about to do;

He, pious without superstition, will strive to direct his deeds to the divine model, since that evil, which in princes is by far the most deadly, has not rarely raged with madness against peoples, or at least cast unworthy chains upon their minds;

He will not want to be regarded by the citizens as a minister of God, so that greater authority and slavish reverence may accrue to him, but he will be held in his own estimation, who has been placed over free men to care for the salvation of men.

Neque rex in omnibus rei publicae gerendae partibus ea instructus prudentia esse necessario debet, quam ab iis poscimus, qui singulas quasque tractant partes, sed sicuti qui olim ingenii et eloquentiae viribus
plebem regebant oratores nec iuris nec militiae nec rationis redituum et vectigalium magnopere periti erant, sed tamen rem publicam gubernabant non sine magna sollertia, ita regia ars universam civitatem moderatur eatenus, ut singulis quidem rebus singulos praeficiat administros, quibus quasi instrumentis utatur, ipsa vero summam omnium, quas illi praeparaverint, rerum complectatur, quae singularum partium praefecti suppeditarint, diiudicet, potissima decernat, quae agenda sint iubeat et mandet.

Thus, to use a very recent example, it is proper even for a prince to have some knowledge of letters and to value them highly, and certainly he himself ought in some measure to direct the literary institutions of the state, and to understand what their force and character are and how they may best be organized; yet he should not, as Dionysius the tyrant of Sicily competed with poets, Nero with singers, the Emperor Hadrian, and Henry VIII and James I, kings of England, with scholars in immoderate rivalry, aspire to the praise of learning, so that of course in this respect too he may be regarded as a prince.

Finally, not the least part of royal wisdom is self-control, by which the prince himself imposes a limit on himself, and modesty, by which he listens to those whom he has seen to be experienced, and allows himself to be taught by them.
Indeed, in such great power it is difficult to apply the reins to the mind:
and yet he who does not know how to command himself will not rightly rule others;
nor will he whose mind is not composed be able to compose his subjects.
But many think that it is kingly to yield to no one, and they take stubbornness and obstinacy for constancy, and a mind disposed tyrannically for a royal one;
Indeed, the greatest princes erred especially in this, that they trusted themselves too much;
and too late they understood how much better it would have been to have obeyed prudent advisers:
There are also those who resent advisers and fear to acknowledge reason as mistress, because they think that by obeying those who show what is right, their own power is diminished.
Moreover, in the choice of friends and in their use, how cautious a prince ought to be, no one fails to understand.

For not only from those who surround him is a conjecture made as to what sort of person he himself is, but the power of the empire depends to a great extent on whether he has chosen good or bad men, and whether he favors the former and restrains the latter, or not.

Whether he allows himself to be deceived by flatterers, who praise even things that are not praiseworthy, or report false things, because they judge those things to be pleasing to him, or whether he can tolerate the honorable freedom of speech, and those who prefer to reveal even unpleasant or sad things rather than conceal them are even more acceptable to him.

For all these things, sharp judgment is needed, which penetrates the people; the orators who governed the people were not greatly skilled in law, nor in military affairs, nor in the management of revenues and taxes, but nevertheless they governed the state not without great skill, so the royal art moderates the whole city to such an extent that it places individual administrators over individual matters, whom it uses as instruments, but it itself embraces the sum of all things that they have prepared, judges what the prefects of individual parts have supplied, decides the most important matters, and orders and commands what must be done.

Thus, to use a very recent example, it is proper even for a prince to have some knowledge of letters and to value them highly, and he himself ought in some measure to direct the literary institutions of the state, and to understand what their force and character are and how they may best be arranged; yet he should not, as Dionysius the tyrant of Sicily strove with poets, Nero with singers, the Emperor Hadrian, Henry VIII and James I, kings of England, with learned men in immoderate rivalry, aspire to the praise of learning, in order that he may be regarded as a prince in this respect too.

Finally, not the least part of royal wisdom is self-control, by which the prince himself may impose a limit on himself, and modesty, by which he may listen to those whom he has seen to be experienced, and allow himself to be taught by them.
Indeed, in such great power it is difficult to apply the reins to one's mind.
And yet, whoever does not know how to command himself will not rightly rule others.
Nor will he whose mind is not composed be able to compose his subjects.

Indeed, the greatest princes erred especially in this, that they trusted themselves too much;
and too late they understood how much better it would have been to have obeyed prudent advisers:

For all these things, there is need of a keen judgment, which penetrates the minds, plans, and characters of men, and especially of a certain simple sense of truth, by which one can choose the best and quickly embrace them.

Therefore, equipped with these arts, and joining courage of mind with wisdom, at the same time benevolent to all men, fair, just, faithful both to his own and to foreigners, he will be a prince, and in all matters he will keep measure;

He will temper severity with leniency, giving to each its due measure in its proper place, neither relaxing justice through soft counsels, nor being inclined to harsher measures by a gloomy disposition, nor prone to suspicions through a certain melancholy.
He will be sparing by reason and again liberal, because he knows that neither is right except with reason.
In short, he will do nothing without reason and judgment.

And whatever he will undertake, although he will not neglect a good reputation, nevertheless he will not do it in order to make his name famous, but he will exercise royal virtue for the sake of virtue.
Indeed, the insane desire for glory has rendered very many princes of the best character, who seemed to have been born for making peoples happy, most hostile both to themselves and to others.
Finally, a king so constituted will become a partaker of genuine happiness.
You may indeed see that the leading houses, although placed on the highest pinnacle, are not rarely lacking in happiness, which more easily falls to the lot of the humble:
But if, according to the old proverb, the wealthy have many things with which to console themselves, nevertheless not a few evils come upon princes, from which the lesser are free.
The greater the place, the greater the burdens and cares;
scarcely any space for rest is left for him who must look out for all:
The lower classes are refreshed by the familiar companionship of the wife and children;

For kings, even if they are not troubled by domestic calamity, or by the disgrace that happened to Octavian Augustus, rarely is there that prosperity of marriage which private individuals are accustomed to enjoy.
Add to this that the things which vex and afflict the whole state, by these the head of the republic is struck more bitterly.
But the royal mind, in having fulfilled all parts of duty and in the consciousness of good, will find the greatest and sweetest reward of its labors;

Nor will he who is subject to fortune compare his lot with the outcome, since fortune is no more enslaved to kings than to those who obey them, but, steadfast and least broken by human misfortunes, he will bear whatever adversities have fallen.

Nor will he compare his lot with the outcome, who is subject to fortune, which is no more enslaved to kings than to those who obey, but, steadfast and least broken by human misfortunes, he will bear whatever adversities have fallen.

In a popular manner, as I promised at the beginning, I have sketched the royal virtue, as far as I could by my own judgment, and not treating everything as fully as perhaps was fitting, because the subject is infinite and the time allotted to me is short;

But directing your attention to those things which I have discussed in summary, you have understood, I believe, even without my reminding you, how greatly Frederick William corresponds to the royal virtue:
Nevertheless, I hope I shall not do something ungrateful, if I repeat the more important outlines of the description.

And so, to keep the series I have begun, Frederick William, in the manner of his ancestors, took up the care of the army, yet he is not excessive in it, nor does he subordinate civil affairs to it, and he so tempered the soldier that he would not fight with the pagans as once, but would live in harmony:

The King himself proved himself keen in military service and a brave warrior, brave also as a man in enduring misfortunes, by which he was not overwhelmed, but was strengthened by them, having emerged greater from a not insignificant calamity, having gathered the fruit of wisdom from the turns of fortune, just as bees produce the sweetest honey from thyme, a most bitter and driest herb.

I am not saying anything more than the truth, but I stop unwillingly far below the magnitude of the deeds, far below those zeal of the people, which the most beloved King won for himself by his counsels and deeds, after the divine help, by his own virtue and the loyalty of the citizens.
Those who were present then remember and will appreciate them.
But what shall I say about the King's industry and endurance of labors?
Who is more removed from pleasures, to which even strong men sometimes yield, who is more removed from all luxury and softness, who is more frugal?
Indeed, no citizen is unaware how small a part of the revenues is spent on the court, with almost all turned to public benefits.

At the same time, Frederick William so tempers severity that, whereas severe princes are usually feared by their subjects, in this prince one cannot even ask what those curious about such matters have often asked: whether it is better to fear the king or to be loved by him.

For those very things which you might think can be accomplished by fear alone, the affection of the prince together with the reverence owed to him accomplishes, and the force of the laws through which he rules.
Indeed, stronger supports and bulwarks of empire than troops and citadels, with which we are supremely fortified.
But piety, the foundation of wisdom, Frederick William does not have on his lips, but in his heart;

nor does he wish to lead and bind the peoples by religious rites and ceremonies, as many kings thought they had to do for themselves, and in a certain way deceive them, but to improve his own by the true knowledge of God;

And his piety is not placed in the empty knowledge of dogmas, nor is it contaminated by blind and superstitious opinions, but it penetrates into the things that it does, and is illuminated by much thought.
Now who better holds the measure of himself?
Does he not combine the modesty of a private citizen with royal power and dignity?
Of which thing I will bring a great proof, even with the risk of offense.
We do not have the liberty, which they call, written on a charter;
Nor is the authority of the civil orders, as they are called, great in this empire:
But I hope that I shall not do something disagreeable to the whole state, if I shall repeat the more important outlines of the description.

Of which thing I will bring a great proof, even with the risk of offense.
We do not have the liberty, which they call, written on a charter;
Nor is the authority of the civil orders, as they are called, great in this empire:
but through the whole administration of the republic a certain moderation is diffused, which Frederick William leads by his commands and example;
whence nothing is done anywhere greedily, nothing violently, nothing by faction, and thus we are freer than those who seem most free.
Consider this system of literary universities:

Although these [schools] were subjected, by a common decree of the German Confederation eight years ago, to the stricter supervision of the prefects appointed over them, have they therefore lost their just freedom of teaching or of learning?
Are they not freer than the British and Gallic [schools], from which these [schools] seem especially to be disturbed by illiberal contentions?
I will not speak more distinctly about the prudence and diligence of Frederick William in choosing and consulting ministers and friends;
nor is it proper for me to name the living;
The dead are evidence, who under his auspices before these twelve years and earlier accomplished the greatest deeds at home and abroad and remain fresh in the memory and minds of the citizens.
On the contrary, the whole tribe of flatterers is banished from this kingdom and from this court.
But the wisdom of the most beloved Prince is perfected by that keen sense of truth, which I mentioned above, which aims with a sure shot at the right, the honorable, and the useful in any matter:
Since this excellent disposition is known to almost everyone, no one doubts that the king will rightly judge whatever things have come to his notice.
Such a man cannot fail to be just, fair, faithful, and kind to all who are worthy of kindness, but at the same time severe toward those who offend.
From this source proceeds the proper measure of punishment or leniency, of generosity or frugality.

Although it has long been proved by very many evidences that all these things are in Frederick William in a distinguished manner and in the way in which they ought to be, nevertheless I will mention two things which this year has brought, one of justice and equity, the other of bountiful liberality.
Of these, the former is of such a kind that thanks were publicly given to Frederick William even by foreigners.

For since for the space of many years no state had been willing to pay what was owed to the creditors of the former kingdom of Westphalia, our King was the first, on his part, to order that they be satisfied under certain conditions.
But the latter pertains to our affairs.

For although Frederick William, as he enriched the other literary universities of this kingdom, so also enriched ours from its foundation with extraordinary resources and repeatedly increased them, yet in respect of stipends by which needy young men might be supported, we were certainly less provided, in so far as in such a great multitude of academic citizens as we flourish with, which for a long time no administration of the republic of arts in Germany has been diffused, there is a certain moderation, which Frederick William sets forth by his commands and example.
From this, nothing is done anywhere greedily, nothing violently, nothing through faction, and thus we are freer than those who seem to be the freest.

Are they not freer than the British and Gallic [assemblies], from which these [assemblies] seem especially to be disturbed by illiberal contentions?
