For since for the space of many years no state had been willing to pay what was owed to the creditors of the former kingdom of Westphalia, our King was the first, on his part, to order that they be satisfied under certain conditions.
But the latter matter pertains to our affairs.

For although Frederick William, like the other literary universities of this kingdom, so also ours from its foundation has exceptionally enriched with resources and has repeatedly increased them, nevertheless with regard to stipends by which needy young men might be supported, we were certainly less furnished to that extent, inasmuch as in such a great multitude of academic citizens in which we flourish, such as no school of arts in Germany has had for a long time, it is fitting that there are very many who must be publicly assisted:
For whom the earlier resources were not sufficient, although they too had been gradually increased.

Therefore this year the most benevolent king has excellently arranged that from the treasury not inconsiderable stipends should be paid out both to others and especially to the sons of deceased clergymen and scholars, who among us should devote themselves to their studies:
and since private individuals very willingly follow the king's example, there is hope that more gifts of this kind will be added in the future:
In the same way, in this same academic year, two merchants of noble mind offered a not inconsiderable gift to the university for the same purpose.

By these arts, Frederick William, although not led by any desire for glory, but because, as Tacitus says most beautifully about Galba, he was neither careless of reputation nor a seller of it, obtained the praise of a good king, and at the same time attained the true happiness of a prince.

He is not outwardly wrapped in the appearance of happiness, surrounded by arms and horses and the display of an army, while within, the voices of desires and the anguish of conscience bear witness against that empty splendor, and the hidden groans of citizens sing ominously to the fame of his name:
but the tranquility of the breast is unfolded in the serenity of the brow;
Whatever fortune distributes, he accepts it with moderation, assigns to each its proper place, so that his mind is neither excessively contracted by adversity nor elated by prosperity.
Finally, in the affection, loyalty, and zeal of his fellow citizens, and in the love and harmony of the royal family, he rests secure.
I seem to myself to have accomplished what I wished.

Let us therefore pray to God, the Best and Greatest, that He, who has recently restored to us from sickness, may long keep him as a joyful prince and father among us, and that He may look after and provide for the Augustan house, which we have congratulated this year also as increased by a most pleasing marriage, and finally that He may look after and provide for this most powerful and flourishing empire, being propitious.
the school has had, it is consistent that there are very many who are to be supported publicly:
for whom the former resources were not sufficient, although they themselves were gradually increased.

Therefore, in this year the most benevolent king has excellently arranged that from the treasury not inconsiderable stipends should be paid out both to others and especially to the sons of deceased clergymen and scholars, who among us devote themselves to their studies:
And since private individuals most willingly follow the king's example, there is hope that more gifts of this kind will be added in the future:
In the same way, in this same academic year, two merchants of noble mind offered a not inconsiderable gift to the university for the same purpose.

By these arts Frederick William, although not led by any desire for glory, but, as Tacitus says most beautifully about Galba, neither careless of his reputation nor a seller of it, obtained the praise of a good king, and at the same time attained the true happiness of a prince.

He is not outwardly wrapped in the appearance of happiness, surrounded by arms and horses and the pomp of an army, while within, the voices of desires and the anguish of conscience bear witness against that empty splendor, and the secret groans of citizens sing an ill-omened accompaniment to the fame of his name:
but the tranquility of the breast is unfolded in the serenity of the brow;
Whatever fortune distributes, he accepts it with moderation, assigns to each thing its proper place, so that his mind is neither excessively contracted by adversity nor exults in prosperity.
Finally, in the affection, loyalty, and devotion of his fellow citizens, and in the love and harmony of the royal family, he rests secure.
I seem to myself to have accomplished what I wanted.

Let us therefore pray to God, the Best and Greatest, that He, who has recently restored to us from illness, may long keep the prince and father happy among us, and that He may graciously look after and provide for this most powerful and flourishing empire, and finally for the Augustan house, which we have congratulated this year as well, having been increased by a most pleasing marriage.

div.head: XVI. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXVIII. habita.

p.s: Since there are very many reasons, listeners, why we celebrate the birthday of Frederick William every year with such great festivity, and these reasons are partly common to the whole state, because it is equally in the interest of all to honor the best Prince, to recall with pious mind the benefits conferred by him upon the state, to give thanks to God the Best and Greatest for his welfare, and to make vows again and again; but partly they are proper and peculiar to us, because he not only founded this school, but also fosters it with more distinguished care, and so loves it that he has very recently adorned it with his name;
Then one thing seems to me so singular that, having set aside other places which I have pursued in previous years, I have decided to dwell on this one today.
I speak of a simple matter, not unknown or doubtful to any of you.

For if nothing contributes more to the prosperity of the human race, not to mention that of individual peoples, than the love of country implanted in the souls of citizens, which in no age has failed to produce the richest fruits and to give birth to the most beautiful deeds;
what should teachers of youth consider more important than to imbue and inflame those whom they have undertaken to form with that very virtue?

Of course, the feelings that a boy and a young man has imbibed with his first training, once they have crept into the innermost recesses of the mind and, as it were, cling to the very marrow and vitals, are retained both most firmly and most enduringly.

And I do not know whether the ancients, especially the Greeks, nourished that most sacred flame, by which it is certain that they alone burned, with anything more than with suitable education and gymnastic and musical training, which, with any pretense of foreign color rejected, accustomed their offspring to ancestral customs, ancestral worship, and ancestral literature and arts.

But we find the love of country and the love of the prince, who satisfies his duty, so united among the peoples who are ruled, that he who loves his country cannot but love the prince, and since the person of the prince contains in itself the whole state as if expressed in a visible image, without that most grateful affection with which we embrace the head of the republic, not even the country could be dear enough to our hearts.

Thus we are bound to the prince and the fatherland by the same law, formula, and faith, not as slaves, for whom there is a master but no fatherland, but as free men, who, just as at home they regard the prince in the place of a father, so in public they regard the king in the place of a parent.

These feelings, with which among us every best person is devoted to Frederick William, these pursuits, scarcely known to that most praised antiquity, intensify the very love of the fatherland, ennoble it, and fill it with wonderful sweetness;
And it is so far from being the case that the prince seizes what is owed to the fatherland, that whatever sincere love he has claimed for himself here, that has been claimed for the fatherland.

Therefore, in the schools, both the higher and the lower, should not the youthful minds be directed to reverence and love for the prince, and together with the teaching of letters must we not work so that the students are penetrated with those feelings?

Although this is not to be done on this one day alone, but on every occasion that presents itself, whether we must use eloquent words or whether it will suffice to set forth those things from which learners can of themselves gather right counsels;

Nevertheless this day, joyful and festive for the whole people, is at the same time most fitting, on which each literary college may testify that it is by no means unmindful of that most weighty duty.

And indeed I trust that you, most delightful colleagues, as many of you as are present, are just as fully aware as I myself am, how earnestly you love and admire Frederick William on account of the virtues divinely implanted in him, on account of his justice and moderation, piety and wisdom, gentleness and fortitude.
We understand our blessings; we understand who is their author:

Would anyone ever have thought that we, who have been captured by the excellent arts of Frederick William and heaped with the greatest benefits, would so forget the oath sworn to the Father of our country as to neglect, if we could by teaching or exhorting bring it about that the love of the citizens toward their most beloved King, which seems scarcely able to be increased, should be strengthened and spread?
to be.

These feelings, with which among us every best person devotes himself to Frederick William, these pursuits, almost unknown to that most praised antiquity, intensify, ennoble, and fill with wonderful sweetness the very love of the fatherland;
And it is so far from being the case that the prince seizes what is owed to the fatherland, that whatever sincere love he has claimed for himself here, that has been claimed for the fatherland.

Therefore, should not the minds of the young be directed in the schools, both the higher and the lower, to reverence and love for the prince, and must not effort be made, along with the teaching of letters, that the students be penetrated with those feelings?

Although this is not to be done on this one day alone, but on every occasion that presents itself, whether we must use eloquent words or whether it will suffice to set forth those things from which learners can of themselves gather right counsels;

nevertheless this day, joyful and festive for the whole people, is at the same time most suitable, on which each literary college may testify that it is by no means unmindful of that most weighty duty.

And indeed I trust that you, most delightful colleagues, all of you who are present, are just as fully aware as I am myself, how earnestly you love and admire Frederick William on account of the virtues divinely implanted in him, on account of his justice and moderation, piety and wisdom, gentleness and courage.
We understand our blessings, we understand who is their author:

And who would ever have thought that we, having been captured by the excellent arts of Frederick William and heaped with the greatest benefits, would forget the oath sworn to the Father of the Fatherland, if we could bring it about either by teaching or by exhorting that the love of the citizens toward the most beloved King, which seems scarcely able to be increased, should be strengthened and spread?
But here someone may now ask:
What is that, then, which, if you take away the bare admonition, learning and youthful training can contribute to arousing love of country and of the prince?

But what do you, who are placed in the very seat of the empire, who ought to have thoroughly known the excellence of this kingdom through closer acquaintance and, as it were, daily use, do to prove that which is said to be your purpose?
And how many of you are there who, shut up within the walls of a museum and bending over aged volumes, deserve well of the republic, of the fatherland?
What of the fact that literature is common to the whole human race?
Because almost all peoples are held together among themselves by the bond of the same arts?

Because the cultivation of letters draws men away from action, and, once drawn away, fixes them in a kind of foreign land and in an imaginary realm of pure notions, while agriculture, commerce, and all other business keeps them in the affairs of the state?
Indeed, excessive devotion to one's country harms even literature itself;

When not a few peoples are carried away by this to arrogance and pride, they cut off the flower of their own learning by despising foreign learning, a fault opposite to that of the Germans, who, marveling at foreign things, disparage their own countrymen enviously.
But does not philosophy, the mother and nurse of all learning, seem to shrink from the conveniences of common life and of the fatherland?

Thus, to mention Thales at once, from whom this science took its beginning, and Anaxagoras and similar men, there were already among the ancients those who would say that they were indeed wise but by no means prudent, and that they had known things difficult, admirable, and altogether divine, but useless, because they did not seek human goods.

And do not say that this is the property of the physicists; he who is said to have first called philosophy down from heaven, to have placed it in cities, and even to have introduced it into homes, that Socrates was far removed from common utility, and, paying little attention to his native soil, when he was asked of what country he was, declared himself a citizen of the world.
The same opinion pleased the Stoics, who nevertheless were no less alien to moral philosophy than Socrates.

And Plato says that those who, from adolescence, are occupied in courts and other public assemblies, seem to have been brought up as slaves, if they are compared with the one whom philosophy has formed:
to him not even the way to the forum is known, he says, nor does he know where the senate-house or any other council of the state is;

And in truth, his body alone is placed in the state and lives in the place of a foreigner, but his soul, having spurned all these things, investigates the things that are above the earth and below, and the whole nature of things, by no means lowering itself to what is near.
Nor does Aristotle not prefer the contemplative life to the active:
and you might say that it is difficult to join both, because literature demands leisure, and business demands strenuous industry.
Indeed, not only philosophers teach such things:
we have even heard emperors proclaiming that it is not fitting for learned men to cast votes concerning the affairs of the state.

Finally, literature is thought to offer some most welcome refuge and a retreat full of solace, where, tossed by the waves of public life, you may rest secure, where no one may disturb those Archimedean circles, but as if in the cloisters of monasteries you may hide away freed from all contagion of miseries.
Are these and many similar things, which I refrain from recounting, held together among themselves by the bond of the same arts?

Because the cultivation of letters withdraws men from action, and having withdrawn them, fixes them in a foreign land, as it were, and in a certain imaginary realm of pure notions, while agriculture, commerce, and all other business keep them in the affairs of the state?
Indeed, excessive love of country harms even literature itself;

When, by this, not a few peoples are carried away to arrogance and pride, they cut off the flower of their own learning by despising foreign learning, with a fault opposite to that of the Germans, who, marveling at foreign things, disparage their own people enviously.
But does not philosophy, the mother and nurse of all disciplines, seem to shrink from the conveniences of common life and of the fatherland?

Thus, immediately, Thales, from whom this science almost took its beginning, and Anaxagoras and similar men, there were already among the ancients those who would say that they were indeed wise but by no means prudent, and that they had known things difficult, admirable, and altogether divine, but useless, because they did not seek human goods.

The same opinion pleased the Stoics, who nevertheless were no more alienated from moral philosophy than Socrates.

And Plato says that those who from adolescence are engaged in lawsuits and other public assemblies seem to have been brought up as slaves, if they are compared with the one whom philosophy has fashioned:
To this man not even the way to the forum is known, he says, nor does he know where the senate-house or any other council of the republic is;

And in truth, his body alone is placed in the state and lives in the place of a foreigner, but his soul, having despised all these things, investigates the things that are above the earth and below, and the whole nature of things, by no means lowering itself to what is near.
Nor does Aristotle not prefer the contemplative life to the active:
And you might say that joining both is difficult, because literature demands leisure, and business demands strenuous industry.
Indeed, not only philosophers teach such things:
we have even heard emperors proclaiming that it is not fitting for learned men to cast votes concerning the affairs of the state.

Finally, literature is thought to offer some most welcome refuge and a retreat full of solace, where, tossed by the waves of public life, you may rest secure, where no one may disturb those circles of Archimedes, but as if in the cloisters of monasteries you may hide away freed from all contagion of miseries.

If any learned man should approve of these and more things of this kind, which I refrain from setting forth, do you think that he will be sincerely faithful and devoted to the prince and to his country, or that he will be affected in a very different way from the Alexandrian poets and men of letters, who were nourished and well kept, chiefly for the sake of display, by kings of foreign stock, who kept the people in check by fear and superstition, a people destitute of a country in their own land?
Indeed, that condition seems to me to differ from ours by an incredible amount.

And I would think that anything should be conceded sooner than that the learned men of this empire should be so alienated from Frederick William and the Prussian people that their learning should be completely separated from the state's policy, and that our minds should not be bound to both the King and the republic by an inner bond of piety.
If we lacked this piety, this very solemnity of this day would not be valued beyond the giving of thanks.

siquis doctus probarit, num eum putatis principi et patriae ex animo fidum et addictum fore, aut multo aliter affectum, atque Alexandrinos fortasse poetas et litteratores, ostentationis causa potissimum alitos et bene habitos a peregrinae stirpis regibus, qui metu et superstitione continebant populum in sua ipsius terra patriae expertem?
Nae ista condicio mirum quantum distare a nostra mihi videtur;

And I would think that anything should be conceded sooner than that the learned men of this empire should be so alienated from Frederick William and the Prussian people that their learning should be completely separated from the state's policy, and that our minds should not be bound to the King and the republic by a deeper bond of piety.
If we lacked this piety, this very solemnity of this day would not be to be valued beyond an act of thanksgiving.

Now, since it seems that there is rather a very close connection between the state and literature, which I do not doubt that the most wise king, aiding the pursuits of learning with such great munificence, has not only himself perceived, but also demands that both teachers and learners keep before their eyes:

Although you perhaps have a better knowledge of these matters than I do, nevertheless, since it is my duty to express your opinions to the best of my ability, I advise that knowledge, by no means estranged from the fatherland, serve the interests of the country in a threefold manner.
For first, what the wise provide for the human race, they provide at the same time for their fellow citizens, and they ought to be citizens at once of the world and of a particular state;
Then, since the fatherland is defined not so much by its soil as by the common character of the people or of the state, education contributes very much to cultivating this character.
Finally, vigorous learning passes into all parts of the state.

For if Aristotle truly taught that man is a political animal, then human life is perfected and completed in the state, and the state itself seems to be nothing other than the natural condition and state of the human race, formed and composed according to the standard of reason;

Therefore, whoever strives to aid the perfection of mortals and the progress of the human race—which is certainly the mark of an educated person—even if he devotes his cares to no particular commonwealth, whether by enlightening minds, or by correcting morals, or by discovering useful things, while deserving well of all men, at the same time earns the favor of his fellow citizens.

When the same person, if he has learned to reason correctly, is not unaware that human nature itself demands that the human race be divided into several societies, he will understand that he too, although a citizen of the world, owes a certain definite state as his fatherland, just as each person has a definite nation and family, and that he must especially love it, whether he will have been born a citizen of that state or granted that right.
What of the fact that those very men who first called themselves worldly-minded did not neglect their fatherland or the republic at all?
Or did Socrates ever leave Athens, except to fight with arms for his fatherland, and once for the sake of seeing the Isthmian games?

Does he not, in that most famous conversation which he held with Crito in prison, although he praises Sparta and Crete, nevertheless declare that he was never desirous of any city other than Athens, nor of any laws other than those of Attica?
That he had resolved to live according to these and to perform the duties of a citizen, and to obey them?
Did he not approve these resolutions both by his life, which was devoted, as to philosophy, so to the correction of the morals and institutions of the citizens, and by his very death?
Did not his country afterwards mourn him, unjustly condemned, and honor him with a bronze statue?
But did the Stoics, because they wished to be citizens of the world, live in idleness?
On the contrary, their adversaries, the Epicureans.
Or M.
Did Antoninus, who affirms that for himself as a man the world is his fatherland and his commonwealth, decline the burdens of empire?
Indeed, these examples clearly demonstrate, if I see anything, that the wisdom which makes its followers citizens of the world does not harm one's country.

For just as commerce, which in this matter is most similar to literature, spreading light through all the regions of the world, while it opens up the intercourse of nations, does not seem to dissolve the bonds of one's fatherland;

that the most holy Christian faith, which wills that the pious have an invisible and heavenly fatherland, does not diminish the love of this earthly one, but rather binds it with religion and stirs it with divine instinct, so that we devote our life to fatherland and prince, and pour out our blood for altars and hearths.
And he thought that it was especially to be cherished, whether he would be a citizen by birth or granted that right.
What of the fact that those very men, who first called themselves world-citizens, by no means neglected their fatherland or the republic?
Or did Socrates ever leave Athens, except to fight with arms for his fatherland, and once for the sake of seeing the Isthmian games?

Does he not, in that most famous conversation which he held with Crito in prison, although he praises Sparta and Crete, nevertheless declare that he was never desirous of any city other than Athens, nor of any laws other than those of Attica?
That he had resolved to live according to these and to perform the duties of a citizen, to obey them?
Did he not approve these resolutions both by his life, dedicated as it was to the improvement of the citizens' morals as well as to philosophy, and by his very death?
Did not the fatherland afterwards mourn him, unjustly condemned, and honor him with a bronze statue?
But did the Stoics, because they wished to be citizens of the world, live in idleness?
On the contrary, the Epicureans were the adversaries of these.
Or was M.
Did Antoninus, who affirms that for himself as a man the world is his fatherland and commonwealth, decline the burdens of empire?
Indeed these examples clearly, if I see anything, demonstrate that the wisdom which makes its followers citizens of the world does not harm the fatherland.

For just as commerce, which in this matter is most similar to literature, spreading light through all the regions of the world, while it opens the intercourse of nations, does not seem to dissolve the bonds of one's country;

that the most holy Christian faith, which wills that the pious have an invisible and heavenly fatherland, does not diminish the love of this earthly one, but rather binds it by religion and stirs it by divine instinct, so that we devote our life to fatherland and prince, and pour out our blood for altars and hearths.

But mortals, placed at the very lowest step of human culture, at first confined their fatherland within the nearest and very narrow boundaries of the field or town where each one had been born and grown up, comparing the familiar and the foreign from their seat and soil;

Indeed, they were bound to their fields, streams, and hills by the sweetest familiarity, and they delighted in places known from infancy, the sight of which affects no one who is even moderately gentle without a pleasant recollection of past times.
Soon, a person more roused and already capable of conceiving higher things in his mind understands that the state, tempered by laws suited to his character, is his fatherland;

Then he is no longer, as it were, bound to the soil, but measures his fatherland by the community of his nation, and first of his own smaller tribe, then of a people embracing several tribes closely related in origin:
just as the Greeks, who began late to be called by a common name, even later and scarcely ever firmly coalesced into one body, although each one had his own country as a republic exceedingly dear;

Just as the provinces of the kingdoms that now exist gradually and not without disturbances and wars came together in such a way that citizens of different provinces recognized a common fatherland for themselves.
And indeed the Greeks judged that the republic, together with liberty, which cannot be separated from it, was especially the fatherland, which, as if confined to no place, could even be transferred.
Thus the Phocaeans, besieged by Harpagus and driven to the last extremity, transferred their homeland to Corsica, and soon afterwards to Velia.
Thus Bias of Priene tried to persuade the Ionians to leave Ionia, sail to Sardinia, and establish a city there, in order to preserve their freedom.
Thus Herodotus reports that Themistocles thought about transferring Athens to Italy.
Thus, wherever the Greeks occupied land in the most diverse regions—Asian, Libyan, Italian—that very land seemed to them to be Greece and was called Greece.
And rightly so;
since a state does not consist of lands and buildings, but of laws and institutions.

Of course, when to the communion of language and customs, without which peoples can never be rightly united into one state, there has been added this civil sharing of rights and duties, of government and obedience, of advantages and dangers, and a certain perpetuity of public and private discipline, by which the natural character may be strengthened;

To these the zeal of the citizens attaches itself, and the love of one's country, which formerly clung to the soil alone, that mute and inanimate thing, is now transferred to this form of the commonwealth, this character of the people, this living and immortal society of souls that have the same end of action and agree in the same counsels; and although this society is formed from all the citizens and can even be preserved to some extent without royal dignity, nevertheless it is best and most perfectly contained in one head of the commonwealth, a legitimate prince.
And this love of country grows the more, the more the people's own character is expressed, the freer the condition of subjects, the more certain the harmony between citizens and the prince.

Nor do I fear to say that even those peoples which have accrued to any state through the outcomes of wars and the fortuitous division of lands can be united among themselves by these bonds, if only there comes to their aid some conformity of primitive character and disposition, which certainly inheres in all nations of Germanic stock, and the rulers of the state are skilled in that weaving work which Plato's Statesman imposes on them, namely joining together dissimilar threads.

Did they not, although this kingdom had grown together from various peoples in a certain way, as if by a chance concourse of elements, ever firmly coalesce into one body, the power of the empire holding a certain balance, although each one had his fatherland exceedingly dear?

Just as the provinces of the kingdoms that now exist gradually, and not without disturbances and wars, so came together that the citizens of different provinces recognized a common fatherland for themselves.

And indeed the Greeks judged that the republic, together with liberty, which cannot be separated from it, was especially their fatherland, which, as if confined to no place, could even be transferred:
Thus the Phocaeans, besieged by Harpagus and driven to extremes, transferred their fatherland to Corsica, and soon to Velia;
Thus Bias of Priene tried to persuade the Ionians to leave Ionia and sail to Sardinia and establish a city there, in order to preserve their liberty;
Thus Herodotus says that Themistocles thought about moving Athens to Italy.
Thus, whatever land the Greeks occupied in the most diverse regions—Asian, Libyan, Italian—that land seemed and was called Greece to them.
And rightly so.
Since a state does not consist of lands and buildings, but of laws and institutions.

Of course, when to the communion of language and customs, without which nations can never be rightly united into one state, there has been added this civil sharing of rights and duties, of government and obedience, of advantages and dangers, and a certain continuity of public and private discipline, by which the natural character is strengthened;

To these the zeal of the citizens attaches itself, and the love of one's country, which formerly clung to the soil, that mute and lifeless thing, is now transferred to this form of the republic, this character of the people, this living and immortal society of souls who have the same end of action and who agree in the same counsels; and although this society is formed from all the citizens and can even be preserved to some extent without royal dignity, nevertheless it is best and most perfectly contained in one head of the republic, a legitimate prince.
And this love of country grows the more, the more the people's own character is expressed, the freer the condition of subjects, the more certain the harmony between citizens and the prince.

Nor do I fear to say that even peoples that have come to any state through the outcomes of wars and the fortuitous division of lands can be united by these bonds among themselves, if only some harmony of primitive character and disposition, which certainly inheres in all nations of Germanic stock, comes to their aid, and the rulers of the state are skilled in that weaver's work which Plato's Statesman imposes on them, namely joining together dissimilar threads.

Does not, although this kingdom has grown together from various peoples as if by some chance concourse of elements, the power of the empire holding a certain balance, and a certain equality of laws and institutions, to which even equal pursuits of letters and arts must be counted, and one who governs all, who is fair to all, the spirit of the most beloved Prince, unite the inhabitants of the Rhine and the Vistula, the Oder, the Elbe, and the Weser, and all the intervening provinces, not by arms, but by the consent of their wills, into this one Prussian name?
Even if there are some (though there are none or very few) who have not yet become sufficiently accustomed to gentle rule, they will soon be charmed by the virtues of this state;
But by the love of Frederick William I judge even those already now captivated, who previously were most hostile to Prussia.

That therefore, which I have said, the character of the people and of the state is manifestly formed to a great extent by public education, especially since those who are placed in charge of affairs are almost all educated in public schools.

Therefore, although, with the connection of the most cultivated lands of Europe having been increased to an immense degree, literature cannot retain as much of a peculiar national character as it once did among the Greeks, nevertheless our discipline ought to harmonize with the inner character of the people and the state, and to bring it as far as possible to perfection.
How this is to be done, I will not explain now:
Nor can this be explained except by examining the institutions of the state, whatever they may be, and the policies which it itself has followed through a long series of years.

But I think no one will deny that the Prussian state is endowed with a certain and indeed excellent character, which, having gained such great strength under its most glorious kings and leaders, has attracted and still attracts very many foreigners, whom it by no means excludes, departing very far from the Spartan rejection of foreigners, and in a certain way transforms them to the nature of the natives.

But if we imagine that pupils have been entrusted to us for that character of the state, to which, if not all, certainly most will concede that freedom of minds is especially fitting, we shall perform our duty both to the fatherland and to Frederick William.

And does a certain equality of laws and institutions, to which even equal pursuits of letters and arts must be added, and one who governs all, who is fair to all, the spirit of the most beloved Prince, unite the inhabitants beyond the Rhine and the Vistula, and the dwellers on the Oder, Elbe, and Saale, and all the intervening provinces, not by arms, but by the agreement of wills, into this one Prussian name?
Even if there are some (though there are none or very few) who have not yet become sufficiently accustomed to gentle rule, they will soon be charmed by the virtues of this state;
But by the love of Frederick William I judge even those already now captivated, who previously were most estranged from Prussia.

That therefore, which I have said, the character of the people and of the state is manifestly formed to a great extent by public education, especially since those who are placed in charge of affairs are almost all educated in public schools.

How this is to be done, I will not explain now:
Nor can this be explained except by examining the institutions of the state, whatever they may be, and the policies which it itself has followed through a long series of years.

But if we imagine that pupils have been entrusted to us with a view to that character of the state, to which, if not all, certainly very many will concede that freedom of minds is especially fitting, we shall render our duty both to the fatherland and to Frederick William.
Thirdly, I said that vigorous learning is spread into all parts of the state;
Since this is well known, I will not pursue it except briefly.
Indeed, when one considers the public utilities of theology, jurisprudence, medicine, natural science, mathematics, and the disciplines of politics and economics, no one will fail to see what I mean.

But philosophy and history are both the foundation of many of these doctrines, and they set forth precepts and examples, by which it is not doubtful that the state's condition and institutions, once heard, can also be corrected;

But above all those [philosophies] oppose with their own light the worst evils of states, the unbridled domination of tyrants and insane superstition, by which cunning men are accustomed to seize the weakness of mortals.
This is the chief reason why both wicked princes and priests greedy for power have been hostile to them at all times.

Finally, these studies of humanity, as they are called, themselves also assist the other disciplines, and it has been established by long use and approved by the judgment of our princes as well, that they, when rightly handled and confined within the just limits of liberal education, are especially suited for educating those whom the state employs in conducting its affairs.
I knowingly refrain from other praises, which may seem a little more remote from the immediate advantage of the state;
Although Cicero, certainly not ignorant of public affairs, did not even in the forum fear to recommend good arts to these men.
But he would be unfair who would wish to confine literature within the limits of common usage.

For not only can you not easily foresee what will be useful, but literature has its own value even without utility, and knowledge, divine and human, explores all things, the innermost recesses of nature and of the mind, and whatever men have done and thought, driven by the innate impulse of discovering truth, for the sake of knowledge itself.

But if anyone should think that only that part of that manifold apparatus of learning should be retained in the state which seems to suit his own purposes, and should undermine the foundations of literature, those hidden things not suited to common use, and should act not much differently than the Cynics, who, because they thought that a man suffices for himself for living rightly, being content with a staff and a wallet and a pot and a cup, or even with a hollow hand instead of these, are said to have despised whatever of furniture and utensils adorns life and makes it more pleasant.

This one thing I think must be conceded: that there is a kind of, as it were, dead learning, or rather a semblance and imitation of learning, which, however much it may boast itself, is utterly illiberal and shadowy, and neither exercises the mind nor sharpens the judgment, nor fills the soul with ideas, nor teaches anything or refreshes and delights, but heaps empty chaff into its granaries, and dwelling among the volumes of books alone, comprehends nothing with the mind.

Therefore, just as we will allow that doctrine to be exiled from the state, so we will say that lofty and profound learning, although it is far removed from common use, together with poetry and the other arts of this kind, is the glory and ornament of that state.
Nor must we fear that we, who perform public duties, will become too estranged from the state, or that we will become bookworms in this city:

Indeed, they oppose that [doctrine] of Frederick with their own light, [opposing] the evils of the tyrants' unbridled domination and insane superstition, by which cunning men are accustomed to seize the weakness of mortals.
This is the chief reason why both wicked princes and priests greedy for power were hostile to them at all times.

Finally, these studies of humanity, as they are called, themselves also assist the other disciplines, and it has been established by long use and approved by the judgment of our princes as well, that they, when properly handled and confined within the just limits of liberal education, are especially suited for educating those whom the state employs in conducting its affairs.
Knowingly I refrain from other praises, which seem to be a little more remote from the immediate advantage of the state;
Although Cicero, certainly not ignorant of public affairs, did not even in the forum fear to recommend good arts to these men too.
But he would be unfair who would wish to confine literature within the limits of common usage.

For not only can you not easily foresee what will be useful in the future, but literature has its own value even without utility, and knowledge, divine and human, explores all things, the innermost recesses of nature and of the mind, and whatever men have done and thought, driven by the innate impulse of the mind to discover truth, for the sake of knowledge itself.

But if anyone should think that only that part of that manifold apparatus of learning should be retained in the state which seems to suit his own purposes, and should undermine the foundations of literature, those hidden things and not suited to common use, and should act not much differently than the Cynics, who, because they thought that a man suffices for himself for living rightly, being content with a staff and a wallet and a pot and a cup, or even with a hollow hand instead of these, are said to have despised whatever of furniture and utensils adorns life and makes it more pleasant.

This one thing I think must be conceded: that there is a kind of, as it were, dead learning, or rather a semblance and imitation of learning, which, however much it may boast of itself, is utterly illiberal and shadowy, and neither exercises the mind nor sharpens the judgment, nor fills the soul with ideas, nor teaches anything or refreshes and delights, but stuffs empty chaff into its granaries, and dwelling among the volumes of books alone, comprehends nothing with the mind.

Therefore, just as we will allow that man to be exiled from the state, so we will say that lofty and profound learning, although far removed from common use, together with poetry and the other arts of this kind, is the glory and ornament of that state.
Nor must we fear that we, who discharge public duties, will be too much estranged from the republic, or that we will become bookworms in this city:

Indeed, that institution of Frederick William, of placing the principal schools especially in the leading cities, besides its other advantages, seems also to have this, that both teachers and students become accustomed somewhat more easily to a just measure of those things which are outside of learning.

William's plan of placing the principal schools especially in the chief cities, besides its other advantages, seems to have this one too, that both teachers and students become accustomed somewhat more easily to a just measure of those things which lie outside of learning.

I have briefly run through what I had promised, listeners, because, since some time is now cut off from the orator previously granted for publicly reciting the opinions that have been delivered concerning literary commissions,
But although I have not today deliberately proclaimed the praises of the most beloved Prince, yet what need is there for me to show that almost all the things I have said are suited to his person?
Frederick William indeed both wills and understands that literature is useful to the state, but he does not derive its dignity from this use:
For I think no state has prescribed a freer course or granted a wider field to them than ours under the auspices of this king.
He so increased the flower of learning in this empire that he may rightly be called the chief supporter of them in Prussia;
He corrected and enlarged everything received from previous kings;
He added so many new honors that he left his predecessors far behind;

Finally, the king unites those three best things, the true, the good, and the beautiful, with each other, and the arts of peace and the prosperities of the civil state with military virtue and power, and teaches piety and moral integrity to the citizens by his example.
Nor are those things of such a kind that they are suitable only for this age.

Just as the things that Frederick the Great did excellently have propagated their fruit to posterity, so Frederick William is going to be beneficial to the state after himself, while, although the present necessities, increased by the iniquity of former times, may demand a huge expense, he does not cease to establish lasting institutions and to scatter the seeds of a future harvest.
And so the salvation of this prince, embracing the prayer of all and the conveniences of the whole state, is [the object of universal desire];
Here he is fair and courteous to all good men of every rank, here a refuge for the wretched, here uniquely popular and civic-minded;
In short, the same things are joyful and sad to him as to the citizens.

Would that the supreme deity might grant our prayers, that Frederick William may enjoy perpetually the happiness he most deserves, and that a green and long old age may befall him, seeing the success of his undertakings;

so that the quiet and lasting peace of the state may answer to that tranquility of mind, by which he has attained the true blessedness of the wise man, and may favor the plans undertaken for the restoration of the city;
finally, that the whole Augustan house may be preserved and increased, and that this security and glory of the empire, once confirmed, may endure for the longest time.

div.head: XVII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXIX. habita.

p.s: The Persians, once a most distinguished people, seem to me to have wisely established, my hearers, that legal action should be taken against a man who, although he could return a favor to one who had deserved well of him, was detected as ungrateful, because they thought that such a man would also neglect the gods, parents, fatherland, and friends, and they judged that an ungrateful man differs in no way from an impious one.
For indeed to pious, gentle, tender minds that most sacred feeling of gratitude is especially sweet;
Nothing stings them more sharply, nothing in the whole nature of things is more atrocious and foul, than a man forgetful of benefits:

And if it is permitted to establish certain grades of harmless pleasures, the sweetest thing seems to me to be doing good, the next sweetest to be grateful for good deeds, the third to be affected by the pleasantness of benefits, and finally to receive less gratitude than is actually due, which indeed no one would demand, who, as is rightly prescribed, should immediately forget what he has done well for others.
But from these, the fourth, and that by far the greatest, has been divinely given to the father of his country, whom we always venerate, indeed both silently and openly, but today more solemnly;
to us the second and third, these also exceptionally good, have been left:
on account of which, lest our piety be missed, deservedly this day is held by us as uniquely joyful, happy, festive.

For who is more beneficent, who more worthy of the praise of grateful citizens, than Frederick William, a prince both vigorous and gentle, restorer of the state in peace and war alike, corrector of morals, establisher of the arts, fair and just to all, generous to the deserving, a comfort to the wretched and afflicted?

Sed ego hoc sollemni die non modo laudatione identidem prosecutus sum eum regem, quem laudanti occinas adeo illud, quod in sophistam Herculis praeconia recitarunt haud inficete Antalcidas Spartanus dixit, „Quis autem illum vituperat?" verum etiam, qualis Fridericus Guilelmus sit, non in sola ipsius persona spectandum censeo:

de qua dicturus sicuti effugiam ipsam speciem assentationis, quamquam mihi inter vos, ut Principi optimo sinceris animis obstrictos, ne metuendam quidem, ita non magis recedam a Friderici Guilelmi egregiis artibus exponendis, quam qui olim Athenis publice constituti erant, ut civium bello caesorum memoriam celebrarent, visi sunt ab argumento deflexisse, ubi patriae enarrabant bona, cui fortes illi bellatores et gloriam commodumque addiderant, et suam ipsi debebant virtutem, educatione et exemplis parentum clarissimis ad res praeclare gerendas formati atque excitati.

Attamen quum considero, quam varias res ac multiplices haec concludat materia, quas ne summa quidem eruditio et peritia cum uberrimis eloquentiae copiis coniuncta exhaurire aliqua ex parte queat, tantum non deterreor ab incepto:
et certe licebit in exigua aliqua particula hinc delibata consistere, quae neque ab re litteraria neque a temporibus esse aliena videatur.
Tempora vero quae dico?

Nimirum ex quo Europae regna ab imperio unius impotenti liberata sunt, si natas in civitatibus aliquot male compositis seditiones, atque inde exortas expeditiones magis quam bella et proelia exceperis, alta pace gavisa haec orbis pars est, coepitque recreari et florere:
Occidens quidem etiamnunc misere commotus et oppressus;
longinquum Orientem vastat bellum, ut servitus atrocissima tolleretur, susceptum;
mediae gentes securae, et praeter leves suspiciones et nescio an dicam minas nihil audetur gravius, dum pacem continet principum sapientia.

Hanc temporum condicionem mihi, qui in litteris occupatus sim, spectanti oblata cogitatio est, quae quum in qualibet re publica tum in nostra civitate inter bellicum et militarem statum atque inter disciplinas artium intercedat ratio:
de qua pauca et exilia disputaturum me vestrae, auditores, aura benignitatis adiuvate.
quod ipse rem publicam fingit et ab illa fingitur vicissim;

de qua pauca et exilia disputaturum me vestrae, auditores, aura benignitatis adiuvate.

Et primum quidem, quum regnum Borussicum vulgo militare dicatur (neque ipse veritus olim sum certa quadam ratione hoc pronuntiare), mireris hoc imperium artium cultu tantum praestare, quantum praestat sine dubio.

Quamquam enim bello aliquando populorum vires et ingenia quasi ex somno excitantur, et quemadmodum tempestates aërem purgant et solum fecundant, sic illa morbis rei publicae, et imprimis luxuriae, negligentiae, ignaviae medentur, quo simul meliorem litterarum tractationem provocari posse non nego;

tamen non quodlibet
bellum has affert prosperitates.
Nam quae bella per solos, ut ita dicam, milites, nullis acrieribus populi studiis geruntur, ea populum aeque quidem atque alia bella affligunt, non aeque erigunt:

quae nec libertatem, qua litterae imprimis crescunt, vindicent rei publicae, nec latiorem orbis terrarum cognitionem afferant, neque utilibus exterorum artibus augeant indigenas, aut quibus nimium vastentur terrae, ea quomodo possint gentibus conducere, non video.
nec Romanis civilia bella boni praestiterunt quidquam;
nec Ludovici Quarti decimi arma eam, quae illo regnante fuit, Gallis litterarum laudem attulerunt;
istud autem triginta annorum bellum sacrum longe perniciosissimum litteras Germaniae universas funditus exstirpavit;
nec bellum septem annorum magnopere excitavit ingenia;
Neapolionis vero expeditiones nec Galliarum nec gentium victarum profuere litteris.
Sed Medica bella aucta libertate eruditionem Graecorum mirum quantum adiuverunt;

Alexander Magnus, dum Orientem aperit, rerum et humanarum et divinarum amplificavit notitiam, et Graecas litteras in barbaris sparsit oris, similliterque expeditiones cruciatae aliquid certe utilitatis praestiterunt Occidenti;

postremo nostra memoria bellum pro libertate susceptum non solum nobilissimorum carminum copia sane dignorum, quae cum Tyrtaeo et Alcaeo componantur, ditavit Germanos, verum etiam animos a frivolis rebus avocatos ad optimum quidque et vero ad litterarum studia nova alacritate capessenda impulit.
Sane alia insuper via bellum ut ceterum civitatis apparatum, ita artes augere potest, ubi id victarum gentium divitias et tributa transfert ad victorem:
qua via Pericles Athenas litteris quibusvis et splendidissimis implevit operibus:
nec bello istum Athenarum cultum deberi, sed insito natura Atheniensibus artium optimarum studio, inde colligas, quod nec Sparta nec Roma ex similibus maioribusque rapinis comparem percepere fructum.
Iam vero quae de bello diximus, eadem videntur etiam pacatae civitatis ei convenire statui, qui unice ad bellum gerendum comparatus sit:

nisi quod
bellum has affert prosperitates.

nec bello istum Athenarum cultum deberi, sed insito natura Atheniensibus artium optimarum studio, inde colligas, quod nec Sparta nec Roma ex similibus maioribusque rapinis comparem percepere fructum.
Iam vero quae de bello diximus, eadem videntur etiam pacatae civitatis ei convenire statui, qui unice ad bellum gerendum comparatus sit:

nisi quod
domestica militia ne id quidem praestat, ut animis civium eos addat stimulos, quos iis bellum populi consensu coeptum admovet.
Denique ut bellum excitet ingenia, pax ea maturare debet;
pacisque artes litterae et sunt et vocantur:

haec alma pax non solum, quod praedicat Bacchylides, opes dispensat, et dulciloquorum flores carminum gignit, iuvenesque ad gymnasia et tibias et comissationes convocat, verum etiam altiora illa disciplinarum et scientiae gymnasia et praestantissimam philosophiae musicen alit, otiumque et opes ut in mitiores conferre artes liceat, efficit.
Nonne enim, ut summi poetae Britannici verbis utar, per bella, quemadmodum arva, prata, arbusta nostra vitiosa germinatione degenerant, sic iuventus artes dedocta efferatur?

Num vero pecunia omni in belli necessitates conversa artibus principes tantam possunt curam impendere, quantam Rex optimus, postquam diuturnis bellis pax laetissima successit, in magnificis per universum imperium litterarum et artium institutis vel condendis vel instruendis posuit?

Num vero pecunia omni in belli necessitates conversa artibus principes tantam possunt curam impendere, quantam Rex optimus, postquam diuturnis bellis pax laetissima successit, in magnificis per universum imperium litterarum et artium institutis vel condendis vel instruendis posuit?

Enimvero imperium Borussicum, quod olim fortasse ob magnum mercenariorum numerum potuit militari potentia unice nixum videri, haud magis militare est, quam unumquodque esse debet, neque eatenus, quatenus id vitiosum habetur.

Nam quum unamquamque civitatem paullo perfectiorem tres potissimum constituant ordines, qui ea quaerat, quae ad victum cultumque necessaria, commoda, iucunda sint, qui ceteros erudiat et doceat, qui armorum vi tueatur parta, et in horum concordia et concentu posita rei publicae salus sit;

merito imperfecta et vitiosa videbitur ea civitas, in qua unus ex his ordinibus aut minus excultus sit aut prorsus neglectus vel oppressus iaceat, unusque reliquos ita vicerit, ut in hunc cuncta vergant, hic in reliquos dominetur.
Ita civitas alia mercatoria, alia sacerdotalis, alia militaris iudicanda est, prout quaeque pars rei publicae nimium emineat:

sic, ut militaris exempla absolutissima, qualia nostra aetate vix nisi inter barbaros reppereris, ex antiquis petam rebus publicis, quae licet tam exiguae fuerint, ut una essent urbe vel paucarum communione circumscriptae, tamen clarissimas variarum, quas civitas induit, formarum imagines offerunt, et ob hoc ipsum, quod simpliciores fuerunt, singula civitatis elementa exhibent distinctiora;

sic inquam Sparta et Creta prope unice militares fuerunt, quod optimatium exercitus praepotens ceteris imperabat ut servis, agros colebant
clientes dure ut plurimum habiti, atque ut agriculturae opus quamvis utile et delectabile, sic mercatura, opificia, reliquus quaestus in nullo erant honore, litterae vero et artes, exceptis gymnicis et musica et siqua alia numinis colendi causa tractanda visa, nimium negligebantur, civesque, quod eximie perspexit Plato, non ad virtutem universam, cuius partibus omnibus perfusa esse res publica debet, sed ad solam fere fortitudinem formabantur;
sic Roma labens, ex quo penes Praetorium vis fuit imperii, militaris regni specimen miserabile extitit.
Sed nostra civitas numne paret militibus?
num maior apud nos quam in aliis regnis pars redituum in exercitum impenditur?
num reliquis rei publicae ordinibus obest exercitus aut numero aut auctoritate aut praerogativa sive sumpta sive concessa?
Nonne rei rusticae optimis institutis, levanda agricolarum condicione, agrorumque imprimis divisione egregie provisum est?
nonne opificia laxandis collegiorum vinculis, instituendis scholis, suo huic quoque ordini honore habendo, denique omni genere subsidiorum adiuvantur?
nonne vectigalia et portoria ita constituta, ea cum exteris pacta conventa sunt, ut quantum fieri potest, etiam mercantibus et negotiatoribus prospiciatur?

Quid quod tantum abest, ut solis armorum viribus locum tutari hoc regnum studeat, ut quum nullos proprios militiae socios habeamus, sed universorum Germanorum foederi adscripti ipsi simus, vectigalium tamen habeamus socios communi nobiscum utilitate libere coniunctos?
Quid autem dicam de artibus et disciplinis?
Num ulla est civitas non modo in Germania sed in universa Europa, quae in illas pro opum et finium amplitudine tantos sumptus fecerit et faciat quam nostra?

quae pari cura et liberalitate omne scholarum genus, et ludos inferiores, qui paganae et plebeiae multitudini aliquatenus instituendae destinati sunt, et gymnasia sive lycea, in quibus ingenuae eruditionis rudimenta traduntur, et universitates litterarias, quae altioribus studiis initiant discentes, colit et fovet;

quae divini numinis cultum non quo populus libentius serviat, sed quo ad pietatem, ad probitatem, ad lenitatem morum imbuatur, tuetur ita, ut sacerdotibus et verbi divini ministris nec detrahantur quae concedi fas est et aequum, nec damnosa concedatur potentia;
quae quidquid ad formandas mentes, ad boni pulchrique sensum excolendum, ad eruditionem latius propagandam idoneum est, magnis impensis conquirit et communi usui proponit;

quae iam nunc
clientes dure ut plurimum habiti, atque ut agriculturae opus quamvis utile et delectabile, sic mercatura, opificia, reliquus quaestus in nullo erant honore, litterae vero et artes, exceptis gymnicis et musica et siqua alia numinis colendi causa tractanda visa, nimium negligebantur, civesque, quod eximie perspexit Plato, non ad virtutem universam, cuius partibus omnibus perfusa esse res publica debet, sed ad solam fere fortitudinem formabantur;

quae iam nunc
Friderico Guilelmo efficiente elegantissimis artificum operibus est ornatissima et in dies fit ornatior.
Sed haec quod aliquoties ex hoc suggestu dedita opera uberius persecutus sum, memor mei consilii tribus hodie verbis significasse satis habeo:

illud vero admirabile, quod tantus iam apud nos bonarum artium flos subnatus est, ut sint qui metuant, ne nimium docti fiamus, nimium ingenuis tribuatur litteris, ac puerilis et iuvenilis institutio parum ad vitae dirigatur usus.
Sane quidquid nimium est, recte dicitur in vitium verti:
tamen sunt quae adversus nimium litterarum cultum, ubiubi provenerit (in hac enim re publica, opinor, nondum provenit), dici non inepte possint.

Nam primum ut populum esse cultissimum longe praestat, ita litteratorum, qui artem factitent, ordo iustum numerum excedere haud minus quam militum potest, et plures quam pro civitatis commodo possunt ad litterarum studia deferri:

quodsi nimium multi artes quaestuarias et negotia spernent, praestantissima ingenia otio litterario unice delectabuntur, etiam qui modico aut nullo ingenio praediti sint, in litteris vitam consumere, his victum parare constituent;
dicas ab agendo nimium revocari cives, et veluti aliquam Indorum vel Aegyptiorum sacerdotalem stirpem contemplationi totam deditam reddi imbelles:
quemadmodum videmus litteratores umbraticos rebus gerendis minime aptos, timidosque et non modo manu, verum ne lingua quidem, sed solo calamo promptos:
ipsas quin etiam litteras in vilem dicas quaestum verti, et semidoctorum misere degentium nugis, ac voluminum digitis magis compositorum quam alta mente conceptorum mole corrumpi disciplinas.

quodsi iis, quae minora sunt, plus tribuitur, quod haud raro accidit in tractandis litteris, hac quoque ex parte nimium fit, idque ita ut simul parum neque operae pretium efficiatur, quod summae res et notiones universae posthabentur minutiis, et plurimi in singulis quibusdam rebus unice occupati non iam ingentem disciplinae suae orbem illum, quantum fieri per mortalium imbecillitatem potest, magno comprehendere animo student:
quin sunt, qui etiam in litteris, ut in opificum officinis, distributione operae praestandae plurimum doceant profici:

quod ut concedam de colligenda

quin sunt, qui etiam in litteris, ut in opificum officinis, distributione operae praestandae plurimum doceant profici:

quod ut concedam de colligenda
scientiae materia rectissime dici, ita dubito, an scientiae ipsi accommodari non possit:
utut est, certe nimium dividi doctas operas posse quis est qui negaverit?
Postremo in ipsa scholastica institutione iustus potest modus migrari.

Quae quum, mea quidem sententia, eum sibi finem debeat propositum habere, ut discipulos non ad certam quandam sive negotiorum sive litterarum partem exercendam condocefaciat, sed liberali formet eruditione, aptosque reddat ei, quam quisque deinceps pro indolis ratione elegerit, disciplinae cum fructu capessendae, simul ut eos iis imbuat studiis, quae, ut ait Cicero, adolescentiam agunt, senectutem oblectant, secundas res ornant, adversis perfugium et solatium praebent:

peccabit praeceptor, qui vel recondita doctrinae alicuius, in qua ipse studiose versetur, adyta recludere tironibus constituerit, ad quae penetrare illi nisi multis aliis rebus posthabitis nequeant, vel eos oneret eo apparatu iisque artis quasi instrumentis, quibus non opus sit ad liberalem institutionem, sed ad tractandam et factitandam artem ipsam.
Sed haec nimia, ubi in corpore litterarum quasi succi plenissimo nata fuerint, facile reseces:
difficilius succureris macie et torpore languentibus.
Neve deside vita enervetur populus, fortissimo cuique barbaro praeda, exercet illum militia nec sinit ignavum fieri.
ut, quae omnium mater est patria, eandem omnes defendere parati sint:
quo fit, ut imperium hoc ea, qua debet, ratione militare sit:

simul, qui copiis praeficiuntur, ita institutos doctrinis videas, ut quemadmodum docti adolescentes militant, sic militum duces haud pauci reperiantur eruditissimi, et perfecta sapientiae ac fortitudinis concordia simus insignes.

Quodsi cum Demosthene civitatibus certam quandam et propriam fortunam tribuere licet, non abnuentibus credo philosophis, haec mihi huius rei publicae videtur bona prae aliis fortuna esse, ut modicis praedita opibus, aliena a luxu, ingenii et armorum excellat viribus:
sed ut arva alternis annis frugibus aliis consita fertiliora sunt, sic illa per intervalla modo armis modo eruditione magis claruit, donec confirmata utriusque virtutis consortio est.
Nam ut priores regiae domus principes omittam, Fridericum Guilelmum Magnum Electorem, etsi litteris quoque academia Tuiscoburgensi condenda benignus fuit, tamen magis nobilitavit bellica gloria;
scientiae materia rectissime dici, ita dubito, an scientiae ipsi accommodari non possit:
utut est, certe nimium dividi doctas operas posse quis est qui negaverit?
Postremo in ipsa scholastica institutione iustus potest modus migrari.

Fridericus Tertius, primus deinceps rex, splendidissime adiuvit bonas artes;
huius filius exercitui deditus;
at magnus ille Fridericus utramque cepit lauream:

et Fridericus Guilelmus, quem nobis divinitus datum hodie grata profitemur mente, postquam adversam non huius imperii, sed orbis terrarum fortunam, quae hoc quoque pro rata parte corripuerat, superavit, et bello restituit regnum et pacis artibus exornavit egregie:

ipse pariter militaris et civilis, fortis mitisque, ipse temperans et moderatus, et eodem temperamento variis rei publicae moderans partibus, parcusque simul nec luxuriae deditus, videtur mihi illam, quam dixi, imperii Borussici fortunam sibi totam demonstrare congenitam.
Neque ille gloriae cupiditate quidquam facit;
itaque quidquid artibus praestat, fit sine iactatione, qua haud pauci ducuntur principes.
Quod ubi considero, vix audeo unum attingere, quod tamen mihi ad argumentum absolvendum superesse videtur, ex bellis an ex litteris maior civitati accedat fama.
Et de hac quidem re non multum dubito.
Nam rebus gestis et magnis facinoribus minora iudico et carmina et pictorum ac statuariorum opera et domestica doctorum studia inventaque quamvis eximia;
nihil est generosius, quam fortis vir anima redimere victoriam promptus.
Cui sententiae suffragatorem habeo Plutarchum, hominem in paucis eruditum eumque etiam in re publica aliquatenus spectatum.

Quum enim nulla civitas artibus et disciplinis esset illustrior quam Athenae, simul illae ut commerciorum frequentia ita potentia militari sic instructae, ut ex tribus, quae supra diximus, vitae generibus essent aptissime mixtae;

tamen quaerendum Chaeronensis philosophus putavit, bellone an sapientia clariores Athenienses essent, neque ille veritus est bellicae Atheniensium virtuti potiorem vindicare laudem, non ausus expeditionibus, proeliis, laboribus cum summa audacia et constantia toleratis, tropaeisque Marathoniis, Plataeensibus, Salaminiis praeferre signa marmorea, tabulas pictas, tragicas comicasque commissiones, dithyramborum furorem, philosophorum sermones, oratorum vim et elegantiam.

Neque immerito in fine commentarioli sophisticam et minutiis adhibitam Isocratis curam spernere prae Chabria et Iphicrate videtur, quod is, dum hi victoriis Graeciam conciliant patriae, domi deses cincinnos orationis torqueret, et nonam longissimae vitae partem, ut ait Chaeronensis philosophus, hoc est prope tres Olympiades, quot annis Hecatompedum et Propylaea exstruxerit Pericles,
Fridericus Tertius, primus deinceps rex, splendidissime adiuvit bonas artes;
huius filius exercitui deditus;

consumeret in retractandis Panegyrici verbis, magis quam miles sonum armorum et phalangum concursum et vulnera, metuens ille ne vocalem cum vocali collideret, vel membrum, quod dicunt, aequale una syllaba proferret brevius.
Attamen litterae quoque et artes latissime splendent, diutissime perdurant;
et fluxa armorum gloria nec mansura, nisi suo illi praeconio scriptores, poetae, sculptores, pictores addiderint perennitatem.
Non tanta esset veterum ducum claritas, nisi eorum facta egregii auctores exaequassent dictis;
non Atheniensium urbs Spartae et ipsi Romae, quae per duces suos et copias multo gessit maiora, praeferretur, nisi illa orbis terrarum extitisses magistra;
non Augusteum saeculum tantopere inclaruisset, nisi litterarum accessisset flos laetissimus;
non Ptolemaeorum regnum celebrius esset Seleucidis aeque potentibus, nisi illi magis favissent doctis:
Mediceae stirpi artes litteraeque maiorem laudem attulerunt quam res gestae;
neque armis sed eruditione qualicunque inde a Ludovico Quarto decimo Galli vicerunt Europam:

Graecique olim litteris subegerunt orbem, suamque linguam in Italiam et Gallias, ultra columnas Herculis et ad Cimmerium Bosporum, in Persidem, ad Syros, in Aegyptum et Libyam et Aethiopiam propagarunt, pridemque exstinctis eorum rebus publicis superfuerunt ingeniorum lumina, ex quibus optimorum studiorum facem accenderunt noviciae gentes;
serisque illorum posteris, ut olim a Romanis, ita nunc quoque a bonis omnibus ob maiorum haec de nobis ipsis merita habetur honos, et optima quaeque apprecamur.
Quin in Germania ipsa exigua urbs, quod summa patriarum potissimum litterarum decora eximia benevolentia et amicitia fovit principalis domus, haud mediocrem nacta famam est:

quam domum inter cetera exempla promptiore nomino voluntate, quod ex illa duabus generosissimis matribus familias regia aucta gens est, quarum altera iam subolem peperit stirpi, altera egregiis civium studiis nuperrime hanc urbem intravit nova nupta.
Et harum quidem matronarum avo contigerat raro fortunae beneficio, ut in eius aetatem incideret sublimium ingeniorum proventus, quae adolescentes Germanorum litteras maturarent et perficerent:
quae quum Friderico Magno defuissent iuveni, senex demum futuras auguratus est vernaculae eruditionis virtutes.

Fridericum Guilelmum vero optamus ut nunquam deficiant, qui domi militiaeque satisfacere magnanimis illius consiliis possint,
consumeret in retractandis Panegyrici verbis, magis quam miles sonum armorum et phalangum concursum et vulnera, metuens ille ne vocalem cum vocali collideret, vel membrum, quod dicunt, aequale una syllaba proferret brevius.

Fridericum Guilelmum vero optamus ut nunquam deficiant, qui domi militiaeque satisfacere magnanimis illius consiliis possint,
et ipsius auspiciis rem publicam optimis rebus augeant.

Qui quum bello non delectetur quamvis strenuus, neque eo nisi ad tutandam utatur patriam, contingat illi grata pax, artibus et disciplinis florentissima, ut ille a prioribus requiescat aerumnis, et fruatur civium amore ac prosperitatibus, quarum auctor ipse est, fruatur domestica felicitate, qua illum imprimis beari scimus omnes, ac nuper, quum filia ex iuncti Occidentis et Orientis solio in natalem redux domum patri dilectissimo in aliquod redderetur tempus, non sine communi urbis laetitia vidimus.

Denique faxit Deus Optimus Maximus, ut Friderico Guilelmo eveniant ea omnia, quae ipsius voluntati et civium votis et bonorum omnium precibus, postremo incrementis rei publicae et magnitudini domus Augustae respondeant maxime.
