div.head: XVIII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXX. habita.

p.s: The day that gave to this commonwealth a king who was the best and dear to everyone, most serene Prince, heir to the throne, most distinguished auditors of all ranks, that festive day is observed every year by the whole people with the same feeling of devotion, because Frederick William continually cherishes the citizens with the same love, with the same steadfastness guards and strengthens the safety of the commonwealth, peace that dispenses all good things, public and private resources, the strength of the army, the flower of arts and letters, and finally all common advantages of all, and whatever private advantages of individuals.
Thus the King, with steadfast counsels, holding the reins with a sure hand, guides the Prussian state on an even course.

But if nothing of great new increments were to accrue to the state, nothing singular and preeminently excellent would attract our minds, the ordinary tenor of royal goodness itself would suffice for nourishing the zeal of the citizens.
But that evenness, which I mentioned, implanted in the Prince's mind and propagated from the Prince into the state, has nothing slothful:
motion accompanies rest;

By this moderation it is brought about that, as the seeds gradually increase, everything that is best matures with a tranquil progress, and when matured, by its own excellence draws the eyes of all others to itself, and from that new nourishment for the gratitude owed to the Prince flows into our hearts.
Now in the year in which, by the care or kindness of Frederick William, the great work was, if not completed, at least well advanced, what should come to our consideration more than that very thing?
Of course, just as one face placed before many mirrors appears whole in each one, so the same virtue of the Prince who governs all things is seen undivided in different matters;
and it will be pleasing to observe it especially in that matter which at every time is, as it were, more present.
Indeed, the arts and sciences, even before that most recent and fatal destruction of the state, were excellently fostered by the kings of Prussia:

But Frederick William, having undertaken greater things afterwards, when the fatherland had scarcely been restored, brought literature, which had previously been hidden in the academy and gymnasia, into the light of this university in his own city, and placed it in the palace nearest to his own residence.
Soon, with the power of the kingdom restored, he founded a treasury of the arts, that famous Museum, opposite the royal citadel, the seat of the empire.
Behold, literature and the arts are most splendidly placed among the ornaments of the princely court!
And indeed our affairs have long been flourishing;

They have survived the fierce and glorious wars along with the other parts of the state, of which we were participants, as the monument conspicuous in this senate-house testifies, and they have grown beyond expectation into a great number of citizens:

But as for the arts, although an excellent school was established long ago, and they have already been approved by their splendid works, nevertheless this new institution adds a crowning touch to them by the abundance and variety of its resources.
Nor indeed is it of no importance for literature that the arts flourish;
for both, as if related by birth, proceed to almost the same final goal, although by a different path, and the one owes much to the other:
so that a state which favors the one and neglects the other seems to take insufficient thought for both:
only by joining both together will you have perfected human culture.

Since it seems not foreign to the solemnity of this day, as the King fosters both with equal care, nor to this place and our person, to set forth the kinship of both, allow me to dwell a little on this matter, not that I may investigate the most splendid subject with a subtle and sufficient philosophical discussion, but that, mindful of the orator's duty, I may contribute something plausible, though unequal to greater things, by touching upon the sum of affairs rather than exhausting it.
Let him turn his eyes to the rest, and from that may new nourishment of thanks due to the Prince be poured into our hearts.
Now in what year the great work was, if not completed, at least advanced, by the care or kindness of Frederick William, what more should come to our consideration than that very thing?
Of course, just as one face placed before many mirrors appears whole in each, so the same virtue of the Prince governing all things is seen undivided in different matters;
And it will be helpful for her to look especially at that matter which at any time is, as it were, more present.
Indeed, the arts and disciplines were already excellently cultivated by the Prussian kings even before that latest and fatal destruction of the state.

But Frederick William, having attempted greater things afterwards, when the fatherland was scarcely yet restored, brought literature, which had previously been more hidden in the academy and gymnasia, into the light of this university, and placed it in the palace nearest to his own house.
Soon, with the power of the kingdom restored, he founded a treasury of arts, that famous Museum, opposite the royal citadel, the seat of the empire.
Behold, literature and the arts are most splendidly placed among the ornaments of the princely court!
And indeed our affairs have long been flourishing;

They have survived the fierce and glorious wars along with the other parts of the state, of which we were participants, as the monument conspicuous in this senate-house testifies, and they have grown beyond expectation into a great number of citizens:

But as for the arts, although an excellent school was established long ago, and they have already been approved by their splendid works, nevertheless this new institution adds a crowning touch to them by the abundance and variety of its resources.
Nor indeed is it of no importance for literature that the arts flourish;
for both, as if sisters by birth, proceed to almost the same ultimate end by a path however different, and the one owes much to the other:
so that whichever state favors the one, neglects the other, seems to take insufficient thought for both:
only by joining both together will you have perfected human culture.

Since it does not seem foreign to the solemnity of this day, as the King fosters both with equal care, nor to this place and our person, to set forth the kinship of both, let it be permitted to me to dwell a little on this matter, not that I may investigate the most brilliant subject with a subtle and sufficient philosophical discussion, but that, although unequal to greater things, mindful of my oratorical duty, I may contribute something plausible, not so much exhausting as tasting the sum of things.

For those who are exclusively occupied with exploring and representing the corporeal nature of things, which is subject to the senses, unless you would call these empty pastimes of the human intellect, I see no other ultimate goal than something divine, from which they proceed, which they explain, and to which they return.

But did not these [studies] emerge, like a mother goddess from the sea waves, from that deep fountain of religions, which you could not measure with any plumb-line, not only among the nations of the East, which have scarcely ever left the cradle of learning, but also among the Greeks, who were the authors of purer science and more polished art, and among the Christian peoples themselves, at the time when they began to cultivate letters and arts?
Do not even now individuals, who approach literature and the arts rightly, are driven at the first moment by a divine instinct, without which nothing excellent is begun and completed?

This is that wonderful love of the deepest things, which you do not yet know but have divined, of things to be sought with tireless zeal, the guide and parent of discovering the true and the beautiful, of science and art.
This reason, innate in mortals, strives to comprehend by thought and the bonds of concepts what it first divined not without admiration and a joyful awe of the deity.
And the very particle of the divine breath, since like is known by like, recognizes in universal nature and in human affairs the supreme mind pervading all things, in which alone truth resides.

In whatever parts, indeed, science is divided and descends, whatever and of whatever kind it treats, whether the hidden principles of the universe, the forms and forces of natural things, the life and constitution of the healthy or sick body, or the recesses of the human mind and the laws of thinking and feeling, whether numbers and figures expressed in space, or the recondite causes of speech and languages, sacred and public affairs, customs and laws, and whatever things have been done at home and abroad, and whatever other human things there are:

Since universities are accustomed to embrace the very broad circle of all these things, ours especially shows even to the less attentive, by the number of teachers and schools that it has, how manifold and varied the disciplines are:
Finally, whatever work is diligently placed in the study of things that are visible, common and trivial, and that do not seem able to be reduced to definite principles;

Nevertheless, we must refer everything to the notions of the mind, and even in those things that fall under the senses, we must search for the traces of divine and human intellect impressed upon them, valuing the greater ones more highly, but not despising even the lesser ones, which often bring unexpected light to the greater ones, to such an extent that we are unwilling that even literature should have its own painters of filth and craftsmen of trifles and fabricators of the tiniest works, such as Myrmecides and Callicrates, sculptors of old, were, not without the authority of nature, a hinge, as something divine, from which they proceed, which they explain, to which they return.

But did not these [studies] emerge, as a mother goddess from the sea waves, from that deep fountain of religions, which you cannot measure with any plumb-line, not only among the nations of the East, which have scarcely ever left the cradle of learning, but also among the Greeks, who were the authors of purer science and more refined art, and among the Christian peoples themselves, at the time when they began to cultivate letters and arts?
Do not even now individuals, who rightly approach literature and the arts, are driven by a divine impulse, without which nothing excellent is begun and completed, as if by a first moment?

This innate reason in mortals, which at first was divined not without admiration and a joyful awe of the deity, strives to comprehend it through thought and the bonds of concepts.

Since universities are accustomed to embrace the very broad circle of all these things, ours especially, how manifold and varied the disciplines are, is shown even to the less attentive by the number of teachers and schools that they have.
Finally, whatever work is placed diligently by scholars in the study of visible things, common and trivial, and which do not seem able to be reduced to certain principles;

Nevertheless, we must refer everything to the notions of the mind, and even in those things that fall under the senses, we must search out the traces of divine and human intellect impressed upon them, valuing the greater ones more highly, but not even despising the lesser ones, which often bring unexpected light to the greater, to such an extent that we are unwilling that even literature should have its own painters of filth and artisans of trifles and fabricators of the tiniest works, such as Myrmecides and Callicrates, sculptors, once were, not without the authority of nature, which itself takes pleasure in constructing even the most subtle things with the greatest diligence.
But to avoid lingering too long over literature, what do the arts attempt to achieve?
By the images, he says, which they fashion, they move our hearts.
But they do not merely move;

They also raise us up and fill us with the noblest sensations, leading us from these sordid concerns of daily life to something that rises above the human and is placed above mortal things, and that is adumbrated in those very images, both revealed and concealed, with matter, as it were translucent, affording access to that eternal beauty which lies hidden within, to those whose sight is not blunted by the contemplation of earthly things alone:
What is impenetrable to reason is nevertheless conceived by the imagination of the mind.

Indeed, the perfect artist in each genre, endowed with the poetic power of generating beauty, which both Plato taught to be common to all arts, and Simonides of Ceos had long before indicated, when he declared that painting is silent poetry and poetry is speaking painting, represents in his work the innate vital and immortal form of each thing, which philosophers call the idea, grasped by that imagination I mentioned, with scarcely any other aid; in this work the soul is wonderfully fused with those things which you perceive by the senses.

Whether it uses words and thoughts woven together in verse, or the rhythms and harmony of sounds, movements in figures and gestures, or the aids of statuary, sculpture, engraving, or of lines and light and shade and colors, so that it may clothe the soul with a body.
This soul, the governor of nature, nowhere appears more excellently than in the human form and face, both the temple and image of the divine power;
From his face shines forth, gathered together, whatever of the divine mind is diffused through the whole universe.

Therefore, in expressing especially the human form, sculpture and painting, which according to the plan of our discussion we will be able to consider most, achieve that which is proposed for the arts.

And yet it is not proposed to imitate slavishly natural and common forms, but to show in excellent forms that which is more excellent than anything: the soul and mind, which penetrates the external appearance.
For the mind is beauty itself, dwelling in and illuminating these earthly things, which are called beautiful, just as the soul dwells in our body;

It is the mind, I say, that which Diotima of Mantinea beheld, the beauty of an admirable nature, for the sake of which, whoever has been led by the love of beauty has undertaken all the earlier labors of knowing this, which neither comes to be nor perishes, neither grows nor is wasted away, but is everlasting and eternal, which by itself, and itself for itself, takes pleasure in the most subtle things of all, when they are most diligently constructed.
But to avoid lingering too long over literature, what do the arts attempt to achieve?
By the images, he says, which they fashion, they move our hearts.
But they do not merely move;

They also raise us up and fill us with the noblest sensations, leading us from these sordid concerns of daily life to something that rises above the human, is placed above mortal things, and is adumbrated in those very images, both revealed and concealed, with matter, as it were translucent, affording access to that eternal beauty which lies hidden within, to those whose sight is not blunted by the contemplation of earthly things alone:

Whether it uses words and thoughts woven together in verse, or the rhythms and harmony of sounds, or movement through figures and gestures, or the aids of statuary, sculpture, engraving, or of lines and light and shade and colors, so that it may clothe the soul with a body.
This soul, indeed, the governor of nature, nowhere appears more excellently than in the human form and face, both the temple and image of the divine spirit;
From his face shines forth, gathered together, whatever of the divine mind is diffused throughout the whole universe.

Therefore, in expressing especially the human form, sculpture and painting — which, according to the plan of our discussion, we will be able to consider most closely — achieve that which has been set before the arts.

But it is not the purpose to imitate slavishly the natural and common forms, but to show in excellent forms that which is more excellent than anything else: the soul and the mind, which penetrates the external appearance.
For the mind is beauty itself, dwelling in and illuminating these earthly things, which are called beautiful, just as the soul dwells in our body;

It is the mind, I say, that which Diotima of Mantinea beheld, the beauty of an admirable nature, for the sake of which, whoever has been led by the love of beauty has undertaken all the earlier labors of knowing it, because it neither comes to be nor perishes, nor grows nor is wasted away, but is everlasting and eternal, by itself with itself uniform and simple, pure and unalloyed, by participation in which all things that appear beautiful are beautiful, but in such a way that, as these are born or perish, it itself remains untouched by mortal contagion.

Therefore, although knowledge and art are closely related in origin, though they employ different powers, different action and work, and are occupied with things of very different appearance, yet in reality they are similar in their own nature; both strive to contemplate the heavenly and eternal in earthly and perishable examples, to trace these back to that, and to immerse the minds of men in that.

With what zeal they come to the aid of the most burning desires of mortals, and as ministers of blessedness itself they lead to the highest good, which the philosopher seems not without reason to seek in the absolute conjunction of the beautiful and the true and of measure or proportion.
Indeed, not even the forces by which each acts are so opposed to each other that in science there is no place for imagination, and in art no place for reason;

But that one is also necessary for that one, lest the knowledge be destroyed by the thinness of the formulas; this one is necessary for the arts, so that the craftsman, while he makes the work, may at the same time understand what and how he makes it.
But here someone may object:
You indeed, imbued with Platonic precepts, say that something sublime is proposed for the arts;

Or has he forgotten how strongly the same wise man, who alone embraced the science of the purest concepts, condemns the talent of the arts, because they are wholly contained in imitation, and that too of things often not the best;
that they render images of images, shadows of shadows:
that poets, ignorant of what they invent, are drawn without reason by an alien force, as if by a Magnesian stone?
Does he not boast of the inveterate and perpetual dissension between philosophy and poetry?

Does he censure that divine Homer, the teacher of Greece, to whom Phidias himself owed the image of Olympian Jupiter, for many reasons, and especially because he instills into men the excessive emotions of the mind, recommended by the most illustrious examples, even of the gods, together with all comedy and tragedy, than which art can produce nothing more magnificent, and, adorned with crowns and anointed with ointments, does he expel him from the perfect state?
Indeed, a man by no means last in judging beauty, on whom Winkelmann himself depends, did not throw out these and similar remarks carelessly;

And I see that Friedrich Schiller, although an excellent poet, once advised somewhat similar things, though adapted differently according to the character of the age, in a treatise which he wrote on the necessary limits to be set to the use of beautiful forms.
For if the arts serve only the senses, flattering lust and desire, delighting the eyes, tickling the ears, which they do not rarely;
they oppress rather than lift up the mind:

nor do they [have anything in common] with that which is uniform and simple, pure and whole, by participation in which all things that appear beautiful are beautiful, but rather [they are] so [opposed] that while these [beautiful things] arise or perish, it [the beautiful itself] remains undefiled by mortal contagion.

And so knowledge and art, though close in origin, although using different powers, different action and work, and occupied with things most different in appearance, yet in reality similar in their own nature, both strive to behold the heavenly and eternal in earthly and perishable examples, to derive these from that, and to immerse the minds of men in that.

With what zeal they come to the aid of the most burning desires of mortals, and as ministers of blessedness itself they lead to the highest good, which the philosopher seems not without reason to seek in the absolute conjunction of the beautiful and the true and of measure or proportion.

Indeed, a man by no means last in judging the beautiful, on whom Winkelmann himself depends, did not throw out these and similar remarks rashly;

and I see that Friedrich Schiller, although an excellent poet, once suggested something similar, though adapted differently according to the character of the age, in an essay which he wrote on the necessary limits to the use of beautiful forms.
For if the arts serve only the senses, flattering lust and desire, delighting the eyes, tickling the ears, which they do not rarely;
they oppress rather than lift up the mind:

And I would not deny that Homeric poetry, which is engaged in vividly presenting things that fall under the senses and in most truthfully describing the emotions of the mind, contributed much to the effect that the minds of the Greeks, which were naturally inclined in that direction, took delight more and more in external appearance, and that the desires to which the mortal race is subject were nourished.
Since Plato was more keenly affected by this disadvantage, being present and in the midst of those men,
Posterity admires the judgment, the causes of which, being very far removed from that age by times and condition, they no longer perceive themselves.

Just as they wonder what it is that he in civil discipline favors the aristocrats, and is hostile to popular rule, since they are no longer oppressed by those evils by which the best men were undoubtedly afflicted at that time.

Nevertheless, I would readily concede that the wise man, wholly occupied with philosophy and turned to contemplate those pure and simple exemplars of things, which are comprehended by reason alone, would have shown himself a rather strict censor of the arts, since he would not wish them to be seen in other images except those which the father of the universe himself had fashioned.
But that philosopher, who combines the deepest knowledge with the highest piety and incomparable charm, would not have spurned the Jupiter and Minerva of Phidias.
He would not have scorned the sanctity of the Virgin Mother of God, transferred into the painting from the mind of Urbino.
Again, you would not deny that, although you are less unjust than Plato toward the arts, in cultivating and esteeming them one may go so far as to fall into vice.
For he who attributes more to imagination, the mother and offspring of the arts, than to reason, in acting easily wanders from the right path;
Moreover, the slothful veneration of images clings especially to those ceremonies that love to subject knowledge to authority, and the zeal for seeking truth to light credulity.
Thus with the very supports of the arts, superstition cast clouds over minds.
Now reason has scattered these;
Those who have been enlightened by its light, why should they not, secure, revere God present in images?
Must the statues be torn down and broken, because there were those who abused them?
Therefore even wisdom will have to go into exile, because it has turned into sophistry.

Let us rather rejoice that the Prince, distinguished by genuine holiness and piety, scorns that rough and gloomy sadness, for which religion is to gaze upon a painted picture, equally as the barbarous disdain for knowledge that has seized some who call themselves pious, and has begun to restore their ornaments also to the temples.
I have passed over one place up to this point, which is about the emotions of the mind.
Why indeed?

Since all art, like poetry, must above all represent those things that require action, and in any action the mind is more or less moved, I would not deny that Homeric poetry, which is concerned with vividly presenting things that fall under the senses and with most truthfully describing the emotions, has contributed much to the result that the minds of the Greeks, which were naturally inclined in that direction, were more and more delighted by external appearance, and that the desires to which the mortal race is subject were nourished.
Since Plato was more keenly affected by this inconvenience, being present and in the midst of those men,
posterity admires the judgment, the causes of which, being very far removed from that age by times and condition, they themselves no longer perceive:

just as they wonder what it is that he in civil discipline favors the aristocrats, and is hostile to popular rule, since they are no longer oppressed by those evils by which at that time the best men were undoubtedly afflicted.

But that philosopher, who combines the deepest knowledge with the highest piety and incomparable charm, would not have spurned the Jupiter and Minerva of Phidias;
He would not have spurned the sanctity of the Virgin Mother of God, transferred from the mind of Urbinate onto the panel.

For he who attributes more to imagination, the mother and offspring of the arts, than to reason, in acting easily deviates from the right path;
Moreover, a slothful veneration of images clings especially to those ceremonies which love to subject knowledge to authority, and the zeal for seeking truth to a light credulity.
Thus with the very aids of the arts, superstition spread clouds over minds.
Now reason has scattered these.
Those who have been enlightened by its light, why should they not, secure, reverence the God present in images?
Must the statues be torn down and broken, because there were those who abused them?
Therefore even wisdom will have to go into exile, because it has turned into sophistry.

Let us rather rejoice that the Prince, distinguished by genuine holiness and piety, scorns that harsh and gloomy sadness, for which religion is to gaze upon a painted picture, and equally the barbarous disdain for knowledge that has seized some who call themselves pious, and has begun to restore their ornaments also to the temples.
So far I have passed over one topic, which concerns the emotions of the mind.
Why, indeed?

For since poetry, and so every art, must above all represent those emotions, because it requires action, and in any action the mind is more or less stirred, in that stirring the whole character of human nature and its innermost recesses are laid open:

If art consists solely in the imitation of desires, and especially of the worse ones, and does not diminish but increases and intensifies them even in the hearts of spectators or listeners, as Plato generally assumed;
That reproach seems to stick and cannot be washed away.
But I judge that not even this is true;

Art rather, while it expresses the excited and agitated passions, partly looks at something greater in them, namely the mind, which acts by their peculiar force and virtue, and partly soothes and calms them in the listener or spectator.

This is, if I am not mistaken, that celebrated purgation of the disturbances of the mind, which Aristotle attributes to poetry and music, meeting, I think, the Platonic doctrines with rather obscure words:

Although fortune has denied us the fuller explanation of this matter which he himself promised, nevertheless from his Politics you may understand, according to his opinion, that just as those who are agitated by sacred frenzy, when they have used sacred songs, are calmed and composed, having obtained medicine and purification, so those who are fearful or compassionate, or generally subject to disturbances of the soul, when they have tasted these emotions by watching, are relieved with pleasure and purified, freed from them to some extent.
Although this can happen in many ways, and Aristotle seems to have aimed at nothing other than a remedy from homeopathy, which is properly referred to the emotions of the mind:

saltem concedetis, auditores, sive tragoediis seu pictura vel sculptura, quam posse ad tragoediam accedere proxime, Nioba et liberi monstrant, misericordiam movent ac metum, artifices perfectos simul efficere, ne miseratione et horrore spectantium opprimantur animi, sed ut, dum metuis, dum miseraris, idem sentias, nostrae huius misericordiae et timoris mollitie superiores esse illos, qui mala perpessi sunt, heroes, altaque mente et invicta tolerantes evasisse fluxae huius vitae casus, sicuti divinus generis humani servator, in quo fingendo iure suo multum elaborarunt artifices, mortis superavit dolores, nec cum cupiditatibus et per ipsas interisse nisi id, quod illi ex mortali traxerant contagio, divina aura eo reduce, unde erat profecta.
Is this a very trivial purification of disturbances?
Does not art, rather, in this its moral character also emulate science, which, moderating and restraining desires, teaches what is to be sought or avoided, what is to be endured or pitied?
Finally, the dignity of art and science is the same, because each has its end in itself, and is not valued by common utility.
Since no one does not concede this concerning the works of artisans:
For who has demanded that the whole nature of the human mind and its innermost recesses be opened up?

That reproach seems to stick and cannot be washed away.
But I do not think even this is true;

Will this be a very small purification of disturbances?
Does not art, rather, in this its moral character also emulate science, which, moderating and restraining desires, teaches what is to be sought or avoided, what is to be borne or pitied?
Finally, the dignity of art and science is the same, because each has its end in itself, and is not valued by common utility.
Since no one does not concede this concerning the works of artisans:

For who has ever demanded, or even now demands, that a statue by Polyclitus or Lysippus, or a painting by Raphael Sanzio or Antonio Correggio, should serve any other purpose than to please by its beauty?

Nevertheless, we often hear this reproach made to literature, and especially by those who govern states, with the greatest injustice, that it is too much occupied with things that provide no practical use for life.
But I think that what is useful by its own nature for forming and elevating the mind, namely the true and the beautiful, is most useful for the human race.

But if literature and the liberal arts also conveniently serve the needs of life, by helping to procure them more correctly and easily, by aiding the crafts, and by equipping the state and the household better and more splendidly;
And that they do indeed provide this, no one doubts.
I do not think that this is to be demanded from them as a debt, but that it should be received with a grateful heart as spontaneously offered.
Just as learning and the arts have never ceased to strive to return due gratitude to the states, princes, and private individuals by whom they have been aided.
Who among us does not greatly rejoice that the most excellent men, whom Frederick William's sound judgment placed over our affairs, think likewise?
Does anyone ever demand that a statue by Polyclitus or Lysippus, or a painting by Raphael or Antonio Correggio, serve any other purpose than to please by its beauty?
Nevertheless, we often hear it reproached to literature, and especially by those who govern states, with the greatest injustice, that it is too much occupied with things that offer no use for life.
But I think that what is useful by its own nature for forming and elevating the mind, namely the true and the beautiful, is most useful to the human race:
But if literature and the liberal arts also serve conveniently the needs of life, by helping trades and by better and more elegantly equipping the state and the household;
which indeed no one doubts that they do:
I do not think that this is to be demanded from them as a debt, but that it is to be received with a grateful mind as spontaneously offered.
Just as learning and the arts have never ceased to strive to return due gratitude to the states, princes, and private individuals by whom they have been aided.
Who among us does not rejoice greatly that the most excellent men, whom Frederick William's sound judgment placed over our affairs, think the same way?

Now we rejoice no less in the arts for this same reason, either because the resources had to be acquired at great expense and it is fitting that the most beautiful things be arranged most splendidly, and also because aid was given with even more distinguished liberality and splendor by a most munificent king.
When I name him, I do not wish anything to be taken away from the praises of our ancestors;

We know that a not inconsiderable part of the furniture was collected at private expense by the earlier princes of the Brandenburg house, Joachim II, Frederick William the Great Elector, Frederick I and II, and by the most merciful King's father, over nearly three centuries.
I do not enumerate these things individually, because I judge that the orator's duty differs from a mere listing of names.
Certainly we owe very many resources to this King, to whom this day is sacred.

And even if he had not added so many and such splendid works, he would nevertheless have to be said to have won the palm, because he gathered together the scattered ornaments of palaces and villas into one, consulting the common good, making private things public.
While these things were being gathered together, it was understood that a house, however spacious, would not suffice even for a carefully selected complete equipment:

From there, besides the plaster casts, an excellent aid for studies, and other things to be preserved separately, the monuments of Egyptian antiquity have been left in a city garden situated not far away, where we see whatever that clever and industrious people fabricated for the adornment of domestic and daily life, as if snatched from the underworld, together with the most ancient images of the gods, not yet rendered with the beauty of the human form in the Greek manner, but hard, stiff, and grim, so that they might be even more significant by their monstrosity.

But on the field, once trampled by military exercises and the crowd of pagans, which is now cultivated with trees in the form of a garden, and which a spring of remarkable height will soon water, where also that great bowl, hewn and polished from native rock, will be placed, a magnificent house of arts occupies the ground snatched from the river, rising aloft with a lofty portico of eighteen huge columns, conspicuous also for its acroteria.

The lower parts will contain a precious collection of ancient and new coins, which in their small images represent the course and changes of the whole art of sculpture, a cabinet of gems with casts and descriptions, and one made most famous by the very name of Johann Winkelmann;
They will contain a very rich collection of highly elegant painted vases, restored to light from the darkness of tombs;
I do not speak of bronze and clay seals of various kinds, lamps, and other manifold utensils of the ancients.

When you have ascended, you will enter the rotunda, whose roof is surmounted by a bold arch, encircled by twenty columns of artificial stone, between which, however they shine, marble images of the gods, although worn by the rust of age, nevertheless gleam with their own splendor;

The remaining chambers adjoin, supported by variegated columns of the same material, displaying statues of gods and heroes and portraits of men, along with herms and busts, with reliefs suitably arranged on the walls:

until in the recess you come to a single new work that has been brought in, a laurel-crowned victor of Europe, who, had he not fallen by the great counsels of Frederick William and by our arms and those of our allies, this house would not stand, nor would it be filled with the decorations that he had carried off.
Now, with the intolerable power of the great man abolished, he himself is placed among the ancients.

I am not afraid that I may seem to have disparaged the merits of our Princes, if I say in passing that these excellent forces, among which one youthful statue of a worshiper in bronze is to be compared to a great number, cannot be compared with the wealth of Italy:
not to mention that we should never equal that people of the gods, who once inhabited Greece.

We read with wonder that even in the age of Roman domination, when the flower of Greece had long since withered, Athens alone contained three thousand statues, and as many Olympia, Delphi, and Rhodes, which was adorned even with a hundred colossi;
and that even the fierce Aetolian people had so many statues at Thermus, where they used to assemble, that the Macedonians destroyed two thousand statues there.

And what shall we say of Rome, which we behold as the world's wonder, when its forms, not yet finished with Greek refinement in the beauty of the human shape, but harsh, stiff, and grim, were made even more expressive by their monstrousness?

But on the field, once trampled by military exercises and the crowd of pagans, which is now cultivated, planted with trees, in the form of a garden, and which a spring of water of extraordinary height will soon irrigate, where also that great bowl, hewn and polished from native rock, will be placed, a magnificent house of the arts occupies the ground snatched from the river, rising on high with a lofty portico of eighteen huge columns, conspicuous also for its acroteria.

The lower parts will contain the precious ancient and new coinage, which in its little images represents the course and changes of the whole plastic art, a cabinet of gems with casts and descriptions, and one made most famous by the very name of Johann Winkelmann;
They will contain a very rich collection of highly elegant painted vases, brought back to light from the darkness of tombs;
I do not speak of the bronze and clay seals of various kinds, lamps, and other manifold utensils of the ancients.

When you have ascended, you will enter the rotunda, which with a bold arching surpasses the roof, encircled by twenty columns of artificial stone, among which, however they shine, the marble images of the gods, although worn by the rust of antiquity, nevertheless shine with their own splendor;

The remaining rooms adjoin, supported by variegated columns of the same material, displaying statues of gods and heroes and statues of men, along with herms and busts, with reliefs suitably arranged on the walls:

until in the recess you come to the one new work that has been brought in, the laurel-crowned victor of Europe, who, had he not fallen by the great counsels of Frederick William and by our arms and those of the allies, this house would not stand, nor would it be filled with the decorations that he had carried off.
Now, with the intolerable power of that great man done away with, he himself is placed among the ancients.

I am not afraid that I may seem to have disparaged the merits of our Princes, if I say in passing that these excellent forces, among which one youthful statue of a worshipper in bronze is to be compared to a great number, cannot be compared with the wealth of Italy:
not to mention that we should never equal that people of the gods, who once inhabited Greece.

We read with wonder that even in the age of Roman domination, when the flower of Greece had long since withered, Athens alone contained three thousand statues, and as many Olympia, Delphi, and Rhodes, which was adorned even with a hundred colossal statues;
Even the Aetolians, a fiercer race, had so many statues at Thermus, where they used to assemble, that the Macedonians destroyed two thousand statues there.
And what shall we say of Rome, the capital of the world?
What great quantities did the Marcelli, Quinctii, Fulvii, Aemilii, Mummii, and Sullae amass from conquered foreign nations!
Three thousand statues were brought by Marcus.
Scaurus, when aedile, displayed them in a temporary theater;
Those who made moderate calculations report that sixty thousand were restored to Roman soil;

Piety, old-fashioned frugality at home, public munificence, and finally the long-continued practice of workshops enriched Greece above all with so many ornaments; how great this was, you may infer from the fact that Lysippus alone is reported to have made fifteen hundred works, and that three hundred and sixty statues, of which many were equestrian or stood on chariots or bigae, were set up by the Athenians for Demetrius of Phalerum, completed in less than three hundred days.

Let us be satisfied if, from the vast shipwreck, some examples have been brought to this northern region, not snatched away, but well earned, so that we may behold the perfection of the art of the ancient sculptors, which our people now successfully emulate.
And what we possess, the King's kindness increases, and will increase.

But what lights and how great are spread before the eyes, when you have approached the most ample treasury of paintings, which stores the illustrious documents of revived art, breathing the milder genius of Christian worship!

Here the whole world of the most noble art, from the austere beginnings of the Byzantine and Tuscan brush, with the works of artists in every genre set forth, of Italians, Germans, Belgians, not with the paintings of different ages and schools confused, but with each suitably joined, lies open to the view.
Here majesty dwells together with the Graces and all charms.
Soon these things will find those by whom they may be worthily proclaimed;
There are among you most discerning judges of all elegance:
I am silent.
Do you understand?
How much did the Marcelli, Quinctii, Fulvii, Aemilii, Mummii, and Sullae amass from conquered foreign nations!
Three thousand statues of Marcus.
Scaurus, as aedile, displayed them in a temporary theater;
Those who made modest calculations report that sixty thousand were returned to Roman soil;

Piety, ancient frugality at home, public munificence, and finally the long-continued practice of workshops enriched Greece above all with so many ornaments; how great this was, you may infer from the fact that Lysippus alone is said to have made fifteen hundred works, and that three hundred and sixty statues, of which many were equestrian or stood on chariots or bigae, were set up by the Athenians for Demetrius of Phalerum, completed in less than three hundred days.

Let us be satisfied if, from the great shipwreck, some examples have been brought to this northern region, not snatched away, but well earned, so that we may behold the perfection of the art of the ancient sculptors, which our artists now successfully emulate.
And what we possess, the King's kindness increases, and will increase.

But what lights and how great are spread before the eyes, when you have approached the most ample treasury of paintings, which stores the illustrious documents of revived art, breathing the milder genius of Christian worship!

Here the whole world of the noblest art, from the austere beginnings of the Byzantine and Tuscan brush, with the works of artists of each kind set forth, of Italians, Germans, Belgians, not with the paintings of different ages and schools confused, but with each suitably joined, lies open to the view.
Here majesty dwells together with the Graces and all charms.
Soon these things will find those by whom they may be worthily proclaimed;
There are among you most discerning judges of all elegance:
I fall silent.
Often we hear in the circles of not inelegant men this royal city reproached because it has no antiquity.
Truly great is the glory in the monuments of the virtues of parents;
but that reproach is greater:
Once there were vigorous Milesians.
There are those for whom nothing is venerable except ruins;
The rust of the Middle Ages, which they long for, does not seem to me to sit well on this republic.
Our antiquity is recent;

This kingdom did not take its growth in the age of papal or imperial power, but with both broken, and only in the last century was it so strengthened by the virtue of Frederick the Great that it could hold its place among the more powerful states by the strength of its intellect and its remaining vigor.

Those who in that century gave new life and form to literature and the arts, for the most part either born or received into this empire—Leibniz, Christian Wolff, Kant, Fichte, and that restorer of the arts, John Winckelmann, full of divine mind.
Other nations grow, others diminish, says he;
Have we not been better provided for, in that we live rather in the dawn of a rising greatness than in the twilight of a declining one?
Therefore it is our duty not to be astonished at ancient things:

and if we must use ancient examples (and we certainly must), we will no more confine ourselves to old things in our own affairs than distinguished men in any field are kept out of this state because they were born abroad.
The King judges ours, whoever they are who are intelligent;
he strives to win them over to us, if it can be done:
All antiquity is ours, from which we may draw, which we may enjoy.

This the most wise Prince sets before the students of the arts, that by the sight of excellent works the eyes and minds may be trained, that a stimulus may be added to the artists, not those who imitate earlier works, but those who wish to learn from ancient masters, having been taught, may dare to attempt new things with their own strength:
In the same way, learning and philosophy itself were roused from their slumber and corrected by nothing more than the revival of ancient literature that had lain neglected.
Thus indeed each later age receives the light handed down from the earlier one together with life, not to rest idly in what has been handed down, but to draw new fruits from what it has received.
For indeed, when I say that we ought not to be fixed in the old ways as if in a stupor, I do not say with impunity that the excellent things which earlier ages produced are to be despised;

The arts themselves are evidence, which in the previous century, having abandoned the footsteps of their ancestors, had so degenerated that the most cultivated princes lacked talents that could produce what the age could bear.
Now, for those who have entered upon a more correct path, the magnanimous studies of Frederick William come to their aid in a timely manner:
He who, because he wishes Prussia to be deprived of no praise, devotes unwearied and equal care to all parts of both the state and of human culture.
May God preserve him, His devout worshiper, safe, and keep him for us as long as possible.

May God so favor his undertakings that both he himself and those who now live may reap the fruit of his plans, and since the best men at the same time look out for posterity, may not only the present outcome prove the excellence of his well-begun works, but also the late success and the judgment of future offspring, so that our descendants may one day hold the memory of Frederick William as sacred and dear as we love and venerate him while he survives.
May God hold these prayers as ratified, as they have been conceived by us piously and sincerely.
Wolf, Kant, Fichte, that restorer of the arts, John Winckelmann, full of divine mind.
Other nations grow, others diminish, says he;
For us, is it not better provided, because we live rather in the dawn of rising greatness than in the twilight of declining?
Therefore it is our duty not to be astonished at ancient things:

And if we must use ancient examples (and indeed we must, without doubt), we will no more confine ourselves to our own ancient affairs than distinguished men in any field are kept out of this state because they were born among foreigners.
The King judges as ours all who are intelligent;
he strives to win them over to us, if it can be done:
all antiquity is ours, from which we may draw, which we may enjoy.

The wisest Prince sets this before the students of the arts, so that the eyes and minds may be trained by the sight of excellent works, so that a stimulus may be added to the artists, not those who imitate earlier works, but those who wish to learn from ancient masters, and, taught by their own powers, may dare to attempt new things:
just as also learning and philosophy itself have been roused from their slumber and corrected by nothing more than by the revival of ancient literature that had lain neglected.

Thus indeed each later age receives the light transmitted from the earlier one together with life, not so that it may rest idly in what has been handed down, but so that from what it has received it may draw forth new fruits.
For when I say that we should not be fixed in the ancients as if in a stupor, I do not mean to say with impunity that the excellent things which earlier ages produced are to be despised;

The arts themselves are evidence: in the previous century, having abandoned the traces of their ancestors, they had so degenerated that the most cultivated princes lacked talents that could produce something able to endure the age.
Now, to those who have entered upon a more correct path, the magnanimous studies of Frederick William come to their aid in a timely manner:
He, because he wishes that no part of Prussia be without praise, devotes equal care, untiringly, to all parts both of the state and of culture.
May God preserve this man, His devout worshiper, safe, and keep him for us as long as possible.

May God so favor his undertakings that both he himself and those who now live may reap the fruit of his plans, and since the best men at the same time look out for posterity, may not only the present outcome prove the excellence of his well-begun works, but also the late success and the judgment of future generations, so that our descendants may one day hold the memory of Frederick William as sacred and dear as we love and venerate him while he survives.
Thus may God hold these prayers as valid, as they have been conceived by us piously and sincerely.

div.head: XIX. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXXI. habita.

p.s: Last year, listeners, when on the most joyful birthday of Frederick William I spoke in this assembly, the first news of that immense upheaval had scarcely reached us, by which, after the fatal error of the Bourbon king, or whatever name one may wish to call that most ruinous undertaking, stirred up the undisciplined ranks of the urban multitude against the praetorians and the remaining soldiers, the leading city of the Gauls, polluted with slaughter and blood, and within the space of a few days stripped of the ancestral kingdom, driven from the ancestral soil, that family was, which a few decades earlier our armies and those of the allies had established and stabilized once and again with most savage battles and much blood.

On that day, when the situation was still perfectly calm and there was the utmost peace, how few were there who understood on the threshold and at the very entrance of what great events we were placed!
But what a change meanwhile invaded nearly all of Europe!
How many misfortunes, discords, seditions, battles, disasters harassed the peace, if this is to be called peace, which daily threatens war!
You would say that the world was shaken and knocked from its hinges, that all the furies of civil war were let loose from the underworld.
For after the Gauls had conquered themselves by a disastrous slaughter, the turbulent populace of the Belgians was inflamed with madness:
By the slaughter at Brussels the forces of the Batavians were broken;
The most populous and most wealthy cities of Belgium, the strongest and best-equipped citadels, into which the allies had expended great sums, revolt;

Finally, the king, who had shown his justice, fairness, and goodness to every best man, having been spurned with the greatest audacity, the Belgians are separated from the Batavians, so that they might fulfill their anger and hatred conceived long ago and nourished with much skill.
Soon the same movement drew part of Germany, which had been most faithful to its princes for a long time;
The duke of Brunswick was driven out by his citizens, the citadel itself having been burned;
There was disturbance among the Chatti, among the Saxons.
Now indeed, while the Prussian kingdom remains inviolate,
(For who would count the Aachen uprising, subdued by the citizens themselves, or those nocturnal games in our city?) Discord leaped toward the East:
With a fierce and immense force the Poles blazed up, already with mutual disasters to the nobility;
The rebellion spread widely through Lithuania and to the farthest Sarmatia.
Not even the Swiss cantons remained quiet;
The kingdom of Hanover was also disturbed, a kingdom that had never governed more innocently, the trouble having arisen from that most celebrated seat of learning, which owes many benefits to kings;
Several provinces of Italy were stirred up and were immediately settled by foreigners.
Britain itself, though it seemed secure in its ancient laws and institutions, was driven by tumults and factions to the point that the question of reforming the form of the republic was discussed.
What shall I say about the Spaniards and the Lusitanians, whom domestic discord has not yet ceased to harass?
They have already forgotten Greece, occupied with their own nearer troubles.
Among these things, armies of nearly all Europe have been prepared with enormous expenses, not indeed for undertaking war, but for maintaining peace.
And lest only the peoples of Europe should be afflicted with those calamities of which they themselves are the authors, nature, laboring by divine will, presses upon us:
From the foul cradle of Asia burst forth a dreadful plague, which, spread more widely day by day through the routes of armies and commerce, now presses upon us, having already entered our borders.

Since this year has brought such great declines of public and private fortune, at which it is no wonder if even the most steadfast are disturbed, would that my voice were so eloquent that with that consolation, which is almost the only one left, and which is uniquely suited and, as it were, proper to these most sacred solemnities, I might soothe the sad memory of evils and cheer your minds on this day, a most abundant source of joy for me, for you, and for the whole fatherland!

For if we consider what it is that our fatherland, along with few lands, has remained at least free from civil disturbances and perfectly peaceful, although some new provinces, and those scattered over very long distances, are not only neighboring in situation but also joined by natural kinship to those peoples who have either fallen completely into madness, or have been not moderately affected by the desire for new things:
What is offered to us before the image of Frederick William, which, like the Castors, calmed the storm and the waves with its serenity, the republic?

Indeed, Frederick William held together what could have fallen apart, not so much by the strength of armies, whose help is unsafe in a civil disturbance, as by those arts which alone you may apply with success even to fervent minds;
He came to the aid of his people in a timely manner, that is, before it was demanded, by lightening burdens of every kind, by removing those things that were hateful to the peoples;
He provided for necessities, so that medicine would not be prepared too late;
He bound and occupied minds with good deeds, so that they were persuaded, the Poles blazed with passion, already ennobled by mutual disasters;
A rebellion spread widely through Lithuania and to the farthest Sarmatia.
Not even the states of Helvetia were quiet;

The kingdom of Hanover was also disturbed, a kingdom that had never before been governed more innocently, the disturbance having originated in that most celebrated seat of learning, which owes many benefits to kings.
Several provinces of Italy were stirred up and were immediately settled by foreigners.
Britain itself, which seemed secure in its ancient laws and institutions, was driven by tumults and factions to the point that the question of reforming the form of the republic was discussed.
What shall I say about the Spaniards and the Lusitanians, whom domestic discord has not yet ceased to harass?
They have already forgotten Greece, being occupied with their own nearer troubles.
Among these things, armies of nearly all Europe are prepared with enormous expenses, not indeed for undertaking war, but for maintaining peace.
And lest the peoples of Europe alone should be afflicted with those calamities of which they themselves are the authors, nature, laboring by divine will, presses upon us.
From the foul cradle of Asia burst forth a dreadful plague, which, spread more widely day by day through the routes of armies and commerce, now presses upon us, having already entered our borders.

Since this year has brought such great declines of public and private fortune, at which it is no wonder if even the most steadfast are disturbed, would that my voice were so eloquent that with that consolation, which is almost the only one left, and which is uniquely suited and, as it were, proper to these most sacred solemnities, I might soothe the sad memory of evils and cheer your minds on this day, a most abundant source of joy to me, to you, and to the whole fatherland!

For if we consider what it is that our fatherland has remained free from civil disturbances and perfectly peaceful, with few lands, although some new provinces, scattered over very long distances, are not only near in situation but also joined by natural kinship to those peoples who have either fallen completely into madness or have been not moderately affected by the desire for revolution:
What is offered to us first but the image of Frederick William, which, like the Castors, calmed the storm and the waves with its serenity, and settled the republic?

Indeed, Frederick William held together what could have fallen apart, not so much by the strength of armies, whose help is unsafe in civil unrest, as by those arts which alone you may apply even to fervent minds with success;
He came to the aid of his people in good time, that is, before it was demanded, by lightening burdens of every kind, by removing those things which are hateful to the peoples.
He provided for necessities, so that medicine should not be prepared too late.

He bound and preoccupied minds with good deeds, so that they were convinced that he wanted nothing but the happiness of the citizens, and that he did not look out for himself and his own power, but for the common welfare.

Finally, both by his administration of the state and by his other virtues, by which he also won for himself the admiration and reverence of foreigners, he brought it about that the citizens loved him equally, just as they both felt and knew that they were loved by him.

Indeed it happens even to the best princes that they are not repaid by the people with the gratitude they deserve, either because factious men by various incitements render the citizens hostile to the prince, or because diverse and unsociable nations have been imprudently united under one master, and one of them spurns him;
Nevertheless, you will find no firmer or more certain pledge of public tranquility than that character of the prince by which the mutual love of the ruler and the parents is fostered.
This the splendid character of Frederick William provides for this kingdom;
this is that consolation with which we are especially delighted, and it is so implanted in your hearts that I bring it forth not more from my own than from your breasts;
This is the public happiness of Prussia, which will be enjoyed as long as these princes rule over us, and the people, most loving of their kings, will preserve their faith whole and uncorrupted.
This, whatever evils press upon it, alone will not perish, and it is not consumed by scarcity or high price of grain, nor by diseases, nor by wars;
On the contrary, it will alleviate whatever inconveniences arise, as long as the prince helps the citizens and the citizens help the prince:
Just as about twenty years ago, by mutual harmony and common steadfastness, we overcame the most severe times of the republic and completed the greatest wars.
He wished nothing except the happiness of the citizens, and he did not look out for himself and his own power, but for the common safety.

Finally, both by his administration of the state and by his other virtues, by which he also won for himself the admiration and reverence of foreigners, he brought it about that the citizens loved him equally, just as they both felt and knew that they were loved by him.

Indeed it happens even to the best princes that the people do not show them the gratitude they deserve, either because factious men with various goads render the citizens hostile to the prince, or because different and unsociable nations have been imprudently united under one master, and one of them spurns him;
Nevertheless, you will find no firmer or more certain pledge of public tranquility than that character of the prince by which the mutual love of the ruler and the parents is fostered.
This the distinguished character of Frederick William provides for this kingdom;
this is that consolation with which we are especially delighted, and it is so implanted in your hearts that I bring it forth not more from my own than from your breasts;
This is the public happiness of Prussia, which will be enjoyed as long as these princes rule over us, and the people, most loving of their kings, will preserve their faith whole and uncorrupted.
This, whatever evils press upon it, alone will not perish, and it is not consumed by scarcity or high price of grain, nor by diseases, nor by wars;
Indeed, it will alleviate whatever inconveniences, as long as the prince helps the citizens and the citizens help the prince:
Just as about twenty years ago we overcame the most serious times of the republic and completed the greatest wars through mutual harmony and common steadfastness.
It pleases those skilled in civil affairs and the rulers of empires themselves that peoples and kingdoms are held together by agreements.

Indeed, although many kingdoms have been compelled by force of arms, and arms and force are contrary to law, unless the sanctity of treaties and of an oath has been added, victors and vanquished will not coalesce by any civil bond.
But those treaties, in establishing which necessity alone presided, that they may be firm by law, are found to be not void only in name.
And so those things, which you may see daily, are changed and abolished by a new agreement, when another necessity presses again.
But love, true and wise indeed, not feigned and foolish, is everlasting;
by which kingdoms are founded much more securely.
Thus the foundation and bond of the family is love, not a contract:
certainly it would have been badly provided for marriage, badly for parents and children, if they were held together by a contract, not by love:

And just as a state, whose image the family reproduces as if in a very small form, when it has grown from primitive simplicity into a more perfect condition, changes the appearance of the family, nevertheless when the mutual love of prince and citizens has perished, the vital force is extinguished, the light of the state is put out.
By agreements the private affairs, by agreements the public affairs are so ordered that nevertheless without love the condition of both is unpleasant and sad.
Therefore not even the Romans, in so great a mass of empire, were unwilling that the prince be called father of the fatherland and that this honorable surname be earned;
so that he might seem to rule the state not only by power and skill and strength of forces, but by the natural affection of a father of a family:

nor has that virtue, which is referred to performing the duties of the fatherland, obtained a name of whatever sort derived from the condition of a pact, but it is called affection and love of the fatherland.

Now indeed this bond of love most closely unites the nation with that prince especially, whose stock, imbued with the ancestral institutions and customs, has through a long and benign hereditary rule contracted familiarity with the people, has not only recently proved beneficent to them, but has from its ancestors handed-down zeal for doing good, and by its deeds has given to the state and the nation a name and glory among foreigners.

Even for this reason, how devoted and bound to Frederick William the greatest part of the Prussian people is, escapes no one who considers what those glorious ancestors accomplished, and what he himself, following in their footsteps, has done.

But if some provinces have only recently been acquired, in which that innate love is not present, besides the distinguished and manifest virtue of the Prince himself, the consensus of very many also draws these, and that virtue of this empire, long since proven by the clearest examples, by which it brings it about that it attracts even strangers by the usefulness, justice, and equity of its institutions and makes them its own.
Thus it happens that mutual love unites the Prince not only with the old, but also with the new Prussians, and that all judge and piously revere him as father of the fatherland.
This story has often been sung by many, that the Prussian state is not native, but artificial:
to me that state seems truly native, whose foundation is love;
which falls most plainly upon our case.
For that one is especially to be regarded as natural which is closest to the family, the natural image of the state;
those that rest on compacts are artificially composed;
and for the most part compacts are born from dissensions, when the natural state has been disturbed.
But the natural state is not perfect, just as the natural man is imperfect.
I hear you:
but not even compacts and constitutions, however much they adorn the state and aid public confidence, are perfect:
And this kingdom also has some instruments of public security:

Finally, if there were only a choice between agreements without affection and affection without agreements, nevertheless, when mutual love of prince and citizens has perished, the vital force is destroyed, the light of the state is extinguished.
By agreements the private property, by agreements the public affairs are so ordered that nevertheless without affection the condition of both is unpleasant and sad.
Therefore not even the Romans, in so great a mass of empire, were unwilling that the prince be called father of the fatherland and that this honorable surname be earned;
so that he might seem to rule the state not by power alone and skill and strength of resources, but by the natural affection of a father of a family:

nor has that virtue, which is referred to the duties of the fatherland to be performed, obtained a name of whatever sort derived from the condition of a pact, but it is called affection and love of the fatherland.

Now indeed this bond of love most closely unites the nation with that prince especially, whose stock, imbued with ancestral institutions and customs, has contracted a familiarity with the people through a long and benign hereditary rule, has not only recently proved beneficent to them, but has inherited from its ancestors a zeal for doing good, and through its deeds has given to the state and the nation a name and glory among foreigners.

Even for this reason, how devoted and bound to Frederick William the greatest part of the Prussian people is, escapes no one who considers what those glorious ancestors accomplished, and what he himself, following in their footsteps, has done.

But if some provinces have only recently been acquired, in which that innate love is not present, besides the distinguished and manifest virtue of the Prince himself, the consensus of very many also draws these, and that virtue of this empire, long since proven by the clearest examples, by which it brings about that it attracts even strangers by the usefulness, justice, and equity of its institutions and makes them its own.
Thus it happens that mutual love unites the Prince not only with the old, but also with the new Prussians, and that all judge him to be the father of the fatherland and revere him piously.
This story has often been sung by many, that the Prussian state is not native but artificial:
to me that state seems truly native, whose foundation is love;
which falls most plainly upon our case.
For that one is especially to be regarded as natural which is closest to the family, the natural image of the state;
those which rest on compacts are artificially composed;
and for the most part compacts are born from dissensions, when the natural state has been disturbed.
But the natural state is not perfect, just as the natural man is imperfect.
I hear you.
but not even compacts and constitutions, however much they adorn the state and aid public confidence, are perfect:
And this kingdom also has some instruments of public security:
Finally, if there were only a choice between agreements without love and love without agreements, who would not prefer the latter?
Add that benefits offered by a willing person are better than those forced:
Gratitude is not felt for extorted favors.

Therefore, although there are things that are missed, the people recently subjected love Frederick William all the more intensely, because he conferred benefits on them willingly, bound by no other law than love, by which a prince is obligated to do good to the people.
It is indeed characteristic of this love that nothing too harsh or violent be decreed, and that all things be conducted without deceit.
By this, kingdoms are especially strengthened.
Indeed, that power cannot be retained long by force, the memory of past events tells us.
And those who strive to circumvent their subjects with arts and cunning fall into even greater hatred.

Nevertheless, many states are governed by this perverse principle, in which the prince is surrounded by cohorts of prefects, magistrates, and officials, not those who agree with the subjects, but who, like a hostile army, suppress with cunning and fear those whose interests they ought to have provided for:

That our republic rests on mutual love, you may also recognize from this, that the ministers of every public kind conspire excellently in mind and counsel with those whom they govern, and are not compelled to oppose their desires.

These ministers themselves in the universities are educated not according to a prescribed formula from the master, but with liberal learning, and they are not considered mercenary servants of the prince, performing slavish service and caring for that Thrasymachean advantage of the more powerful, but, obeying the prince with due deference, they have this duty enjoined upon them: that they strive to accomplish what they understand to be best in common for the king and the people.
Therefore, Frederick William wants intelligent men to be in charge of the state.
Hence no class of citizens was excluded from access to honors.
This is what is uniquely fitting for mutual affection.
For when a certain order of conducting the state enjoys the prerogative, the rest are slaves or close to servitude;
who, even if they obey in some part, certainly do not love those in command:
and very many are offended, if the state is like an inheritance of a few.
There are nevertheless those who want the people to serve perpetually;

They, although they take care of nothing more than that the people should not become intelligent, among the other arts employ this worst art or rather force upon their minds, so that they render them, as far as possible, dull, stupid, superstitious, not even refraining from sacred things, so that they may use these also for accomplishing their plans, with a purpose the more wicked the farther they are from the love which they pretend, and moreover equally foolish as if a father should wish his children to be foolish, so that they may be more obedient.
Among us there is nothing of that sort;
Our institutions of schools and churches, for educating and enlightening, who would not prefer this one?
It is added, that benefits offered by a willing giver are more excellent than forced ones:
gratitude is not felt for extorted favors.

Therefore, although there are things that are desired, they love Frederick William so much the more, even those recently subjected, because he conferred benefits on them willingly, bound by no other law than that of love, by which a prince is bound to do good to the people.
Indeed, it is characteristic of this love that nothing too harsh or violent should be decreed, and that all things be conducted without deceit:
By this, kingdoms are especially strengthened.
Indeed, the memory of past deeds tells us that power cannot be retained for long by force;
And those who strive to ensnare their subjects with tricks and cunning incur even greater hatred.

Nevertheless, many states are governed by this perverse principle, in which the prince is surrounded by cohorts of prefects, magistrates, and officials, not men who are in harmony with their subjects, but who, like a hostile army, suppress them by cunning and fear, those whose interests they ought to have looked after:

You may also recognize from this that our republic rests on mutual love, because the ministers of every public kind agree excellently in mind and counsel with those whom they govern, and are not forced to oppose their desires.

These ministers themselves in the universities are not educated according to a prescribed formula from a master, but with a liberal education; nor are they considered mercenaries of the prince, performing servile labor and caring for that Thrasymachean advantage of the more powerful, but, obeying the prince with due deference, they have this duty enjoined upon them: that what they understand to be best in common for the king and the people, they strive to accomplish.
Therefore, Frederick William wants intelligent men to be in charge of the state.
Hence no class of citizens is excluded from access to honors.
This is what is uniquely fitting for mutual affection.
For where a certain order of conducting the state enjoys a prerogative, the rest are slaves or close to slavery;
who, even if they obey in some part, certainly do not love those in command:
and very many are offended, if the state is like an inheritance of a few.
There are, however, those who want the people to serve forever;

Since they take no greater precaution than that the people should not become intelligent, among their other arts they employ this worst art or rather force upon their minds, so as to render them, as far as possible, dull, stupid, and superstitious, not even refraining from sacred things, so that they may use these too for accomplishing their plans, with a purpose all the more wicked the further they are from the love which they pretend, and moreover as foolish as if a father should wish his children to be foolish, so that they may be more obedient.
Among us there is nothing of that sort.

Our institutions of schools and churches serve to educate, enlighten, and console minds, and with few exceptions of light-shunning men, we seek a sincere, simple, and vigorous piety, by which the King excels, not a feigned and cunning one or wrapped in clouds, and truly or in appearance sad.

Now I need not explain the administration of justice, in which the paternal authority of Frederick William is not missed insofar as justice, by its nature severe and inexorable, admits of pardon and yields place to the leniency of a gentle prince:
Who does not see that the administration of taxes and public revenues is directed entirely to the advantage of the people?
For neither is silver collected for the use of the royal house and court, nor is effort given to filling the private treasury of the king:
Wealth taken from the people is not used to support a life of extravagance, nor to strengthen unjust power;
but what the subjects pay is spent on public necessities and utilities, and, if anything remains, on honor:
Thus the money returns to where it was sought.
Nor are taxes imposed in such a way that as much as possible is paid, but so that the burdens are very light, and commerce and private gains are hindered as little as possible:

What of the fact that alliances with foreign peoples were made not without a temporary loss of revenues, as I think, only so that private individuals might have a greater and freer opportunity of acquiring wealth?

Although, however, the state also flourishes more if private citizens are not poor, nevertheless the King does not help them for this reason, that a richer return from it might flow back to himself, just as masters or shepherds tend their flocks;
But the grateful people feel that he is led by fairness and love.
Finally, in no part of the state does the mutual love by which this commonwealth is held together seem to me to shine forth more than in military affairs.
For where that bond embraces the prince and the people, there is no need of mercenary soldiers, no bodyguard collected from foreigners;
The citizens will guard the king best.

Indeed, from ancient times it was held both by the common people and by philosophers among the most important things by which a king and a tyrant were distinguished, that the former was guarded by hired mercenaries from his own people, the latter by those from foreigners.
For the former seem to guard the prince against foreigners, the latter against citizens.
But you will also read of guards chosen from the natives, who are no more civil or popular.
A certain class of soldiers, not very prudently established and not properly restrained, easily becomes hostile to a well-ordered republic, to the mass of the people, and to the nobles themselves.
This happened to the Romans in the age of the emperors.
Therefore a king who has been compelled to entrust himself to such an army is far different from ours.

Among us, there are not fierce soldiers who serve to console minds, and with few exceptions of light-shunning men, we seek a sincere, simple, and vigorous piety, by which the King excels, not a feigned and cunning one or one wrapped in clouds, and truly or in appearance sad.

Now I need not explain about the administration of justice, in which the paternal rule of Frederick William is not lacking insofar as justice, by its nature severe and inexorable, admits of pardon and yields a place to the gentleness of a mild prince:
Who does not see that the administration of taxes and public revenues is directed entirely to the advantage of the people?
For neither is money collected for the use of the royal house and court, nor is effort given to filling the private treasury of the king:
Wealth taken from the people is not spent on leading a prodigal life, nor on strengthening unjust power;
but what the subjects pay is spent on public necessities and utilities, and, if anything remains, on honor:
Thus the money returns to where it was sought.
