Nor are taxes imposed in such a way that as much as possible is paid, but so that the burdens are very light, and commerce and private gains are hindered as little as possible:

What of the fact that alliances with foreign states were made not without a temporary loss of revenues, as I think, only so that private individuals might have a greater and freer opportunity of acquiring wealth?

Although, however, the state also flourishes more if private citizens are not poor, nevertheless the King does not help them for this reason, that a richer return from it might flow back to himself, just as masters or shepherds tend their flocks;
But the grateful people feel that he is led by fairness and love.
Finally, in no part of the state does the mutual love by which this city is held together seem to me to shine forth more than in military affairs.
For where that bond embraces the prince and the people, there is no need for mercenary soldiers, no bodyguard collected from foreigners;
citizens will protect the king best.

Indeed, in ancient times, among the most important things by which a king and a tyrant were distinguished, this was held both by the common people and by philosophers: that the former was guarded by his own citizens, the latter by hired foreigners;
For the former seem to guard the prince against foreigners, the latter against citizens.
But you may also read of guards chosen from the natives, who are no more civil or popular for that reason;
A certain class of soldiers, not very prudently established nor properly restrained, easily becomes hostile to a well-ordered republic, to the multitude of civilians, and to the very nobles.
This happened to the Romans in the age of the emperors.
Therefore a king who has been compelled to entrust himself to such an army differs greatly from ours.
Among us there are no fierce cohorts of soldiers, often more troublesome to their own side than formidable to the enemy.

From the whole people, with no distinction of place where each one was born, by the most just selection, legions are equipped, not to guard the king at home, who is most safe among his own, but to defend the fatherland from foreigners.

Nor are soldiers, as once, kept under the standards until old age, so that they become thoroughly hardened and inured to obedience hateful to themselves and to every kind of cruelty, but after a few years, having been properly subdued and trained, they are discharged by a lawful discharge to their own people, always ready to return to the ranks at the king's command.
Whereas formerly nothing was so hateful to the pagans as military service, now no one except the most cowardly refuses this honorable service, which is not inhuman, not too burdensome.

Is this a slight proof that the Prince is dear to the citizens, that the fatherland is dear, and that private individuals do not separate their own advantage from the interests of the Prince and the fatherland?
cohorts, often more troublesome to their own men than formidable to the enemy;

From the whole people, with no distinction of place where each one was born, by a most just selection, legions are equipped, not to guard the king at home, who is most safe among his own, but to defend the fatherland from foreigners.

Nor are soldiers, as in former times, kept under the standards until old age, so that they become thoroughly hardened and inured to obedience hateful to themselves and to every kind of cruelty, but after a few years, having been properly subdued and trained, they are discharged by a lawful discharge and returned to their own people, always ready to return to the ranks at the king's command.

Although in former times nothing was so hateful to the pagans as serving in the army, now no one except the most cowardly refuses this honorable military service, which is not inhuman, not too burdensome.

Is this a slight proof that the Prince is dear to the citizens, that the fatherland is dear, and that private individuals do not separate their own advantage from the interests of the Prince and the fatherland?
Thus far I have considered the public counsels of Frederick William, by which mutual love, the honor and strength of the Prussian state, has been brought about.
But in order that the prince may be equal to all the duties of the empire:
if he, as a private person, is not equally innocent, and is not only not better, but somewhat worse than an ordinary citizen;
if at home he is either too harsh or excessively patient and indulgent;
Prodigal, and where there is leisure, given to idleness, pleasures, and delights, or on the other hand too sparing and gloomy;
if he is not a good father of the family, if he is harsh to his household:
something will leak out even outside, and either his softness and secret lusts will hand him over to contempt, or his untimely severity will diminish the people's love.

The suspicious minds of the citizens, if anything adverse to the republic should happen, will transfer the blame to the ruler, because he who presides badly over his own household does not seem able to preside rightly over the state, and private vices spread into the republic.
Indeed, Frederick William wins the wills of his subjects by his private virtues no less than by his public ones.
He who judges that a king should not be granted any more license in morals than any private person.
who combines the duties of a father of a family and of a prince with an excellent balance;
He is at once courteous and energetic, splendid and generous without extravagance, moderating himself for the state as much as for himself.

Finally, just as he respects the judgment of men, because he respects those whom each person loves, so reverence for the divine power perfects the virtue of a private individual, as far as is permitted to mortals.

Therefore, whether we consider the public or the private life of Frederick William, we understand that he himself is the source of that love by which I have judged the happiness of Prussia to be contained.

Quodsi tamen hoc rege haud immunes ingentium malorum fuimus et sumus, si bella primum adversa, mox secunda quidem sed tanto cruentiora gesta sunt, unde magna vis aeris alieni contrahenda rei publicae fuit, si in pace modo quaestus inopia et agrorum sterilitas urget, modo ipsa fertilitas et frugum copia indeque accidens vilitas annonae fundorum possessores et colonos premere, quin nonnullis etiam nimia populi frequentia, cui alendae vix sufficere agricultura, opificia, commercia queant, adducere discrimina videtur, si quum maxime belli metus et nata ex tot turbis communis animorum agitation et morbi grassantis saevitia cum caeli intemperie angunt, magnasque in exercitus et tuendos imperii limites etiam adversus amicos postulant impensas:

What else can you conclude, except that by a hidden law of fate or by the design of divine providence, evils afflict both men and nature, which no mortal prudence, and not even the kindness of the best prince, can guard against or heal?
This can be illustrated not now for the first time, by an example, although ancient, yet, I think, not foreign to our affairs.
Certainly no ruler was ever more benevolent in spirit toward the human race, none was so clement and gentle, as Marcus.

Antoninus the Philosopher, so beloved by all that he was called by some father, by others brother, by others son, as each one's age suggested, and at his funeral all were certain that he, lent by the gods, had returned to the gods, and with one voice the Senate and People called him a propitious god.

Profecto is, qui Platonis sententiam, felicem fore civitatem, si aut philosophi imperent, aut imperantes philosophentur, non modo in ore habuit, sed suo exemplo demonstrare conatus est, et qui quamvis sapiens non quod sibi, sed quod prudentissimis placeret, ratum esse voluit, profitens aequius esse, ut ipse tot et talium amicorum consilia sequeretur, quam ut tot et tales amici unius ipsius sequerentur voluntatem, is inquam non omisisse quidquam censendus est, quo civium adiuvaretur felicitas.
But he foresaw it himself, and at the time when he was adopted into the kingdom he argued what evils the empire contained in itself:

Among these, I think that this was not the least for him: that the world was afflicted with the greatest calamities under the prince himself, and, as an old writer says, almost nothing can be said or thought by which mortals are wont to be exceedingly tormented, that did not rage during his rule.
Nowhere was there rest from arms:
The East, Illyricum, Italy, Gaul, and Germany are the regions in which, as I have judged, the happiness of Prussia is contained through wars.

Quodsi tamen hoc rege haud immunes ingentium malorum fuimus et sumus, si bella primum adversa, mox secunda quidem sed tanto cruentiora gesta sunt, unde magna vis aeris alieni contrahenda rei publicae fuit, si in pace modo quaestus inopia et agrorum sterilitas urget, modo ipsa fertilitas et frugum copia indeque accidens vilitas annonae fundorum possessores et colonos premere, quin nonnullis etiam nimia populi frequentia, cui alendae vix sufficere agricultura, opificia, commercia queant, adducere discrimina videtur, si quum maxime belli metus et nata ex tot turbis communis animorum agitation et morbi grassantis saevitia cum caeli intemperie angunt, magnasque in exercitus et tuendos imperii limites etiam adversus amicos postulant impensas:

What else can you conclude, except that by a hidden law of fate or by the counsel of divine providence, evils afflict both men and nature, which no mortal prudence, nor even the kindness of the best prince, can guard against or heal?
This we may illustrate, not now for the first time discovered and approved, by an example, though ancient, yet, I think, not foreign to our affairs.
Certainly no prince was ever more benevolent in spirit toward the human race, none was so clement and gentle as M.

Antoninus the Philosopher, so beloved by all that he was called by some father, by others brother, by others son, as each one's age suggested, and at his funeral all were certain that he, lent by the gods, had returned to the gods, and with one voice the Senate and People called him a propitious god.

Profecto is, qui Platonis sententiam, felicem fore civitatem, si aut philosophi imperent, aut imperantes philosophentur, non modo in ore habuit, sed suo exemplo demonstrare conatus est, et qui quamvis sapiens non quod sibi, sed quod prudentissimis placeret, ratum esse voluit, profitens aequius esse, ut ipse tot et talium amicorum consilia sequeretur, quam ut tot et tales amici unius ipsius sequerentur voluntatem, is inquam non omisisse quidquam censendus est, quo civium adiuvaretur felicitas.
But he foresaw it himself, and at the time when he was adopted into the kingdom he argued what evils the empire contained in itself:

Among these, I think that not the least happened to him, that the world was afflicted with the greatest calamities under the prince himself, and, as an ancient writer says, almost nothing can be said or thought by which mortals are wont to be exceedingly distressed, which did not rage while he ruled.
Nowhere is there rest from arms:
The East, Illyricum, Italy, Gaul, and Germany were afflicted by wars;
Cities were swallowed up and buried by an earthquake;

Inundations of rivers oppressed them, locusts were harmful to the fields, a most severe famine, and finally the greatest evil, a pestilence rushing in with repeated and increased force over several years.

For after the Roman soldier, under the leadership of Avidius Cassius, plundered and burned Seleucia of Babylonia, a city inhabited by four hundred thousand, or as others have reported, six hundred thousand people, situated between the Tigris and the Euphrates, contrary to all law and right;

In that city, not far from the recess of the Persian Gulf, whence that disease, which has now begun to spread through Europe, entered western Asia, the plague is said to have been born, released from the narrow opening of the temple of Apollo or from a golden chest, as superstitious rumor reported, by an original taint.
Soon the pestilential breath was carried through the soldiers and the commerce of the rivers into Mesopotamia and especially Nisibis, and from there it filled the Parthians and the whole world, L.

And the contagions, spreading through the armies of Verus and Cassius into all the provinces through which they were returning, which polluted everything from the borders of Persia all the way to the Rhine and into Gaul with deaths, destroyed nearly all the troops, and having spread throughout all Italy, also consumed at Rome many thousands of men and not a few of the nobles.
And this indeed was the state of the Roman empire under those delights of the human race, M.
Aurelius:

Concerning this, not a contemporary, upon whom suspicion of flattery might fall, but some later person not undeservedly said that it seemed divinely granted that while the law of the world, or of nature, or whatever else unknown to men produces those evils, the counsels of the prince, as remedies, should bring relief.
Who would fear to apply the same opinion to Frederick William?

Of course, what happens even to a good prince, that he often, weary from the experience of adverse circumstances and from cares, relaxes his exertion and diligence, the constancy of Frederick William does not allow:
He did not become hardened to the misfortunes of the citizens;

As soon as any calamity, of whatever kind, has invaded any part of the kingdom, he strives to help each person not only when warned but of his own accord, not only mindful of his royal duty but from a human feeling of compassion, bearing another's distress as if it were his own, just as a father helps his children, a brother his brother, a son his parents.
Therefore, as the Senate and People of Rome [have decreed] M. [something], ...

Antoninus, so we have long proclaimed that Frederick William was divinely sent to the state, and we proclaim it now especially, and we give thanks to the supreme deity, because, if our age had to endure both the unusual evils of nature and to see those things in which the state could scarcely stand unmoved, when it was afflicted;
cities swallowed up and buried by an earthquake;

The floods of the rivers pressed upon them, locusts were hostile to the fields, there was a most severe famine, and finally the greatest evil, a pestilence that for several years rushed in with repeated and increased force.

For after the Roman soldier, under the leadership of Avidius Cassius, plundered and burned, contrary to all law and right, Seleucia of Babylonia, a city inhabited by four hundred thousand, or as others have reported, six hundred thousand people, situated between the Tigris and the Euphrates;

In that city, not far from the recess of the Persian Gulf, whence that disease, which has now begun to spread through Europe, entered western Asia, the plague is said to have been born, released from a narrow opening, as superstitious rumor reported, from the inner sanctuary of the temple of Apollo or from a golden chest:
Soon the pestilential breath was carried through the soldiers and the trade of the rivers into Mesopotamia and especially Nisibis, and from there it filled the Parthians and the whole world.

And the armies of Verus and Cassius, as the contagion spread through all the provinces through which they were returning, which from the borders of Persia all the way to the Rhine and into Gaul polluted everything with deaths, destroyed nearly all the soldiers' forces, and having spread throughout all Italy, at Rome too consumed many thousands of men and not a few of the nobles.
And this indeed was the state of the Roman empire under those delights of the human race, M.
Aurelius:

Concerning him, not a contemporary, upon whom suspicion of flattery might fall, but some later person not undeservedly said that it seemed to have been granted by divine providence that, while the law of the world or of nature or whatever else unknown to men produces those evils, the counsels of the prince, as remedies, should bring relief.
Who would fear to apply the same opinion to Frederick William?

Of course, what happens even to a good prince, that he often, wearied by the experience of adverse circumstances and by cares, relaxes his exertion and diligence, the constancy of Frederick William does not permit:
He did not become hardened to the misfortunes of his citizens;

As soon as any calamity, of whatever kind, has invaded any part of the kingdom, he strives to help each person not only when warned but of his own accord, not only mindful of his royal duty but moved by human compassion, bearing another's distress as if it were his own, just as a father helps his children, a brother his brother, a son his parents.
Therefore, just as the Senate and People of Rome, for Marcus...

Antoninus, so we have long proclaimed that Frederick William was divinely sent to the state, and we proclaim it now especially, and we give thanks to the supreme deity, because, if our age had to endure both the unusual evils of nature and to see those things in which the state could scarcely stand unmoved, unless that prince reigned who would bind the minds of his people with the bond of mutual love, a king has fallen to our lot most just, most merciful, most kind, in whose love the state might find rest.

Finally, we make vows to God, the Best and Greatest, that Frederick William, together with the whole August house, may be preserved safe and most flourishing; that under his leadership our fatherland may be increased day by day with firmer and more liberal institutions; that the most sacred bond of love may not be broken by any imprudence or wickedness; that, if it can be done, an end may be put to the slaughters by which nations are worn away; and that peace, the nurse of arts and letters, the mother of all good things, may be strengthened, and that common fear may cease and security be restored.

Unless that prince reigned who would bind the hearts of his people with the bond of mutual love, a most just, most merciful, most kind king fell to our lot, in whose love the commonwealth would rest content.

Finally, we make vows to God, the Best and Greatest, that Frederick William, together with the whole August house, may be preserved safe and most flourishing; that under his leadership our fatherland may be increased day by day with firmer and more liberal institutions; that the most sacred bond of love may not be broken by any imprudence or wickedness; that, if it can be done, an end may be put to the slaughters by which nations are worn away; and that peace, the nurse of arts and letters, the mother of all good things, may be confirmed, and that common fear may cease and security be restored.

div.head: XX. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXXII. habita.

p.s: Just as, when the civil year has ended, it is pleasing even for a prudent man to recall what pleasant and what adverse things the nearest course of the sun has brought, although he knows well that the motion and flux of things is neither held back nor interrupted by these boundaries which we fix, but that it runs on continuously with infinite force toward the eternal goal;

Thus we, the audience, we whom piety bids to count the years from the most auspicious birthday of Frederick William, have been accustomed in this assembly, when we act, to recall especially the memory of each preceding year, and to draw fresh matter for rejoicing from the events most recently accomplished, which flowed in from all sides with joyful abundance.

A year ago, when I spoke from this place, it was almost more my task to dispel the sad expectation of impending calamity by setting forth the virtues of our excellent King, than to speak of our prosperity:
So many evils threatened, so many disturbances took away security.
What shall I say now about this year, listeners?
Should I judge the fierce spirits as composed, or as not yet composed?
Shall I speak of the victories and defeats of foreigners and civil wars, in which, whichever side was victorious, it is compelled not to afflict enemies, but its own people?
Or, to dwell on our own affairs, the fatal disease, which we foresaw approaching the previous year, shall I say was overcome with a small loss or a very great one?

Certainly it exhausted the public resources, certainly it snatched away from the kingdom great leaders, and from us a great wise man, just as about four lustra earlier the plague had carried off Fichte.
Certainly, the attendance at our school has diminished somewhat.
But accidental losses are repaired where vigor, virtue, prudence, and industry survive;

but if morals are corrupt, and ignorance and stupidity, and the barbarous injustice and harshness of the empire have gradually and little by little reduced everyone to weakness, the people die with a slow wasting away.
Hitherto, indeed, the world, suspended between hope and fear, trembles as to where this state of affairs is about to turn out.

Our commonwealth, amid the general disturbance which seemed likely to bring extreme violence even to the wise, as if tested by fire, rests in the mutual affection of the King and the people, which perhaps you remember when I explained more fully.
Meanwhile the word liberty resounded everywhere, which would that it could be borne more easily than procured:
To remain moderate, to harm when excessive, not a few have forgotten; not a few, by the appearance and pretext of liberty, have fallen into extreme madness.

Indeed, to temper liberty with laws in such a way that a limit is maintained, which liberty itself strives to exceed, not indeed by its own nature, but by a fault joined with it, is a matter of great skill and the highest wisdom:

For since liberty is such that it is permitted to do what you ought to will, and you are not compelled to do what it is right to be unwilling to do, at no age have peoples not seemed free to themselves, unless it were permitted to do whatever they wished, imitating themselves those whom they least approve, unbridled spirits, to whom not that which is just and right pleases, but that which pleases seems just and right.
But if I consider the nature of this kingdom:

But I often and carefully consider, not because my own pursuits call me here, but because the praises of Frederick William are to be pursued by me, and I am devoted to him and to the Prussian state with my whole soul:
I seem to see that we enjoy a greater liberty than can be displayed, while many who seem to themselves most free are in reality slaves.
For true liberty is placed in morals and in the common consent of all good men;
And, as Tacitus attributes to our ancestors, among us good morals prevail more than good laws do elsewhere.
These guard against the measure being exceeded on either side;
these draw even the unwilling, they repress violence however great;

if these have been corrupted, if citizens have become unaccustomed to obeying laws and magistrates, to holding dear ancestral institutions, to keeping faith and oath, to being bound by the religion of the supreme deity, what then does the name of liberty profit?
But by what means especially do you think that character is formed?

I think no one of you will disagree with me, if I say that the life of the prince contributes much to that matter, and that the wise man, whom the kingdom took from us, snatched away a great thing, as the plague had carried off Fichte almost four lustra before;
Certainly it diminished the attendance of our school to a moderate degree.
But accidental losses are repaired, where vigor, virtue, prudence, and industry remain;
But if corrupt morals, ignorance and stupor, barbaric injustice and harshness of rule have gradually and little by little brought all to languor, the people die by a slow wasting away.
Hitherto, indeed, the world, suspended between hope and fear, trembles, wondering where this state of affairs will turn out.

Our republic, amid the general disturbance which seemed likely to bring extreme violence even to the prudent, as if tested by fire, rests in the mutual affection of the King and the people, which perhaps you remember I have explained more fully at some time.
Meanwhile the word liberty resounded everywhere, which would that it could be borne more easily than procured:
That it should remain moderate, that it should harm when excessive, not a few have forgotten; not a few, slipping under the appearance and pretext of liberty, have fallen into extreme madness.

Indeed, to temper liberty with laws in such a way that a measure is maintained, which liberty itself strives to exceed, not indeed by its own nature, but by a fault joined with it, is a matter of great skill and the highest wisdom:

For since liberty is such that it is permitted to do what you ought to wish, and you are not compelled to do what it is right not to wish, at no age have peoples not seemed free to themselves, unless it were permitted to do whatever they wished, imitating themselves those whom they least approve, unbridled spirits, to whom not what is fair and just pleases, but what pleases seems fair and just.
But if I consider the nature of this kingdom:

But I often and carefully consider, not because my own pursuits call me here, but because the praises of Frederick William are to be pursued by me, and I am devoted to him and to the Prussian state with my whole heart:
I seem to see that we enjoy a greater liberty than can be displayed, while many who seem to themselves most free are in reality slaves.
For just liberty is placed in the morals and the common consent of all good men;
And, as Tacitus attributes to our ancestors, among us good morals prevail more than good laws do elsewhere.
These guard against exceeding the limit on either side;
these draw even the unwilling, they restrain violence however great;

if these have been corrupted, if citizens have become unaccustomed to obeying laws and magistrates, to holding dear ancestral institutions, to keeping faith and oath, to being bound by the religion of the supreme deity, what then does the name of liberty profit?
But by what means especially do you think that morals are formed?
I think no one of you will disagree with me, if I say that the life of the prince contributes much to that matter, and also the things that are done publicly by him and his ministers.
I will not sketch for you the image of Frederick William, which you hold as if by daily sight, which is inscribed in your hearts, which has been described by me more than once;
This has often been explained by me before, that he by his example equally corrected morals, just as other princes corrupted them.
And in governing the state you may find nothing excessive, nothing too unjust, nothing cruel:
By his moderation the King mitigates his rule and lightens whatever burdens.
Concerning these matters, since I have spoken not once before, now I will embrace everything in a few words.
Indeed, violent domination keeps its subjects in check through fear, but we are governed by love and reason:
the people do not fear the prince, but they revere him;
the prince does not fear his own people, but he loves them.
That not everything pleases everyone is human;
and concerning matters that are debated with the greatest intensity at any time, the judgment of the present age is corrupted by partiality and flattery, by hatred and anger:

What is good, what is useful, posterity weighs with a sure balance by weighing the wills, causes, and outcomes; they enjoy the good deeds of their ancestors as much as grandchildren rest in the shade of trees that their parents planted, as they pay for the imprudence and faults of their predecessors, just as future generations pay off the debt contracted in the age of their fathers.
Now indeed, beyond those things that are done publicly, character is shaped by education and training.
In this, divine matters hold the first place.

Concerning these, the more erroneous the opinions of men are, the more superstitious anxiety prevails, or the more prone to impiety is their fickleness, so much the more widely does the corruption of morals spread.
Examples also have great influence here, and it is agreed that Frederick William's mind excels in this matter too with remarkable moderation.

At the same time, in no state, I think, have sacred matters been more wisely ordered than in ours, and better directed to that end, that unskilled minds may be imbued with those things which it is in the interest of all to know, that as much knowledge as they acquire, so much may the upright teachers minister to them, and finally that they may not be bound by ceremonies, but by inner sense and, as far as possible, by free intellect be led to God.
But if public education governs morals, schools of every kind, in which boys and adolescents are instructed, have no small influence on that most important matter;
among which, since universities are especially conspicuous, according as these have been arranged, morals can be changed somewhat for the better or worse.
What need is there of words?
Rightly, both from teachers and from students, integrity of morals is demanded;
Rightly, if a life that is not honorable enough and is dissolute disgraces them, let them be conducted publicly through him and his ministers.
I will not sketch for you an image of Frederick William, which you hold as if by daily sight, which is inscribed on your hearts, which has been described by me more than once;
This has often been explained before me: that he by his own example corrected morals just as much as other princes corrupted them.
And in governing the state, you would find nothing excessive, nothing too unjust, nothing cruel.
By his own moderation the King mitigates his rule and lightens whatever burdens there are.
Although I have spoken about these matters more than once before, now I will embrace everything in a few words.
Of course, a violent tyranny keeps its subjects in check through fear, but we are governed by love and reason:
The people do not fear the prince, but they revere him;
the prince does not fear his own people, but he loves them.
That not everything pleases everyone is human;
and concerning matters which are conducted with the greatest effort at any time, the judgment of the present age is corrupted by zeal and flattery, by hatred and anger:

What is good, what is useful, posterity weighs with a sure balance by weighing wills, causes, and outcomes, and they enjoy the good deeds of their ancestors as much as grandchildren rest in the shade of trees that their parents planted, as they pay for the imprudence and faults of earlier generations, just as future offspring pays off the debt contracted in the age of the fathers.
Now indeed, beyond those things that are done publicly, character is shaped by education and training.
In this, divine matters hold the first place.

Concerning these, the more erroneous the opinions of men are, the more superstitious anxiety prevails, or the more prone to impiety is their fickleness, so much the more widely does the corruption of morals spread.
Examples also have great influence here, and it is agreed that Frederick William's mind excels in this matter too by a remarkable moderation;

At the same time, in no state, I think, have sacred matters been arranged more wisely than in ours, and better directed toward that end, that untrained minds may be imbued with those things which it is of interest to all to know, that as much of knowledge as they may take in, so much may good teachers minister to them, and finally that they may not be bound by ceremonies, but by inner feeling and, as far as possible, by free intellect may be led to God.
But if public education governs morals, schools of every kind, in which boys and adolescents are instructed, have no small influence on this most important matter;
among which, since universities are especially conspicuous, according as these have been arranged, morals can be changed somewhat for the better or worse.
What need is there of words?
Rightly, integrity of morals is demanded from both teachers and students;
Rightly, if a life that is not honorable enough and is dissolute disgraces the order, they are blamed;

Nor is it in any way to be tolerated that what was once said more frequently than now, if not openly, at least secretly and in a roundabout way, that the private life of great scholars is not to be examined according to the commonly accepted moral norms.
For shall we impose this duty on princes, that they unite honesty with power, and shall we grant to a learned and talented man that he may set forth bad examples?
But a burning passion has carried me away in another direction than the one toward which I was heading.
I have said that customs have very great influence in this kingdom, and that education is subservient to customs:

Therefore, rightly, among us great importance is attached to public education and to the propagation of literature and the liberal arts, which, among the other instruments of empire, the most clement King uses both most wisely and most liberally:
Since this argument pertains especially to us, grant me this indulgence, listeners, that I may dwell on it a little.

and therefore rightly among us very much is attributed to public education and to the propagation of liberal arts, which among the other instruments of empire the most clement King uses both most wisely and most liberally:
Since this argument especially pertains to us, grant me this indulgence, listeners, that I may dwell on it a little.
How truly and wittily did that elegant man, who recently lived among us as a guest, call Prussia the land of schools and camps!
And indeed the excessive frequency of camps undoubtedly oppresses the peoples:
Therefore, with the military system more properly established, Frederick William reduced the standing armies:
the same man increased the number of schools, which can hardly be made greater than is right;

For never under this sky will that happen which we read was done in the Indian Ocean through the fault of imprudent preachers of the divine word, that the common and pagan multitude, having abandoned their trades and agriculture, wholly occupied in reading and reciting sacred formulas and prayers, perishes by the most extreme kind of idleness and misery.

Then indeed, when the state lay prostrate under the greatest calamities, we saw letters, as it were, establish sanctuaries, and with the strength of the fatherland restored and its borders extended, learning grew marvelously.
I am not the sort of person who disparages the good qualities of others and seeks praise for my fatherland by despising them.

I freely confess that many things in Britain are excellently established and invented, and many in Gaul, and the more willingly because the learned men of those most learned peoples now by no means despise our [institutions], and even partly prefer them to their own:

Indeed, in certain arts, and especially in those which require great apparatus, or whose resources must be gathered with the aid of immense commerce and distant voyages, our poverty cannot enter the contest with the wealthier.
Nor is it surprising if the princes of greater kingdoms nourished our cities, much more populous and abounding in richest resources, and most distinguished talents.

Indeed, even some cities of Germany itself, inferior to Prussia, have their own distinctions, of which they may justly boast, and they have contributed and still contribute much to the flourishing of literature and the arts.
Nevertheless, foreigners especially celebrate that care which, under the auspices of Frederick William, is publicly devoted to nurturing studies;
Nor is one part or another fostered while others are neglected, but provision is made evenly and consistently for almost all desires.
The splendor of great academies dazzles the eyes in other places, while the rustic multitude, for the most part, has not even learned to distinguish and write the elements of letters.
Who would wish that so great a number of most useful men, on whose strength the state rests, should be utterly uncultivated like cattle, so that, of course, it might obey more readily?
Therefore we take pains that these too may be educated according to their own capacity:
Although this matter is hindered by very great difficulties, nevertheless will accomplishes much when combined with judgment.
What shall I say of the urban games of every kind, by which the age of boys is formed;
the schools, which by a new institution have undertaken to teach those who do not indeed profess literature, but transfer it to the use and enjoyment of common life;
the gymnasia, by which young men are prepared for higher knowledge;
technical exercises of any kind;
the academies, as they call them, of architecture, painting, sculpture;
Finally, our universities, equipped and adorned with all resources?
But also teachers, who would be adequate for the duties, had to be prepared;
Therefore, seminaries for popular and scholarly teachers were established, and certain other things that would serve the cultivation of certain individual disciplines.
How many training schools have recently been founded for physicians and surgeons, both civil and military, to be more perfectly trained in learning and practice!

And lest anything should anywhere be lacking of the necessary equipment, which in so great a mass of present erudition, lest it should seem too small, ought to be most abundant and, I might almost say, immense, the King's munificence has supplied the most ample libraries, museums filled with the most precious and most elegant works of art and with natural objects collected from all over the world, and gardens, and other things of this kind, and he increases them daily.

Although these benefits are common to the whole kingdom, because no province of it is placed after the others, nevertheless our university has this, as it were, a prerogative, that since it is situated in the very seat of the empire, into which very many resources flow of their own accord, and which it is fitting to be distinguished with all ornaments, we abound in many things, which one would hardly find in smaller cities:
Wherefore we owe a greater gratitude to the most kind King.

Now indeed let it be permitted to wander a little more widely, so that from the inner condition of literature itself we may understand what I said above, that they contribute what is just and fitting to morals.

And lest anything should ever be lacking of the necessary equipment, which in so great a mass of present learning, lest it should seem too small, ought to be most abundant and, I might almost say, immense, the King's munificence has supplied the most ample libraries, museums filled with the most precious and most elegant works of art, and with natural objects collected from all over the world from every side, and gardens, and other things of this kind, and he increases them daily.

Therefore we owe the greater gratitude to the most kind King.

Now indeed let it be permitted to wander a little more widely, so that from the inner condition of literature itself we may understand what I said above, that liberty is rightly contained within morals.
For since literature cannot be rightly handled unless varied material of every kind is collected, for which unwearying industry is required;
since many things must be held in memory, the proper path of each discipline and, as it were, the form of art must be learned by long use and practice;
Much effort and labor must be spent on these matters.

But we must be careful that minds weighed down by learning and constrained by formulas, however learned, do not lose that which literature is especially able to provide: the light and freedom of the mind.
It is not enough to be learned.
Wisdom is needed.
I call the wise man free, as the Stoics do.
That you may in some way be a perfect grammarian, a perfect physicist or mathematician, that you may have thoroughly learned any other art or science whatsoever:
If this, which I demand, is lacking, the greatest thing will be lacking.

Without doubt, even if minds are bound by certain prescribed laws and are constrained by the formulas of their superiors, which it is impious to transgress, one or another art that is less entangled in them can be cultivated with great success;
which the Society of Jesus has shown by outstanding examples:

For with the wisest policy he had decided that he should also excel in letters, partly because he revered and loved them, partly because he understood that his glory and power were increased and strengthened by them:

But the closer each discipline is to wisdom, the more it is engaged in the highest utilities of the human race—not those that pertain to livelihood and gain, but those that are placed in notions that illuminate the mind—the more each is hindered by such bonds, until the mind, by its own force, which you would scarcely tame, breaks through the prison.
Thus philosophy, since it especially hammers out those notions I mentioned, cannot make progress without freedom.
Nevertheless, for almost all ages, men equally ignorant and powerful have especially opposed this, and yet they have not achieved what they wanted.

Anaxagoras, who was the first to think that the universe was adorned and governed by mind, was accused as impious by the superstitious, condemned by the Athenians, although they were the most cultured of all Greeks, and they would have punished him more severely, had he not had Pericles as his patron, a man far superior in his native city and in the age in which he lived:
After the philosopher died, the people of Lampsacus erected altars to him as to a god.
What happened to Socrates, no one does not know;
He was thought to corrupt the youth, he who eminently corrected their morals, who called the mind back from external and visible things to itself, so that it might know itself:
After the citizens killed him with poison, soon they repented of the public atrocity.
And that I may come closer to our times, Iordanus was kept in confinement.

What happened to Socrates, no one does not know;
He was thought to corrupt the youth, he who eminently improved their morals, who called the mind back from external and visible things to itself, so that it might know itself:
After the citizens killed him with poison, soon they repented of the public atrocity.
And to come closer to our own times, the foolish and bloodthirsty inquisitors burned Giordano Bruno alive, who rightly called himself a lover of wisdom.
Our age admits that he was free from our impiety; it detests these men.
René Descartes, who was regarded as an atheist by some religious contemporaries, soon seemed to have furnished the strongest weapons against atheists;

Many have inveighed against Benedict Spinoza, not without fury, because he taught that human freedom consists in the knowledge of God, that the knowledge of God leads to the love of God, and that in the love of God the happiness of mortals is placed.
These are covered by darkness, while his name remains and will remain, and even those wise men who shrink from his doctrines confess that he was most holy and most acute.

What of the fact that in the previous century turbulent adversaries of the arts expelled Christian Wolf from this kingdom, who professed to be conducting the cause of God and natural religion against him?
But King Frederick honorably recalled him, and no one today doubts that Wolfian philosophy is nothing more innocent.
Finally, in our memory, Fichte was accused of impiety:
This state provided him a refuge, and we who have lived with him know that he was a pious man.
The sight of all men does not endure the light of history:
Nevertheless, this also penetrates whatever darkness is spread before it.
For the curious posterity of earlier ages searches out nothing, not even the most hidden things;
long time opens nothing, which rewards virtue and punishes crimes with the perpetuity of memory.
Although offenses may lie hidden for a while, although slander may obscure integrity:

Soon there will come a worthy herald of glorious deeds, a keen chastiser of vices, who, like that Tacitus, having attained eternity through the monuments of his genius, may rescue the conscience of the human race from oblivion.
But why do I speak of history?
Not even mathematics did they spare.
Who would believe that a lawsuit was brought against the astronomical discoveries of Copernicus and Galileo on account of superstition, if we had not received it from our ancestors?

What, to avoid mixing the cradle of the most holy religion with human affairs, shall we say about Luther and those who, before him and with him, undertook to reform the sacred rites with the boldest enterprise?
Wherever we turn our eyes, we see errors defended by prejudiced opinions, and the knowledge of truth delayed.
Nor is it the question whether the human race advances or stands still, but who advances eagerly, who are left behind weary.
Indeed, when the freedom of the mind is taken away, not only is progress hindered, but ruin is accelerated.
What we read in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, that the stupid and cruel inquisitors burned alive Aristodemus of Cumae in Italy, surnamed Brunus, who rightly called himself a lover of the divine:
That he was free from our impiety, the age concedes; these it detests.

Wherever we turn our eyes, we see errors defended by prejudiced opinions, and the knowledge of truth delayed:
nor is it the question whether the human race advances or stands still, but who advance eagerly, who are left behind weary.
Indeed, when the freedom of the mind is taken away, not only is progress hindered, but ruin is accelerated.

We read in Dionysius of Halicarnassus that Aristodemus, the tyrant of Cumae in Italy, in order that no generous and manly spirit might arise in any citizen, by abolishing gymnasia and exercises of arms, wished to effeminate the young offspring, and ordered that the boys, like virgins, should let their hair grow, adorn it with flowers, curl it in ringlets, and gather it into knots, let variegated robes fall to their ankles, be led by female pedagogues carrying fans and parasols to dancing schools and to flute-players and to baths, where, after being anointed with ointments, they might be adorned before a mirror.
This was gradually accomplished not so much by weakening bodies as by enervating and dulling minds, as the Roman Empire declined in both respects.
Indeed, even that age did not lack brilliant talents;
but to avoid envy, they hid at home, not without public detriment:
virtue and honor and whatever remained of good counsels perished;
but greed grew and corrupt ambition, and the cunning of pretenders and flatterers prevailed;
Finally, with the strength of the empire broken, the vast and flourishing regions of Europe and Asia fell as prey to the barbarians.

And so, although it is understood that license, which is by no means to be tolerated, and pernicious attempts that overturn the foundations of the republic, must be altogether restrained, and that the monstrous passion for revolution must be suppressed;
and to letters of any kind and to talents laboring in any discipline, so that kingdoms do not perish along with the enfeebled strength of minds, a just freedom is granted:
especially since what is true and what is false must be demonstrated by reason and arguments, not established by power and decrees.
And in this most serious matter, what influence customs have can now be said in a few words.

For when in former times even among more civilized peoples punishment had been inflicted with the most bitter and capital penalties upon those whom the magistrates had often judged by the most foolish decisions to have committed offenses, since not only heretics and those accused of impiety, whose vengeance was to be committed to God as avenger rather than to mortals, but also enchanters and magicians, who never existed at all, were condemned to the fire:
Thus, as humanity and a certain simple wisdom were gradually disseminated, with manners softened, deeds that were once deemed worthy of impartial judges were now called abominable crimes.

The number of those madmen gradually diminished, who thought that one must attack established beliefs and opinions with chains and iron, and that whatever of others' opinions on any matter of greater importance displeased them should be dragged to punishment.
Finally, this moderation, common to almost all, overcame the laws and the princes, who are for the ancients the living and animated laws.
Thus liberty grew with customs, which is truly Christian.

For it is no more true that the tyrant, in order that no noble and manly spirit might arise in any citizen, by abolishing gymnasia and military exercises, wished to effeminate the young generation, ordered the boys to let their hair grow like virgins, to adorn it with flowers, to curl it in ringlets, and to gather it into knots, to let variegated robes fall to the ankles, to be led by female pedagogues carrying fans and parasols to dancing schools, to the flute-players, and to the baths, where, after being anointed with ointments, they were to be adorned before a mirror.
This was gradually accomplished not so much by weakening bodies as by enervating and dulling minds, as the Roman Empire declined in both respects.
Indeed, even that age did not lack brilliant talents;
but to avoid envy, they hid at home, not without public detriment:
virtue and honor and whatever remained of good counsels perished;
but greed grew and base ambition, and the cunning of pretenders and flatterers prevailed;
Finally, with the strength of the empire broken, the vast and flourishing regions of Europe and Asia fell as prey to the barbarians.

And in this very serious matter, what influence customs have can now be said in a few words.

For when in former times even among more civilized peoples punishment had been inflicted with the most bitter and capital penalties upon those whom the magistrates had often judged by the most foolish courts to have committed crimes, namely not only upon heretics and those accused of impiety, whose vengeance was to be committed rather to God as avenger than to mortals, but also upon enchanters and magicians, who never existed at all, condemned to the fire:
Thus, as humanity and a certain simple wisdom were gradually disseminated, and manners were softened, deeds that were once deemed worthy of impartial judges were now called abominable crimes.

The number of those madmen gradually diminished, who judged that one must attack with chains and iron against established beliefs and opinions, and that whatever of others' opinions on any matter of greater importance displeased them should be dragged to punishment.
Finally, this moderation, common to almost all, overcame the laws and the princes, who, according to the ancient arbiters, are living and animated laws.
Thus liberty grew with customs, which is truly Christian;
For our most holy religion demands no other servitude, any more than civil servitude.
These customs, this moderation among us was confirmed by him who confirmed the kingdom, Frederick the Great;
These Frederick William does not disapprove, commanding himself as much as his own people.
The immortal name of Greek and Latin literature reminds me.

It is well known that Frederick, when advanced in age, ordered that the classical Greek and Latin authors, by whose aid learning and the arts had been restored, and who from the revival of intellectual culture had served scholastic instruction, should be treated in the gymnasia with greater diligence and in such a way especially that not only the words of the writers should be committed to memory, but also that minds should be imbued with the matter, the sentiments, the doctrine contained in them, and with the method and system of discourse which they had set forth for subsequent ages.

Nempe ille quum libera cogitatione uti suos vellet, qua sola duce inveterati errores et prava generis cuiuslibet instituta corrigi possunt, rectissime haec antiqua et communia generi humano bona probavit, non modo quod imprimis perfecta sunt, sed quod, quid bonum, quid fugiendum sit, virtutes et vitia, populorum et principum res gestas, quibus illi magnitudinem et gloriam vel decrementa et postremo interitum sibi pararunt, integro ex illis iudicio cognoscere licet, non illo occupato praeceptis sententiis, intempestivis studiis, metu odiisque et cupiditatibus, quas praesens quoque aevo et in quaque civitate rerum status excitare solet.

But if the tender minds of the pupils cannot derive this utility from it, at least a certain form is impressed even on the unwilling, and men, attracted by the excellence of the best models, will retain what as boys they began to love, and the exercises of youth will prelude the counsels of a riper age.

Since the wisest men, who preside over public education in this kingdom, perceive this, under the auspices of Frederick William the most ancient institution of scholastic discipline flourishes, although the more inexperienced, who estimate every matter by the weight of silver that redounds from it to the state and to private individuals, may wish it to be abolished or diminished.
But do you think that the learning of literary universities ought to be less liberal?
But these were established for the formation of public ministries, and are maintained for this purpose.
I hear it, but I am not persuaded.
Not yet at that time, when the universities were being born, had a fixed order of officials, in a certain way separated from other men, been established;

And indeed the state may rightly demand that our discipline send forth pupils who can at some time sustain the duties of the republic, because our most holy religion demands this service more than any other civil service.
These customs, this moderation among us was confirmed by him who confirmed the kingdom, Frederick the Great;
These Frederick William does not disapprove, ruling himself as much as his own people.
The immortal name of Greek and Latin literature reminds me.

It is well known that Frederick, when advanced in age, ordered that the classical Greek and Latin authors, by whose aid learning and the arts had been restored, and who, from the revival of intellectual culture, had served scholastic instruction, should be treated in the gymnasia with greater diligence and in such a way especially that not only the words of the writers should be committed to memory, but also that minds should be imbued with the matter, the sentiments, and the learning contained in them, by the method and system of discourse which they had set forth for subsequent ages.

Indeed, when he wished to use free thought, by which alone as guide inveterate errors and the corrupt institutions of any kind can be corrected, he most rightly approved these ancient and common goods of the human race, not only because they are especially perfect, but because from them one can learn with an unbiased judgment what is good, what is to be avoided, virtues and vices, the deeds of peoples and princes, by which they procured for themselves greatness and glory or declines and finally destruction, not with that judgment preoccupied by precepts and opinions, untimely pursuits, fears, hatreds, and desires, which the present age and the state of affairs in every state is wont to excite.

But if the tender minds of the students cannot derive this benefit from it, certainly a certain form is impressed even upon the unknowing, and men, attracted by the excellence of the best models, will retain what as boys they began to love, and the exercises of youth will foreshadow the counsels of a more mature age.

But do you think that the learning of universities ought to be less liberal?
But these were established for the purpose of forming public ministries, and are maintained for this use.
I hear it, but I am not persuaded.
Not yet then, when the universities were being born, had a certain order of officials, separated in a way from other men, been established;

And indeed the state can rightly demand that our discipline send forth students who may at some time be able to sustain the duties of the republic, because those will be equal to this task who are intelligent in every kind of literature, and states are governed by reason and understanding:
Moreover, the learned and wise seek and teach the truth, which is at once good and useful, and together with this they inspire love of country, without which nothing in the world remains sound.
But the truth, which we seek, is one; error is manifold.

I think that the truth cannot be one thing in Spain, another in Britain, another in Germany, but only according to the nature of the climate and the character of the peoples is one nation more prone than another to a certain corruption of morals and other errors at a particular time.
Whose duty would it have been to meet these [errors], if not that of the learned?

In order to accomplish this more safely, they must take care that they do not allow themselves to be swept away by the waves of events or by any other force when they are about to cross, but that they hold well-fortified the lofty temples of learning, from which a view opens in every direction.

Where it is permitted to follow this path when teaching, and where moreover universities, which derive their very name from the fact that they are colleges or bodies governing their own affairs by fixed laws, are not deprived of the rights that belong to them, nor are governed too strictly or more severely than is right, but moderately and benevolently by those whom the prince adds as curators and, as it were, guardians, there true academic freedom seems to me to be preserved.

By this is also comprehended that, since equals are to be judged by equals, and equals are not indeed in skill and age, in which it is fitting that the judge excel, but in place and rank, teachers distinguished in learning are for studious youths, the governance of morals and the judgments which pertain to morals are exercised by the teachers.

For you yourselves know, my dearest fellow soldiers, that that liberty does not consist in the license of feasts and contests, nor in the tyranny of clubs, and your modesty and integrity have brought it about that, although the magistrates pay attention, scarcely any punishments have had to be employed for a long time.

If you continue this course vigorously, you will satisfy the wishes of the best king, and you will show that you feel gratitude toward him for such great benefits as he has conferred upon us all, not only in words but in your conduct.

Eandem gratiam universi et agimus et habemus Friderico Guilelmo, scholae nostrae statori et altori, qui non modo traditum a maioribus litterarum adiuvandarum studium retinet ac tuetur, sed illos longe superat munificentia et benignitate, ac per omnes provincias regni late propagati bonis artibus tam novas et florentissimas sedes condidit, quam vetustas lautius instruxit, neque institutionem publicam artioribus adstringit formulis, sed debitam tantum sacris legibusque reverentiam iniungit
pares erunt, qui intelligentes in quoque genere litterarum sint, et ratione atque intellectu gubernantur civitates:
Moreover, learned and wise men seek and teach the truth, which is at once good and useful, and together with it they inspire love of country, without which nothing in the world is sound.
But the truth, which we seek, is one; error is manifold.

I think that it cannot be that one thing is true in Spain, another in Britain, another in Germany, but only that, according to the nature of the climate and the character of the peoples, one nation is more inclined than another to a certain corruption of morals and to other errors at a certain period.
Whose duty was it to meet these [errors], if not that of the learned?

In order that they may accomplish this more safely, care must be taken that they do not allow themselves to be carried away by the waves of events or by any other force when they are about to cross, but that they hold well-fortified lofty temples of doctrine, from which a view opens in every direction.

Where it is permitted to follow this path when teaching, and where moreover universities, which derive their very name from the fact that they are colleges or bodies governing their own affairs by fixed laws, are not deprived of the rights that belong to them, nor are governed too strictly or more severely than is right, but moderately and benevolently by those whom the prince adds as curators and, as it were, guardians, there true academic freedom seems to me to be preserved.

By this is also included that, since equals are to be judged by equals, and equals are not indeed in skill and age, in which it is fitting that the judge excels, but in place and rank, teachers distinguished in learning are for studious young men, the governance of morals and the judgments which pertain to morals are exercised by the teachers.

For you yourselves know, my dearest fellow soldiers, that that liberty does not consist in the license of carousals and contests, nor in the tyranny of clubs, and your moderation and integrity have brought it about that, although the magistrates are attentive, scarcely any punishments have had to be employed for a long time.

If you continue this journey vigorously, you will satisfy the wishes of the best king, and you will show that you have gratitude to him for such great benefits as he has conferred upon us all, not only in words but in your conduct.

We both express and feel the same gratitude to Frederick William, the founder and nourisher of our school, who not only maintains and protects the zeal for supporting literature handed down from our ancestors, but far surpasses them in munificence and kindness, and throughout all the provinces of his widely extended kingdom has established for the good arts abodes as new and flourishing as antiquity furnished more sumptuously, nor does he confine public instruction within narrower formulas, but only enjoins upon teachers the reverence due to sacred things and laws.
May what Frederick William most desires happen to this republic, lasting peace and tranquility, and may this strengthen the state, not weaken it;

May the gentleness of government, by which Frederick William won for himself reverence and love, while the authority of the laws remains strong and the power of the empire intact, bring to completion the happiness of the people, toward which the most benevolent King has been accustomed to direct his counsels alone, and may virtue and faith, charity and concord, which are more powerful than any power, strengthen this kingdom and defend it from every danger.
Finally, we utter the most sacred vows, that Frederick William with the whole Augustan house may be preserved by divine power, safe, sound, and unharmed.
while they teach.
Would that what Frederick William most desires, that may happen to this republic, lasting peace and tranquility, and may it strengthen this state, not weaken it;

May the gentleness of government, by which Frederick William won for himself veneration and love, while the authority of the laws remains strong and the power of the empire intact, bring to completion the happiness of the people, toward which the most benevolent King has been accustomed to direct his counsels alone, and may virtue and faith, charity and concord, which are more powerful than any power, strengthen this kingdom and defend it from every danger.
Finally, we make the most sacred vows, that Frederick William, with the entire Augustan house, may be preserved safe, sound, and unharmed by divine power.

div.head: XXI. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXXIII. habita.

p.s: You have gathered together with me, listeners, so that, just as today not only throughout this entire city, but through all provinces and all cities, towns, and fields of the empire widely extending, joyful celebrations are conducted by the citizens, so in this place you might be participants and witnesses of that piety with which our literary republic, founded and flourishing under the auspices of Frederick William, would honor its founder and preserver.

For indeed we, if anyone else, ought not only to feel gratitude toward the most gracious Prince, but there are also many reasons why we should publicly declare with what feelings our hearts are filled.

Among these, this is not the least, that for some years now discord has been more and more nourished and spread, which threatens to break the pleasant and useful alliance of princes and peoples, and that this very discord is thought to have taken root especially in the literary universities.
But if I consider how great vicissitudes we have seen from that time, when our school was founded by the distinguished institutions of Frederick William;

The span of a few years seems to enclose such great floods and outcomes of events and such headlong successions of very different plans and wills, that you would believe the world to be moved and to run with an accelerated impetus, and even he who has not been pressed by any Epimenidean sleep cannot find his little sheep.
Hastening time in so short a span administers so much experience of things, that we seem to be born gray like Cycnus and Tarchon.
We who first saw the state afflicted by a disastrous war and, as it were, sent under the yoke:
but in the greatest calamity, the constancy of the most beloved King and the agreement of the Prince and the people consoled every best man, who had together decided either to stand or to perish:
Never was mutual love kindled by sharper goads;
never was the whole republic held together by firmer bonds of faith and love:

Therefore, the more these words of veneration and piety, spoken and acclaimed to the best King, displeased the foreign master full of suspicions, the more gladly and intently they were spoken and acclaimed.
Soon, with minds and strength strengthened through adversity, the King conquered with his allies, and not only restored the empire, but also increased it;
From the fields stained with blood, a most joyful harvest of good things came forth;
Glory was followed by security, wealth, public and private prosperity;
Nor did our state alone enjoy tranquility and concord, but the Germans as a whole agreed among themselves and with us.
But since the human race is prone to excess, not all endured moderate happiness for long.
From those who pursue vain things, the torches of disturbances were kindled and thrown.
Already the present hour's fruit is not allowed us to enjoy without cares, because evil hope, while from every side, like a sword over the head, some fear of the future hangs over us.

Yet in this revolution of affairs, which, even if for a while the force of the disease has either spontaneously abated or has been repressed, can seem to no one except the improvident to be slight or hardly worthy of mention, the Prussian state stood safe, the faith of the people safe, the love of the Prince safe:
The times have changed; we have not changed in them:

And with the same ardor with which we especially venerated the name of Frederick William in the solemnities celebrated in this hall, with that same ardor today we pray to the supreme deity that he may bestow upon that excellent soul all those goods by which mortals can be blessed and the minds of rulers can be refreshed.

These vows I pour forth on behalf of all of you, I who, not so much an orator as an interpreter and herald of your feelings, stationed publicly on this platform every year, seem to myself to have looked deeply into the virtues of Frederick William and to have embraced them in manifold thought.
You would believe, and even one who had not been oppressed by any Epimenidean sleep, that he could not find his own little sheep.
Haste, shortening life, supplies experience of many things in a brief time, so that we seem to have been born old, like Cycnus and Tarchon.
We who first saw the state afflicted by a disastrous war and, in a manner, sent under the yoke:

But in the greatest calamity, every good man was consoled by the constancy of the most beloved King and the agreement of the Prince and the people, who had together decided either to stand or to perish:
Never was mutual love kindled by sharper goads;
Never was the whole commonwealth held together by firmer bonds of loyalty and love:
The more these words of veneration and piety, spoken and acclaimed to the best of kings, displeased the foreign master full of suspicions, the more gladly and intently they were spoken and acclaimed.
Soon, with spirits and strength strengthened through adversity, the King conquered with his allies, and not only restored the empire, but also increased it;
From the fields stained with blood, a most joyful harvest of good things springs forth.
Glory was followed by security, wealth, and public and private prosperity.
Nor did our state alone enjoy tranquility and concord, but the Germans as a whole agreed among themselves and with us.
But since the human race is prone to excess, not all endured moderate happiness for long.
From those who pursue vain things, the torches of disturbances were kindled and thrown.
Now the evil hope does not allow us to enjoy the fruit of the present hour without cares, while from every side, like a sword over the head, some fear of the future hangs over us.

Yet in this turning of affairs, which, even if for a while the force of the disease has either relaxed by itself or has been checked, cannot seem to anyone but the imprudent to be light or of little account, the Prussian state has remained safe, the faith of the people safe, the love of the Prince safe:
The times have changed; we have not changed with them.

And with the same ardor with which we especially venerated the name of Frederick William in the solemnities celebrated in this hall, with that same ardor today we pray to the supreme deity that he may bestow upon that excellent soul all those goods by which mortals can be blessed and the minds of rulers can be refreshed.

These vows I pour forth on behalf of you all, I who, not so much an orator as an interpreter and herald of your feelings, stationed publicly on this platform every year, seem to myself to have looked into the virtues of Frederick William from within and to have embraced them with manifold thought.

Now after I have already announced at the very threshold of my speech what you, my listeners, most expected from me, it will be permissible to digress a little from the present subject, so that at the end I may return to the point from which I began.
Yet I will not entirely digress from my purpose.
Indeed, the discord with which the world is now troubled has arisen more from an agitation of minds than from any other somewhat greater cause.
And it is an evil, but an evil admitted by providence, which from the very evils brings forth good things:
By this one consolation is the grief assuaged which less favorable events bring.
I shall say nothing new, nothing recondite, nothing more distinguished either in the richness of learning or in the weight or subtlety of thoughts:
That whatever mortals have done and performed, has been done and performed for the most part through struggles, the memory of nearly all things reminds us.

For as it pleased Empedocles of Agrigentum that the nature of things is moved by these two principles, discord and friendship, and as Heraclitus of Ephesus attributed to all things a resisting union of bow and lyre and a harmony from dissonant elements, and without opposites there is no composition and generation:
so contention stirs and nourishes human affairs, lest they fall apart through idleness and sloth, and thus the outcome is prepared, which has been established by divine will.

This is especially what poetry sketches out, which Aristotle rightly judges to be more philosophical and more excellent than history, because the former presents universal truths, the latter particular facts;

Therefore, when in tragedy, that mirror of a more severe life, it accomplishes and brings to its conclusion any more serious action, not without discord of the parts, which entangles the characters in very many difficulties and dangers, it shows generally, although in individual plays, from what elements human life and fortune are composed.

And, as it is fitting that the learned should attend to this above all, although the powers of the mind, in the highest harmony which nature has formed, nevertheless diverge into different directions, and impel those in whom this or that power prevails to embrace various sects of life and studies;

These very varied studies, although they all proceed from the same source and express in different forms one and the same divine reason of the human mind, are nevertheless separated and dissociated and fight among themselves, until at last they are reconciled more perfectly.
Indeed, the most ancient cognitions of the human mind, in which truly something divine was inherent, were concerned with the consciousness of the supreme deity, which we call religion;
From this source especially flowed the most ancient civil institutions, from this the arts and sciences, of which philosophy is the chief.
But when religion had formed the names, figures, and natures of the gods, and had taught that they had done and suffered those things which are contained in mythical doctrines and narratives;
Soon after came the philosophers, who, on those very primitive notions, ...
Nor, however, will I depart entirely from my purpose.
Indeed, the discord with which the world is now troubled has arisen more from the agitation of minds than from any other cause, and that to a somewhat greater degree.
And it is an evil, but an evil admitted by providence, which brings good out of the evils themselves.
By this one consolation the grief is alleviated, which the less favorable circumstances bring.
I shall say nothing new, nothing recondite, nothing more distinguished either in the richness of learning or in the weight or subtlety of thoughts:
The memory of almost all things warns that whatever mortals have done and accomplished has been done and accomplished to a great extent through contests.

For just as it pleased Empedocles of Agrigentum that the nature of things is moved by these two principles, discord and friendship, and Heraclitus of Ephesus attributed to all things a resisting union of bow and lyre and a concord from dissonants, and without opposites there is no composition and generation:
Thus contention stirs and nourishes human affairs, so that they do not fall apart through sluggishness and indolence, and thus the outcome is prepared, which has been established by divine will.
Poetry especially sketches this, which Aristotle rightly judges to be more philosophical and more excellent than history, because that presents universals, this particulars;

Therefore, when in tragedy, the mirror of a more severe life, it accomplishes and brings to an end any more serious action, not without discord of the parts, which entangles the characters in very many difficulties and dangers, it shows generally, although in individual plays, from what elements human life and fate are composed.

And, as it is fitting that the learned should attend to this above all others, although the powers of the mind, in the highest harmony which nature has formed, nevertheless diverge into different directions, and impel those in whom this or that power prevails to embrace the various sects of life and studies;

These very varied studies, although they all proceed from the same source and express in different forms one and the same divine reason of the human mind, are nevertheless separated and dissociated and fight among themselves, until at last they are reconciled more perfectly.
Indeed, the most ancient cognitions of the human mind, in which truly something divine was inherent, were concerned with the consciousness of the supreme deity, which we call religion;
From this source especially the most ancient civil institutions flowed, from this the arts and sciences, of which philosophy is the chief.
But when religion had formed the names, figures, and natures of the gods, and had taught that they had done and suffered those things which are contained in mythical doctrines and narratives,
Soon after came the philosophers, who, imbued with those very primitive notions and spurred on to discover higher things,

These men, using a purer reason, condemned mythology as a whole, and just as Jupiter deprived his father of power and bound him, they conquered the old discipline, while this, like Saturn devouring his offspring, in turn defeats those ethnic heretics with their own weapons.
This discord is as old as the cradle of philosophy.
Thus Heraclitus and Xenophanes judged Homer and Hesiod, the authors of divine tales, worthy of the greatest disgrace because of the things they had said badly about the gods;
And they say that Pythagoras reported that he had seen Homer and Hesiod paying the penalties in the underworld for the stories they had handed down.
Thus Plato expels Homer from his most perfect republic, and rejects all those little stories about the gods, whether changed into human form or affected with mortal habits.

Finally, this division recurs in almost every age, because priestly discipline wishes to rest on what has been handed down and rejects novelty by its own right, while science dares to know beyond what has been handed down and to trust common judgment:

until after the troublesome controversies of many centuries both sides have reached the point that the teachings of neither are understood to be entirely contrary to the other, but both theology recalls its own doctrines to the principles of science, and philosophy not only concedes but demonstrates that the forms in which the consciousness of the divine power has been comprehended in religions are necessary and have proceeded from the divinity of the mind itself:
This agreement seems to be gradually brought about from our age onward.
But what about the arts?
Were not sculptors and painters driven by divine inspiration to express, through visible images, that one and hidden thing which our ancestors beheld only with reverence?
Was not the whole chorus of arts from the beginning devoted to the ceremonies and worship of the gods?
Was not music also, and all poetry, filled with divine spirit, celebrating and adorning sacred rites from their very origins?

But what formerly conspired uniquely, religion and the arts, were afterwards more than once so divided that images were broken, and nothing seemed more wicked than statues and scenic performances, finally so that actors, as if impious, were excluded from participation in sacred rites and burial.

Now, although these and similar matters have been agitated with the greatest effort in the past, how few are there among priests or theologians who are hostile to painted tablets, or who think that theaters, even in this decline of scenic poetry, are the abodes and workshops of evil demons?
Even greater dissensions between the priests of the sacred rites and the rulers of states had arisen quite early, and they were imbued with them and spurred on to discover higher things.

These, using a purer reason, condemned the whole mythology, and just as Jupiter deprived his father of power and bound him, they conquered the old discipline, while this, like Saturn devouring his offspring, defeats those ethnic heretics in turn with their own arms.
