This discord is as old as the very cradle of philosophy.
Thus Heraclitus and Xenophanes judged Homer and Hesiod, the authors of divine fables, worthy of the greatest disgrace for the things they had said badly about the gods.
And they say that Pythagoras reported that he had seen Homer and Hesiod paying the penalties in the underworld for the stories they had handed down.
Thus Plato expels Homer from his most perfect republic, and rejects all those little stories about the gods, whether changed into human form or affected with mortal habits.

Finally, this division recurs in almost every age, because priestly discipline wishes to stand firm in what has been handed down and rejects novelty by its own right, while science dares to know beyond what has been handed down and to trust common judgment:

until after the troublesome controversies of many centuries both sides have reached the point that the precepts of neither are understood to be entirely contrary to the other, but both theology recalls its teachings to the principles of science, and philosophy not only concedes but demonstrates that the forms in which the consciousness of the divine power has been comprehended in religions are necessary and derived from the divinity of the mind itself:
which agreement seems to be gradually brought about from our age onward.
But what of the arts?
Were not the sculptors and painters, by divine inspiration, impelled to express that one and hidden thing through visible images, which our ancestors beheld only with reverence?
Did not the whole chorus of arts from the beginning serve the ceremonies and worship of the gods?
Did not music also and all poetry, filled with divine spirit, celebrate and adorn the sacred rites from their very origins?

But what formerly conspired uniquely, religion and the arts, were afterwards more than once so divided that images were broken, and nothing seemed more wicked than statues and scenic performances, finally so that actors, as if impious, were excluded from participation in sacred rites and burial.

Now, although these and similar matters were once debated with the utmost effort, how few are the priests or theologians who are hostile to painted panels, or who think that theaters, even in this decline of dramatic poetry, are the abodes and workshops of evil demons?
Even greater quarrels arose quite early between the priests of the sacred rites and the rulers of the states.

For already in the heroic age of the Greeks, in which nevertheless the minds of men were wholly bound by the bonds of religion, such as it was, and scarcely any somewhat more brilliant civil wisdom had yet emerged, the king accuses the augur of ambition, falsehood, and fraud, and the augur accuses the king of contempt of the gods, pride, and tyranny:

And although the Christian faith may seem to have set the boundaries of both parties with more inward and certain limits, the more sacred that faith was and the greater the papal power became, the more fiercely the conflict blazed up, which was not even extinguished by wars waged to the point of extermination, but is even now nourished openly or secretly in many lands of Europe:
Although the reform of the sacred rites, begun in the fourth century before our era and accomplished not without bloodshed, was a prelude to the firm peace that posterity will enjoy.

Moreover, the political science, just as it comes into conflict with the priests, so also with those who devote themselves to the knowledge of a more recondite and abstruse philosophy, although that same reason, which the lovers of wisdom seek, seems to permeate the state in a somewhat more perfect way, since, as is professed by the philosophers themselves, a man not moderately skilled in public affairs, M., ...

Tullius says that law, that rule by which states are governed, is the highest reason implanted in nature and established and perfected in the human mind, which should command the things that ought to be done and forbid their opposites.
And yet, to say nothing of the desires and party interests by which the powerful are sometimes carried away, whether they are princes or leaders of factions:

As all human things are corrupted, a law is not infrequently passed according to the advantage of the powerful, and that pernicious opinion of some sophist, that the just is what is useful to the stronger, is confirmed by long experience of events.
And although Machiavelli, by no means the last among the prudent, may have proved this, yet it is impious for a wise man to approve it.

And those who conduct public affairs necessarily plunge themselves into the immense floods of individual matters, and, tossed about by them, they generally become dull for the contemplation of universal notions, just as those among the learned who are especially engaged in investigating particular things are accustomed to be drawn away from the understanding of those same notions:
on the contrary, philosophers in any matter pursue that general thing, which they call the idea, being sometimes less skilled in individual things than they ought to be.
And likewise those people readily acquiesce in the present state of affairs, whatever the time, and strive to preserve it as much as possible or to correct it by slow progress:
These, often neglecting what is placed before their eyes — a fault for which Thales is reproached — are intent on the more perfect future state of the human race.

For even in the heroic age of the Greeks, when nevertheless the minds of men were wholly bound by the bonds of religion, such as it was, and scarcely any more brilliant civil wisdom had yet emerged, the king accuses the augur of ambition, falsehood, and fraud, and the augur accuses the king of contempt of the gods, pride, and tyranny:

And although the Christian faith may seem to have set the boundaries of both parties with more inward and certain limits, the more sacred that faith was and the greater the papal power, the more fiercely the conflict blazed up, which was not even extinguished by wars waged to the point of annihilation, but is even now nourished openly or secretly in many lands of Europe:
Although the reform of the sacred rites, begun in the fourth century earlier and accomplished not without bloodshed, was a prelude to the firm peace which posterity will enjoy.

Moreover, civil discipline, just as it comes into conflict with priests, so also with those who devote themselves to the knowledge of a more recondite and abstruse philosophy, although that same reason, which the students of wisdom seek, seems to permeate the state in a somewhat more perfect way, since, as a man not moderately skilled in public affairs declares on the authority of the philosophers themselves, M.

Tully, that law by which states are governed, is the highest reason implanted in nature and established and perfected in the human mind, which commands the things that are to be done and forbids the contrary.
And yet, to say nothing of the desires and party interests, by which the powerful are sometimes driven off course, whether they are princes or leaders of factions:

As all human affairs are corrupted, a law is not infrequently passed according to the advantage of the powerful, and that pernicious opinion of some sophist, that the just is what is useful to the stronger, is confirmed by long experience of things.
Although Machiavelli, by no means the last among the prudent, may have proved this, yet it is impious for a wise man to approve it.

And those who conduct public affairs necessarily plunge themselves into the immense floods of individual matters, and being tossed about by them, they generally become dull for the contemplation of universal notions, just as those among the learned who are especially engaged in investigating individual things are accustomed to be called away from the understanding of those same notions:
on the contrary, philosophers in any matter pursue that general thing, which they call the idea, being sometimes less skilled in individual things than they ought to be.
And likewise those people easily acquiesce in the present state of affairs, whatever the time, and strive to preserve it as much as possible, or to correct it by slow progress:

These people, often neglecting what is placed before their eyes (which is reproached against Thales), occupy themselves with a more distant thought about the future, more perfect condition of the human race, and, as if by divination, anticipate it.
Now there is enough of reasons why the one party resists the other.

Therefore, the one example we know of perfect harmony between philosophy and politics, namely the power of the Pythagorean society in Italy, we see passed away in a short time, because turbulent men had stirred up the common people against those most holy and most wise men and had burned down the meeting-houses of the Pythagoreans.

At Athens, indeed, when the discipline of morals first began to be treated more subtly by the philosophers, the wise men censured the rule of the people as imprudent, inconstant, and tyrannical; and, on the other hand, men hostile to them who were conducting the state, such as that Anytus was, kept shouting that the youth were being corrupted by the philosophers, inasmuch as they were calling them away from respect for popular government:

Nor was there any other cause so deep-seated why the leader and founder of Attic philosophy was condemned, than that he had had Critias and Alcibiades, most eager for revolutionary changes, as disciples and followers.

Soon Plato exaggerated the incompatibility of public affairs and knowledge to such an extent that he said that those who from youth had been occupied in courts and around the forum were compared, as slaves to free men, with those who had been educated in philosophy and studies of this kind.
so that he thought that these, from their earliest age, did not even know the way to the forum, nor where a court or council or any other public assembly of the state was held;

But they say that they have neither heard nor seen the laws and decrees, whether spoken or written, and that they do not even in their dreams think about bribery and conspiracies for creating magistrates and about forming clubs, but that in reality only their bodies dwell in the state, while their minds, deeming all those things trivial or worthless, are occupied with higher thoughts.

at civiles istos et causidicos acerrimos, qui rideant philosophi imperitiam, ubi quis eos ad supera erigere tentasset, aut ipsi digrederentur a tali quaestione, „Quid tibi ego iniuriae feci aut tu mihi?" ut inquirerent, quid esset iustitia et iniustitia ipsa, et quid hae a sese et ab aliis notionibus omnibus differrent, aut si a sententia hacce, „Beatus est rex multum possidens auri", ad quaestiones de regni natura et de humana felicitate et miseria generatim considerandas transissent;

Therefore, when they ought to render an account of these matters, they are seized with dizziness as if placed on a high watchtower, from which they are not accustomed to look out, and, being at a loss for counsel and taking it ill, they utter barbarous words.
After this, because philosophers, with their thought projected further ahead, occupy, as it were, a royal command, and, as if by divination, they prescribe a tempered condition.
Now there is enough of reasons why the one party resists the other.

Therefore, the one example we know of absolute harmony between philosophy and politics, the power of the Pythagorean society in Italy, we see passed away in a short time, because turbulent men had stirred up the people against those most holy and most wise men and had burned down the meeting-houses of the Pythagoreans.

At Athens, indeed, when the discipline of morals first began to be treated more carefully by the philosophers, the wise men reproved the rule of the people as imprudent, inconstant, and tyrannical; and, on the other hand, men hostile to them who were conducting public affairs, such as that Anytus was, kept shouting that the youth were being corrupted by the philosophers, inasmuch as they were calling them away from respect for popular government:

Nor was there any other so intimate cause why the leader and founder of Attic philosophy was condemned, than that he had had Critias and Alcibiades, most eager for new things, as disciples and followers.

Soon Plato exaggerated the incompatibility of public affairs and knowledge to such an extent that he said that those who from youth had been occupied in courts and around the forum were compared to those who had been educated in philosophy and studies of this kind, as slaves to free men.
so that he thought that these, from the beginning of life, did not even know the way to the forum, nor where a court or assembly or any other public meeting of the state was held.

But they say that they have neither heard nor seen the laws and decrees, whether spoken or written, and that they do not even in their dreams think about bribery and conspiracies for creating magistrates and about forming clubs, but that in reality only their bodies dwell in the state, while their minds, deeming all those things trivial or of no account, are occupied with higher thoughts:

But those most keen civil lawyers and advocates, who might laugh at the philosophers' lack of skill, if anyone had tried to raise them to higher things, would either themselves depart from such a question, "What wrong have I done to you, or you to me?" to inquire what justice and injustice itself were, and how these differed from each other and from all other notions, or if they had passed from this saying, "Blessed is the king who possesses much gold," to questions about the nature of a kingdom and about human happiness and misery considered generally;

Therefore, when they ought to render an account of these matters, they were seized with dizziness as if placed on a high watchtower, from which they were not accustomed to look out, and being at a loss for counsel and taking it ill, they uttered barbarous words.
Afterwards, because the philosophers approved almost exclusively a kingly rule, tempered indeed and liberal, they were harassed by many dangers;
after the death of Alexander the Great, Aristotle himself, accused of impiety, left the city;

Theophrastus, when he was accused by Hagnonides, pleaded the same cause, indeed, more successfully; but afterwards he too was forced to withdraw for a short time, when Sophocles, son of Amphiclides, had carried a law that no one should preside over a school of philosophers unless it had pleased the Senate and the People.
Whoever did otherwise, it was a capital offense.
By this decree all philosophers seem to have been driven from Athens, until a year later, when the law was repealed and Sophocles was fined, permission to return was granted.

At Rome too we have learned that in the sixth century of the city, after words had been spoken about philosophers and rhetoricians, the Senate so decreed that the Praetor should take heed and see to it, as seemed to him to be in the interest of the state and consistent with his good faith, that they should not be at Rome.

Why should I mention Domitian, who banished the teachers of wisdom and all philosophers from the city and from Italy, as Tiberius once banished actors, and, as Tacitus says, drove every good art into exile, and that because of the praises alone that were bestowed upon Paetus Thrasea and Priscus Helvidius by Arulenus Rusticus and Herennius Senecio?
What of the fact that under the Emperor Justinian the pagan philosophers had to seek refuge in Persia?

And so we see that philosophers were hated by those in power for very different reasons, sometimes because they favored the rule of the best, sometimes because they favored royal power, sometimes because they favored ancient institutions and ceremonies.
But in our age this discord has almost become obsolete:
gradually many things that the wise have taught have been received into the laws themselves:
it is agreed that the state ought to be illuminated by the lights of knowledge;

And the learned understand that their own discipline ought not to be opposed to the public one, but that by both, morals are to be corrected, the misery of mortals is to be alleviated, the darkness of error is to be dispelled, and finally a more perfect state of the human race is to be brought about.

But if men have not yet attained that which, in Plato's judgment, is the highest good, namely that either philosophers should rule or rulers should philosophize, nevertheless the two are not even now separated by so great an interval as then, when it was difficult for that man not to write a satire against the state.
But you would wonder more at the fact that knowledge did not even maintain a perpetual harmony with the arts, than at what I have so far set forth.

Indeed, that does not seem to have been accidental, that he who was almost the first to turn his mind from the contemplation of natural things to the mind itself, was a sculptor, himself indeed like Silenus, but not displeasing to the Graces, whom he is said to have fashioned with extraordinary beauty:
but he repented of his art and of the Graces expressed in marble, indeed and liberal, they approved uniquely, having been afflicted with many dangers;
After the death of Alexander the Great, Aristotle himself, accused of impiety, left the city.

Theophrastus, indeed, when accused by Hagnonides, pleaded the same case more successfully, but afterwards he too was forced to withdraw for a short time, when Sophocles, son of Amphiclides, had carried a law that no one should preside over a school of philosophers unless it pleased the Senate and the People.
Whoever should do otherwise, it was a capital offense.
By this decree all philosophers seem to have been banished from Athens, until a year later, after the law was repealed and Sophocles was punished, the right of return was granted.

At Rome too we learn that, at the end of the sixth century of the city, after speeches were made about philosophers and rhetoricians, the Senate so decreed that the Praetor should take heed and see to it, as seemed to him in accordance with the public interest and his own good faith, that they should not be in Rome.

What shall I say of Domitian, who banished the professors of wisdom and all philosophers from the city and Italy, as Tiberius once did the actors, and, as Tacitus says, drove every good art into exile, and that on account of the praises alone bestowed upon Paetus Thrasea and Priscus Helvidius by Arulenus Rusticus and Herennius Senecio?
What of the fact that under the Emperor Justinian the pagan philosophers had to seek refuge in Persia?

And so we see that philosophers were hated by those in power for the most diverse reasons, sometimes because they favored the rule of the best, sometimes because they favored royal power, sometimes because they favored ancient institutions and ceremonies.
But in our age this discord has almost become obsolete:
gradually many things that the wise have taught have been received into the laws themselves:
it is agreed that the state ought to be illuminated by the lights of knowledge;

And the learned understand that their own discipline ought not to be opposed to the public one, but that by both, morals are to be corrected, the misery of mortals is to be alleviated, the darkness of error is to be dispelled, and finally a more perfect state of the human race is to be brought about.

But if men have not yet attained that which, in Plato's judgment, is the highest—that either philosophers should rule or rulers should philosophize—still the two are not even now separated by as great an interval as then, when it was difficult for that man not to write a satire against the state.
But you would wonder more at the fact that science did not even maintain a perpetual harmony with the arts, than at what I have so far set forth.

Indeed, that does not seem to have been accidental, that he who was almost the first to turn the mind from the contemplation of natural things to the mind itself, was a sculptor, himself indeed like Silenus, but not unpleasing to the Graces, whom he is said to have fashioned with extraordinary beauty:
but he regretted his art and the Graces expressed in marble, because he preferred to look upon the inner Graces of the human mind.
And his student, by far the most outstanding in talent, experienced almost the same fate.

He, who was born in a certain sense for poetry, and while still quite young had practiced almost all the genres of this art, and had composed an epic poem, emulating Homer, as well as lyric poems and tragedies, is said soon to have burned the whole heap of his verses in fire, so that he might practice only the music of philosophy.

We see, then, that these people, for reasons not very different from those for which later certain Christian sects despised poetry and all imitative arts (and there is none that is not imitative), rejected them, as being those which would render and represent images of images, shadows of shadows, not pure and absolute notions of things and, if one may use a Ciceronian word, their essence.

And if Aristotle was less hostile to the arts, whose nature he tried to investigate like that of all other things, philosophy certainly afterwards, if not in express words, yet by its neglect, for a long time despised them, until in the previous century it embraced them when they were flourishing, though it had spurned them when they were declining and for the most part lying prostrate, and with a new name, however inconvenient, formed a new part of its discipline, which would be entirely concerned with establishing the principles of the arts.

Thus this separation also was endured by the age, and it was understood that both art and science tend toward the same end, namely that in these fleeting and fragile forms of things, which fall under the senses, the traces of the divine mind may be recognized.
But indeed, just as the reason of the whole universe is seen expressed in its individual parts, as if in some smaller image of the world;

Thus we see that the same division which has obtained and to some extent still obtains among the most important kinds of studies to which the human mind applies itself is repeated within the very boundaries of those studies.

Therefore in no discipline have countless sects arisen, of which some attribute more to history, others to philosophy, others again to reason, others to faith or to some obscure sense of truth, and others to experience;
From all of which, amid manifest discord, a certain hidden harmony is brought together.
From all things one, and from one all things.

Finally, if the mind itself is by its own nature compelled to descend into these conflicts, why should not the necessities and desires urge on, by which the wars of peoples are inflamed, both foreign and domestic?
because he preferred to look upon the inner Graces of the human mind.
And his disciple, by far the most outstanding in talent, met with almost the same fate;

He, who was born, as it were, for poetry, and who, while still quite young, had practiced almost all the genres of this art, and had composed an epic poem, emulating Homer, and also lyric poems and tragedies, is said to have soon burned the whole heap of his verses in fire, so that he might practice only the music of philosophy.

We see, therefore, that these men, for reasons not unlike those for which later certain Christian sects despised poetry and all imitative arts (and there is no art that is not imitative), spurned them, as being those which would render and represent images of images, shadows of shadows, not pure and absolute notions of things and, if one may use a Ciceronian term, their essence.

And if Aristotle was less unfair to the arts, whose nature he tried to investigate like that of all other things, philosophy certainly afterwards, if not in express words, yet by its neglect, for a long time despised them, until in the previous century it embraced them when they were flourishing, though it had spurned them when they were in decline and for the most part lying prostrate, and with a new name, however inconvenient, formed a new part of its discipline, which was wholly concerned with establishing the principles of the arts.

Thus this age also endured this separation, and it was understood that both art and science tend toward the same end, so that in these fleeting and fragile forms of things, which fall under the senses, the traces of the divine mind may be recognized.
But indeed, just as the principle of the whole universe is seen expressed in its individual parts, as if in some smaller image of the world;

Thus we see that the same division which has obtained among the most important kinds of studies to which the human mind applies itself, and which to some extent still obtains, is repeated within the very boundaries of those studies.

Therefore in no discipline are there not innumerable sects born, of which some attribute more to history, others to philosophy, again others to reason, others to faith or to some obscure sense of truth, others to experience;
From all these, in the midst of manifest discord, a certain hidden harmony is brought together.
From all, one; and from one, all.

Finally, if the mind itself is compelled by its own nature to descend into these conflicts, why should not the necessities and desires, by which the wars of peoples are inflamed, both foreign and domestic, urge it on?
These things so far.
Now I will briefly finish what seems to remain to be said.
For God is free from error, evil, and discord.

Mortals must both endure evils and grieve, because something good must always be opposed to what is necessary, be moved by disturbances, experience joys and hardships and human weakness, so that they may come forth more approved and more purified from trials, err, so that error may be corrected, disagree, so that they may be seized by a so much more vehement desire for concord.
And these dissonant things must be brought together into a harmony:
The more men have accomplished this, the more they will be assimilated to God.
And indeed harmony is not brought about by removing and rooting out opposing forces, but by combining and tempering them.
Nor does the temperature of the sky come about by removing the cold or the hot, and again neither by the moist nor the dry;
Music itself, which especially strives for consonance, mixes contraries, the high and the low, the fast and the slow, and sometimes even admits dissonances, which it resolves:
Take away the dissimilar, and harmony itself is destroyed.

But in the state, the one who is at the head of the highest affairs is of all men the most suited to reconciling opposites, and he will be able to accomplish this more certainly, the greater the power with which he has been endowed.
If he, moreover, is utterly free from desire, he will also calm the desires of his subjects, not kindle them;
if he is provident and kind, he will consult the needs of the same people, so that not even a pretext is left for the instigators of revolution.
Who, therefore, could be a more desired governor of the republic in this age than Frederick William?
He shaped the people toward consensus, in which the highest virtue of the state is placed;
he, abhorring most far from all pride, by his own example also accustomed the citizens to moderation;
he provided for the comforts and fortunes of his subjects;

Here, in the common fatherland, as Pliny says of Pompey and Trajan, by his authority, counsel, and good faith, he opened up roads, restored routes to the lands, and mingled kindred peoples with commerce that had been forbidden for too long.
He, giving to each his own, also keeps those diverse spheres in which the studies of the human mind are engaged so composed in this kingdom that none stands out to the detriment of the rest.
Civil power does not oppress the church, nor does the church invade the duties of the state;
Neither the arts nor the sciences are neglected by the state, no formula is prescribed to those who teach, nor do the masters of knowledge cross their own boundaries;
In short, all arts and disciplines dwell together in harmony.
Let those states divide these, in which the church is separated from the state, and literature is separated from both:
among us they have grown together firmly;
we do not fear contamination.
But this moderation, spread throughout the entire state, is a pledge of lasting happiness.

Pride perishes by its own blows, and whatever excessively exalts itself is, by divine ordinance, always opposed by something good in the order of nature and of human affairs, to be disturbed by perturbations, to experience joys and sorrows and human weakness, so that they may come forth more approved and more purified from trials, to err, so that error may be corrected, to disagree, so that they may be seized by a so much more vehement desire for concord.
And these dissonant elements must be brought together into a harmony:
The more men have accomplished this, the more they will be assimilated to God.
And indeed harmony is not brought about by removing and eradicating opposing forces, but by combining and tempering them:
nor by removing the cold or the hot does the mildness of the sky come about, and again neither by the moist nor the dry;
music itself, which especially strives for consonance, mixes contraries, the high and the low, the swift and the slow, and admits even sometimes dissonances, which it may resolve:
Remove the dissimilar elements, and harmony itself will be sustained.

But in the state, the one who presides over the highest affairs is of all the most suited to reconciling opposites, and he will be able to accomplish this the more surely, the greater the power with which he has been endowed.
If he is moreover entirely free from desire, he will also calm the desires of his subjects, not kindle them;
If he is prudent and kind, he will consult the needs of the same people, so that not even a pretext is left for the instigators of new things.
Who, therefore, could be a more longed-for governor of the republic in this age than Frederick William?
He shaped the people into consensus, in which the highest virtue of the state is placed;
he, abhorring most far from all pride, by his own example also accustomed the citizens to moderation;
he provided for the comforts and fortunes of his subjects;

Here, in the common fatherland, as Pliny says of Pompey and Trajan, by his authority, counsel, and good faith, he opened up roads, restored routes to the lands, and united kindred peoples by commerce that had been forbidden for too long.
He, giving to each his own, also keeps those diverse spheres in which the pursuits of the human mind are engaged so composed in this kingdom that none stands out to the detriment of the rest.
Civil power does not oppress the church, nor does the church invade the duties of the state;
Neither are the arts and sciences neglected by the state, nor is a formula prescribed to those who teach, nor do the masters of knowledge cross their own boundaries;
In short, all arts and disciplines dwell together in harmony.
Let those states divide these, in which the church is separated from the state, and literature is separated from both:
among us they have grown together firmly;
we do not fear contamination.
But this moderation, spread throughout the whole state, is a pledge of lasting happiness;
pride perishes by its own blows, and whatever excessively exalts itself is sooner or later cast down from the order divinely established of nature and of human affairs, with a ruin the more fatal.
Seized by this pride, certain ambitious men have drawn away a part of the youth, which is wont to admire forbidden things and to lend an ear to corruptors;

She has forgotten that even in the freest states it was anciently established that young men, however liberally educated and treated, were nevertheless not allowed to mix freely in the conduct of public affairs, but were under the supervision of cosmetae, gymnasiarchs, and sophronistae.

She does not know that, as the writer most devoted to freedom has taught, obedience and modesty, if industry and vigor are present, attain to that praise which others have attained through precipitous paths, but have become famous through ambitious ruin, to no advantage of the state.
Since he said this about that age which had endured the most unjust masters, how much more truly will it be said about the most equitable and just kingdoms?
But who would defend and repel that disease with better counsels and a more favorable success than the serene and temperate mind of Frederick William?
To whom, without any suspicion of flattery, one may exclaim with the poet:
You truly are the most opportune physician, and Paean favors your fortune!
And so in the kindness, virtue, and wisdom of Frederick William this republic finds its rest;
From him and from his excellent counsels it has and expects whatever good things are attainable in this state of affairs and according to the resources and strength of this kingdom.

For him, with that love with which he himself embraces his own, with that piety which you all know to be in him, we again pray from the divine power a most prosperous course of his undertakings, and a long, vigorous old age, not saddened by any evil or any sickness;

We, bound even by his benefits, are obliged to him with the highest religious reverence, and we, reverently, desire and pray again and again that in his grace and favor a perpetual and most firm protection may be placed for this school founded by him.
Once established, sooner or later it is cast down with a ruin all the more deadly.
With this pride now seized, certain ambitious men have drawn away a part of the youth, which is wont to admire forbidden things and to lend an ear to corruptors;

She has forgotten that even in the freest states it was anciently established that young men, however liberally educated and treated, were nevertheless not allowed to mix freely in the conduct of public affairs, but were under the supervision of cosmetae, gymnasiarchs, and sophronistae.

It does not know that, as the writer most devoted to freedom has taught, obedience and modesty, if industry and vigor are present, reach that height of praise to which others have become famous through precipitous paths, but with ambitious ruin that is of no use to the state.
Since he said this about that age which had endured the most unjust masters, how much more truly will it be said about the most equitable and just kingdoms?
But who could defend and repel that disease with better counsels and a more favorable outcome than the serene and temperate mind of Frederick William?
To whom, without any suspicion of flattery, one may exclaim with the poet:
You truly are the most opportune physician, and Paean favors your fortune!
And so in the kindness, virtue, and wisdom of Frederick William this republic finds its rest;
From him and from his excellent counsels it obtains and expects whatever good things are possible to attain in this state of affairs and according to the resources and strength of this kingdom.

For him, with that love with which he himself embraces his own, with that piety which you all know to be in him, we again pray from the divine power for the most prosperous course of his undertakings, and for a long, vigorous, and unclouded old age, unmarred by any evil or any sickness.

We, bound even by his benefits, are obligated to him with the greatest religious reverence, and we, reverently, desire and pray again and again that in his grace and favor a perpetual and most firm protection may be placed for this school founded by him.

div.head: XXII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXXIV. habita.

p.s: Fuit anni millesimi octingentesimi noni mensis Augusti dies sextus decimus, minister Regis illustrissime, auditores omnium ordinum spectatissimi, quum Fridericus Guilelmus Regimontii, ubi tum sedem regni habebat, rescriberet ad plures ex ministris et consiliariis, placere sibi et rata esse, quae illi de condendo Berolini studio generali, ut vocabant maiores, rettulissent, atque eam sibi rem adeo videri gravem tantoque momento futuram ad altiorem animorum eruditionem non solum in re publica Borussica verum etiam ultra huius fines latius disseminandam et propagandam, ad viros in quovis genere litterarum principes alliciendos et huic imperio conciliandos, postremo ad academiarum Berolinensium variorumque, quos haec urbs contineret, apparatuum et institutorum litteris inservientium quasi in unum corpus coniunctionem cum fructu perficiendam, ut nollet differre institutionem talis scholae, quae antiquo universitatis litterariae nuncupata nomine et iure honorum academicorum impertiendi instructa et ornata in hac urbe et in his, ubi nunc convenimus, collocaretur aedibus.
I pass over the other additions, some of which were soon carried out, others postponed to better times and entrusted to favorable circumstances.
That day, colleagues, created this leisure for us; it provided for your studies, fellow soldiers;
The very title, which the most kind king ordered to be inscribed on this house, refers that donation, plainly royal, to that year.

Therefore, although our duties were only begun a year later, and indeed this school was to be dedicated with solemn rites only in the eighth year, we shall trace and count the beginnings of the university from that year and that truly natal day:

Since, by this most just calculation, in a few days, in which we are celebrating this assembly for the birthday of Frederick William, the Frederick William University will have completed five lustra, I think it has traversed the first and perhaps most laborious stadium of the contest not without honor;
Why should we not, on the most auspicious birthday of the founder, also celebrate the memory of our own, as it were, birth?
For this memory is to be recalled solely to the praise of Frederick William;

Thus it will be at the same time less ambitious, less alien to the reasoning of this time, which now especially does not allow universities to boast about their affairs and to congratulate themselves greatly, and finally more suitable to that modesty, by which modesty we who were present know that the dedication of the university, celebrated seventeen years ago, was also excellently performed.

But as it has always been a pleasure for me to give thanks in the name of Frederick William and in your name, listeners, and in my own person, for the greatest benefits with which he has blessed us and the whole state;
so this duty ought to seem more acceptable every year, the longer we experience that we have remained in the King's favor by the addition of each year.
Yet there is something by which this joy of mine is disturbed.

If I compare myself with my own mind, I do not, by Hercules, doubt that there will be no one who can proclaim the King more earnestly and sincerely than I, and who can seem more worthy to undertake this office, which I today sustain on behalf of you all.
But the strength must suffice for the mind;

Although these things are thought to be strengthened by frequent practice, yet who does not understand that moderate abilities are exhausted by more frequent use, and that the edge of the mind is blunted by much fighting, and that a style of speaking already too well known by much hearing easily brings disgust to learned ears, unless whenever you speak, you vary it with the greatest art and distinguish it with new ornaments?

Therefore I seem to myself to be able to be charged with the fault of rashness, I who dare to illustrate the same subject, although it is noble and magnificent, now for the twenty-first time in an oration.
Shall I then yield my place?
Not yet, not even now, as long as your indulgence, listeners, remains, which I know has never failed me before and will not fail me today.

For you yourselves, my dearest colleagues, will rather impute that rashness of mine to yourselves than to me, who would prefer that I be kept under the standard after so many campaigns than be presented with the discharge staff.

And the concern that arises, lest my speech should now be unworthy of the King, I dispel with those words with which the great interpreter of nature, Pliny, uses in a similar case, offering his work to Titus, son of Vespasian:

"But truly," he says, "rustics and many peoples supplicate the gods with milk, and they appease them with salted meal alone, because they do not have frankincense." And why would you desire frankincense, where the work praises the craftsman?

For the King's wisdom and kindness will have been abundantly praised, when I have sketched with what counsels, how generous and magnanimous, by what novel and never-before-attempted path he founded this seat of the arts;
His prudence is abundantly evident, when I shall have shown by my counsels that these things are to be recalled to the praise of Frederick William alone;

Thus it will be at once less ambitious, less alien to the reasoning of this time, which now especially does not allow universities to boast about their affairs and to congratulate themselves greatly, and finally more suitable to that modesty, by which modesty we who were present know that the dedication of the university, celebrated seventeen years ago, was also excellently performed.

But as it has always been a pleasure to me to give thanks in the name of Frederick William and in your name, my hearers, and in my own person, for the great benefits with which he has blessed us and the whole state;
so this duty ought to seem more acceptable every year, the longer we experience that we have remained in the King's favor by the addition of each year.
Yet there is something by which this joy of mine is disturbed.

If I compare myself with them in my mind, I do not doubt, by Hercules, that there will be no one who can proclaim the King more earnestly and sincerely than I, and who can seem more worthy to undertake this office, which I today sustain on behalf of you all.
But strength of mind is needed to suffice for the task.

Although these things are thought to be strengthened by frequent practice, yet who does not understand that moderate abilities are exhausted by more frequent use, and that the edge of the mind is blunted by much fighting, and that a style of speaking already too well known by much hearing easily brings disgust to learned ears, unless as often as you speak, you vary it with the greatest art and distinguish it with new ornaments?
Therefore I seem to myself to be able to be charged with the fault of rashness, I who dare to illustrate the same subject, although noble and magnificent, now for the twenty-first time in an oration.
Shall I then yield my place?
Not yet, not even now, as long as your indulgence, listeners, remains, which I know has never failed me before and will not fail me today.

For you yourselves, dearest colleagues, will rather impute that rashness of mine to yourselves than to me, since you would prefer that I, after so many campaigns, be kept under the standard rather than be presented with the discharge staff.

And the concern that arises, lest my speech be no longer worthy of the King, I dispel with those words with which the great interpreter of nature, Pliny, uses in a similar case, offering his work to Titus, son of Vespasian:

"But the country folk and many nations supplicate the gods with milk," he says, "and they offer only salted meal, because they do not have frankincense." And why would you desire frankincense, where the work praises the craftsman?

For the King's wisdom and kindness will have been abundantly praised, when I have sketched with what counsels, how generous and magnanimous, by what new and previously untried path, he founded this seat of the arts;
His prudence is abundantly evident, when I have shown that success answered his counsels;

His constancy is abundantly evident, when I have shown that nothing was relaxed through the changes of times, but that our affairs were preserved and increased by Frederick William through constant zeal and munificence.
success answered his counsels;

His constancy is abundantly evident, when I have shown that nothing was relaxed through the changes of times, but that our affairs were preserved and increased by Frederick William through constant zeal and munificence.

For if we except that age in which literary universities were born in great cities, because into these flowed all the learning which at that time existed outside the monasteries, and if we by our right deny that certain universities, which even in this century seem to survive in some principal cities, are universities except in name;
This was a new undertaking, listeners, that Frederick William wanted these schools to be established especially in the more important cities.

They were then distributed in such a way that of the three parts of the kingdom, Prussia properly so called had its seat of the liberal arts at Königsberg, Silesia at Breslau, and the remaining German provinces, which indeed survived from the great shipwreck, at Berlin.
Thus it seemed possible that, since larger cities and seats of government provide a more splendid apparatus, on this side at least more could be accomplished with less expense;
so that, because a small band could not dominate the youths, however numerous, in a large town, the morals of the academic citizens might become more modest;

Moreover, so that those very capitals of provinces might be reconciled to a higher and more subtle science, and that those things which held the first place in position and rank should not be secondary to literature, and so that the learned might be less separated from the administrators of the highest government, but that learning might in a way penetrate into the state, and that the learned, in turn, might become less alien to the management of public affairs, and less, as they say, bookish.
But novelty then brought it about that this matter seemed full of risk:
The corruption of youth was feared, the snares of pleasures and luxury, by which great cities were infected:
That academic freedom, which the lovers of the old discipline value most highly, was also feared.
Indeed, most people forgot that even the less frequented towns, and especially those in which literary universities have been established, have their own secret lusts;
that there, not rarely, more licentious drinking parties and Bacchanalia are celebrated than in the very foremost cities;
and that the crowdedness of the city does not harm just liberty, provided only that arrogance and insolence are absent, since it allows each person to live in his own way;
and that liberty is not such that it is permitted to insult citizens with impunity and to hold every most innocent person up to ridicule.
In short:

The outcome has so confirmed Frederick William's judgment that, since neither the charm of the place, nor the abundance of wine, nor the indulgence shown to insolence has enticed anyone to come here, no part of the youth has spent its time more innocently than this band of ours, none has been more distinguished for eagerness in study, industry, and seriousness—indeed, as most people now admit, and especially the governors of states—nothing is more useful than this most tranquil residence of universities in capital cities.
Indeed, I would explain this topic even more fully, were it not that, while I am engaged in it, I recall that it has already been deliberately treated by me long ago:
For who would not experience that, in treating the same subject, the same thought or sentiment repeatedly recurs?

And moreover I fear that, although I strive to avoid all ostentation in our affairs, I may seem unwittingly to disparage the allied universities, which are most closely connected with us in common interests, and to compare our advantages with the disadvantages of others:
which would have been more unjust at no time than now.
For indeed almost all of them deserve very well of literature.
Nor indeed did Frederick William think that all things should be reduced to one form:

It has retained even those universities with which other towns are adorned and enriched, and has furnished these very ones far more splendidly, and moreover has founded in the most ancient town on the bank of the Rhine a new school of the finest arts, the eye of the fatherland's river, the bright jewel of the Prussian crown.

But how truly the wisest king prophesied that the great power of our university would also lie in this, that all the literary equipment of every kind, which was scattered throughout this city, would be properly arranged, enlarged, and set before the common use.
For these treasures have become especially famous from that very time, from which they were liberally turned to the benefit of the university.

Nor would they ever have attained such great abundance, usefulness, and dignity, nor would they themselves have brought such great adornment to the city, had not the Friedrich Wilhelm University more keenly stimulated the studies of Berlin.

For this is the condition of studies in Germany, that neither the schools which they call special, whose meagerness and languor please some people, nor the academies, however learned and splendid, nor any other scholastic institutions add such great stimuli to minds, nor inflame youthful spirits with such great ardor for cultivating the good arts with the utmost exertion, as this discipline of universities, without which, as the culture of the European peoples is now indeed constituted, literature does not seem able to thrive and flourish.

But the fact that the excellent Prince had persuaded himself that the institution of this university would contribute greatly to the formation of minds, not only in abundance, nor did the indulgence of insolence entice anyone to come here, no part of the youth has lived more innocently than this our band, none has been more distinguished in the eagerness, industry, and severity of studies, indeed, as many now confess, and especially the presidents of republics, that nothing is more useful than this most tranquil habitation of universities in the principal cities.
Indeed, I would explain this topic even more fully, were it not that, while I am engaged in it, I recall that it has already been explained by me deliberately long ago:
For who would not have it happen that, in treating the same subject, the same thought or sentiment should repeatedly recur?

And moreover I fear that, although I strive to avoid all ostentation in our affairs, I may seem unwittingly to disparage the allied universities, which are most closely connected with us in common interests, and to compare our advantages with the disadvantages of others.
This would have been more unjust at no time than now.
For indeed almost all of them deserve very well of literature.
Nor indeed did Frederick William think that all things should be reduced to one form.

It has also retained the universities, even those with which other towns are adorned and enlarged, and has furnished these very ones far more splendidly, and moreover has founded in the most ancient town on the bank of the Rhine a new school of the finest arts, the eye of the fatherland's river, the bright jewel of the Prussian crown.

But how truly the wisest king prophesied that the great power of our university would also lie in this, that the literary equipment of every kind, which was scattered throughout this city, would be properly arranged, enlarged, and set out for common use.
For these treasures have become especially famous from that time onward, since they were liberally turned to the benefit of the university.

Nor would they ever have attained such great abundance, usefulness, and dignity, nor would they themselves have brought such great adornment to the city, had not the Friedrich Wilhelm University more keenly stimulated the studies of Berlin.

For this is the condition of studies in Germany, that neither the schools which they call special, whose weakness and languor pleases some, nor the academies, however learned and splendid, nor any other scholastic institutions add such great stimuli to minds, nor inflame youthful souls with such great ardor for cultivating the good arts with the utmost exertion, as this discipline of universities, without which, as the culture of the European peoples is now indeed constituted, literature does not seem able to thrive and flourish.

But that the best prince had persuaded himself that the establishment of this university would greatly contribute to forming minds, not only in the lands subject to him but also beyond the borders of the empire—how greatly do you think this has been confirmed by the outcome?
For since from its very beginnings the number of citizens has been so great that it has equaled moderate universities, ours [has been] such.

Then, after the most fortunate calamity happened, that we dismissed not unwillingly the noble youth summoned to the camp, who at that time had devoted themselves of their own accord for the safety of the King and the fatherland, since with the whole people they were about to redeem and recover our liberty and the Prussian glory and the integrity of the empire and other goods with their blood, not only was the damage done to this school immediately repaired, but by continuous increases the number of citizens soon grew so much that in a short time we surpassed all the other universities.
Even the plague, which three years ago carried off very many of our fellow students, did not greatly diminish our numbers;
so from all the provinces and from the rest of Germany and even from foreign lands the flower of youth has flowed in anew.
For how excellent a wrestling-school of studies Frederick William has opened here for the young, both the natives and foreigners see.

Nor do I fear so much that I will greatly incur the criticism of the experts, when perhaps I shall say somewhat more ambitiously in passing, that by the fame of this school of ours it is brought about that the virtue of the Prussian kingdom is better understood, while young men of good character, flowing here from all sides, more closely come to know the goods and advantages of this state, and, as I have often experienced myself, are gradually imbued with and drawn to the reputation of the Prussian name, even unwilling and in a way unknowing.

But if Frederick the Great, in order to promote the growth of learning in his own and foreign lands, took care to equip the academy of sciences munificently, which under that king flourished especially with men who were leaders in their respective fields, particularly distinguished mathematicians and philosophers, Frederick William, in order to attain the same end, preferred that institution which almost everyone affirms to be truly German, and which is far more effective for that purpose;

And by summoning professors to teach in the university, he not only wonderfully nourished the learning of this city, but also provided the most abundant opportunity for increasing, from the common people at the same time, that society which Frederick the Great had uniquely loved.
To the lands themselves subject to him, but also beyond the borders of the empire, how greatly this was approved by the outcome, do you judge?
For since from its very beginnings the number of citizens was such that it equaled our modest universities;

Then, after the most fortunate calamity happened, that we dismissed not unwillingly the noble youth summoned to the camp, who at that time had devoted themselves of their own accord for the safety of the King and the fatherland, since with the whole people they were about to redeem and recover our liberty and the Prussian glory and the integrity of the empire and other goods with their blood, not only was the damage given to this school immediately repaired, but by continuous increases the number of citizens soon grew so much that in a short time we surpassed all other universities.
Indeed, the plague, which three years ago drove away very many of our fellow students, did not greatly diminish our numbers;
so from all provinces and from the rest of Germany and even from foreign lands the flower of youth has flowed in anew.
For how excellent a training ground for studies Frederick William has opened here, both the natives and foreigners see.

Nor do I fear so much that I will greatly incur the criticism of the experts, when perhaps I shall have said somewhat more ambitiously in passing, that by this celebrated gathering of our school it is brought about that the virtue of the Prussian kingdom is better understood, while young men of good character, flowing here from all sides, come to know more closely the goods and advantages of this commonwealth, and, as I have often experienced myself, are gradually imbued with and drawn to the reputation of the Prussian name, even unwilling and in a way unknowing.

But if Frederick the Great, by munificently equipping an academy of sciences, sought to promote the growth of learning in his own and foreign lands, which under that king flourished especially with men preeminent in their kind, particularly distinguished mathematicians and philosophers, Frederick William, in order to attain the same end, preferred that institution which almost all declare to be truly German, and which is far more effective for that purpose;

And by summoning professors to teach in the university, he not only wonderfully nourished the learning of this city, but also provided the most abundant opportunity for increasing, from the common people at the same time, that society which Frederick the Great had loved uniquely.

This is an old glory of the Prussian kingdom, listeners, and it has not been boasted by its own natives with vain grandiloquence, but has been celebrated by the mouth of every most learned nation, because its power has rested no more on arms than on the cultivation of minds.
This indeed was more keenly observed during those years in which the state lay prostrate, struck by a most disastrous calamity:
How much more does it delight to recall the memory of that time, in which the wisdom of Frederick William was so employed that from the very adversities it drew forth the greatest prosperities.

Then nothing was left undone, by which the powers hidden in hearts and minds, which you could not exhaust by imposing taxes, nor by placing garrisons, nor by any other injustice, might be nourished and fostered with the most diligent care.
To this care we owe our life, colleagues and fellow soldiers, not the life that nature gave in common with the animals, but the life by which our minds are vigorous:
This care any schools of the good arts in this kingdom have experienced.
But oh, the pain!

We have degenerated so much in these five lustra that there are already those who say that when the schools were restored, this ruin was sown, which now creeps through all Germany, so that the most audacious youth may attempt revolution.

By a wonderful inclination of minds, that character of German schools which was once hateful to enemies is now approved by foreigners, but displeases some of our own people, who think they are led by love of country.
Formerly, the most talented men defended them against external slander, among whom were also the teachers of this school, especially distinguished.
Now a war, as it were civil, has blazed up concerning them.

And what you may especially grieve, lest they seem to have utterly brazen-faced, like informers, they commit crimes and outrages, which may be imputed with some appearance of truth to the universities and to the other schools.

Indeed, most of those who judge in journals and in certain assemblies of the civil orders what schools and universities are or ought to be, do not have a better knowledge of their nature and character than adolescents have of republics, whose thoughtless judgments about these matters those very critics of public education rightly take amiss.

At one moment we are envied and reproached for this shadow of the form and right of the guilds, because we are said to have retained something from the Middle Ages, being too tenacious of ancient institutions;
at another time, quite the contrary, we are thought to despise the old and to grasp at the new, and to be eager for liberty, or rather license.
But to those who judge rightly, the one will seem most justly tempered with the other:
for those bonds of the guilds have been so loosened that nothing has been left that is more illiberal;
license, as far as lies in our power, we restrain:
But when one has not been able to eradicate it root and branch, why is it surprising that we have not succeeded in what even the bravest and most powerful leaders could not accomplish?
And we claim freedom for ourselves to this extent, that we think no one should teach anything that he himself does not approve:

Not that those things which are to be taught, nor how, can be commanded, but that whatever each person has understood to be true by accurate inquiry, from him not memory, which the wisdom of Frederick William used in such a way that from the very adverse circumstances it drew forth the greatest prosperities.

Then nothing was left undone by which the powers hidden in hearts and minds, which you could not exhaust by imposing tributes, nor by placing garrisons, nor by any other injustice, might be nourished and fostered with the most diligent care.
To this care we owe our life, colleagues and fellow soldiers, not the life that nature gave in common with the animals, but the life by which our minds thrive:
This care any schools of the good arts in this kingdom have experienced.
But oh, the pain!

We have degenerated so much in these five five-year periods that there are already those who say that when the schools were re-established, this ruin was sown, which now creeps through all Germany, so that the most audacious youth attempts revolution.

By a wonderful inclination of minds, that character of German schools which was once hateful to enemies is now approved by foreigners, but displeases some of our countrymen, who seem to themselves to be led by love of fatherland;
Formerly, the most ingenious men defended those [studies] against external calumny, among whom there were also especially distinguished teachers of this school;
now a war, as it were civil, has blazed up concerning them.

And what you may especially deplore, lest those men seem to have utterly effronteried their face like informers, they commit crimes and outrages, which may be imputed with some appearance of truth both to the universities and to the remaining schools.

Indeed, most of those who judge in journals and in certain assemblies of the civil orders what schools and universities are or ought to be, do not know their nature and character better than adolescents know public affairs, whose thoughtless judgments about these matters those very critics of public education rightly take amiss.
Now we are envied and reproached for this shadow of form and of the right of associations, because we are said to have retained from the middle age, being too tenacious of ancient institutions;
now quite the contrary, we are thought to despise the old, to catch at the new, and to be eager for liberty or rather license.
But to those who judge rightly, the one will seem most justly tempered with the other:
for those bonds of associations have been so relaxed, that nothing is left more illiberal;
license, as far as lies in us, we restrain:
But when one cannot tear it out by the roots, why should it be surprising that we have not succeeded in doing what not even the bravest and most powerful leaders could accomplish?
And we claim freedom for ourselves to this extent, that we think no one should teach anything that he himself does not approve:
that it cannot be commanded what should be taught or how, but that whatever one has understood to be true by careful inquiry, from that one is not allowed to deviate a finger's breadth:

Nor is it to be taught for this reason, that the listener may take down in writing or in memory what is handed down, but that the students themselves may become accustomed to penetrate the inner sanctuaries of literature by free thought;

Nor should these young men be trained and instructed like slaves, according to certain fixed doctrines, from a prescribed rule, for specific duties, which they would then perform and carry out without feeling; but rather, the inner reason of divine and human affairs itself, as far as we are able, should be explained, and youthful minds should be filled with the most burning love of the true, the good, and the beautiful.
When the King wished this, he did not say that he was founding a university, so that young men might be trained for ministries and public offices:
although it is not doubtful that they are also formed for these by the right instruction of arts and sciences:
but so that he might provide for the cultivation of minds both in his own lands and beyond the borders of the empire.
But that these crimes of a few did not flow from the teaching of universities is clearer than light;

And if it is permissible to judge other schools by our own, it was not even the gentleness of the academic discipline, which is not as great as it is thought to be, that brought it about that those things could be committed.
Truly other forces drove Gaul, Italy, Belgium, Poland, Spain, and Portugal;
By the same movements and the common flaw of the age, whose origins it is not ours to investigate, some German youths were drawn to undertake new things, not incited by the discipline of the schools.

But as in barbarous ages, when pestilence was raging, the superstitious common people, ignorant of how to investigate the natural causes of things, used to accuse the Jews, as those who had poisoned wells and springs:
so in more cultivated ages certain ingenious men took delight in this, that they demonstrated to the credulous that the seeds of all the greatest disturbances had been scattered by the learned.

Who does not know, I ask, how often that oft-repeated story has been told, that philosophy, as they called it, and the philosophers and the authors of encyclopedias brought about that great revolution in France, by which the whole world was shaken more violently than by an earthquake?
Indeed, if those philosophers were able to accomplish so much, we will not despair that German philosophy from pure concepts will one day bring forth some new world:
which ability comedy has not dared to grant up to this point.

What of the fact that some have even been pleased by this, and it has been received with applause from certain quarters, since the notions which we seem to hold about the condition of the ancient states are so imperfect and false that we do not hold even the first elements of the civil discipline of the Greeks and Romans except as confused and corrupted by the most shameful errors;
it is permitted to depart a finger's breadth aside;

Nor is it to be taught for this reason, that the listener may take down what is handed over either with pen or with memory, but that the students themselves may become accustomed to penetrate the inner sanctums of literature with free thought.

Nor should these young men be trained and instructed like slaves, according to certain fixed doctrines, from a prescribed rule, for specific duties, which they would then perform and execute without feeling; but rather the inner reason of things divine and human, as far as we are able, should be explained, and youthful minds should be filled with the most burning love of the true, the good, and the beautiful.
Since the King wished this, he did not say that he was founding a university in order that young men might be trained for the ministries and public offices:
although it is not doubtful that they are also formed for these things by the right instruction of arts and sciences:
but so that he might provide for the cultivation of minds both in his own lands and beyond the borders of the empire.
But those crimes of a few men, it is clearer than light that they did not flow from the teaching of universities;

And if it is permissible to judge other schools by our own, it was not even the mildness of the academic discipline, which is not so great as it is thought to be, that brought it about that those things could be committed.
Truly other forces drove Gaul, Italy, Belgium, Poland, Spain, and Portugal;

By the same movements and the common flaw of the age, whose origins it is not our task to investigate, some German youths were drawn to attempt new things, not incited by the discipline of the schools.

But as in barbarous ages, when pestilence was raging, the superstitious common people, ignorant of how to investigate the natural causes of things, used to accuse the Jews, as those who had poisoned wells and springs:
so in more cultivated ages certain clever men took delight in this, that they demonstrated to the credulous that the seeds of all the greatest disturbances had been scattered by the learned.

Who does not know, I ask, how often that oft-told tale has been repeated, that philosophy, as they called it, and the philosophers and the authors of encyclopedias brought about that great revolution in France, by which the whole world was shaken more violently than by an earthquake?
Indeed, if those philosophers were able to accomplish so much, we shall not despair that German philosophy will one day, from pure concepts, bring forth some new world:
This ability, which comedy alone has dared to grant them up to now.

What of the fact that some have even been pleased by this, and it has been received with applause by certain people, since the notions which we seem to hold about the condition of ancient states are so imperfect and false that we do not hold even the first elements of Greek and Roman civil discipline except confused and corrupted by the most shameful errors;

It can now be understood how correct and true the interpretation of ancient writers is rendered in the schools, on how firm foundations rests the knowledge of the ancient civil liberty, with which the teachers of the schools imbue their pupils:

Indeed, both teachers and learners hunt after certain obscure and unformed sensations instead of clear and distinct notions and opinions, with which they stir their minds even to the point of disturbance, arrogating to themselves judgment about civil institutions, which not even men most experienced in public affairs have been able to fully understand up to this point, instead of a modest and honest confession of ignorance.

Therefore, it must be asked whether it is consistent with reason that young offspring, from childhood, should be accustomed, trained, and educated at public expense to a superficial and lightly tasted estimation of public affairs, and to the formation of false, corrupt, and pernicious notions about them.

Since this has now prevailed for several centuries, but in our century is pursued more eagerly than ever, it is not surprising if with incredible haste the abolition of any public rights is now demanded and conceded with equanimity, and the peoples of Europe, corrupted in their morals by this vice of public education, rush unwittingly and fall back into barbarism.
Those who toss about these and similar things most confidently, do they not describe for us the teachers of the schools as so many Gracchi?
Do they not affirm and prophesy that civil disturbances of any kind and even barbarism itself are brought on by the handling of Greek and Latin literature?
Yet others complain rather that boys are over-exercised by the subtlety of grammarians;
and certainly much is attributed to grammatical precepts in our schools and has never not been attributed:

Finally, those schoolmasters, in whom so much distrust is placed, are partly so occupied with the most serious and abstruse studies that they scarcely have time to examine public affairs, and the pupils are so trained by learning every kind of liberal education that scarcely any leisure is left for transacting the affairs of others.
Indeed, I would not deny that the love of just liberty and the hatred of unjust tyranny are nourished by the study of ancient literature;
And our ancestors thought that this should be counted among the most important benefits of these studies, together with every excellent prince.

ceterum ex scholastica nostra disciplina legibus apte temperata et ex studiis antiquitatis non maiore praetextu saeculi repetas labem, quam siquis, quemadmodum Graeci harmoniis mollioribus et licentioribus discendis ignavos et intemperantes puerorum reddi animos sibi persuaserant, ita hanc aetatis quasi intemperiem a musicis nostris repetat, vel a theatris, in quibus sane
intelligi iam posse, quam recta et vera scriptorum veterum explicatio reddatur in scholis, quam firmis fundamentis nitatur cognitio libertatis veterum civilis, qua scholarum magistri imbuant discipulos:

Indeed, both teachers and learners, instead of clear and distinct notions and opinions, hunt after certain obscure and unformed feelings, by which they stir their minds even to the point of disturbance, and, instead of a modest and honest confession of ignorance, they arrogate to themselves judgment concerning civil institutions, which not even men most experienced in public affairs have been able to fully understand up to this time.

Therefore, it must be asked whether it is consistent with reason that a young offspring, from childhood, should be accustomed, trained, and educated at public expense to a superficial and lightly tasted estimation of public affairs, and to the forming of false, corrupt, and pernicious notions about them.

Since this has now prevailed for several centuries, but in our century is pursued more zealously than ever, it is not to be wondered at, if with incredible haste the abolition of any public rights is now demanded and conceded with equanimity, and the peoples of Europe, corrupted in their morals by this vice of public education, rush unwittingly and fall back into barbarism.
Those who toss about these and similar things most confidently, do they not describe for us the teachers of the schools as so many Gracchi?
Do they not affirm and prophesy that civil disturbances of any kind and even barbarism itself are brought on by the handling of Greek and Latin literature?
Yet others complain rather that boys are over-exercised by the subtlety of grammarians;
and certainly much is attributed to grammatical precepts in our schools, and never has not been attributed:

Finally, those schoolmasters, in whom so much distrust is placed, are partly so occupied with the most serious and abstruse studies that they scarcely have time to examine public affairs, and the students are so trained by learning every kind of liberal education that scarcely any leisure is left for attending to the affairs of others.
Indeed, I would not deny that the love of just liberty and the hatred of unjust tyranny are nourished by the study of ancient literature.
And our ancestors judged that this should be counted among the most important benefits of these studies, together with every excellent prince.

Moreover, from our scholastic discipline, properly tempered by laws, and from the study of antiquity, you would not more justly derive a blemish on account of the pretext of the age, than if someone, just as the Greeks had persuaded themselves that the minds of boys were rendered idle and intemperate by learning the softer and more licentious harmonies, should in like manner derive this, as it were, intemperance of the age from our musicians, or from the theaters, in which indeed we not rarely hear the most famous poets, the glories of Germany, proclaiming civil liberty.
Finally, in the Prussian schools, to whom, I ask, are those pernicious precepts taught?
And if anything of this sort has been taught by one or another, are the whole schools therefore to be slandered?
Away, then, with those accusations:

let us rather congratulate Frederick William, because, as the old proverb has it, he did not hesitate to sow, and he did not sow dragon's teeth, from which a deadly and bloody crop might spring up, but he has brought back a joyful and innocent harvest of the best studies;
And let us be confident in the clemency of the most excellent Prince and in the character of the Prussian state, which do not allow that anything be decreed against literature more unjustly.

For what can the state most justly adopt that which the most honorable man Isocrates used in the Athenian republic, when he was accused of the same crime as formerly the son of Sophroniscus, that he corrupted the youth by his instruction?
For he used to say that the Athenians excelled all other states in literature.

Therefore, if they wished to be hostile to those who strove to surpass their contemporaries in the same arts by which the Athenians surpassed all others, and who used that learning of which Athens had been the leader and parent, the city would condemn itself by its own judgment, and would do the same as if the Lacedaemonians punished the teachers of the military art, or the Thessalians those who taught the methods of horsemanship.
We hear, not rarely, the most famous poets, the glories of Germany, proclaiming civil liberty.
Finally, in the Prussian schools, to whom, pray, are those pernicious precepts handed down?
And if anything of that sort has been handed down by one or another, are the whole schools therefore to be slandered?
Away, then, with those accusations!

Let us rather congratulate Frederick William, because, as the old proverb says, he did not hesitate to sow, nor did he sow dragon's teeth, from which a deadly and bloody crop might spring up, but he has brought back a joyful and innocent harvest of the best studies.
And let us rely on the clemency of our excellent Prince and on the character of the Prussian state, which do not allow that anything be decreed against literature more unjustly.

For what can that rightly be applied to a state, which the most upright man Isocrates employed in the Athenian republic, when he was accused of the same crime as the son of Sophroniscus once was, namely that he was corrupting the youth by his instruction?
For he used to say that the Athenians excelled all other states in literature.

Therefore, if they wished to be hostile to those who strove to surpass their contemporaries in the same things by which the Athenians surpassed all others, and who used that education of which Athens had been the leader and parent, the city would condemn itself by its own judgment, and would do the same as if the Lacedaemonians punished the teachers of the military art, or the Thessalians those who taught the methods of horsemanship.

Now, to return to the point from which I may perhaps have slightly deviated: since often the princes, in the first fervor of promoting letters, promised much, but soon failed, either through negligence, or from weariness, or because they thought that the studies and characters of teachers and students did not meet expectations;
Frederick William, having by natural goodness attained a union of constancy with munificence, preserved and enlarged the university with no less benevolence than he had founded it.
I will not speak of the far most extensive increases of the apparatus, nor will I pursue the individual details that pertain to this matter:
