For these things, although necessary and precious, just as they are devoid of life, so they lack force and vigor, unless the keen, ready, and vigorous talents of the teachers have been added.

In this matter there is need of constant diligence and kindness, so that, since the life of man is short, the successions may be worthy and illustrious, and lest, however great the names that have celebrated the school, it should gradually decline to lesser ones, as often the titles and goods, not the virtue, of excellent men are transferred to their heirs.
And how great, indeed, do you think the number of colleagues is, to whom successors have had to be given within this short space of a few lustra?
Twenty-five full professors, together with seven extraordinary professors, opened this school.
Of those twenty-five, no more than ten survive.
Even of those who later joined as ordinary professors, eight have died, only six have departed elsewhere.
Of the extraordinary professors, three have met their fate.
Twenty-two, mostly the younger ones, have changed their position.
And how great were those men, indeed in fame and memory of men they still are, whose sweetest friendship fortune has begrudged us!
Today we celebrate a birthday, listeners, not a funeral:
therefore let all mourning and lamentation be absent:
but it was nevertheless permitted to indicate in a word how great losses had to be repaired for the most merciful King;
of which two, and among these the last, are almost irreparable:
those which could be repaired have been so repaired that at the same time the number of teachers has increased as much as in no literary university of Germany ever.
This is the King's disposition toward us;
But the royal house favors us no less, and especially you, fellow soldiers.
For although this university was never not well-equipped with those things that pertained to literature,
Nevertheless, another kind of support was lacking, intended for relieving the need and poverty of the citizens:
Only older schools are accustomed to enjoy an abundance of such supports, because the earlier age was more inclined to pious generosity.
Indeed, this necessity has been moderately provided for by private individuals, chiefly by supplying food.

But nothing more distinguished, nothing more desirable could have happened to us, than that the heir to the throne and the other most serene princes of the imperial house and their most serene consorts have recently contributed such large sums, so that they alone equal the benefits of all the others.
Nor was the gift most pleasing merely on account of its magnitude.
Moreover, the courtesy of the donors and the confidence with which they entrusted this matter to the Senate to be administered, themselves plead in favor of this seat of the arts.
We indeed, colleagues and fellow soldiers, cannot return thanks to Frederick William and the royal line, nor even offer thanks worthy of such great gifts;
but we can take care that our plans, institutions, studies, and life do not displease the Father of the fatherland:
This I promise to you all in your name, that we will do diligently.

But may God, the Best and Greatest, reward the King with the highest goods and prosperity, and keep him safe and unharmed with his beloved son, the heir to the kingdom, and his whole flourishing house!
Have successors been given in the space of the lustra?
Twenty-five full professors with seven extraordinary ones opened this school;
Of those twenty-five, no more than ten survive.
Even of those who later joined, eight of the regular members have died, only six have departed elsewhere;
of the extraordinary members, three have met their fate;
twenty-two, especially the younger ones, have changed their abode.
And how great were those men, indeed in fame and memory of men they still are, whose sweetest friendship fortune has begrudged us!
Today we celebrate a birthday, listeners, not a funeral:
therefore let all grief and lamentation be absent:
But it was nevertheless possible to indicate in a word how great losses had to be repaired for the most merciful King.
Of these, two, and among them the most recent, were almost irreparable.
Those that could be repaired have been repaired in such a way that at the same time the number of teachers has grown as much as in no other literary university in Germany.
This is the King's disposition toward us.
But no less does the royal house favor us, and especially you, fellow soldiers.
For although this university was never without the most ample provision for those things that pertained to letters,
yet another kind of support was lacking, one destined for relieving the need and poverty of the citizens:
of which supports, only the older schools are usually able to enjoy an abundance, because the earlier age was more ready for pious generosity.
Gradually, indeed, this need too has been moderately provided for by private individuals, especially in providing food.

But nothing more distinguished, nothing more desirable for us could have happened, than that the Prince, heir to the throne, and the other most serene Princes of the August house, and their most serene consorts, have recently contributed such great sums, so that they alone equal the benefits of all the others.
Nor was the gift welcome only because of its magnitude:
The very courtesy of the donors and the confidence with which they entrusted it to the Senate for administration also plead on behalf of this seat of the arts.
We indeed, colleagues and fellow soldiers, cannot return thanks to Frederick William and the royal line, nor even give thanks worthy of such great gifts;
but we can take care that our plans, institutions, studies, and life do not displease the Father of the fatherland:
this indeed I promise that we will do diligently in your name on behalf of all of you:

May God, indeed, the Best and Greatest, reward the King with the highest goods and prosperities, and keep him safe and unharmed with his noble son, the heir to the kingdom, and with his entire most flourishing house!

div.head: XXIII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXXV. habita.

p.s: Among most peoples, just as among us, listeners, the parents, relatives, and all who wish well to the parents and the newborn child consider each person's birthday to be happy and auspicious, and they celebrate it every year with great joy and solemn festivity.
Good hope receives the new offspring with a joyful omen;
We give thanks to God, we pour out prayers and make vows for the tender infant, whom we bring to the altar to be purified;
We congratulate the birth of a new star, an immortal soul, which, like a spark, has flashed forth from the divine fire and has penetrated into this mortal little body:

Finally, although we are anxious about his safety, with God's favor we expect that he will reach a more robust age, will excel in uprightness, honor, and virtue, and will someday be a comfort to his own.
There were few nations, and those rather uncultivated, to whom it seemed otherwise:
which is what Herodotus has handed down about the Trausi.

For among these people, who followed a custom that was, I know not whether more severe or more soft and effeminate, but certainly more gloomy, they used to surround the newborn child with relatives lamenting and bewailing his fortune;
but the one who had died they buried with rejoicing and jesting, and they proclaimed blessed the one who had escaped so many and such great evils.
Nor are these people entirely without reason.
For we enter upon a path of life that is steep, rough, and precipitous;
we are tossed about by the roughest waves and storms:
In short, no one is happy before death.
How many are there who emerge safe and unharmed from these calamities by which we are surrounded on every side?
Most indeed fall short of their undertakings and prayers;
there are those who seem to have been born neither for their own advantage nor for that of other men:
and not a few are stained with crimes and shameful deeds, and become famous for the magnitude of their vices rather than their virtues:
Who would not think that death is to be desired more than life for such men?

And although these things apply to all men of any rank, even to those who are born in a humble station, yet they are especially suited to those who are born to the throne, because these are born not for themselves and for their father and mother alone, but for the republic and all citizens, and they are called by their very birth not to manage their own private fortune, but to conduct the great affairs of the empire.
And so they are received not only by their parents and relatives, but by the whole people with congratulatory greetings and immense exultation of spirit.
For the people feels and understands how great a pledge of tranquility and public security is placed in the perpetual succession of legitimate princes.

It understands that the fortune of the empire depends on the heir of the kingdom, and that according as the lots of birth have fallen, either the happiness of the republic or most disastrous losses are portended.
But the omens are obscure:
It is not clear by evident signs whether the Graces, courtesy, gentleness, or cruelty and the Furies stood by at his birth:
The outcome proves each one.
Certainly this outcome is not in our power alone;
Human affairs obey the more powerful laws of providence and fate, established by divine will:

Yet the counsel of the divine power uses men as instruments, and indeed especially kings in public affairs, but in those matters which pertain to the cultivation and advancement of the mind and spirit, then both those same kings and others whom you might call kings in their own kind, as living and acting with their own free will.
Whatever instrument resists that plan is thrown away as useless before the work is completed, and what had been accomplished by it becomes void.

I call happy the one for whom that part of the common work has succeeded, which he has received as assigned by the supreme maker of all things, that is, the one who knows how to direct his plans so that they harmonize with the hidden plan of the supreme divinity.
The outcome approved him.
From the birth of this man, that foul and inhuman mourning of the Trausi was deservedly absent.

I declare the King happy, who after a long rule, after various vicissitudes, to which the human race is subject, constantly endured, as often as these most sacred birthdays return, may repeatedly acclaim:
God favors your cares, God, who destined you, that you might be the dispenser of those good things, of those prosperities which he wishes to confer upon this people;

You, who seem to adapt your actions to the counsels of providence, as far as we can judge with human understanding, and not to resist the course of events established by divine will, and to handle with ready and sure hand what has been entrusted to you!
You increase the happiness of the empire every year;
you understand that human affairs are governed not by anger but by the love of the supreme deity and are accomplished through the infinite courses of ages:
You, comparing and composing yourself to his example, as far as mortal nature permits, prefer freedom to servitude, obedience tempered by reason to necessity, gentleness to savage severity.
We venerate you as king, we love you as father!
Their private fortune is to be governed, but for the great affairs of the empire they are called by their very birth.
Therefore they are received not only by their parents and relatives, but by the whole people with congratulatory greetings and immense exultation of minds:

God favors your cares, God, who destined you, that, what good things, what prosperities he wishes to confer upon this people, you might be the dispenser of them;

You, who seem to adapt your actions to the counsels of providence, as far as we can judge with human understanding, and not to resist the course of things established by divine will, and to handle with ready and sure hand what has been entrusted to you!
You increase the happiness of the empire every year;
you understand that human affairs are governed not by anger but by the love of the supreme deity, and are accomplished through infinite courses of ages:
You, comparing and composing yourself to his example, as far as mortal nature permits, prefer freedom to servitude, obedience tempered by reason to necessity, gentleness to savage severity.
We venerate you as king, we love you as father!

I have said that kings and those who in every kind of human culture excel in outstanding wisdom, and rule as if with royal power and write laws for the less gifted, less clear-sighted multitude, are instruments which providence uses to carry out its plans.
But what are these plans?

Who, I ask, even if he seems by far the wisest, would dare to define what are the reasons and ways of providence, whence it proceeds and whither it tends, what ends it has set for the human race, and, once you have known the end, by what means it impels mortals so that they may at some time reach the goal?
Indeed, it would be the part of a prophet to know and to discuss these things:

Yet if one who is skilled in past events is rightly considered a prophet turned backward, this man, from those traces which have been impressed upon earlier ages, may have divined a little about the ends of human affairs.

And although I seem to myself to discern this, which he has divined, scarcely after a long interval and as through a mist, and so it happens that what is itself small and obscure is represented to me by my blunter vision as even more minute and dimmer, yet it pleases me, even with an unpolished voice, as far as can be done within the narrowness of time, to sketch out what sort of thing it is that hovers before my eyes.

For if this visible nature of things, which nevertheless seems to many to be devoid of mind, is not moved by a random impulse, nor are the stars whirled about by some blind rotation, but the masses, intervals, spaces, and times are balanced and arranged in a lawful order:

Shall we think that the mind, which alone was able to compose and adorn rude matter into the form of the world, alone to establish a law for the whole mass, when it was first implanted in the human race, was driven without law, wandered, was carried recklessly wherever chance gave it headlong?

Or shall we say that human affairs have indeed their appointed changes, but just as the sky and the stars, moving in a circle perpetually, after completing their course return to the same place from which they set out, so human affairs too, imitating the heavenly order, are driven as it were by certain whirlwinds in a circle, and after completing the circle, after so many ages, after so many and such great labors of mortals, have not advanced a step, but have been thrown back to the beginning of the course, and that the human race, pierced like the leaky jars of the Danaids, performs a task, perpetually pouring in water which perpetually flows out?
Indeed it is a common saying that what once existed returns again and again, and that nothing new happens under the sun:
but it is equally true that the same things never return, and that one does not step into the same river twice;

Indeed, while in human affairs earlier ages seem in a certain way to be repeated, nevertheless these [words] — 'I have said that kings and those who in every kind of human culture excel in outstanding wisdom, and rule as it were with royal power and write laws for the less gifted, less clear-sighted multitude, are instruments by which providence uses to carry out its plans' — are [true].
But what are these plans?

Who, I ask, even if he should seem by far the wisest, would dare to define what are the reasons and ways of providence, whence it proceeds and whither it tends, what ends it has set before the human race, and, once you have learned the end, by what means it impels mortals so that they may at last reach the goal?
Indeed, it would be the part of a prophet to know and to discuss these things.

Yet if one who is skilled in past events is rightly considered a prophet turned backward, this man, from those traces which have been impressed upon earlier ages, may have divined a little about the ends of human affairs;

And although I seem to myself to discern this, which he has divined, scarcely after a long interval and as through a mist, and so it happens that what is itself small and obscure is represented to me by my blunter vision as even more minute and duller, yet it pleases me, even with an unpolished voice, as far as can be done within the narrowness of time, to sketch out what sort of thing it is that hovers before my eyes.

For if this visible nature of things, which nevertheless seems to many to be devoid of mind, is not moved by a random impulse, nor are the stars whirled about by some blind revolution, but the masses, intervals, spaces, and times are balanced and arranged in a lawful order:

Shall we think that the mind, which alone was able to shape and adorn rude matter into the form of the world, alone to establish a law for the whole mass, when it was first implanted in the human race, was driven without law, wandered, was carried recklessly wherever chance gave it headlong?

Or shall we say that human affairs have indeed their appointed changes, but just as the sky and the stars, moving in a circle perpetually, after completing their course return to the same place from which they set out, so human affairs too, imitating the heavenly order, are driven round as it were by certain whirlwinds, and after completing the circle, after so many ages, after so many and such great labors of mortals, have not advanced a step, but have been thrown back to the beginning of the course, and that the human race, pierced like the leaky jars of the Danaids, performs a task, ever pouring in water that ever flows out?
Indeed, it is a common saying that what once existed returns again and again, and that nothing new happens under the sun.
But it is equally true that the same things never return, and that one cannot step into the same river twice.
Indeed, while in human affairs earlier ages seem in a certain way to be repeated, nevertheless these things, which you might think to be the same, have greatly changed their character.
By this change, although with a slow motion, the human race progresses and advances, striving of its own accord toward perfection.

For such is the nature of the mind, that, although the body, which we share with the beasts, only reproduces bodies no better than those from which they were born, the reason implanted in the mind grows with the succession of ages, because each later person, taught by the earlier one, increases the resources of the mind, and purges, corrects, and amplifies what was previously known and discovered;
But while the body serves, let the mind be free and command itself, and as the powers of the mind grow, freedom grows, which no one will think I confuse with license:
For license uses only the appearance of freedom, so as to exercise the most savage tyranny:

Now with freedom increased gradually and step by step, we shall be less constrained by the bonds of necessity, because we govern ourselves, and with a milder rule day by day love and clemency will reign instead of severity and vengeance.
This is that law which history, unless I am mistaken, promulgates as prescribed for human affairs by providence.

But when I dare to propose this, although I would not deny that, just as by a natural evil cities are shaken by earthquakes and are swallowed up by a chasm of the earth, and the most fertile regions are devastated by floods, and great families are destroyed by pestilence;

Thus you might think that whole nations and ages are attacked by diseases of the mind, and that many things happen otherwise than is consistent with that law, which I have mentioned, and with the wisdom and goodness of the divine will;
that obstacles are thrown in the way of the human mind's course;
that barbarism sometimes breaks in;
that some states grow, others decline;

that peoples, once most adorned with every kind of civilization, fall asleep in torpor and grow old in idleness, and that the whole human race does not rejoice at the same time in equal flourishing, but that the seats of more perfect culture and learning change in turn:

Nevertheless, I am not more disturbed by these things than anyone somewhat more intelligent will doubt about providence, if he has seen not a few of the best men oppressed by diseases and poverty, shut up in prison, tortured by torments, and disgraced, while meanwhile others, to use the words of a certain most eloquent man, covered with all kinds of crimes, live in the greatest pleasures and enjoy the most favorable fortune in all their affairs.
But I think that the human race takes growth from its very impediments, because in the struggle strength is nourished and sinews are stretched:

And those who resist reason already on the point of victory, we see them generally carried away as if by a river and overcome, whom I said a little before are to be cast aside as now useless instruments, remnants of a past age, not supports for the present:
Finally, a more refined culture, however much it changes its seat, which you might think to be the same, has greatly changed the character:
By this change, although with a slow motion, the human race advances and makes progress, striving of its own accord toward perfection.

For such is the nature of the mind, that, although the body, which we share with the animals, only reproduces bodies no better than those from which they were born, the reason implanted in the mind grows with the succession of ages, because each later person, taught by the earlier one, increases the resources of the mind, and purges, corrects, and amplifies what was previously known and discovered;
But although the body serves, let the mind be free and command itself, and while the powers of the mind grow, freedom grows, which no one will think I confuse with license:
For license uses only the appearance of freedom, so that it exercises the most cruel tyranny:

Now, with freedom increased gradually and step by step, we will be less constrained by the bonds of necessity, because we moderate ourselves, and with a gentler rule day by day, love and mercy will reign instead of severity and vengeance.
This is that law which history, unless I am mistaken, proclaims as prescribed for human affairs by providence.

But when I dare to set this forth, although I will not deny that, just as by a fault of nature cities are shaken by earthquakes and are swallowed up by a chasm of the earth, and the most fertile regions are devastated by floods, and great families are destroyed by pestilence;

Thus you might think that whole nations and ages are attacked by diseases of the mind, and that many things happen otherwise than is consistent with that law, which I have mentioned, and with the wisdom and goodness of the divine nature;
that hindrances are thrown in the way of the human mind's course;
that barbarism sometimes breaks in;
that some states grow, others are diminished;

that peoples, once most adorned with every kind of civilization, fall into a torpor and grow old in sloth, and that the whole human race does not rejoice at the same time in an equal bloom, but that the seats of more perfect culture and learning change in turn:

Nevertheless, I am not more disturbed by these things than anyone a little more intelligent will doubt about providence, if he has seen not a few of the best men oppressed by diseases and poverty, shut up in prison, tortured by torments, and afflicted with disgrace, while meanwhile others, to use the words of a certain most eloquent man, covered with all kinds of crimes, live in the greatest pleasures and enjoy the most favorable fortune in all their affairs.
But I think that the human race takes growth from the very obstacles, because in the struggle strength is nourished and sinews are stretched.

And those who resist reason already on the point of victory, we see them generally carried away as if by a river and overcome, whom I said a little before are to be cast away as now useless instruments, remnants of a past age, not supports for the present.
Finally, a more refined culture, although it changes its abode, gradually spreads wider and wider, takes root more deeply, and is established more firmly.
Now let it be permitted to illustrate what I have said with a few examples.
It is agreed that the beginnings of culture are to be sought in the East.

There in ancient times, what each person had to handle was not determined by one's own will, nor by one's character and talent, but with the tasks assigned by family, the origin of each person cast the die for his entire life:
which now in this culture of states is restricted to the princes alone.
Therefore the human mind obeyed the necessity of nature;
this necessity had subjected the greatest part of men to the harshest servitude;
nor was there any place left for flight, nor did anyone seek better things:
so much did servitude itself please.
Marriages were uncertain, almost like those of brute animals:
they were maidservants rather than mothers of families:
states were almost none, but there was for the most part a most unjust domination.
Arts were not neglected;

But the unformed shapes, which had been born and fashioned by a certain natural impulse, have been consecrated forever and have remained unmoved, because the mind, not yet mature, preferred to acquiesce in what had been handed down, and was not yet equal to undertaking new inventions and attempting more perfect works:

In the same way, the priests among the Egyptians most diligently sanctioned those figures and songs which seemed to them to be proper, and they took care that no sculptor or painter or any other craftsman should fashion or invent anything else besides those.

From this it came about that things which had been drawn or carved many thousands of years before did not differ from the most recent ones, nor were they more beautiful or more deformed, but were made with exactly the same skill.
But literature and learning were generally confined within the boundaries of religions, not differing much from mythology.
But the poetry and wisdom of the Indians, as if by divination, opened up a more sublime understanding of things.
And the nation of the Jews, although not even itself freed from superstitious fear, occupied a more sacred opinion concerning the supreme deity.
Now the Greeks, with a freer movement of their intellects, broke those bonds by which the East was constrained, and escaped from custody.
Liberty shone forth in the republic, if not tempered in the most just manner, at any rate as the mother and leader of the greatest deeds and most beautiful achievements.
Private affairs, even marriages, which they say Cecrops instituted, were arranged according to the law of a more correct reason.
Arts and letters advance, as he says, with winged step.
The form of beauty, immortal and eternal, a visible image of the eternal mind, is expressed in most perfect and, as it were, living and walking images.
Philosophy begins to penetrate the inner sanctuaries of nature and of the mind with deep thought.
Nevertheless, it gradually spreads more and more widely, and sends its roots deeper, and is established more firmly.
Now let it be permitted to illustrate with a few examples what I have said.
It is established that the beginnings of civilization are to be sought in the East.

There in ancient times, what each person had to handle was not determined by one's own will, nor by one's natural disposition and talent, but with tasks assigned by family, one's origin cast the die for one's entire life.
This, in the present culture of states, is restricted to the rulers alone.
Therefore the human mind obeyed the necessity of nature;
This necessity subjected the greatest part of mankind to the harshest servitude;

Marriages were uncertain, almost like those of brute beasts:
They were maidservants rather than mothers of families:

The arts were not neglected;

But the unformed shapes, which had been born and fashioned by a certain natural impulse, have been consecrated forever and have remained unmoved, because the mind, not yet mature, preferred to acquiesce in what had been handed down, and was not yet equal to undertaking new inventions and attempting more perfect works:

In the same way, the priests among the Egyptians, whatever figures and songs seemed to them to be proper, these they established most carefully, and they took care that no sculptor or painter or any other craftsman should fashion or invent anything else besides those.

From this it came about that things which had been sketched or carved many thousands of years before did not differ from the most recent ones, nor were they more beautiful or more deformed, but were made with exactly the same art.
But literature and learning were generally confined within the boundaries of religions, not differing much from mythology.
But the poetry and wisdom of the Indians, as if by divination, opened up a higher understanding of things.
And the nation of the Jews, although not even it was freed from superstitious fear, occupied a more sacred opinion concerning the supreme deity.
Now the Greeks, with a freer movement of their intellects, broke those bonds by which the East was constrained, and escaped from custody.
Liberty shone forth in the state, if not tempered in the most just manner, at least as the mother and leader of the greatest deeds and most beautiful achievements.
Private affairs, even marriages, which they say Cecrops instituted, were arranged according to the law of a more correct reason;
Arts and letters advance, as he says, with winged step;
The form of beauty, immortal and eternal, the visible image of the eternal mind, is expressed in most perfect and, as it were, living and walking images:
Philosophy begins to penetrate the inner sanctuaries of nature and the mind with deep thought.
Nevertheless, traces of ancient inhumanity and harshness remain:
some are free, others are slaves;
and not yet does the female sex have its own honor;
and not yet is the common people freed from immense superstition, although the wise see the truth.
And Greece was also infected with other vices;
these things rather brought destruction upon it than the Macedonians and Romans.
I will not speak of the kingdom of the Persians, overthrown by Alexander the Great:

Although even through this man the light of the mind was propagated, as is shown by the Egyptian kingdom and the strength and power of Alexandrian learning, which was greater and more useful than it seemed to most people.
Soon Rome imposed laws on the world.

Although it was inferior to Greece in learning, yet it not only adorned the institutions of life and the public and domestic affairs better, but that very part of civilization which it owed to the Greeks it spread widely among the barbarous peoples of old, and tamed the wild nations, to whom amid arms it gave at the same time laws, and prepared the soil for a new sowing.
The beginnings of the Christian religion made this greatest sowing, just as from the smallest seeds huge things are born.

For just as Aeschylus established that after the ancient gods, that stern and harsh offspring of eternal night, more gentle and more intelligent gods, more favorable to men, succeeded, he, that first one, as it seems to me, divined with a lofty mind that the progress of the human mind gradually grew stronger.

Thus the Christian religion, after the old ceremonies were abolished, tamed the world, and not only reconciled the mortal race to God, but also strove to reconcile man to man, people to people, and all to grace and freedom, and to bring it about that, as that excellent poet famously declared, you may be just without necessity and hence not without a share of the blessed life, but never perish utterly.
Indeed, long ago, the providence of the divine mind had laid the foundations for that better understanding of divine and human affairs;
Nor do I fear to affirm that there were long ago not a few who judged and discoursed most worthily about these matters;

Already Plato, as it were, proclaimed the sovereignty of purer reason, and Socrates and the Stoics, although they did not deny that the duties of a good citizen also must be performed, exalted humanity above the state:
Those who profess this opinion are so far from causing harm to the state that they are even likely to improve civil affairs according to the laws of humanity.
Indeed, there were those who, with a truly Christian sense, valued humanity itself solely by its likeness to divinity.
But nevertheless both the priests and those who administered the state resisted, until the Christian cause prevailed.
However, I would not want us to be too angry with men of lofty genius, who, fixed in the excellence of earlier learning, [retain] traces of its ancient inhumanity and harshness:
some are free, some are slaves;
and not yet has its own honor been given to the female sex;
and not yet was the common people freed from immense superstition, although the wise see the truth.
And Greece was also infected with other vices;
these things rather brought destruction upon them than the Macedonians and Romans.
I will not speak of the kingdom of the Persians, which was overthrown by Alexander the Great:

although even through him the light of the mind was spread abroad, as is shown by the Egyptian kingdom and the strength and power of Alexandrian learning, which was greater and more useful than it has seemed to most people.
Soon Rome imposed laws upon the whole world;

Although it was inferior to Greece in learning, yet it not only adorned the institutions of life and the public and domestic affairs better, but it also spread widely among the barbarian peoples of old that part of civilization which it owed to the Greeks, and it civilized the wild nations, to whom amid arms it gave at the same time laws, and prepared the soil for a new sowing.
This greatest sowing, as from the smallest seeds huge things are born, the beginnings of the Christian religion made.

For just as Aeschylus established that after the ancient gods, that stern and harsh offspring of eternal night, there succeeded milder and more intelligent gods more favorable to men, he, the first, as it seems to me, augured with a lofty mind that the progress of the human mind gradually grew stronger.

Thus the Christian religion, after the old ceremonies were abolished, tamed the world, and not only reconciled the mortal race to God, but also strove to reconcile man to man, people to people, and all to grace and freedom, and to bring it about that, as that excellent poet famously declared, you may be just without necessity and hence not without a share of the blessed life, but never perish utterly.
Indeed, the providence that foresees had long since laid the foundations for that better understanding of divine and human affairs;
Nor do I fear to affirm that there were not a few long ago who judged and discoursed about them most worthily;

Already Plato, as it were, proclaimed the dominion of purer reason, and Socrates and the Stoics, although they did not deny that the duties of a good citizen also had to be performed, exalted humanity above the state:
Those who profess this opinion are so far from causing harm to the state that they are even likely to correct civil affairs according to the laws of humanity.
Indeed, there were those who, with a truly Christian sense, valued humanity itself solely by its likeness to divinity.
But both the priests and those who administered the state nevertheless resisted, until the Christian cause prevailed.

However, I would not want us to be too angry with men of lofty genius, who, fixed in the excellence of earlier learning and dazzled by its splendor, followed the ruin of the old discipline with a not ignoble grief:
for these too seemed to themselves to be filled with God, and they did not yet understand those good things which the new superstition, as they called it, was about to bring;

And a greater madness of Christian fanatics excuses them, who raged against those who disagreed with such cruelty as might perhaps befit the furious ministers of Bellona among the Comans, not those who had been instructed in the precepts of charity by a divine teacher.

Indeed, after the Christian religion brought such great light and improvement to the human race, and subdued so many barbarous nations under its gentle yoke, which, roused from their ancient seats, had invaded and reduced to subjection the most cultivated lands of Europe;
soon that very religion, no less than the affairs of the Greeks and Romans once, worn out as if by old age, decayed, and was corrupted in various ways.

For although it had freed bodies to a great extent, it had especially freed minds, and led them into a new servitude, from which not even philosophy, which is by its nature most free, could sufficiently vindicate itself:
The pontifical power even attempted to subject kingdoms and princes to a not very equitable rule:

The unlearned clergy, for the most part devoid of good literature, dissolved in softness and luxury, were polluted by lust, avarice, treachery, and any evil arts more than the priests of the pagan gods once were.

These and other evils, not without providence, I think, were remedied by the great things which, from the fifteenth century onward and shortly after, the human mind accomplished, using not arms but the strength of intellect:
Although afterwards even arms were taken up, because power sought to impose force upon intellect.
For first, by the most bitter contentions of the most excellent men, literature was renewed.

Whatever survived from antiquity was brought out of the darkness and turned with the greatest zeal to this end, that the fog by which minds had been obscured might be dispelled, that a sound judgment about things divine and human might be established, that preconceived opinions by which the freedom of the mind is hindered might be cast aside, and that a more refined cultivation of intellects might be restored:

And to this lively movement the recently invented printing press brought enormous weight, which not only disseminates whatever is entrusted to it so quickly and over such immense spaces that this Daedalian contrivance at last seems to have made words truly winged and flying, but at the same time also gives to these flying words a bronze-like firmness and permanence, and brings it about that common understanding can now scarcely be suppressed by anyone's force.
A new flower of the arts, especially of painting, had appeared, which arts themselves, if dazzled by the splendor of poetry, were mourning the ruin of the old discipline with no ignoble grief:
For these too seemed to themselves to be filled with God, and they did not yet understand those good things which the new superstition, as they called it, was about to bring;

And it excuses those [Christians] the greater fury of Christian fanatics, who raged against dissenters with such cruelty as might perhaps befit the frenzied ministers of Bellona among the Comans, not those who were instructed by a divine teacher in the precepts of charity.

Indeed, after the Christian religion brought such great light and improvement to the human race, and subdued so many barbarous nations under its gentle yoke—nations that, roused from their ancient seats, had invaded and brought under their dominion the most cultivated lands of Europe—
soon that very religion itself, no less than the affairs of the Greeks and Romans once, as if worn out by old age, withered away, and was corrupted in various ways.

For although it had freed bodies to a great extent, it had especially freed minds, and led them into a new servitude, from which not even philosophy, which is by its nature most free, could sufficiently vindicate itself:
The pontifical power even attempted to subject kingdoms and princes to a not very equitable rule:

The unlearned clergy, for the most part lacking in good letters, dissolved in softness and luxury, were defiled by lust, avarice, treachery, and any evil arts whatsoever, more than the priests of the pagan gods were once.

These and other evils, not without providence, I think, were remedied by the great things which, from the fifteenth century onward and shortly after, the human mind accomplished, using not the strength of arms but the power of intellect:
Although afterwards even arms were taken up, because power strove to bring force against intellect.
For first, by the most bitter contentions of the most excellent men, literature was restored.

Whatever survived from antiquity was brought forth from darkness and turned with the greatest zeal to this end, that the darkness by which minds had been clouded might be dispelled, that a sound judgment concerning things divine and human might be established, that preconceived opinions by which the freedom of minds is hindered might be cast aside, and that a more refined cultivation of intellects might be restored:

And to this lively movement the recently invented printing press brought enormous weight, which not only disseminates whatever is entrusted to it so quickly and over such immense spaces that this Daedalian contrivance seems at last to have rendered words truly winged and flying, but at the same time also provides an airy firmness and permanence to these flying sayings, and brings it about that common understanding can now scarcely be suppressed by anyone's force.

A new flower of the arts, especially of painting, has arisen, which arts themselves, if you except a few genres of poetry and a certain not-to-be-despised form of architecture, had lain prostrate after the destruction of Greek and Roman antiquity.

Now what was more desired than a more correct and more holy constitution of sacred things and a salutary restoration of the church, attempted indeed earlier by one and another, but suppressed by fire through the barbarous cruelty of priestly tyrants?
Luther therefore undertook this reformation of sacred rites with a bold enterprise and accomplished it:
which, without doubt, would have brought forth more joyful fruits sooner, had not most atrocious wars intercepted the harvest.
But with the world somewhat pacified, in many lands of Europe letters and disciplines grew with continuous success:
the most important peoples so cultivated their languages and especially poetry, that they could emulate antiquity;
the studies of history, nature, and mathematics were advanced very far by the assiduous labors of innumerable scholars;

Philosophy, however, through many successive steps, which it seems superfluous to enumerate before this assembly of most learned men and studious youths, especially since some of those who excelled in philosophy lived in the very Prussian kingdom, partly in this very city and among ourselves, ascended to the highest and broadest knowledge.
I am not the sort of person who would marvel at the greatness of this age and think that our learning is perfect and complete in all respects;

But he would be unfair and no less ungrateful to our ancestors, whose benefits we enjoy, than to the present generation, if he denied that the human race has made great progress, and that civilization is growing day by day better, more liberal, and more humane; which, after a new world besides emerged, as it were, from the ocean more than three hundred years ago, now surrounds and occupies this whole terrestrial globe, whereas in the most flourishing times of Greece it was confined to the narrow circuit of the Mediterranean Sea.

Already now even barbarians are beginning to taste and to love the arts of more civilized Europe, and peoples who had languished in idleness and long torpor are rising again and recovering their strength.

Therefore, both princes and peoples ought to serve the common interests of the human race by increasing them, and each one ought to strive according to his ability to satisfy the position in which he has been placed.
No man returns into his cradle, no one offers himself to be bound in swaddling clothes;
Nor shall we fall back more completely into the condition of the East or of Greek antiquity, or of the so-called Middle Ages.

Nevertheless, since not all peoples, as we indicated above, move at the same pace, nor do they advance with equal effort, you would have accepted a few types and a certain definite form of architecture not to be despised, which had lain neglected after Greek and Roman antiquity had been abolished.

Now what was more desired than a more correct and more holy constitution of sacred things and a salutary restoration of the church, attempted indeed earlier by one and another, but suppressed by fire through the barbarous cruelty of priestly tyrants?
Therefore Luther undertook this reformation of sacred rites in a bold enterprise and accomplished it:
This, without doubt, would have brought forth more joyful fruits sooner, had not most atrocious wars intercepted the harvest.
But with the world somewhat pacified, in many lands of Europe literature and learning grew with continuous success:
the most distinguished peoples so cultivated their languages and especially their poetry that they could rival antiquity;
the studies of history, nature, and mathematics were advanced very far by the constant labors of countless scholars;

Philosophy, however, through many successive steps, which it seems superfluous to enumerate before this assembly of most learned men and studious youths, especially since some of those who excelled in philosophy lived in the very Prussian kingdom, partly in this very city and among ourselves, ascended to the highest and broadest knowledge.
I am not the sort of person who would marvel at the greatness of this age and think that our learning is perfect and complete in every respect;

But he would be unfair and no less ungrateful to our ancestors, whose benefits we enjoy, than to the present generation, if he denied that the human race has made great progress, and that culture is growing day by day better, more liberal, and more gentle; which, after a new world besides emerged, as it were, from the Ocean more than three hundred years ago, now surrounds and occupies this whole terrestrial globe, whereas in the most flourishing times of Greece it was confined to the narrow circuit of the Mediterranean Sea.

Already now even the barbarians are beginning to taste and to love the arts of more civilized Europe, and peoples who had languished in sluggishness and long torpor are beginning to rise again and recover their strength.

Therefore, both princes and peoples ought to serve the common interests of the human race by increasing them, and each one ought to strive according to his ability to satisfy the position in which he has been placed.
No man returns to his cradle, nor offers himself to be bound in swaddling clothes.
Nor shall we fall back more completely into the condition of the East, whether of Greek antiquity or of the so-called Middle Ages.

Yet since not all peoples, as we indicated above, move at the same pace, nor do human affairs advance with equal effort, some through indolence and stupidity retain for a longer time a worse condition;
others at least promptly follow the foreign impulse and allow themselves to be dragged along;
Some are leaders beyond others in undertaking better things, especially when they have been stirred and driven by the talent of some outstanding man.

And sometimes provinces have even been divided among these, with one people deserving well by cultivating literature or arts exceptionally, another by ordering public affairs or other institutions of life more correctly.
But those peoples who are leaders to better things and in every age, and who do not follow too late, these, however small, alone almost come into the census of humanity;
The rest, like proletarians, are counted almost in no number except that of heads.
Thus those small Athens, placed by Pericles especially on the highest summit, were the eye of the world and the delight of every most learned person;

The Persian kingdom, extending most widely through the vast regions of Asia, is held in a much lower position by just estimators of things, who compare nations by the virtue of the mind, not by the multitude of slaves:
But the Scythians, Sarmatians, and Huns, however strong and powerful they may have been at some time, you would count among the last of mortals.

But I will say in very few words how much this kingdom, which is now called by the name of Prussia, has contributed and contributes to the progress of mind and reason among the more civilized states of the modern age.
The lineage of our princes, together with the peoples who then obeyed them, was among the first to join in the reformation of sacred things;

And today Frederick William is regarded as the leader and, in a certain way, the defender of the evangelical confession, the same man as the wisest reconciler of parties once in disagreement, thinking that all good men ought to be united by mutual love, not to be separated by hatreds on account of certain doctrines scarcely, and not even scarcely, understood.

Frederick the Great taught by example and by law to tolerate those who held a different persuasion about divine matters, and he granted [the freedom] to think what you wish, and to say what you think.
Barbarous and cruel institutions, once sanctioned by the laws themselves, have been abolished.
The Prussian kings greatly fostered literature and the arts, but no one more brilliantly than Frederick William.
By this merit, just as he consulted the whole of Germany, so he also holds forth a torch to the same and to all Europe for the society of commerce to be extended more widely every year.
And this very thing may also be counted among the progress of the human race.

Now if no one who is a bit more prudent fails to understand that many things are still lacking for the perfection of humanity, and that in not a few matters the present state is so far surpassed by earlier centuries, and that any human society, as soon as it has begun to establish itself, [and] human affairs, some through sloth and stupidity retain for a longer time a worse state;
others certainly follow the foreign impulse in time and allow themselves to be dragged along;
Others, more than the rest, are leaders for undertaking better things, especially when they have been stirred and driven by the talent of some excellent man.

And sometimes provinces have even been divided among these, with one people deserving well by cultivating literature or arts exceptionally, another by ordering public affairs or other institutions of life more correctly.
But those peoples who are leaders to better things and in every age, and who do not follow too late, these, however small, alone almost come into the census of humanity;
The rest, like proletarians, are counted almost only by the number of heads.
Thus that little Athens, placed especially by Pericles on the highest pinnacle, was the eye of the world and the delight of every most learned person;

The Persian kingdom, extending most widely through the vast regions of Asia, is placed in a much lower position by just estimators of things, who compare nations by the virtue of the mind, not by the multitude of slaves:
But the Scythians, Sarmatians, and Huns, however strong and powerful they may have been at times, you would count among the last of mortals.

But I will say in very few words how much this kingdom, which is now called by the name of Prussia, has contributed and contributes to the progress of mind and reason among the more civilized states of the modern age.
The line of our princes, together with the peoples who then obeyed them, was among the first to undertake the reformation of sacred things;

And today Frederick William is regarded as the leader and, in a certain way, the defender of the evangelical confession, the same man, the wisest reconciler of parties once in disagreement, thinking that all good men ought to be united by mutual love, not to be separated by hatreds on account of certain doctrines scarcely, and not even scarcely, understood.

Frederick the Great taught by example and by law to tolerate those who held a different persuasion about divine matters, and he granted [the freedom] to think what you wish, and to say what you think.
Barbarous and cruel institutions, once sanctioned by the laws themselves, have been abolished.
The Prussian kings fostered literature and the arts to an extraordinary degree, but no one more brilliantly than Frederick William.
By this merit, just as he consulted the whole of Germany, so he also holds a torch before it and the whole of Europe for extending the community of commerce more widely every year.
And this too may be counted among the progress of the human race.

Now if no one who is even a little more prudent fails to understand that many things are still lacking for the perfection of culture, and that in not a few matters the present state is so far surpassed by earlier centuries, and that any human society, as soon as it has begun to establish itself, is carried backward, and that for minds as for bodies there is need of frequent motion to preserve health, lest the juices stagnate and become corrupted, and lest, as Tacitus says, even the sweetness of idleness itself creep in, and sloth, at first hated, afterwards be loved;

If, moreover, it must be conceded that the whole affairs of the human race are governed by one mind and reason, and consequently that from the knowledge and science of divine and human things alone, institutions both public and private proceed, depend, and improve somewhat better:

That which seems to have moved Cicero, a man far wiser than most of those who despise him, to say that philosophy produced cities, called scattered men together into a society of life, and joined them to one another first by dwellings, then by marriages, then by the sharing of letters and words, and that it was the inventor of laws, the teacher of morals and discipline:

Therefore, if those things which I have said are true, this glorious task has been imposed upon the most honorable leisure of all who devote themselves to learning: that they should provide those things by which public and private welfare may be increased.
This is first accomplished by preserving the memory of the best things, which the earlier age has produced.
Whoever destroys or neglects that memory, which removes that knowledge to which our life owes itself, seems to me to be, as it were, a parricide.
Then that only field, which our parents left to us as heirs, must be cultivated and worked with new labor, lest it become barren, and from it new crops must be generated.
Of these things, one belongs to historical learning in each kind of erudition, the other to rational meditation.
But both of these have been entrusted to us, the teachers of universities, so that we may hand over the knowledge of our age to the young men who will be the teachers of a future age.
We sow the seeds;
we scarcely see the ripe fruits.
But if we are rightly minded, we will so form our pupils that they may advance beyond what we ourselves have achieved:

And to use an old saying, when we are weary with years, just as in the games of the gymnasia among the Greeks, we hand the burning torches to a fresh runner, what wonder if he, having entered upon a new course, will run more swiftly than we, exhausted?
The Spartans ordered their boys to promise in a public ceremony, in song, that they would one day be much braver than those who then excelled in courage.
So why should we not willingly allow ourselves to be surpassed by those who come after us?
By this path the mind and reason emerge victorious, virtue grows, and the human race is formed toward the end divinely appointed for it.
This path is approved by Frederick William, who, if he had not wished to be walked on in this way, would not have so greatly supported literature and the arts:

for these do not lead to any other than this one, being carried backwards, and that just as bodies, so minds need frequent motion to preserve health, lest the juices stagnate and become corrupted, and lest, as Tacitus says, even the sweetness of idleness itself creeps in, and laziness, at first disliked, is later loved;

If, moreover, it must be conceded that all the affairs of the human race are governed by one mind and reason, and consequently that institutions, both public and private, derive, depend upon, and advance from almost only the knowledge and science of divine and human things, being somewhat better:

That which seems to have moved Cicero, a man far wiser than most of those who despise him, to say that philosophy gave birth to cities, called scattered men together into a society of life, and joined them to one another first by dwellings, then by marriages, then by the sharing of letters and words, and was the inventor of laws, the teacher of morals and discipline:

Therefore, if what I have said is true, whoever devotes themselves to learning has this noble task imposed upon their most honorable leisure: to provide those things by which public and private welfare may be increased.
This is first accomplished by preserving the memory of the best things, which an earlier age has produced.
Whoever destroys or neglects that memory, which removes that knowledge to which our life owes itself, seems to me to be, as it were, a parricide.
Then that only thing, which our parents left to us as heirs, must be cultivated and exercised with new labor, lest it become sterile, and from it new things must be generated.
Of these things, one belongs to historical learning in each kind of erudition, the other to rational meditation.
But both of these have been entrusted to us, the teachers of universities, so that we may hand over the knowledge of our age to the young men who will be the doctors of a future age:
We sow the seeds;
we scarcely see the ripe fruits.
But if we are rightly minded, we will so form our pupils that they may advance further than we ourselves have progressed.

And to use an old saying, when we are weary with years, just as in the gymnasium games among the Greeks, we hand the burning torches to a fresh runner, what wonder if he, entering upon a new course, will run more swiftly than we, exhausted?
The Spartans ordered their boys to promise in a public ceremony, in song, that they would one day be much braver than those who then excelled in courage.
So why should we not willingly allow ourselves to be surpassed by those who come after us?
By this path the mind and reason emerge victorious, virtue grows, and the human race is formed toward the end divinely appointed for it.
This path is approved by Frederick William, who, if he had not wished to be walked on in this way, would not have so greatly supported literature and the arts:
for these do not lead to any other path than this one:
he would not have founded this our wrestling school of the best studies.
Therefore, what was for me today the beginning of speaking, let the same be the end.

So often, when I have been discoursing on these solemn occasions, such a great light of royal wisdom, liberality, humanity, and gentleness has arisen for me, that, since I judge that man to be perfected by these virtues who offers himself as the most suitable instrument for carrying out the counsels of providence, I think that Frederick William so fulfills the great office entrusted to him that he serves not only the growth of the republic but also of human affairs with the most favorable success.
Therefore we venerate him as king, we love him as father.
I have spoken.

Therefore, what was for me today the beginning of speaking, let that be the end.

So often, while I have been discoursing on these solemn occasions, such a great light of royal wisdom, liberality, humanity, and gentleness has arisen for me, that, since I judge that man to be perfected by these virtues who offers himself as an instrument most apt for carrying out the counsels of providence, I think that Frederick William fulfills the office entrusted to him in such a way that he serves not only the growth of the republic but also of human affairs with the most favorable success.
Therefore we venerate him as king, we love him as father.
I have spoken.

div.head: XXIV. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXXVI. habita.

p.s: There are two things, listeners, from which anyone who has decided to praise either a state or a prince or a private citizen can seek material for praise: fortune and virtue.
And fortune indeed, although it is not in our power, nevertheless itself also has its admirers:

In part rightly and correctly, because, as proverbial wisdom teaches, each person contributes something to shaping his own fortune, and the highest prosperity comes by the benefit of nature and of the divine will, whose favor no one doubts to count among things praiseworthy;
In part by a more imprudent estimation, which the crowd generally follows, marveling at the splendor of birth, wealth, and power.
But who does not know the fragility of fortune?
Who has not seen that he who was but lately regarded as most fortunate has been struck down by sudden ruin and overwhelmed by the waves of calamity?
Therefore virtue alone is that which, in the judgment of the wise, is worthy of praise.
I, now about to speak of a prince, will not boast of the title of felicity, with which Rome did not disdain to adorn her Augusti, more through foolish flattery than from the truth of the matter:
I will take my stand on virtue.
This is indeed a great subject, and one that demands a great orator:
for one may declaim about happiness, but not likewise about virtue:
But you, in accordance with your indulgence, will judge my speech not by what I have accomplished, but by what I have intended.
But if you ask by what means the virtue of a prince is completed and perfected, although the answer may seem difficult, I have one that is both ready and very simple.

I affirm that the prince, because he must fulfill all duties in his own household as a private master, and because publicly he is not occupied with one or another single business, but presides over the whole of affairs and embraces all parts of the state, cannot be considered perfect unless he is equipped with all the virtues that human nature can attain.
Since no single mortal seems adequate for this task, you might say that the perfect virtue of a prince can be conceived in the mind, but not realized in practice.

Therefore, both the lot of a prince is miserable, since, however excellent he may be, he still cannot attain the highest good, and a harsh necessity is imposed on men to obey those who, even with the most strenuous effort, cannot reach universal princely virtue, but must be content with certain small parts or fragments of virtue.
And indeed such is the weakness of the human race that it can accomplish nothing perfect without divine aid.
Nevertheless, I deny that anyone is equal to attaining all the virtues.
Therefore, I do not even concede that a prince can fail to be sufficient, in some part, for all his duties.

For if the virtues were so constituted that they dwelt in separate abodes, as it were, and did not remain harmonious in one seat, and wherever one had entered, the other would rush out and withdraw from there, or would resist outside the doors and threshold;
You would rightly doubt whether anyone could satisfy all his duties, whether private or public.
But I see that the greatest philosophers decide otherwise, and it is by far the safest to follow them in a matter which cannot be rightly judged except by philosophers.

For it is not the case that, just as the mouth, nostrils, eyes, and ears are distinct and different parts of the face, so the individual virtues are parts of the whole of virtue divided and separated from one another; nor is it the case that, just as one who has been deprived of eyes nevertheless retains the ears and the other parts of the face, so one who lacks wisdom or courage can nonetheless be adorned with the remaining virtues:
But there is one virtue which embraces each and every one of them, and each individual virtue contains both the rest and the whole.
There is none that excludes any other, none is contrary to any other.
To discuss especially the cardinal virtues, as they are called: justice in itself contains wisdom, temperance, fortitude;

And courage—I mean true courage, not what is commonly counted as courage—boldness carried by blind impulse, courage, I say, belongs to no one unless he is both just and wise and in that which I would have wished.
But if you ask by what things the virtue of a prince is perfected and completed, although the answer may seem difficult, I have one answer, both ready and very simple.

I affirm that the prince, who, both as a private master, ought to discharge all the duties in his household, and publicly is not occupied with one or another single business, but presides over the sum of affairs and embraces all parts of the state, cannot be considered perfect, unless he is furnished with all the virtues by which human nature can attain possession.
Since no single mortal seems adequate for this task, you might say that the perfect virtue of a prince can indeed be conceived in the mind, but not realized in practice.

Therefore, both the lot of a prince is miserable, since, however excellent he may be, he still cannot attain the highest good, and a harsh necessity is imposed on men to obey those who, even with the most intense exertion, cannot reach universal princely virtue, but must be content with certain small parts or fragments of virtue.
And indeed such is the weakness of the human race that it can accomplish nothing perfect without divine aid.
Nevertheless, I deny that anyone is equal to attaining all the virtues.
Therefore, I do not even concede that a prince can fail to some extent to fulfill all his duties.

For if the virtues were so constituted that they dwelt in separate abodes, as it were, and did not remain together in one seat, and wherever one had entered, the other would rush out and withdraw from there, or would resist outside the doors and threshold;
You would rightly doubt whether anyone could satisfy all his duties, whether private or public.
But I see that the greatest philosophers decide otherwise, and it is by far the safest to follow them in a matter that cannot be rightly judged except by philosophers.

For it is not the case that, just as the mouth, nostrils, eyes, and ears are distinct and different parts of the face, so the individual virtues are parts of the whole of virtue, divided and separated from one another; nor is it the case that, just as one who has been deprived of eyes nevertheless retains the ears and the other parts of the face, so one who lacks wisdom or courage can nonetheless be adorned with the remaining virtues:
But there is one virtue which embraces each and every one of the individual virtues, and each individual virtue contains both the rest and the whole.
There is no virtue that excludes any other, and there is no virtue that is contrary to any other.
To discuss especially the cardinal virtues, as they are called, justice contains in itself wisdom, temperance, and fortitude.
And courage—I mean true courage, not what is commonly regarded as courage, boldness carried by blind impulse—courage, I say, belongs to no one unless he is both just and wise and temperate.
And similarly the rest in turn.

To add sanctity, can anyone be considered holy who is not also intelligent, just and fair, of temperate and moderate character in any circumstances of life, and finally, when the situation demands it, even courageous?
Therefore, in whatever position each person is placed, he must share in the whole of virtue, so that he may properly perform his duty;
And so far is it from being the case that one cannot become possessed of it, that whoever has thoroughly attained one virtue holds the whole.
Therefore it is less fitting to ask anxiously whether anyone can attain the whole royal virtue.
How these things are present in our most merciful King, both all of you who have come here to venerate him know well, and I have often either sketched in passing or explained with deliberate effort:
Today I will confine myself to considering a single virtue.
For although all virtues dwell together in the greatest harmony, yet different circumstances, different times, and different outcomes demand that one virtue be brought forward especially.
Frederick William indeed fell into that age which commanded one virtue to be shown after another.

His steadfastness of mind and courage in the great calamity both of himself and of the state, and in waging the most savage wars; his wisdom and justice in restoring and ordering the commonwealth, which we saw shaken and prostrate; his moderation in calming and soothing the minds that had been stirred or exasperated by various goads.
Indeed, Frederick William is most temperate; he is born for the reconciliation of citizens, nations, and peoples.
which is especially needed now.

Indeed, whether in the very bosom of the state or outside it somewhat greater disturbances have arisen, before it has come to arms, no art will be more effective than moderation combined with constancy, which makes leading men fair to all parties and does not allow them to be carried away by passions:
Thus it happens that, like gods from on high and serene, they look down securely upon the turbulent crowd and the fleeting and, for the most part, vain passions of the fickle multitude.
By this moderation, as far as possible, both seditions and wars are guarded against, which greed and pride provoke and nourish.
Let him be moderate;
and similarly the rest in turn.

To add sanctity, can anyone be considered holy who is not also intelligent, just and fair, with temperate and moderate character in any part of life, and finally, when circumstances demand it, even courageous?
Therefore, in whatever position each person is placed, he must share in universal virtue, so that he may rightly perform his duty.
And so far is it from being the case that anyone can be possessed of it, that whoever has thoroughly obtained one virtue holds the whole.
Therefore it is less fitting to ask anxiously whether anyone can attain the whole royal virtue.

How these things are present in our most merciful King, both all of you who have come together here for reverence of him know well, and I have often either sketched in passing or explained with devoted effort.
Today I will confine myself to considering a single virtue.
For although all virtues dwell together in the greatest harmony, yet different circumstances, different times, and different outcomes demand that one virtue be brought forward especially.
Frederick William indeed fell into that age which commanded one virtue to be shown after another:

His steadfastness of mind and courage in the great calamity both of himself and of the state, and in waging the most savage wars; his wisdom and justice in restoring and ordering the commonwealth, which we saw shaken and prostrate; his moderation in calming and soothing the minds that had been stirred or exasperated by various goads.
Indeed, Frederick William is most temperate; he is born for the reconciliation of citizens, nations, and peoples.
which is especially needed now.

Indeed, whether in the very bosom of the state or beyond it somewhat greater disturbances have arisen, before it has come to arms, no art will be more effective than moderation combined with constancy, which makes leading men fair to all parties and does not allow them to be carried away by passions:
Thus it happens that, as it were, gods from on high and serene look down securely upon the turbulent crowd and the fickle multitude's passions, which are for the most part transient and vain.
By this moderation, as far as possible, both seditions and wars are guarded against, which desire and pride provoke and nourish.
What then?
Does not empire itself seem by its very nature to be impatient of limit?
Is it not difficult for those who, from their very birth, have been placed at the highest pinnacle not to become proud?
Whom almost no one contradicts, whom no one dares to correct?
Who see everything placed in their own hand, everything done at their nod, destined by divine will to hold the place of gods on earth?
Indeed, a good natural disposition is needed, lest the leading men fall into that fault to which the very position in which they are placed easily gives them a headlong tendency.

But a self-controlled prince never forgets that he shares the common human weakness with even the humblest person, and that although the prince is indeed a living and breathing law, yet because the prince's will stands in place of law, his own will must be established according to the norm of reason, which alone ought to govern all things, not according to arbitrary desire and lust, and that although he has been divinely placed in charge of the highest affairs, he is a man commanding men.

Finally, the less any sane person dares to compare himself with him, and the greater the interval by which the prince's dignity and majesty are separated from all other mortals, the more moderately can one deal with those who depend entirely on him.
But someone may say that these things are trite and common;
more recondite things are desired.

I indeed, although I think that commonplaces are not to be avoided, provided they are true, and I judge them to be safer for me, because one who wishes to bring forth more recondite matters about the principate ought to have been much engaged in public affairs, from which no one is more remote than I am, since I lurk in the shadow of the school, not unwillingly:
Nevertheless, I will try to discuss these matters briefly, in which the prince's moderation, if not solely, certainly to a great extent and especially, may seem to shine forth.
I will arrange this argument into three places, of which two pertain to domestic matters, the third to foreign affairs.
First I say that the prince should not, with excessive zeal, exalt any one way of life in the state above the rest, and disregard these:

But if any part is nourished too much, while the rest truly wither, it is clear that this part becomes burdensome to them, and the state is sick, since the harmony, concord, and just proportion of the individual limbs have been removed, just as the body does not enjoy full health when some one organ swells excessively and draws away the juices from the others.
The second point is that the prince should not involve himself in the partisan zeal and anger of factions, which arise in most states;
Third, that he be fair to foreign nations as well and be far removed from envy and hatreds, with which one people is accustomed to attack another.

Nam primum quamquam privado non modo hanc damus veniam, ut ad unam aliquam rem animum appellat potissimum, sed hoc ipsum putamus utile ac necessarium esse, propterea quod singuli singulis quibusdam rebus vel artibus tractandis et suapte natura aptiores sunt et exercitatione fiunt etiam sollertiores, dum ii, qui in nulla arte habitant et perseverant, sed huc illuc volitantes, veluti apes ex floribus, variis ex disciplinis trahere aliquid nutrimenti et carpere fructus solent,
opus est indole, ne principes incurrant in id vitium, ad quod eos ipse locus, quo positi sunt, facile dat praecipites;

But a self-controlled prince never forgets that he shares the common human weakness with even the humblest person, and that although the prince is indeed a living and animate law, yet because the prince's will stands for law, his own will must be established according to the norm of reason, which alone ought to govern all things, not according to arbitrary desire and lust, and that although he has been placed by divine will over the highest affairs, he is a man commanding men.

Finally, so that no sane person may dare to compare himself with him, and so that the dignity and majesty of the prince may be separated from all other mortals by a greater interval, the more moderately one can deal with those who depend entirely on him.
But someone may say that these things are trite and common;
more recondite things are desired.

I indeed, although I think that commonplaces are not to be avoided, provided they are true, and I judge them to be safer for me, because one who wishes to bring forth more recondite matters about the principate ought to have been much engaged in public affairs, from which no one is more remote than I am, since I lurk in the shadow of the school, not unwillingly:
Nevertheless, I will try to discuss these matters briefly, in which the prince's moderation, if not solely, certainly to a great extent and especially, may seem to shine forth.
I will arrange this argument into three places, of which two pertain to domestic matters, the third to foreign.
First I say that the prince should not, with excessive zeal, exalt any one sect of life in the state above the rest, and neglect these.

But if any part is nourished too much, while the rest truly wither, it is clear that this part becomes too heavy for them, and the state is sick, since the harmony, concord, and just proportion of the individual members have been removed, just as the body does not enjoy full health when one particular organ swells excessively and draws away the juices from the others.
The second point is that the prince should not involve himself in the partisan zeal and anger of the factions that arise in most states.
Third, that he be fair to foreign nations as well, and be far removed from envy and hatred, with which one people is accustomed to attack another.

For first, although we grant this indulgence not only to a private individual, that he should apply his mind especially to some one thing, but we also think this very thing useful and necessary, because individuals are by their own nature more suited to the handling of certain particular things or arts, and by practice become even more skillful, while those who do not dwell and persevere in any art, but flitting about here and there, like bees from flowers, are accustomed to draw some nourishment and pluck fruits from various disciplines, attempt many things and are imbued with some rough learning, but neither are they perfected themselves nor do they accomplish anything at all:

Nevertheless, a leader, who is not engaged in handling individual matters and performing some particular duty, but holds the reins of government, ought not to hold any art or business so dear as to think that the rest are to be neglected or despised, but, just as a divine power that governs all things provides for all parts of this world, he ought to embrace everything with equal care, to judge all kinds of life with keen judgment according to their own dignity and importance, and to show himself kind to all of them.
In this matter no one will deny that sometimes mistakes are made.
For some princes care only for military matters, others for civil affairs:
or they favor lucrative arts, crafts, and commerce, and think that liberal education is unprofitable and not worthy of public care;
or they neglect too much those things that are altogether necessary for acquiring wealth:
