indeed, from these very things, sometimes agriculture, sometimes commerce has seemed more excellent to princes.
There are those who favor the arts, but care little for literature;

And from literature we have just seen that mathematics and the natural sciences were neglected by them, and that these alone pleased them, but whatever pertains to the cultivation of the human race and the memory of deeds done displeased them greatly, and philosophy was especially hateful;
again others, devoted and enslaved to sacred rites and ceremonies, careless of profane matters, even the most serious;
Others, estranged from sacred rites, or even hostile to them.
Frederick William, what moderation, how wise, how just, he has maintained and maintains in all these matters, there is none of us who does not understand:
He presents a prince almost perfect, as far as human nature allows, burdensome to no kind of life or business, favorable to all, giving to each his due honor.

Now, to come to the second point, where great danger threatens the state from a great agitation of minds, the temperate prince is indeed on watch and keeps guard for the safety of all, lest the republic suffer any harm;
he goes to meet destructive and wicked attempts in good time, so that medicine may not be prepared too late:

And yet he does not serve the interests and counsels of any party, whether these have arisen from the precepts of some civil doctrine, which we see happening from time to time in our age, or are adapted to the advantages of some order or class of citizens;
He does not court the popular breeze, nor the favor of the aristocrats.
He does what Solon, the wisest and most equitable of legislators and the most excellent example of moderation and self-restraint, declares that he did:

"To the common people I have granted only as much power," he says, "as is enough for them to attempt many things and to be imbued with some rough learning, but they neither perfect themselves nor accomplish almost anything."

Nevertheless, a leader, who is not engaged in handling individual matters and performing some particular duty, but holds the reins of government, ought not to hold any art or business so dear as to think that the rest are to be neglected or despised, but, just as the divine power that governs all things provides for all parts of this world, he should embrace everything with equal care, judge all kinds of life according to their own dignity and importance with keen discernment, and show himself kind to all of them.
In this matter no one will deny that sometimes mistakes are made.
For some princes care only for military matters, others for civil affairs:
or they favor gainful arts, handicrafts, and commerce, and think that liberal education is unprofitable and not worthy of public care;
or they neglect too much those things which are altogether necessary for acquiring wealth:
indeed, of these very things, sometimes agriculture, sometimes commerce has seemed more excellent to princes.
There are those who favor the arts, but care little for literature;

And from literature we have just seen that mathematics and the natural sciences were neglected by them, sometimes that these alone pleased them, but whatever pertains to the cultivation of the human race and the memory of deeds done displeased them greatly, and philosophy was especially hateful:
Again, others devoted and enslaved to sacred rites and ceremonies, careless of profane matters, even the most serious;
Others, alienated from sacred rites, or even hostile to them.
Frederick William, what moderation, how wise, how just, he has maintained and maintains in all these matters, there is none of us who does not understand:
He presents a prince almost perfect, as far as human nature allows, burdensome to no kind of life or business, favorable to all, giving to each his due honor.

Now, to come to the second point, where danger threatens the state from great agitation of minds, the temperate prince is indeed on watch and keeps guard for the safety of all, lest the republic suffer any harm;
He goes to meet destructive and nefarious attempts in good time, so that medicine may not be prepared too late:

And yet he does not serve the interests and plans of any party, whether these have arisen from the teachings of some civil doctrine, which we see happening from time to time in our age, or are adapted to the advantages of some order or class of citizens.
He does not court the popular breeze, nor the favor of the aristocrats.
He does what Solon, the wisest and most just of legislators and the most excellent example of moderation and self-restraint, declares that he did:
"I granted the plebs only as much power as is sufficient," he says, "neither taking anything away from their honor nor adding too much;
But those who were endowed with power and strong in resources, for these too I provided, lest they suffer anything unworthy:

I stood firm for both sides, surrounding them with a shield, and I did not allow either to win unjustly." By this means it cannot happen but that the prince wins the hearts of all, even of those who, perhaps because they have recently come under his rule, have not yet grown together with the new master in that mutual bond of affection by which the other subjects are united.

Moreover, because he knows that no one contends with him for the highest place, he will not unwillingly descend from his eminence, so as to hear the wishes of the citizens and to listen to the counsels of the experienced.

He alone is truly above all, who understands that he can obey the admonitions of each one while preserving his authority; he alone is truly free from the laws, who has bound himself to the law voluntarily, and does not think that he does violence to his own will by observing the law.

Even if some have offended, although their audacity and impious deeds deserve punishment, he will prefer leniency and clemency to the most severe punishment and will incline to the more humane side, as far as the guardianship of morals and the security of the empire permit:
For temperance is the mother of clemency; pride gives birth to cruelty.

Who would deny that this is to be counted among the most important blessings of this age, that we have ceased to take pleasure in cruelty when punishing crimes, and that most of us understand that the very harsh punishments, which our ancestors used very frequently, are not suitable except for rude ages and for uncultivated manners and minds, which have persuaded themselves that the savagery of a crime must be either equaled or surpassed by the savagery of the punishment, so that fierce and wild men might be deterred by the cruelty of retribution?
There have long been those who think that it is not even lawful to condemn anyone to death.

However this matter may be judged (for I do not interpose my own opinion, since it makes no difference), all the more humane agree on this: that it is unworthy of a state to teach cruelty by its own example, and that too with no public advantage.

For it is so far from being the case that crimes are prevented by this means, that while a person commits them, hardly anyone is mindful of the laws and punishments, but is driven by anger and hatred and mad desires, or hopes that he can escape punishment and hide from the avenger, that even crimes seem to be provoked by cruel punishment, because wicked and bold men are trained to cruelty by the example of the state.
The law itself has not rarely pointed out and has given birth to crime:

As Seneca, who lived in that age in which the frequency of punishments could teach attentive men what fruit the most severe punishments could bear, is about parricide, and neither detracting anything from his honor nor adding too much;
But those who were endowed with power and were strong in resources, for these also he was provident, lest they suffer anything unworthy:

I stood firm for both sides, surrounding them with my shield, and I did not allow either to win unjustly." By this means it cannot happen but that the prince wins the hearts of all for himself, even of those who, perhaps because they have recently come under his rule, have not yet grown together with the new lord in that mutual bond of affection by which the other subjects are united.

Moreover, because he knows that no one contends with him for the highest place, he will not unwillingly descend from his height, so that he may hear the wishes of the citizens and listen to the advice of the experienced.

He alone is truly above all who understands that he can obey the admonitions of each person while preserving his authority; he alone is truly free from the laws who has bound himself to the law willingly, and does not think that he is doing violence to his own will by observing the law.

Even if some have offended, although their audacity and impious deeds deserve punishment, he will prefer leniency and clemency to the most severe punishment and will incline to the more humane side, as far as the guardianship of morals and the security of the empire permit.
For temperance is the mother of clemency; pride gives birth to cruelty.

Who would deny that this ought to be counted among the most important blessings of this age, that we have ceased to take delight in cruelty in punishing offenses, and that most of us understand that the most severe punishments, which our ancestors employed very frequently, are not suited except to rude ages and to uncultivated manners and minds, which have persuaded themselves that the savagery of crime must be either equaled or surpassed by the savagery of the punishment, so that fierce and savage men might be deterred by the cruelty of retribution?
There have long been those who think that it is not even lawful to condemn anyone to death.

However this matter may be judged (for I do not interpose my own judgment, since it makes no difference what I think), all the more humane agree on this: that it is unworthy of a state to teach cruelty by its own example, and that too with no public advantage.

For it is so far from being the case that crimes are prevented by this means, that while a person commits them, hardly anyone is mindful of the laws and punishments, but is driven by anger and hatred and mad desires, or hopes that he can escape punishment and hide from the avenger, that even wrongdoings seem to be provoked by cruel punishment, because wicked and bold men are trained to cruelty by the example of the state.
The law itself has not rarely pointed out and given birth to crime:

As Seneca, who lived in that age in which the frequency of punishments could teach attentive people what fruit the most severe punishments could bear, saying about parricide, "The greatest prudence," he says, "of the most profound men and most skilled in the nature of things preferred to pass over an incredible crime and one placed beyond audacity, rather than, while they punish it, to show that it can be done:"

And so they began with the law of parricide, and the punishment showed them the crime. But when the state itself uses milder laws, the minds of all citizens are gradually imbued with a sense of gentleness, which our Christian religion also demands, and morals are softened;

And not to speak only of laws and institutions, whether written or unwritten, the prince especially, who, as we said above, is a living and breathing law, according as he has been gentle or fierce, by his example will shape the multitude of the more ignorant, which is governed more by examples than by precepts, either to humanity or to barbarous cruelty.
But when a common movement adds sharper goads to minds and disturbs tranquility, you may see that most people sin more from error than from a bad mind:

If these are not to be forgiven, certainly a lighter punishment should be inflicted, and only desperate and incurable natures, lest they be able to harm again, should be restrained with harsher penalties.
Indeed, the more people are punished, the more enemies rise up again, just as the Hydra regenerated two heads for each one cut off.

And if fear is needed (and it is certainly needed in the state of affairs I have mentioned, lest impunity increase audacity), certainly a moderate amount must be applied, because excessive fear makes people more stubborn.

"For moderate fear," as that same wise writer whom I just brought forward says, "restrains the mind, but constant and sharp fear, driving to extremes, rouses those lying in idleness to boldness and urges them to try everything." Now, lest I linger too long on these matters, to which the sequence of events and the course of my speech has brought me, [I turn to] not the character and nature of this kingdom:

For these things, even if Frederick William were not by nature most gentle and most mild, and rather bore the character of a father of his subjects than of a master, nevertheless could scarcely invite anyone to propose these things, because almost all cruelty has long been banished from our state:
I pass on to the third of the arguments which I have set forth.

For just as in one and the same state, both the interests of different orders—as they themselves think—are different and accordingly their pursuits are different, and moreover each person according to his own feeling or the principles with which he has been imbued, and according to the opinions either his own or those of his patrons, thinks that one form of the republic and other institutions are advantageous:
so peoples differ in their customs and talents;
Different things seem fair, just, and useful to different states.

Different peoples use different laws, which confirm that discrepancy, saying, "With the greatest prudence," he says, "the most profound men, most skilled in the nature of things, preferred to pass over an incredible crime and one placed beyond audacity, rather than, while avenging it, to show that it could be done."

And so parricides began with the law, and the punishment showed them the crime. But when the state itself uses milder laws, the minds of all citizens are gradually imbued with a sense of gentleness, which our Christian religion also demands, and morals are softened;

And not to speak only of laws and institutions, whether written or unwritten, the prince especially, who, as we said above, is a living and breathing law, according as he has been gentle or fierce, by his example will form the multitude of the more ignorant, which is ruled more by examples than by precepts, either to humanity or to barbarous cruelty.
But when a common movement adds sharper goads to minds and disturbs tranquility, you may see that most people sin more from error than from a bad disposition:

If these are not to be forgiven, certainly a lighter punishment should be inflicted, and only those dispositions that are desperate and incurable should be restrained with harsher penalties, lest they be able to harm again.
Indeed, the more people are punished, the more enemies rise up again, just as the Hydra regenerated two heads for each one cut off.

And if fear is needed (and it is certainly needed in the state of affairs I have mentioned, lest impunity increase audacity), certainly a moderate amount must be applied, because excessive fear makes people more stubborn.

"For moderate fear," as that same wise writer whom I just brought forward says, "restrains the mind, but constant and sharp fear, driving to extremes, rouses those lying in idleness to boldness and urges them to try everything." Now, lest I linger too long on these matters, to which the sequence of events and the course of my speech has brought me, [I turn to] the character and nature of this kingdom:

For these things, even if Frederick William were not by nature most gentle and most mild, and rather bore the character of a father of his subjects than of a master, nevertheless could scarcely invite anyone to propose these things, because almost all cruelty has long been banished from our state:
I pass on to the third of the arguments which I have set forth.

For just as in one and the same state, both the interests of different orders—as they themselves think—are different and accordingly their pursuits are different, and moreover each person according to his own feeling or the principles with which he is imbued, and according to the opinions, whether his own or those of his patrons, that he has been taught, thinks that one form of the republic and other institutions are advantageous:
so peoples differ in their customs and natural dispositions;
Different things seem fair, just, and useful to different states.
Different peoples use different laws, which confirm that discrepancy which nature itself has established.
Thus it happens that one nation is alienated from another:
Neighboring peoples especially are wont to cause offenses, because one seems to stand in the way of another's advantages:
And especially great states, from an innate desire of acquiring, strive to extend the boundaries of their empire and to take possession of neighboring lands.

But if hatred has been increased by frequent wars and by many mutual disasters, then animosities are kindled more fiercely, so that they seem scarcely ever able to be extinguished, and, hidden in the inmost hearts, they are readily brought forth at every opportunity.

I think there is no one among our elders who has not burned with this hatred himself, at the time when the proud enemy, after he had continually provoked the most just and most self-controlled king and finally forced him to wage war, with the army defeated in battles, tore apart this kingdom and harassed the Prussian lands most unjustly;

And I freely confess that in these very orations in which I celebrated the praises of Frederick William, I not infrequently indulged a somewhat irritated mind and yielded to the hatreds which the reason of the times demanded.
But with the causes removed, the effects must be moderated;

As it is the mark of a man too prone to anger to extend hatreds to the end of life, so a state, which it befits to be more temperate than individuals, ought to lay aside enmities as soon as an opportunity for reconciliation has been made.

Igitur quoniam nulla aetate atque apud nullum populum desunt qui sibi in eo placeant, ut alant discordias et instigent ad simultates exercendas, ille princeps imprimis laudandus est, qui privatos superet moderatione, et munus sibi a Deo commissum esse hoc sentiat, non ut certaminum strage suos exterosque affligat, quod faciunt qui nulla alia causa nisi ambitionis et cupiditatis explendae suscipiunt bella, sed ut pace adiuvet genus humanum, cui merito exprobratum est, quod homini plurima ex homine sint mala, quum ne beluae quidem nisi in diversa genera saeviant ac ne leonum quidem feritas inter se dimicet.

Certainly it is understood more and more day by day that the human race tends toward that end, that peoples may securely enjoy common goods, not only those who are of the same stock, as the Germans are now almost all most closely united with us, but also those of a different stock, and that all nations may come together into a great society of the whole human race.

And so it has been shown by earlier times, and now by these most recent events, that the most serene mind of Frederick William was so disposed that no one is more suitable than he to bring about this better state of affairs.
And so the swords that were just now threatening battles have been sheathed and bound, and the fears by which we were held in suspense for several years have been dispelled.
as nature herself has established.
Thus it happens that one nation is estranged from the other.
Neighboring states are especially prone to cause friction, because one seems to obstruct the interests of the other.
And especially great states, with an innate desire for acquisition, strive to extend the boundaries of their empire and to take possession of neighboring lands.

But if, through frequent wars and many mutual disasters, resentment has grown, hatreds are kindled more fiercely, so that they seem scarcely ever able to be extinguished, and, buried deep in the heart, they are readily brought forth on any occasion.

I think there is no one among our elders who has not burned with this hatred himself, at the time when the proud enemy, after he had continually provoked the most just and most self-controlled king and finally forced him to wage war, with the army defeated in battles, tore apart this kingdom and most unjustly harassed the Prussian lands;

And I freely confess that in these very orations, in which I was celebrating the praises of Frederick William, I not infrequently indulged a rather irritated spirit and yielded to the hatreds which the reason of the times demanded.
But with the causes removed, the effects must be moderated;

As it is the mark of a man too prone to anger to extend hatreds to the end of life, so a state, which it befits to be more temperate than individuals, ought to lay aside enmities as soon as an opportunity for reconciliation has been made.

Igitur quoniam nulla aetate atque apud nullum populum desunt qui sibi in eo placeant, ut alant discordias et instigent ad simultates exercendas, ille princeps imprimis laudandus est, qui privatos superet moderatione, et munus sibi a Deo commissum esse hoc sentiat, non ut certaminum strage suos exterosque affligat, quod faciunt qui nulla alia causa nisi ambitionis et cupiditatis explendae suscipiunt bella, sed ut pace adiuvet genus humanum, cui merito exprobratum est, quod homini plurima ex homine sint mala, quum ne beluae quidem nisi in diversa genera saeviant ac ne leonum quidem feritas inter se dimicet.

Certainly it is understood more and more day by day that the human race tends toward that end, that peoples may securely enjoy common goods, not only those who are of the same stock, as the Germans are now almost all most closely united with us, but also those of a different one, and that all nations may come together into a great society of the whole race.

And indeed, that the most serene mind of Frederick William was so disposed, that no one is more suitable than he for bringing about this better state of affairs, the earlier times have shown, and then these most recent ones;
And so the swords that were just now threatening battles have been sheathed and bound, and the fears by which we were held in suspense for several years have been dispelled;
Finally, Frederick William is not only the most certain founder and preserver of the republic, but also of peace.
From that moderation of his, both the people and the learned can take an example for themselves, so that, by attributing too much to their own customs, they may not be unfair to foreigners.
For although it is proper and pious to hold one's fatherland dearer than all things and to prefer it and its institutions to foreign ones, unless these are manifestly better;
From this source, how much strength accrues to a state, the Lacedaemonians and Romans excellently teach:

Nevertheless, just as parents, through a foolish love of their offspring or rather of themselves, love and approve even the faults of their children, so often peoples rejoice in their own blemishes and even boast of them, and do not wish to be corrected, but spurn and hate the physician who announces a hidden disease and judges a cure necessary, while they applaud flatterers, who keep saying that not only is the body sound, but most perfect, and that this nation surpasses all other mortals:
Hence it cannot happen that the people are gradually given over to sloth and listlessness.

At the same time, because it alone pleases itself, just as the Chinese please themselves, it is lifted up with pride above the other nations, and despises and scorns them before itself, and disparages their virtues:
And since the Jews once seemed to do this notably, hatred of the human race was reproached to them, and they themselves incurred the hatred of all.
What of the fact that this popular envy, with the most perverse rivalry, rages even in literature?

Since these are common to all nations, that injustice, which looks not so much at what is being done as at who does it, and which is distressed by the good arts of foreigners and disparages their merits, ought to be considered more remote from nothing than from them.
Finally, Frederick William is not only the most certain founder and preserver of the republic, but also of peace.
From that moderation of his, both the people and the learned can take an example for themselves, so that, by attributing too much to their own customs, they may not be more unfair to foreigners.
For although it is proper and pious to hold one's fatherland dearer than all things and to prefer it and its institutions to foreign ones, unless these are manifestly better;
From this, how much strength accrues to the state, the Lacedaemonians and Romans excellently teach:

Yet just as parents, through a foolish love of their offspring or rather of themselves, love and approve even the faults of their children, so often peoples rejoice in their own blemishes and even boast of them, and do not wish to be corrected, but spurn and hate the physician who announces a hidden disease and judges a cure necessary, while they applaud flatterers, who keep saying that not only is the body sound, but that it is most perfect, and that this nation surpasses all other mortals.
Therefore it cannot happen that the people are gradually given over to sloth and listlessness.

At the same time, this people, because it alone pleases itself, just as the Chinese please themselves, is lifted up with pride above the other nations, and despises and scorns them before itself, and disparages their virtues:
And since the Jews once seemed to do this notably, hatred of the human race was reproached to them, and they themselves incurred the hatred of all.
What of the fact that this popular envy, with the most perverse rivalry, rages even in literature?

Since these are common to all nations, that injustice ought to be considered more remote from nothing than from them, which looks not so much at what is performed, as at by whom, and is distressed by the good arts of foreigners and disparages their merits.

Perhaps, listeners, I will seem to have departed too far from the praises of Frederick William, and to have spoken more generally about the moderation of a prince, with other opinions mixed in besides, which did not even pertain to the princely virtue.

But I did not want to repeat what has been set forth by me more than once about Frederick William's generous mind, and yet I have recalled the most important parts of the argument to the person of the most beloved King.
Now if I wanted, I could add more.

For also in private life, especially in marriage, and in the whole domestic and family sphere, in choosing and cultivating friends, in the just measure of liberality and frugality, and in other almost countless matters, the self-control and moderation of the Prince is so clearly seen that it is all too easy to demonstrate from these things as well, as from those which he does publicly, the most temperate character of Frederick William.

But I confine myself altogether to narrower limits, because it is not fitting even for a moderate prince to be pleased with a more detailed eulogy, and I consider it enough to have indicated one or two things and to have pointed a finger at his excellent institutions and plans.

But if it seems that the eulogy should be moderated, nevertheless it should not be moderated in the feelings of affection, piety, and grateful mind, with which all citizens of this literary university ought to and do accompany the most kind Prince.
However, not many words are needed:
A genuine feeling of gratitude completes the action with a more concise speech.

Therefore, since I have often deliberately discussed what Frederick William had done for literature and the arts throughout so many years of his reign, although they were disturbed by the tumults of wars, with what care and at what great expense he had provided for every kind of school, not only, as ambitious princes are wont to do, for those from whose dignity something might seem to accrue to the splendor of the empire, but especially with what zeal, with what liberality, under what equitable laws he had founded, adorned, and cherished this our seat of learning,
Now, in your name, I shall give thanks to the most gracious King for two things, one of which pertains to moderation, the other to generosity.

For after that nearly incurable plague of secret societies, which we saw growing worse up to conspiracy and arms, wrested from the German Confederation a common decree, by which academic discipline might be established on a more prudent basis;

Because among us almost everything had been arranged correctly and according to the standard, in accordance with a strict and just norm, nothing was taken away from our dignity and authority, and very few new institutions were added, which we accepted with the most willing mind.

This ought also to be an incentive to you, fellow soldiers, so that, as you have almost all approved the honesty and innocence of your character up to this point, you may in the future satisfy the will of the most beloved Prince by preserving the same.

He who very recently gratified the university he founded with a most welcome gift, in that, although the buildings which he most generously gave us more than twenty-five years ago together with the establishment of this school, although they are very spacious and magnificent, are no longer in good repair, that eminent man, who as minister of royal wisdom and kindness governs the affairs of universities and schools excellently, yielding to our prayers has granted sufficient money, from which they might not only be restored, but also be better adapted to the needs that have arisen in the meantime, especially with the increased number of both teachers and students.
This work will be accomplished over the course of several years in such a way that no hindrance arises from it for holding lectures.

It is not even fitting for a prince to be pleased with a more detailed eulogy, and I am satisfied to have indicated one or two things and to have pointed a finger at his famous institutions and plans.

But if it seems that we should moderate our praise, nevertheless we should not moderate the feelings of affection, devotion, and gratitude with which all citizens of this literary university ought to and do honor our most kind Prince.
Although not many words are needed:
With a more restrained speech, true feeling of gratitude completes the action.

Therefore, when I have often deliberately discussed what Frederick William had done well for literature and the arts throughout so many years of his reign, although they were disturbed by the tumults of wars, with what care and at what great expense he had provided for every kind of school, not only, as ambitious princes are wont to do, for those from whose dignity something seems to accrue to the splendor of the empire, but especially with what zeal, with what liberality, under what equitable laws he had founded, adorned, and cherished this our seat of learning,
Now, in your name, I shall give thanks to the most gracious King for two things, one of which pertains to moderation, the other to generosity.

For after that almost incurable plague of secret societies, which we saw growing worse up to conspiracy and arms, extorted from the German Confederation a common decree, by which the academic discipline might be established on a more prudent basis;

Because among us almost everything had been arranged correctly and according to a strict and just standard, nothing was taken away from our dignity and authority, and very few new institutions were added, which we accepted with the most willing mind.

This ought also to be an incentive to you, fellow soldiers, so that you may satisfy the will of the most beloved Prince by preserving for the future the same honesty and innocence of character that you have almost all approved up to now.

He has very recently benefited the university he founded with a most welcome gift, in that, although the buildings which he most generously gave us more than twenty-five years ago together with the establishment of this school, although they are very spacious and magnificent, are no longer in good repair, a distinguished man, who as minister of royal wisdom and kindness governs the affairs of universities and schools excellently, yielding to our entreaties has granted sufficient money, from which they might not only be restored, but also be better adapted to the needs that have arisen in the meantime, especially with the increased number of both teachers and students.
This work will be accomplished over the course of several years in such a way that no hindrance arises from it for holding lectures.
And indeed, after so many other favors, Frederick William has heaped these benefits upon us.
But to no part of the state is he equally kind.

Therefore, however much the earlier kings have deserved well of this empire, just as the king excels in power, so the people seems to flourish more joyfully than ever, especially since with lasting peace and with wise and salutary institutions both public and private resources are more and more restored, and tranquility has succeeded the disturbances;

And there is hope that it will come to pass that Frederick William, rejoicing in vigorous old age, just as he has not been wearied by years, so may he not be wearied by doing good, and at the same time, along with his life, most dear to his citizens, may he bring forth the happiness of his citizens.

Would that therefore God, the Best and Greatest, may assent to those vows, which indeed always, but on this his birthday with more sacred ceremonies, all the provinces, cities, and colleges of the kingdom undertake for the health of Frederick William.
But if those prayers shall not have been in vain, the common safety of the Prussians will be assured.
And indeed, after so many other favors, Frederick William has heaped these upon us;
but to no part of the state is he equally kind.

Therefore, however much the earlier kings have deserved well of this empire, just as the king is powerful, so the people seem to flourish more joyfully than ever, especially since with lasting peace and with wise and salutary institutions both public and private resources are more and more restored, and tranquility has succeeded the disturbances;

And there is hope that it will come to pass that Frederick William, rejoicing in vigorous old age, just as he has not been wearied by years, so may he not be wearied by doing good, and at the same time, along with his life, most dear to his citizens, may he prolong the happiness of his citizens.

May God, the Best and Greatest, therefore favor those vows which always indeed, but on this his birthday with more sacred ceremonies, all the provinces, cities, and colleges of the kingdom undertake for the health of Frederick William.
But if those prayers shall not have been in vain, the common safety of the Prussians will be ratified.

div.head: XXV. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXXVII. habita.

p.s: The task that has been entrusted to me, listeners, on this most auspicious day, which the piety of the citizens has publicly dedicated and consecrated to the honoring of the name of Frederick William, from this most spacious place of speaking, although I understand with most people that it is as honorable to every most distinguished man and pleasant to me, so on account of the dignity of the matter it is especially serious, and that an oration would better correspond to the gravity of the subject, where not I alone am adorned with this splendid prerogative, but in turns another orator succeeds another each year:

Yet so far am I from confessing that I am exhausted by frequent repetition, and from thinking that the praises of Frederick William have long since been exhausted by me, that I even deny that in any year an orator need fear that he may repeat, unknowingly and unwillingly, what he has said before, and thus affect with some weariness those who may happen to remember his earlier words.

When I say this, I would not have it understood as if I thought that each latest year brings entirely new material to the speaker, by which alone, being more richly set forth, you could sufficiently celebrate a most beloved Prince:
Rather, I would count this among the chief blessings of this kingdom, that not so many new things happen every year.

An orator could congratulate the Roman Republic and the Roman Emperors, who waged wars almost without interruption and rarely kept the temple of Janus closed, on some notable success in almost every single year.

And even in a peace that is not well settled, when affairs fluctuate this way and that, and there is need day by day of new devices and counsels, so that an empire threatening ruin is held together from time to time, new laws and institutions are founded every year, which you might refer to the praise of the prince:

But the auspices of this kingdom of Frederick William have not only kept it peaceful from foreign wars for a long time, but have also brought it to a certain equitable state of affairs, indeed not lacking in movement, but rejoicing in quiet movement, in which, unless something extraordinary happens, nothing single stands out so much that in these greatest and most sacred solemnities it seems right that the speech be directed uniquely to that one thing, and that all material for praise be sought from it.
Nor does he himself seem to wish that the things which are being done by our Prince in a distinguished manner should be praised individually and too lavishly.
And the things that were done in secret, although they are extraordinary and not entirely unknown, ought not to be publicly discussed.
But I do not lack new arguments:

The human mind is so constituted that scarcely anyone, in illustrating those matters which are set forth by the free course of thought and words, would fall upon exactly the same opinions, connected with one another in the same series, and the same words, after any considerable interval.

This is the difference between a free mind and the necessity of nature: that nature, at the same season every year, regenerates the same plants, flowers, and fruits, while the human mind, at whatever time, is driven by other impulses and produces and brings forth other thoughts and reasonings.
Yet the mind is not moved by a random impulse:
different times remind us of different things.

But this most peaceful and most fortunate condition of the Prussian state has brought me now to no other thought more than to contemplating the benevolence of Frederick William, which he shows to all in common.
For we are well off, because he does good to us:
but he does good, because he wishes well from the heart.
to one saying something new, by which alone, when more fully expounded, you could sufficiently celebrate the most beloved Prince:
I would rather count this among the chief blessings of this kingdom, that so many new things do not happen every year.

For the Roman Republic and the Roman Emperors, who waged wars almost without interruption and rarely kept the temple of Janus closed, an orator could have congratulated some notable success in almost every single year;

And even in a peace that is not well established, when affairs fluctuate this way and that, and there is need day by day of new devices and counsels, so that an empire threatening ruin is held together from time to time, new laws and institutions are founded every year, which you might refer to the praise of the prince:

But the auspices of Frederick William have not only kept this kingdom peaceful from foreign wars for a long time, but have also led it to a certain equitable state of affairs, indeed not lacking in movement, but rejoicing in quiet movement, in which, unless something extraordinary happens, nothing single stands out so much that in these greatest and most sacred solemnities it seems right that the speech be directed uniquely to that one thing, and that all material for praise be sought from it.
Nor does he himself seem to wish that the things which are being done by our Prince in a distinguished manner should be extolled individually and too lavishly.
And those things which were done in secret, although they are excellent and not entirely unknown, it is not fitting to discuss publicly.
But I do not lack new arguments:

The human mind is so constituted that scarcely anyone, in illustrating those matters which are unfolded by the free course of thought and words, would fall, after a somewhat long interval, upon exactly the same opinions connected with one another in the same series and the same words.

This is the difference between a free mind and the necessity of nature: that nature, at the same season every year, regenerates the same plants, flowers, and fruits, while the human mind, at whatever time, is driven by other impulses, and hammers out and brings forth other thoughts and reasonings.
Yet the mind is not moved by a random impulse:
different times remind us of different things.

But this most peaceful and most fortunate condition of the Prussian state has brought me down to no other thought more than to contemplating the benevolence of Frederick William, which he shows to all in common.
For we are well off, because he does good to us:
but he does good, because he wishes well from the heart.
I affirm that to the benevolent spirit of Frederick William is chiefly owed this happiness of the state, this flourishing of letters in the state:
For nothing is more salutary to states than the benevolent mind of the prince.

As I am about to illustrate this opinion, I pray that the breeze of your goodwill may also be present to me, listeners, and I ask pardon from you in advance, that since I am not speaking in the forum, not in the senate-house, not before the people, but before an assembly of the learned and of those eager for learning, it may be permitted to mix in here and there something that may seem to smell rather of the shade of the school than to be suited to the light of a public assembly.
But if we ask what benevolence is:

Just as it is established that some are by nature inclined to sadness, severity, and cruelty, so the feeling of benevolence, although it is cultivated by reason and practice, is not acquired by art, but comes as a gift of nature, and is a certain innate disposition and constitution of the mind, by which you desire that all those with whom you associate have as many good things as possible, and you pursue them with love.
But since the Prince, as the one among all, was born to make citizens happy and ought to provide for their safety and all their prosperity;
This disposition of mind is truly princely, and is the mother and nurse of almost all civic virtues.
By this virtue the Emperor Titus, whom an ancient writer says was by nature most benevolent, earned that most beautiful praise, that he was called the love and delight of the human race;

By this virtue the prince, as far as can be done through human weakness, emulates the highest divinity, to which, in order that they may be assimilated according to their powers, it befits both the rest of mortals to strive with all their might and truly the princes, who from ancient times have seemed to hold the place of gods on earth.
For God, as our religion especially teaches, embraces the whole human race with immense love, and is the most benevolent author and dispenser of all good things:
Nor is it moved by envy or hatred, which two vices are contrary to goodwill.

For envy pursues those who seem to be happy, because they have been increased and adorned with goods and virtues; it attacks and casts down the splendid, raising up obscure names, and it is distressed by the prosperity of others, even if the envious man perceives no harm to himself from it;

And hatred is that disposition of the mind which watches for and eagerly seeks the opportunity to do harm with pleasure, because those who hate think that the one they hate is either evil or stands in the way of their own interests.
From these things nothing falls to God.

For neither can that opinion, which you know was especially pleasing to Herodotus, that divine envy casts down whatever exalts itself too much, and that it does not allow anything to be magnificent, but that the anger of god spares humble conditions, be reconciled with the purity and sincerity of the divine mind:
although there is some truth in that opinion, insofar as if any are more proud, they are accustomed to fall with a heavier ruin by their own fault:

But Plato long ago decided much more correctly that the maker of the world, for that reason also, should be surrounded by a breeze of goodwill; and I ask pardon of you, listeners, and of my own accord, that since I am not speaking in the forum, not in the senate-house, not before the people, but before an assembly of the learned and of those eager for learning, it may be permitted to mix in something here and there that seems rather to smell of the shade of the school than to be suited to the light of a public assembly.
But if we ask what goodwill is:

Just as it is established that some people are naturally inclined to sadness, severity, and cruelty, so the feeling of goodwill, although it is cultivated by reason and practice, is not acquired by art, but comes as a gift of nature, and is a certain innate disposition and constitution of the mind, by which you wish for all people, with whom you associate, as many good things as possible, and you pursue them with love.
But since the prince, as the one person, was born to bless all citizens and ought to provide for their safety and all their prosperity;
This disposition of mind is truly princely, and is the mother and nurse of almost all civic virtues.
By this virtue the Emperor Titus, whom an ancient writer says was by nature most benevolent, earned that most beautiful praise, that he was called the love and delight of the human race;

With this virtue the prince, as far as can be done through human weakness, emulates the highest divinity, to which, in order that they may be assimilated according to their powers, it befits both the rest of mortals to strive with all their might and truly princes, who from ancient times have seemed to hold the place of gods on earth.
For God, as our religion especially teaches, embraces the whole human race with immense love, and is the most benevolent author and dispenser of all good things:
And it is not moved by envy or hatred, which two vices are contrary to goodwill.

For envy attacks those who seem to be happy, because they have been increased and adorned with goods and virtues; it invades and casts down the splendid, raising up obscure names, and it is distressed by others' prosperity, even if the envious man perceives no harm to himself from it;

And hatred is that disposition of mind which watches for and eagerly seeks the opportunity to do harm with pleasure, because those who hate think that the one they hate is either evil or stands in the way of their own interests.
From these things nothing falls to God.

For indeed, that which you know was especially pleasing to Herodotus, that divine envy casts down whatever exalts itself too much, and that it does not allow anything to be magnificent, but that the anger of god spares humble conditions, that cannot be reconciled with the purity and sincerity of the divine mind:
although in that opinion there is some truth to this extent, insofar as if any are more proud, they are accustomed to fall with a heavier ruin by their own fault:

But Plato long ago decided much more correctly that the maker of the world, for this very reason, because he is good, was free from the feeling of envy, and therefore wished to make all things as like himself as possible;

Nor does it seem right to attribute hatred to the divine nature, and the anger and vengeance that flow from hatred, since not even a good man indulges in revenge, and not even a wicked man should be punished for that reason, that he suffer evil and become worse, but that he be corrected by the appearance of evil and the offense be expiated.
Now I would not fear to apply these same things to a prince.

A good prince, just as no one envies him, because he is so placed above all that no private person can be compared with him, neither envies anyone, nor again pursues anyone with hatred, not even a guilty person:
And if any punishment is needed, so that public safety may be provided for, he does not satisfy his soul with punishment, but punishes unwillingly and pities the necessity of punishing.
Indeed, because good princes are not disturbed by those emotions of the mind, but are led by kindness and goodwill, they are deservedly called serene and most serene.
And that state which is governed by these arts seems to come closest to perfection, not the one which is held together by force of arms and cunning, however firmly.
But who is more serene than our King, who more kind to all?

Finally, who is there that does not understand that, by this especially noble disposition of Frederick William, which all citizens feel in their inmost hearts, it has been brought about that the Prussian kingdom, after so many vicissitudes of fortune, has flourished most happily, and amid various and most violent disturbances has rejoiced and rejoices in unbroken tranquility?
He himself, because he was good, was removed from the feeling of envy, and therefore wished to make everything as similar to himself as possible;

Nor does it seem right to attribute hatred to the divine nature, and the anger and vengeance that flow from hatred, since not even a good man indulges in revenge, and even a wrongdoer should not be punished so that he suffers evil and becomes worse, but so that he is corrected by the appearance of evil and the offense is expiated.
Now I would not fear to apply these same things to a prince.

A good prince, just as no one envies him, because he is so placed above all that no private person can be compared with him, neither envies anyone, nor again pursues anyone with hatred, not even a guilty person:
And if any punishment is needed, so that public safety may be provided for, he does not satisfy his mind with punishment, but punishes unwillingly and pities the necessity of punishing.
Indeed, because good princes are not disturbed by those emotions of the mind, but are led by kindness and goodwill, they are deservedly called serene and most serene:
And among these arts by which a state is governed, that one seems to come closest to perfection, not the one that is held together by force of arms and cunning, however firmly.
But who is more serene than our King, who more kind to all?

Finally, who is there that does not understand that it is especially through this noble character of Frederick William, which all citizens feel in their inmost hearts, that it has been brought about that the Prussian kingdom, after so many changes of fortune, has flourished most happily, and amid various and most violent disturbances has rejoiced and rejoices in unbroken tranquility?

I have discussed these matters, listeners, to this end, that since kings rightly seem to command by divine authority, I might demonstrate that benevolence has been enjoined upon princes from the very nature of the divine mind, insofar as we mortals can attain to it.
But one cannot do good unless one acts by reason:
Therefore this is the chief point of princely benevolence: that whoever reigns should follow reason as his guide.
But the reason by which a provident deity governs the whole nature of things established a law in the communion of human life, which, as the old poet says, is the queen of mortals and immortals:
Therefore, from reason and from the law that reason brings, a benevolent prince will administer the republic, not from whim and caprice.

Only he will truly be said to rule with divine authority, who, as our most temperate King does perpetually, guards himself by reason, which dwells in him, and takes care that nothing more ill-advised or unjust escapes him, and employs it in governing the state:

Unless perhaps someone, not fearing to utter an insult against God, will affirm that even Nero, Commodus, Caracalla, and similar monsters, who were called to power by birth or inheritance, have by divine authority harassed and afflicted the human race, and that whatever was done by the most cruel princes was rightly done:

Just as once Anaxarchus of Abdera, who had entered upon a certain peculiar path of philosophizing and scorned the common judgment of men, when he saw Alexander the Great deeply afflicted with grief because of the murder of Clitus, reproved the king, whom the whole world might admire, because, cast down like a slave, he wept, respecting the institutions of men and fearing reproaches:
He should not serve vain opinion;
He himself was the law and the standard of what is right and just;
For this reason, Justice and Themis are represented as sitting beside Jupiter, so that whatever has been done and performed by the ruler should be considered just and lawful.
Rather, that which is divine in a prince is extinguished as soon as he has completely deviated from what is right, just, and pious, and is polluted by crimes.

Moreover, a prince who derives all his plans from reason, not from caprice, will also desire that reason and understanding be diffused and disseminated throughout the whole state; and since those goods which are in the power of men, namely knowledge and virtue, surpass all others, he can be more beneficent to the whole state in no way than by so aiding and directing the study of letters that letters may both flourish and be turned to the common use.

They will, however, be turned especially to the common good, when men are placed at the head of the individual parts of the state, who, besides the probity and skill altogether necessary for conducting affairs, have been cultivated with accurate learning, the fruit of which they may each in his own place scatter abroad.
Since they are formed especially in universities, Frederick William has with good reason devoted the greatest care to founding, partly correcting and restoring them.

Nor indeed, while he adorns these, has he neglected the other schools, but with equal kindness he aids all, and he also looks after the common and rural multitude, so that it may be able to become possessed of those rudiments without which it can scarcely attain to culture.
Nevertheless, the most wise King did not provide subsidies to literature only to the extent that they are of advantage to the state and repay the favor by use.
If this were to happen, it would be a bad provision for literature, which cannot return favors in the same measure in which it received them.
For his own sake, and for the sake of the ministers worthy of this king, literature seems to need to be supported.
In this you may discern the genuine affection of princely benevolence.

For it is not kindness that, as if in a purchase, should count what it has done to Caracalla and similar monsters, who were called to power by birth or inheritance, to have harassed and afflicted the human race by divine authority, and that whatever was done by the most cruel princes was rightly done, will affirm:

Just as once Anaxarchus of Abdera, who had entered upon a certain peculiar path of philosophizing and scorned the common judgment of men, when he saw Alexander the Great deeply afflicted with grief because of the murder of Clitus, reproved the king, whom the whole world might admire, because, like a slave, he wept prostrate, revering the institutions of men and fearing reproaches:
He should not serve vain opinion;
He himself was the law and the norm of what is right and just;
For this reason, Justice and Themis are represented as sitting beside Jupiter, so that whatever has been done and performed by the ruler should be considered just and lawful.
Rather, that which is divine in a prince is extinguished as soon as he has completely deviated from what is right, just, and pious, and is polluted by crimes.

Moreover, a prince who derives all his plans from reason, not from caprice, will also desire that reason and understanding be spread and disseminated throughout the whole state; and since those goods which are within human power, knowledge and virtue, surpass all others, he can be more beneficial to the whole state in no way than by so supporting and directing the studies of literature that literature both flourishes and is turned to the common use.

They will, however, be turned especially to the common good, when men are placed at the head of the individual parts of the state, who, besides probity and skill altogether necessary for conducting affairs, have been cultivated with accurate learning, the fruit of which they may each in his own place spread abroad.
Since they are formed especially in universities, Frederick William has with good reason devoted the greatest care to founding, partly correcting and restoring them.

Nor indeed, while he adorns these, has he neglected the other schools, but with equal kindness he aids all, and he also looks after the common and rural multitude, so that it may be able to become possessed of those rudiments without which it can scarcely attain to culture.
Nevertheless, the most wise King did not provide subsidies to literature only to the extent that they benefit the state and repay the favor by use;
When this happened, it would have been ill-advised for literature, which cannot return the same measure of gifts as it received.
For his own sake and for the sake of ministers worthy of this king, literature seems to need support.
In this you may discern the genuine affection of princely benevolence.
For it is not kindness that, as in a purchase, calculates what it receives, and it is by no means kingly but characteristic of servile baseness to look to the profit of benefits.

Finally, Frederick William, not only in literature but in fostering any parts of the state whatsoever, does not look to his own advantages, but seeks the good of his citizens, which the greatest philosopher long ago taught to be the mark of a good prince and which Frederick the Great approved by his own judgment, and to this he directs all his counsels:

By this very fact it is brought about that the royal house and the people are joined by a mutual bond of love, and that this kingdom has so coalesced with this republic that they cannot be separated without damage and ruin to the people themselves.
Let him take it back, and it is by no means kingly but characteristic of servile baseness to look to the profit of one's favors.

Finally, Frederick William, not only in literature but in fostering any parts of the state whatsoever, does not look to his own advantages, but seeks the benefit of his citizens, which the greatest philosopher long ago taught to be the mark of a good prince and which Frederick the Great approved by his own judgment, and to this he directs all his plans:

By this very fact it is brought about that the royal house and the people are united by a mutual bond of love, and so this kingdom has grown together with this republic that they cannot be separated without harm and ruin to the people themselves.
There is not one way, listeners, by which the benevolent mind of a prince may aid the affairs of the citizens.
First, by the mere feeling of affection, by mere courtesy and popularity, by mere judgment and approval, he nourishes, excites, and inflames the zeal of men.

If the prince holds no class of parents in low esteem, if he shows that the farmer, the artisan, the merchant, and the learned man are dear to him, if he deigns them with his address, approves, praises them, by this very token of goodwill he is generous without a gift.

Pericles, not indeed a king, but equal to kings in his authority, because he was on familiar terms with Anaxagoras, Damon, and Phidias; Scipio Aemilianus, because he had Polybius and Panaetius in his company; that same Scipio and Laelius, because they cultivated Terence—these men, by their judgment, nourished literature and the arts.
It was reproached against Frederick the Great that, by despising native poets and writers and by preferring foreigners, he hindered the education of the Germans.
Although he has a valid excuse, which it is pointless to mention, nevertheless you may infer from this how harmful the judgment of so great a prince was thought to be.
But the prince gives a greater and more effective proof of goodwill, who grants to each class of men in the state as much freedom in conducting their own affairs as is possible for the safety of all.
Indeed we rightly call a good prince the father of his country:
In this there is this, that he rules over subjects not as slaves but as free people:
For the father of a family is the parent of free children, not of slaves;
For him to be like the prince in this matter, that seems to be the true power of paternal authority, from which some wish that royal power was born.

Enimvero ea res publica non potest libera haberi, in qua ad quodcunque te negotium contuleris, quamcunque artem exercebis, quodcunque opus suscipient cives, circumstant undique et impediunt leges, decreta, vectigalia, monopolia, vel aerarii causa vel prava ad rem publicam cuncta trahendi cupiditate nimiaque anxietate
constituta:
id quod in nonnullis rebus publicis, quae videntur liberrimae, haud raro constat accidere.

In this matter, how wisely Frederick William maintained a balanced policy, and how much he supported agriculture, crafts, and trade with wiser laws and by restoring due liberty without harming anyone, I need not explain to those who know.
Now indeed, what is more necessary for literature than liberty?

Since some of these are engaged in investigating natural things, others in the memory of deeds done, others in mathematics, others in philosophy, whether natural or moral, and in politics, which are included in moral philosophy, and finally others are mixed from the philosophical and historical or physical kind, to which I refer theology, the knowledge of law, and medicine;
Although some of these seem able to flourish even without freedom, because even the most suspicious person does not regard them as suspect:

For who will fear from arithmetic and geometry, from the history of plants, from grammar and metrical doctrine or archaeology of the arts and similar literature, that the republic may suffer any harm?

Nevertheless, none of the most important branches of literature, not even poetry, which I have not mentioned earlier only because it is more remote from the studies of universities, can reach its full flower, if different laws are to be followed for them than those which are founded in the very nature and character of the art itself:
And when those most important ones are corrupted, the rest will contribute little to the cultivation of the mind.

For to mention but a few examples, if a philosopher is not allowed to direct the course of his mind wherever his deepest meditation carries him, but a certain fixed limit of philosophizing is prescribed, which the opinion of others has established as a rule;

If the historian and the politician are not allowed to report events as they happened, but are forced to conceal some things, to gloss over others, and to approve what sound reason does not approve, or not to approve what it does approve;
if the theologian and the jurist are forbidden to inquire further into the causes of divine and human affairs and of what is just and right than seems expedient to those in power;

If a natural philosopher must fear that what he has discovered by investigating the nature of things, because it seems contrary to certain doctrines which men have set up as divine, may be publicly condemned as impious:

Science, which by its nature strives toward perfection, will halt its progress as far as the state is concerned, and with science the human race, whose progress science and intellect move and measure.
Students who swear by the words of their teacher are criticized.
Do we want teachers to swear allegiance to the opinions of others, who cannot even be considered as teachers?
Thus it is established:
a thing that in some republics, which seem very free, is not rarely found to happen.

In this matter, how wise a moderation Frederick William maintained, and how much he supported the cultivation of fields, manufactures, and commerce with more prudent laws and by restoring due liberty without detriment to anyone, I need not explain to those who know.
But indeed, what is more necessary for literature than freedom?

Of these, while some are engaged in the investigation of natural things, others in the memory of past deeds, others in mathematics, others in philosophy, whether natural or moral, and in politics, which are included in moral philosophy, and others finally are mixed from the philosophical and historical or physical kind, to which I refer theology, jurisprudence, and medicine;
Although some of these seem able to flourish even without freedom, because even the most suspicious person does not suspect them.
For who will fear from arithmetic and geometry, from the history of plants, from grammar and metrical doctrine or archaeology of the arts and similar letters, that the republic might suffer any harm?

Nevertheless, none of the most important branches of literature, not even poetry, which I have not mentioned earlier only because it is more remote from university studies, can reach its full flower, if other laws are to be followed for them than those which are founded in the very nature and character of the art itself:
And when those most important ones are corrupted, the rest will contribute little to the cultivation of the mind.

For to mention but a few examples, if a philosopher is not allowed to direct the course of his mind wherever his deepest meditation carries him, but a certain fixed limit of philosophizing is prescribed, which the opinion of others has established as a rule;

If the historian and the politician are not allowed to report events as they happened, but are forced to conceal some things, to gloss over others, and to approve what sound reason does not approve, or not to approve what it does approve;
if the theologian and the jurist are forbidden to inquire further into the causes of divine and human affairs and of what is just and right than seems expedient to those in power;

If a natural philosopher must fear that what he has discovered by investigating the nature of things, because it seems contrary to certain doctrines which men have set up as divine, may be publicly condemned as impious:
Science, which by its nature strives toward perfection, will halt its step as far as the state is concerned, and with science, the human race, whose progress science and intellect move and measure.
Disciples who swear by the words of their master are blamed.
Should we want teachers to swear allegiance to the opinions of others, who cannot even be considered as masters?
Thus it will happen that the voice sticks in the throat of the teacher:
sensible men will become silent:
truth will yield to pretense.
Science itself teaches what is right, good, and beautiful, and to that extent is impatient of authority, insofar as what is commanded is not in accordance with reason.
And often science anticipates by many centuries the truth not perceived by the multitude.

What of the fact that the teachings of the learned, which a few centuries ago seemed impious to the multitude, now the common people themselves approve, and laugh at the superstition of their ancestors, who condemned them?
And do we understand that what the earlier age held pious is impious, cruel, and wicked?
For such is the power of knowledge, that it overcomes whatever obstacles are thrown in its way, even iron and fire.
There is indeed, there is a course destined for the human mind by providence and divinely predetermined, which it, even if it sometimes pauses for a little while, pursues with unimpaired strength:
The very intervals, the very obstacles add new strength, and the very windings and bypaths of errors are wont to lead the runner back to the straight course.
And so nothing from literature seems to be feared for the republic;

And the errors of learned men, by which I do not deny that even states have sometimes been disturbed, although I deny that those who disturb human affairs are truly learned, those errors, I say, are refuted by arguments:
But wantonness and impudence, unless contempt is preferable, must be chastised, and fierce spirits must be restrained.
Indeed, the kindness and wisdom of Frederick William has not separated us, who are strangers to these vices, with a harsher guard:
We enjoy perfect freedom of teaching and learning;
This is not the least reason why we should be bound to Frederick William with all our heart.
And we all feel this and are most grateful.

But besides fear, envy also can assail literature, if it is sometimes fostered too eagerly and equipped with more ample and more splendid resources, and learned men are increased with honors and wealth, although to those envious ones they seem useless and undeservedly preferred to more useful men;

In short, just as we have often heard that dancers or singers or mimes are begrudged their rather lavish salaries, not even this is right, because something must be granted even to the refined arts, which move and delight the minds of the elegant with eyes and ears and shape the sense of beauty, among more civilized peoples, and because those things which no one else can perform, since the charm of voice and gestures comes as a gift of nature, if indeed it is worth the effort to hear and watch them, are to be rewarded all the more generously, the more people you find at a cheaper wage who are equal to handling common business.
Among us, I think, this whole class of things has become obsolete, so that the voice of the teacher sticks in his throat:
sensible men will become silent:
truth will yield to pretense.
Science itself teaches what is right, good, and beautiful, and is impatient of authority only insofar as what is commanded is not in accordance with reason.
And often science anticipates by many ages the truth not perceived by the multitude.

What of the fact that the teachings of the learned, which a few centuries ago seemed impious to the multitude, now the common people themselves approve, and laugh at the superstition of their ancestors, who condemned them?
And do we understand that what the earlier age held pious is impious, cruel, and wicked?
For such is the power of knowledge, that it overcomes whatever obstacles are thrown in its way, even iron and fire.
There is indeed, there is a course destined for the human mind by providence and divinely preordained, which it, even if it sometimes pauses for a little while, pursues with unimpaired strength:
The very intervals, the very obstacles add new strength, and the very windings and bypaths of errors are wont to lead the runner back to the straight course.
And so nothing from literature seems to be feared by the state;

And the errors of learned men, by which I do not deny that even states have sometimes been disturbed, although I deny that those who disturb human affairs are truly learned, these errors, I say, are refuted by arguments:
But insolence and impudence, unless contempt is preferable, must be chastised, and fierce spirits must be restrained.
Indeed, the kindness and wisdom of Frederick William has not separated us, who are strangers to these vices, with a harsher guard:
We enjoy perfect freedom of teaching and learning;
This is not the least reason why we should be bound to Frederick William with all our heart.
And we all feel this and are very grateful.

But besides fear, envy can also assail literature, if it is sometimes fostered more intently and equipped with more ample and more splendid resources, and learned men are increased with honors and wealth, although to those envious ones they seem to be useless and undeservedly preferred to more useful men;

In short, just as we have often heard that dancers or singers or mimes are begrudged their more lavish salaries, this is not even right, because something must be granted among more civilized peoples even to the refined arts, which move and delight the minds of the elegant with eyes and ears and shape the sense of beauty, and because those things which no one else can perform, since the grace of voice and gestures comes from a gift of nature, if indeed it is worth the effort to hear and watch them, are to be rewarded all the more generously, the more people you find with cheaper wages who are equal to performing vulgar tasks.
Among us, I think, this whole kind of envy has become obsolete, which has attacked the learned on this side and that:
Indeed, since it is a matter of private individuals, it now seems it should not have been mentioned at all.
But princes can also envy the learned:
To this pertains the fact that they bear with difficulty the disagreement of the more learned and wiser, and do not want to be defeated by them.

Truly rare is the example of this matter, and so much the more illustrious is the Emperor Hadrian, a prince of ambiguous reputation, but of immense intellectual ability, and who seems to have surpassed the vices of nature by his virtues and by doing good, not inconsiderably, and not often to have forgotten what he had promised, that he would so conduct the state as to know that it was the people's affair, not his own:

He, therefore, since from boyhood he had been excellently imbued with Greek and Latin literature, and had devoted no contemptible attention to music, painting, and kindred arts, indeed held grammarians, rhetoricians, philosophers, geometers, musicians, painters, architects in the closest intimacy, and honored and enriched professors of every kind, but with excessive ambition, because he wished to appear more learned than all, he mocked, ridiculed, and oppressed with envy every most learned man; and Apollodorus the architect, who had criticized his diagrams rather freely, he not only drove into exile, but finally, with his characteristic cruelty, even killed.
Even under such a prince, however fond of literature, literature can hardly retain its freedom;

And wittily Favorinus of Arelate, when he had been rebuked by Hadrian and had come off badly with the Emperor, and was therefore criticized by his friends, replied that he had to put up with it that the one who had thirty legions should seem more learned.
It is a matter of envy, because he attacked the learned on this side and that:
Indeed, although that is a matter for private individuals, now it seems it ought not to have been mentioned at all.
But princes can also envy the learned:
To this belongs the fact that they bear with difficulty the disagreement of the more learned and wiser, and do not wish to be defeated by them.

A rare example of this indeed, and the more illustrious for that, is the Emperor Hadrian, a prince of ambiguous reputation, but of immense intellectual ability, and who seems to have surpassed the vices of his nature by his virtues and by doing good, not to a small extent, and not often to have forgotten what he had promised, that he would so conduct the state as to know that it was the people's business, not his own:

He, therefore, since from boyhood he had been excellently imbued with Greek and Latin letters, and had devoted not contemptible effort to music and painting and the kindred arts, indeed held in the closest intimacy grammarians, rhetoricians, philosophers, geometers, musicians, painters, architects, and honored and enriched with wealth professors of every kind, but with excessive ambition, because he wished to appear more learned than all, he mocked, ridiculed, and oppressed with envy every most learned man; but Apollodorus the architect, because he had criticized his diagrams rather freely, he not only drove into exile, but finally, with his characteristic cruelty, even killed.
Even under such a prince, however fond of literature, literature can hardly retain its freedom;

And wittily Favorinus of Arelate, when he had been rebuked by Hadrian and had come off badly with the Emperor, and was therefore criticized by his friends, replied that he had to put up with it that the one who had thirty legions should seem more learned.
I have lingered longer, listeners, in illustrating those matters in which, although no small part of princely goodwill is discerned, yet it may seem less evident.
Now I will briefly finish those things that are set before us.
It is a sign of goodwill to bestow rewards, which are chiefly honorary.
Indeed, by ambition, which is the desire for honors, men are driven almost equally to wrong and to right actions.

And a state that excessively cultivates the ambition of its citizens seems to corrupt them rather than to raise them to virtue, and of its own accord brings it about that the honors, which it had wished to use for rousing their spirits, gradually lose their value and no longer serve their purpose.

This you may clearly perceive in the ancient states, from the time when, with the severity of morals simultaneously slipping away and love of country diminished, they used to bestow honors and distinctions not so much as gifts but rather to squander them.
Yet a good prince will show his goodwill, common to all orders, when he excludes no order from those honors which it is customary to bestow on the well-deserving.
I come to those things by which alone most people think benefits are to be measured, to pecuniary subsidies.

Most people need these at all times, and since private resources are not sufficient, so that by their contribution the needs of the needy may be provided for, recourse is had to the state and to the head of the state, the prince.
Help must be given to the sick, the weak, widows, and orphans:
at one time scarcity of crops, lack of food, and want of employment press hard;
at another time cheapness of provisions afflicts the farmers, a plague breaks out, estates and fields are overwhelmed by sudden flood, men and cattle are carried off;
As soon as the money supply fails, with gold and silver coinage as it were absorbed and consumed for various uses, the people are oppressed by debt.
Our age has experienced every one of these calamities;

and for all of them, in his kingdom, Frederick William brought the most provident and most benign remedy, whether by remitting or lightening burdens, or by lending and giving money, or by any good plans and institutions.
But even in the greatest integrity of all things, many and most excellent things cannot be accomplished, unless the expenses are provided from the public treasury;

But indeed the condition of the liberal arts and letters is now such that they must for the most part be publicly supported, because the work they provide is greater than the profit from the fee that would be paid by a private individual, and because our present state of learning demands manifold and most ample apparatus, and finally because both artists and scholars need leisure in order to produce good works, which seem scarcely able to be completed when a taskmaster daily presses and urges on.
Behold, a most beautiful material for royal munificence is set before us; shall we say that any king has more perfectly embraced it than Frederick William?
