So much for his generosity:
I see that one thing remains for me, in which the king's benevolent spirit is especially to be observed.
For I said that a good prince is unwilling to exact punishment and pities the necessity of punishing:
and so, as far as the public safety allows, he is uniquely inclined to forgive.

Titus not only did not punish two patrician men who had been convicted of the very attempt to seize the empire, but, after warning them not to dare anything further, he admitted them to his private dinner, and promised them that if they wanted anything, he would grant it.
The next day, while he was watching the gladiators, he placed the same men around himself, and when weapons of the fighters were offered to him, he handed them over to them to inspect.
Similarly, once Octavian Augustus, after he realized that by severity he had scarcely accomplished anything, with L.
He had dealt with Cinna, the grandson of Gnaeus Pompeius, his own would-be assassin:
but this is true of Octavianus, either because of his own merits or because of those who deserve remembrance.
I come to those things by which alone most people think benefits are to be measured, to financial subsidies.

Most people need these at every moment, and since the resources of private individuals do not suffice, so that by their contribution the needs of the needy may be provided for, recourse is had to the state and to the head of the state, the prince.
We must come to the aid of the sick, the weak, the widows, and the orphans:
at one time the barrenness of the crops oppresses, the scarcity of provisions, the lack of profit;
at another time the cheapness of provisions ruins the farmers, a plague breaks out, fields and plains are submerged by a sudden flood, men and cattle are carried off;
at another time the money system fails, with gold and silver coinage as it were absorbed and consumed for various uses, and the people is burdened with debt.
Of these calamities our age has experienced not one but all;

And in his kingdom Frederick William brought the most provident and most benign remedy to all, whether by remitting or lightening burdens, or by lending and giving money, or by any other beneficial measures and institutions.
But even in the greatest integrity of all things, many and most excellent things cannot be accomplished unless the expenses are provided from the public treasury.

But indeed the condition of the liberal arts and letters is now such that they must for the most part be publicly supported, because the work they provide is greater than the profit from the fee that would be paid by a private individual, and because our present state of learning demands manifold and most ample apparatus, and finally because both artists and scholars need leisure in order to produce good works, which seem scarcely able to be completed when a taskmaster presses and urges daily.
Behold, a most beautiful material for royal munificence is set before us; shall we say that any king has more perfectly embraced it than Frederick William?
So much for his generosity:
I see that one thing remains for me, in which the king's benevolent spirit is especially to be observed.
For I said that a good prince is unwilling to exact punishment and pities the necessity of punishing:
and so, as far as public safety permits, he is uniquely inclined to forgive.

Titus not only did not punish two patrician men who had been convicted of actually aspiring to the empire, but, after warning them not to dare anything further, he admitted them to his private dinner, and promised them that if they wanted anything, he would grant it.
The next day, when he was watching the gladiators, he placed the same men around himself, and when weapons of the fighters were offered to him, he handed them over to them to inspect.
Similarly, once Octavian Augustus, after he realized that he had scarcely made any progress by severity, with L.
He had acted with Cinna, the grandson of Gnaeus Pompeius, who was his own would-be assassin:
but in Octavian's case, either his own prudence or, as has been handed down to memory, the prudence of his wife Livia managed this;
In Titus's case, certainly, it was not prudence that persuaded him to do that, but greatness of soul and innate clemency:

Although even the most severe will not deny that pardons are useful to human and public affairs, not even that most severe Cato the Censor denied it, but even in a speech which he delivered in the Senate on behalf of the Rhodians, he publicly professed it.
I do not praise impunity for crimes, nor would I have promised that by pardoning crimes are entirely prevented:
But still, fierce spirits seem to be disarmed more by clemency than by harsh punishment.
It has been handed down that it was managed by the prudence of Livia, the wife.
Certainly it was not prudence that persuaded Titus to do that, but greatness of soul and innate clemency:

Although even the most severe will not deny that pardons are useful to human and public affairs, even that most harsh Cato the Censor did not deny it, but even in a speech which he delivered in the Senate on behalf of the Rhodians, he publicly professed it.
I do not praise impunity for crimes, nor would I have promised that by forgiving, crimes are entirely prevented:
But nevertheless, the fiercest spirits seem to be disarmed more by clemency than by harsh punishment.
I have sketched, as far as I could in a brief speech, the image of a benevolent prince, listeners, and at the same time indicated in many places how much Frederick William corresponds to this image:

Nor, however, do I think that anyone has missed this meaning either in those places or in the remaining parts, since the whole life of Frederick William testifies to everyone that for whose sake I have chosen this subject, namely the serenity and benevolence of the King, free from hatred and envy.

From this most noble disposition of mind, whatever good deeds arise, we, who are engaged in teaching and learning literature, have not only experienced and experience daily, but the whole state and very many of the subjects individually, whom it has aided and blessed either with rewards or with wealth or by pardoning and with every kind of favor;

And not only the state and the citizens, but also foreigners, because he was moderate, gentle, forgetful of anger and offense, did not want feuds to be prolonged and perpetuated, but he stood forth as a peacemaker, the leader and author of sincere reconciliation.
In a few words I have said a very great matter.
But what the most merciful King has bestowed and bestows upon us will never fade from our minds:

Keep these things diligently in mind, my dearest fellow soldiers, you who are being prepared in this school of arts founded by Frederick William for the pursuit of literature and the discharge of the duties of the state, and take care that by uprightness of character, by eagerness in your studies, by embracing now all the best counsels, and finally by love for the excellent Prince, who alone is the parent of liberal obedience, you show yourselves worthy of that kindness with which you have been judged worthy by the Father of the fatherland.

Finally, I pray to God, the Best and Greatest, that, just as under the auspices of that prince, through whose leadership Prussia, having been led through the greatest dangers of old, has remained whole, and now flourishes, having been restored and increased, so it will stand firm and unmoved hereafter; that He may further provide for the safety of Frederick William, and may favor and add perpetuity to the benefits conferred through his hands upon the state; and together with the most beloved King, may He keep the Augustan house safe and unharmed.

div.head: XXVI. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXXIX. habita.

p.s: Since, in these most holy annual solemnities, which the piety of the citizens has dedicated to the best King, I have been accustomed to speak almost from the very cradle of our school, and since I had reluctantly omitted the previous year, because I was occupied with public duties, and my dearest colleague, whom we then heard with the greatest pleasure elegantly, copiously, and gravely discoursing on the praises of Frederick William, had succeeded in my place:

I was hoping that it would happen that, if by chance my strength had been weakened or exhausted by frequent repetition without my knowledge, I would be refreshed by this rest, and that the example of an excellent orator would kindle not my will, of which I have so often given proof, but the emulation and ardor of my talent.
But contrary to expectation, the matter turned out.
Up to this point I had compared myself with myself;
it was permitted to me to yield to a pleasing hope, that I would not descend below myself:

Now, in the most blessed and most abundant abundance of resources, that very thing breaks and afflicts me, by which I had seemed to myself to be able to be raised up, since, with old age now approaching and the weapons of eloquence exhausted, I am not so strong either in weight of thoughts or in richness of speech or in lungs, that I could contend with stronger and unimpaired men, to whom I would rather yield than be compared.

But if weariness should steal upon me, and I should not equal the vigor of previous years, I ask that you transfer to this time some of that zeal with which you once seem to have pursued me as I spoke, and that you allow my mind to be refreshed by the memory of your former kindness, which would not be refreshed by resting.

What of the fact that I think I may by my own right not only beg but demand your indulgence, because the more prudent you are, my hearers, the more you understand into what a critical position he is placed who, having very often and in every part discharged the praises of the King, is compelled either, by repeating what he has said before, not to satisfy himself, or, by departing further from his purpose, to answer less well to the dignity of this day and to your great expectation?

Therefore, relying on you, I proceed to speak, intending to use this moderation, that neither my reverence in honoring the King may be lacking, nor may I fear to depart somewhat from the praise of the most beloved Prince.

For to linger today on literature, we Prussians do not only proclaim—we who might be regarded as touters of our own affairs—that literature has been aided by none of the present princes, by none of those who previously held this kingdom, not even by Frederick the Great, who nevertheless was imbued with the best arts and was himself learned, both a poet and a philosopher, with such great care and munificence as by Frederick William, but also all foreigners profess it with remarkable agreement.
He himself especially founded, preserved, enlarged, and adorned this most flourishing seat of the good arts;
He spares no expense to provide for our needs;
He does not cease to repair losses, to add new distinctions, to summon distinguished professors here, and to increase the equipment and apparatus of learning:

The very fact that we have been compelled to assemble today in an unusual place testifies that the Prince's generosity is not exhausted, since he is magnificently restoring our almost royal buildings, which he gave us about thirty years ago, with equally royal expenditure.
Nor has he done and does he do less for other universities;
finally, throughout the whole kingdom, he protects schools of every kind and the literary republic with admirable kindness.

Thus Frederick William earned this praise, than which nothing can more adorn a prince, that he is considered in his kingdom the most ready and most fortunate establisher, nourisher, and preserver of letters.

But when I consider how much literature owes to Frederick William, this thought has occurred to me: what it is that a prince can contribute to the flourishing of literature at any time and in any state of the republic, and what he cannot contribute even with the utmost diligence.
I shall therefore now undertake the role of a just examination of the true state of affairs rather than of vague praise that wanders here and there.
by which I hope that I shall bring it about that it becomes clear that Frederick William has accomplished everything that lies within the power of a prince.
and I shall not fear to depart somewhat from the eulogy of the most beloved prince.

For, to dwell for a moment on literature today, we Prussians do not merely boast—though we might be regarded as touters of our own affairs—that letters have been aided by none of the present princes, by none of those who formerly held this kingdom, not even by Frederick the Great, who nevertheless was imbued with the finest arts and was himself learned, a poet, and a philosopher, with such great care and munificence as by Frederick William; but all foreigners also declare this with wonderful unanimity.
He himself especially founded, preserved, enlarged, and adorned this most flourishing seat of the good arts;
he spares no expense to provide for our needs;
he does not cease to repair losses, to add new distinctions, to summon distinguished professors here, and to increase the equipment and apparatus of learning:

The very fact that we have been compelled to assemble today in an unusual place testifies that the Prince's generosity is not exhausted, since he is magnificently restoring our almost royal buildings, which he gave us about thirty years ago, with equally royal expenditure.
Nor has he done and does he do less for other universities;
finally, throughout the whole kingdom he protects schools of every kind and the literary republic with admirable kindness.

Thus Frederick William earned this praise, than which nothing can more adorn a prince, that he is considered in his kingdom the most ready and most fortunate establisher, nourisher, and preserver of letters.

But when I consider how much letters owe to Frederick William, this thought has occurred to me: what it is that a prince can contribute to the flourishing of letters at any time and in any state of the republic, and what he cannot contribute even with the utmost diligence.
I shall therefore now undertake the role of a just examination of the true nature of things rather than of a vague and wandering eulogy.
By this I hope to achieve that it may be evident that Frederick William has accomplished everything that lies within the power of a prince.
Therefore, to begin with those things which a prince cannot accomplish, these are of two kinds:
For some things cannot be accomplished at all by helping and assisting, while others cannot be accomplished under certain conditions.
For what about the question that has been debated, whether literature can be advanced by any rewards, by any external aids and supports that are to be supplied?
What about the fact that the Medici seemed to have accomplished too little with the greatest zeal and generosity, while Louis XIV, king of the French, even seemed to have done some harm?
Lest anyone think this judgment is too inexperienced, it is helpful to cite Lessing as its author, or at least as its supporter, the most prudent judge of all matters pertaining to literature.
Of course, great talents are born spontaneously, not cultivated by culture.

But those men truly open up paths of literature that no one's feet have trodden before; those men are the leaders and standard-bearers for the rest of the common crowd of scholars, and they are moved by their own strength rather than by the supports of others, and they move others.
For talent is stimulated by the very obstacles, and the greater the difficulties to be overcome, the more it is strengthened and stands out.

This is especially evident in poets, but in none more clearly than in Shakespeare, the prince of British poets, who, born in a humble station and equipped with very meager instruments of learning and attracted by rewards either none or very slight, by his innate virtue attained to the highest rank.
Finally, I would proclaim the felicity of that age, which not only produced a prince who fostered literature and the arts, but also those talents which could satisfy the desires of such a prince.
so that by the splendor of these men the kingdom of that one may be illuminated, and that the prince may be the harbor and refuge of talents worthy of the highest favors.

But certain kinds of literature, and those the most noble, especially poetry and those things most closely related to poetry, when they have been brought to perfection by the efforts of most distinguished men, are accustomed generally to halt their step and, as it were, to rest upon the laurels already won.

Just as among the Greeks after Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides no one arose who could be compared with them in tragedy, so among the Germans no one has yet surpassed or equaled Schiller and Goethe.
You would do an injustice to your contemporaries if you said that the excellence of the race had died out throughout the whole nation.

But those who succeed are pressed by the examples of their predecessors, and, as it seems, by a natural law, each nation cannot attain the highest point in any kind except once, until by a singular gift of providence a wholly new age is born and, as it were, a great year of nations returns, in which another generative spring is brought, a new crop of talents springs up, and finally the human race hastens to complete a new course with its strength recovered and even increased;
Just as a tree in the same year produces flowers and fruits only once, but as the year turns, it regenerates them most joyfully.
But what we have said about poetry, the same can be seen in philosophy, whose history contains almost all the vicissitudes of the human mind.

Indeed, this [philosophy] among the Greeks, from Thales onward all the way to Aristotle, poured forth in a certain continuous stream of the most weighty thoughts, and was soon divided into rivulets, one or two of which watered the Stoa and the gardens of Epicurus;
then, the longer it survived, the more, if one may grant Lessing some divine quality, [it was] the most prudent judge of all those things that pertain to literature.
Of course, great minds are born spontaneously, not sown by cultivation:

But those men truly open up paths of literature that no one's feet have trodden before; those men are the leaders and standard-bearers for the rest of the common crowd of scholars, and they are moved by their own strength rather than by external supports, and they move others.
For talent is stimulated by the very obstacles, and the greater the difficulties to be overcome, the more it is strengthened and stands out.

This is especially visible in poets, but in none more clearly than in the prince of British poets, Shakespeare, who, born in a humble station and equipped with very scanty means of education, and attracted by rewards either none or very slight, by his innate excellence attained to the highest rank.
I would indeed proclaim the felicity of that age, which not only produced a prince who fostered letters and arts, but also those talents which could satisfy the desires of such a prince.
so that both the kingdom of that one may be illuminated by the splendor of these, and the prince may be the harbor and refuge of minds worthy of the highest favors.

But certain kinds of literature, and those the most noble, especially poetry and those things most closely related to poetry, when they have been brought to perfection by the efforts of most distinguished men, are accustomed generally to halt their step and, as it were, to rest upon the laurels of their fathers;

Just as among the Greeks after Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides no one arose who could be compared with them in tragedy, so among the Germans no one has yet surpassed or equaled Schiller and Goethe.
You would do an injustice to your contemporaries if you said that the excellence of the race had died out throughout the whole nation.

But those who succeed are pressed by the examples of their predecessors, and, as it seems, by a natural law, each nation cannot attain the highest point in any kind except once, until, by a singular gift of providence, a wholly new age is born and, as it were, a great year of nations returns, in which another generative spring is brought, a new crop of talents springs up, and finally the human race hastens to complete a new course with its strength recovered and even increased;
Just as a tree produces flowers and fruits only once in the same year, but, as the year turns, regenerates them most joyfully.
But what we have said about poetry, the same may be seen in philosophy, whose history contains almost all the vicissitudes of the human mind.

Indeed, among the Greeks, from Thales onward all the way to Aristotle, it poured forth in a certain continuous stream of the most weighty thoughts, then was divided into rivulets, one or two of which watered the Stoa and the gardens of Epicurus;
then, the longer it survived, the more it grew old, unless you except certain divine minds;
the same was brought back in the Middle Ages and flowed down again;

Finally, after many attempts of great men had been interposed, it was strengthened by Kant on new foundations, and then by Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel, of which triumvirate two were ours and among the foremost of ours, it was increased with such great increments and carried to such a point that this succession also seems to have been exhausted and that one now halts somewhat.

And when this point has been reached, the nation is accustomed to reap no small fruit of its studies, so that not only are there some notable men who are the guardians and stewards of literature, but with the resources for acquiring learning increased, and with easy access to it granted, and with the method and system of treating every art with some success made known to all, which those who led the way had discovered and prescribed, learning has been spread and disseminated more widely, and has many authors not to be despised, none of whom so stands out as to surpass the rest by a long interval.

Thus it happens that, with the resources of learning, which were once possessed by a few rich men, being divided among many, the literary republic, which the aristocrats had previously held in a certain way, is changed into a kind of popular state.
The sum of all these things, if I see correctly, does not depend on the will of the prince:
but the fatal course of the human mind, obeying its own laws and eternal order, draws them to a destined end, dragging mortals unwilling and resisting;

A divine power presides over them, which sends forth and recalls talents, and, as with the whole human race, so also for individual peoples, it has appointed and marked out for each its own ages, stamped with certain definite signs.
If you have taken up talents, it has grown old:
The same was brought back in the Middle Ages and again flowed away;

Finally, after many attempts of great men had intervened, it was strengthened by Kant on new foundations, and then by Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel, of which triumvirate two were ours and among the foremost of our men, and it was increased by such great advances and carried to such a point that this succession also seems to have been exhausted, and now it has stopped somewhat.

Atque huc quum perventum est, simul eum studiorum fructum haud exiguum percipere gens solet, ut non pauci aliqui et insigniores viri litterarum custodes et dispensatores sint, sed auctis comparandae eruditionis subsidiis facilique ad eam aditu dato et vulgata per omnes artis cum aliquo successu tractandae via et ratione, quam invenerant et praeceperant ii, qui familiam duxerunt, eruditio latius sparsa et disseminata sit, multosque nec contemnendos auctores habeat, quorum nullus ita emineat, ut longiori reliquos intervallo superet.

Thus it happens that, when the resources of learning, which were once possessed by a few rich men, are divided among many, the literary republic, which the aristocrats had formerly in some measure held, is changed, as it were, into a popular state.
The sum of all these things, if I see anything, does not depend on the will of the prince:
but the fatal course of the human mind, obedient to its own laws and to the eternal order, draws them on, and hurries mortals, unwilling and struggling, toward the destined end;

A divine power presides over them, which sends forth and recalls talents, and, as for the whole human race, so for individual peoples, it has appointed and marked out for each its own ages, distinguished by certain definite signs.
I have said that the prince, moreover, cannot accomplish certain things that pertain to the flourishing of literature under certain conditions.
Thus there are, to use these examples, several kinds of literature that cannot be brought to completion except in a certain state of the republic.

Among these, eloquence holds the first place—I mean civil eloquence, not sacred, not the shadowy eloquence of the schools, which, even if it retains the color and appearance of a polished speech, would nevertheless have lost its juice and blood.
Indeed, no one denies that this eloquence was not the last part of the ancient learning of the Greeks and Romans:
But for this to flourish, two civic virtues are needed.

For citizens ought to be so inclined to the cultivation of the finer arts and of all humanity, that they not only cultivate their native language with the greatest zeal, but also eagerly inquire into all those matters which pertain to maintaining human society, to establishing, preserving, and correcting laws and rights, and to enjoy that freedom which affords speakers the opportunity of showing how much eloquence avails in the commonwealth:

Since these two things had come together exceptionally in the Athenian state, while in other states, although by no means unacquainted with the arts, they had come together less, among the Greeks that art of speaking stood out as almost peculiar to them, and the single Attic city flourished with more orators than all the rest of Greece together.

Although this art can hardly be said how much influence it has in public affairs, because it gives back to liberty, its parent, its nurse, because it reveals the hidden decay of states and public pretense, because it warns of impending dangers, because it provides, exhorts, reproaches, drives out idleness, depresses the inactive and those unequal to conducting affairs, and brings to the helm of the republic the most prudent, the bravest, the most ready:
Nevertheless, it also exercises great power in literature.

For orators together with philosophers and poets form and shape diction, and they lift up minds with the weight of their thoughts, and they sharpen the sense of elegance, and they educate ears, and what I judge to be most important, they increase the force and strength of language wonderfully.
Take away the orators:
you will have cut off much of the sinews of the language, you will have snatched away from the poets themselves, the philosopher, the writer of history much nourishment full of healthy juice;
how much all of them are nourished by eloquence can be conjectured from Greek literature.
But eloquence has no place in every republic:
And so not even the Ptolemies, although they were very fond of literature, were able to restore eloquence.
I do not contend that that supreme freedom, which gave birth to and nourished the oratorical art, should be preferred to this stable condition of affairs and public security:
Nay, if the old wisdom rightly taught that the half is more than the whole, it might perhaps be better to be half-free:

I affirm this, led by the inner causes of things, that this kind of literature cannot be cultivated in those forms of government in which the system is not otherwise established than if it is rendered to one person.

And I do not fear to transfer the same thing in some measure to history, which cannot be well written except by an eloquent and fluent writer, which moreover demands nearly the same freedom of speech as eloquence, because this is the first law of history, that you should not dare to say anything false, but should say whatever is true, and finally which brilliant minds will flee from and shrink to approach, when they have first perceived that things must be concealed and suppressed, not those which displease themselves, but those which displease any other judges whatsoever, and that with no public benefit they would bring upon themselves envy and offenses, if one is unwilling either to pretend or to dissemble.

Although the indulgence of a good prince will alleviate these disadvantages as much as the condition of the empire will allow, yet how much they may suffer, especially in more serious times of the republic and in great upheaval, is neither clear to all nor easy to understand.

However this may be decided, whoever weighs the matter fairly, since I have freely professed what I have established, will understand in treating the subject we are discussing that both the times must be regarded and the state and condition of the republic, which prevails at each season.
The principle of government will endure it, yet how much it endures, especially in the more serious times of the republic and in great upheaval, is neither clear to all nor easy to understand.

Whatever may be decided about this, whoever weighs the matter fairly, since I have professed to have established it freely, will understand, in treating the subject we are discussing, that both times must be considered and that the state of the republic and its condition, whatever it may be at any time, must be considered.
I turn now to the more cheerful and pleasant explanation of those things which, whatever the state of the city may be, depend on the prince.
And although he is not the sower of talents, nevertheless he can seek them out, recognize them, foster them, bring them to light, and finally use them in various ways.

But the correct use will be this: that he does not wish to rule their pursuits himself and give them laws, but that he conforms to their course, which is spontaneously borne toward that which is most excellent.

And since in the ruder age of any people a prince can most especially lay the foundations of a more civilized life and of all learning by founding and equipping schools, which we know Charles the Great once did, and which we now see must be done and is being done in Greece, in order that inveterate barbarism may be driven out:

tum qui eruditionem per regnum suum iam disseminatam acceperit, ut accepit Fridericus Guilelmus, quod nova quaeque aetas nova sibi adminicula deposcit, nec quae prioris aetatis necessitatibus sufficere videbantur, sufficiunt praesenti, immensam habet litteris benefaciendi materiam, quae in eo posita est, ut suppleat quae maiores imperfecta reliquerunt, ut si praesertim prolati fines imperii fuerint, novas bonarum artium addat sedes, ut scholas quaslibet et cetera litterarum instituta ad eum, qui adductus sit, meliorem eruditionis et scientiae statum et ad communem utilitatem accommodet, denique ut nihil omittat, quo et conservari parta et ad bonam frugem praesentia converti, et nova artium incrementa parari, nova lumina elici latiusque spargi possint.
For the human mind never rests:
But if, as we have said, certain studies sometimes relax, others are kindled all the more fiercely.

Indeed, let him demand that we waste our labor, whoever should desire that it be demonstrated by me that, in all these longings of literature, none of those princes who are now and who formerly were has satisfied and satisfies Frederick William more prudently, more effectively, more munificently; that no one, led by so great and so sincere goodwill of mind, by his own sole will of doing good, with no spur of ambition, has been so far from ostentation and extravagance as from unseasonable parsimony and tenacity.

But allow me to look a little more closely at those arts by which the prince and the prince's ministers seem to deserve best of all literature, especially in that condition of the literary republic which now exists.

For since learning has now grown to such an extent that in almost every field there is an abundant supply of those who are imbued with a plausible appearance of knowledge, and not only imbued with this appearance, but also equipped with those aids of learning which seem to make them fit for instructing the young;
the greater the number of competitors, the easier is the choice, and again the more difficult:
easier, if it is considered enough to have placed a not unworthy man in the chair;
It is more difficult, if one asks who is most worthy.
But indeed the most worthy must be sought:
This matter, difficult in itself, is often voluntarily disturbed by ambition and favor, sometimes even by envy, which attacks the highest, careless of the lesser.
I praise the golden mean, provided it is not placed at the summit:
Rewards, honors, magistracies, offices, any duties whatsoever become worthless, unless they are conferred upon the most worthy.
But among such great cares of empire, how few are the princes who can descend to this, that they themselves choose professors and teachers of every kind?

And so, to whatever perfection literature will be able to attain by its own virtue without a skilled guide, it is of the greatest interest to literature what sort of men the king entrusts with the care and direction of public instruction.

For this province, if any other, demands a man who is equipped with the other virtues, and especially endowed with a liberal mind, and a lover of all literature and of the learned and the studious, and so trained in a certain circle of all disciplines that he knows each individual part of these, and discerns with keen judgment what in each kind is excellent.
a man of no ordinary but of exceptional talent, so that, since like generally delights in like, he may favor the mediocre rather than the excellent among the learned;
a shrewd judge of talents and most observant of opportunities, so that he may win over those whom he has approved;

finally, one capable of great designs, so that he may not be content with acquiring the meager and most necessary supplies of learning, nor rest satisfied with preserving present conditions, but may attempt something more magnificent, something worthy of so great an empire, of so great a prince.

It would not be beside the purpose, nor, I think, unpleasant to you, my hearers, if, just as the lyric and tragic poets of the Greeks used the personae of ancient heroes in such a way that by describing their characters, deeds, and fortune, whether prosperous or adverse, they expressed the virtues of the famous men who then flourished or signified the condition of present affairs—not what things or what men they were—but if I may be allowed to look a little more closely at those arts by which the prince and the prince's ministers, in that condition of the literary republic which now especially exists, seem to have deserved best of all literature.

For since learning has now grown to such an extent that in almost every field there is an abundant supply of those who are imbued with a plausible appearance of knowledge, and not only imbued with this appearance, but also equipped with those aids of learning which seem to make them fit for instructing the young;
the greater the number of competitors, the easier is the choice, and again the more difficult:
easier, if it is considered enough to have placed a not unworthy man in the chair;
It is more difficult, if one asks who is most worthy.
But indeed the most worthy must be sought:
This matter, difficult in itself, is often voluntarily disturbed by ambition and favor, sometimes even by envy, which attacks the highest, careless of the lesser.
I praise the golden mean, provided it is not placed on the summit:
Rewards, honors, magistracies, offices, any services whatsoever become worthless, unless they are conferred upon the most worthy.
But amid such great cares of empire, how few are the princes who can descend to this, that they themselves choose professors and teachers of every kind?

And so, to whatever perfection literature can attain by its own virtue without a skilled guide, it matters greatly to literature what kind of men the king entrusts with the care and governance of public instruction.

For this province, if any other, demands a man who is not only equipped with the other virtues, but especially endowed with a liberal mind, and a lover of all literature and of the learned and the studious, and so instructed in a certain circle of all disciplines that he knows each individual part of these, and discerns with keen judgment what is excellent in each kind;
a man of no ordinary but of exceptional talent, lest, because like generally delights in like, he should favor mediocre rather than excellent scholars;
a shrewd judge of talents and most observant of opportunities, so that he may win over those whom he has approved;

finally, one capable of great designs, lest he be content with acquiring the meager and most necessary supplies of learning, or rest satisfied with preserving present conditions, but so that he may undertake something more magnificent, something worthy of so great an empire, so great a prince.

It would not be beside the purpose, nor, I think, unpleasant to you, my hearers, if, just as the Greek lyric and tragic poets used the personae of ancient heroes in such a way that, by describing their characters, deeds, and fortune, whether prosperous or adverse, they expressed the virtues of the famous men who then flourished, or indicated the condition of present affairs—not declaring what thing or what men they meant, to whom they wished these things to be referred, because sometimes the nature of poetry did not permit it, sometimes another reason dissuaded them, but leaving the interpretation to the hearers, to whom, as if looking into a mirror, the image of the man described or of the thing signified would present itself of its own accord—

You will not regret it, I assure you, if I now, in nearly the same manner, call to mind the memory of an immortal man, who, not in this our own, but in the common fatherland Germany, in the last century, deserved excellently of literature.

I mean Münchhausen, who, under the auspices of George II, King of the Britons, founded the Georgia Augusta University and for more than thirty years governed it with tireless diligence and embraced it with fatherly love:
Whom, when he was dead, the Göttingen people mourned, as children mourn a father, because they knew that they owed to him all their goods and as much as each one owes to his own parents;

Whom, to use the words of Heynius, a most trustworthy authority, they did not fear as a master, although gentle and well deserving, but they all addressed and loved as a patron, a helper, a best friend, most devoted to their interests;
To whom they freely brought their cares, wishes, and desires;

He who by his counsel, authority, and action would resolve or alleviate their difficulties, or if what was sought had to be refused, would refuse with a calm brow, gentle words, and kind address, like an indulgent father to his children.
When I now recall these things before you, dearest colleagues, who have experienced and are experiencing the same daily, do you, I ask, need an interpreter?
And there were in Münchhausen nearly all things that would render him most suitable even for governing letters in a larger kingdom.
He had formed in his mind a sketch of all the disciplines, and he knew the dignity, necessity, usefulness, growth, and decline of each, and the connection of all with one another.
He understood the character of the age.
Nor was his spirit unequal to the new undertaking, however arduous.
Indeed, he was deficient in no branch of literature, except that he was somewhat more estranged from philosophy, whose face at that time was not very cheerful.

And he was almost the first to bring together all kinds of studies, a great part of which had previously been cultivated outside the boundaries of the university, into this most ample body of academic discipline.
In this matter, however, how great a gap has been left in our age and in our republic under the auspices of Frederick William, there is no need for me to explain.

But in the selection of learned men, which Heynius most rightly calls the second anchor of the academic republic, it is wonderful how fortunate a discoverer of talents he showed himself, and he shrank from no burden of care:

I pass over how great the preparations were that they sought to have brought back, declaring that sometimes the principle of poetry did not allow it, sometimes another reason dissuaded, but leaving the interpretation to the audience, to whom, as if looking into a mirror, the image of the man described or of the thing signified would present itself of its own accord:

I assure you, you will not regret it, if I now, in nearly the same manner, call to mind the memory of an immortal man, who, not in this our own, but in the common fatherland Germany, in the last century, deserved excellently of literature.

I mean Münchhausen, who, under the auspices of George II, King of the Britons, founded the Georgia Augusta University and for more than thirty years governed it with tireless diligence and embraced it with fatherly love:
Whom, when he was dead, the people of Göttingen mourned, as children mourn a father, because they understood that they owed to him all their goods and as much as each one owes to his own parents;

Whom, to use the words of Heynius, a most trustworthy authority, they did not fear as a master, although gentle and well deserving, but they all addressed and loved as a patron, a helper, a best friend, most devoted to their interests;
To whom they freely brought their cares, wishes, and desires;

He who by his counsel, authority, and action would resolve or alleviate their difficulties, or if what was sought had to be refused, he would refuse with a calm brow, gentle words, and kind address, like an indulgent father refusing his children.
When I now recall these things before you, dearest colleagues, who have experienced the same and experience them daily, do you, I ask, need an interpreter?
And there were in Münchhausen almost all the qualities that would make him most suitable even for governing a larger realm.
He had formed in his mind a sketch of all the disciplines, and he knew the dignity, necessity, usefulness, growth, and decline of each, and the connection of all with one another.
He understood the character of the age.
Nor was his mind unequal to a new undertaking, however arduous.
Indeed, he was deficient in no kind of literature, except that he was somewhat more estranged from philosophy, whose face at that time was not very cheerful.

And he was almost the first to bring together all kinds of studies, a great part of which was previously cultivated outside the boundaries of the universities, into this most ample body of academic discipline.
In this matter, however, how much of a gap has been left in our age and in our republic under the auspices of Frederick William, there is no need for me to explain.

But in the selection of learned men, which Heynius most rightly calls the second anchor of the academic republic, it is wonderful how happy a discoverer of talents he showed himself, and he shrank from no trouble of care:
I pass over how great apparatus he collected, how much labor and assiduity he himself expended on equipping the university library, especially that most copious and most select one.

But Heynius, especially that man skilled in academic governance, in which he himself later held great authority, does not dwell at length on any part of his praises in that speech in which he paid his due respects to Münchhusius almost seventy years ago, nor does he insist more earnestly on any point than that Münchhusius, when he led literature, as it were, out of the cells of monasteries into the field and dust of civil life, at the same time knew the freedom of thinking, feeling, and writing:
He says that this aegis, this Palladium of the university, is this:
And if any wicked fraud of a man should snatch it away, then at last he thinks he will have a reason to fear for the fortune of the university:

For this reason he proclaims that Münchhausen brought new light into almost all disciplines, especially into the historical and the discipline of public law, which it greatly matters for princes and states to be handed down whole and undefiled, and that he illuminated everything far and wide.
Such, therefore, was that Münchhausen:

Looking at him, I am moved in my mind both for his own sake and because of the admirable judgment of our most wise, most kind, most just King in choosing his magnificent plans' administrator, a judgment most useful to our affairs.
How much labor and diligence he himself spent on equipping the university library, especially that most abundant and most select one.

But Heynius, especially that man skilled in academic governance, in which he himself afterward held great authority, does not dwell at length on any part of his praises in that speech with which he paid his due respects to Münchhusius almost seventy years ago, nor does he insist more earnestly on any point than that Münchhusius, when he led literature, as it were, out of the cells of monasteries into the field and dust of civil life, at the same time knew the freedom of thinking, feeling, and writing:
This is the aegis, this is the Palladium of the university.
But if any wicked fraud of a man should snatch it away, then at last he thinks he will have reason to fear for the fortune of the university.

For this reason he proclaims that Münchhausen brought new light into almost all disciplines, especially into the historical and the public law discipline, which it is of great importance to the princes and states to be handed down whole and undefiled, and that he illuminated everything far and wide.
Such, therefore, was that Münchhausen.

When I look at him, I am moved in my mind both for his own sake and because of the admirable judgment of our most wise, most kind, most just King in choosing his administrator of magnificent plans, a judgment most useful to our affairs.
While I am setting these things forth, listeners, I have taken up a great subject implicitly, by unfolding and explaining which I could have pursued the praises of Frederick William more eloquently.
But what shall I set forth, which everyone does not see, feel, and understand from the daily use of royal beneficence?
However, let no one take in a bad sense what I have discussed about those studies which a prince cannot support in any state of the republic:
although I know that all ill-will is absent from you, and the consciousness of my devotion, most devoted to the best King, reassures me:
I freely affirm that that liberty, without which the life of universities is not vital, by which the highest glory and ornament of letters is contained, remains safe and sound among us.

Recall, you who are older, as many of you as have been present here with me from the beginning of this school, when at that time a great part of you were summoned here by Frederick William from other seats of learning, recall the condition which then existed in other universities and especially in ours, of which none of us was then ashamed, and compare with it this condition which we now enjoy.
What, by your faith, have we lost?
How little has changed among us in these six lustra, in these most serious times for universities?
For Frederick William does not approve those who try to obstruct the lights of the mind:
this citadel, this bulwark of our freedom, as long as we do not fail ourselves.
That we may not fail ourselves, the dignity of knowledge contributes on the one hand, and on the other a certain continuity of discipline and of purposes long since confirmed.

For our ancestors most wisely established this, that they founded these colleges of learned men, which are called by the name of universities, not because they embrace the whole circle of letters, but because they are bodies endowed with their own rights and composed in the likeness of a commonwealth.
In these, unless they are corrupted by the evil arts of ambitious men, excellent counsels are handed down from ancestors to posterity by a constant succession.

That our school too, at that age, was reduced to this form of a college, at a time when, of course, many thought that these ruinous remnants of the barbarous age should be entirely removed—will it seem wonderful that this should be mentioned among the benefits conferred upon us by Frederick William?
There is indeed, there is very great power in this communion and fellowship of studies, institutions, necessities, and utilities.
Those who individually had been weak, to them union adds strength;
Disagreements of opinions, accidental quarrels, private enmities yield to the public good, and we are like children of one family under a King as patron.
That grief and mourning, equally domestic and public, is evidence, if any of us has been taken from us by death and from literature.

O that our colleague, endowed with the most excellent gifts of mind and talent, had not recently been lamented! No one thought that all the advantages and disadvantages of the university pertained more to himself, no one was a more certain and sincere friend, no one was more benevolent to fellow students.
I consider it a religious duty not to mention him in these solemn ceremonies, at which he was never absent from venerating the King.

Whom the very logic of this speech of mine demands that I mention not more for his own sake than for the sake of praising the state, because in him it was made clear how much liberty this empire can bear.
For this man, as we despair of being able to find an equal successor, so we pray that a completely unequal one may not follow.

As I now would profess these things in three words, I was moved by piety, which is the mother of all virtues, not that piety consisting of formulas and ceremonies, but dwelling in the hearts of men, not that foul nurse of hatreds and discords, by which the priestly sedition and the obstinacy of the Roman curia disturbed the security of this most tranquil city, but the teacher of charity and love, with which Frederick William embraces his people.
But what is piety without gratitude that remembers benefits?
Who does not approve of those who repay with evil deeds those who have deserved well of them, those Guilelmus-like men who try to obstruct the lights of the mind?
This is the citadel, this the bulwark of our liberty, as long as we do not fail ourselves.
That we may not fail ourselves, on the one hand the dignity of knowledge, on the other a certain continuity of discipline and of purposes long since confirmed, brings it about.

For our ancestors most wisely established this, that they founded these colleges of learned men, which are called by the name of universities, not because they embrace the whole circle of letters, but because they are bodies endowed with their own rights and formed in the likeness of a commonwealth.
In these, unless they are corrupted by the evil arts of ambitious men, excellent plans are handed down from ancestors to posterity by a constant succession.

Will it seem surprising that this is counted among the benefits conferred upon us by Frederick William, that our school too was reduced to this form of a college at that time, when, of course, very many thought that these ruinous relics of the barbarous age should be entirely removed?
There is indeed, there is very great power in this communion and fellowship of studies, institutions, necessities, and utilities.
Those who individually had been weak, to them union adds strength.
Disagreements of opinions, accidental quarrels, private enmities yield to the public good, and we are like children of one family under a King as patron.
That grief and mourning, equally domestic and public, is evidence, if any of us has been taken from us by death and from literature.

O that our colleague, endowed with the most excellent gifts of mind and talent, had not so recently been lamented! No one more than he considered all the advantages and disadvantages of the university to pertain to himself; no one was a more certain and sincere friend; no one was more benevolent to his fellow students.
I consider it a religious duty not to mention him in these solemn ceremonies, at which he was never absent from venerating the King.

Whom the very logic of this speech of mine demands that I mention not more for his own sake than for the sake of praising the state, because in him it was made clear how much this empire can bear of liberty.
As we despair of being able to find an equal to succeed this man, so we pray that his successor may not be wholly unlike him.

As I now profess these things in three words, I was moved by piety, which is the mother of all virtues, not that piety consisting of formulas and ceremonies, but dwelling in the hearts of men, not that foul nurse of hatreds and discords, by which the priestly sedition and the obstinacy of the Roman curia disturbed the security of this most tranquil city, but the teacher of charity and love, with which Frederick William embraces his people.
But what is piety without a grateful remembrance of benefits?
Who would not call those who repay with evil deeds those who have deserved well of them not only inhuman but savage and wild, since not even the tamer beasts are devoid of all sense of gratitude?

But if the remaining virtue of Frederick William, beneficent to all, and the sanctity of the oath did not bind us to devote ourselves to him, nevertheless the remembrance of the benefits with which he has heaped this university ought to bring it about that whatever he expects from us (for he expects nothing that cannot be performed without violating religion), that we should strive diligently and strenuously to perform.
At this point, fellow soldiers, I must urge you to repay with gratitude, in the ways you can, the most merciful King, who takes exceptional care of your prosperity.
I mean love of the Prince and affection for the fatherland, diligence in studies, reverence for the laws, and modesty and strictness of morals.
Although I advise that thanks should be given to the best Prince, I do not do so because this admonition seems necessary to me now, but to indulge my own feelings.

For the more ungrateful we have seen those men toward the King, whose power, dignity, and resources he alone restored, the more earnestly do all good men love Frederick William, and congratulate him on the constancy of his purposes, and hope that he will be the avenger and preserver of the highest goods of the soul for his people, and that he will not yield to superstition, which is growing everywhere, and is nourished secretly and openly, by deceits and by authority, and threatens a most grievous servitude.
I pray you, God, Best and Greatest, that you would ward off and avert this evil from our state;

I pray that you may grant to Frederick William a vigorous old age, free from all distress; that you may direct his counsels to the strengthening of the safety of his people; that you may preserve the harmony and mutual affection of the ruling family and the people; and finally, that you may keep safe the magnanimous Prince, heir to the kingdom, in whom the nearest hope of the fatherland is placed, together with his august consort restored to us by your favor, and the entire royal house.
Would he not call them not only uncivilized but savage and wild, since even the gentler beasts do not lack every feeling of gratitude?

But if the remaining virtue of Frederick William, beneficent to all, and the sanctity of the oath did not bind us to devote ourselves to him, nevertheless the remembrance of the benefits with which he has heaped this university ought to bring it about that whatever he expects from us (for he expects nothing that cannot be performed without violating religion), that we should strive diligently and strenuously to perform.
At this point I must urge you, fellow soldiers, that you also, in the ways you can, show gratitude to the most merciful King, who takes exceptional care of your prosperity.
I mean love of the Prince and love of country, diligence in studies, reverence for the laws, and modesty and strictness of morals.
Although I do not do this because I think this admonition is necessary for me now, but to indulge my own feelings, when I urge that thanks should be given to the best Prince.

For the more ungrateful we have seen those men toward the King, whose power, dignity, and resources he alone restored, the more earnestly do all good men love Frederick William, and congratulate him on the constancy of his purposes, and hope that he will be the avenger and preserver of the highest goods of the soul for his people, and will not yield to superstition, which everywhere grows strong, and is nourished secretly and openly, by deceits and authority, and threatens a most sad servitude.
I pray you, God, Best and Greatest, that you would defend and avert this evil from our state;

I pray that you may grant to Frederick William a vigorous old age, free from all distress; that you may direct his counsels to the strengthening of the safety of his people; that you may preserve the harmony and mutual affection of the ruling family and the people; and finally, that you may keep safe the magnanimous Prince, heir to the kingdom, in whom the nearest hope of the fatherland is placed, together with his august consort restored to us by your favor, and the entire royal house.

div.head: XXVII. Friderici Guilelmi III. laudatio d. XXVII. m. Iunii a. MDCCCXL. dicta.

p.s: I, who from my youth, with the continuous success of many years, have celebrated in my speech the most joyful solemnity of that day on which Frederick William was born for the happiness of the fatherland, most distinguished men, most learned men, most honored fellow soldiers, now about to pay the last rites to the ashes of the Father of the Fatherland, with what feeling do you think I am affected, with what confidence equipped, to approach so great a matter, so grave and arduous, so sad and mournful?

Indeed, each of you, as many as are present, can infer the feeling of my mind from your own mind, and from the common grief and longing of all, since we mourn the death of a king so beloved that every best man, if it had been possible, would have been willing to redeem his life with his own death.
I fear that few sufficiently realize how much confidence fails me, and rightly fails me.
For although there are many things that make the praise of a living master difficult and uncertain, nevertheless in performing that duty the mind is raised and strengthened by not a few things:
the serene image of a flourishing prince presents itself to the speaker, which may fill the orator with joy;
the mind of the speaker is moved by most pleasing and sweetest emotions, when he congratulates a good king on his successes and makes vows for his safety;
The joyful faces of the audience add strength to my weak powers, and even spur on the slow.

But in these most mournful solemnities everything is arranged to disturb and confound the mind: the sad appearance of the place, your grief, the mourning of the republic, and finally my own sorrow and distress, which would break even a stronger man and close the mouths of the eloquent.
To be brief:
If your kindness has conceived any good opinion of me from my frequent praises of the surviving King, that opinion seems to me to have been extinguished by the death of that excellent King.

Indeed, I who had wished rather to hide myself in solitude and silently ponder with myself the virtues of the deceased Prince, silently to grieve the bitter misfortune, after some time was indeed granted for collecting my mind, I am dragged into the light, which I cannot bear, as if one had exposed a sick man, to whom darkness brings relief, to the endurance of the sun's glare.
Therefore the spirit is cast down;
I despair of fulfilling so great a task as has been entrusted to me today by you, my dearest colleagues, who trust me too much not so much because of my skill as because of my goodwill.
Nevertheless I will speak as best I can, since I cannot speak as I wish.

Finally, to strengthen myself as much as possible, I will not indulge in tears, but I will restrain my lamentation and tearful cries, which do not even seem fitting for the funeral rites of a brave man:

I shall try to recall both myself and you somewhat from the bitterness of grief, and to lift up our minds by contemplating the life of our most beloved King, not so much his death, by which we have been struck down, as his life, which has been and is salutary for the citizens, for the Prussian kingdom, and for all Europe, as far as my strength suffices.
You would have exposed yourself to the sun to be endured.
Therefore the mind is cast down;
I despair of fulfilling so great a task as has been entrusted to me today by you, dearest colleagues, who have trusted too much in my good will rather than in my skill.
But I will speak as best I can, since I cannot speak as I wish.

Finally, to strengthen myself as much as possible, I will not indulge in tears, but I will restrain my lamentation and tearful cries, which do not even seem fitting for the funeral rites of a brave man:

I shall try to recall both myself and you somewhat from the bitterness of grief, and to lift up our minds by contemplating the life of our most beloved King, not so much his death, by which we have been struck, as his life, which has been and is salutary for the citizens, for the Prussian kingdom, and for all Europe, as far as my strength suffices.
When I say 'life,' I mean something great, and perhaps something greater than I seem to mean.

For this is not the only life that our bodies live, and the soul in the body, but a future life follows this one lived on earth, that constant and perpetual life following this fleeting and fragile one.

Indeed, if there is anything that offers us a better hope of dying, that can console those who are left mourning for the death of a dear one, what consolation is more effective, what is more worthy of a philosopher and a Christian man, than that we not only hope and believe, but know that, when the bonds of the body are loosened and the prison broken, the soul, a particle of the divine breath, freed, returns to the kindred spirits above from which it came forth?
That the life we now lead is a pilgrimage, pleasant by the sight and survey of various things, agreeable by the abundance of favorable circumstances, sweet by pleasures;

The same life is troublesome with cares and tumults, obstructed with rough places and dangers, filled with miseries and evils, which not even he who is placed on the highest pinnacle can escape, being subject to the more severe misfortunes and greater losses, the more ample the goods and the higher the place.

When this earthly journey has been traversed, the death that follows is the beginning of a higher life, and the ancient sages, anticipating the divine precepts of our faith, rightly conjectured that what we call life is that death, and what we call death is life.
Therefore, since death seems to begin the true life, this life which we now live is a meditation on death:

We divine and believe that for those who have lived justly and piously, who in the greatest fortune have never forgotten that they are mortal, and have so lived as to know that human souls, stripped and laid bare of all pomp and splendor at some time, will render an account to the supreme judge of all those things which they have administered in this earthly province, that life will be more blessed, when they are brought back to the supreme deity.

So that you cannot tell whether death is rather to be congratulated for the good, who indeed, besides the common weakness of mankind, conscious of no fault of their own, die with good hope, while the same death terrifies the wicked and the criminal.
Therefore the Father of the fatherland has not died, but has been carried up to a more blessed seat, which is firmer and more sublime than the very royal throne he had obtained;
Therefore he is not to be lamented:
But we who are left behind, measuring our grief from our own longing, not from the most blessed condition of the heavenly soul, nevertheless stand sorrowfully at the funeral with good reason.
This immortality, which truly belongs to the divine part of man, I think I am not mistaken if I call it divine;
But there is also another human immortality, which must not be counted in the last place, and that is not simple but divided into two parts.

And indeed, next to that divine immortality is the second one, the immortality of a name, which is preserved by the memory of deeds and by the monuments of talent, virtue, and kindness that each person has left behind.
In this regard, a great prerogative has been given to princes.
For we are all born and die indiscriminately, and with equal foot death, to use a common phrase, strikes the towers of kings and the huts of the poor.
Nor is the richest man, at his last breath, different from a beggar, nor a king from a private citizen or a slave.
But they differ in the comforts and discomforts of life, in the resources and outcomes of their affairs.

For a prince, indeed, from his very birth, there falls to him an immense abundance and opportunity for great deeds and for benefiting the human race, and again license for idleness, luxury, cruelty, and any evil arts whatsoever, which we generally see go unpunished.
Indeed, the memory of a conspicuous vice is propagated to posterity just as much as that of virtue.
But we do not attribute immortality of name except to virtue.
This is the second immortality of Frederick William, that not only we have admired and do admire his virtue, but future ages will proclaim it;

Because the things he accomplished brilliantly at home and in war will live no less in the memory of men than the mighty deeds of Frederick the Great, and will be handed down forever by historians with the highest praise, as long as the good arts, which he fostered with such great zeal, do not become obsolete.

We divine and believe that that life will be happier for those returning to the supreme deity, because he left to his people, to Germany, to all Europe, lasting monuments of the best counsels and benefits of such a kind that they would benefit not only his contemporaries but also posterity, who will rest under the shade of the trees that he planted and will gather the harvest that the province had produced.

So that you cannot tell whether death is rather to be congratulated for the good, who indeed, besides the common weakness of mankind, conscious of no fault of their own, die with good hope, while the same death terrifies the wicked and the criminal.
Therefore the Father of his country has not died, but has been carried up to a more blessed seat, which is firmer and more sublime than the very royal throne he had obtained;
Therefore he is not to be lamented:
But we who are left behind, measuring our grief by our own longing, not by the most blessed condition of that heavenly soul, nevertheless stand here sorrowfully at the funeral, and rightly so.
This immortality, which in reality belongs to the divine part of man, I think I am not mistaken in calling divine;
But there is also another human immortality, which is not to be counted in the last place, and that not simple but divided into two parts.

And indeed, next to that divine immortality is the second one, the immortality of the name, which is contained in the memory of deeds and in the monuments of talent, virtue, and kindness, which each person has left behind.
In this, a great prerogative has been given to princes.
For we are all born and die indiscriminately, and with equal foot death, to use a common word, strikes the towers of kings and the huts of the poor.
Nor is the richest man, at his last breath, different from a beggar, nor a king from a private citizen or a slave.
But they differ in the comforts and discomforts of life, in the resources and outcomes of their affairs.

For a prince, by his very birth, obtains an immense abundance and opportunity for great deeds and for benefiting the human race, and again license for idleness, luxury, cruelty, and any evil arts whatsoever, which we generally see go unpunished.
Indeed, the memory of a conspicuous vice is propagated to posterity just as much as that of virtue.
But we do not attribute the immortality of a name except to virtue.
This is the second immortality of Frederick William, that his virtue not only we have admired and do admire, but future ages will proclaim it.

He left to his people, to Germany, to all Europe, lasting monuments of the best counsels and, even amid the pressing necessities of the present time, benefits of such a kind that they would profit not only his contemporaries but also posterity, who will rest under the shade of the trees that he planted and will gather the harvest that he sowed.
Thirdly, why should we not esteem the eternity of the stock and race, by which even that which is mortal is propagated?
The most flourishing offspring of Frederick William lives and thrives, sons and grandsons, those already now supports of the empire, these in time to come to follow in the footsteps of their fathers;
the son has taken up the kingdom equal to his father, whom we now venerate as our most serene lord with no less piety than his most blessed father:

who, by his innate virtue, will protect the state; by his affability, even before his principate, he has already won the hearts of all; with prudence and kindness he will diligently provide for all the prosperity of his people.

Truly, how great a consolation for so great a loss and relief of grief is this, that to the Prince, uniquely beloved, has succeeded a King of most robust age, distinguished by the most beautiful gifts of mind and talent, equipped with the best arts, whose public and private virtues we have come to know through use and experience and the benefits conferred upon us, whose excellent character I would not hesitate even now to celebrate more fully, were it not that an untimely eulogy of a Prince just beginning seemed to be in this common and deepest sorrow.

But as for the other immortality, which I called the immortality of fame, since leading men cannot attain it by one single path, and especially either by military glory or by the arts of peace, this has long been the good fortune of Prussia, that its kings excel in both kinds of glory.
But different men have entered upon different paths of performing glorious deeds;

Most blessed Father of the Fatherland, by what character, by what deeds, by what institutions, by what vicissitudes of fortune, and finally with what success he earned this eternity of his name, there is none of you, listeners, who does not understand that I must discuss this uniquely, avoiding any digressions of speech, and who does not uniquely desire to hear it.

Since I have set forth these matters individually and in detail, almost throughout the whole course of my life, with the greatest zeal and with admiration for royal virtue, I shall now make, as it were, a very brief summary of them.
I shall speak simple words;
true feeling does not run out into a luxuriant and exultant style of speech.

When I consider the character of Frederick William, I do not hesitate to recount the series of his many virtues, both because I myself know that all these virtues were in him, and because I would judge your loyalty poorly if I thought that any of you would decide otherwise.
For why was he so dear to all, why did he pass away mourned by all, why was he so missed, if not because of the very many virtues that stood out in him?
There was indeed an admirable union and harmony of the good arts in that man:

But this, just as sharp and deep sounds are tempered into a harmony, so in the human mind is brought about by moderation and temperance, which seems to me to have been that virtue of the most blessed Father of the Fatherland, from which nearly all the others flowed, by which they were held together as by a very strong bond.
This he never failed to maintain both publicly and privately.
For Frederick William was not indeed a good prince, but he was of ambiguous reputation in private life;
not good at home, but unequal to the conduct of the state:
which in so great fortune seem able neither easily to be united nor separated, private and public virtues were equally conspicuous in him.

A most faithful and loving husband, an excellent head of a household, gentle and courteous toward domestic servants, so averse to the luxury of the court that in his daily food and dress he scarcely equaled the splendor of a somewhat wealthier private citizen, he restored the ancient simplicity and strictness of morals, a most useful example to the citizens.

Now, since a perfect prince ought to excel both in courage and in clemency and wisdom, Frederick William proved himself brave not only by leading an army and by military glory and by enduring hardships, but also by constancy of mind in bearing any calamities whatsoever:

He, no less than Frederick the Great, combined with that strength of mind wisdom and gentleness, I mean the genuine wisdom of the mind, which would not aspire to the praise of manifold learning, and would differ greatly from the cunning and deceits by which, as many think that peoples are to be ruled, so Frederick William, a most upright and honest man, thought that nothing was to be done through those arts, but through faith and sincerity;

And being strict when the situation demanded it, whenever it could be done without public harm, he never failed to give way to more lenient measures, like a prudent and humane physician preferring milder remedies to fire and the knife.
Being fair and just to all, he not only took the greatest care that no one should suffer injury, but he also strove to repair any injury whatsoever.

With what feelings he had been disposed toward those by whom he had been wronged, who did not read in that will of his, drawn up thirteen years ago, by the promulgation of which Frederick William the Fourth auspiciously began his reign, with the deepest emotion and with tears that welled up unbidden?
Indeed, that heart of his must have been imbued with not even the slightest sense of humanity and harder than flint and adamant, whose heart that royal will did not touch!

What shall I say of the piety and holiness of the most blessed King, with which he worshipped and revered the divine power, which never allowed that the union and harmony of the good arts should turn him aside from a right conscience?

But this moderation and temperance, just as sharp and grave sounds are tempered into harmony, so it works in the human mind; which seems to me to have been that virtue of the Father of his Country, most blessed, from which nearly all the others flowed, by which they were held together as by a very firm bond.

What shall I say of the piety and holiness of the most blessed King, with which he worshipped and revered the divine deity, which never allowed him to depart a finger's breadth from a right conscience?

But with what excellent moderation did he combine liberality and munificence with frugality, being neither tenacious of wealth nor prodigal, having spent much on the flourishing of literature and the arts and on the necessities of the church, having spent much to aid provinces afflicted by famine, pestilence, cheapness of provisions, or inundations of rivers, and having moreover bestowed no small sums from his private treasury to relieve the poverty and straitened circumstances of individuals who had fled to him!
He never hardened himself against anyone's misfortune, but amid the very cares of empire, which would bid a heart to be encased in triple bronze, he retained human compassion.
And the most modest of all princes we know did nothing for display and ostentation, and if not careless of fame, at least not eagerly or ambitiously desirous of it.
On the contrary, the virtues which I said were conspicuous in him, he himself did not want to be conspicuous.

He was led by no party spirit, favored no class of citizens above others, and was not subject to the voices, whispers, and goads of any servants—as the Roman emperors of old were to their freedmen—nor of courtiers, if indeed a prince has courtiers, nor of informers or spies, like that famous Marcus.
Antoninus always maintained his own character most steadfastly.
These things are almost all very closely connected with continence and moderation, which I have indicated was, as it were, peculiar to the most blessed King.

He who held the supreme command of so great a state had nothing more important or more ancient than that he should command himself with a composed mind, keeping far away hatreds, angers, desires, and any emotions of the mind that disturb too much.
What wonder, then, if the same moderation which he himself employed in his whole life, he shared with the state?

For through all parts of the state, through the minds of the king's friends and ministers, magistrates, soldiers, citizens, this moderation, which alone promises lasting happiness to the people, has spread from the highest place;
From this source was born public tranquility, a certain even-balanced condition of the kingdom, a calm course and progress of affairs, neither headlong nor sluggish.

When to this was added that singular goodwill toward all subjects and the intimate feeling of benevolence and courtesy, and popularity combined with majesty, when in administering the empire he sought not his own advantage but the safety of the people, which he believed had been entrusted to him by divine providence, and when moreover he wished to do everything not by his own judgment alone, but not unwillingly listened to those who were distinguished in each field, and yielded to their wishes:
which, in such great power, would hardly depart from itself even a nail's breadth?
