When, in addition, that singular goodwill toward all subjects, that intimate feeling of benevolence, that courtesy, and that popularity combined with majesty, came to him; when in administering the empire he sought not his own advantage but the safety of the people, which he believed had been entrusted to him by divine providence; and when, moreover, he was unwilling to do everything by his own judgment alone, but not unwillingly listened to those who were esteemed in every field, and yielded to their wishes:
That which a prince, in such great power, obtains from himself with difficulty, unless he has firmly resolved in himself to obey reason alone:

He brought it about that not only was his rule borne easily, being circumscribed by almost no agreements, by no laws except those which the King alone had given, but also that the greatest harmony of the whole commonwealth arose, never disturbed except by chance and, as it were, playful gatherings of the city crowd, and mutual love between King and people, by which the kingdom is held much more firmly than by the strength of armies;
so that the people might feel and understand that their own safety could not be separated from the safety of the King;

that the King might live as secure among a people enjoying just liberty as a father of a family among good children, and finally that he might draw those very provinces, which had recently been added by the outcome of wars, into that same consensus of goodwill and love, reverence, and admiration of royal virtue.
By these arts was accomplished whatever the most glorious Father of his Country did during his forty-three years of reign.

In what condition Frederick William the Third received his father's kingdom is known to no one, neither among the older nor the younger generation.

After the King, whose distinguished character is known to have been prophesied as that of Frederick the Great, had gained control of the highest affairs, he corrected morals, restored the resources of the treasury, which had been exhausted by the war of which he himself had been a witness in his youth and by lavish expenditures, and he either restored or confirmed the force of laws and the freedom of thought and speech that had been sanctioned by Frederick the Great, and he earnestly devoted his efforts to maintaining peace.
The first years of his reign flowed by in a calm course;
Although there were those to whom the peace, which was then held, seemed to have been a little too sluggish and remiss.
Meanwhile, by the treaty of Lunéville, the borders of the kingdom were advanced without bloodshed, with more territory received than had been lost.
Soon a sad reversal of all things followed.
For mortals must experience prosperity and adversity, rejoice and grieve.
And although kings hold the place of gods on earth, they are nevertheless not exempt from the lot of men, so that they are overtaken by the vicissitude and injustice of fortune.
Indeed, the best of kings fell with us into that age in which the immense power of one man shook the world with continuous disturbances.
Drawn along by this common ruin of the human race, Frederick William endured such great evils as no one could bear unless he were a most steadfast and most brave man.
God had willed that his pious worshiper should be tested like gold by fire, so that he might shine forth all the more brightly:
and, relying on God's help, he overcame the evils, however great they were.

A most just and most religious prince, I will not say with what difficulties he was then entangled, with what snares he was assailed, with what injuries and insults he was provoked and challenged to a war which he had uniquely striven to avoid:
it is hardly pleasing to renew old angers and to perpetuate feuds scarcely yet in some measure extinguished.
Why say more?

One most fatal day destroyed a most powerful and best-equipped army, overthrew a whole kingdom, and afflicted the Prussian people with the utmost calamities that had to be endured for more than six years.
The King was conquered, but conquered by whom?
Indeed, by that man who conquered all, until he was conquered by the combined forces of all, not without God as his helper.
The war was ended by a peace, which was more ruinous than the war itself:
the kingdom was punished by the loss of the greater part of its territories;
Against the King's will, so many most loyal peoples were dismissed unwillingly.
On the lands that Frederick William retained, very harsh conditions were imposed.

To the King was added the most bitter heap of grief: his dearest wife, snatched away by untimely death, the mother of so many children, the companion of such great misfortunes, and the darling of the people both while she flourished and after she died.
Yet Frederick William was not overwhelmed by the waves of such a storm, but emerged more noble and stronger and greater than himself.
For the greater the loss of territory was, the more zealous care he devoted to strengthening the forces of the kingdom that remained.

To pass over everything else at this point, although Frederick William, even when the Prussian state was flourishing, had favored literature exceptionally and had conferred many benefits especially upon the universities, particularly those of Halle and Erlangen, nevertheless, after the strength of arms was broken, he understood more keenly that the forces of the mind, which are stronger than arms themselves, must be roused and strengthened.
But he saw this most wisely, that it should be accomplished especially by aiding literature.
Therefore, for nurturing these, greater expenses were then made in the greatest straits of the treasury than ever before.
But I recall myself from this most abundant material of praise, to which I see that I must return afterwards.

When they contributed money, arms, and any military equipment whatsoever, not only those who were powerful in resources, but even the poor, brought whatever little each had, to the King and the fatherland.
I am moved in my soul when I recall those times;
But indeed the brevity of the hour, which has been granted to me for speaking, compels me to cut short not only my words but even my very thoughts.
Nor will I proclaim so many most noble victories:
I do not pass over the victory of Culm, a great part of which is acknowledged to be owed to the counsel and courage of the King himself.
His valor in Gaul was equal, and the moderation of the victor was no less.
This is the reward of the victories won in both wars, that now it has left to Frederick William the Fourth, our most gracious Lord, a greater empire than he had received.

But that he left not only more, but also more firmly and more flourishingly, we owe to that wisdom, by which, after overcoming dangers and enduring labors, he restored the state through the arts of peace, which was not even then disturbed, when all Europe trembled with a new commotion.

For when, ten years ago, so many new things, discords, seditions, and civil wars were harassing the neighboring nations, the Prussian state stood peaceful and unmoved, not so much because it was held together by skill and arms, as because the minds of the citizens were bound and obliged by the benefits of Frederick William; and although there were things that were desired, the mutual affection of the ruler and the subjects compensated for those compacts and rights which the peoples then longed to extort.

The day would fail me, listeners, if I wished to enumerate all those things, or even a great part of them, however briefly, which the most blessed Father of his Country instituted excellently in ordering the state during the three and forty years of his reign.
Nevertheless, piety demands that I run through briefly those parts of the state which he especially brought to a better condition.
I have said that he was fair to all orders;
The same man embraced almost all parts of the republic with equal care.
The division of the whole kingdom was changed, the whole system and form of administering the provinces;
Cities and towns were enlarged by new constitutions, so that citizens could manage their own affairs more conveniently, more usefully, more freely through their own magistrates and decurions;
The workshops were loosened from the bonds of the guilds, not only released, but so tempered that access to making work might not be too much closed off;
The farmers were freed from slavery, and the fields themselves became more fertile after the division was established.
Where once there were vast sands, now there are roads excellently paved.
The taxes were established in a new way, not so that as much as possible should be exacted, but so that they should be most equitable.
The towns, once closed by the guards of the tax-farmers, are now open day and night.

Trade, once hindered in many ways, is now most ready and most free, since a most beneficial treaty has been concluded with very many states of Germany, not for the sake of profit but so that the resources of the citizens might grow and the opportunity of seeking might be more ample and easier, concerning the commonality of revenues, and it is equally most acceptable to foreigners as to our own people.

Iam vero rem militarem, quae tamen videbatur sub prioribus regibus optime instructa esse, novo instituto ita ordinavit Fridericus Guilelmus, ut quum prius milites magna ex parte mercenarii essent, aegre isti poenis suppliciisque atrocissimis cohibiti, ceteri vero ex inferioribus subiectorum classibus conscriberentur, et per multos annos continuos retinerentur in manipulis, nunc stipendia honestissima facili obsequio mereantur cives universi, seu sponte sumpta militia sive iusto delectu, et illi post annum, hi post triennii spatium exauctorentur, temporaria posthac militia non nimium molesta quotannis exercitandi, civesque et milites non ut antea alteri ab alteris alienati sint, sed in unum quasi coaluerint corpus.
There was a time when it was charged against Prussia that it was too military:
But the last years of the most blessed King, in a very different part of the state, were subject to various judgments.
For long before, he had at heart to establish a certain order of sacred rites, not because he was devoted to ceremonies or wanted to strengthen his rule by fostering superstition:
For no one doubts that he was imbued with true piety and that he propagated it into the minds of the citizens by his own example.
But, if I am not mistaken, because he judged that in these matters not too much should be left to the discretion of individuals.

For my part, although I think that everyone should have his own judgment about divine matters (and Frederick William thought no differently), the most blessed King seems to me to have done this excellently, that he strove to reconcile both Protestant confessions and did reconcile them.
But if they cry that something in this matter was done too sharply, whose fault this was, let the judgment rest with others.
The Germans, indeed, with one voice have long proclaimed Frederick William as the leader and defender of the evangelical faith;

And he deserved that reward of his zeal which befell him, that he was permitted to celebrate two secular festivals of the reformation of religion, the one of the church restored by Luther, the other of the deliverance from the yoke of the Roman pontiff;
where once there were vast sands, now there are roads excellently paved;
The revenues were established in a new way, not so that as much as possible should be exacted, but so that they should be most equitable.
The towns, once closed by the guards of the tax-farmers, are now open by night and by day.

Trade, once hindered in many ways, is now most ready and most free, after a most beneficial treaty was concluded with very many states of Germany, not for the sake of profit but so that the resources of the citizens might grow and the opportunity of seeking might be more ample and easier, concerning the commonality of revenues, and it is equally most acceptable to foreigners as to our own people.

Iam vero rem militarem, quae tamen videbatur sub prioribus regibus optime instructa esse, novo instituto ita ordinavit Fridericus Guilelmus, ut quum prius milites magna ex parte mercenarii essent, aegre isti poenis suppliciisque atrocissimis cohibiti, ceteri vero ex inferioribus subiectorum classibus conscriberentur, et per multos annos continuos retinerentur in manipulis, nunc stipendia honestissima facili obsequio mereantur cives universi, seu sponte sumpta militia sive iusto delectu, et illi post annum, hi post triennii spatium exauctorentur, temporaria posthac militia non nimium molesta quotannis exercitandi, civesque et milites non ut antea alteri ab alteris alienati sint, sed in unum quasi coaluerint corpus.
There was a time when it was attributed to Prussia as a fault that it was too military:
But the last years of the most blessed King, in a very different part of the state, were subject to various judgments.
For indeed he had long had it at heart to establish a certain order of sacred rites, not because he was devoted to ceremonies or wanted to strengthen his rule by fostering superstition:
For that he was imbued with true piety and propagated it into the minds of the citizens by his example, no one doubts.
But, unless I am mistaken, he judged that in these matters not too much should be left to the discretion of individuals.

For my part, although I think that everyone should have his own judgment about divine matters (and Frederick William thought no differently), the most blessed King seems to me to have done this excellently, that he strove to reconcile both Protestant confessions and did reconcile them.
But if they cry out that something in this matter was done too sharply, whose fault this was, let the judgment be with others.
The Germans, indeed, with one voice have long proclaimed Frederick William as the leader and defender of the evangelical faith.

And he deserved that reward of his zeal which befell him, that he was permitted to celebrate two secular festivals of the reformation of sacred rites, one of the church restored by Luther, the other of the evangelical doctrine received from his ancestors in the Brandenburg land.
Yet the same man, with his characteristic fairness, strenuously protected the Catholic church in his kingdom.
Who does not know how much the Roman Pontiff himself owed to him, when he was restored to his dominion?
Who does not know that by royal munificence the dignity and splendor of the Catholic Church were restored in this kingdom?

For this reason it is the more to be lamented, that when the royal mind could not endure priestly obstinacy, the old age of the most pious King, if not afflicted, was at least saddened by the difficulties and disturbances which arose from that source.
I pass on to the other pursuits of Frederick William, for which greater gratitude was shown to him and is still shown.
For he was so generous to literature and the arts that he surpassed both all the universities and very many kings in the number and magnitude of his benefactions.

And he not only supported literature by his generosity, but also, although at this age a certain part of studies, both of the learned and of those eager for learning, was greatly suspected, nevertheless he treated us most liberally and gently.
We have retained the freedom of speaking and teaching;
As for writing, whether you would rather call it freedom or license, what seemed to be diminished is to be attributed not so much to the royal will as to the common failing of this age.
It is not unpleasant to recall at this point with what courtesy that great-hearted man dealt with the learned, to whom at last the most wise King had entrusted the supreme care of public education;

from which it can be understood with what sort of men, with what talent, with what skill in literature, with what sincerity of mind endowed, and finally how civil and indulgent the most blessed King judged that this province should be entrusted.
But we have very recently conducted the funeral of this most excellent man too, not without tears.
Under the auspices of Frederick William, moreover, both academies, that of the sciences and that of the arts, were better established.
Apparatus of every kind, necessary for the pursuit of the disciplines, were procured in the choicest and most abundant manner.
The literary universities, both the old ones restored and better equipped, and new and most celebrated ones founded at great expense.

By a new and most salutary arrangement, the King has placed our university in the very seat of the kingdom, and not in a less conspicuous place, but in the most frequented and most adorned street of the city, and in the immediate neighborhood of his own house and within his own view, and in these royal buildings, which he began to splendidly restore in the last few years:
And so that there might be proofs of the greatest affection with which he embraced learning, he wished both our university and the beloved Rhenish one to bear his name.
And so, just as the Greek cities of old honored their founders with heroic honors, so also did the Brandenburg land, having received the evangelical doctrine from its ancestors.
Nevertheless, with his characteristic fairness, he vigorously protected the Catholic church in his kingdom.
Who does not know how much the Roman Pontiff himself owed to him, when he was restored to his dominion?
Who does not know that by royal munificence the dignity and splendor of the Catholic Church were restored in this kingdom?

For this reason it is the more to be lamented that, since the royal mind could not endure priestly obstinacy, the old age of the most pious King, if not afflicted, was at least saddened by the difficulties and disturbances that arose from this.
I pass on to the other pursuits of Frederick William, for which greater gratitude was felt and is felt toward him.
For he was so generous to literature and the arts that he surpassed both all the universities and very many kings in the number and magnitude of his benefactions.

And he not only helped literature by his generosity, but also, although at this age a certain part of studies and of the learned and of those eager for learning was greatly suspected, nevertheless he treated us most liberally and gently.
We have retained the freedom of speaking and teaching;
As for writing, whether you would call it freedom or rather license, because it seemed to be diminished, it is to be attributed not so much to the royal will as to the common fault of this age.
It is not unpleasant to recall at this point with what courtesy that great-hearted man treated the learned, to whom at last the most wise King had entrusted the supreme care of public education;

from which it can be understood with what sort of men, with what talent, with what skill in literature, with what sincerity of mind endowed, and finally how courteous and indulgent the most blessed King judged that this province should be entrusted.
But we have very recently conducted the funeral of this most excellent man too, not without tears.
Under the auspices of Frederick William, moreover, both academies, that of the sciences and that of the arts, were better established.
Apparatus of every kind, necessary for the cultivation of the disciplines, were procured in the most select and abundant manner.
The literary universities, both the old ones were restored and better equipped, and new and most celebrated ones were founded at great expense.

By a new and most salutary institution, the King placed our university in the very seat of the kingdom, and in a place no less conspicuous, but in the most frequented and most adorned street of the city, but in the immediate neighborhood of his own house and in his own view, but in these royal buildings, which he began to splendidly restore in the last few years:
And so that there might be proofs of the greatest affection with which he embraced learning, he wished both our university and the beloved Rhenish one to bear his name.

Therefore, just as the Greek states of old honored their founders with heroic honors, what religion, what piety, what veneration of ours can be so great that it does not fall short of the thanks that must be paid to the most blessed soul of Frederick William, our hero?

He also increased the gymnasia and the schools lower than these with no small subsidies, and ordered many popular and rural games to be established, in which the common and rustic multitude might be instructed in the precepts of the Christian faith and the first rudiments of letters, not thinking that men would be the more ignorant, but the more refined, and therefore easier to govern.
Moreover, how much the cultivation of the arts grew and advanced under this King is evident.

With truly Periclean zeal he roused sculptors, painters, architects, musicians, actors, and thymelic performers, thinking it a civic duty, following the example of Octavian Augustus, to share in the pleasures of the people.

He founded that magnificent treasury for the arts, filled it with the most elegant works, and opened it to all with the freest access, so that artists might have models to follow, and the minds and eyes of all might be delighted and educated.
He so changed the face of the city that almost wherever we cast our eyes, we see monuments of royal magnificence.
The one thing that seemed to be missing, the monument to Frederick the Great, he ordered to be founded when he was already on the point of death.

O that joyful and at the same time sad spectacle, when the heir to the kingdom, at his father's command and amid the greatest enthusiasm of the people, with his own hand inaugurated that work, while in these most auspicious circumstances, together with the nobles and magistrates, the immense multitude that was present lacked nothing but the presence of the Father of his country, about whom we were already then anxiously worried!
O happy Prussia, whose honor and glory Frederick William kept in his heart even to his last breath!

I declare the rule of the most blessed king fortunate, a rule which, although it was not free from the gravest evils, drew prosperity from those very evils, bringing so wholesome a remedy to them that Frederick William seemed to have been sent by divine providence, who, relying on the love of his people, would emerge as the restorer and renewer of the Prussian state in war and peace.
He also died fortunate.
For although with him ruling almost the whole world was changed, the mutual love between King and people among us has not changed:
witness is this universal grief, that mournful sight as of a captured city:

For indeed, although a change of ruler is accustomed to hold minds suspended between hope and fear, there is no place for any fear among us, since Frederick William IV has attained power with the highest hope and confidence of the people, but the tears that burst forth were drawn out by nothing other than that love.

They have honored him with honors; what religion, what piety, what veneration of ours can be so great that it does not fall short of the thanks that must be paid to the most blessed soul of Frederick William, our hero?

He also increased the gymnasia and the schools inferior to these with no small subsidies, and ordered that many popular and rustic games be established, in which the common and rural multitude might be instructed in the precepts of the Christian faith and the first rudiments of letters, not thinking that men would be the more difficult to rule the more ignorant they were, but the more cultivated.
Moreover, how much the cultivation of the arts grew and advanced under this King is evident.

With truly Periclean zeal he roused sculptors, painters, architects, musicians, actors, and choral performers, thinking it a citizen's duty, after the example of Octavian Augustus, to share in the pleasures of the people.

He founded that magnificent treasury for the arts, filled it with the most elegant works, and opened it to all with the freest access, so that artists might have models to follow, and the minds and eyes of all might be delighted and educated.
He so changed the face of the city that almost wherever we cast our eyes, we see monuments of royal magnificence.
The one thing that seemed to be missing, the monument to Frederick the Great, he ordered to be founded when he was already on the point of death.

O that joyful and at the same time sad spectacle, when the heir to the throne, at his father's command and amid the greatest enthusiasm of the people, inaugurated that work with his own hand, while in these most auspicious circumstances nothing was lacking, with the nobles and magistrates and the immense multitude that was present, except the presence of the Father of his country, about whom we were already then anxiously worried!
O happy Prussia, whose honor and glory Frederick William kept in his heart even to his last breath!

Felicem praedico Regis beatissimi principatum, qui principatus, quum non liber a gravissimis malis esset, ex ipsis malis elicuerit prosperitatem, tam salubrem illis medelam afferens, ut Fridericus Guilelmus visus sit divinitus missus esse, qui populi sui nixus caritate rei publicae Borussicae bello et pace evaderet restitutor et instaurator.
Felix ipse etiam obiit.
For although under his rule almost the whole world was changed, the mutual affection between King and people among us has not changed:
witness is this universal grief, that mournful sight as of a captured city:

For although a change of ruler is wont to hold minds in suspense between hope and fear, there is no place for fear among us, since Frederick William IV has taken possession of affairs with the highest hope and confidence of the people; but those tears that burst forth were elicited by nothing other than that love.
The King departed from the palace, surrounded not by guards but by sorrowful crowds of citizens, with the entire Augustan family standing by him.
The Empress, his most beloved daughter, had flown from the throne of the East;
The dying king bade farewell to his son-in-law, the Emperor.
He left the kingdom to his most august son, whom he knew would follow in his footsteps.

We therefore give thanks to you, God, Best and Greatest, that after you did not wish the Father of the Fatherland to live longer among us, but received into your bosom a most holy man on the most holy day on which we celebrate the outpouring of your Spirit, you gave Frederick William the Fourth, our most merciful Lord, as successor to the kingdom, whom we trust will hold as ratified whatever the best of everyone expects of him, and will add a crowning glory to the greatest benefits that the most blessed father conferred upon the fatherland, he excellently perceiving what a new principate, new times demand.

Preserve, I pray, and keep safe the most august King with his consort the most august Queen and the whole August house, and fill his most noble and generous mind with the best counsels, by which he may confirm the harmony of the commonwealth handed down from his father, procure for the most loyal people all advantages and utilities, and protect and increase the honor and glory of the Prussian name and the safety, security, and majesty of the kingdom.
So may God help us, as these vows have been religiously made by us.
I have spoken.
The King departed from the palace, surrounded not by guards but by sorrowful crowds of citizens, while the entire imperial family stood by him:
the Empress, his dearly beloved daughter, had flown from the throne of the East;
dying, the King bade farewell to the Emperor, his son-in-law.
He left the kingdom to his most august son, whom he knew would follow in his footsteps.

We therefore give thanks to you, God, Best and Greatest, that after you did not wish the Father of the Fatherland to live longer among us, but received into your bosom a most holy man on the most holy day on which we celebrate the outpouring of your Spirit, you gave Frederick William the Fourth, our most merciful Lord, as successor to the kingdom, whom we trust will hold as ratified whatever the best of everyone expects of him, and will add a crowning glory to the greatest benefits that the most blessed father conferred upon the fatherland, he excellently perceiving what the new principate, the new times demand.

Preserve, I pray, and keep safe the most august King with his consort the most august Queen and the whole August house, and fill his most noble mind with the best counsels, by which he may confirm the harmony of the commonwealth handed down from his father, procure for the most loyal people all kinds of advantages and utilities, and protect and increase the honor and glory of the Prussian name and the safety, security, and majesty of the kingdom.
So may God help us, as these vows have been solemnly made by us.
I have spoken.

div.head: XXVIII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi IV. celebrandis d. XV. m. Octobris a. MDCCCXLI. habita.

p.s: In conventu hoc laetissimo, quem primum hodie agimus, auditores, ut Regis dilectissimi natalicia rite pieque celebremus, non mihi videtur fas esse aliud dicendi exordium sumere nisi ex gratibus Deo Optimo Maximo agendis meo nomine vestroque et rei publicae universae, quod postquam non licet superstitem colere eum principem, ad cuius venerationem totiens nos in hanc curiam convocaverat communis gratulatio et veluti patris caritas, sanctissimo legitimae successionis iure voluerit imperium transferri in Dominum hunc clementissimum, quem difficilius sit non diligere, non laudare, quam intimo affectu diligere, verissima oratione laudare.

For since everything human is fragile and subject to many changes, and since a change of ruler brings anxiety to kingdoms, especially after a long reign, whose citizens have experienced such great kindness that better things seem scarcely possible to be hoped for, but because nothing is accustomed to remain long in the same state, losses can be feared:

What can be received from God by more devoted minds as a gift, than that which was most earnestly sought by the prayers of all, namely that the most excellent blessings should remain, which the most blessed Father of the fatherland had bestowed upon the state, so that the heir of the empire might nourish the seeds sown by him and scatter new ones, about to yield a most abundant and most joyful harvest?

Adhuc resonant et resonabunt perpetuo non tam auribus nostris quam mentibus illae Regis voces gravissimae, ex commoto effusae pectore egregiorumque testes consiliorum, illae legatorum et populi acclamationes nulla simulationis aut assentationis suspicione notatae, quibus mutua illa caritas, quae patrem beatissimum cum populo suo coniunxerat, confirmata inter successorem atque universas regni provincias omnesque ordines rei publicae, et documentis certissimis ita declarata est, ut orbem terrarum pervagaretur fama praeclarae huius et quae fere sine exemplo est concordiae, ut ad novi sideris ortum omnes gentes
converterent oculos, Borussiaeque fidem, felicitatem, robur perspecta haberent etiam increduli, metuerent etiam audaciores:

And if that sudden heat, or rather ardor and impulse of love, could not be openly continued, love itself relaxed nothing, but like a river that had overflowed, returned to its channel and enclosed and restrained by its banks, it holds a moderate course and promises perpetuity with even temper.
The King follows in his father's footsteps, his father's admonitions, neither too eager for new things, nor too tenacious of the former state:

And so, by a gentle and not precipitate step, the state is led to better things; and although not yet two years have passed since Frederick William IV took possession of the supreme power, we have seen and heard many things which before were unheard of;
The minds of the citizens have been roused, raised, and inflamed, not by a turbulent movement, but by an inner impulse and instinct, which proceeds from the King, and which the King moderates.
But as for what I said, that the praises of this king are most ready at hand, I do not want it to be taken as said in such a way that I should be thought able to praise the king worthily.

To speak the truth, what I said in the funeral oration, in which I venerated the shades of the most blessed king, that together with his death it seemed to me that whatever eloquence there was in me had perished — and I well understand how slight it was — that I now feel has plainly happened.

Indeed, having for nearly thirty years accustomed myself, as it were, to the life, character, institutions, and deeds of Frederick William III, by repeatedly considering and explaining them, I had conformed my own mind to his nature and my own disposition to his genius:
For unless you have thoroughly insinuated yourself into the nature of the one you wish to praise, success will not answer to your undertaking:

Now, although our most merciful Lord has recently regenerated the father, yet he himself is endowed with a peculiar and distinctive character, wonderful in its excellence; I see that a different talent must be assumed for speaking, and, as it were, a different role; and I do not trust that this loftiness of mind can be equaled by my words, nor that my speech, already fading and growing old, can be compared to the force, vigor, and ardor of this new empire.

There are, moreover, those who think that this empire should not be proclaimed as truly German and popular in this learned or dead and foreign language, which they disdain of their own accord, but in the native and common language open to the understanding, which I myself confess I gladly use on other occasions.

Yet this thought raises and strengthens me, although I am weak in strength, that just as on the birthday of the most blessed father of the fatherland it was customary for the greatness of my office to be remitted and granted, so that I might depart a little from the praises of the King to other things, which, when they turned their eyes to affairs, would have the faith, happiness, and strength of Prussia clearly seen even by the incredulous, and would be feared even by the bolder:

And if that sudden heat, or rather ardor and impulse of love, could not be openly continued, love itself relaxed nothing, but like a river that had overflowed, returned to its channel and enclosed and restrained by its banks, it holds a moderate course and promises perpetuity with even temper.
The King follows in his father's footsteps, his father's admonitions, neither too desirous of new things, nor too tenacious of the former state.

And so, with a gentle and not hasty step, the state is led to better things, and although not yet two years have passed since Frederick William IV took possession of the supreme power, we have seen and heard many things which before were unheard of;
The minds of the citizens have been stirred, raised, and kindled, not by a turbulent movement, but by an inner impulse and instinct, which proceeds from the King, and which the King moderates.
But as for what I said, that the praises of this King are most ready at hand, I do not want it to be taken as said in such a way that I should be thought able to praise the King worthily.

To speak the truth, what I said in the funeral oration, in which I venerated the shades of the most blessed King, that together with his death I thought that whatever eloquence there was in me had perished — and I well understand how slight it was — that I now feel has plainly come to pass.

Indeed, I had, over nearly thirty years, accustomed myself, as it were, to the life, character, institutions, and deeds of Frederick William III, by repeatedly considering and explaining them, and had conformed my own mind to his disposition.
For unless you have thoroughly immersed yourself in the character of the one you wish to praise, success will not answer to your undertaking.

Now, although our most merciful Lord has recently regenerated the father, yet he himself is endowed with a special and peculiar character, wonderfully excellent, and I see that a different talent must be assumed for speaking, and a different, as it were, person, and I do not trust that this loftiness of mind can be equaled by my words, nor that my speech, already fading and growing old, is comparable to the force, vigor, and ardor of this new empire:

There are, moreover, those who think that this empire should not be proclaimed as truly German and popular in this learned or dead and foreign language, which they disdain of their own accord, but in the native language open to the common understanding, which I myself confess I gladly use on other occasions.

Attamen viribus me quamvis defectum erigit et confirmat haec cogitatio, quod quemadmodum in Patris patriae beatissimi nataliciis de magnitudine muneris mei id remitti et concedi solebat, ut a Regis laudibus paullulum digrederer ad alia, quae cum rebus
nostris coniuncta essent, sic etiam hodie suffecisse aliquatenus videbor vel certe veniam impetrabo, si tantum de Rege dilectissimo dixero, ut nemo pietatem nostram desideret, nemo non quantopere Domino clementissimo obstricti et devoti simus, intelligat, sed simul id mihi sumpsero, ut dum de regia virtute expono, haud verear aliquid de litterarum ratione admiscere, de quibus coram vobis, qui in his occupati estis, et in sollemnibus Principi litterarum amantissimo dicatis disputantem quis est paullo cultior qui arbitraturus sit in re versari ab instituto aliena aut longe repetita?

Since these things were connected with our own, so even today I shall seem to have been sufficient to some extent, or certainly I shall obtain pardon, if I say so much about the most beloved King that no one may miss our devotion, no one may not understand how greatly we are bound and devoted to the most clement Lord, but at the same time I shall have taken this upon myself, that while I set forth the royal virtue, I shall not fear to mix in something of the nature of letters, about which, before you who are occupied in these things and in the solemnities dedicated to the Prince most loving of letters, who is a little more refined who is going to think that I am engaged in a matter foreign to my purpose or far-fetched?

The royal power over all human affairs is the greatest and most serious, and it is surrounded by very many cares and requires immense keenness of mind, goodness, industry, and diligence, so that the interests of the state may be provided for and the safety of the people may be looked after, who are destined to reach the highest prosperity, when the king, on whose nod everything depends, will manage affairs wisely, kindly, vigorously, and promptly; but they are destined to perish or certainly to suffer great calamities, if they obey an imprudent, cruel, lazy, and negligent master.
What has been said in general terms, I indeed scarcely dare to apply and explain at length to the praise of our King;
yet those things which are both most true and manifest do not seem to be entirely passed over in silence at this place.

Therefore I will not be silent, that no easily found leader can be found, who is more skilled in all matters pertaining to the administration of the state, both ancestral and foreign institutions, the needs of the people and the plans by which the state is to be governed, and more instructed in letters and good arts, and more ready in speaking, and endowed with a keener sense of the beautiful and the good and the true, and more reverent of sacred things without superstition:
by which things I think the greatest part of wisdom is contained:
Again, there is no one who is of a milder and more merciful disposition, who is more inclined to bring help and to confer benefits:
But how tolerant of business he is, and almost beyond his strength energetic and industrious, we who love him deeply have learned not without some anxiety.

Now in royal life this is the most difficult thing: since it is not fitting that most of those whom the king uses as administrators and counselors should excel and be practiced except in individual fields, the king, who wishes to fully suffice for the burden placed on his shoulders, ought to embrace all parts of the state with a great mind, to grasp, if not every smallest detail of very diverse matters, at least the sum, and finally to join and mix these diverse things with his own mind in such a way that from them, as from variations of sounds, one harmony is produced.
And peace and war are very different things:
The king must excel in the arts of both, at least in this form and condition of the state in which we Prussians live.
Therefore, so that these may be tempered with just measure not only in the state but in the very mind of the king, extraordinary greatness of soul is needed, which rarely falls to a mortal:
It had fallen to the lot of one man in the previous century, to the light and leader of Prussia and Germany, indeed of all Europe, Frederick the Great.
Frederick William IV, at the very beginning of his reign, declared in a most solemn voice what path he would follow:
He proclaimed that he would keep peace in his own lifetime, unless he were provoked to war;
but that he would wage war, trusting in the love and valor of his people and in that common ardor of all by which his father had conquered.
He did not threaten war in order to keep peace;
He kept peace, because he declared that he preferred it, and yet he did not fear war, for which Prussia in peace itself is never unprepared.
Thus, by acting neither arrogantly nor timidly, the dangers that were feared a year ago were overcome, and security was restored.

Meanwhile, although he may not wish all the forces of the state to be turned to military service, he provides excellently for military affairs, and if anything seems to require correction in this excellent and almost completely perfect military establishment, which his father instituted, he diligently strives to correct it.
But in the domestic affairs of the republic, what things are to be done in our age and indeed in this kingdom, it is both difficult to discern, and it is not within my duty or ability to set forth;

except that some things, which are not derived from the inner and business-like knowledge of civil affairs but are of common and popular judgment, it will be permitted to pour forth as it were in a medley.

For since most nations have been raised to that height, that they are not led like herds of creatures devoid of reason, as in the age of Saturn, according to Plato's opinion, by gods, but the people, together with those who hold the reins of government, either deliberate or decide through their representatives about the most important matters:

It was understood in this republic as well, which increases the strength of arms by the powers of the mind and the vigor of spirits, that citizens must be stirred up, so that they may apply their minds to public affairs, lest this kingdom be surpassed by others in the excellence of its institutions and the vigor of its people and civic skill, and lest the minds of the citizens grow languid and be dulled, and, oppressed by sleep and inactivity, they should abandon the state in times of danger.
At the same time, however, the force of the empire must be kept whole and undivided, and tranquility must be maintained, which easily disturbs more agitated minds.
How difficult it is to reconcile these with each other, there is no need to explain:
they are peace and war:
In the arts of both, at least in this form and condition of the state in which we Prussians live, the king must excel.

Therefore, in order that these things may be tempered with just measure not only in the state but in the very mind of the king, extraordinary greatness of mind is needed, which rarely falls to a mortal:
It had fallen to one man in the previous century, to the light and leader of Prussia and Germany, indeed of all Europe, Frederick the Great.
Frederick William IV, at the very beginning of his reign, declared with a most solemn voice what path he would follow:
He declared that he would keep peace during his lifetime, unless he were challenged to war.
But he said he would wage war, trusting in the love and courage of his people and in that common ardor of all by which his father had conquered.
He did not threaten war in order to retain peace;
He retained peace because he declared that he preferred it, yet he did not fear war, for which Prussia in peace itself is always prepared.
Thus, by acting neither arrogantly nor timidly, the dangers that were feared a year ago have been overcome, and security has been restored.

Meanwhile, although he may not wish all the resources of the state to be turned to military service, he provides excellently for military affairs, and if anything seems to need correction in this distinguished and almost completely perfect military establishment that his father instituted, he diligently strives to correct it.
But in the domestic affairs of the republic, what things are to be done in our age and indeed in this kingdom, it is both difficult to discern, and it is not within my duty or ability to set forth;

except that some things, which are not derived from the inner and business-like knowledge of civil affairs but are of common and popular judgment, it will be permitted to pour forth as it were in a medley.

For since most nations have been raised to that height, that they are not led like herds of creatures destitute of reason, as in the age of Saturn, according to Plato's opinion, by gods, but the people, together with those who hold the helm of government, through their ambassadors, either deliberate or decide concerning the most weighty affairs:

It was understood in this republic as well, which increases the strength of arms by the power of intellect and the vigor of minds, that citizens must be stirred up, lest this kingdom be surpassed by others in the excellence of its institutions and the vigor of its people and civic skill, and lest the minds of citizens grow languid and be dulled, and, oppressed by sleep and inertia, they should abandon the state in dangers, so that they apply their minds to public affairs.
At the same time, however, the full and undivided force of imperial power must be retained, and tranquility must be retained, which easily disturbed by more agitated minds.
How difficult it is to reconcile these with each other, there is no need to explain:
Whoever has reconciled them will rightly deserve that splendid praise which Tacitus attributes to the Emperor Nerva, because he united things formerly irreconcilable, the principate and liberty.
But that this very purpose belongs to the wisest King, it will be enough to have indicated in a word.

In this very difficult matter, the prince will make the most progress if nature has so formed him that he attracts the interests of men by his kindness and affability, and does not fear to humble himself and to mingle with the people;
which he can do without any loss of dignity, he who is placed so far above all that no one dares to compare himself with him:
Charm and wit will also please, provided that he does not hurt with witty remarks, which are easily forgiven in a private person, but never in a prince.
He will free the good from fear, having removed the spies and informers;
He will not even inflict punishments on the wicked himself, but he will leave any crimes whatsoever to be judged by whole and undaunted judges according to the laws, which are common and fair to all;

By his uprightness and prudence he will bring it about that everyone is convinced both that he himself wishes to consult the interests and safety of the citizens, and that he understands perfectly what is beneficial, what is harmful, and by what means the former are obtained and the latter avoided.
He will not wish to favor any one order, to summon this one alone into council, and to disregard the rest.

When this happens, envy will be stirred up against that order to which the prerogative has been given, even if this very thing imposes no burden on those who are placed after, and the harmony of the republic will be dissolved.
To the people, to use Solon's words, it will give as much as suffices, and it will take care that the powerful and wealthy have nothing unjust.

He will no more provide for the treasury and the public purse than for the private property of his subjects, because he who rules over the poor is not himself rich, and a good prince has as much as all men have.
He will foster the cultivation of the fields, the crafts, and the commerce.
He will reduce taxes and tributes as far as the necessities of the state allow, and will so arrange them that they themselves and their collection are as little burdensome as possible.
He will show his generosity not in things that quickly perish, but in those that may be a lasting ornament to the state and bring enduring benefits.

He will not think that only those are faithful to him who praise whatever he himself has said and done, but he will add confidence to those who, with an upright and steadfast mind and relying on the consciousness of a good intention and duty, openly and modestly profess what has seemed right to them.

He will restrain the trials for treason as far as can be done without public harm, being more a despiser than an avenger of slander and slight injury, not rejoicing in punishments but in the love of the citizens.

He will command himself as well as the citizens, and not until he has won them over will he justly earn that famous praise which Tacitus attributes to the Emperor Nerva, because he united things formerly incompatible, the principate and liberty.
That this very thing is the purpose of the wisest king will be enough to have indicated by a word.

In this most difficult matter, the prince will make the greatest progress whom nature has so formed that he attracts the interests of men by kindness and courtesy, and does not fear to lower himself and to mingle with the people;
which he can do without any loss of dignity, he who is placed so far above all that no one dares to compare himself with him:
Charm and wit will also please, provided that he does not hurt with witty sayings, which are easily forgiven in a private person, but never in a prince.
He will free the good from fear, once the spies and informers have been removed;

He will not even inflict punishments himself on the wicked, but he will leave any charges whatsoever to be judged by whole and undaunted judges according to the laws, which should be common and fair to all;

He will not wish to favor any one order, to summon this one alone into council, and to disregard the rest.

When this happens, envy will be stirred up against that order to which the prerogative has been given, even if this very thing imposes no burden on those who are placed after, and the harmony of the republic will be dissolved.
To the people, to use Solon's words, it will give as much as suffices, and it will take care that the powerful and wealthy have nothing unjust.

He will no more provide for the treasury and the public purse than for the private property of his subjects, because he who rules over the poor is not himself rich, and a good prince has as much as all men have.
He will foster the cultivation of the fields, the crafts, and the commerce.
He will reduce taxes and tributes as far as the necessities of the state allow, and will so arrange them that they themselves and their collection are as little burdensome as possible.
He will show generosity not in things that quickly perish, but in those that may be a perpetual ornament to the state and bring lasting benefits.

He will not think that only those are faithful to him who praise whatever he himself has said and done, but he will add confidence to those who, with an upright and constant mind and relying on the consciousness of a good intention and duty, profess candidly and modestly what has seemed right to them.

He will restrain the trials for treason as much as can be done without public harm, being more a despiser than an avenger of slander and slight injury, not rejoicing in punishments but in the love of the citizens.
He will command himself just as much as the citizens, and while he does not want them to be ruled by passions, he himself will not be ruled by them.
Thus he will be true and sincere, so that his word will be more certain than the oath of others.
With all these things set before you, will any of you demand, listeners, that I explain at length how the character of our most merciful King responds?
Of course, if I were speaking before those who did not know him, someone might say that I must recount and describe each of his virtues;

But you, just as you recognize the king's face in a painted picture, even if his name is not written below, so in the things I have set before you, you will recognize, not indeed all the excellent gifts of Frederick William, which it would be long to pursue, nor his perfect image, but nevertheless certain features as if sketched.
He wishes to be ruled by his desires; by these he himself will be ruled.
Thus he will be true and sincere, so that his word will be more certain than the oath of others.
With all these things set before you, will any of you demand, listeners, that I explain with deliberate effort how the character of our most merciful King responds?
Of course, if I were speaking before those who did not know him, someone might say that I must review and describe each of his virtues;

But you, just as you recognize the king's face in a painted picture, even if his name is not written below, so in the things I have set forth, you will recognize, not indeed all the excellent gifts of Frederick William, which it would be long to pursue, nor his perfect image, but nevertheless certain features as if sketched in outline.
I have not yet touched upon those things, colleagues and fellow soldiers, which pertain especially to us.

For since from the character of Frederick William IV a most beautiful augury had long since been taken of the future most flourishing flower of arts and letters, which nevertheless had been so nourished by Frederick William III that it seemed that one had to be satisfied if they suffered no loss;
The most merciful king now already seems to have surpassed even the highest hope:

He showed how favorable he was to good studies not only at the very beginning of his reign, when he received most graciously the embassies sent by the first colleges of letters and arts, and, what is by far most pleasing to those who receive benefits, even without waiting until he was asked, he most lavishly increased the revenues of this particular university; but he also summoned here the most distinguished ornaments of Germany, with annual salaries liberally established, not only so that each one might practice and teach his own art among us, but also so that he himself might enjoy their presence.

For he loves learned men for the sake of learning, but he loves learning and the arts not because they offer some advantage or use, whatever it may be, to a ruler, but so that he may be a most skilled and most refined judge of them, on account of the excellence inherent in them, that is, on account of the true and the beautiful.
But the good is not separated from these, since it flows from the same divine source as the true and the beautiful, which three, being the best, are contained inseparably.

But in human affairs, however, not entirely indeed but to some extent, they are seen as so separated that science seeks the true, art strives to produce the beautiful, and the good is the aim of the state and of the institutions of public and private life founded by divine will.

But science, in which I will now dwell alone, is concerned partly with the knowledge of pure concepts, which we call philosophy, partly with mathematics demonstrating quantity, partly with the observation and description of natural things and laws, and partly with the history of the human race and of all those things which human reason has devised and established—of states, customs, and institutions both sacred and profane, of languages, literatures, and arts—which must be explained.

And from these parts of knowledge, those disciplines also either depend on or are mixed with them, which are found joined together in the three particular bodies of the universities according to the ancient custom.

And since science, which indeed is true science, cannot be contrary to science, because truth cannot be contrary to truth, that is, to itself, and false, all those parts of knowledge must necessarily agree among themselves.
They are indeed different:
but just as in the natural universe each star occupies its own place, and the world is held together and moved by the harmony of all;
so all disciplines, as it were so many lights and stars of the human mind, in this rational and literary universe of men, are joined together and harmonious with one another.
The common end of all is truth, because all are occupied in knowledge, not utility, not pleasure;
Nevertheless, they also have utility, just as they have pleasure.
But in our age many people so basely and servilely pervert the force and purpose of knowledge, that they think it should be directed solely to that which is connected with it as useful;

If we obey these, we must fear that the highest usefulness of knowledge and literature may perish, because those who judge the dignity of all things by usefulness are not wont to perceive what the greatest and purest usefulnesses are, placing with dull judgment usefulness especially in bread and money and the comforts and pleasures of life, just as those who are pleasure-lovers do not pursue the purest pleasures of the mind, but luxurious and lustful ones.
But I call that the greatest utility which is most closely connected with the end that is set before the human race.
But since the end of each thing is placed in its notion, I think that humanity is the end of the human race:
not that I deny that mortals ought to take pains to become like God, nor that I deny that each one was born for his country and state, not for himself alone and his parents;

But I think that both are comprehended by humanity itself, since it is true that man was created in the image of God and that man's reason proceeded from the divine, and by its own nature, as Aristotle teaches, man is a civil animal.
Therefore, for humanity, men are to be educated and instructed;
which alone is liberal and perfect education.

But if men are formed for anything else, education is to be explained partly by the observation and description of the necessities of things and of laws, partly by the history of the human race and of all those things which human reason has devised and established, of states, customs, and institutions both sacred and profane, of languages, literature, and arts.

And from these parts of knowledge, those disciplines also either depend on or are mixed with them, which are found united in three particular bodies of literary universities according to ancient custom.

And since science, which indeed is true science, cannot be contrary to science, because truth cannot be contrary to truth, that is, to itself, and false, all those parts of knowledge must necessarily agree among themselves.

so all disciplines, as it were so many lights and stars of the human mind, in this rational and literary universe of men, are joined together and harmonious with one another.

But I call that the highest utility which is most closely connected with the end that is set before the human race.

not that I deny that mortals ought to take pains to become like God, nor that I deny that each one was born for his country and state, not for himself alone and his parents;

But I think that both are comprehended by humanity itself, since it is true that man was created in the image of God and that man's reason proceeded from the divine, and by its nature, as Aristotle teaches, man is a civil animal.
Therefore, men are to be educated and instructed for humanity;
which alone is liberal and perfect education.

But if men are formed for anything else whatsoever, education is either restricted to the necessities of life, that is, of the body, or, neglecting the highest end, is directed toward something fortuitous.
Suppose, as someone used to say, that men should be educated in such a way that each one corresponds as much as possible to the form of the state in which he was born;

The standard will be unstable and harmful to humanity, because among the same nations different forms of government prevail, and the human race cannot be brought to a better condition unless public institutions are corrected, with reason as their guide, according as the minds of the citizens have become more cultivated.
But education cultivates the minds and the reason.

Would not indeed one wonder who would want knowledge (for in this is contained almost the whole education, and for this reason I have begun this discussion), who would want knowledge, I say, and what follows from it, the truth, to be one thing in a popular state, another in a government of the best, another among peoples who are ruled by kings?
On the contrary, to the state, whatever its form is, he will rightly adapt and accommodate himself, whose mind has been properly cultivated to humanity.
What shall I say about the education that must be arranged differently for the different classes of citizens?

For the rustic and urban common people are imbued only with the first elements of letters and with the precepts of morals and the rudiments of sacred doctrine, so that they become partakers of humanity only insofar as it is permitted to those whom poverty and labor do not leave leisure:
From this it is understood that these too are educated, although imperfectly, toward the same end as the rest:

Indeed, so far is it from being the case that an education separated from the rest of mankind and from humanity suits the nobles, that if they are trained by a special discipline, they seem to be educated more for pride and a certain empty elegance and for perpetuating certain fictions of opinions, than for virtue and wisdom.
It is rather fitting for them to exercise and shape their body and mind most diligently of all with any good arts, lest they be noble only in name.
Finally, according as each person is destined for the handling of a certain business, different things are certainly to be learned by different people;

but all are to be formed, as far as possible, in common for humanity, and the higher the rank in which each one was born and the higher things he aims at, the more earnest effort he ought to give, so that he may unite humane learning with the practical skill and cleverness which is altogether necessary.

There are certainly, there are excellent goods of the mind, removed from all business affairs, which if they are partly retained and partly increased, the human race progresses; if they are abolished or diminished, it rushes into worse things:
Among these, besides piety and good morals, I count poetry and the other elegant arts, and the liberal cultivation of the mind joined with freedom of spirit.
He is not enslaved to any one part of knowledge, but is restricted to common life, that is, to the body, or, with the highest end neglected, is directed toward something fortuitous.

Among these, besides piety and good morals, I count poetry and the other elegant arts, and the liberal cultivation of the mind joined with freedom of spirit.
This man is not enslaved to any part of science, but is common to all literature;
But some disciplines are referred to common use more than others.

Therefore those who judge the dignity of knowledge from this alone slander one or another discipline, of which, like that Strepsiades of Aristophanes, a truly rustic man and unskilled in the fine arts, they see no use for the common people or for procuring a livelihood.
And indeed in our age, two disciplines in particular, which seem to contribute much to culture, have the most bitter detractors and adversaries: philosophy and the study of antiquity.
They cry out against the mother of all learning, certain revived Anytuses and Meletuses, shouting that she is hostile to religion, hostile to the state;

In my view, the reason of the human mind, which philosophy explains, does not seem able to conflict either with religion or with the state, but rather to purify the former from superstition and the latter from the perversity of its institutions.
Granted that philosophers may err somewhat:
Have the lawgivers and the teachers of sacred discipline erred in nothing?
I know that what we have just heard is not, as it seemed to Plato, a pagan and impious man, that these our states can be instructed from the precepts of philosophy:

But philosophy gradually educates and enlightens minds, and while it enlightens them, it gradually corrects laws and institutions, not those that pertain to fields and rivers and forests, but those by which the highest principles of the human race are contained.
We would still be burning innocent little old women, if not for philosophy's warning, the most savage and stupid laws had been abolished.

How much more humane, therefore, is Cicero, formed by experience of affairs much more than by the subtlety of the schools, and exercised in the dust and wrestling-ground of the greatest of all states, who calls that philosophy innate in the human race, which those devoted to wisdom strive to perfect, the guide of life, the searcher-out of virtue and the expeller of vices, and says that it gave birth to cities and was the inventor of laws, the teacher of morals and of discipline.
And so our Prussia rightly attracted and cherished the greatest philosophers from Leibniz down to those whom the present age has produced.
Now I do not wish to discuss the literature of antiquity at greater length, lest I seem to be boasting about my own studies.

I would only wish that those who desire that the tender minds of boys and young men be nourished in schools especially by other and technical subjects, remember that the matter is not only that future theologians and jurists should take from Greek and Latin literature as much as is most necessary for moderately understanding the sources of their discipline, nor that future physicians should learn the vocabulary of their art, but that all who are about to approach any science [should take] the most abundant [supply], which earlier peoples [left] in all literature;

tantum meminerint velim, qui aliis rebus et technicis potissimum teneras puerorum et adolescentulorum mentes nutriri in scholis cupiunt, non id solum agi, ut ex Graecis Latinisque litteris futuri theologi et iurisconsulti tantum delibent, quantum ad disciplinae suae fontes mediocriter cognoscendos maxime necessarium sit, neque ut medici futuri artis suae vocabula discant, sed ut omnes, qui ad scientiam quamlibet accessuri sunt, opulentissima, quam priores gentes
cultissimae succedentibus reliquerunt saeculis, perfruantur hereditate, atque ut optimis formentur exemplaribus, quibus plerique omnes, qui litteris inclaruerunt, formati sunt, quibus ipse Fridericus Magnus, qui tamen Gallicis potissimum litteris instructus erat, gymnasiorum alumnos institui voluit, non ille ratus aliis artibus aut noviciarum linguarum et librorum usu compensari illa studia posse;

I would wish that those who fear harm to the Christian faith from ancient literature remember that the Emperor Julian forbade Christians to open schools of rhetoric and letters, in order that they might become more uncultivated, and that he was reproached for this by Gregory, a most holy man, because he had begrudged Christians those goods which were common to all men.

But if literature will seem to be held in high regard only insofar as it appears to serve the common utilities and conveniences of life, and not for nourishing the lights of the mind, then certainly philosophy and the study of antiquity are to be despised, and along with these a great part of the rest of history, and I know not whether even some part of the physical and mathematical disciplines will be [despised]:
Thus indeed the usefulness of knowledge, which I mentioned, will perish, and at the same time the freedom of the mind, which those cannot retain who refer everything to gain and profit.
Indeed, it is to be feared that the freedom of the republic also may be endangered, if citizens exclusively seek and pursue that which I called useful.
For then, the fatter the fodder with which one feeds them, the more willingly they will accept each as master, and they will rest in a placid servitude.

But noble citizens, taught to look at something greater than profit and the pleasures of life, devote for their fatherland, for liberty, and for their legitimate prince not only all their goods but life itself.
By this art Prussia grew;
these plans pleased the earlier kings.
But what of Frederick William the Fourth?
He provides for the resources of the citizens;
With the most salutary institutions, having called the envoys of the people into counsel, it strives to bring about whatever seems to conduce to the prosperity not of individuals but of all.

But with deep mind it perceives that the safety of the republic is placed not in the mere comforts of life, but that those highest goods of the soul are to be blessed, whom providence has entrusted to its own care.

To be sure, to return at last to the point from which I seem to have digressed, our most gracious Lord is so constituted by his own nature that he is filled, as it were, with a divine inspiration by the love of truth and beauty, and he loves letters and arts not for the sake of some base advantage but for their own sake, and if he seeks any utility from them, he regards especially that liberal and most excellent one which I have tried to explain.

They left them to the most cultivated succeeding centuries, so that they may enjoy the inheritance, and so that they may be formed by the best models, by which almost all who have become famous in letters have been formed, by which Frederick the Great himself, who nevertheless was chiefly instructed in French literature, wished the pupils of the gymnasia to be trained, not thinking that those studies could be compensated by other arts or by the use of modern languages and books;
