I have completed what I had proposed to say, listeners, about to describe the most generous character of Frederick William.

And yet, since the minds of subjects are wont to be assimilated to the mind of the prince, I do not fear that in this most flourishing kingdom those counsels and wills may ever prevail which are unworthy of free men.

And you, dearest fellow soldiers, whom, while the most blessed Father of the Fatherland was still alive, your parents raised in the most delightful hope of liberty and security, which Frederick William IV makes firm, you, I say, will give your effort, so that you may zealously emulate the liberal character of the wisest king, as much as a private person can emulate a prince.
This also is included, that you should show to the King, who governs his people with a liberal rule, both now and hereafter, a liberal obedience in your duties.
For he does not demand servile obedience.
The time has passed when you were to be warned and dissuaded, lest you be drawn into that audacity, for which the clemency of Frederick William the Fourth recently granted pardon to the condemned;
You must be urged to that which I said at the beginning of my speech is very easy, namely to love him by whom we are loved.
Although there is no need for this exhortation, nevertheless I added it, to indulge my mind and my love.
We all understand our blessings;
We must strive to be seen worthy of their use.

Let us, the elders, enter joyfully into this new age of Prussia that is rising, because it has fallen to our lot to see an age than which none could have been established more happily for ripening the fruits that an earlier generation sowed.
You younger ones, strong with fresher powers, gird yourselves, so that you may follow the ardor of Frederick William IV and respond to his expectation.

Finally, whatever great and excellent thing is undertaken here, may God, without whom nothing can be brought to lasting completion, assist it, and may He preserve for him the spirit which He gave, and may He, to whose safety the prayers of all are directed, protect him whole and unharmed for the public welfare, together with his most august Queen consort, through the longest span of time.
I have spoken.
I have completed what I had proposed to say, listeners, about to describe the most generous character of Frederick William.

But since the minds of subjects are accustomed to be assimilated to the mind of the prince, I do not fear that in this most flourishing kingdom those counsels and wishes may ever prevail which are unworthy of free-born men;

And you will give your effort especially, dearest fellow soldiers, whom, while the most blessed Father of the Fatherland is still alive, your parents raised in the most pleasant hope of liberty and security, which Frederick William IV makes valid; you, I say, will give effort, so that you may zealously emulate the liberal character of the wisest king, as much as a private person can emulate a prince.
This also is included, that you should show to the King, who governs his people with a liberal rule, both now and hereafter, a liberal obedience in your duties.
For he does not demand servile obedience.
The time has passed when you were to be warned and dissuaded, lest you be drawn into that audacity, for which the clemency of Frederick William the Fourth recently granted pardon to the condemned;
You must be urged to that which I said at the beginning of my speech is very easy, namely, to love him by whom we are loved.
Although there is no need of this exhortation, nevertheless I have added it, to indulge my own mind and my love.
We all understand our blessings;
We must strive that we may seem worthy of their use.

Let us, the elders, enter joyfully upon this new age of Prussia that is now rising, because it has fallen to our lot to see an age than which none could have been founded more happily for ripening the fruits that an earlier generation sowed.
You, the younger ones, strong with fresher powers, gird yourselves so that you may follow the ardor of Frederick William IV and respond to his expectation.

Finally, whatever great and excellent thing is being undertaken here, may God, without whom nothing can be accomplished that will endure, assist it, and may He preserve for him the spirit which He gave, and may He, to whose safety the vows of all have been directed, protect him whole and unharmed for the public welfare, together with the most august Queen his consort, through the longest span of time.
I have spoken.

div.head: XXIX. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi IV. celebrandis d. XV. m. Octobris a. MDCCCXXXXII. habita.

p.s: Although I perceive that this duty, which I undertake every year on behalf of all of you, listeners, of speaking words at the most sacred solemnities dedicated to the far best Prince, is most difficult, nevertheless it is to me both honorable and also pleasant and delightful.

For although it may seem tedious to dwell on the same subject on the same day every year, and it may seem flattering to praise the same prince, however worthy, with lavish praise, whether with the same repeated encomiums or with newly devised ones, on a fixed day as if by command:

This thought removes these scruples: that hardly anyone expects or demands that today we should discuss nothing but the King's praises, but rather the orator, provided he tries to satisfy both his own and your piety, is granted some remission of the burden's weight, and is permitted to treat some particular subject, certainly such that it is not so alien to the sanctity and solemnity of this day that it cannot be referred to the Prince's person, to the Prince's love and praise, nor be considered in some degree suited to your minds, who have come together to revere the King.

And so, when I reflected with myself that, after I had spoken at length and deliberately last year about the virtues of the most beloved king, no one would hold it against me if, for the sake of variety, I chose a subject of that kind—not one that I would explain, complete, and perfect with philosophical subtlety, but one in which I might rather wander somewhat more freely in an oratorical manner—as I have often done at the birthday celebrations of the blessed father of the fatherland, with your approval:

I have proposed to myself to undertake an inquiry concerning the very love of country and of the prince, which, as you will concede, is more fitting and appropriate to these solemnities than any other.
For, to begin with this point on which all agree, we all love the most kind King, and we have gathered in this place for the purpose of publicly testifying this love.
We also greatly esteem the King for his virtues, and we revere him for his majesty, but love and affection are stronger than judgment and reverence.
And indeed not only those whom he has benefited pursue the King with such love, but he is dear to all citizens, even those who have not seen him, who have only heard of him by report:
Finally, the love of a prince, as of a fatherland, is something greater, which far exceeds the measure of private advantage and the feeling of a grateful mind.
There is a certain piety, which, if it were lawful for Christian men to compare any mortal with God the Best and Greatest, you would say is to be compared with the piety that is owed to his divinity.

But the loyalty with which a king is loved, as it does not seem to me to flow from the divine authority of the kingdom—although any rule can be regarded as having proceeded from God—yet God and a prince differ by an immense interval:
so I do not doubt that it is most closely related to that loyalty with which each person honors his own parents.

Since the Romans understood this, they publicly and by decree honored good emperors, and sometimes even bad ones, with the title of Father of the Fatherland, which has a greater feeling of affection than the word parent.
The Germans do not confer this name on their princes as a formal title, but they bestow it spontaneously from the feeling and will of their hearts.
And again, those who obey a king are considered to be free citizens of the state and consequently of the prince.

Therefore Frederick the Great, whom I do not hesitate to name as the principal author of the public and domestic discipline of our kings, says that a well-governed kingdom ought to be like a family, whose father is the prince, and the citizens truly free:
For he says citizens, not subjects, as many kings prefer to hear:
and that good and bad things are common among them;
for neither can the prince rejoice in happiness, where the people labors in misery.
And from this, in my judgment at least, it is gathered that the love of a prince cannot be separated from the love of one's country:
For because he is the father of his country, therefore those who love rightly love him.
But what can be more delightful than to speak at once of one's country and of one's prince, and of the most intimate union of the love with which we cherish both the one and the other?
Since this subject is especially suited to the celebration of this day, it can now be understood that I have not without reason called this office, which I have undertaken today, pleasant.

Yet I will not be allowed to enjoy this pleasure fully, unless the breeze of your kindness fills the sails of my speech, and the indulgence of my audience responds to the weakness of my powers, of which I am fully aware, which I would beg from you more earnestly, had I not often experienced it before.
Therefore, relying on this, even now, whatever I am about to say, I will say with confidence.
even those who have not seen him, who have only heard of him by report:
Finally, the love of a prince, as of a fatherland, is something greater, which far exceeds the measure of private advantage and the feeling of gratitude.

There is a certain piety, which, if it were permissible for Christians to compare any mortal with God the Best and Greatest, you would say is to be compared with the piety that is owed to his divinity.

But the loyalty with which the king is loved, as it seems to me, does not flow from the divine authority of the kingdom; for although any rule can be regarded as having proceeded from God, yet God and a prince differ by an immense interval:
so I do not hesitate to call it most closely related to that loyalty with which each person honors his own parents.

Since the Romans understood this, they publicly and by decree honored good emperors, and sometimes even bad ones with vile flattery, with the title of Father of the Fatherland, which carries a greater feeling of affection than the word 'parent'.
The Germans do not confer this name on their princes as a formal title, but they spontaneously grant it from the conviction and will of their hearts.
And conversely, those who obey a king are considered to be free citizens of the state and consequently of the prince.

Therefore Frederick the Great, whom I do not hesitate to name as the principal authority for the public and domestic discipline of our kings, says that a well-governed kingdom ought to be like a family, whose father is the prince, and the citizens truly free:
For he says citizens, not subjects, as many kings prefer to hear:
and that good and bad things are common among them;
for neither can the prince rejoice in happiness, where the people labors in misery.
And from this, in my judgment at least, it is gathered that the love of a prince cannot be separated from the love of one's country:
For because he is the father of his country, therefore they love him who love rightly.
But what can be more delightful than to speak at once of one's country and of one's prince, and of the most intimate union of the love with which we cherish both the one and the other?
Since this argument is especially suited to the celebration of this day, it can now be understood that I have not without reason called this office, which I have undertaken today, a pleasant one.

Yet it will not be permitted to me to enjoy this pleasure fully, unless the breeze of your kindness fills the sails of my speech, and the indulgence of my audience responds to the weakness of my powers, of which I am fully aware, which I would entreat from you more earnestly, had I not often already experienced it.
Therefore, relying on this, even now, whatever I am about to say, I will say with confidence.

But for me, who am about to say something about my fatherland, it seems hardly necessary to warn, although everyone is especially accustomed to the place where he was born and brought up, and most gladly rests in the memory of those things which there surrounded his infancy and boyhood, yet that the fatherland cannot be confined within the narrow bounds of that place;

Indeed, although each person's fatherland is connected with a certain region, nevertheless it is not constituted by this surface, these fields, these mountains and forests, rivers and lakes, these houses and timbers, and this heap of stones, those mute and inanimate things, which, as Tacitus says, are liable to fall and be rebuilt indifferently, but rather by this society of men, in which we were born, which is indivisible and in a way eternal, whether one prefers to call it a nation or a commonwealth.

That this fellowship is not, as it were, bound to the soil, but can be transferred from one place to another and extended and enlarged, the Greeks especially, burning with the greatest love of their fatherland, both determined and proved by examples:

And in our age too, who would deny that true Germany is not a certain definite land, which geographers call by this name, but that it is that [land] in which the community of the German nation has been established and flourishes, [namely] Prussia and the fatherland of the Prussians, not these provinces alone, which are either upper...

They may have been included under this name even earlier than a century ago, but this entire community of nations, which by the virtue and auspices of our kings have coalesced into one very strong body;

Finally, who would not say that if any people, driven from their seats, has established its republic in a foreign land, by it indeed only the soil has been changed, but the fatherland has been transferred rather than lost?
And so we measure the boundaries of the fatherland by the boundaries of the people;

The language of the people and its literature, customs and habits, common institutions both private and public, which are strengthened by education and laws, finally the memory of ancestors and the glory of distinguished deeds, which is propagated from them to posterity, these seem to me to be, as it were, the strongest bonds of the fatherland.
And indeed we rejoice that very many lands of Prussia are contained in all these things;
But no kingdom of the whole world, nor any state, has more famous examples of ancestors:

And although indeed this very thing the royal stock especially has exhibited, I cannot but mention in a word that this, which is placed in the memory of former times, would by no means have been enjoyed by Prussia, unless the greatness of our princes had stood out so much.
One happiness did not fall to this state, which is placed in the communion of religions:

For religion, and especially the Christian religion, by which mortals ought to be joined in brotherly love, the more serious and destructive divisions there once were, the more gladly it rests in the memory of those things which surrounded its infancy and childhood there, yet it cannot be confined within the narrow boundaries of that place;

Indeed, although each person's fatherland is connected with a certain region, nevertheless it is not constituted by this surface, these fields, these mountains and forests, rivers and lakes, these houses and beams, and this heap of stones, those mute and inanimate things, which, as Tacitus says, are liable to fall and be rebuilt indiscriminately, but rather by this society of men, in which we were born, individual and in a way eternal, whether one prefers to call it a nation or a republic.

That this fellowship is not, as it were, bound to the soil, but can be transferred from one place to another and extended and enlarged, the Greeks especially, burning with the greatest love of their fatherland, both determined and proved by examples:

And in our age too, who would deny that true Germany is not a certain definite land, which geographers call by this name, but that it is that [land] in which the society of the German nation has been established and flourishes, and that Prussia and the fatherland of the Prussians are not these provinces alone, which are either upper...

They may have been included under this name even earlier than a century ago, but this whole community of nations, which through the virtue and auspices of our kings has coalesced into one very strong body,

Finally, who would not say that if any people, driven from their own seats, has established its republic in a foreign land, only the soil has been changed, but the fatherland has been transferred rather than lost?
And so we measure the boundaries of the fatherland by the boundaries of the people.

The language of the people and its literature, customs and habits, common institutions both private and public, which are strengthened by education and laws, and finally the memory of ancestors and the glory of distinguished deeds, which is propagated from them to posterity—these seem to me to be, as it were, the strongest bonds of the fatherland.
And indeed we rejoice that very many lands of Prussia are held together by all these things;
But no kingdom of the whole world, nor any state, has more famous examples of its ancestors:

And although it was especially the royal line that displayed these very things, I cannot but mention in a word that this, which is placed in the memory of earlier times, would by no means have been a source of joy to Prussia through a most effective bond, had not the greatness of our princes stood out so much.
One happiness did not fall to this state, which is placed in the communion of religions:

For religion, and especially the Christian religion, by which mortals ought to be joined in brotherly love, the greater and more pernicious discords it once stirred up and will be able to stir up in our age too, if fanatical fury, to which some are inclined, is nourished zealously and skillfully;

So much the happier does that state seem to me to be, in which either most people all profess the same faith, or if any diversity of sects prevails, the one party bears with the other with gentle minds, and no sect is subject to a foreign master.

But if the boundaries of the fatherland, as I said, are to be determined by the boundaries of the people, and the fatherland consists not so much in the soil as in the fellowship of men and in the state, it must be granted that many have a double fatherland, one narrower, the other wider, because that one people is divided into several nations, and, what seems to be of greater importance, into several states, whether these are entirely separate or joined by treaty, and either differing in the form of government or, what is far better, equipped with the same institutions and laws.

For states that use very different laws will never coalesce well, but they will be suspicious of one another, both because the citizens of the one that has been established more freely will distrust those to which the less free one is subject, and will judge not undeservedly that danger to their liberty threatens from them, and because the masters of this less free republic will fear that from that more free one the love of liberty may be spread and propagated to their own subjects and may make them more impatient of rule.
But for us Prussians, to whom, as for the other Germans, a twofold fatherland has been given, as it were, by divine providence, he would be peevish who should think that we ought to grieve.

Rather, the magnanimity of our kings, and especially of Frederick William IV, must be proclaimed, who, although the institutions of our republic differ somewhat from those of most Germans and seem to be less popular, nevertheless did not wish themselves not to be Germans, nor did they wish their Prussians not to be Germans.

Therefore Frederick William III, not content that he had joined the federation by which the whole German name is held together, useful indeed as it seems especially against foreigners, established this more useful union of commerce and customs, by which certainly the greatest part of the Germans is now united.
But Frederick William the Fourth, our most beloved King, both in sad and in joyful circumstances declares, and in this very year has declared, that our common fatherland is Germany:

who, when the Hamburgers were afflicted by that pitiable calamity, was the first of all princes to declare that this common misfortune had befallen the Germans, which was to be repaired by us to the best of our ability;

And a little later, when he wished to honor literature, by which the Germans are especially united among themselves, and the arts, he did not want the rest of Germany to be distinguished from Prussia in this matter.
He stirred it up, and he will be able to stir it up in our age too, if the fanatical madness, to which some are inclined, is nourished zealously and skillfully;

So much the happier does that state seem to me to be, in which either nearly all profess the same faith, or if any diversity of sects prevails, the one party bears with the other with gentle minds, and no sect is subject to a foreign master.

But if the boundaries of one's country, as I have said, are to be determined by the boundaries of the people, and if one's country consists not so much in the soil as in the fellowship of men and in citizenship, then it must be granted that many have a twofold country, one narrower and one broader, because that one people is divided into several nations, and, what seems even greater, into several states, whether these are completely separate or joined by treaty, and either differing in their form of government or, what is far better, equipped with the same institutions and laws.

For states that use very different laws will never coalesce well, but they will be suspicious of one another, both because the citizens of the one that is more freely constituted will distrust those to which the less free one is subject, and will judge, not without reason, that danger to their liberty threatens from them, and because the masters of this less free republic will fear that from that more free one the love of liberty may be disseminated and spread to their own subjects and make them more impatient of rule.
But for us Prussians, to whom, as to the other Germans, a twofold fatherland has been given, as it were, by divine providence, he would be peevish who should think that we ought to grieve;

Rather the magnanimity of our kings, and especially of Frederick William the Fourth, is to be proclaimed, who, although the institutions of our republic differ somewhat from those of most Germans and seem to be less popular, nevertheless did not wish themselves not to be Germans, did not wish their Prussians not to be Germans.

Therefore Frederick William III, not content that he had joined the federation by which the whole German name is held together, useful indeed as it seems especially against foreigners, established this more useful union of commerce and customs, by which certainly the greatest part of the Germans is now united.
Frederick William IV, however, our most beloved King, both in sad and in joyful circumstances declares, and in this very year has declared, that our common fatherland is Germany:

who, when the Hamburgers were afflicted by that pitiable calamity, was the first of all princes to declare that this common misfortune had befallen the Germans, which was to be repaired by us to the best of our ability;

And a little later, when he wished to honor with letters, by which the Germans are especially united among themselves, and with arts, he did not want the rest of Germany to be distinguished from Prussia in this matter.
And very recently, when he celebrated those truly magnificent Cologne festivities, he clearly indicated with his usual eloquence how much he valued the harmony of the Germans.
Finally, there is no land of Germany that receives Germans as its own, not as foreigners, more readily and more willingly than our Prussia.
Now indeed, we are not bound by a pact, as some used to say, to love this fatherland, both the broader and the narrower one.
For no one loves from a pact.
But just as the source of any love is the inner harmony of minds, so we love our fatherland because our character agrees with the nature of the whole people and state;

Moreover, this love is increased by the recollection of benefits owed to the fatherland, which has both educated us and protected us and equipped us with all goods of mind and body, and daily equips us:

Hence it happens that the fatherland is loved more easily and more intensely, which has set before itself that which the princes of Prussia have set before themselves, namely to enrich their citizens with any good things, both external and internal, as much as possible.
But by what things do we show that we are held by love of the fatherland?
By civic virtue, I think.
But in what does civic virtue consist?
In this, I think, that you be a good citizen.
But who is a good citizen?
Frederick the Great answers:

"A good citizen," he says, "is he who follows this immutable law, that he be as useful as possible to that society to which he is assigned." Therefore, he by whom we wish the fatherland to be loved must be a citizen and accordingly free.
For he who is above the citizen will be a lover of domination, not of the fatherland;
he who is below the citizen does not have a fatherland.
Thus among the ancient nations in the eastern kingdoms ruled tyrannically, you would find no love of country, because in them there were no citizens, but only masters and slaves;

and in the middle age, as they call it, if you except free cities, it was not love of country that drove men to great deeds, but the impulse of religions and what seems to have been loyalty to masters in place of love of country.
But what shall I say about liberty?
For whoever is not free is not even a part of the people, nor even a person, but a possessed thing;
And an old author wittily said:

“Fifteen free men are a people, as many slaves a household, as many prisoners a prison.” What wonder, then, that those who are imbued with genuine love of country are most devoted to liberty, and that civic virtue and love of liberty are considered almost the same thing?
It is a proof, what Demosthenes says about the Athenians.

"For who of the Greeks, who of the barbarians does not know," he says, "and from the Thebans and from those who previously had power, and most recently, when he celebrated those solemn Agrippinian games, truly magnificent, with his usual eloquence he clearly indicated how much he valued the harmony of the Germans:
Finally, there is no land of Germany that more easily and more willingly receives Germans as its own, not as foreigners, than our Prussia.
Now indeed, we are not bound by a pact, as some used to say, to love this fatherland, both in its broader and narrower sense.
For no one loves from a pact.
But just as the source of any love is the inner harmony of souls, so we love our fatherland because our character agrees with the spirit of the whole people and state.

Moreover, this love is increased by the recollection of benefits owed to the fatherland, which has both educated us and protected us, and has furnished us with all goods of mind and body, and daily furnishes us:

Hence it happens that the fatherland is loved more easily and more vehemently, which has set before itself that which the princes of Prussia have set before themselves, namely to enrich their citizens with any goods, both external and internal, as much as possible.
But by what things do we show that we are held by love of our country?
By civic virtue, I think.
But in what does civic virtue consist?
In this, I think: that you be a good citizen.
But who is a good citizen?
Frederick the Great answers:

"A good citizen," he says, "is one who follows this immutable law, so as to be as useful as possible to the society to which he is assigned." Therefore, he whom we wish to be loved by the fatherland must be a citizen and accordingly free.
For he who is above the citizen will be a lover of domination, not of the fatherland;
he who is below the citizen does not have a fatherland.
Thus, among the ancient nations in the eastern kingdoms ruled tyrannically, you would find no love of country, because in them there were no citizens, but only masters and slaves;

and in the so-called Middle Ages, if you except free cities, it was not love of country that drove men to great deeds, but religious fervor and what seems to have been loyalty to lords in place of love of country.
But what shall I say about liberty?
For whoever is not free is not even a part of the people, not even a person, but a possessed thing.
And an ancient author wittily said:

“Fifteen free men are a people, the same number of slaves a household, the same number of prisoners a prison.” What wonder, then, that those who are imbued with genuine love of country are most devoted to liberty, and that civic virtue and love of liberty are considered almost the same thing?
It is a proof, that Demosthenes says this about the Athenians.

"For who does not know that of the Greeks, of the barbarians," he says, "and from the Thebans and from those who had previously been powerful, the Lacedaemonians, and from the king of the Persians, the Athenians would most easily and with much gratitude have obtained, that having received whatever they wanted and with their own affairs retained, they would do what was commanded and would allow another to rule over the Greeks?"
Indeed, that was not their ancestral custom, not tolerable, not implanted by nature:
For they were not then seeking an orator or a praetor, by whose service they might happily be slaves, but they thought that they should not even live, unless it were permitted to live with liberty:
For each one of them thought that he was born not only for his father and mother, but also for his fatherland:
But he who thinks that he was born for his parents alone will await the death that is destined by fate and comes of its own accord;

But he who also [thinks he was born] for his country will want to die, lest he see it enslaved, and will fear disgrace and insults more than death, which must be endured in an oppressed country." Thus he [said].
Therefore, by the best use of liberty, not by serving best, is love for one's country maintained:

But since servile flattery and obsequiousness, that worst plague of the human race, is no small part of servitude, he is not to be judged as loving his country who approves, praises, and extols whatever is done in his state, but he who brings to light the hidden evils of the state, chastises those that are open, attacks imprudence and perverse counsels, if he can, modestly and humbly, but if need be, even sharply and severely.
By this art Demosthenes and Cicero earned the gratitude of their country.
By this art, among the ancients, comedy itself was useful to the state, which, because many in our age cannot bear it, told the truth by laughing most freely.

Indeed, some bitterness, although troublesome to those who have not yet become accustomed to freedom of speech, is preferable to indolent endurance; and he who is content with that endurance does not differ much from the man whom that wisest lawgiver Solon judged worthy of severe punishment—I mean the man who, in the discord and sedition of the people, was unwilling to take the side of either party, but withdrew solitary and separated from the common evil of the state.

For here it cannot happen that he is held by love of country, since he lives for himself, not for the state, and is not moved by its advantages or disadvantages, but led by private utility and, almost according to Epicurus' teaching, indulging in sluggish leisure and careless of public safety, and if not a traitor to his country, certainly next to a traitor.

Would the Athenians have very easily and with great favor obtained from the Lacedaemonians and from the Persian king that, having received whatever they wanted and having retained their own affairs, they should do what was commanded and allow another to rule over the Greeks?
Indeed, that was not ancestral to them, not tolerable, not innate in their nature:
For they were not then seeking an orator or a praetor, by whose service they might serve happily, but they thought that they should not even live, unless it were permitted to live with freedom:
For each one of them thought that he was born not only for his father and mother, but also for his country.
But he who thinks he was born only for his parents will await death destined by fate and coming of its own accord;

But he who [thinks he was born] for his country as well will want to die, lest he see it enslaved, and will fear disgrace and insults, which must be endured in an oppressed country, more than death.” These words he [said].
Therefore, the love of one's country is contained in the best use of liberty, not in serving best.

But since flattery and obsequiousness, that worst plague of the human race, are no small part of servitude, he is not to be regarded as loving his country who approves, praises, and extols whatever is done in his state, but rather he who brings to light the hidden evils of the state, chastises those that are open, attacks imprudence and perverse counsels, if he can, gently and humbly, but if need be, even sharply and severely.
By this art Demosthenes and Cicero earned the gratitude of their country.
By this art, among the ancients, comedy itself was useful to the state, which, because many in our age cannot bear it, told the truth by laughing most freely.

Indeed, some bitterness, although troublesome to those who have not yet become accustomed to freedom of speech, is preferable to indolent patience; and he who is content with that patience differs not much from the man whom that Solon, the wisest lawgiver, judged worthy of sharp censure — I mean the man who, in the discord and sedition of the people, was unwilling to take the side of either party, but withdrew alone and apart from the common evil of the state.

For here it cannot happen that he is held by love of country, since he lives for himself, not for the state, nor is he moved by the advantages or disadvantages of this state, but being led by private advantage and, almost according to Epicurus' teaching, indulging in sluggish leisure and careless of the public safety, and if not a traitor to his country, certainly next to a traitor.

While I speak of the fatherland, not of the prince, hearers, nevertheless both the matter itself and this occasion and my own piety have impelled me, at the same time, to make mention both of the earlier kings of the Prussians and of the magnanimous counsels of Frederick William IV:

Now I come to that point, to which perhaps you had even earlier expected that I would proceed, namely, to consider what relation exists between the fatherland and the prince, between love of the fatherland and love of the prince.
This matter, before these two years, shortly after Frederick William IV had assumed the government, I remember that I touched upon in another solemn assembly.

But just as the Theban poet, most copious in the songs with which he celebrated the victors of the games, did not avoid treating the deeds of Hercules and Achilles and the Aeacidae at different times, yet in such a way that he would set forth differently about them in different places, so I hope that I will not now say exactly the same thing about the same subject.
We see that it has been asked whether love of one's country was peculiar to free states, in which, at least among the ancients, it especially stood out, or whether it also had a place in kingdoms.

Indeed, what we said a little earlier, that he who is above the citizen is a lover of domination, not of the fatherland, someone might twist this to mean that the fatherland cannot be dear to the prince himself, but that he alone is dear to himself, since, like Louis XIV, king of the French, he himself alone seems to himself to be the state.

Therefore it is all the more valuable to point out that the Athenians, who nevertheless were devoted exclusively to liberty and popular government, established the most brilliant examples of love of country set forth by their ancient kings, from Erechtheus, who had sacrificed his daughter for his country, and from Codrus, who, lest Athens should yield to the enemy, had offered himself to certain death.

And indeed, as long as the prince does not fail to know—what is certain that Frederick the Great did not fail to know, and that our most merciful lord does not fail to know—that he too is a citizen, who could be more inflamed with love of country than the head of the state, on whom especially the safety of the country depends?
But what shall we say about those who are subject to kings?
It is pleasing to recall what that same Frederick the Great decided about this matter.

When he discusses the love of one's country, after he has denied that there are no citizens in kingdoms, he says that well-constituted kingdoms, since their administration is wise and full of kindness, in his age come closer to the rule of a few than to tyranny, and that only laws reign in them:

Since the Greeks say that these [laws] rule even in a popular government, it can be understood, if indeed both statements are true, that well-constituted states, whatever their form may be, are equally just and fair.

But descending to particulars, Frederick says that all who are admitted into the councils, who are occupied in administering justice, who manage revenues, taxes, and commerce, who undertake embassies, who command armies, who provide for public safety at home, and besides, who cast votes in the affairs of individual provinces, will pass over, so that we may consider what relation exists between the fatherland and the prince, between love of country and love of the prince.
I remember that I touched upon this matter in another solemn assembly a little after Frederick William IV had obtained the empire, before these two years.

But just as the Theban poet, most copious in the songs with which he celebrated the victors of the games, did not avoid treating the deeds of Hercules and Achilles and the Aeacidae at different turns, yet in such a way that he would set forth differently about them in different places, so I hope that I will not now say exactly the same thing about the same subject.
We see that it has been asked whether love of one's country was peculiar to free states, in which, at least among the ancients, it especially stood out, or whether it also had a place in kingdoms.

Indeed, what we said a little earlier, that he who is above the citizen is a lover of domination, not of the fatherland, someone might twist to mean that the fatherland cannot be dear to the prince himself, but that he alone is dear to himself, since, like Louis XIV, king of the French, he himself alone seems to himself to be the state.

Therefore it is all the more worthwhile to mention that the Athenians, who nevertheless were devoted solely to liberty and popular government, established the most brilliant examples of love of country set forth by their ancient kings, from Erechtheus, who had sacrificed his daughter for his country, and from Codrus, who, lest Athens should yield to the enemy, had offered himself to certain death.

And indeed, as long as the prince does not fail to know—what is certain that Frederick the Great did not fail to know, and that our most gracious lord does not fail to know—that he too is a citizen, who could be more inflamed with love of country than the head of the state, on whom especially the safety of the country depends?
But what shall we say about those who are subject to kings?
It is pleasing to recall what that same Frederick the Great decided about this matter.

When he discusses the love of one's country, after he has denied that there are no citizens in kingdoms, he says that well-constituted kingdoms, since their administration is wise and full of kindness, in his age come closer to the rule of a few than to tyranny, and that only laws reign in them:

Since the Greeks say that these [laws] rule even in a popular government, it can be understood, if indeed both statements are true, that well-constituted states, whatever their form may be, are equally just and fair.

But descending to particulars, Frederick says that all who are admitted into councils, who are occupied in administering justice, who manage revenues, taxes, and commerce, who undertake embassies, who command armies, who provide for public security at home, and besides, who cast votes in the affairs of individual provinces—all these, as many as there are, are participants in supreme power in kingdoms:

Therefore, the prince should not be a tyrant, who has no law except his own will (not to mention his lust), but he should be, as it were, the center of a circle, in which all lines from the circumference meet.

If there is any kingdom in Europe into which these things do not fit aptly, that is the Turkish empire, and one or another that has not yet learned to perfectly combine the interests of private individuals with the interests of the rulers, being ignorant of its true advantage.
He adds, what I mentioned a little earlier from that source, that a well-governed kingdom is like a family, and that good things are common to rulers and parents alike.
This community and concord, when it has been well cemented, produces a feeling of gratitude, so that good citizens come to be so united with the state that they cannot separate themselves from it.
For if they are separated, they will lose everything and gain nothing.
After these things have been discussed by that great man, what I have said generally about love of country fits together excellently:
namely, in kingdoms too love of country will have a place, if the kingdom is at the same time a state and in this state there is liberty.

But nevertheless, the love of country is one thing in a popular and aristocratic government, another in a monarchy, inasmuch as the safety of the kingdom and of the ruled nation can hardly be separated from the safety of the prince, and when the princely house is overthrown, the state of the republic rarely remains untouched, and in a monarchy the love of country itself is transferred entirely to the person of the prince as the father of his children.

For it is so far from being the case that liberty diminishes and breaks the love of the prince, that a prince cannot be loved except by free men, while by slaves he may rather be feared; and the more freely a kingdom has been established, the more sincerely and vehemently the prince is wont to be loved, especially where, as in our age in Britain, power has been confirmed by long duration of time, and has not been acquired only recently, nor against the will of a great multitude of citizens; and most of all where the prince himself has established liberty of his own accord, and has not waited until it was wrested from him by force or by the untimely opportunity of adverse circumstances.

Therefore, since love of country and love of the prince admirably conspire, the latter will be approved by almost the same arts as the former, that is, not by illiberal servitude, but by the virtue of a good citizen, such as we have indicated above, and by the right use of liberty, which Frederick William IV does not begrudge us, but rather supports and increases.
But it would be a long story to speak about this matter;
Now I will set forth another point, which above, when I spoke about the fatherland and love of country, I deliberately omitted.
For since not a few kingdoms are composed of several nations, and all, as many as there are, are participants in the supreme power in those kingdoms, ...
Therefore, let the prince be not a tyrant, who has no law except his own will (not to say his lust), but let him be like the center of a circle, in which all the lines from the circumference meet.

If there is any kingdom in Europe into which these things do not fit well, that is the Turkish empire, and one or another that has not yet learned to perfectly unite the interests of private individuals with the interests of the rulers, being ignorant of its true advantage.
He adds, what I mentioned a little earlier from him, that a well-governed kingdom is like a family, and that goods are common to rulers and parents alike.
This community and concord, when it has been well cemented, produces a feeling of gratitude, so that good citizens come to be so united with the state that they cannot separate themselves from it;
For if they are separated, they will lose everything and gain nothing.
After these points have been excellently discussed by that great man, what I said in general about love of one's country fits in well:
namely, in kingdoms too love of one's country will have a place, if the kingdom is at the same time a state, and in this state there is liberty.

But in a popular government and in the rule of the optimates, the love of country is one thing, and in a monarchy it is another, inasmuch as the safety of the kingdom and of the ruled nation can hardly be separated from the safety of the prince, and when the princely house is overthrown, the state of the republic rarely remains untouched, and in a monarchy the love of country itself is transferred entirely to the person of the prince as the father of his children.

Tantum enim abest, ut libertas amorem principis imminuat et frangat, ut non possit diligi princeps nisi a liberis, a servis vero potius metui videatur, atque ut, quo liberius constitutum regnum sit, eo sincerius et vehementius amari princeps soleat, praesertim ubi, ut nostra aetate in Britannia, confirmata longinquitate temporis potentia, non nuper demum, neque invita magna civium multitudine, parta sit, et maxime ubi princeps ipse instituerit libertatem sua sponte, neque exspectaverit, donec ea vel vi vel rerum adversarum opportunitate importuna extorqueretur.

Therefore, since love of country and love of the prince admirably agree, the latter will be approved by almost the same means as the former, that is, not by illiberal servitude, but by the virtue of a good citizen, such as we have indicated above, and by the proper use of liberty, which Frederick William IV does not begrudge us, but rather promotes and increases.
But it would be tedious to speak at length on this matter;
Now I will set forth another thing, which I deliberately omitted above, where I spoke about the fatherland and love of the fatherland.

For since there are not a few kingdoms composed of several nations, and these differing in language and customs, and since moreover the provinces of the same kingdom, even if the characters of their inhabitants do not differ so much that they seem to be of different stocks, nevertheless, because they had been completely separated for a long time, are accustomed to be more or less estranged from one another, and their inhabitants to indulge in a certain degenerate love of country, which is love of province;
Those who preside over such states, or give their effort, so that that diversity of nations and provinces may be removed:

This will be brought about especially then, when the whole force of the empire will be placed in the city, the seat of the kingdom, almost as the ancients comprehended the whole state in one city, Attica in Athens, Laconia in Sparta, Arcadia in Megalopolis, and Rome, mistress of the world, that immense Roman state:
or they tear those nations, subject to one ruler, into different kingdoms, and, wonderfully delighted with these distinctions of provinces, they strive to preserve and increase these very things.
With what difficulties each method is hindered, with what disadvantages it labors, it is not my task now to explain:

That seems clear: different nations, and even provinces that are too much alienated from one another, cannot be firmly united into one commonwealth, unless they understand that their common interests are contained in this union, and that as soon as this alliance has been dissolved, the safety of each individual will be endangered, and the parts, now weak, will fall as prey to a more powerful enemy.

But this fellowship, which rests solely on utility, will be greatly strengthened by the love of the prince, who, as it were, from these elements of the whole kingdom, will have bound and obliged all parts to himself by the magnitude of his benefits.
Who among you, listeners, does not see even without being warned why these things are now mentioned by me?

Who does not see that, as formerly by the kindness and clemency of Frederick William III, so now by that of Frederick William IV, the nations that obey the Prussian rule, though separated not only by language and customs but also by the chances of fortune and by their desires and expectations, are united, as far as possible, into one body, and that they, if not in all things, yet certainly in love for their excellent King, conspire with one unanimous feeling?

In language and customs, since moreover the provinces of the same kingdom, although the dispositions of their inhabitants do not differ so much that they seem to be of different stocks, nevertheless because they had been completely separated for a long time, are accustomed to be more or less estranged from one another, and their inhabitants to indulge in a certain degenerate love of country, which is love of province;
Those who preside over such states, or give their effort, so that that diversity of nations and provinces may be removed:

That which will then especially be brought about, when the whole force of the empire will be placed in the city, the seat of the kingdom, almost as the ancients comprehended the whole state in one city, Attica in Athens, Laconia in Sparta, Arcadia in Megalopolis, Rome, the mistress of the world, that immense Roman one:

or they tear those nations, which are subject to one ruler, into different kingdoms, and, wonderfully delighted with these distinctions of provinces, they strive to preserve and increase these very things.
With what difficulties each of the two methods is hindered, with what disadvantages it labors, it is not my task to explain now:

That is evident: different nations, and even provinces that are too much alienated from one another, cannot be firmly united into one commonwealth, unless they understand that their common interests are contained in this union, and that as soon as this alliance is dissolved, the safety of each individual will be endangered, and the parts, now weak, will fall as prey to a more powerful enemy.

But this fellowship, which rests solely on utility, will be greatly strengthened by the love of the prince, who, as if from these elements, has bound and united to himself all parts of the kingdom, formed from them, by the magnitude of his benefits.
Who among you, listeners, is there who does not see even without being warned why these things are now being mentioned by me?

Who does not see that, as formerly by the kindness and clemency of Frederick William III, so now by that of Frederick William IV, the nations that obey the Prussian rule, though separated not only by language and customs but also by the chances of fortune and by their desires and expectations, are united, as far as possible, into one body, and that they, if not in all things, yet certainly in love for their excellent King, conspire with one unanimous feeling?
Therefore, by the gift of this harmony, which is placed in the love of our most dear Prince, I judge Prussia to be strong and happy:
strong not only in favorable circumstances, but also in adverse ones, if they should ever occur, and not only against external enemies, but also against internal dissensions;

He is happy not by abundance of wealth and luxury, but by the virtue of his citizens, who, devoted to the fatherland and the Prince, would rather suffer anything than violate their faith, and let all recognize the excellent will of the King joined with wisdom.
For the King wishes to be the author of evil to no one, but the author of all good things to everyone;
Nor do I fear that anyone may think that I am courting favor with flattery, if I have compared his most gentle nature, leniency, and courtesy with Titus.
And indeed no part of the state is lacking to him, but an equal care embraces all, just as befits one who holds the helm of the whole empire;

yet he so favors literature and the arts and all things that pertain to the cultivation of minds, that unless you knew how much effort he devotes to equipping the military, to establishing and amending law, to agriculture, to aiding crafts and commerce, you would have been ready to believe that he spends his whole time in liberal studies.
But indeed, he cannot rightly favor literature who thinks that it should be governed so that it serves to strengthen domination or to defend certain opinions.
Literature cannot flourish unless it is free.
Therefore, a prince who wishes their flower to increase will hold nothing more important or more ancient than to grant that one may think what one wishes and say what one thinks.
That our most merciful Lord wishes this in general is established by the most certain documents.
But those who twist their face to his nod, he will rather despise than love.
For when all things become worthless through servitude, then nothing is more abject than letters that serve.

But genuine science, which seeks universal, necessary, and immutable notions, which depends on itself alone, not on things, plans, or chance events, which has its end placed within itself, and finally which, being impatient of any authority whatsoever, whether pontifical, princely, or academic, pursues by the straight path the course that reason demonstrates and prescribes, and does not anxiously look around to see what pleases each of the bystanders.
It is especially in our interest that the rulers of states should be persuaded that this is the nature and character of science.
But Frederick William IV, a king of the most liberal disposition, is persuaded of this.

Will anyone therefore think, listeners, that in a state in which literature and especially these literary universities had retained their freedom at that age, in which the most unjust tyranny of a very powerful and almost omnipotent man, because it feared danger to itself from the free movement of minds, was most hostile to literature and especially to this discipline of universities?

In that subsequent age, when because of the reckless undertakings of some young men the German universities had been brought into such suspicion that we seemed likely, under new laws, to suffer anything rather than to break faith, and all may recognize the king's excellent will joined with wisdom.
For the king wishes to be the author of evil to no one, but the author of all good things to all.
Nor do I fear that anyone may think that I am seeking favor by flattery, if I compare his most gentle disposition, his leniency, and his courtesy with Titus.
And indeed he is not lacking to any part of the state, but he embraces all with equal care, as befits one who holds the helm of the whole empire;

Yet he so favors literature, the arts, and all things that pertain to the cultivation of minds, that unless you knew how much effort he devotes to training the military, to establishing and amending law, to agriculture, to crafts, and to supporting commerce, you would have believed that he spends all that time in liberal studies.
Nor indeed can he rightly favor literature who thinks that it should be so governed that it serves to strengthen domination or to defend certain opinions.
Literature cannot flourish unless it is free.
Therefore a prince who desires that their flower should grow will hold nothing more important or more ancient than to grant that one may think what one wishes and say what one thinks:
which our most merciful Lord wishes universally, is established by the most certain proofs:
but those who twist their mouth to his nod, he will despise rather than love.
For when everything becomes worthless through servitude, then there is nothing more abject than letters that are enslaved.

But genuine science, which seeks universal, necessary, and immutable notions, which depends on itself alone, not on things, plans, or chance events, which has its end placed within itself, and finally which, being impatient of any authority, whether pontifical, princely, or academic, pursues by the straight path the course that reason demonstrates and prescribes, and does not anxiously look around to see what pleases each of the bystanders.
That this is the nature and character of science, it is especially in our interest that the rulers of states should be persuaded of.
But Frederick William IV, a king of the most liberal disposition, is persuaded of this.

Will anyone therefore think, listeners, that in a state in which literature and especially these literary universities had retained their freedom at that age, in which age the most unjust tyranny of a very powerful and almost omnipotent man, because it feared danger to itself from the free movement of minds, was most hostile to literature and especially to this discipline of universities?

In that subsequent age, when because of the rash undertakings of some young men the German universities had been brought into such suspicion that we seemed to need to be publicly restrained and guarded by new laws and institutions:

In that republic now, with Frederick William IV holding the reins of government, will letters and schools of letters suffer any loss of liberty, as long as they themselves vigorously defend their own affairs?
By Hercules, no one will think this.

Rather let us give thanks to the most gracious Father of his country, because he supports literature not only by paying salaries, by providing equipment, by supplying expense of every kind, and by conferring other benefits, but also grants to those who teach and those who learn that freedom which the wisest men agree, and have agreed in every age, to be the soul and vital force of literature;
Let us give thanks to the Father of his country, because he regulates the whole commonwealth in the same manner with liberal, good, and wise institutions:

Let us give thanks to God, the Best and Greatest, because He so shaped the mind of Frederick William that there is no one who does not understand that a better king could not have been desired by the citizens nor given by the supreme deity.

Finally, we send most holy prayers to the supreme deity, that he may look after the welfare of Frederick William and assist his counsels, and preserve him together with his consort, the most august queen, and the whole august house for the republic, whose flower and happiness cannot be separated from the safety of the royal family, and that he may strengthen and confirm the forces of the empire and the virtue and concord of the citizens.
and that they must be restrained and guarded by public institutions.

In that republic, then, while Frederick William IV is handling the reins of government, will literature and the schools of literature suffer any loss of liberty, as long as they themselves vigorously defend their own interests?
By Hercules, no one will think this.

Let us rather give thanks to the most gracious Father of our country, because he supports literature not only by paying salaries, by providing equipment, by supplying expenditure of every kind, and by conferring other benefits, but also grants to those who teach and those who learn that freedom which the wisest men agree, and have agreed in every age, to be the soul and vital force of literature;
Let us give thanks to the Father of our country, because he governs the whole commonwealth in the same manner with liberal, good, and wise institutions:

Let us give thanks to God, the Best and Greatest, because He so shaped the mind of Frederick William that there is no one who does not understand that a better king could not have been desired by the citizens nor given by the supreme deity.

Finally, we send most holy prayers to the supreme deity, that he may look to the welfare of Frederick William and aid his counsels, and preserve him together with his most august consort the Queen and the entire August house for the commonwealth, whose flower and happiness cannot be separated from the safety of the royal family, and that he may strengthen and confirm the forces of the empire and the virtue and concord of the citizens.

div.head: XXX. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi IV. celebrandis d. XV. m. Octobris a. MDCCCXXXXIII. habita.

p.s: I think that none of you, most distinguished and most honored auditors of all ranks, judges that there is anything more fitting, anything more proper, than the giving of thanks, which the whole commonwealth, and especially this our literary university, which has appointed me as its speaker, together with the other schools of the liberal arts in this kingdom, owes to the most gracious Prince, for those solemn rites which are consecrated to the observance of the memory of that day on which the supreme deity willed that Frederick William should be born into the hope of succession, so that the safety and dignity of this empire and the welfare and opportunities of the citizens might be provided for.

When I consider that, in carrying out this duty, two ways especially can be entered upon: the one, that whatever the King has done excellently, whether from the time he took up the government, or in this one year which has flowed from the immediately preceding solemnities, should be enumerated one by one and weighed, and how much good from this has overflowed into whatever parts of the state, should be explained with deliberate effort;

The other, so that in some chosen singular argument, which may not be alien from the person of the King or from this most noble royal stock, yet pertains especially to the condition of letters, as if reflected in a mirror, a certain part of that virtue by which the best King excels may be represented:

Indeed, I feel that I am barely, and not even barely, equal to undertaking the former path, and I do not think that I will seem to you, and especially to my most learned colleagues, who both know my weakness and are themselves much more prudent than I, to be sufficiently suited for undertaking so great a province, I say, I who have constantly held that course of life which has hidden me far away from public affairs and from the contemplation of present things in the shade of the school and the seclusion of letters.

But as for that one, which I mentioned in the second place, although I may not be equal to it, yet perhaps I will seem able to claim it for myself with some right, because it is closer to scholastic learning than to the handling of civil and public affairs.

What about the fact that, if something else and greater were demanded or expected from this orator, you would see neither me nor anyone else from that family of closet scholars, to which I count myself, placed on this platform, but rather someone from the jurists, who, as common opinion holds, are usually especially skilled in public affairs, or at least a philosopher or a professor of political doctrine?

There is present a distinguished man, the Rector of this university, who is about to lay down the office he has most successfully administered, and he, having once been notably engaged in public affairs, and being so renowned for his knowledge of events from the remotest antiquity down to the present, for his subtlety and fairness of judgment, for his elegance of mind, and finally for his eloquence and freedom of speech, that no one could sustain that more ample and weighty office with greater success than he.

Therefore I think, listeners, that the fact that I have been appointed almost alone from this most distinguished college of professors to speak on behalf of all, this has this force, that it is permitted in this place to propose something of such a kind as I indicated a little before, yet in such a way that it must be explained so that that whole argument, whatever it is, is brought back to the sense of gratitude owed to our most merciful Lord, and that this sense, like the soul the body, permeates what we say.

In this system, besides eloquent praises, there is also a certain silent praise, one indeed more modest and more inward and more sincere, than that which may boast many bombastic phrases of grandiloquent words.

Dicam igitur hodie de litteris, nec tamen de litteris generatim, sed quatenus de iis bene mereri principes possunt, ac ne hanc quidem rem tractabo integram, sed praemissa una et altera sententia magis generali continebo me posthac in ea quaestione, quid principis de singulis litterarum partibus iudicia conferre ad doctrinarum florem vel queant vel nequeant, eamque magno Friderici Magni exemplo illustrabo, quo uti tanto mihi videtur aptius esse, quanto Fridericus Guilelmus Quartus, quod ex veteri praecepto simile non cognoscitur nisi a simili, illius herois magis agnoscit ingenium, idque etiam ab aequalibus suis posterisque vult agnosci, quippe qui digna et illius et suo nomine monimenta a patre beatissimo vix inchoata condere praeclaro consilio summisque studiis instituerit.

But if I doubt that I will achieve this by setting forth these matters, that my speech may please and be approved, certainly I desire that you not miss my good will, and I want pardon sought and obtained from you both for the things I shall have said and for the things I shall have omitted.
What about the fact that other things also seem to me to need to be excused today?

I mean the use of the Latin language, which, though already abolished from our university, you would not see me or anyone else from that family of recluses, in which I am counted, placed on this platform, but rather some one of the jurisconsults, who, as common opinion holds, are wont to be especially skilled in public affairs, or at least a philosopher or a professor of political science?

There is present a distinguished man, the Rector of this university, who is about to lay down the office he has most successfully held, and one who formerly distinguished himself in public life, and who is so renowned for his knowledge of events from the remotest antiquity down to the present, for his subtlety and fairness of judgment, for his elegance of mind, and finally for his eloquence and freedom of speech, that no one could sustain that more important and weighty office with greater success than he.

Therefore I think, listeners, that the fact that I have been appointed almost alone from this most distinguished college of professors to speak on behalf of all, this has this force, that it is permitted in this place to propose something of such a kind as I indicated a little before, yet in such a way that it must be explained so that that whole argument, whatever it is, is brought back to the sense of gratitude owed to our most merciful Lord, and that this sense, like the soul the body, permeates what we say.

In this system, besides eloquent proclamations, there is also a certain silent praise, indeed more modest and more inward and more sincere than that which may boast many bombastic phrases of grandiloquent words.

Dicam igitur hodie de litteris, nec tamen de litteris generatim, sed quatenus de iis bene mereri principes possunt, ac ne hanc quidem rem tractabo integram, sed praemissa una et altera sententia magis generali continebo me posthac in ea quaestione, quid principis de singulis litterarum partibus iudicia conferre ad doctrinarum florem vel queant vel nequeant, eamque magno Friderici Magni exemplo illustrabo, quo uti tanto mihi videtur aptius esse, quanto Fridericus Guilelmus Quartus, quod ex veteri praecepto simile non cognoscitur nisi a simili, illius herois magis agnoscit ingenium, idque etiam ab aequalibus suis posterisque vult agnosci, quippe qui digna et illius et suo nomine monimenta a patre beatissimo vix inchoata condere praeclaro consilio summisque studiis instituerit.

But if I doubt that I will achieve this by setting forth these matters, that my speech may please and be approved, certainly I desire that you not miss my good will, and I want pardon sought and obtained from you both for the things I shall have said and for the things I shall have omitted.
What of the fact that even other things seem to me to need to be excused today?
I speak of the use of the Latin language, which rumor has reported to have been already abolished from our university, and, what is more important, the scarcity of academic citizens.
But that one, if indeed there is need of an excuse, the law excuses; if anyone is released from it, this seems to have been granted to the person, not to the matter.

But this solitude around us is not because piety has relaxed, but because our cohorts of fellow soldiers, which used to celebrate this most sacred assembly elsewhere, are detained far from the city by legitimate holidays that are not very opportune.
Fame has reported that there is, and, what is more important, the scarcity of academic citizens.
But that one, if indeed there is need of an excuse, the law excuses, by which if anyone is released, this seems to be given to the person, not to the matter.

But this solitude around us is not because piety has relaxed, but because our cohorts of comrades, which used to celebrate this most sacred assembly elsewhere, are detained far from the city by legitimate holidays that are not very opportune.

I take my beginning from that division, which I remember I explained more fully at the end, in the oration delivered before you, in which I praised Frederick William III, the most blessed father of his country, while he was still alive.
At that time I distinguished what could contribute to the flourishing of literature, and what could not, even with the utmost care and diligence applied.
And what could not [be done], that was of two kinds:
For these either were not at all placed in the power of the prince, or were not [placed] under certain conditions.
The prince cannot bring it about that great talents are born, which nature produces of its own accord or the gift of the deity;

And by a certain fatal order and a course of ages divinely prescribed, just as peoples themselves, so in each people the arts and disciplines take their beginnings, their growth, and again grow old with languor.
Indeed, Frederick the Great, in that essay from which I shall quote more a little later, auguring future glory for German letters, hopes that when we shall have our Medicis, talents will flourish;
that Augustuses will bring it about that there will be Virgils;

Although Germany produces men equal to the most laborious investigations, both philosophers and other most ingenious men, and everything you might require, nothing is lacking except a Prometheus who would snatch the celestial fire with which to kindle them:

But rather, whenever literature and the arts flourished more joyfully, the same age, through a certain felicity of the times, produced both poets, learned men, and distinguished artists, who, since the path was already prepared beforehand, might advance further, and leading men powerful in wealth and influence, who would favor literature and the arts;
Nor could you easily say which side was provoked by the other.

However it may be, no one will deny that, unless the character of the age itself inclines toward a more perfect state of the arts and sciences, this cannot be brought about even by the munificence of princes or by the offering of any rewards; and that, to use this example, in the seventeenth century German poets such as Goethe and Schiller later became would not have emerged, even if some Saxon duke had then cultivated poets as recently the noble house of the princes of Weimar cultivated them.

Now, to touch in a few words upon those letters which cannot be advanced under certain conditions of the state, I have once used the example of eloquence, which cannot be cultivated unless, with fear removed, you have given freedom of speech, and not only freedom, but also places and subjects in which eloquence can be shown;
Nor is the method of writing history different, in which we Germans especially limp.

But who does not understand that philosophy and those disciplines that are most closely related to it are not permitted, under the priestly or pontifical domination which they commonly call hierarchy, to know anything beyond the elementary exercises of boyhood?

Haec et talia consideranti mihi, ut Rex noster clementissimus egregius omnis elegantiae iudex et artium ac litterarum amantissimus est, novitque quidquid ingeniosum, pulchrum, magnificum est, dignoscere a promiscuo et vulgari, atque eos, qui optima praestant, requirit, invitat, ad sese perducit, imprimis optandum hoc videtur, illum ut largus ingeniorum proventus ne deficiat, quibus possit succurrere munifice, atque ut illi ipsius saeculi indoles et status civitatis copiam faciant bonas artes quaslibet adiuvandi cum fructu, magnanimisque eius consiliis et exspectationi respondeat eventus.

For at this age, if I am not mistaken, almost all are found to be devoted solely either to the utilities and conveniences of life, which, under the guidance of science itself, have been so greatly increased by recent discoveries that anyone who had predicted them in earlier centuries would have seemed to be mad;
or they turn to examining the condition of public affairs not without desire and partisanship, toward which goal poetry itself is carried with no small impetus;

Or they begin to stir up controversies about those matters which seem to pertain to religion, and indeed to arouse or nourish certain disturbances connected with this matter, and to mix sacred things with public affairs:

From these inclinations of minds, just as a foreseeing deity can draw great benefits, so how much danger to the liberal arts may threaten or how much growth may be about to come from them, I, who am not a soothsayer, do not care to divine.
But many things, without doubt, and excellent ones, by which the good arts may be aided, depend in any state of the commonwealth on the will of the prince:
that it may bring to light the talents which have been born;

that it may preserve and increase the instruments and aids of learning handed down from our ancestors, and give the people the opportunity of learning by establishing schools of every kind, and supply expenses not only most necessary but sufficient and generous;
so that he may show that he holds letters in high regard, and that he may honor men of letters with no less honors than those who perform public duties;

that they cannot be advanced by wholesome and liberal conditions, I once used the example of eloquence, which cannot be cultivated unless, with fear removed, you have given freedom of speech, and not only freedom, but also places and subjects in which eloquence can be displayed;
Nor is the method of writing history different, in which we Germans especially limp.

But who does not understand that in philosophy and in those disciplines which are most closely related to it, under priestly or pontifical domination, which they commonly call hierarchy, it is not permitted to know more than the rudiments of childhood?

As I consider these and similar things, since our most merciful king is an excellent judge of all elegance and a great lover of arts and letters, and knows how to distinguish whatever is ingenious, beautiful, and magnificent from the common and vulgar, and seeks out, invites, and draws to himself those who excel in the best things, this especially seems to me to be desirable: that the generous crop of talents may not fail, talents which he can assist munificently, and that the character of his age itself and the state of the commonwealth may provide the opportunity to support any good arts with profit, and that the outcome may answer his magnanimous plans and expectation.

For at this age, if I am not mistaken, almost all men are found to be intent solely on the utilities and conveniences of life, which, under the guidance of science itself, have been so greatly increased by recent inventions that anyone who had predicted them in former centuries would have seemed to be mad.
or they turn to examining the condition of public affairs not without desire and partisanship, toward which goal poetry itself is carried with no small impetus;

that he may order and temper with wholesome and liberal laws and institutions both the whole literary enterprise and the schools of letters, both lower and higher, and the colleges destined for transmitting or cultivating learning.
That these things may be brought about, much care, effort, and diligence must be applied.

nor does that seem necessary, especially since I have not now for the first time begun to speak about these matters.
Therefore I proceed to that which I said a little while ago I would especially dwell upon in explaining.

There is no one who does not know that Frederick the Great almost entirely despised the literature of the Germans, such as it appeared in his own age, or at least conceived a very moderate opinion of it;

And he, in a special little commentary, which he entitled 'On German Literature,' not only attempted to disclose the causes by which the Germans, although endowed with the best natural disposition, were hindered from equaling the other more learned nations in the cultivation of letters and the elegant arts, but also sought out remedies and gave advice, by which it might be brought about that our fatherland's language and literature and all kinds of learning should be improved, and the rough rust of minds should be rubbed off.
I am not the sort of person who would think myself able to judge more wisely than so great a man on matters of the greatest importance.

Nevertheless, to confess what I feel, as he says that even good Homer sometimes nods, so I think I will not have many adversaries when I have classified that little book, which I believe was poured forth by Frederick extemporaneously, not composed with care and diligence, among the lighter works of the philosopher king, being not particularly conspicuous either in the order of its subject matter or in the weight of its opinions.
When I say this, I by no means deny that excellent things are also contained in this treatise, and indeed prophetic words;
