While Italy was refined by the good arts, he says that Germany was agitated by theologians and torn into two factions, distinguished by fanatical instinct and by hatred and envy, each inflamed against the other:

Soon after, when in Gaul the plans once conceived by Francis the First for restoring the humanities had been renewed, and under King Louis the Fourteenth it had been brought about that Paris no longer yielded to Rome and Florence, which had been illuminated by the Medici with the lights of arts and learning, Germany was afflicted and exhausted by the most disastrous slaughter of the Thirty Years' War, with twenty armies, now victorious, now vanquished, one after another bringing such depopulation, solitude, and vast devastation that farmers abandoned their fields and villages, inhabitants their towns, and everything lay deserted, uncultivated, and squalid.

Nor was Germany immediately revived by the Peace of Westphalia, but it had to be defended first against the Turks, who filled everything with immense terror, and then against the arms of the French, who had entered the German provinces to extend their own borders.

While Vienna, the capital of the empire, was besieged, while villages, towns, and fortresses of the Palatinate were destroyed by fire and sword, along with the very tombs of the princes, it was not possible for poetry to be cultivated there.

Therefore, the accidents of fortune and continuous wars, which would exhaust the resources and men of the fatherland, not a scarcity of talents, stood in the way of the Germans then, so that they did not achieve what other nations achieved.
Those losses had to be repaired first by cultivating the fields, restoring buildings, propagating offspring, fostering the industry of artisans, and increasing trade.
By these means, wealth later grew, not without luxury.
At the same time, the love of literature was revived.
Nevertheless, to use a Horatian word, traces of the countryside remain.

In order that these may be extinguished and that literature of every kind may be corrected and perfected, he gives many precepts individually, both pertaining to the regulation of gymnasia and to the schools of universities:
From this discussion I will sample a few things, though not preserving exactly either the order of topics or the divisions which he himself used.
For the fact that the German style is neither clear nor exact, he attributes to the neglect of good studies:

But this opinion has arisen from the fact that, since the learned Germans seemed to be stuck in trifles and in fastidious and rotten erudition, many, in order to wash off the stain of that reputation, have dismissed Greek and Latin literature, from whose most abundant springs they had drawn, by whose excellent examples the Italians, French, and British had been formed.
Thucydides and Xenophon must be handled, so that strength and grace may be won for one's words;
the vehemence of Demosthenes must be rendered;
Sallust, Julius Caesar, Tacitus, and Marcus Antoninus are to be read, so that a brief, sententious, and grave style may be formed;
He adds Aristotle's Poetics and Horace's Epistle to the Pisos, and one or two French books.

But for us, from the controversies and disputes about religion that were undertaken, there has arisen an abundance of contentious men, who would discuss obscurely things that cannot be understood, defend and attack the same arguments, and mix insults with the fallacies of sophists.

He says that our first learned men, as among all peoples, were men who, by heaping up one thing after another, filled their memory, men of the study, destitute of judgment, Lipsiuses, Freinshemiuses, Gronoviuses, Graeviuses:
A certain Gaul from the cohort of friends, as I think, would have supplied their names, scarcely proper to Germany, to the most august patron about to write this little book:

These slow-moving restorers of some obscure expressions, which are found in old manuscripts, have indeed rendered useful service to some extent, yet not all industry and diligence ought to be consumed on those trifling matters and consequently of slight importance.

But nevertheless, what is especially to be lamented, they won the applause of all Europe, since they wrote in Latin, in order to boast of their Latinity and even to carry off the admiration of foreign scholars of the same stripe.
I pass over with what right that great man censured these scholars, whom without doubt he knew too little:
but we owe him thanks, because he vindicated the dignity of ancient literature:
Unless perhaps this is rather an accusation than a vindication, because Frederick the Great defended them.
But let them disparage them, both those who disparage Frederick the Great and those who praise him, and they try to drive them out;
Though driven out, they will always return, just as they returned in that age in which literature was reborn, and immortal and eternal they will survive the memory of obscure adversaries.

In the other disciplines, however, because only one method of teaching and learning can be correct and this must be followed, he wants a definite standard to be prescribed for each professor.
Therefore he directs his speech to the teachers of each discipline in turn, namely to the professors of philosophy, of medicine, of law, and of history.
For example, from the things he discusses about the teaching of philosophy, I cite a few sentences.
He does not expect from the philosopher that he should contribute anything to forming and polishing the language.
this is the business of the poet and the orator;
the province of the philosopher is the refutation of errors, the exploration and discovery of truth.
He should not, as is commonly done, be wholly devoted and enslaved to some particular system of opinions, which they call a system;

For students who will go forth from the instruction of such a philosopher will be filled everywhere with precepts and opinions, and will have known only a small part of the doctrines devised by men, and not all the errors and absurd fictions.

He says that one who is about to teach philosophy must begin with an exact definition of this discipline, and then the various systems from the most remote age must be explained in order of time and judged or refuted.
He adds examples taken from the opinions of the Stoics and Epicureans.
For example, if the Stoics say so.

That the human soul is a particle of the divine breath, that it is the professor's duty to teach this, that this statement contains a contradiction, because if man were a particle of God, it would be necessary that man be endowed with infinite knowledge, and that if God inhabited men, it would come to pass that a British God would fight with a French God or a Spanish God, and that from that doctrine it would be a consequence that any crimes of men whatsoever are perpetrated by God.

Now after he has spoken about certain other ancient philosophers, he demands that the master of philosophy clearly expound the teachings of Galileo, and in explaining them not omit to rebuke the stupidity of the Roman clergy, who refuse to believe that the earth moves and rebel against the antipodes;
He says that one must speak about Copernicus, Tycho, whom he names late, about Descartes, Newton, Leibniz:
He brings forward his monads and pre-established harmony:
He says that this is a story invented by a most ingenious man;
This is what must be demonstrated by the professor.
Spinoza, he says, the professor will refute without any trouble, in the same way as the Stoics;

But if that same man seems to deny the supreme deity, nothing will be easier for the teacher than to crush him to ashes, especially when our professor demonstrates the end of each thing, for which it was destined:
For the whole nature of things, from the smallest thing up to man, speaks testimony about divinity.

To pass over other things, a professor who is endowed with common sense says that he will not forget the wise Locke, that one among metaphysicians who embraced sound reason and rejected the dreams of imaginations, who followed experience as far as it could lead, and prudently stopped where it began to fail as a guide of the journey.
Finally, when it comes to morals, the professor will say a few words about Socrates, and will bestow due praise on M.
Antoninus, and he would have expanded more fully in setting forth Cicero's work on duties, the best of all, as many as have been written and can be written on morals.
This is, in brief, the sum of the rules to which that great man wishes the schools of philosophers to be directed.

But if the hour were not pressing, and if I did not fear that, while I myself am not getting tired, I would weary your patience, I would have related these things more fully, and I would have added those things which in a similar manner he teaches to the remaining teachers.
Indeed, whoever has considered all these things will also admire in these matters the genius of a great prince, instructed and adorned with varied and manifold learning;

He will admire the fact that the king, amid his greatest and most serious occupations, not only handled literature himself, but placed part of his leisure in examining the way and method by which literature was to be taught.
Yet in that discussion you may detect excellent judgments mixed with lighter ones:
And reverence due to that great man brought it about that I willingly passed over certain things which have been sufficiently and more than sufficiently reproached to him by his critics.

Of course it could not happen that a man, however endowed with all the gifts of the mind, when he did not wish to confine himself to general notions, but descended to the individual parts of nearly all disciplines, to which he could not devote more than a superficial effort, should be less wise than those who dwell entirely in these individual parts.
And I think that Frederick the Great, in his wisdom, tacitly conceded this.

For although he did not hesitate, as a private citizen, to express his opinion on matters about which even men who excel neither in force of intellect nor in abundance of learning have been accustomed to judge both in the past and especially at the present time, nevertheless, since it is especially characteristic of a king to distrust oneself in many things and to listen to those who excel in each art, he by no means carried out what seemed to him regarding the teaching of letters.

He himself, indeed, when he advises that something be changed in the formation of Germanic words, so that they may become more pleasant and sonorous, says wittily that if the Emperor and the eight Electors were to pass laws on this matter in the solemn assemblies of the Empire, the zealous followers of Teutonic barbarism would receive these decrees with laughter and would drown them out with that cry:

"Caesar is not above the grammarians." The emperor appointed Quintilian as professor of eloquence;
the precepts of eloquence were established not by the emperor, but by Quintilian.

But how little is it that we see literature accomplish in those kingdoms, where certain fixed doctrines are to be taught by teachers according to a certain method, and where pupils are to be educated according to certain publicly approved compendia, and even the very manuscripts of the teachers' commentaries are subjected to the examination of censors?
What, to use a most brilliant example, would Kant have accomplished, if he had been forced to teach that philosophy according to the precepts of Frederick the Second, his master, however great?

Whence I seem rightly to gather that the judgments of princes concerning individual parts of literature, especially insofar as they pertain to the way and method of transmitting disciplines, can contribute not much to bringing about the perfection of learning.
I do not deny that a state, which in its bosom cherishes and nourishes science, ought to make laws by which the public education of youth is regulated;
but these laws are of whatever sort they are:
for concerning these it is not my part to decide:

As long as there will be caution that the highest matter not be corrupted by pernicious doctrines, the wise prince will no more impose his own judgment about individual disciplines on the teachers of the good arts.

But if the prince loves literature, if he loves it so much that he favors no part of it, that he is equally kind to all, and is persuaded that all [parts] by their own nature tend to the common prosperity of the human race, what can more favor the course of literature than this judgment of the prince?
Indeed, this has been and is no small felicity of the Prussian state, that almost all its princes have conceived this opinion about literature:

Frederick William IV, however, our most gracious Lord, both before he attained the supreme power and afterwards after he assumed the government, has testified his most ardent zeal for the liberal arts by such manifest proofs that from the very beginning no one could doubt that from this king, as far as it lies with a prince, a new and truly golden age of literature would come forth.
What then do you think, listeners?
Would anyone rather wish that this king impose unjust laws on the professors of universities than Frederick the Great, and command from his own will what and how should be taught?

Indeed, the most illustrious man, to whom he entrusted the care of public education, declared most clearly and most certainly that the wisest king was persuaded of this very thing which has now been set forth by me, when he saw that Caesar was above the grammarians, by what right he is above the philosophers or above the rhetoricians or above the authors of history.
