But if the prince loves literature, if he loves it so much that he favors no part of it, that he is equally kind to all, and is persuaded that all [parts] by their own nature tend to the common prosperity of the human race, what can more favor the course of literature than this judgment of the prince?
Indeed, this has been and is no small felicity of the Prussian state, that almost all its princes have conceived this opinion about literature:

Frederick William IV, however, our most gracious Lord, both before he attained the supreme power, and afterwards after he obtained the empire, has testified his most ardent zeal for the good arts by such manifest proofs, that from the very beginning no one could doubt that from this king, as far as it lies in a prince, a new and truly golden age of letters was about to proceed.
What then do you think, listeners?
Would anyone rather wish that this king, more than Frederick the Great, should impose unjust laws upon the teachers of universities, and command from his own discretion what and how should be taught?

Immo vero id ipsum, quod a me nunc expositum est, persuasum habere sapientissimum Regem, vir illustrissimus, cui ille institutionis publicae curam commisit, planissime et certissime declaravit, quum
oratione apud Bonnenses nuperrime habita exponeret, nolle Regem ad novum et meliorem, quem adducturus sit, statum adducendum suo iussu et imperio uti, neque eum de hac re mittere mandata ad ministros suos nec decreta facere, sed cupere tantum atque exoptare, ut multa ingenia et vires excitentur, quae agant sua sponte.
This is of course the mark of a prince who values literature highly and loves literature.
But there is an old saying: no one can love what he does not know.
What one does not know, he is wont to hate.
Therefore those who are unskilled in the good arts are wont to be hostile to them, and the more cultivated a prince is himself, the more diligently he provides for literature.

God has therefore granted this benefit to our fatherland, that He adorned Frederick William IV with such great gifts of intellect, that he might comprehend in his lofty mind the whole world of the finest arts.
But I would not want what I have just said to be taken in such a way that only he who knows science perfectly loves it;
But as Plato thinks, none of the gods philosophizes nor desires to become wise, because he is already wise, nor does anyone who is wise philosophize at all;

And again, those who are completely destitute of knowledge are least desirous of becoming wise, because ignorance has this as its worst feature, that he who is not good and intelligent thinks himself to be sufficiently furnished with virtue and knowledge:

Thus we judge that he loves learning, not the one who thinks himself to be stuffed with all wisdom, but the one who, like that Platonic Love, is in the middle between knowledge and ignorance and seems to himself to be so, and therefore philosophizes, that is, strives for wisdom.

He truly understands that, just as no single person has ever been perfectly wise, and the wiser each person is, the more keenly he perceives how much there is that he does not know, so the human race has in no age reached such a summit of knowledge that one could now stop and nothing would need to be added to discoveries, but one must rest content in handing down those things that have been established before.
Indeed, the future is contained in the past, just as the tree is contained in the seed:
But seeds are entrusted to mother earth, so that from them the sprouting greenness may be drawn forth, not stored away like the dead.
That Frederick the Great, however, judged no differently than we do, is sufficiently established.
He thought that by that path, which was described by him, not prescribed, it could be brought about that a new order of ages might be born for German literature.
And it was born of its own accord.

The great king had foreseen in his mind that the best times for the literature of the fatherland were approaching, times in which honor was to be established for our learning throughout nearly all of Europe, and, to use his own words, as he recently explained in a speech delivered before the people of Bonn, that the king did not wish to use his command and authority to bring about a new and better state, which he is about to introduce, nor to send mandates to his ministers about this matter, nor to make decrees, but only to desire and long for many talents and energies to be roused, which would act of their own accord.
This is of course the duty of a prince who values literature and loves it.
But there is an old saying that no one can love what he does not know;
and that what one does not know is wont to be hateful to him.
Therefore those who are unskilled in the good arts are wont to be hostile to them, and the more cultivated a prince himself is, the more diligently he provides for literature.

God therefore granted this benefit to our fatherland, that He adorned Frederick William IV with such great gifts of intellect, that he comprehended in his lofty mind the whole world of the finest arts.
But I would not want what I just said to be understood in such a way that only the one who knows science perfectly loves it;
But just as Plato thinks that no god philosophizes, nor desires to become wise, because he is already wise, nor does anyone who is wise philosophize at all;

and again, those who are completely destitute of knowledge least desire to become wise, because ignorance has this worst feature, that one who is not good and intelligent thinks himself to be sufficiently equipped with virtue and knowledge:

Thus we judge that he loves learning, not the one who thinks himself to be filled with all wisdom, but the one who, like that Platonic Love, is in the middle between knowledge and ignorance and seems to himself to be so, and therefore philosophizes, that is, strives for wisdom.

He truly understands that, just as no single person has ever been perfectly wise, and the wiser each person is, the more keenly he perceives how much there is that he does not know, so the human race has in no age reached such a summit of knowledge that one could already stop and nothing would need to be added to discoveries, but one must rest content in handing down those things that have been established before.
Indeed, the future is contained in the past, just as the tree is contained in the seed.
But seeds are entrusted to mother earth, so that from them the green growth may be drawn forth as it sprouts, not stored away like the dead.
That Frederick the Great, moreover, judged no differently than we do is sufficiently established.
He thought that by that path, which he himself had described, not prescribed, it could be brought about that a new order of the ages should be born for German letters.
And it was born of its own accord.

The greatest king had foreseen in his mind that the best times for the literature of the fatherland were approaching, times in which honor would be established for our learning throughout nearly all of Europe, and, to use his own words, like Moses he was looking from afar at the promised land, though he was not going to enter it:
except that to some extent he had already entered without knowing it.
The diligence and kindness of Frederick William III helped the good fortune of these times, which will never fall from the memory of men;
We pray to the highest deity that this fortune may not fail our fatherland.

Divine providence has given us Frederick William IV, a most clement, best, and wisest prince, who not only preserves the good things that he received as handed down, but also, with new plans and inexhaustible new liberality, has excellently aided not only the other parts of the state but also all the best studies.

For these benefits we all, first of all, feel and express gratitude to God, the Best and Greatest, the King of kings, the Lord of lords, from whose nod all things depend; then to the most august Prince, under whose leadership, command, and auspices the Prussian kingdom is increased and adorned.

Finally, I make a most sacred vow, which alone embraces all our prosperity, that God, the Best and Greatest, may grant to Frederick William and to the most august Queen his consort, together with the whole royal house, perpetual health and safety.
Just as Moses saw the promised land from afar, yet was not to enter it:
except that to some extent he had already entered without knowing it.
The diligence and kindness of Frederick William III aided the good fortune of these times, which will never fade from the memory of men;
We pray to the supreme deity that this fortune may not fail our fatherland.

Divine providence has given us Frederick William IV, a most gracious, best, and wisest prince, who not only preserves the good things that he received as handed down, but also, with new plans and with inexhaustible new liberality, admirably assists the best studies, as well as the other parts of the state.

For these benefits we all, first of all, feel and express gratitude to God, the Best and Greatest, King of kings, Lord of lords, from whose nod all things depend, and then to the most august Prince, under whose leadership, command, and auspices the Prussian kingdom is increased and adorned.

Finally, I make a most sacred vow, which alone embraces all our prosperity, that God, the Best and Greatest, may grant perpetual health and safety to Frederick William and to the most august Queen, his consort, together with the entire royal house.

div.head: XXXI. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi IV. celebrandis d. XV. m. Octobris a. MDCCCXXXXV. habita.

p.s: Since it has never seemed to me not especially difficult, most distinguished and most honored auditors of all ranks, on this day from this place before this your assembly, not in my own name alone, but in that of the great university composed of various and most ample bodies of most learned men, to speak about the supreme ruler of so great a republic, about whom even if you have proclaimed the best and most excellent things, nevertheless you understand that your words fall far short of his magnificence and goodness confirmed by deeds;

When I compare the present times with the earlier ones, which nourished my youth, strengthened and exercised my manhood, it seems to me that the condition in which we now live, whether one should call it happiness or a difficulty mixed with happiness, greatly hinders the orator.

For if there is anything by which an orator can diminish the magnitude of this office to his own advantage, I think that it is placed in that license which is usually granted to everyone, namely, that having digressed a little from the main point, he may occupy himself with some other argument not too trivial, to which he feels his powers are either equal or at least less unequal:
Therefore, I greatly fear that this expedient, by which a mediocre talent could to some extent help itself, has been snatched from our hands.

Of course, since it befits one who is going to speak in the name of the college and by public mandate to take pains and carefully see to it that, like a contractor to the owner, he approves his work to as many as possible and gains common assent;
Indeed, the state of affairs was calm and tranquil, in which you would achieve that with some diligence applied.
Now the minds are more agitated.
But in this movement, though not unfruitful, yet inconvenient, in this distraction of parts, how few things are there, dissonant and turbulent, in which most agree?
Wherever you turn yourself, offense is more ready and more certain than favor.

You would believe that an orator, even one who lives far from anger and partisanship, and removed from that ambition which leads many astray, in literature alone, practices warfare rather than the art of peace.
While he desires and strives, if not to please everyone, which is not possible in any matter, at least to avoid offense, what he has said and what he has not said are blamed.

And suspicious envy, which is wont of its own accord to scent out hidden thoughts, almost drives the speaker to the point that, just as the Greek comic poets sometimes deformed their actors with masks having a mouth drawn beyond the human nature and monstrous eyebrows, lest if they bore any chance resemblance to some powerful Macedonian, he should seem to have been deliberately mocked by them, so he composes things utterly discordant and abhorrent from any principles of life.

But amid such great dissensions, nevertheless, one thing remains as a resource, the greatest hope and anchor of public safety, in which all agree: I mean the love of the best Prince, whose veneration has today called you here, most distinguished and most honored listeners, so that you might learn, through my interpretation, however I am equipped, with what feeling this school of ours, devoted to the liberal arts, is affected toward the Father of the Fatherland.
This is the sixth year now, listeners, since Frederick William the Fourth succeeded his most blessed father, who was also the most loving father of the people.

Many things have happened in the meantime to me personally, of the state in which we now live, whether one ought to call it happiness or difficulty mixed with happiness, most of all seems to hinder the orator.

For if there is anything by which an orator can diminish the magnitude of this office to his own advantage, I think that it is placed in that license which is usually granted to everyone, namely, that having digressed a little from the main point, he may occupy himself with some other argument not too trivial, to which he feels his powers are either equal or at least less unequal:
I greatly fear, therefore, that this expedient, by which a mediocre talent has been able to help itself to some extent, may have been snatched from our hands.

Of course, since it befits one who is going to speak in the name of the college and by public mandate to take pains and carefully ensure that, like a contractor to the owner, he approves his work to as many as possible and wins common assent;
Indeed, the state of affairs was calm and tranquil, in which you would achieve that with some diligence applied.
Now minds are more agitated:
But in this movement, though not unfruitful, yet inconvenient, in this distraction of parts, how few things are there in which the majority agree, being discordant and turbulent?
Wherever you turn yourself, offense is more ready and certain than favor:

You would believe that the orator, even one who lives far from anger and partisanship, and removed from that ambition which drives many astray, dwelling in literature alone, is rather waging war than practicing the art of peace:
while he desires and strives, if not to please everyone, which is not possible in any matter, at least to escape blame, they criticize what he has said and what he has not said;

And suspicious envy, which is wont of its own accord to scent out hidden feelings, almost drives the speaker to the point that, just as the Greek comic poets sometimes deformed their actors with masks having a mouth drawn beyond the human nature and monstrous eyebrows, lest if these should by chance bear a resemblance to some powerful Macedonian, he should seem to have been deliberately mocked by them, so he composes things utterly discordant and abhorrent from any principles of life.

But amid such great dissensions, nevertheless, one great resource remains, the hope and anchor of public safety, in which all agree: I mean the love of the best Prince, whose veneration has today called you here, most distinguished and most honored listeners, so that you might learn, with me as interpreter, however I am equipped, with what feeling this school of ours, devoted to the liberal arts, was affected toward the Father of the Fatherland.
This is the sixth year, listeners, since his most blessed father, who was also the most loving father of the people, was succeeded by Frederick William the Fourth.
Many things in the meantime have happened, joyful, auspicious, excellent, others sad, deadly;
and causes already seem to be building up for future changes, which you might doubt where they will end up:
but through things as sad and adverse as they were joyful and prosperous, the love of the Prince remained constant.
But what is the source of this affection?
I answer very briefly:
the Prince's character.
For kindness begets affection:

Since this cannot be feigned nor acquired by art, but is a good implanted by nature, unless the prince is by nature inclined to benevolence, he cannot win for himself the love of his people, by which alone, as a bond, nations that are ruled can be firmly held together.

What, then, could have happened more happily to the Prussian kingdom than that it obtained a prince who was by nature courteous, gentle, kind, and generous, who by his very character might draw forth the love of the people?
But what theme could be more fitting for these solemnities, what more delightful, and finally what more suited to the person of the most beloved King than princely kindness?
But if in sketching the image of a benevolent prince, it is at the same time established that the character of Frederick William is set forth in outline;

I think that I am doing a favor to myself, who have myself experienced the favor of the most august King and am devoted to him with all my heart, and that I am doing a favor to you who cultivate him with equal piety, when I describe in outline, both by tacitly adopting the opinions of the most approved authors in this field and by explaining my own reasoning, what the nature of princely kindness is and what power it has, and, as far as the narrowness of time permits, the rest, being more constrained than before by the magnificent speeches of my colleagues which are to be delivered today.
Indeed, I do not deny, this kind of speaking which I now undertake is closer to moral philosophy than to a solemn oration;

but the more I feel that my eloquence, or the appearance of eloquence, if any ever existed in me, has been worn out by use and extinguished by age and ill health, and that I am kept in this duty longer than is good for my reputation and especially for the dignity of this most sacred solemnity, the more it seems suited to my condition.
Joyful, auspicious, excellent, and other things sad and fatal.
And already causes seem to be being built for future changes, so that you might doubt where they will turn out.
But through things so sad and adverse as joyful and prosperous, the love of the Prince has remained constant.
But who is the source of this love?
I answer very briefly:
The Prince's character.
For kindness begets love:

Since this cannot be feigned nor acquired by art, but is a good implanted by nature, unless the prince is by nature inclined to benevolence, he cannot win the love of his own people, by which alone, as a bond, nations that are ruled can be firmly held together.

Therefore, what could have happened more happily to the Prussian kingdom than that it obtained a prince who was by nature courteous, gentle, benevolent, kind, who by his very character draws forth the love of the people?
But what subject can be more suitable for these solemnities, what more delightful, and finally what more adapted to the person of the most beloved King than princely kindness?
But if by sketching the image of a benevolent prince, it is established that the character of Frederick William is also presented in the sketch;

I think I am doing a favor to myself, who have myself experienced the favor of the most august king and am devoted to him with all my heart, and I think I am doing a favor to you, who cultivate him with equal piety, when I describe in outline, both by tacitly citing the opinions of the most approved authors in this genre and by explaining my own reasons, what the nature of princely kindness is and what power it has, and, as far as the narrowness of time permits, the rest, since we are more constrained than before by the magnificent speeches of my colleagues, which are to be delivered today.
Indeed, I do not deny that this kind of speaking which I now undertake is closer to moral philosophy than to a formal oration;

but the more I feel that my eloquence, or whatever appearance of eloquence there ever was in me, has been worn away by use and extinguished by age and ill health, and that I am kept in this office longer than is good for my reputation and especially for the dignity of this most sacred solemnity, the more that seems to me suited to my condition.
Therefore, to begin with that, what that is about which I am about to speak, I call it kindness: a disposition of the mind to do good to those who are in need of good.

This cannot exist without gentleness and mildness, and it is joined with compassion and clemency, except that we are so affected by compassion that we are afflicted in mind together with the wretched, while the affection of kindness is purer and more pleasant, and because clemency consists in remitting sins or punishments and penalties of the guilty, but kindness bestows benefits on the innocent.
And kindness surpasses justice and equity:
For the man who is just and fair gives to each person as much as he owes, obeying only the law and reason;

the one who is kind gives even what he does not owe, or more than he owes, and although he calls reason and judgment into use, nevertheless he indulges his spirit somewhat, so that he may satisfy his inclination to do good;
Then indeed justice conforms itself to the laws established by men, while kindness obeys the divine and likewise truly human precept of love, which Christ promulgated.
Now although this is a virtue common to all men, who nevertheless can be more kind than a prince?

For no one has a greater capacity for doing good than a prince, not only because he is powerful with the greatest resources of all, but also because his mere will alone, even if no advantage should accrue to you from it, is so much a benefit, adding value and dignity to the gift, that he can show his kindness through those things which are usually called by the name of honors:

In these matters, it is not what is given that matters, but with what mind and intention it is given, and you should not value them by silver nor weigh them on a scale, but measure them by the spirit.
And he has such a great abundance of people to whom he can do good, as no one else has.

To say nothing of foreigners, to say nothing of the afflicted, the whole people over whom he rules, and every single one of them, the highest, the middle, the lowest of citizens, have entrusted themselves and all their possessions to his good faith and will, and they can not demand his favor but experience it:
A private individual comes to the aid of one or another of the needy;
From the nod of the prince hangs the fortune of cities and peoples; either the prince's grace and serenity cheers all, or his anger strikes all with fear and sadness.
Again, whom does kindness more befit than a prince?

For if a king, as some think, reigns by divine authority, and in the kingdom itself there is something divine, which I approve to this extent, that I should judge a good prince to have approached nearer to divinity, by as much as a bad one has been pressed down below humanity;

The king will be a kind of image and vicar among mortals of the divine power, and by his example he will have to correspond not more in power than in goodness, which is held to be so great in God that he bestows upon us all good things by pure grace, without regard to merits.
Or if a prince exercises power entrusted to him by men, this has been entrusted to him so that those who obey may fare well.
It is added that for a Christian king at least nothing can be dearer than the happiness of the people;

and since in a prince not the mediocrity of a private person but the highest and absolute virtue is required, you would hardly miss in him the charity from which kindness flows, that is, kindness surpasses justice and equity:
for he who is just and equitable gives to each only as much as he owes, obeying only the law and reason;

He who is kind gives even what he should not, or more than he should, and although he may call reason and judgment into use, yet he indulges his spirit somewhat, so that he may satisfy his inclination to do good.
Then indeed justice composes itself to the laws established by men; kindness obeys the divine and truly human precept of love, which Christ promulgated.
Now although this is a virtue common to all men, who nevertheless can be more kind than a prince?

For no one has a greater opportunity for doing good than a prince, not only because he is powerful with the greatest resources of all, but also because his mere will alone, even if no advantage should accrue to you from it, is so much a benefit, adding value and dignity to the gift, that he can show his kindness through those things which are usually called by the name of honors:

In these matters, it is not what is given that matters, but with what mind and intention it is given, and you should not value them by silver nor weigh them on a scale, but measure them by the spirit.
And he has such a great abundance of people to whom he can do good, as no one else has.

To say nothing of foreigners, to say nothing of the afflicted, the whole people over whom he rules, and every single one, the highest, the middle, the lowest of citizens, have entrusted themselves and all their possessions to his good faith and will, and they can not demand his favor but experience it:
A private individual comes to the aid of one or another of the needy;
From the nod of the prince hangs the fortune of cities and peoples; and either the prince's grace and serenity cheers all, or his anger strikes all with fear and sadness.
Again, whom does generosity become more than a prince?

For if a king, as some think, reigns by divine authority, and in the kingdom itself there is something divine, which I approve to this extent, that I should judge a good prince to have approached the nearer to divinity, by how much a bad one has been depressed below humanity;

The king will be a kind of image and vicar among mortals of the divine power, and by his example he will have to correspond not more in power than in goodness, which is held to be so great in God that he bestows upon us all good things by pure grace, without regard to merits.
Or if a prince exercises power entrusted to him by men, it has been entrusted to him for this purpose, that those who obey may fare well.
Add to this that nothing can be dearer to a Christian king, at least, than the happiness of his people;

and since in a prince not the mediocrity of a private person but the highest and absolute virtue is required, you would hardly miss in him that charity from which kindness flows, that is, that virtue which seems to Christians rightly the most important.

Indeed, the vice contrary to kindness is by no means fitting for the highest ruler of the state, but a gentle, mild, and merciful disposition, conscious of its own human nature, is fitting, lest, placed in the highest position, it rise too high.
But a sharp and agitated temperament is more suited to conducting wars than to ruling the state; a covetous, wrathful, and fierce one is fit for managing affairs neither at home nor abroad.
the virtue which is rightly considered most important by Christians.

The opposite vice to kindness, indeed, is by no means fitting for the highest ruler of the state, but a gentle, mild, and merciful disposition, conscious of its own human nature, is fitting, lest, placed in the highest position, it rise too high.
But a sharp and excitable temper is more suited to conducting wars than to ruling the state; a covetous, wrathful, and fierce one, however, is fit neither at home nor abroad for managing affairs.
Now, to place the matter in a clearer light, let it be permitted to explain briefly what benefits a kind king confers, and on whom, and in what manner.
To the first question I answer with an old saying:
The fatherland owes everything to a good prince.
Therefore, as many kinds of goods as there are, so many are the parts of royal kindness:
But there are some goods of the soul and internal, others of fortune and external.

Therefore, although nature may partly bestow these external advantages and partly talent, labor, and industry may produce them, yet scarcely any kingdom shows more clearly how much in these matters depends on the goodness and wisdom or the harshness and imprudence of rulers than this Prussian one, which, amid the barrenness of so many lands and amid unusual calamities, flourished through the zealous and indefatigable cares of Frederick William, while other states, blessed with most fertile soil and a most healthful climate, languish through the perversity of their laws and institutions.

For the kindness of a good prince opens paths to every honorable kind of gain for the prudent through right counsels, and frees farmers, artisans, and trade from the most troublesome bonds and unjust laws, by which they can be so constrained that they can scarcely move their limbs:
In the matter of revenues, in their method and collection, a good prince takes care that the resources of citizens are not diminished nor the poorer classes oppressed;
he does not seek the profit of the treasury, but provides for the necessities of the state:
Finally, he knows that the prince has as much as all the citizens together, and that whenever the situation demands it, the willing will contribute more than can be extorted from the unwilling.

And since generosity is honorable in time, necessary, and sometimes even useful to the state itself, it repairs losses either accidental or sent by heaven, and with his munificence he kindly relieves the want and misery of men.

Iam vero etsi non possumus sine externorum possessione bonorum vitam bene sustentare, tantum me iudice abest, ut prava ista, quae hac aetate permultos invasit et variis de causis magnopere commendatur, opinio probanda sit, ex qua vel primus huic generi bonorum locus tribuitur, vel ea omissis reliquis prope omnibus unice spectanda sunt, nec quidquam praeter externorum
bonorum curam a principe exspectandum et exoptandum, et qui hac re satisfecerit, principalibus satisfacisse officiis videtur;

so that I should think that, if this error has completely taken hold of the minds of men and has clung to their inmost marrow, states are corrupted by the worst and most shameful cowardice, and the human race is about to be destroyed.

Of course, those who judge the dignity of life solely by the enjoyment of those goods cannot help but, charmed by the daily ease of living and captivated by the allurements of this, of course, their own happiness, no longer dare anything for retaining, defending, and recovering the highest goods of the mind, and consider it enough if they are allowed, secure and safe, even with insult, to do and to feel what is commanded, and to serve a most unworthy servitude.
Therefore a good prince strives to provide for his citizens especially the goods of the mind, as far as it lies in his power:

This is directed to the end that they may be imbued with reverence and piety toward the deity, not that they may be infected and bound by superstition, which would nourish discords and tear apart those whom love ought to unite;
that good morals may be propagated;
finally, that reason and intellect, which is the source of true piety and an honorable life, may be cultivated, not merely ostentatiously paraded.

Since the knowledge of the liberal arts, of philosophy, of history, and of natural science, and the whole vast circle of every kind of discipline, are brought back to this point, what the kind kings could accomplish by undertaking the patronage of science and letters, the Prussian empire, to say nothing of earlier times, from Frederick the Great down to Frederick William IV, the most generous cultivator and defender of the good arts, has excellently shown:
For by their favor, literature has been so firmly established in these lands that we yield to no nation in learning, and even surpass very many.
At the same time, by these studies, superstition has been driven back to some extent.

When last year, in the solemn rites performed elsewhere for the most beloved King, I had pointed out that this was owed in large part to natural science, and had said by way of example that no one is now frightened by eclipses of the sun and moon, by which in former times unlearned minds had been struck;

vir ingenio, virtute, auctoritate spectatissimus, qui Lipsiae eandem quam ego in hac urbe artem profitetur, nescio an illis verbis provocatus concessit quidem solis defectionibus, quas oculis cernimus, hodie neminem terreri, sed alias dixit easque perniciosissimas conduplicari tenebras et occaecare noctis ac nimbum nigrorem, qui eo tantum a deficiente sole differat, quod solis orbem quando relictura sit umbra sciamus, ex istis autem tenebris nec quando neque an lux ac non potius crassa caligo sit emersura, sit cuiquam
bonorum curam a principe exspectandum et exoptandum, et qui hac re satisfecerit, principalibus satisfacisse officiis videtur;

so that I think that, if this error has completely taken hold of the minds of men and has clung to their innermost marrow, states will be corrupted by the worst and most shameful cowardice, and the human race will go to ruin.

Of course, those who measure the dignity of life solely by the enjoyment of those goods cannot help but, charmed by the daily ease of living and captivated by the allurements of this, their own happiness, no longer dare anything for retaining, defending, and recovering the highest goods of the mind, and consider it enough if they are allowed, secure and safe, even with insult, to do and to feel what is commanded, and to serve the most unworthy servitude.
Therefore a good prince strives to provide the citizens with the goods of the mind above all, as far as it lies within his power:

This aims at their being imbued with reverence and piety for the divine, not at their being infected and bound by superstition, which would nourish discord and tear apart those whom love ought to unite;
that good morals may be propagated;
finally, that reason and intellect, which is the source of true piety and an honorable life, may be cultivated, not merely ostentatiously paraded.

Since the knowledge of the liberal arts, philosophy, history, and natural science, and the whole vast circle of all kinds of disciplines, is brought together here, what the benevolent kings could accomplish by undertaking the patronage of science and letters, the Prussian empire, not to mention earlier ones, has admirably demonstrated from Frederick the Great down to Frederick William IV, the most generous patron and defender of the fine arts:
For by their favor, literature has been so firmly established in these lands that we yield to no nation in learning, and even surpass very many.
At the same time, by these studies, superstition has been to some extent driven away.

When last year, in the solemn rites for the most beloved King held elsewhere, I had pointed out that this was largely due to natural science, and had said by way of example that no one is now frightened by eclipses of the sun and moon, by which unlearned minds were once struck;

A man most distinguished in talent, virtue, and authority, who at Leipzig professes the same art that I do in this city, whether provoked by those words, I do not know, conceded indeed that no one today is frightened by the eclipses of the sun, which we perceive with our eyes, but he said that other and most pernicious darknesses are doubled and that the blackness of night and clouds blinds, which differs from the eclipsed sun only in this, that we know when the shadow will leave the sun's disk, but from those darknesses neither when nor whether light, and not rather thick darkness, will emerge, is known to anyone.

But those shadows of ours nevertheless seem to me to have less distinction, because they are not so much natural, as once they were, arising from the character of the age, as smoke artificially made in certain very well-known kitchens, which the blasts of the winds scatter.

This kingdom will not be overshadowed by those things, nor the serenity of the wisest king, who, pious and religious, not fanatical, will, in accordance with the most sacred institution of the Prussian state, allow to each his own opinion and judgment concerning matters which we do not know, but believe.
Finally, the most precious good of the mind is liberty, most closely connected with reason, the prerogative of man among the other animals.
And so a kind prince, as a man among men, as a free man among free men, commands;
But a Christian prince especially knows that slavery of both body and soul has been abolished by the teachings of Christ, although excessive lust for domination may have retained or brought it back;

And that Frederick William IV at the very beginning of his reign declared excellently that he wished to be a Christian king, that declaration the whole administration of the state proves to have been made in such a way that he wished to rule free men with love and to lead them by reason to obedience to be rendered under just laws, not to coerce slaves by force.
What of the fact that by this truly royal path the dignity of the empire itself is excellently provided for?
For this is so much more excellent, as those who obey are more excellent.

Therefore, he who uses citizens as if they were slaves makes his rule worse, in proportion as slaves are worse than free men, although he has more right over slaves than over free men; and it was rightly said long ago that the master of slaves is not much above the possessor of cattle.

Indeed, just liberty, which is not ignorant of obeying laws, magistrates, and the prince, quickly increases the strength, resources, and fame of the empire, and again together with it the remaining goods perish;
but licentiousness must be restrained, and most truly thus far Galba advised Piso:
“You are about to rule men who can endure neither complete slavery nor complete liberty.” And these indeed seem to me to be the most important kinds of benefits;
But if we ask for those things which a good prince gives, the answer is ready:
to the worthy and the needy.
For the reward must be paid to virtue, even if he who excels in virtue should be less grateful;
the prince's kindness pardons even those who are too free, whom he sees to be well-disposed, and with him that saying does not hold:
“Compliance makes friends, truth makes enemies”;
but flatterers, who are born for the ruin of princes and states, he keeps far away.
Then, just as law and statutes, although they ought to be equal for the poor and the rich, for the noble and the commoner, and to protect both parties from injury, so it has been recognized.

But those shadows of mine nevertheless seem to have less distinction, because they are not so much natural, as they were of old, which arise from the character of the age, as they are smoke artificially made in certain very well-known kitchens, which the blasts of winds scatter.

This kingdom will not be overshadowed by those men, nor the serenity of the wisest king, who, being pious and religious, not fanatical, will, in accordance with the most sacred institution of the Prussian state, allow to each his own opinion and judgment concerning matters which we do not know but believe.
Finally, the most precious good of the mind is liberty, most closely connected with reason, the prerogative of man among the other animals.
And so a kind prince, as a man among men, as a free man among free men, gives commands;
But a Christian prince especially knows that slavery of both body and soul has been abolished by the teachings of Christ, although excessive lust for domination may have retained or brought it back;

And that Frederick William IV, at the very beginning of his reign, expressly declared that he wished to be a Christian king, the whole administration of the state testifies that it was so said that he wished to rule free men with love and to lead them by reason to obedience to be rendered under just laws, not to coerce slaves by force.
What of the fact that by this truly royal path the dignity of the empire itself is excellently provided for?
For this is so much more excellent, by how much more excellent are those who obey:

Therefore, he who uses citizens as if they were slaves renders his rule worse, by how much slaves are worse than free men, although he has more right over slaves than over free men, and rightly was it said long ago that the master of slaves is not much above the possessor of cattle.

Indeed, just liberty, which is not ignorant of obeying laws, magistrates, and the prince, quickly increases the strength, resources, and fame of the empire, and again together with it the remaining goods perish;
but license must be restrained, and most truly thus far Galba advised Piso:
"You are about to rule men who can endure neither complete slavery nor complete liberty." And these indeed seem to me to be the most important kinds of benefits;
But if we ask for those things which a good prince gives, the answer is ready:
To the worthy and to the needy.
For the reward must be paid to virtue, even if he who excels in virtue should be less grateful;
The prince's kindness forgives even those who are more outspoken, whom he sees to be well-disposed, and with him that saying does not hold:
“Compliance wins friends, truth begets hatred”;
But flatterers, who are born for the ruin of princes and states, he keeps far away.

Then, just as the law and statutes, although they ought to be equal for the poor and the rich, for the noble and the commoner, and ought to ensure that no injustice is done to either side, nevertheless seem to need to be established in such a way that security is provided especially to those who, because of their lowliness, are more exposed and subject to arrogance, or for this reason, that wrongs and evils inflicted on the more humble and obscure escape notice more easily without an avenger, but if an injustice has been done to someone more distinguished, the whole world cries out:

Thus the imperial kindness does not turn the good of all to this end, that it makes the rich and the nobles and those who have an abundance of resources in their own and their relatives' and friends' means even richer and feeds them more lavishly and more sumptuously;

But it comes to the aid of the peasant afflicted by the barrenness of the fields, by the overflowing of the rivers, to towns laid waste by fire, to orphans, widows, the disabled, for whom the household means may be more limited; it provides for boys and girls with alimentary allowances, and other things of this kind:

In this category, there is no need for me to describe how merciful our King is with his most beloved Queen, who, indeed, not content with having received reports from the governors about the state of the provinces and the condition of the people, leaving behind the splendor and delights of palaces, themselves visit squalid huts and dilapidated cottages, so that they may learn of the misery of mortals and bring aid to the wretched.
And in this matter especially, observe, listeners, how much more excellent and more commendable kingship is than the rule of the people or of a few.
For where a turbulent multitude rules the state:
although in this age certainly in Europe it rules almost none:
the goods of the rich are seized and divided, by which the greedy common people may be fed;
but to the rule of the best men nothing is more hostile to the common people:
these consult for themselves alone at the expense of the lesser ones;
these pass laws useful to themselves, calamitous to the rest;
These men have no concern for the lower classes, no compassion, but they procure their own advantages generally from the inconvenience of those others.
just as Aristotle reports that in certain states governed by the will of a few, the magistrates themselves, when about to assume power, were solemnly bound by such a formula:
“I will be hostile to the common people, and as far as I can, I will take care that their condition be miserable.” But a wise and kind king grants to each side as much as is fitting:
It provides the wealthy with a secure and certain possession of their goods;
It cherishes and revives the common people as much as possible;
It knows how to bring about peace and harmony among the different parts of the state, the ways of life, and the orders of citizens, and it strives to do so.

Neque enim ille ea tantum beneficentiae parte, quae in externis bonis posita est, inferiores incolarum classes impertit, sed quoniam, quo amplior divitibus facultas est liberos omni genere eruditionis et elegantioris doctrinae instruendi, eo neglectior solet rusticae et in frequentibus potissimum urbibus
fiat, tamen videntur ita instituendae esse, ut iis potissimum, qui ob humilitatem superbiae magis expositi et obnoxii sunt, praestetur securitas, vel eam ob causam, quod damna et mala tenuioribus et obscuris data sine vindice latent facilius, sin cui illustriori facta iniuria sit, totus reclamat orbis:

Thus the imperial kindness does not turn the good of all to this end, that it makes the rich and the nobles and those who have an abundance of protection in their own resources and in those of their relatives and friends even richer and feeds them more lavishly and more sumptuously;

but it comes to the aid of the peasant afflicted by the barrenness of the fields, by the overflowing of the rivers, to the towns devastated by fire, to the orphans, to the widows, to the infirm, whose household means are rather narrow; it provides for the boys and girls with alimentary allowances, and for other things of this kind:

In this category, there is no need for me to describe how kind our most merciful King is with his most beloved Queen, who, indeed, not content with having received reports from the governors about the state of the provinces and the condition of the people, leaving behind the splendor and delights of palaces, themselves visit squalid huts and shabby cottages, so that they may learn the misery of mortals and bring help to the wretched.
And in this matter especially, observe, listeners, how much more excellent and more commendable a monarchy is than the rule of the people or of a few.
For where a turbulent multitude rules the state:
although in this age certainly in Europe it rules almost no one:
the goods of the rich are plundered and divided, by which the greedy populace may be fed;
but to the rule of the aristocrats nothing is more hostile to the people:
these consult only for themselves at the expense of the lesser ones;
these pass laws useful to themselves, calamitous to the rest;
These people have no concern for the lower classes, no compassion, but they procure their own advantages generally from the disadvantage of those others.
just as Aristotle reports that in certain states governed by the will of a few, the magistrates themselves, when about to take up power, were solemnly bound by such a formula:
“I will be hostile to the common people, and as much as I can I will take care that their condition be miserable.” But a wise and kind king grants to each side as much as is fitting:
It provides the wealthy with a secure and certain possession of their goods;
It cherishes and revives the common people as much as possible;
It knows how to bring about peace and harmony among the different parts of the state, ways of life, and orders of citizens, and it strives to do so.

Neque enim ille ea tantum beneficentiae parte, quae in externis bonis posita est, inferiores incolarum classes impertit, sed quoniam, quo amplior divitibus facultas est liberos omni genere eruditionis et elegantioris doctrinae instruendi, eo neglectior solet rusticae et in frequentibus potissimum urbibus
operariae multitudinis educatio atque institutio esse, curabit, ut haec quoque eius discipline particeps fiat, sine qua hominum vita ne humana quidem esse videatur, neve litteris et artibus laetissime florentibus, ut floruerunt in Aegypto regnantibus Macedonicae stirpis regibus et in Italia Mediceis aliisque principibus munificentissimis, nihilo minus vulgus, quod iisdem temporibus factum videmus, misere ac serviliter derelinquatur incultum.
So much for relieving the needy.
What shall I say about the guilty?

For although a kind prince will readily show mercy to them and will moderate the severity of punishments and penalties, yet no one will deny that the laws must be enforced, and that the head of the state must be formidable to the guilty, and indeed to them alone, and that the rights, judgments, and morals of the state must not be corrupted by a perverse indulgence, which differs greatly from kindness.

Finally, so that I do not entirely omit the third of the questions I proposed above, it is so established that a kind and wise prince bestows benefits: first, that he restrains his kindness with judgment, and does not throw away benefits rather than give them, nor corrupt favor by the profusion of favor, diminishing the value of rewards;

Moreover, so that, whatever he himself has understood will be beneficial to the citizens, that certainly, if he rules over somewhat more civilized nations, he should not thrust it upon the unwilling, but rather should strive to lead the common people to a better estimation of good and evil, in which he himself excels, by shaping their minds and eradicating their corrupt opinions.

Since I have been brought to this point, I cannot help but recall a certain opinion of Fichte, which seems to be opposed with a hostile front to this whole discussion that we have undertaken concerning the principal's kindness, and to overturn our [views] from the foundation.

Etenim vir magnus, sapientiae et virtutis et libertatis exemplum, huius universitatis olim decus in paucis insigne, quem maiores natu vidimus ex hoc ipso suggestu fulmina eloquentiae torquentem, in luculenta quadam commentatione hortatur omnes, qui tantae rei pares sint, „ut bellum internecivum indicant primo isti errori, omnium malorum nostrorum ac miseriae fonti venenato, principis esse felicitati nostrae providere, atque ut eum errorem per omnes latebras, per universum scientiae nostrae orbem persequantur, ubiubi delituerit, donec deletus fuerit ex orbe terrarum et in Tartarum reversus, unde emerserit." „Nescimus", inquit, „quibus rebus felicitas nostra adiuvetur;

But if the prince knows this and it is his role to lead us to it, we must follow him with closed eyes, and he does for us whatever pleases him; and for those who seek that the education and instruction of the working multitude be provided, he will take care that this too becomes a part of his discipline, without which human life does not even seem to be human; and lest, while letters and arts flourish most joyfully, as they flourished in Egypt under the kings of the Macedonian stock and in Italy under the Medici and other most munificent princes, the common people, which we see happened at the same times, be left wretchedly and slavishly uncultivated.
So much for relieving the needy.
What shall I say about the guilty?

For although a kind prince will have clemency readily available for them and will moderate the severity of punishments and executions, yet no one will deny that the laws must be enforced, and that the head of the state must be formidable to the guilty, and indeed to them alone, and that rights, judgments, and the morals of the state must not be corrupted by a perverse indulgence, which differs greatly from kindness.

Finally, so that I do not entirely omit the third of the questions I proposed above, it is so established that a kind and wise prince bestows benefits, first, that he restrains his kindness by employing judgment, and does not throw away benefits rather than give them, nor corrupt favor by the profusion of favor, diminishing the value of rewards;

Moreover, so that, whatever he himself has understood will be beneficial to the citizens, he certainly, if he rules over somewhat more civilized nations, should not thrust it upon the unwilling, but rather should strive to lead the people to a better estimation of good and evil, in which he himself excels, by shaping their minds and uprooting their corrupt opinions.

Since I have been brought to this point, I cannot help but recall a certain opinion of Fichte, which seems to be opposed with a hostile front to this whole discussion that we have undertaken concerning the principal's kindness, and to overturn our [views] from the foundations.

Etenim vir magnus, sapientiae et virtutis et libertatis exemplum, huius universitatis olim decus in paucis insigne, quem maiores natu vidimus ex hoc ipso suggestu fulmina eloquentiae torquentem, in luculenta quadam commentatione hortatur omnes, qui tantae rei pares sint, „ut bellum internecivum indicant primo isti errori, omnium malorum nostrorum ac miseriae fonti venenato, principis esse felicitati nostrae providere, atque ut eum errorem per omnes latebras, per universum scientiae nostrae orbem persequantur, ubiubi delituerit, donec deletus fuerit ex orbe terrarum et in Tartarum reversus, unde emerserit." „Nescimus", inquit, „quibus rebus felicitas nostra adiuvetur;

But if the prince knows this and it is the prince's role to lead us to it, we must follow him with closed eyes, and he does for us whatever he pleases, and to those who ask he answers with pledged faith that this is necessary for our happiness;
He binds the neck of the human race with a noose, and cries out:
Be silent, be silent;
All these things are done for your advantage.
You, prince, are not our God:
From God we expect happiness, from you the protection of our rights;
We do not want you to be kind to us; we want you to be just." These words he spoke, as he was naturally sharp, somewhat more harshly, more stubbornly, more obstinately:
For us speaking today it will be possible to blunt these stings, which the injustice of earlier times had sharpened.
Indeed, with the sharpness removed, we elicit from the words of our immortal colleague this milder sentiment:

A good prince, such as we describe, does not drag the people to happiness by the neck, nor make them blessed by force, but with reason as their guide and the sweet-speaking goddess Persuasion as their helper, he so shapes them that they learn to judge correctly about their own happiness.
He answers with confidence that this is necessary for our happiness.
He binds the neck of the human race with a noose, and shouts:
Be silent, be silent;
All these things are done for your benefit.
You are not, O prince, our God:
from God we expect happiness, from you the protection of our rights;
we do not want you to be kind to us, we want you to be just." These words he spoke, as he was by nature harsh, somewhat too harshly, too stubbornly, too obstinately:
for us, speaking today, it will be permitted to blunt these stings, which the injustice of earlier times had sharpened.
Indeed, with the harshness removed, we elicit from the words of the immortal colleague this milder sentiment:

A good prince, such as we describe, does not drag the people to happiness by the neck, nor make them blessed by force, but with reason as their guide and with the sweet-speaking goddess Suadela as their helper, he so shapes them that they learn to judge correctly about their own happiness.
After I have set these things forth a little more fully, it is permitted, listeners, to comprehend in summary what the power of this royal kindness is.

For first, even if no advantage should accrue from it to the prince, and even if no gratitude should be shown to him, the very feeling of kindness itself renders him blessed, because the greatest pleasure is in doing good, and the sweetest fruit of right deeds is to have done them:
He who has subdued the whole world with much blood will be considered great by most, yet he cannot delight his mind with his crimes;
He who has deserved well of the state by his innocent virtues, he alone will enjoy the sweetest fame of himself.

And if the judgments of contemporaries are corrupted by anger and passion, by slander and flattery, the memory of future ages, which alone is the most certain witness and judge of truth, can be neither abolished by any prohibitions nor by scissors nor by a little hammer nor by fire; it weighs with an even scale the wills, the counsels, the deeds.
"The benevolent virtue of Croesus does not die," says the poet;
But Phalaris, the merciless burner with the bronze bull, is pursued everywhere by hostile rumor. Then he who by doing good shows that he loves, is loved in return:
But the mutual love of king and citizens is the clearest fountain of public happiness and the one impregnable bulwark of empire.
Hence, as the rule of a kind prince is more pleasant for both prince and citizens, so it is more peaceful, more stable, and more lasting.

For, as Seneca says, one obeys a commander who is more lenient more readily, because the human mind is by nature stubborn and strives against what is contrary and difficult, and follows more easily than it is led.

Thus it happens that he who knows how to gain the approval of the citizens for his commands exercises power and retains his authority with less effort than he who has decided to accomplish everything by force.
Finally, since with Aristotle, the most sagacious author of political wisdom, there are especially two things by which kingdoms are overthrown, hatred and contempt;
Contempt indeed follows cowardice, fickleness, rashness, inexperience, imprudence; but that those who have power may not be despised, wisdom and vigor, which win authority, bring it about:
Hatred, however, is contracted by injustice, injuries, pride, cruelty, and the other things of this kind; and, on the other hand, kindness makes it so that neither a master nor a prince is hated.

Therefore you may see that half of the task of ruling rightly is placed in kindness; and unless the people experience it from the prince, there is reason to fear that they may be separated from each other.

Indeed, the king differs greatly from the tyrant in these very arts, because the former, such as Isocrates, Seneca, Erasmus of Rotterdam, and Frederick the Great established him, as one governing the state by the consensus of all, rules his subjects with affection, beneficence, faith, truth, and sincerity;
the tyrant, such as Machiavelli established him, having at hand that saying, "Let them hate, provided they fear";
With this worst of guardians, fear and violence, and with the snares of informers and spies, he keeps the slaves in check, and leads them by fraud, lies, pretense, and dissimulation:
King and people are united by mutual trust and common interest;
The tyrant fears and is feared, desires to be feared and fears being feared, and measures advantages not from what benefits his subjects, but from his own private power.
Will anyone therefore reproach me, if I say that the duty is fulfilled especially by the kindness of a Christian king, as I indicated above?

Indeed, Erasmus, in a book most full of good fruit, which he wrote on the education of a Christian prince to Charles, the grandson of Maximilian, who shortly afterward was created Emperor, did not hesitate to go so far as to affirm, disregarding the custom prudently and decorously received, as my opinion holds, in the titles of princes, that dominion, empire, kingship, majesty, and power are words of the pagans, and to declare that Christian empire is nothing other than an administration, a guardianship, a beneficence.
Kingdoms are overthrown by hatred and contempt.
Contempt indeed follows cowardice, fickleness, rashness, inexperience, imprudence; but that those who hold power may not be despised, wisdom and energy, which win authority, bring it about:
But hatred is contracted by injustice, wrongs, pride, cruelty, and the rest of that kind; and again, that neither master nor prince may be hated, kindness brings it about;

Therefore, you may see that half of the art of rightly retaining power lies in benevolence; and unless the people experience it from their prince, there is reason to fear that they will be torn apart from one another.

For the king differs greatly from the tyrant especially in these qualities, because the former, such as Isocrates, Seneca, Erasmus of Rotterdam, and Frederick the Great have portrayed him, governing the state by the consent of all, rules his subjects with love, beneficence, faithfulness, truth, and sincerity;
A tyrant, such as Machiavelli establishes, having at hand that saying, "Let them hate, provided they fear,"
With this worst of guardians, fear and violence, and with the snares of informers and spies, he keeps the slaves in check, and leads them by fraud, lies, pretense, and dissimulation:
The king and the people are united by mutual trust and common advantage;
The tyrant fears and is feared, and desires to be feared and fears being feared, and measures advantages not from what benefits his subjects, but from his own private power.
Will anyone therefore reproach me, if I say that the duty is fulfilled especially by the kindness of a Christian king, as I indicated above?

Indeed, Erasmus, in a book most full of good fruit, which he wrote about the education of a Christian prince to Charles, the grandson of Maximilian, who shortly afterward was created Emperor, did not hesitate to go so far that, despising the custom prudently and decorously received, as my opinion holds, in the titles of princes, he would affirm that dominion, empire, kingdom, majesty, and power are words of the pagans, and that the Christian empire is nothing other than an administration, a guardianship, a beneficence.
But I see that I must hasten to the end, lest I cut short the time of the highest magistrates of the university, who are to speak after me.

Nor does it seem that I should take up the matter, which I have once and again treated in my peroration, so that I may remind you, most honored fellow soldiers, of your affairs, and what you owe to the dearest King, what it is fitting for you to perform, what to omit, by which you may respond to the most wise counsels of the Father of the fatherland, I will set forth with deliberate effort:
This province, indeed, they will now claim by their own right, to whom the discipline of morals has been entrusted.
I will briefly finish what, after I have discussed the royal kindness, seems to remain, and I will turn my foot back to the place from which I began.
For Frederick William is without doubt that prince who thinks that a day has been lost for him on which he has not benefited someone;
He is the prince who looks not to his own advantage, but to that of those whom God has entrusted to him to protect;
who wishes his presence to be felt by doing good, not by terrors, and desires above all that all may be well;
who with gracious address attracts the zeal of citizens, and not only is called most serene, but with serene brow and calm mind refreshes all who have had the opportunity to associate with him.

Just as he now thrives and flourishes with the prayers of all, so we wish that his happiness, which cannot be separated from the prosperity of the Prussian state, may remain firm and undisturbed, that his noble spirit may never be saddened by adverse circumstances, and that, with the same candor, faith, and love with which he provides for the interests of his people, the whole people may reward his virtue, insofar as those below can repay the supreme moderator of the state.

May God, the Best and Greatest, preserve the most august King, together with the Queen, his consort, the best of women, the most faithful partner in whatever matters may bring either pleasure or anxiety to the King's mind, and may He keep them safe, secure, and unharmed forever for the welfare of this kingdom.
I have spoken.
After I have discussed the royal kindness, there seem to remain for me [these things], and I shall turn my step back to the point from which I began.
For Frederick William is without doubt that prince who thinks that a day has been lost for him on which he has not benefited someone;
he is the prince who looks not to his own advantage, but to that of those whom God has entrusted to him to protect;
who wishes his presence to be felt by doing good, not by terrors, and desires above all that all may be as well as possible;

He who attracts the pursuits of citizens with friendly address, and not only listens most serenely, but with a serene brow and calm mind refreshes all those who have had the opportunity to associate with him.

Just as he now thrives and flourishes through the prayers of all, so we pray that his happiness, which cannot be separated from the prosperity of the Prussian state, may remain firm and undisturbed, that his noble spirit may never be saddened by adverse circumstances, and that, with the same candor, faith, and love with which he provides for the interests of his people, the whole people may reward his virtue, insofar as those below can show gratitude to the supreme ruler of the state.

May God, the Best and Greatest, preserve the most august King with his consort, the best Queen, the most faithful partner in whatever matters may bring either pleasure or anxiety to the King's mind, and may He keep them safe, secure, and unharmed forever for the welfare of this kingdom.
I have spoken.

div.head: XXXII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi IV. celebrandis d. XV. m. Octobris a. MDCCCXXXXVI. habita.

p.s: For the due celebration of these most sacred solemnities, which have been dedicated to the best Prince, all of you who are present, hearers of every rank, each to be honored in his own place, easily perceive as a whole that something greater is being transacted in this assembly than a simple congratulation to be offered on the birthday of one man, however excellent.

For since the prince and the fatherland are so joined as it were in one body, that neither he can be safe unless the state is safe, nor can the fatherland enjoy prosperity without the safety and security of the prince;

Although the eternity of the state may seem able to remain through any changes of kings, nevertheless I judge that with the birth of a king the state is born again and regenerated, and that with the birth of a prince the fates and fortune are born for the city, which will be either favorable or unfavorable according as the Fates of that birth have stood by propitious or angry.
Thus the birthday of the prince is the birthday of the fatherland.

This opinion, except in those states in which the principate is handed over not by hereditary right but by election, holds and will hold in all the rest, whatever the form of the kingdom and the power of the prince may be:

whether he alone with his ministers holds the reins of government, or the people and the commons are participants through their representatives in the making of laws, the imposing of taxes, and the commanding of tributes;

And again, whether the minds of the citizens, languid with torpor and intent solely on their own private affairs, care nothing for public matters, or whether they understand that whatever pertains to the republic pertains to themselves, and are carried with the greatest fervor to know, judge, and, as far as is allowed, to handle the affairs of the state.

When the king makes all the duties of the state his own office, and the people, careless of the republic, follow the leader like a flock follows the shepherd, which some call a paternal and patriarchal government;

Whether the leader provides for the necessities of the people and has persuaded himself that his own advantage and the interests of the citizens are not separate, or whether he uses the resources and bodies of his subjects to satisfy his own desires out of lust or ambition, who does not see that the fates of the people are born together with the fate of the leader, that whatever has turned out well for the leader falls in some part upon the people itself, and that the Achaeans pay the penalties for the imprudent plans of their leader, and that the subjects are even more bitterly surrounded and afflicted by the evils of their master?

But if, instead of that brutish and stupid servitude, citizens begin to apply themselves to the care of common affairs, especially townspeople to governing their own small republics in the manner of municipalities, and to come into a share of public administration;

How much it matters what the character of a prince is, whether cruel or gentle, gloomy or cheerful, stern and harsh or mild and kind, suspicious and distrustful of every good man, or full of joyful confidence, too tenacious of his authority and power, and taking it as a diminution of himself however small a prerogative the citizens may have obtained, or inclined to yield something of his power and to grant to the colleges and civil orders as far as this can be done without public harm!
As I say these things in general, so they are especially suited to the person, character, plans, and institutions of Frederick William IV, the most gracious king.

For although the Prussian kingdom has not been established in that most free form in which, after we were victorious, both the conquered and several peoples who had been allies in the wars and victories were united, nevertheless that inactivity and indolence, which in earlier ages had held not only almost all Germans but also these lands, dragging out a slow life which is like death;
has been repelled:

And although Frederick William III, the most blessed father of his country, had understood that the state had to be restored and, in a new way and by new measures, corrected and adorned, nevertheless, with the self-restraint and moderation that were his, he especially strove that the state might pass its time in calm tranquility, and that he would rather strengthen it with these new forces than, after so many disturbances, so many revolutions, so many endured hardships, wish to set these new forces in motion.

The most joyful vigor of Frederick William IV roused and even impelled minds that had been almost lulled to sleep by long quiet, and loosened the reins of government, and with magnanimous counsel sent the people forth, as it were, from the starting-gates into the broadest field, in which they could run to the appointed goal.
Behold the fates of the republic, fitting and innate to the genius of the prince!

He gave to almost all these things a new and more beautiful appearance and form, so that one who had been oppressed by an Epimenidean sleep before these seven years, today, having returned, would scarcely recognize his homeland;
He proved to be the author of many and great goods for us:

If evils seem to be mixed with these, these are not new, but some part of the affairs has lain hidden, to fall upon the people themselves, and the Achaeans to pay the penalties of the imprudent leader's plans, and the subjects to be surrounded and harassed even more bitterly by the master's evils?

But if, in place of that brutish and stupid servitude, citizens begin to apply themselves to the care of common affairs, especially townspeople to governing their small republics in the manner of municipalities, and to come into a share of public administration;

How much it matters what the character of a prince is, whether cruel or gentle, sad or cheerful, stern and harsh or mild and kind, suspicious and distrustful of every good man, or full of joyful confidence, too tenacious of his own authority and power, and taking it as a diminution of himself however small a prerogative the citizens may have obtained, or inclined to yield something of his power and to grant to the colleges and civil orders as much as can be done without public harm!
As I say these things in general, so they are especially adapted to the person, character, plans, and institutions of Frederick William IV, the most gracious king.

For although the Prussian kingdom may not have been established in that most free form, in which, after we had been victorious, both the conquered and several peoples who had been allies in the wars and victories were united, nevertheless that inactivity and indolence, which in earlier ages had held not only nearly all Germans but also these lands, dragging out a slow life, which is like death;
has been driven away:

And although Frederick William III, the most blessed father of his country, had understood that the state needed to be restored and, in a new way and by new measures, to be corrected and adorned, yet with his characteristic self-restraint and moderation he especially strove that the commonwealth should pass its time in calm tranquility, and that he would rather strengthen it with these new forces than, after so many disturbances, so many revolutions, so many endured hardships, wish these new forces to be set in motion.

The most joyful vigor of Frederick William IV roused and spontaneously impelled minds that had been almost lulled to sleep by long quiet, and loosened the reins of government, and with magnanimous counsel sent the people forth, as it were, from the starting-gates into a very broad field, in which they could run to the appointed goal.
Behold the fates of the republic, fitting and innate to the genius of the prince!

He gave to nearly all these things a new and more beautiful face and appearance, so that one who had been oppressed by an Epimenidean sleep before these seven years would today, on returning, scarcely recognize his homeland.
He proved to be the author of many and great goods for us.
If evils seem to be mixed in with these, these are not new, but they had previously lain hidden under scars drawn over and poorly covered.
Indeed, nothing is more dangerous than an ulcer that creeps secretly and gnaws away the most excellent parts of the body;
And he has made great progress who understands how much is lacking, how much remains.
There are those who grieve that we do not yet enjoy perfect freedom of speech and writing;
but by the kindness of the best King it has been granted that we may complain openly that we do not enjoy it:
Now I ask you, is not this very thing an excellent liberty, and to which not much is lacking for full liberty?
Truly happy mortals, who know their own good things;
but I know not whether the beginning of happiness is to know one's own evils, which cannot be healed unless known.
There was a time when our wisdom was boasted of not without pride;
but we understand that there are also others who are wise.

Indeed, those men consult the fatherland badly, badly interpret the love of the fatherland, who, just as the Spartans of old, very brave men indeed and not unwise in other respects, but too ignorant of foreign affairs, praise nothing except their own and are uniquely pleased with themselves;

And most rightly does Sophocles' Haemon advise that those who seem to themselves alone to be wise and to have a tongue or a mind that no one else has, if they are opened up, are found to be empty and vain.

Since this is evident in individual men, so we see entire peoples, when, on account of the excessive opinion which they have conceived of their own virtue and prudence, they have preferred to rest content with their present goods rather than to seek new ones, soon cast down from the dignity acquired by great men and through great deeds, and lose the very goods they had, and be conquered by lesser men who strive vigorously toward higher things.
We indeed owe to Frederick William IV not only the greatest benefits but also the knowledge of disadvantages.
After these things were brought to light, indeed we live a life somewhat less comfortable, which before seemed easy, and we proceed on a more obstructed path and here and there we stumble;
but we remember the famous watchword:
“Through hardships to the stars.” And by this movement indeed all parts of the state are seized:

There are added other important considerations arising from other causes, and not from accidental ones, by which these times of the republic are rendered, in an unusual manner, either more difficult or at least memorable beyond others.
Nor, however, is it my task to explain these things:

I will not speak about the things that happened this year, whether favorable or adverse, not about the Polish uprising that was quickly suppressed, not about the partial change in the form of the courts, not about the manifold movements of the churches and about the two assemblies that were connected with these, convened by the pious king and held in our city, not about the sudden [event] that was formerly badly covered under healed scars.
Indeed, nothing is more dangerous than an ulcer that creeps secretly and gnaws away the most excellent parts of the body;
And he has made great progress who understands how much is lacking, how much remains.

but we understand that there are also others who are wise.
