but we remember the famous watchword:
"Through hardships to the stars." And by this movement indeed all parts of the state are seized:

There are added other moments of things flowing from other causes, and not from fortuitous ones, by which these times of the republic are rendered in an unusual manner either more difficult or at least memorable beyond others.
Nor, however, is it my task to explain these things:

I will not speak of the things that happened this year, whether favorable or adverse, not of the Polish uprising quickly suppressed, not of the judicial system changed in some part, not of the manifold movements of the churches and of the two assemblies, which are connected with these, convened by the pious King and held in our city, not of the sudden financial calamity that had threatened, the straits of the loan societies, the public bank established on a new plan, not of the matter of establishing the tolls and taxes and of the disputes arising from this both domestic and of the allied states:
All these things, and whatever more there are of this kind, I pass over, since they are foreign to my person and to my studies;

except that it must be said, as far as I can see, that in these matters many things were done by the excellent King with foresight, caution, gentleness, and kindness, nothing too harsh, nothing proud, nothing rash, nothing excessive.
For us, literature is closer and more immediate;
And who among you, listeners, does not understand that these very things have either been seized by this, as it were, whirlwind of affairs, or can be seized?
Here let me be allowed to linger a little.

It had broken in with a financial calamity, with the straits of the loan-societies, with the public bank established on a new system, not only concerning the establishment of the port-duties and taxes, and the disputes arising hence both domestic and of the allied states:
I pass over all these things, and whatever more there are of this kind, as being foreign to my person and to my studies;

except that it must be said, as far as I can see, that in these matters many things were done by the best King providently, cautiously, gently, kindly, nothing too harsh, nothing proud, nothing rash, nothing excessive.
To us literature is nearer and closest;
And who among you, listeners, does not understand that these very things have either been seized by this, as it were, whirlwind of affairs, or can be seized?
Here let me be allowed to linger a little.
Therefore I would not deny that the condition of literature in our memory has experienced somewhat the fortune of common vicissitudes.

At the time when this our literary university was founded and most splendidly equipped, the studies of earlier ages were both sufficiently established and were flourishing more joyfully day by day, especially in the Prussian kingdom, however afflicted, and they seemed then to be among the principal supports by which the restoration of the shaken republic could be accomplished;
Literature was highly valued and loved by the very restorers of the republic, one or two of whom were by far the most learned;
Trust was placed in the learned, those keen and fearless champions against the common enemy, and greatly hated by the most cunning foe;
It was judged to be excellently invested, whatever expense had been laid out for establishing any branches of learning whatsoever:
Finally, there was the greatest harmony between the republic and literature.
Soon that part of them which had been summoned to wage war seemed to have turned the arms it had taken up against the enemy against the state.
Nevertheless, the public care for advancing literature then relaxed nothing, nor was anything mixed into the plans for adopting it that was foreign to literature.

Frederick William IV, however, even before he took up the supreme command of affairs, revealed an extraordinary love of the fine arts through distinguished proofs, and after he succeeded his father, he surpassed the expectation that he had aroused.
Meanwhile, a long peace had opened up the whole world and had inflamed the studies of the learned;
hence the apparatus of learning was increased, the necessities of literature were increased;

As knowledge grew to an immense extent, the number of learned men increased, who sought an honorable place for themselves and their studies, and it increased to such a degree that we rather suffer from abundance than from scarcity, and those things which in other times would have been most welcome now seem ungrateful and burdensome.

But two things now seem to me, especially at this very moment, to bring some difficulty to literature, not indeed new ones but repeated with new force: the one, that very many demand that literature be turned to the common use of life; the other, that certain pious men and some clerics think nothing is true or tolerable unless it agrees with their own opinions or beliefs about the divine word.
Both of these are especially hindered by those studies which are customarily called liberal, namely antiquity and philosophy.

Indeed, ancient literature is hateful both to those who refer all knowledge and the pursuit of knowledge to common utility, and to those who want erudition to be confined within the limits of the Christian faith:
Nevertheless, I judge that neither of these parties prudently consults its own interest by slandering those studies, much less the proper education of the human race.

But as for me, although I am burdened not so much by the reproach of reclusive learning as by the undeserved suspicion of the opposite vice, and although in defending the literature of antiquity I will seem to want to defend or even to boast of my own work, I shall discharge this part of my speech with as few words as possible.

For those who demand that literature be brought into common use, and who do not want it to lurk in the shadow of the school, but to approach especially those questions which are most vigorously debated in this age;

Because the most serious questions about true freedom of mind and civil liberty are now being discussed, they seem to be devastating their own altars and hearths, when they want to expel from the education of youth the ancient literature, the most faithful nurses of that true liberty, because they are the nurses of humanity:

Although I concede that those who teach these letters have detracted something from the genuine usefulness of these studies, because, forgetting the wise admonition of Aristotle, who does not want boys being liberally educated to be trained in music even to the point where one who is being prepared for practicing the art of music is instructed, they have begun to imbue their pupils more with the more subtle precepts of the art, which are necessary for future grammarians, than to shape their minds by reading the ancient authors toward humanity.

Indeed, a part of this culture is refined speech, which the leading authors of the new literature, if you except a few who were learned by nature alone, have shaped according to Greek and Roman models:
and especially the masculine speech of the Romans, which surpasses Greek itself in strength of force, even now seems to me to be the best teacher of a clear, elegant, exact, and serious style.
I say this not with the intention of defending this custom of speaking Latin handed down from our ancestors.
For my own [words], especially since they may seem troublesome and unpleasant to my country, which at other times would have been most welcome.

But two things now seem to me, especially at this moment, to bring some difficulty to literature, not indeed new ones, but repeated with new force: the one, that very many demand that literature be turned to the common use of life; the other, that certain pious men and some clerics think that nothing is true or tolerable unless it agrees with their own opinions or views about the divine word.
Both of these things are hindered especially by those studies which are customarily called liberal, namely antiquity and philosophy.

Indeed, ancient literature is hateful both to those who refer all knowledge and the pursuits of knowledge to common utility, and to those who want erudition to be confined within the limits of the Christian faith:
Nevertheless, I judge that neither party consults its own interest prudently by slandering those studies, much less the proper education of the human race.

But because I, although I am not so much burdened by the reproach of bookish learning as by the undeserved suspicion of the opposite vice, will seem, by defending the literature of antiquity, to wish either to defend or to boast of my own, I will discharge this part of my speech with as few words as possible.

For those who demand that literature be brought into common use, and do not want it to lurk in the shadow of the school, but to approach especially those questions which are most agitated in this age;

Because the most serious questions about true freedom of the mind and civil liberty are now being discussed, they seem to be devastating their own altars and hearths, when they want to expel from the education of youth the ancient literature, the most faithful nurses of that true liberty, because they are the nurses of humanity:

Although I concede that those who teach these letters have detracted something from the genuine usefulness of these studies, because, forgetting the wise admonition of Aristotle, who does not even want boys being liberally educated to be instructed in music to such an extent as one who is being trained for the practice of the art of music, they have begun to imbue their pupils more with the more subtle precepts of the art, which are necessary for future grammarians, than to shape their minds to humanity by the reading of ancient authors.

Indeed, a part of this culture is polished speech, which the leading authors of the new literature, if you except a few who were learned by nature alone, have shaped according to Greek and Roman models:
and especially the masculine Roman oratory, which surpasses Greek itself in strength of force, even now seems to me to be the best teacher of a clear, elegant, exact, and serious style.
I say this not with the intention of defending this custom of speaking Latin that has been handed down from our ancestors.

For it matters little to me, especially since I am most devoted to the language of my fatherland, in which language it is spoken, provided that it is spoken well; and I will even rejoice when, freed from the necessity of speaking in Latin, to which most people now give ear with difficulty, I shall be in a condition similar to that of Laberius, who, a Roman knight, was compelled at the age of sixty to act in mimes at the games:

I do not say this, I say, with that intention, but because I disagree with those who think that however much industry young men have spent on learning the Latin language thoroughly, they would have invested it with greater profit in their native or French speech.

Now those who fear a threat to the faith from the literature of the Gentiles, although I doubt that they can be overcome or appeased by my arguments, nevertheless I would have them warned that the Emperor Julian forbade Christians, in order to afflict them, that pagan discipline and instruction, and that those who reformed our sacred rites in the sixteenth century were aided by nothing more than the revived studies of antiquity, and that those men who most favored and supported the reformation of the church were the most thoroughly instructed and polished in ancient literature.
By a better example, by a more refined judgment, the most wise King benefits us:

This king, with the most liberal mind, embraces, cherishes, and sets before us whatever is beautiful and good, whatever is worthy of being known, whether it was born in ancient Athens, or in Egypt, or in Gaul or Britain, in the most remote times, or in the middle ages, or very recently.

But will the Germans indeed tolerate that the sad peevishness of a few should bring into neglect literature, which has been cultivated in Germany for a long time with especial care, literature that nourishes youth, strengthens manhood, and delights old age?
that the Greek and Latin Muses should be forced to seek refuge among the Gauls, where already now Henricus Stephanus, revived, is undertaking greater things in this kind than any German can?

even among the Italians, to whom very recently Paris Zaiottus of Trent, a man both experienced in public affairs and equipped with knowledge of the best works that the more recent age has produced among any of the European peoples, in a most elegant book, which equals many of our pedagogical pamphlets, which he wrote on youthful literature, has excellently recommended the ancient authors;
Finally, among the Roman Fathers of the Society of Jesus themselves, who pursue these studies of antiquity not without success and defend them against adversaries?
Furthermore, I have warned that philosophy, which I, together with Plato, judge to be the greatest good given to mortals by God, is opposed to what is customarily demanded of literature in this age.

When I say philosophy, I do not mean only that philosophy for which I, who am most fond of language, use this name; it matters little in which language it is spoken, provided it is spoken well; and I will even rejoice when, freed from the harsh necessity of speaking in this Latin tongue, to which most people now lend a reluctant ear, I shall be in a condition similar to that of Laberius, who, a Roman knight, at the age of sixty was compelled to act mimes in the games:

I say this, I repeat, not with that intention, but because I disagree with those who think that however much industry young men have devoted to learning the Latin language thoroughly, they would have invested it with greater profit in their native or French speech.

Now those who fear that the Christian faith is endangered by the literature of the pagans, although I doubt that they can be convinced or appeased by my arguments, nevertheless I should like to warn them that the Emperor Julian, in order to afflict the Christians, forbade them that pagan learning and education, and that those who reformed our sacred rites in the sixteenth century were helped by nothing more than by the revived study of antiquity, and that the men who most favored and assisted the reformation of the church were those most thoroughly trained and polished in ancient literature.
By a better example, by a more refined judgment, the most wise King benefits us:

He embraces, cherishes, and sets before us with the most liberal mind whatever is beautiful and good, whatever is worthy of being known, whether it was born in ancient Athens, or in Egypt, or in Gaul or Britain, in the most remote times or in the middle ages or very recently.

But will the Germans indeed tolerate that the sad peevishness of a few brings into neglect the literature which has been especially cultivated in Germany for a long time, which nourishes youth, strengthens the prime of life, and delights old age?
that the Greek and Latin Muses are forced to seek refuge among the Gauls, where already now Henricus Stephanus, revived, is undertaking greater things in this kind than any German can;

Even among the Italians, whom recently Paris Zaiottus of Trent, a man both experienced in public affairs and equipped with knowledge of the best works that the more recent age has produced among any of the European peoples, in a most elegant book, which rivals many of our pedagogical treatises, which he wrote on youthful literature, has exceptionally recommended the ancient authors;
Finally, among the Roman Fathers of the Society of Jesus themselves, who pursue these studies of antiquity not without success and defend them against adversaries?
Moreover, I have warned that philosophy, which I judge together with Plato to be the greatest good given to mortals by God, is opposed to what is customarily demanded of literature in this age.
When I say philosophy, I mean not only that which bears this name properly, but also that very broad field of learning in which this order, which they call philosophers, is exercised:
And the other orders also share in these studies, if, as was once counted a glory, they pursue their disciplines with a philosophical mind, as they say.

These disciplines, if it is permissible to use the technical terms of art in this assembly of most learned men, are partly empirical, which are occupied with discovering and establishing the forms, elements, forces, and laws of nature by means of the senses and instruments through observation and experiment;

Some are historical, which investigate, arrange, and compose deeds and whatever has been founded and accomplished by men, from handed-down sources with interpretation and critical art applied, and trace them back to their causes by the same method;
From this kind is also the whole learning of philologists and grammarians, truly very varied:
Some are mathematical, which measure pure quantity with the mind and scrutinize its laws with subtle investigation;

Some are speculative, which embrace in their lofty mind the divine and human principles of things, the purest notions expressed in the nature of things and founded in the human mind, and the entire principles, causes, and ends of civil and moral life.

Although from all these disciplines excellent fruits flow into human affairs, nevertheless, if anyone should wish that their measure be limited by the usage of daily life, there is no need for me to explain to the learned that he would both mutilate them disgracefully and sordidly, and would cut off the very fruits he seeks.

These disciplines cannot flourish unless they themselves determine, from their own principles, both where they begin, and where they tend, and how far it is either permissible or advantageous for them to proceed.
He destroys philosophy who limits it by a law that it itself has not imposed upon itself.
But the office of philosophy, he says, is nothing other than to explain what has been given.
That is, as it seems to some, to give an account of them in such a way that they are proved to be true and correct.
I hear.
Of course, if superstition is given, philosophy will explain superstition and will be adorned with magical and theurgic doctrines and arts, as by the divine Iamblichus;

If slavery has been given, it is the task of philosophy, as Aristotle did, to explain slavery, and there are different kinds of philosophy: one for those times and places where a great part of mankind is oppressed by slavery, another where all are free.

On the contrary, this is the adulterine philosophy, which is obscured by the mists of present things, which serves the times either unknowingly or deliberately, and does not seek what it ought, but conceals evils with paint, and does not [seek] what is most beautifully proper to philosophy, but also that very broad field of doctrines, in which this order, which they call philosophers, is exercised:
And even the remaining orders are participants in these studies, if, as was once counted as a praise, they treat their disciplines with a philosophical mind, as they say.

These disciplines, if it is permitted for an orator to use the terms of art in this assembly of most learned men, are partly empirical, which are occupied with observing and experimenting to discover and establish the forms, elements, forces, and laws of nature by means of the senses and instruments;

Some are historical, which investigate, arrange, and compose the deeds and whatever has been founded and accomplished by men, from handed-down sources, with interpretation and critical art applied, and trace them back to their causes by the same method;
From this kind is also the entire learning of philologists and grammarians, truly quite varied:
Some are mathematical, which measure pure quantity with the mind and scrutinize its laws with subtle inquiry;

partly speculative, which embrace in their lofty mind the divine and human principles of things, the purest notions expressed in the nature of things and founded in the human mind, and the reasons, causes, and ends of all civil and moral life.

Although from all these disciplines excellent fruits flow into human affairs, yet if anyone should wish that their measure be limited by the usage of daily life, there is no need for me to explain to the learned that he would both mutilate them disgracefully and meanly, and cut off the very fruits he seeks.

These disciplines cannot flourish unless they themselves determine from their own principles both where they begin, and where they tend, and how far it is either permissible or advantageous to proceed.
He destroys philosophy who limits it by a law that it has not itself imposed upon itself.
But the office of philosophy, he says, is nothing other than to explain what has been given.
That is, as it seems to some, to give an account of them in such a way that they are proven to be true and correct.
I hear.
Of course, if superstition is given, philosophy will explain superstition and will be adorned with magical and theurgic doctrines and arts, just as by the divine Iamblichus;

If slavery has been given, it is the task of philosophy, as Aristotle did, to explain slavery, and there are different kinds of philosophy: one for those times and places where a great part of mankind is oppressed by slavery, another where all are free.

On the contrary, this is the adulterous philosophy, which is obscured by the mists of present things, which serves the times either unknowingly or deliberately, and does not seek what it ought, but conceals evils with paint, and does not, as Cicero most beautifully says of philosophy, seek out virtue and expel vices, but strengthens and perpetuates vices.
Nor does philosophy serve as a handmaid to theology, as was once proposed rather arrogantly.

When I have been brought to this point, it occurs to me that in our age some people attribute very much to those things which they are accustomed to call positive, but that the whole circle of disciplines, which philosophers embrace, is not taught as positive:
whence it can happen that, if nothing else, at least the disciplines of philosophers are brought into contempt.
But it also occurs to me that we mortals are very often led not by things but by the images of things, words:
Hence the grammarian's province seems the more serious, since he is engaged in defining the meaning of words.
For indeed things cannot be clearly discerned unless the words are discerned.

Indeed many, who are so greatly moved by that word, are, I confess, rather unskilled, but nevertheless not a few, chiefly for this reason seem to wish to praise nothing but positive things, because whatever is not positive, they think is negative, confusing affirmation with position.
That contrariety holds in mathematics and in certain parts of physics, as in the doctrine of electricity:
in human affairs, about which we are now dealing, the negative contrary is not the positive;

But from the Greeks, from whom the Latin language has borrowed these technical terms, it is called positive, because it is established by men and fixed or sanctioned by a certain convention of men; and the opposite of positive is that which flows and stands from the very nature and reason of the thing, and is valid by its own nature.

Therefore, to begin with examples from philologists, which will seem too common and perhaps ridiculous to fastidious ears, grammarians made syllables that are long by nature opposed to syllables that are long by position or by rule:

And those who thought that the words of a language were invented by whim, by arbitrary decision, by the chance agreement of men, as did Democritus and Aristotle, called these artificial words positive;

But those who judged with Plato that words were connected with notions by a certain natural principle, struck out by the necessity of nature and mind, or rather born spontaneously, denied that language is positive;
Similarly, Strabo says that some things established among peoples come about by nature, others by convention and practice and use:

And just as law, so religion is partly positive, which is usually handed down in written form, and partly natural, not written on tablets and documents, but inscribed without letters on the minds and hearts of men.
This positive [law and religion], therefore, rest on authority:

by which authority there is altogether need for ruling men, and in domestic affairs Cicero declares that it is the seeker of virtue and the expeller of vices, but that it strengthens and perpetuates vices.
Nor is philosophy more the handmaid of theology, as was once proposed with sufficient arrogance.

When I have been brought to this point, it occurs to me that in our age some people attribute very much to those things which they are accustomed to call positive, but that in that whole circle of disciplines which philosophers embrace, the positive is not taught:
from which it can happen that, if nothing else, at least the disciplines of philosophers are brought into contempt.
But it occurs to us at the same time that we mortals are very often led not by things themselves but by the images and names of things.
For this reason the province of the grammarian seems the more serious, since he is engaged in defining the meaning of words.
For indeed things cannot be properly understood unless the words are understood.

Indeed, many who are so strongly moved by that word, being indeed less skilled, I admit, but nevertheless not few, especially for this reason seem to want to praise nothing unless it is positive, because whatever is not positive, they think it is negative, confusing affirmation with position.
That opposition holds in mathematics and in certain parts of physics, as in the doctrine of electricity:
In human affairs, about which we are now speaking, the negative is not the opposite of the positive;

but from the Greeks, from whom the Latin language has borrowed these technical terms, that is called positive which has been set down by men and established or sanctioned by a certain convention of men, and that is opposite to the positive which flows and holds from the very nature and reason of the thing, and is valid by its own nature.

Therefore, to begin with examples from philologists, which will seem too common and perhaps ridiculous to fastidious ears, grammarians made syllables that are long by nature opposed to syllables that are long by position or by rule:
And those who thought that the words of a language were invented by whim, by arbitrary choice, by the chance agreement of men, as did Democritus and Aristotle, called these artificial words positive;

But those who judged with Plato that words were connected with notions by a certain natural principle, produced by the necessity of nature and mind, or rather born spontaneously, denied that language is positive;
Similarly, Strabo says that some institutions come to peoples by nature, others by convention and practice and use:

And just as law, so religion is partly positive, which is accustomed to be handed down in writings, and partly natural, not written down in letters and tablets, but inscribed without letters on the minds and hearts of men.
These positive [laws and religions], therefore, rest on authority:

which authority is altogether necessary for governing men both in domestic and in public affairs, not only in the peaceful state of the commonwealth but also in the disturbed and turbulent one, especially amid arms:

Therefore, even the most free and at the same time most cultivated peoples did not hesitate in crises to take refuge in dictatorship, from whose harsh necessity the very highly approved authority of royal power frees us.
But the instrument of science is reason and intellect;
Therefore in science there is no place for authority.
Just as philosophers scorn it, so they will approve the positive sciences, which they have found to be true and correct;
But who would presume to prescribe to anyone that he should praise what is false and wrong?

Although the philosopher will regard these very things with reverence, as long as they are supported by the consensus of the many, unless they are extremely harmful, just as the ancient wise men, especially Socrates, although they thought more correctly about divine matters than the common people, nevertheless worshipped the publicly accepted gods with supplication, ceremonies, and sacrifices, and openly rejected only those stories that could not be reconciled with the majesty and perfection of the divine power:
When they denied that these were true, they did not deny the divinity, they did not remove piety, but they established this, and about that they decided more worthily.
Moreover, in matters that pertain to knowledge, they do not follow authority except dull, lazy minds, slow and weak for thinking.
For it is easy to swear by the words of another.

The path of understanding, or rather the narrow track, is difficult and rough and overgrown with the brambles of much doubt, and it was rightly said long ago that the sinews and joints of wisdom are not to believe rashly.

But what about the fact that all literature, even if it does not want to be immersed in the whirlpool of everyday affairs, nevertheless must treat many matters about which positive authority, whether of the state or of the church, must decide?
Would you not say that here already science has been driven to a standstill?
But we have, if I am not mistaken, even in this crisis something with which to console ourselves.
For although the human race is tenacious of handed-down things, and rightly so, lest it rush headlong at the sudden onset of any moments whatsoever;

tamen quod ii, qui publici et sacri regiminis gubernabla tenent, litteris ipsi excoluntur et ad res gerendas instituuntur, iussa et placita positiva ex praeceptis scientiae paullatim colorem ducunt, et communis gentium consensus, postquam longo temporis spatio quae sanxerat prava vel certe minus probabilia secutus est, multisque parricidiis in homines sapientissimos et innocentissimos commissis inquinati sunt iudices fanatici, ad meliorem frugem convertitur duce ratione victrice, quam a Deo, ratione summa et absoluta, nobis insitam impie ingratus
rebus et in publicis, quum in pacato civitatis statu non tum in commoto ac turbido, praesertim inter arma:

Therefore, even the most free and at the same time most cultivated peoples have not hesitated in times of crisis to take refuge in dictatorship, from whose harsh necessity the supreme and most approved authority of royal power exempts us.
But the instrument of science is reason and intellect;
therefore in science there is no place for authority.
Just as philosophers scorn it, so they will approve the positive things, which they have found to be true and right;
But who would presume to prescribe to anyone that he should praise what is false and wrong?

Although the philosopher will regard these very things with reverence, as long as they bear the consensus of the many, unless they are excessively harmful, just as the ancient wise men, especially Socrates, although they thought more correctly than the common people about divine matters, nevertheless worshipped the publicly accepted gods with supplication, ceremonies, and sacrifices, and openly rejected only those stories that could not be reconciled with the majesty and perfection of the divine deity:
When they denied that these were true, they did not deny divinity, they did not remove piety, but they established this, and about that they decided more worthily.
Moreover, in matters that pertain to knowledge, they do not follow authority except dull, lazy minds, slow and weak for thinking.
For it is easy to swear by another's words.

The path of understanding, or rather the narrow track, is difficult and rough and overgrown with the brambles of much doubt, and it was rightly said long ago that the sinews and joints of wisdom are not to believe rashly.

But what of the fact that all literature, even if it does not wish to be plunged into the whirlpool of everyday affairs, nevertheless must treat many matters about which positive authority, whether of the state or of the church, must decide?
Would you not say that here already science has been reduced to a standstill?
But we have, if I am not mistaken, even in this crisis, something to console us.
For although the human race is tenacious of transmitted things, and rightly so, lest it rush headlong at the sudden onset of any moments;

Nevertheless, because those who hold the helm of public and sacred government are themselves cultivated by literature and trained for conducting affairs, the positive commands and decrees gradually take on a color from the precepts of science, and the common consensus of nations, after it has for a long time followed what it had sanctioned as perverse or at least less probable, and after fanatical judges have been stained by many murders committed against the wisest and most innocent men, is converted to a better way of life, with reason as its victorious guide, which, implanted in us by God, the highest and absolute reason, he who slanders it would have impiously and ungratefully denied.
Therefore, whatever is positive has, as it were, its own ages from the Etruscan discipline, its own courses and advances, not without a provident divine will.

And each nation, which indeed dares to be wise, at whatever age it establishes for itself through its leaders, learned together with the people, positive institutions, which at whatever age correspond most to the understanding of the nation.
Thus, unless the fates of the people incline toward destruction, it comes about that, with the good things of the ancestors preserved, the iniquities and evils of earlier times are removed.

Finally, although some nations run ahead and others are left behind, nevertheless the whole human race seems to tend toward this, that that ancient disagreement of position and of nature or reason gradually becomes obsolete.

For indeed, since that law is most fair and most just which, not fabricated according to arbitrary will and caprice, sets before us the very nature and reason of the things contained in the law, expressed in words, a fair and just law cannot conflict with reason; and most truly did the Stoics, with Cicero as interpreter, establish that law is the highest reason implanted in nature, which commands what must be done and forbids the contrary.

If I have argued these points correctly, do you not think, listeners, that literature, even that which lies hidden at home and does not declaim in the forum, has great power and usefulness for correcting the state of affairs?

But why, in almost no part of human affairs, is peace so difficult to establish between those different and almost hostile things that we have mentioned, as in divine matters, which nevertheless ought to be uniquely suited for pacifying the world torn apart by profane hatreds, it is not my place to examine, since I am not a theologian:
One thing may be allowed to mention, which can be accepted even as spoken by my mouth.
We have recently mourned several colleagues who were very closely connected to many of us by long association and especially dear, among them two theologians:

Of these, the one who departed first was undoubtedly devoted to the positive doctrines of the most holy faith, but the same man did not hesitate to use philosophical contemplation in theological matters, and with great effort he seems to have had the purpose that, as far as it lay in his power, that sad discord between philosophy and theology might be removed.
But what is more destructive and troublesome than discord, what more pleasant and useful than concord?

Would that we all, colleagues and fellow soldiers, might therefore strive, so that, with that concord by which our school once grew, then of all orders, who, because all parts of literature are bound by an inner bond, have been joined in this one and indivisible body of the university, there might be someone who would slander.
Therefore, whatever is positive has, as it were, its own ages from the Etruscan discipline, its own courses and advances, not without divine providence.

And each nation, which indeed dares to be wise, at whatever age it establishes positive institutions for itself through its leaders, learned in common with the people, which institutions at whatever age best correspond to the understanding of the nation.
Thus, unless the fates of the people hasten to their destruction, it comes about that, with the good things of the ancestors preserved, the iniquities and evils of former times are removed.

Finally, although some nations run ahead and others are left behind, nevertheless the whole human race seems to tend toward this, that that ancient disagreement of position and of nature or reason more and more becomes obsolete.

Indeed, since that law is most fair and most just which, not fabricated according to arbitrary will and caprice, sets forth the very nature and reason of the things contained in the law, expressed in words, a fair and just law cannot conflict with reason, and most truly did the Stoics, with Cicero as interpreter, establish that law is the highest reason implanted in nature, which commands what must be done and forbids the contrary.

If I have argued these points correctly, do you not think, listeners, that literature, even that which lies hidden at home and does not declaim in the forum, has great power and use for correcting the condition of affairs?

But why, in almost no part of human affairs, is peace so difficult to establish between those different and, as it were, hostile things which we have mentioned, as in divine matters, which nevertheless ought to be uniquely suited for pacifying the world torn apart by profane hatreds, it is not my place to examine, since I am not a theologian:
This one thing may I be allowed to mention, which can be accepted even as spoken by my mouth.
We have recently mourned several colleagues who were most closely connected to many of us by long association and especially dear, among them two theologians:

Of these, the one who departed first was undoubtedly devoted to the positive doctrines of the most holy faith, but the same man did not hesitate to use philosophical contemplation in theological matters, and with great effort he seems to have had the purpose that, as far as it lay in his power, that sad division between philosophy and theology might be removed.
But what is more destructive and troublesome than discord, what more pleasant and useful than concord?

Would that we all, colleagues and fellow students, therefore devoted our efforts, so that that harmony by which our school once grew—then of all orders, who, because all parts of literature are bound by an inner bond, are united in this one and indivisible body of the university in the ancient and approved manner, then of teachers and learners, then of the civil and literary commonwealth—might remain and be strengthened, and that we all, removed from ambition and any desire whatsoever, might seek, pursue, and express in discipline and character the true, the good, and the beautiful!
And when we do this, what else are we doing than imitating the most noble example of Frederick William IV, the most humane king?

This king, from the time when I had the opportunity, both in other public assemblies and from this platform, of celebrating and venerating him with speeches every year, I have never ceased to proclaim that his intellect was devoted to the best arts and letters, and not only to learning, but also, which is rarer in a prince, to the love of learned men; finally, that his pursuits, entirely removed from vulgar pleasures and delights, were turned toward whatever is excellent, honorable, grave, and sublime; and just as he himself excels in these, so he desires his peoples to be raised to that point of perfection and praise, so that the people may rightly be deemed worthy of a magnanimous king, and the king worthy of most cultivated and most faithful peoples.
We see, therefore, to end where I began, that the fortune of our prince, born with him, is our fortune, by a most auspicious nativity.
From kings, to whom a long reign has fallen, the ages of peoples are derived and counted.

But I judge this century of Prussia to be most fortunate, if God in his mercy grants it, even amid the difficulties of the times, and to be so hereafter, under the leadership and auspices of Frederick William IV.

We pray to God, the Best and Greatest, on this day sacred to the rejoicing fatherland, with pious vows and supplications, that the life of the most beloved King may be prolonged as long as possible for the welfare of the state and of the good arts, and that he may flourish with the august Queen and with the entire royal house in the highest and perpetual prosperity.
I have spoken.

May it remain and be strengthened both for teachers and learners, and for the civil and literary republic, and may we all, removed from ambition and any desire, seek, pursue, and express in discipline and morals the true, the good, and the beautiful!
When we do this, what else are we imitating than the most noble example of Frederick William IV, the most humane king?

Hunc regem ex quo mihi copia fuit quum in aliis conventibus publicis tum ex hoc suggestu orationibus quotannis celebrandi ac venerandi, nunquam non praedicavi illius ingenium optimis artibus et litteris deditum, et non solum eruditionis, sed etiam, quod rarius in principe, eruditorum amorem, denique studia a vulgaribus deliciis et voluptatibus prorsus remota, ad egregium quidvis et honestum et grave et sublime conversa, quibus sicut ipse excellit, ita populos suos eo perfectionis atque laudis evehi cupiat, ut digni populi rege magnanimo, dignus rex populis cultissimis et fidissimis merito habeatur.
We see, therefore, to conclude where I began, that the fortune of our prince, born with him, is our fortune, by a most auspicious nativity.
From kings, to whom a long reign has fallen, the ages of peoples are derived and counted.

But I judge this age of Prussia to be most fortunate, if God in his mercy grants it, even amid the difficulties of the times, and to be so hereafter, under the leadership and auspices of Frederick William IV.

We pray to God, the Best and Greatest, on this day sacred to the rejoicing fatherland, with pious vows and supplications, that the life of the most beloved King may be prolonged for the welfare of the republic and of the good arts as long as possible, and that he may flourish with the august Queen and with the entire royal house in the highest and perpetual prosperity.
I have spoken.

div.head: XXXIII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi IV. celebrandis d. XV. m. Octobris a. MDCCCXXXXVII. habita.

p.s: Since it is difficult for one man, for very many reasons, O hearers, to celebrate every year, in the same solemnities, in the same place, in the same assembly of most learned men, in the name of the same college, the praises of the same prince, however distinguished he may be;

Then, because variety, which the most refined audience requires and the orator desires, cannot generally be derived except from the subject matter, lest he weary both himself and his hearers with boredom, I think that the greatest difficulty lies in the selection of the subject matter.

But if, whenever one must speak about Frederick William IV, a king especially energetic, the orator can never lack an extremely abundant supply of material, still I do not know whether that very abundance rather than scarcity hinders him in his choice.
What, then, can be more pleasing to one about to speak, what more desirable, than that state, that condition of affairs, which leaves no room for choice?
Indeed, this convenience falls to my lot today, listeners.

For this year Frederick William has performed so many distinguished deeds in the state, that whoever, in these solemnities dedicated to his name, should choose to treat of other matters rather than these public affairs, must seem foolish; and that not even an educated man, although he may be little versed in public affairs, unless he wishes to seem a mere closet scholar, can avoid those things which have attracted and moved the minds of all men, not only citizens but all mankind; and finally, that not even this need be feared, that one who speaks about the state before young men should incur reproach.
For that time has passed when only the ministers and officials of the princes seemed able to judge concerning the state.

He was annoyed if anyone else expressed an opinion on such matters, and especially learned men were relegated to their own doctrines alone, being either kept away from or deterred from those things that pertained to the state, and they were compelled, if ever they had to give advice about public affairs, to conceal many things and to pass over them or to indicate them with great caution and as if from a distance.
It is understood at last that the saying of Sophocles' Creon and of Louis XIV, king of the Gauls, is false, that he sells the king for the state;

It is understood that the republic, as it is called from the people, and the state, as it takes its name from the citizens, is thus the possession of the citizens and the people, that is, of a gathering of men united and joined together, if not by a community of origin and stock, which is far more excellent, at least by a community of law, statutes, and utility.

Indeed Plato rightly advises that it is just for each person to do his own work, and I do not deny that it is for some to command and manage public affairs, for others to serve in the military, for others to do manual labor, for others to attend to sacred rites and to practice and teach the liberal arts and sciences:

But because the affairs of the state are common to all, whoever thinks that they pertain to himself does not act as a stranger but as his own, and these common concerns are not neglected by any part of the citizens without common harm, and no one who is a bit more prudent, wherever he is placed, ought to be entirely free from this care.
What indeed shall I say about the young men devoted to literature, from whom a great part of this audience is composed?

That these men in the earlier age mixed themselves too much in civil affairs, which I recently explained they did not so much by their own fault as by that of the times, so that they are unequal to counsels and deliberation and to acting prudently, and are headlong toward changing the institutions of the state which they have not yet sufficiently known, and accordingly, especially in troubled times, are more to be restrained than urged on;

Nevertheless, they ought to be imbued with love of country and be the more inflamed by this flame, the more vehemently youthful minds are carried to any studies, and it is fitting that they be by no means indifferent to those things which are prosperous or adverse for the state, and especially that they take pains to be instructed in civic learning by a method both philosophical and historical, and learn to judge correctly about public affairs.

Therefore I do not hesitate to touch upon that subject which today alone offers itself and presents itself to all, and to adapt my speech to the present circumstances of our state, not that I may enumerate each individual matter, but that I may endeavor to embrace some more important heads and, what is especially characteristic of science, to refer them to some single principle.
The saying of Louis XIV, king of the French, which he boasts of as king for the state;

It is understood that the republic, as it is called from the people, and the state, as it derives its name from the citizens, is thus the possession of the citizens and the people, that is, a gathering of men united and joined together, if not by a community of origin and stock—which is far more excellent—then at least by a community of law, of statutes, and of common advantage.

Indeed Plato rightly instructs that it is just for each person to do his own business, and I do not deny that it is the role of some to command and to manage public affairs, of others to serve as soldiers, of others to do work, of others to attend to sacred rites and to practice and teach the liberal arts and letters:

But because the affairs of the state are common to all, he who thinks that they pertain to himself does not act as a stranger but as his own, and these common affairs are not neglected by any part of the citizens without common harm, and no one who is a little more prudent, wherever he is placed, ought to be entirely free from this care.
But what shall I say about the young men devoted to literature, from whom a great part of this audience is composed?

That they in the earlier age mixed themselves too much in civil affairs, which I recently explained that they did not so much by their own fault as by that of the times, so that they are unequal to counsels and deliberation and to acting prudently, and are headlong toward changing the institutions of the state which they have not yet sufficiently known, and accordingly, especially in troubled times, are more to be restrained than urged on;

Nevertheless, they ought to be imbued with love of country and to be the more inflamed by this flame, the more vehemently youthful minds are carried to any studies, and it is fitting that they be by no means careless of those things which are prosperous or adverse for the state, and especially that they take pains to be trained in civic learning by a method both philosophical and historical, and learn to judge rightly about public affairs.

Therefore I do not hesitate to touch upon that argument which today alone offers itself and presents itself spontaneously to all, and to adapt my speech to the present circumstances of our state, not that I should enumerate any single matters, but that I should endeavor to embrace some more important heads and, what is especially characteristic of science, to refer them to one certain principle.

Therefore, to begin from this starting point, I have not undertaken to say anything new to you, listeners, but something that has long been understood by most and by myself in some part in the previous year.
proposed.
For when in the former reign, after so many calamities brought upon the state by foreign wars, everything seemed to need to be settled for peace;
Frederick William IV wanted this settled state to be moved:
And he has accomplished and repeatedly accomplishes what he has determined.
The state, however, is moved in two principal ways: either by war or in peace.
And you might wonder at the former movement indeed, because that Platonic Socrates recognizes almost only it:

After he described the best state, he says that in considering it he experienced almost the same thing that usually happens to a viewer when looking at a beautiful image, whether painted or sculpted, since it is motionless, namely that a desire comes over him to see it moved and to see it undergoing some contest of those things that suit the body:

Thus they say that someone would gladly listen to a narrator telling how that perfect republic will wage war against other states and, in waging war, will achieve those things that are suitable for the education and learning received in that illustrious state, both in joining battle and in conducting negotiations through ambassadors with other states.
But that he wished his state to be moved almost only by war, is not at all surprising:
For he speaks of the perfect state, which has never existed among any people, nor does it exist now, nor, I think, can it ever be founded because of the character of men:

But that state, since from its very birth it has attained the highest degree, enjoys perpetual and almost divine tranquility and stability, and is neither corrupted nor improved, and lacks internal motion.
A different motion from that which Plato discusses, Frederick William excited;
For he did not receive the state handed down to him in a perfect condition, and he promised that he would preserve peace in his own age, if it were allowed, when he began his reign.
Nor indeed does he wish the state to become obsolete through peace with a sluggish and inactive quiet, but rather that the institutions of the state itself be moved and advanced.
This movement, if it is properly guided, is much more healthful than war.

Of course, when in earlier centuries political science was concerned almost exclusively with external matters, with friendships and enmities among kingdoms, with treaties and peace and war, with the extension of boundaries and the acquisition of territories by arms or by agreements or by marriages, and when in this science he seemed the best who was most skillful and cunning in devising and deceiving, not using skill but tricks, while the just conception of politics, which the Greeks had established and the most distinguished recent authors had cultivated, was in most states and especially in Germany already almost consigned to oblivion;

In our own age, at last, it has been more keenly observed that the primary province of the statesman pertains to the domestic affairs of the state, to establishing and ordering the commonwealth, to the rights and duties of empire, magistrates, citizens, and orders.
This art, in this kingdom at least, Frederick William IV especially recalled as if from exile and restored.
But the state is moved in two ways especially, either by war or in peace.
And indeed you might wonder at the former motion, because that Platonic Socrates recognizes almost alone.

who, after he described the best republic, says that in considering it something almost the same happened to him as usually happens to a beholder when looking at a beautiful image, whether painted or sculpted, since it is motionless, namely that a desire comes over him to see it moved and undergoing some contest of those things that suit the body:

Thus they would gladly listen to someone narrating how that perfect republic will wage war against other states and, in waging war, will achieve those things that are suitable for the education and learning received in that illustrious state, both in joining battle and in conducting negotiations through ambassadors with other states.
But that he wished his state to be moved almost solely by war is no wonder.
For he speaks of the perfect state, which has never existed among any people, does not exist now, and, I think, on account of the character of men, can never be established.

But that state, since from its very birth it has attained the highest degree, enjoys perpetual and almost divine tranquility and stability, is neither corrupted nor improved, and is free from internal motion.
A different motion from that which Plato discusses, Frederick William excited.
For he did not receive a perfect state handed down to him, and he promised that he would preserve peace in his own age, if it were allowed, when he began his reign.
Nor indeed does he want the state to become obsolete through peace with sluggish and inactive quiet, but to be moved and advanced the very institutions of the state.
This movement, if it is properly guided, is much more healthful than war.

Of course, when in earlier centuries political science was concerned almost exclusively with external matters, with friendships and enmities among kingdoms, with treaties and peace and war, with the extension of boundaries and the acquisition of territories by arms or by agreements or by marriages, and in this science he seemed best who was most skillful and cunning in devising and deceiving, not using art but arts, while the true conception of politics, which the Greeks had established and the most distinguished recent authors had cultivated, was in most states and especially in Germany already almost consigned to oblivion;

Only in our own age has it been recognized more keenly again that the primary province of the statesman pertains to the domestic affairs of the state, to establishing and ordering the commonwealth, to the rights and duties of government, magistrates, citizens, and orders.
This art, in this kingdom at least, Frederick William IV especially recalled as if from exile and restored.
Thus he gave the state an inner movement, and that a civil one, not a military one.
Now, that this movement of states is manifold and varied, there is no one who does not see:
And so, about to speak on it, I enter an immense field of discussion, in which, lest I be carried far and wide, I will only touch upon a few and the nearest points, in a general way.
I will not say that one movement is of those proceeding forward, another of those going backward:
For no politician can deliberately want this man, who makes no progress, because he wants the state to be preserved, but by a backward movement it tends to destruction and slides into ruin:
And if ever a good ruler of the state checks the course or turns it back, he does not do this so that the state does not advance, but so that it is not hurled headlong with too violent a rush;

Just as a cautious general sounds the retreat, so that those who have advanced too far may not perish, and so that, having been recalled, they may advance more safely at a suitable place and time thereafter.

But it is worth the effort to describe in a few words a certain natural and, as it were, lawful motion and revolution of states, which, in the fortunes of ancient republics, the simpler their principles were, the more distinctly one may perceive.
And it seems to me that from the memory of those ancient things, something is gained even for judging our own, by looking into them as into a mirror.

For although man is by nature a social animal, not a solitary one, and not because individuals seemed to themselves too weak, by agreement, nor because some more powerful person had subdued the rest, by force and arms, were men brought together into a state, but this community of men was born rather in some way by natural instinct than founded, and from spontaneously uniting kindred stocks peoples were formed, to some extent self-sufficient, and from villages cities were contracted:
Then, in the likeness of a family, that which they call the patriarchal kingdom arose, in which the king was in the place of a father, at once the leader of troops, the priest, and the judge.

These kings, in that age in which the credulous multitude easily persuaded itself that gods had descended to men and that men had been made gods, were regarded as sons of the gods, especially of Jupiter, because Jupiter was the king of the gods, not only among the Greeks but also among the barbarians.

What about the fact that the Old Testament itself reports that mighty giants were born from the sons of God, the angels, or as Greek Christian authors call them, the Watchers, who consorted with the daughters of men?

And so kings born from the gods seemed to reign with divine authority, and one or two indeed with such divine counsels, like that Minos, companion of great Jove, and Numa, partner of the bed of the nymph Egeria.
Therefore, a theocratic element having been mixed with the kingdom gave an inner motion to the state, and that a peaceful one, not a warlike one.
Now, that this motion of states is manifold and varied, there is no one who does not see.
Therefore, about to speak about it, I enter an immense field of discussion, in which, lest I be carried far and wide, I will only touch upon a few and the nearest things in a general way.
I will not say that one motion is of those advancing, another of those going backward.

For no politician can bring himself to want this, which advances nothing, deliberately, because he wants the state to be preserved; but by a backward motion it tends toward ruin and slides into destruction.
And if ever an upright governor of the state checks its course or turns it back, he does this not so that the state may not advance, but so that it may not be hurled headlong with too violent a rush.

Just as a cautious general sounds the retreat, so that those who have advanced too far may not perish, and so that, having been recalled, they may advance again more safely at a suitable place and time.

But it is worth the effort to describe in a few words a certain natural and, as it were, legitimate motion and revolution of states, which, in the fortunes of ancient republics, the simpler their principles were, the more distinctly one can perceive.
And it seems to me that from the memory of those ancient things, something is gained even for judging our own affairs, by looking into them as into a mirror.

For although man is by nature a social animal, not a solitary one, and not because individuals seemed to themselves too weak, by agreement, nor because some more powerful person had subdued the rest, by force and arms, were men brought together into a state, but this community of men arose by natural instinct rather in a certain way than was founded, and from spontaneously coming together kindred stocks peoples were formed to some extent self-sufficient, and from villages cities were contracted:
Then, in the likeness of a family, that which they call the patriarchal kingdom arose, in which the king was in the place of a father, and at the same time leader of the troops, priest, and judge.

These kings, in that age in which the credulous multitude easily persuaded itself that gods descended to men and that men were made gods, were regarded as sons of gods, especially of Jupiter, because Jupiter was the king of the gods, not only among the Greeks but also among the barbarians.

What of the fact that the Old Testament itself reports that mighty giants were born from the sons of God, the angels, or as Greek Christian authors call them, the Watchers, who consorted with the daughters of men?

And so kings born from gods seemed to reign with divine authority, and one or another, indeed, with divine counsels, such as that Minos, companion of great Jupiter, and Numa, partner of the bed of the nymph Egeria.
Therefore, something theocratic was mixed with the kingdom:
For where God is said to reign, a priest reigns, or any prince endowed with priestly and augural auspices.
In this natural monarchy the people obeyed not unwillingly, as bees follow the queen, as the flock follows the shepherd;
By the will of the ruler and by ancestral institutions, the state was administered without laws, if indeed this is to be called administration:

Except that already in Homer we read that kings deliberate with a council of nobles or heroes, who are themselves also called kings, and that the common people are called together into an assembly, so that the king may share his plans with them.
Even then the name of tyranny was unknown along with its concept, because king and tyrant were not distinguished by any fixed mark.

But that form of government could not be maintained any longer than the faith that the rulers were of divine origin and divine right, which a more refined political science, such as Aristotle's, does not recognize, lasted.
But soon the crimes of the rulers and the growing intelligence of men destroyed that faith.
Hence, as I think, a threefold revolution of affairs arose:
For either the patriarchal dominion passed into hereditary tyranny, which managed everything by force and cunning, or into a kingdom established by skill and laws, or into the dominion of the nobles.
Examples of this tyranny are the kingdoms of the East, such as those of the Assyrians, Persians, and Egyptians, although not even these were without some tempering of laws:

Certainly the Persians had their own permanent royal judges, who could not be removed except for a crime, those interpreters of laws and institutions, and in this matter superior to the king's own judgment;

And the kings of the Egyptians were not allowed to judge or to punish anyone according to their whim, but only according to what the laws had prescribed for each crime, and they used to proclaim themselves blessed because by this institution it had been provided that they should not stray from duty through ignorance or desire.
Moreover, it has been handed down that the judges of Egypt were bound by oath, so that even at the king's command they would not render an unjust verdict.
Among the Greeks, however, those ancestral kings were gradually bound by laws;

And not even thus, if you except the Spartan kingdom divided between two and a few colonies of Sparta, did they long endure, and the power of the Laconian kings was so diminished that you can scarcely recognize a royal power.

For in almost all states the royal dignity has been abolished, partly because kings had abused their power, partly because the aristocrats, especially since the strength of the common people was not yet established, were reluctant to have the state ruled by one man:

Therefore the rule of a few succeeded the kingship, and then that of the nobles, that is, as I shall use the definition of Aristotle and Frederick II, the great Emperor of the Germans, it was something of those:
For when God is said to reign, a priest reigns, or any prince endowed with priestly and augural auspices.
In this natural monarchy the people obeyed without reluctance, just as bees follow their queen, as the flock follows the shepherd;
At the will of the ruler and according to ancestral institutions, the state was administered without laws, if indeed this is to be called administration:

Except that already in Homer we read that kings deliberate with a council of nobles or heroes, who are themselves also called kings, and that the common people are called together into an assembly, so that the king may share his plans with them.
Even then the name of tyranny was unknown along with its notion, because king and tyrant were not distinguished by any fixed mark.

But that form of government could not be maintained any longer than the faith in the divine origin and divine right of the rulers lasted, which a more refined political science, such as Aristotle's, does not recognize.
But that faith was soon destroyed by the crimes of the rulers and the growing intelligence of mankind.
From this, as I think, a threefold revolution of affairs arose.
For either the patriarchal dominion passed into hereditary tyranny, which managed everything by force and cunning, or into a kingdom established by skill and laws, or into the dominion of the nobles.
Examples of this tyranny are the kingdoms of the East, such as those of the Assyrians, Persians, and Egyptians, although not even these were without some tempering of laws:

Certainly Persia had its own permanent royal judges, who could not be removed except for an offense, those interpreters of laws and institutions, and in this matter superior to the king's own judgment;

And the kings of the Egyptians were not allowed to judge or to punish anyone according to their whim, but only according to what the laws had prescribed for each crime, and they used to declare themselves blessed because by this institution it had been provided that they should not stray from duty through ignorance or desire.
Moreover, it has been handed down that the judges of Egypt were bound by oath by the kings, so that they would not render an unjust verdict even at the king's command.
Among the Greeks, however, those ancestral kings were gradually bound by laws;

And not even thus, if you except the Spartan kingship divided between two and a few colonies of Sparta, did they long endure, and the power of the Laconian kings was so diminished that you can scarcely recognize the royal dignity.

For in almost all states the royal dignity has been abolished, partly because kings had abused their power, partly because the aristocrats, especially since the strength of the common people was not yet established, resented that the republic was ruled by one man:

Therefore, the rule of a few succeeded the kingship, and next that of the nobles, that is, to use the definition of Aristotle and of Frederick II, the great Emperor of the Germans, of those who prevailed by the ancient virtue of their ancestors and by the ancient wealth of their families, especially by the possession of large estates:

This form of government is usually accompanied by public servitude, whether one prefers to call these slaves farmers Helots, or Penestae, or clients, or serfs bound to the soil, or by any other name whatsoever.

Then, after either a large part of the nobles ceased to be wealthy, or virtue deserted the nobles, and many indeed who had been born in a middling or obscure position began to prevail by wealth, and partly also by virtue, the empire was transferred to the rich, and the rights of citizens were defined according to census and classes:
This kind of state has the proper name of timocracy, in which the equites generally had the greatest influence:

until, not without the seditions of factions, with almost all the prerogatives of the classes abolished, the supreme power passed into the hands of the plebs, and all citizens, with no distinction of birth or wealth, were judged by equal law.

It also happened that, amid the struggles between the optimates and the plebs, a very powerful man arose, who, under the pretense of protecting the plebs, seized a tyranny, unjust indeed, but not infrequently fruitful:
In Greece, however, few tyrannies, and those very mild, were long-lasting;
At Rome, late in the day, when the state was exhausted by civil wars, tyranny was established under the name of principate by military power.

But that absolute liberty, by which citizens of every fortune are considered equal, is not usually brought about except by an increased population, especially of artisans, and through great disturbances, particularly wars, in which the common multitude has deserved exceptionally well of the safety of the state, by which the minds of all are inflamed, the strength of all is increased, and ambition is intensified, demanding a share of honors as a reward for virtue;
just as the Persian wars matured democracy at Athens:
And if any state has sustained the sign of liberty, others quickly follow;

so that at almost the same time, after the Pisistratids were expelled, Clisthenes established a freer state of the republic in Athens, and the aristocratic councils of the Pythagoreans in Italy were destroyed, and kings were expelled from Rome, and soon the Ionians rebelled against the Persians.

Now this popular government, at which the ancient philosophers were greatly angry, Plato indeed considers to be one, and he says that no one gives it different names, whether the multitude rules over the wealthy violently or moderately, and again whether it carefully observes the laws or neglects them:

Most people, however, call that a popular state in which the laws prevail and in which honor is given to the laws, the magistrates, and good morals; but they call ochlocracy that in which the republic is managed according to the decrees of the people and the people decide whatever they please.
Nor can the moderate rule of the people long endure;
who would prevail by the ancient virtue of their ancestors and by the ancient wealth of their families, especially by the possession of large estates:

which form of empire public slavery is accustomed to accompany, whether it has pleased to call these slaves agricultural Helots, or Penestae, or clients, or serfs of the soil, or by any other name whatsoever.

This commonwealth has the proper name of timocracy, in which the knights generally had the greatest influence:
