just as at Athens the Persian wars hastened the democracy:
And if any state has sustained the sign of liberty, others quickly follow;

so that at almost the same time, after the Pisistratids were expelled at Athens, Clisthenes established a freer state of the republic, and the aristocratic councils of the Pythagoreans in Italy were destroyed, and at Rome the kings were expelled, and soon the Ionians rebelled against the Persians.

Now this popular government, at which the ancient philosophers were greatly angry, Plato indeed considers it one, and says that no one gives it different names, whether the multitude rules over the rich violently or moderately, and again whether it carefully observes the laws or neglects them:

Most people, however, call that a popular state in which the laws prevail and in which honor is given to the laws, the magistrates, and good morals; but they call ochlocracy that in which the republic is administered according to the decrees of the people and the people decide whatever they please.
Nor can a moderate rule of the people long endure;
for the people is wont to run riot insolently and, through contempt of the laws, to slide into any kind of wrongs and to exercise tyrannical power:

Just as flatterers attend a tyrant, so leaders of the people, whom they called demagogues, attend the plebs, flattering its desires and serving its iniquity, and turning everything from laws and magistrates to the lust of a turbulent multitude.
From this tyranny of the plebs, the transition to the tyranny of individuals is easy.

Thus excessive liberty not only afflicts the people with unworthy servitude, while it seems free to itself, because it obeys the unbridled license and madness of the mob and its leaders, but it also brings about the destruction of all liberty.

These, speaking with Polybius and Cicero, were among the ancients the cycles and revolutions of changes and vicissitudes in states, this being the order of nature according to which their condition was changed and again revolved to the same point.
There are indeed those who deny that the states of our age can be comprehended in the kinds of republics which the ancients established;

But I think that the constitutions of more recent states also can conveniently be compared with those forms, which, if they are not usually found pure nowadays, were also among the ancients mixed and compounded in more than one way:

Therefore I think that the revolutions of modern states are not greatly different from those orbits which I have described, except that modern kingdoms have been remarkably strengthened by a nearly new institution, to which I shall soon come.
For the common people are wont to be insolently wanton and, through contempt of the laws, to slide into any injuries whatsoever and to exercise tyrannical power.

Just as flatterers attend a tyrant, so leaders of the people, whom they called demagogues, attend the plebs, flattering its desires and serving its wickedness, and turning everything from laws and magistrates to the lust of a turbulent multitude.
From this tyranny of the plebs, the transition to the tyranny of individuals is easy.

Thus excessive liberty not only afflicts the people, while it seems free to itself, with unworthy servitude, because it obeys the unbridled license and fury of the mob and its leaders, but it also brings about the destruction of all liberty.

These, speaking with Polybius and Cicero, were nearly the cycles and revolutions of changes and vicissitudes in republics among the ancients: this is the order of nature, according to which their condition changed and revolved back again to the same point.
There are indeed those who deny that the states of our age can be comprehended in the kinds of republics which the ancients established;

But I think that the constitutions of more recent states, along with other very wise men, can also be conveniently compared to those forms; and if they are not usually found pure nowadays, even among the ancients they were mixed and compounded in more than one way.

Therefore I do not think that even the revolutions of more recent states differ greatly from those cycles which I have described, except that the more recent kingdoms have been remarkably strengthened by a nearly new institution, to which I shall soon come.
Now I must explain to what end I have proposed these things, listeners.

For since these movements and changes are partly necessary and useful, partly natural indeed but harmful and yet not inevitable, the supreme ruler of the state ought to provide that, when the opportunity for the necessary ones has first come, they may be brought about by the most peaceful and easiest path, lest they be extorted by force too late, while the harmful ones are warded off and repelled;
Then, that the individual elements of the state, which prevail in those individual forms, may be so connected with one another that each form may contain and include the other;
Finally, that by the combination of these forms, as far as possible, a perfect and firm state may be established, and that it may not languish in inactivity, but may thrive with healthy motion.
These are the plans which Frederick William the Fourth, as far as I can see, has set before himself;
He wants this course to be held in that motion which he has excited.

But of those forms which I have mentioned, some cannot be regarded as republics, but are degenerate forms of just forms, and corrupted by perversity of morals, lack of self-control, luxury, avarice, and ambition:
Thus tyranny is a corruption of kingship, exceeding the measure;

Timocracy or plutocracy and any oligarchy are imperfect or vicious imitations of the true aristocracy, that is, the rule of the most approved and wisest men, established by selection, which I deliberately omitted above;
Finally, ochlocracy is the worst departure from popular government.

Moreover, although monarchy, the rule of the best, and popular government seem to many to be just forms of the state, nevertheless among these, to the ancient philosophers themselves, who had been educated and trained in popular states, if the individual kinds are compared with one another and one is to be approved separately by itself, legitimate monarchy has seemed the best.

Finally, both the ancient wise men and the most prudent of the more recent ones, except for a few praisers of the excessive power either of princes or of the people, arrived at the point that they especially approved of a fourth kind, which, being blended and tempered from those three, would be.
Of this constitution you may see certain seeds and sprouts, quite imperfect, in the Laconian state, and even more imperfect in other ancient states;
Our age has surpassed antiquity, which discovered this kind of thing by thinking, but cultivated it too little by experience.

This one is the most just and the most firm, and indeed the most firm, because although it may be greatly disturbed, it is not moved by passing over into another, but it has a motion like that of the celestial globes, returning as it were in a circle upon itself and fixed in one constant center of gravity.
This comprehends the advantages of each kind under the auspices of royal authority, avoids the disadvantages, and the fall that is prone to neighboring vices;

Indeed, from these very more corrupt forms, if you except ochlocracy, it can sometimes receive something that, mixed with good, is salutary, just as poisons, with the moderate admixture of a harmless species, bring about a most effective medicine.

Frederick William IV, therefore, when he had received the state prudently administered, equipped with a strong army recruited from the citizens themselves, flourishing in the industry of farmers and artisans, in commerce, revenues, literature, and the arts, because he did not want everything to be done for the people, as they say, and nothing by the people, after the modest beginnings of his most blessed father, laid the foundations of truly political institutions:
Judging the people to be of age and mature, he brought them forth into the light and led them into the wrestling school;

But because what is needed is practical experience and trial, and not even the counsel of the wisest men can foresee everything at one time, he decided not to settle the state with institutions left unchanged, corrupted as they were by greed and ambition:
Thus tyranny is the corruption of kingship, exceeding the proper measure;

Timocracy or plutocracy and any oligarchy are imperfect or vicious imitations of the true aristocracy, that is, the rule of the most approved and wisest men, established by selection, which I deliberately omitted above;
Finally, ochlocracy is the worst departure of popular rule.

Moreover, although monarchy, the rule of the best, and popular government seem to many to be just forms of the state, nevertheless among these, to the ancient philosophers themselves, who had been educated and trained in popular states, if the individual kinds are compared with one another and one is to be approved separately by itself, legitimate monarchy has seemed the best.

You may see certain seeds and germs of this constitution, quite imperfect, in the Laconian state, and even more imperfect in other ancient states;
Our age has surpassed antiquity, which discovered this kind of thing by thinking, but cultivated it too little by experience.

This one is the most just and most firm, and indeed most firm, because although it may be greatly disturbed, it is not moved by passing into something else, but has a motion like that of the celestial globes, returning as it were in a circle upon itself and fixed in one constant center of gravity.
This [form of government] comprehends the advantages of each kind under the auspices of royal authority, avoids the evils, and [avoids] the fall that is prone to neighboring vices;

Indeed, from these very more corrupt forms, if you except ochlocracy, it can sometimes receive something which, mixed with good things, may be salutary, just as poisons, with the moderate admixture of a harmless species, bring about a most efficacious medicine.

Frederick William IV, therefore, when he had received the state prudently administered, equipped with a strong army recruited from the citizens themselves, flourishing in the industry of farmers and artisans, in commerce, revenues, literature, and the arts, because he did not want everything to be done for the people, as they say, and nothing by the people, after the modest beginnings of his most blessed father, laid the foundations of truly political institutions:
Judging the people to be of age and adult, he brought them forth into the light and led them into the wrestling school;

But because what is needed is practical experience and trial, and not all things can be foreseen at one time even by the counsel of the wisest men, he decided not to settle the state with institutions that were immovable, but he wants these very things to grow and unfold gradually, like a tree growing from a shoot and, with its root strengthened, spreading its branches.

This first of the kings of Prussia, in order that all parts of the state might act together, held those great assemblies of all provinces and orders in his own city and in his own palace, to which all citizens and foreigners turned their eyes:
We saw and heard the King not concealing his plans, but with the greatest eloquence he possesses, opening them most sincerely;
And with the most free opportunity of speaking granted, there followed equal zeal of the people's envoys, fervor, with temperance and moderation, energy and noble boldness of speech.
By these lawful contentions the state is healthfully moved, like the air by the blowing of winds;
strength is strengthened and concord is rather brought together than discord is nourished, just as different sounds, grave and acute, are mixed into a harmony;
and the difficulty of entering upon a plan is diminished, and the rashness of deciding is guarded against.
Nothing is born except from contraries.
But all agree that the reins of empire must be retained for the security and power of the republic:

and what in a patriarchal kingdom has been granted to the prince by some religion, so that he might seem to reign by divine right, that in the best form of state is retained by right reason to such an extent that royal majesty, placed above any partisan struggles and subject to no one, may be sacred and inviolable;

Nor should the fact that in that same fatherland a king was regarded in the place of a parent seem unworthy of the state of the republic which we have entered upon, but by ancient institution the king is even now to be judged the father of the fatherland and, with the sweetest feeling of affection and piety, is to be loved as a father by his children, and is loved among us.

Now, how much Frederick William granted to the nobles and the other delegates of the people, so that the republic might approach more closely that which is tempered from those three kinds, is not the place of this occasion to recount and examine individually:

I have enough to have mentioned that something has been remitted from the highest power and granted to those who are distinguished by the antiquity of their families and who are more furnished with resources:

And in the timocratic element there is also something mixed in from the most just aristocracy, because not the richest are called to the office of embassy on account of their greatest wealth, but the most approved of the wealthy, chosen by the citizens.

But if it pleases some that wealth should be assessed not only from lands but also from movable funds, which are now especially the sinews of affairs, and that moreover access to the supreme council of the state should be given to the leading men of the church and of the colleges of learned men, since about these matters there is debate on both sides, but this very thing wishes to grow and unfold gradually like a tree growing from a shoot and spreading its branches when its root is strengthened.

But if some think that wealth should be assessed not only from landed estates but also from movable money, which now especially are the sinews of things, and that in addition access to the supreme council of the state should be given to the leading men of the church and the legates of the learned colleges, since on these matters one can argue on both sides, we leave them to the judgment of future time.

However it may be, the king's wisdom, together with the most prudent men, judges that not all ranks should be removed from the state, nor that equal honor should be granted to the highest and the lowest, and that rights indeed should be equalized, but according to dignity and proportion, not according to numbers, lest equality itself be most unjust.
Finally, I do not seem to myself either ridiculous or rash, if I say that there is something even popular in this kingdom.

For is this not characteristic of a popular government, to lighten the burdens and misery of the poor, not by plundering the goods of the rich, but by transferring taxes especially onto the wealthy and by seeking a remedy for the poverty that is growing and spreading more widely day by day, as the King had proposed?
Is it not popular for urban guilds, which are established by the free votes of all citizens, to be entrusted with very many things that were formerly commanded through the officials of the princes?

By this it comes about that a broad field is opened to the citizens, in which, by handling their own and lesser matters, they may make trial of their political prudence, being about to approach public and greater affairs more prepared.
What if that is popular, that those who practice a gainful art are admitted to the comitial embassy?
For those who are more hostile to the plebs keep these from conducting public affairs;

Just as at Thebes it was once provided by law that no one should be allowed to hold public office unless he had been free for ten years from the market of goods for sale and from a gainful occupation.
But especially I judge it popular that in this kingdom, by the favor of Frederick William, the greatest matters have already begun to be transacted openly.
For kingdoms tempered by no other forms and the rule of the best love to cover all things in darkness, because they think that the principle of ruling cannot stand firm if it is rendered to all:
And clandestine judgments have especially been instruments of unjust power.
We have seen the proceedings of the assemblies most quickly and most fully and most exactly communicated daily to all;
we know that it has been granted to the councils of towns to conduct their municipal affairs in the presence of the citizens;

We see that in this city, the seat of a kingdom, all trials, and especially public ones, are held with the greatest seriousness, with open doors, when the case concerns treason and high treason, and at the same time such freedom of defense is granted to the defendants and their advocates that the citizens of states which seem to themselves most free marvel and are astonished, and recognize how far in this kingdom we are from slavery, with which our detractors used to clamor that we were oppressed.
Indeed, the rule of the most merciful King is so secure, so firmly supported by the affection of his subjects, that it can bear things which in other kingdoms would seem to be intolerable.

This is the pledge of just liberty;
By this most favorable movement it increases and adorns the republic.
Finally, a place in the state has been given even to eloquence, which formerly was left to the homilies of priests.
Nor do I fear to declare that even the freedom of writing and of the very newspapers was greatly increased under this King, although it has not yet been exempted from censorship.
For the most wise King knows that after divine providence, human affairs are moved and governed by mind and thought;

But the thought of the mind is carried freely, and its course, once it has been confirmed by the spirit of the age, cannot be checked by any force, but it sweeps along those who rashly oppose it, casting them down:
Only the faults, which are accustomed to cling even to good undertakings, must be corrected, and excessive impulses must be moderated and restrained.

By this path Frederick William forms and urges the citizens to help the common welfare and to overcome the allurements of idle leisure and pleasures, and he brings it about that those who previously, as happens especially in kingdoms, were careless of the state and sought virtue in a life far removed from such cares, now turn virtue to public use and exercise it in their occupations, and that each citizen in his own place strives by his counsels and labors to render the state safer and more excellent.

By this path Frederick William forms and urges the citizens to aid the common safety and to overcome the allurements of idle leisure and pleasures, and he brings it about that those who previously, as happens especially in kingdoms, were careless of the republic and sought virtue in a life far removed from such cares, now turn virtue to public use and exercise it in their occupations, and that each citizen in his own place strives by his counsels and labors to render the state safer and more excellent.

But now the sails must be furled, my listeners, and it is not permitted to wander too far afield, especially since, after the most pleasing reverence for the royal name, which is common to all, both for me and for my successor there remain to be said and done those things which properly pertain to this school of letters.
And I seem to myself to have accomplished what I wanted;

And I especially desire, being fully conscious of my own weakness, that what I have said may seem to you to have been discussed plausibly and appropriately to the occasion and to the dignity of the matters.

Surely he would be ungrateful who does not acknowledge how many and how great are the things that we owe to the wisdom, kindness, industry, and unwearied zeal and care of Frederick William IV for accomplishing everything that is best in the state, and who would measure these things by his own or anyone else's particular plans and wishes rather than by what the best king has actually accomplished.

Let us therefore make an effort, listeners most distinguished in every rank, each in his own place, that we may both feel and, as far as can be done by the younger generation, repay to Frederick William IV the gratitude due for benefits conferred upon the whole state and upon each individual, and that the harmony and safety of the republic and the majesty, splendor, and power of the kingdom may be perpetuated and strengthened.

Finally, pray with me to God, the Best and Greatest, that He may protect and preserve, as long as possible, His most religious and piously devoted worshipper, adorned with so many and such great virtues, and the author to us of so many blessings, the most clement King, together with the august Queen and the entire royal house.
I have spoken.
